மருவினா னசோத மத்தின் வானவ னாகித் தோன்றி
வருகயல் விழியாள் நாக வசுவும்வந் தமர னுக்கு
மருவிய தேவி யாகி மயலுறு கின்ற வன்றே.
reading: By dharma meditation he leaves his body, is born as a god in the Asodhama heaven, and Nagavasu also becomes a consort of a god.
nuance: The heaven is named அசோதமம்; the name is not found in the earlier verses, and the spelling may be corrupt.
event: Nagadattan dies in meditation and is reborn as a god; Nagavasu is reborn as a god's consort.

tamil: அங்கைந் துபல்ல மாயு வமரனாய்ச் சுகித்து விட்டு
இங்குவந் தரச னானா யினியந்தத் தேவி வந்து
தங்குநின் மனைவி யானாள் தவமுனி யுரைப்பப் பின்னும்
எங்களுக் கந்த நோன்பு யினிதுவைத் தருள வென்றான்.
reading: The sage tells the hero that after five palyas as a god he came here as king and that the goddess is now his wife, and the hero asks him to give that vow to them.
nuance: Here the work gives the hero's good fortune a cause in his own past conduct, not in grace or chance. The sentence runs from the sage's words into the hero's request, so the speaker is not one voice throughout; the speech is the sage's up to line 3 and the narrator reports the request.
event: The sage explains the hero's present kingship and marriage as the fruit of his earlier vow, and the hero asks for the vow.

tamil: திங்கட் கார்த்திகையி லாதற் சேர்ந்தபங் குனியி லாதற்
பொங்கன லாடி யாதற் பூரண பக்கந் தன்னில்
தங்குமாண் டைந்து நோற்றான் றானைந்து திங்க ளன்றே.
reading: The vow is set out: taken on the fifth day of the bright fortnight in certain months, kept for five years and five months.
nuance: The list of months in lines 1 and 2 is hard to take apart (the words ஆதல், ஆடி, பங்குனி, கார்த்திகை run into a rule whose exact calendar is unclear). The sense of a fixed periodic fast is clear; the exact schedule is not.
event: The sage fixes the days and the length of the vow.

tamil: இந்தநற் கிரமந் தன்னி லினிமையி னோன்பு நோற்று
அந்தமி லருகர் பூசை யருண்முனி தானஞ் செய்தால்
இந்திர பதமும் பெற்று இங்குவந் தரச ராகிப்
பந்ததீ வீனையை வென்று பஞ்சம கதியு மாமே.
reading: Keeping the fast in this order, worshipping the arhats and giving to ascetics, one reaches Indra's station, then kingship, conquers the binding deed and reaches the fifth state.
nuance: The release promised is reached through kingship and gifts: the householder's path is placed before the ascetic's, as the fast and the giving come first and the end of deeds last.

tamil: என்றவ ருரைப்பக் கேட்டு யிறைஞ்சிக் கைக்கொண்டு நோன்பை
சென்றுதன் பவனம் புக்கான் சேயிழை யோடு மன்னன்
நன்றுடன் செல்லு நாளு ணயந்தரன் வந்தி றைஞ்சி
உன்னுடைத் தந்தை யுன்னை யுடன் கொண்டு வருக வென்றான்.
reading: The hero accepts the vow and enters his palace with his wife; Nayantaran then bows and tells him his father calls him.
nuance: Lines 3-4 report Nayantaran's words; the speech is not set off by a closing particle, so it could be taken as narrator's paraphrase.
event: The hero takes the vow home; the minister Nayantaran summons him to his father.

tamil: அமையுநன் கமைச்சன் சொல்லை யருமணி மார்பன் கேட்டு
சமையுநாற் படையுஞ் சூழச் சாலலக் கணையி னோடும்
இமையவற் கிறைவன் போல வெழில்பெறப் புக்க வன்றே.
reading: Hearing the minister, the hero rides out on an elephant with his army, his wife Salalakshana and his friends, like Indra's lord.
event: The hero sets out in state, with his army, wife and friends, to join his father.

reading: The father comes to meet him; the hero bows at his feet, the father lifts and embraces him, and they go home and live happily.
event: Father and son meet, embrace and go home.

reading: The women he married with the rite are called to him; he stays with them, and the father, free of attachment, sets the son on the throne.
nuance: Line 4 (பற்றறச் செயந்தரனும் பார்மகன் வைத்தான்) is read as the father, without attachment, setting up the son as king; the subject is uncertain, and the order of 156 and 157 overlaps.
event: The brides are brought to the hero, and his father arranges to hand over the kingdom.

reading: The father crowns Naga Kumara, leaves his pleasures, bows at the sage's feet and, one-pointed in mind, takes the form of the Lord.
nuance: The father takes the way the sage's prophecy (verse 44) had promised for the son. For the son the prophecy of austerity and release is left open here, since he is crowned.
event: The king crowns his son, leaves the throne and takes up the ascetic's life under a sage.

title: ஐந்தாம் சருக்கம் 158-170 (2/2)
theme: The hero crowns his son and takes the monk's form, conquers his karma and reaches liberation after teaching as a kevali, his companions and wives follow, and the poet closes with a promise to those who hear the tale and a sermon that nothing helps the soul but virtue.
source_issues: Verse 167 has broken word division in its number-words, so the years cannot be read with confidence.
Verse 158 does not name the one who destroyed the two deeds in line 1, and the story's earlier king is assumed.
Verse 164 line 4 and verse 166 line 1 have word-divisions the build could not clean (அச்சேத்தியபேத்தியர்).

cast.role: the hero, king who becomes a monk and a kevali
the king named only by his destroyed karma (the earlier king, from verse 158)
the queen who leaves her son and takes austerity
the hero's brother or companion who receives half the kingdom
the hero's brother or companion, who reaches liberation with Vyalan
the chief queen who takes austerity
Ilakkanai's son, crowned king
the kevali before whom the king takes the monk's form
the nun at whose feet Ilakkanai bows
the gods who praise and worship the liberated brothers
the world addressed in the closing sermon

reading: The one who destroyed the two deeds reaches the world of bliss, and Prithivi Devi, leaving her great son and bowing at the feet of the sage Sirimati, takes up hard austerity and reaches the Achyuta heaven.
nuance: The first line gives the fruit (the world of bliss) for one who has destroyed both karmas, but the verse does not name him; the earlier verses make the king the likeliest, which is read here, not stated. The queen's reward is a heaven (அச்சுதம்), a lesser end than the first line's.
event: Prithivi Devi leaves her son, bows to the nun Sirimati, takes austerity and reaches the Achyuta heaven; the earlier king, who has destroyed his karmas, reaches the world of bliss.

reading: The king gives half his kingdom to Vyalan, gives gifts to his many friends, and firmly sets Ilakkanai, chief of his wives, in the rank of chief queen.
event: Naga Kumara gives half the kingdom to Vyalan, rewards his companions and installs Ilakkanai as chief queen.

reading: A good son named Devakumaran is born to Ilakkanai, learns the arts and the bow, and daily goes out with the chariot and elephant.
event: Ilakkanai bears a son, Devakumaran, who is trained in the arts, the bow, chariot and elephant.

reading: The lord, seated on a fine throne in his hall, attended by eight thousand bright-crowned kings and two fly-whisks, sits in splendour.
nuance: The splendour here is drawn at full height, just before the next verse turns it to renunciation.

reading: While the king sits at ease, a cloud that has gathered dissolves, and with dispassion arising he crowns the young prince and rises gladly to take up the hard austerity.
nuance: The text names the vanishing cloud as the moment of the turn but does not say it is the cause; the verse leaves a quick reader to supply the lesson of impermanence. The crowning of the son comes before the going forth, so the king's duty is discharged first.
event: Seeing a cloud vanish, the king grows dispassionate, crowns his son Devakumaran and leaves to take austerity.

reading: The king bows at the feet of the stainless Amalamati, the kevali, and with many kings looking on takes the form of the faultless one, and Ilakkanai and the other wives bow at the feet of the nun Pathumai.
event: Naga Kumara bows to the kevali Amalamati and takes the monk's form before many kings; Ilakkanai bows to the nun Pathumai.

tamil: நறுங்குழ லிலக்க ணையு நங்கை மார்தங் கூட
உறுதவந் தரித்துக் கொண்டு வுவந்தவர் செல்லு நாளுள்
மறுவில்சீர் முனிவ னாய னாக குமாரன் றானும்
இறுகுவெவ் வினைகள் வென்று யினிச்சித்தி சேர்ந்த தன்றே.
reading: Ilakkanai and her companions take up hard austerity and go on gladly, and in those days the faultless sage Naga Kumara, having overcome the binding deeds, reaches the final perfection.
nuance: The verse gives the king's end as the conquest of karma (வினைகள் வென்று), not as a gift of any god; the women's austerity is told but their end is not said here.
event: Ilakkanai and the women take austerity; the monk Naga Kumara conquers his harsh deeds and reaches siddhi.

tamil: வியாளமா வியாளர் தாமும் விழுத்தவத் தனயை யென்னு
நயாவுயிர் தியானந் தன்னா னாலிரு வினைகள் வென்று
செயத்துதி தேவர் கூறிச் சிறந்தபூ சனையுஞ் செய்ய
மயாவிறப் பிறப்பு மின்றி மருவினார் முத்தி யன்றே.
reading: Vyalan and Mavyalan, through meditation on the soul and the supreme austerity, overcome the two deeds, are praised and worshipped by the gods, and reach liberation with no more death or birth.
nuance: Meditation on the soul (உயிர் தியானம்) is the named means; no grace or god is given a part, which is the point the Jain account would press against a path of release by a Lord's favour.
event: Vyalan and Mavyalan conquer their karmas by meditation, are praised by the gods and reach liberation.

tamil: அருந்தவ யோகந் தன்னா லச்சேத் தியபேத் தியர்தம்
இருவினை தம்மை வென்று வின்புறுஞ் சித்தி சேர்ந்தார்
மருவுநற் றவத்தி னாலே மற்றுமுள் ளோர்க ளெல்லாம்
திருநிறைச் சோத மாதி சேர்ந்தின்பந் துய்த்தா ரன்றே.
reading: By hard yoga these indivisible and unbreakable ones overcame the two deeds and reached the joyful perfection, and all the others too, through firm austerity, enjoyed the bliss of heaven.
nuance: Two ends are set side by side: those who conquer both deeds reach perfection (சித்தி), while the others by austerity go to a heaven of enjoyment, so austerity alone does not give the same fruit to all.
event: The two brothers reach siddhi by yoga; the rest, by austerity, reach heavenly bliss.

tamil: நாகநற் குமரற் காயு நான்காண் டைஞ்நூற் றிரட்டி
ஆகுநற் குமார கால மைந்து முப்பத் திரட்டி
ஆருநற் றவத்தி லாண்டு வறுபத்து நான்க தாமே.
reading: The verse counts the years of Naga Kumara's life as the years of youth, of rule in the earthly land and of austerity, which together come to a long span.
nuance: The numbers in the Tamil (the first lines are broken into words and units) cannot be fixed cleanly, so the arithmetic is not relied on.

tamil: மறுவறு மனைய வர்க்கு மாதவர் தமக்கு மீந்த
பெறுமிரு நிலங்க ளெங்கும் பெயர்ந்து நற்கே வலியாய்
அறமழை பொழிந்த கால மறுபத்தா றாண்டு சென்றார்
உறுதவர் தேவர் நான்கு முற்றெழு குழாத்தி னோடே.
reading: Having moved on as a kevali through both lands he had given to the faultless wives and the great sages, he poured out a rain of dharma for sixty-six years with sages and gods in four groups around him.
nuance: Dharma is figured as rain falling on the lands, a teacher's giving without return, and the teacher is already liberated in knowledge before he is freed from the body.
event: As a kevali Naga Kumara teaches dharma for sixty-six years among sages and gods.

tamil: இதன்கதை யெழுதி யோதி யின் புறக் கேட்ப வர்க்கும்
புதல்வர்நற் பொருளும் பெற்றுப் புரந்தரன் போல வாழ்ந்து
கதமுறு கவலை நீங்கிக் காட்சிநல் லறிவு முன்பாய்ப்
பதமிகு மமர யோகம் பாங்குடன் செல்வ ரன்றே.
reading: Those who write and recite this story and those who hear it with joy will gain sons and wealth, live like Indra, shed anger and sorrow, hold right faith and knowledge, and reach the heavens.
nuance: This is the usual promise at a poem's close: reward comes from hearing and copying the tale, which is put alongside conduct rather than in place of it.

tamil: மறமின்றி யுயிர்க் கிடர்செய் மற்றொன்று மில்லை யென்றும்
திறமிது வுணர்ந்து தேறித் தீக்கதிப் பிறவிக் கஞ்சி
மறமிதை விட்ட றத்தில் வாழுமின் னுலகத் தீரே.
reading: Apart from virtue nothing else helps the soul, and nothing else harms it as vice does; knowing this and fearing rebirth in a bad state, the world is told to leave vice and live in virtue.
nuance: The closing sermon is a rule, not an event: it puts the whole story's moral in two statements, one about what supports the soul and one about what harms it. Fear of an evil birth is the stated motive, not love of virtue for itself.

title: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து 1-9
theme: The invocation praises the omniscient one, free of birth and its three companions, whose word ends the suffering of souls, as the only god; the poet then makes his apology to the assembly (his work came in a dream and, like the moon, may carry a spot) and sums up the story to come: the demoness Neelakesi, unable to break a sage's penance, takes the great one's dharma, turns from violence and sets out to answer the schools, beginning with the view that accepts flesh.
source_issues: Verse 7, line 3: 'திறத்த.: துரை' renders the aytham as '.:'; read திறத்தஃது உரை.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Jain sage whose penance Neelakesi cannot break
the lesser demons who seek out Neelakesi for help

reading: The poet praises as god the one whom the good worship, who has none of the four that begin with birth, whose word removes the suffering of souls and makes them rise to joy, the ancient lamp of dharma who knows all things.
nuance: The verse does not name the Jina; it defines god by marks (freedom from birth and the three that follow it, omniscience, a teaching that ends suffering) rather than by creation or grace. That this is the Jain omniscient teacher rests on those marks and on the later verses that name the Jina (சினவரன், 148); the claim is tagged Jain on that basis. The god acts through his word (சொல்), not by intervening.

reading: Those who have drunk the nectar of dharma he gave need not be named one by one; out of a devotion built by bowing over many days, the poet says, there is one thing he has to tell here.
nuance: Line 2 (இன்னார் இனையர் என வேண்டுவது இல்லை) can mean that the saints are too well known to need naming, or that no distinction of persons matters for those who drink the dharma; the reading is not fixed.

reading: The poet asks the learned not to throw his work aside in anger as speech not found in the old Agama: he bowed at the broad feet of the one who walked on cool lotuses, lay down, and saw it in a dream, and tells it as he saw it.
nuance: The apology anticipates the charge that a debate poem is a novelty outside scripture, and answers it by vision rather than by citing a text.
event: The poet bows at the lotus-walker's feet, lies down and sees the work in a dream.

reading: Neelakesi, a demoness in the form of a woman with dark kohl-lined eyes who did unrestrained harm, took the great one's dharma; her dark and evil heart turned, she rose into holiness, and she had the glory of turning the whole wide world from violence.
nuance: The verse plays on நீல (dark) three times: her name, the dark eyes, and the dark heart that turns. The conversion is the cause of her public work; the debates are framed as the reform of a world's violence (மறம்), not as a scholastic contest.
event: Neelakesi the demoness takes the great one's dharma, is transformed, and turns the world from violence.

reading: The poet says he became clear as the god taught, took all he then understood as great, and, with his own ignorance as his only strength, set out to establish it in the assembly of eloquent poets, where none will now fault the verse.
nuance: The last line can be read as confidence (no one will now scorn the verse, since its matter is the god's) or as a hope; மாவென்று கொண்டேன் in line 2 is also open.
event: The poet, taught by the god, sets out to present his work before the assembly of poets.

reading: Even the white moon that the sea-girt world beholds and loves every day is not spotless; so the poet will not ask that all his words be taken as merit, and if there is a fault here, he will not refuse to own it.
nuance: A conventional apology to the assembly, but turned: the moon's spot is used to claim the right to a fault, not to be ashamed of it.

reading: Since people take as meaningful even the cry of a bird, the poet argues, the world, if it wants dharma of excellent virtue, should not discard this work as speech fit for scorn but accept it.
nuance: Line 1 (தெள்ளி நரைத்துத் தெருளாது உறு தீமை செய்யும்) is obscure: it may describe the bird, or those who, though grey and learned, act without understanding. The argument is a fortiori: if a bird's call is heeded as an omen, a teaching of dharma deserves a hearing.

reading: The lesser demons, who went searching through country, king, city and the forest around it because their god's refuge had been taken away, went and seized on the great demoness, and she, in enmity, tried many times to frighten the sage.
nuance: கடவுள் புகல் நீக்குதல் (the removing of refuge in the god) refers back, in the story told later (35 to 45), to the sage stopping the blood offering at the goddess's shrine; the verse compresses that, and the one she frightens is not named here.
event: The lesser demons, deprived of their offerings, seek out Neelakesi, who repeatedly tries to frighten the sage.

reading: Unable to disturb the penance of the one she had seen, she took the form of a woman with a doe's glance, and after she gave up violence, all that followed, beginning with the view that accepts flesh, the poet will tell to the assembly as he saw it.
nuance: ஊன் கொண்ட காட்சி (the view that has taken flesh) names the first debate by its issue, the eating of flesh, which the Kundalakesi debate charges against the Buddhist teaching (163); the poem's polemic is announced through an ethical charge before any metaphysics.
event: Failing to break the sage's penance, Neelakesi takes a woman's form and gives up violence; the poet announces the debates to follow.

title: தருமவுரைச் சருக்கம் 10-33 (1/6)
theme: The sermon sarukkam opens with the setting: the rich Panchala land, walked through its tinais and explained as needing no palai, its two kinds of good people (generous householders and those who strive to wear away their deeds), its four varnas, its king Samudrasaran and his capital Pundavarthanam; then, near the town of Palalaiyam, a burning ground of pyres, corpses and demons with a shrine of the demon-mother, where a sage of earth-like patience takes up his dwelling.
source_issues: Verse 33 does not end: line 4 breaks off mid-word (தெரிந்) and the sentence runs into 34, which names the sage.
Verse 33, line 3 carries a stray full stop after தான் and is longer than its fellows; தான் may be an intrusion.
Verse 26, line 3: கலலிவான் looks corrupt.
Verse 27, line 2: பங்கொள் is doubtful.
Verse 10, lines 2 and 3 do not divide cleanly (திணையின்னணி தங்கி யேங்குந் / தாஞ்சால வாழ்நா டளிரீனுந்).

cast.role: king of the Panchala land, ruling from Pundavarthanam
the Jain sage whose penance Neelakesi cannot break

reading: The poet opens on the land praised by many as Panchala, where mango groves swell, parrot chicks in the marutham country drip with sweet juice, and the long-lived country puts out fresh shoots.
nuance: பார்த்தி நாடே may name the land as the king's (a form of பார்த்திவன்) or carry a personal name; lines 2 and 3 (திணையின்னணி தங்கி யேங்குந் / தாஞ்சால வாழ்நா டளிரீனுந்) do not divide cleanly, so the reading of the middle is open.

reading: This land of unfading wealth is the most esteemed in the flowering world; its goodness cannot be told in full, yet some must be said, and it is not a land where guests who come must fear hardship.
nuance: The modesty formula (its good cannot be told, but some must be) frames the whole description that follows. Line 4 (பாடா விருந்தார் பரிவஞ்சும் படிய தன்றே) is compressed; taking it as guests not fearing want is one reading.

reading: In the marutham fields, valai fish leap in the flowing water, herons rest with spread wings, dark-striped waterhens cry as they stride, and red paddy shines with ripe ears in every direction.
nuance: Verses 12 to 16 are built on one pattern: each line piles up adjectives in -அன on a single plant or creature and ends on its name, and the five verses walk through the tinais (fields, groves, shore, forest, hills).

reading: Areca palms rise among bamboo, coconuts drop ripe fruit, jack and banana bear sweet segments, fragrant blue lilies open by the houses, and sturdy marutham trees stand in flower.
On the backwater shore, fragrant screwpine, golden-flowered punnai and gnazhal spread their scent, and neythal lilies bloom unmatched along the creeks.
In the forest country the kodal opens its clusters among the creepers, the thondri glows like flame, the kaayaa blossoms by the fields, and the mullai opens its fragrant buds.

On the hills the naagam is in bud and scent, the vengai blooms as if announcing that the time for work has come, the kaanthal stands by the gem-bright rock, and the kurinji flowers beside the springs.
nuance: கணி வேங்கை calls the vengai the astrologer: its flowering tells the season (வினையுடையன பொழுது இவை), an old Tamil convention the poet keeps inside a Jain work.

reading: The people of the land enjoy dance and song without pause, see the assemblies of the renowned and hear their music, know both the lovers' quarrel and the union that follows, and give wealth freely to their men and women servants.

The householders keep giving and right conduct, rise in goodness with honour and without deceit, and others, having left the troubles of home for forest and hill, strive with knowledge to wear away the deeds they have done.
nuance: The ideal land holds both lives side by side: the householders' தானம் and சீலம் and the striving of those who aim that their deeds should wither (செய்வினைகள் நைய முயல்வாரும்). Wearing down past karma by knowledge and effort fits Jain teaching, but the verse does not name a school, so no claim is tagged. Line 3 (கானமொடு கல்லடரு ளில்லிடரு நீங்கி) is divided here as forest, rock and leaving the home's troubles; other divisions are possible.

reading: Brahmins and others together make up the four varnas, flawless and excellent, none straying from the path given to it, and so the land has the good of rising ever higher.
nuance: A Jain poet counts the four-varna order, each keeping its own path, among the land's merits. நந்திமிசை சேறல் in line 4 is read as growth upward (நந்தி, flourishing); it could also carry a religious sense that the verse does not make clear.

reading: Since the land is known for its goodness, since its months each have three rains, and since the harshness of the seasons is hardly seen there, it is no defect that it has no palai country.
nuance: The verse closes the tinai catalogue of 12 to 16, which named four landscapes, by explaining away the missing fifth: the dry palai arises from drought and harsh seasons, and this land has neither. The three rains a month, elsewhere a fruit of righteous rule, here are simply the land's own goodness.

reading: The king who rules this land happily is Samudrasaran, among men here what Surendra, told of in heaven, is among the gods.
event: Samudrasaran rules the land.

reading: In strength he is a lion, in command he is called Death itself, to his people he is a protecting mother, and to his enemies a mass of fire in his anger.
nuance: The verse joins the two faces of kingship that the ethics books keep apart, terror (கூற்றம்) and a mother's care (போற்று தாய்), and assigns them to different objects: the first to his command and his foes, the second to the குடி.

reading: This guardian of a realm where evils had ended and prosperity played, the lord whose long hands give in every direction, has his city in a quarter called Pundavarthanam.
The gates of its tall, rich walls seem to swallow all who enter and spit them out again, and the walls rise so high that they block the white moon's course and seem to measure the sky.
Swift horses, herds of elephants and rows of fine-wheeled chariots crowd the great gate of the royal palace, with a roar like the sea beating its waves.
Smoke of agil, clusters of cloth banners on the jewelled streets and pure fragrant powder rise to the clouds and cover the sky, so that the great city gives no room to daylight.
nuance: Line 3 (முகிற்றலைக் கலலிவான் மூடி) has a doubtful word (கலலி); the sense of the clouded sky is clear from the rest.

reading: Near that great city is a town called Palalaiyam, and it has a great burning ground where corpses fall, whose clamour, rising night and day, has spread its fame over the water-girt world.
nuance: The poem moves straight from the splendid capital to its cremation ground: the prosperity of 10 to 26 is the frame for the place where the story begins. பங்கொள் in line 2 is doubtful.

reading: Tall bamboos and vaagai trees mingle with thorny indu and eengai so thickly that it is dark, and among them deep-eyed ghouls and owls cry out and throw the minds of those who see it into turmoil.
The smoke and flames of the pyres are its lamps in the dark; owls and jackals howl in turn; at midnight the aandalai birds gather and call; it is a ground given over to evil.
Garlands, spread white skulls, charred firebrands, torn cloth from the biers, abandoned biers and bones lie scattered among the cactus, a fearful sight.
Crows clamour, ghouls shriek with their kin and drag at the hanged, many corpses dangle, red-eared vultures roost there, so that it is very hard for any who have a body to come near.
nuance: யாக்கை கொண்டவர்க்கு (for those who have taken a body) names the living by their bodies at the very place where bodies end; the phrase prepares the sage's choice to live there.

reading: Where fierce banyans and thick-trunked trees gather, the dust of the pyres rises and bodies crowd, and swarming hosts of demons that strike down and eat bodies press round, there stands a shrine made for the mother of the kooli demons.
nuance: The goddess is not named; கூளி தாய் (mother of the demon hosts) and இறைவி (33) mark her as the burning-ground goddess whom the next verses show receiving a lamb's blood (35). The flesh-eating demon hosts around her shrine set up the poem's first quarrel, over offering flesh.

tamil: பொறையு மாற்றலும் பூமியு மேருவு மனையான் தான்.
reading: In the goddess's shrine, taking it as his dwelling for four months, there lived in that forest no one could dwell in a man like the earth in patience and Meru in strength, of restrained mind, who had discerned the endless things...
nuance: The sentence runs on into 34, which names him (முனிச்சந்திரன்). உறையருங் காட்டகத்து உறைவான் plays on the word: he dwells in the place no one can dwell, so his first act is a feat of endurance. Four months (ஈரிரு திங்கள்) fits the rains retreat when Jain monks stay in one place, though the verse does not say so.
event: A sage takes the goddess's shrine in the burning ground as his dwelling for four months.

title: தருமவுரைச் சருக்கம் 34-56 (2/6)
theme: The sage Munichandra stops a goat sacrifice vowed for a child by arguing that the child came from karma, not the goddess, and gives the worshippers a clay substitute and the householder's five abstentions; the demons who lose their offerings bring the goddess Neelakesi, whose terrors fail against his unmoved penance.
source_issues: Verse 43, line 3 carries an editor's bracketed (றெண்ணி), and line 4 (யிரந்தோர் வன்றெய்வங் கொணர்ந்திவற் கடிதுமென்) is metrically short; the verse appears defective.
Verse 34, line 4: முத்தின் யான் does not construe as divided; the word division may be wrong.
Verse 56, line 4: நடுங்கும் னுடம்பென has a stray ன் before உடம்பு, probably for நடுங்குமென் னுடம்பென.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Jain sage whose penance Neelakesi cannot break
the lesser demons who seek out Neelakesi for help
the worshippers who bring a goat to be killed for the goddess in thanks for a child

reading: The narrator introduces the sage named Munichandra: he knows the existents by measuring them with the means of valid knowledge, is great in the virtues that begin with the restraints, and by the twelve kinds of penance cuts the chain of births.
nuance: The vocabulary is technical Jain: அத்திகாயங்கள் (the astikayas, the extended existents), குத்தி (gupti, the restraints of mind, speech and body) and பத்தின் மேல் இரு, ten and two, the twelvefold penance. The sage is defined first as one who knows by அளவை, which prepares his later role as teacher of a debater. The opening of line 4 (முத்தின் யான்) does not construe clearly.

tamil: நின்றக் கோண்மின மெனச் சொல்லி நெறியறி வுறுவோ
னொன்றற் பல்வகை யுயிர்க் கொலை யுரைமின மெனவே.
reading: At the temple, when some were carrying out the rite of cutting off the head of a goat that knew nothing for the deity, the sage who knew the way told them to stop and to say why they would kill a life for one end.
nuance: The sage's first move is a question, not a ban: he asks the worshippers to give their reason, which sets up the exchange of 36 to 40 as a small debate. The goat is called அறிவிலா மறி, the goat without understanding, which makes its killing the taking of a life that cannot consent.
event: As worshippers prepare to behead a goat for the temple deity, the sage stops them and asks why they kill.

reading: The killers answer that the broad-shouldered woman standing here had no child, that they made a vow about it to this goddess Modi of the host, that a child was born, and that they have brought the goat to cut it in thanks.
nuance: மோடி is a name of the fierce goddess; the sacrifice is a vow repaid (நேர்த்தி in later usage), a gift for a gift. The poem names the worshippers by their act, கொலையாளர், the killers, before they have argued at all.
event: The worshippers explain that the goddess granted a barren woman a child and the goat is the vowed thank-offering.

reading: The sage asks which became the child, the flesh-body or the life: if the body, it is of the parents' blood; if the life, it came to a human birth by the deed it did before; so what did the god give the woman with honeyed hair?
nuance: The argument splits the child into body and soul and finds no share left for the goddess: the body has a natural cause, the soul a karmic one. It denies the gift, not the goddess's existence, so the vow lapses for want of anything to repay.
event: The sage answers that the child's body came from its parents' blood and its life from its own former deeds.

reading: The sage proposes that, since the gods are content even when what was vowed to them is made in figure, the worshippers make a goat of clay and give it, and then neither they nor the gods will bear blame or sin.
nuance: A pastoral compromise: the sage does not ask the worshippers to break their vow but to keep it with an image, and he speaks as if the gods accept this. Lines 1 and 2 (ஏறி யானை இருங்கலைகள் நேர்ந்தார், perhaps vows of an elephant to ride or great stags) do not construe securely; the clay goat of line 3 is plain.
event: The sage tells them to offer a clay goat in place of the living one.

tamil: கொன்ற வன்னே கொடியனென வுலகங் கூறு மதனாலு
மொன்ற நூலா ருரைகளோ டொப்ப முடியு மதனாலு
மின்றி னின்று மிதுவொழிதி ராயி னுங்கட் கிருமைக்கு
நன்றி தென்றான் வெந்நரகம் புகுதல் விலக்கு நாவினான்.
reading: The sage whose tongue keeps men from the hot hell tells them that the world calls the killer cruel and the words of the scriptures agree, so if they give up this practice from today it will be good for them in both lives.
nuance: He argues from two authorities his hearers already accept, common opinion and the scriptures, not from Jain doctrine; the appeal is to a shared ground before the doctrinal list of 40.
event: The sage urges the worshippers to give up killing from that day.

tamil: கோறல் பொய்த்தல் கொடுங்களவு நீக்கிப் பிறர்ம னைகண்மேற்
சேற லின்றிச் செழும்பொருண்மேற் சென்ற சிந்தை வேட்கையினை
யாறு கிற்பி னமருலக நுங்கட் கடிய தாமென்றான்
நீறு மோடு நிழன்மணியும் பொன்னு நிகரா நோக்குவான்.
reading: The sage, who looks on ash, potsherd, shining gem and gold alike, tells them that if they put away killing, lying and theft, do not go after other men's wives, and calm the mind's craving for wealth, the world of the gods will be within their reach.
nuance: These are the five lesser vows of the Jain householder (not killing, not lying, not stealing, not going to another's wife, limiting possessions), given in order. The reward named is the world of the immortals, not release: the sage asks of lay worshippers a householder's discipline, while his own epithet (gold and potsherd alike) marks the ascetic's equanimity.
event: The sage gives the worshippers the five abstentions of the householder.

tamil: ஏத்து தற்கேற் றானிரங்கி யின்ன வைசொல் லக்கேட்டுப்
பாத்தி யோயெம் பழவினையும் பாறு கென்று பணிந்துதாம்
யாத்து நின்ற வம்மறியும் மறமு முடனே கொண்டுபோய்க்
காத்து மென்றார் கருவினையு ணீங்கு நல்ல கருத்தினார்.
reading: Hearing the compassionate words of the one worthy of praise, the worshippers bowed, prayed that their old deeds too might be undone, and took the tethered goat away with them, promising to keep it safe.
nuance: The converts at once think of their own karma (பழவினை), so the sage's argument about the child's karma in 37 has been taken home. Line 3 (அம்மறியும் மறமும்) can be read as taking away the goat and their violence, or the goat and the dharma (அறமும்); either way the goat leaves alive.
event: The worshippers bow to the sage, pray to be freed of their old deeds, and lead the goat away alive.

tamil: ஆய மெல்லா மதுசொல்லிப் போக வவணே வாழ்கின்ற
பேயுங் கூடிப் பெரிதுமகி சூழ்ந்து தம்பெற் றிசொல்லி
னாயு மாக்க ருத்துமில னாவ னிவனங் கட்கென்னிற்
reading: When the whole company had gone away telling of it, the demons who lived in that place gathered in great distress and spoke of their plight, saying that this man had no regard for them at all.
nuance: The cost of the conversion falls on the spirits of the place, who lose the offerings they lived on. Lines 3 and 4 are obscure and the demons' words cannot be fixed.
event: After the worshippers leave, the demons of the temple gather to lament.

reading: The demons say that when the hot sun rises they have no standing, being hidden like dark night and hard to see, and they resolve to roam many lands and settlements and bring back a strong deity to drive this man away.
nuance: The demons are weak by day and must borrow strength; the plan of 44 to 46 begins here. The verse is defective: line 3 carries an editor's bracketed (றெண்ணி) and line 4 ends short.
event: The demons resolve to search for a powerful deity to drive the sage off.

reading: Saying there is no use staying, they set out through the Kasi country, the Chedi country and many lands without finding one, and in the southern direction they met the great goddess Neelakesi and eagerly told her this.
nuance: Neelakesi is here a மாதெய்வம், a great deity, where the invocation called her a பேய் (4); the poem lets the demons' own estimate of her stand. She is found in the south after the northern lands fail.
event: The demons search Kasi, Chedi and other lands in vain and find the goddess Neelakesi in the south.

reading: The demons weep to Neelakesi that the sage forced his way into their place, told many that feeding the bali of cooked food and flesh is sin, does not care what becomes of their clamorous forest, and has tormented them, and they put themselves under her protection.
nuance: The sage's teaching reaches us here in the mouth of its victims: what the worshippers heard as a release, the demons report as an invasion (வலிசெய்து புகுந்து). The meaning of line 3 is not secure.
event: The demons complain to Neelakesi that the sage has stopped their offerings and ask her protection.

reading: Neelakesi asks why they weep: let the one who is set on hard penance sit there passing his time, and she will show him to the vultures to eat; beating her hands and crying 'rise', she went and sat in the field where corpses are laid.
nuance: She treats the penance as idleness (பொழுது போக்குதல்); the phrase பொருத்தம் அஃது உடைத்தே (that has its fitness) reads as scorn, though its exact turn is not certain.
event: Neelakesi promises to feed the sage to the vultures and goes to the cremation ground where he sits.

reading: Going through the dark and rising up again and again, she boasts of herself before the ascetic, saying she will swallow him if she frightens him and that she will roll the high peak of a mountain onto him.
nuance: Her threats are self-praise (தன்னை வியக்கும்); the line that seems to say he has no power to delude or to resist (மருட்டிறம் இலன்) is damaged by word division.
event: Neelakesi appears before the sage in the dark and threatens to swallow him and crush him with a mountain.

reading: The sage, who had clearly grasped the good precepts and the holy word of the Jina, who knew without limit the many things of the three times, and who knew besides that the vyantara spirits frighten in this way, judged that this was Neelakesi's want of the right path.
nuance: வியந்தரம் is the Jain class of wandering demigods (vyantara): the sage meets the goddess with a category, as a known kind of being acting according to its kind, not as a power to be feared. Her violence is read as a lack of நெறி, to be cured, not as wickedness.
event: The sage recognizes the terrors as the work of a vyantara spirit and judges her to lack the right path.

reading: The sage knew that, though she frighten him with her transformations, he would make her understand her own powerlessness, and that if in a little while she gained the arts of meaning through learning, she would come to the good path of dharma and grace.
nuance: விகுர்வணை is the Jain term for a deity's power to change form (vikurvana). The sage plans to teach, not to defeat: the line about learning the arts of meaning (பொருட்டிறங்களைப் புலமையில்) foreshadows her later career as a debater.
event: The sage resolves to bear her terrors and foresees that she will come to the dharma.

reading: She rises to touch the sky like a mountain, roars like rock struck on rock, bursts like a cloud thundering through the air, thrusts out her tongue like a serpent, and roams about as many and as few.
nuance: The run 50 to 54 is a catalogue of a deity's transformations, each verse built on repeated similes; பலவெனச் சிலவென (as many, as few) shows her changing number as well as shape.
event: Neelakesi takes terrifying forms to frighten the sage.

reading: She laughs with fire flaring between her long gleaming fangs, roars with a din like a storm of rain, opens the great cave of her mouth like a pit and calls, and stands to bewilder him, thrusting her hand into her long hair and panting.
event: Neelakesi takes terrifying forms to frighten the sage.

reading: She stamps her feet so the earth is shattered to dust, beats her belly, falls like fire screaming, and whirls everywhere like a circle of burning brands.
event: Neelakesi takes terrifying forms to frighten the sage.

reading: She hurls stones fiercer than fire, sets white arrows to a bow and shoots them, grinds her teeth saying she will close with him in wrestling, and with those teeth divides the fat of many corpses.
event: Neelakesi takes terrifying forms to frighten the sage.

reading: She takes a form and then hides as if formless, sings with a clattering din, dances a drama crying that her great hunger be eased, and says again and again that she will pass right through him before she gives over.
nuance: அரும்பசி களைக, ease my great hunger: in the middle of the terrors the goddess's own need shows, the hunger left by the offerings the sage has stopped (45). Line 1 (ஓடு முட்குடை) is obscure.
event: Neelakesi takes terrifying forms to frighten the sage.

reading: Though she became elephant, great striped tiger, fierce bull, killing lion and other beasts of great rage, he did not flinch, and she held back, thinking this was no refuge for her and that the fullness of his penance would burn her.
nuance: The sage does nothing: his penance acts by being unmoved, and it is the assailant who imagines it as fire. The story bears her thought out, since she withdraws and in time takes his dharma (4).
event: The sage stays unmoved through her beast forms, and Neelakesi gives up the attack.

reading: Neelakesi says she had thought to destroy his penance by fear but did not know him: this victor has no other magic but great virtue, and unless he wills it she cannot come before him; and she shrank, her body trembling as if poisoned.
nuance: She sets virtue (விழுக்குணம்) against magic (விச்சை): she reads his strength as the absence of the very powers she was using. Line 1's construction (அழிக்குவன் தவம் என அறியேன்) can also mean she did not know he would undo her; the sense of defeat is clear either way.
event: Neelakesi admits she cannot overcome the sage and shrinks back trembling.

title: தருமவுரைச் சருக்கம் 57-79 (3/6)
theme: Having failed to terrify the sage Munichandran, Neelakesi takes the form of the princess Kamalekai and tries to seduce him; he sees through her, answers her feigned fears and wiles, and when she weeps over her birth begins a sermon on birth, the four states of birth, the seven hells and the grading of beings by their number of senses.
source_issues: Verse 64 is printed with the number 6; it is read as 64, since the next verse is 65.
Verse 61, line 3 (கூலி யான்குறை யுளதெனக்) is obscure and may be corrupt.
Verse 64, line 3 (பணிந்தவரட் காசிடை) does not divide cleanly; the phrase that says to whom the sage speaks is unclear.
Verse 76, lines 3-4 (முழுச்செவி கிண்ணர்கள், முவ்வாதம் அல்லார்) are hard to construe and may be corrupt.
Verse 71, line 4 ends with a stray semicolon in the text.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Jain sage whose penance Neelakesi cannot break
the troops who sing and dance as Neelakesi worships in her disguise

reading: Seeing that the sage's power is such that the fire of his austerity would destroy her and there is no way to counter it, the demoness of Death-like cruelty drops her rage, humbled, and bows, praying that her cruel deeds be quenched.
nuance: The verse names the sage by his ஆற்றல் (power) and her by Death, கூற்றம்: the contest is staged as austerity against death. Whether the bow is already pretence is left open; the next verse shows her planning a feigned worship with the same kind of plea.
event: Neelakesi, unable to frighten the sage, ends her rage and bows to him, asking that her cruel karma be quenched.

reading: She reasons that if she takes the shape of a young woman and, under cover of a feigned worship that prays for her old bound deeds to perish, breaks his inner restraint in that shape, he will abandon his fire-like vow.
nuance: The plan turns the language of release from karma (பழவினை கெடுக) into bait: the plea a penitent would make is to be her disguise. Her target is named precisely: not his body but his மனநிறை, the containment of his mind.
event: Neelakesi resolves to take a young woman's form and break the sage's vow through feigned worship.

reading: At the end of the night she appears in the very form of Kamalekai, the king's only daughter, radiant as the goddess of fortune, and goes with garlands, sandal paste and cool flowers to worship.
nuance: She borrows a real person's form, the king's daughter, so the deceit also puts a princess's good name at risk. Line 4's words of praise (சேமம் காவல சேவடி போற்று) may be addressed to the shrine's guardian; who they address is not plain.
event: Neelakesi appears in the form of the princess Kamalekai and sets out with offerings to worship.

reading: As she bows, circles the place and worships, troops sing the praises due and dance the thunangai while her girdle sways under her garment, and she, in her lovely form, resolves to approach the ascetic.
nuance: Who the கணங்கள் are, her own spirit retinue playing attendants or the shrine's troops, is not said.
event: Neelakesi worships at the shrine while troops sing and dance, then resolves to go near the sage.

reading: Standing where the famed ascetic can hear, she orders the guards to stop at the gate and come no further, the servants to see to what is needed, and her people to come close when she has some want.
nuance: The speech is played for the overhearing sage: a princess's orders to her household are her credentials. Line 3 (கூலி யான் குறை உளது) is obscure.
event: Neelakesi, as the princess, dismisses her guards and servants within earshot of the sage.

reading: Coming to the shrine, she bows to the great ascetic seated at the foot of a broad-leaved banyan and prays that her cruel deeds be quenched, she who wears the wondrous shining form she had wished for.
nuance: Line 3 repeats the plea of verse 57 almost word for word (என்செய் கருவினை தணிக்க), now spoken through a borrowed body as a lure.
event: Neelakesi, disguised, bows to the sage under the banyan and asks that her karma be quenched.

tamil: வேண்டிய வுருவத னாலும் வேட்கைசெய் யுருவத னாலுங்
காண்டகு மடவர லுருவங் காமுறு வதுநனி தாங்கி
யீண்டிய மிகுகுணத் திறைவ னியல்பினை யெனையது நினையா
நீண்டதோர் கொடியயற் கொடிபோ னிறைதவ வருளென நின்றாள்.
reading: Bearing a desired and desire-making form, the beauty of a young woman, and giving no thought at all to the nature of the lord rich in virtues, she stands like a creeper beside a tall creeper and asks the sage of full austerity for his grace.
nuance: The simile of a creeper by a creeper puts her as clinging to him; the verse stresses that the form is both chosen (வேண்டிய) and made to rouse desire (வேட்கைசெய்).
event: Neelakesi stands close beside the sage in her borrowed form and asks for his grace.

tamil: உடம்பொடு முயிரிடை மிடைந்த வொற்றுமை வேற்றுமை விகற்பிற்
றொடர்ந்தபல் வினைகளைத் துணிக்குஞ் சுதநெறி முறைமையு மறிவான்
னிடம்பக மகளிவள் பெரிது மிராசபுத் திரியல ளெனவே.
reading: The sage, who knows the scriptural way that cuts the many deeds bound up in the soul's union with and difference from the body, steadies his yoga and says that this woman is a deceiver and no king's daughter at all.
nuance: ஒற்றுமை வேற்றுமை, the body and soul as one and as other, may be the Jain view that they are one in one respect and distinct in another; that is my reading. Line 3, where he speaks (பணிந்தவரட் காசிடை), is obscure, so it is unclear whether he says it to her, to himself or aside.
event: The sage, fixed in yoga, perceives that the woman is a deceiver and not the princess.

tamil: என்னைஈண் டைக்கு வரவென் றருந்தவன் வினவலு மெழிலார்
பொன்னனாள் புடைபெயர்த் திட்ட பொலங்கல மனங்கலக் குவபோன்
reading: When the sage asks why she has come, the golden lady, her ornaments clinking like a parrot's chatter, says she has come to pay what is due for boons she once prayed for.
event: Asked why she has come, Neelakesi says she has come to fulfil vows for boons granted.

tamil: யாதுநீ கொண்ட வரமென் றருந்தவ னியல்பினின் வினவ
வேதினாட் டிறையெங்க ளிறைமே லியல்பின்றி யெழலொழி கெனவே
போதுசாந் தவியொடு புகையும் பொருந்திய பொருந்தெய்வக் கெனலு
மோதிஞா னியிது வாயி னுரையழ கீதென மொழிந்தான்.
reading: Asked what boon she sought, she says it was that the king of a hostile land not rise unlawfully against her father, with flowers, sandal, oblation and incense for the god, and the knowing sage answers that if so, her words are fair.
nuance: The sage's reply (உரை அழகு ஈது) can be plain assent or a dry remark on a well-made story; he already knows she is not the princess.
event: Neelakesi names a vow for her father's safety from a hostile king, and the sage comments on her answer.

tamil: தோடுகொண் டொருசெவி விளங்கத் துளங்குவ மகரமொன் றாடப்
பாடுவண் டோடுசுரும் பரற்றப் பல்கலம் வயிரவில் வீச
வாடுகொம் பனையவ ருரைக்கு மச்சமோ பெரிதுடைத் தடிகள்
காடுகண் டாற்பிறர்க் கறியேன் கவற்றுவ தொக்குமீ தெனக்கே.
reading: With a jewel on one ear, a makara earring swinging on the other, bees humming and gems flashing, she says the fear such tender women speak of is great indeed, and that whatever others feel, this forest troubles her.
nuance: The demoness of the burning ground claims to be afraid of her own haunt.
event: Neelakesi, in her finery, tells the sage that the forest frightens her.

tamil: மணிநகு நெடுமுடி மறவேன் மன்னவன் மகளெனின் மடவாய்
அணிநகை யாயமோ டாடி அரும்பெறற் சுற்றமோ டிருப்பாய்
பிணிமிகு பேய்வன மிதனுட் போதுற லொருதலை பிறவோ
துணிவொடு துறந்தவர்க் கல்லாற் றுன்னதற் கரிதிது பிறர்க்கே.
reading: The sage answers that if she were the daughter of the king of the jewelled crown and fierce spear she would be playing with her companions and sitting among her kin, and that this disease-ridden demon forest is hard for any to enter except those who have renounced with resolve.
nuance: He tests her story against what a princess's life would be, without accusing her outright.
event: The sage questions why a king's daughter would come into a demon forest that only renouncers approach.

tamil: வேணுவோ டினையன பிறவும் வியப்புறு பெருவனம் வினவிற்
பேணுதற் கரிதிது பெரிதும் பிணிதரு பேய்வன மெனவே
வாணுதன் மயிர்குளிர்த் துரைக்கும் மாதவத் தடிகளென் றானுங்
காணுதற் கரியன வுருவங் கண்டறி வனகளு முளவோ.
reading: With bamboo and such things, she says, the great forest is a wonder, yet hard to bear, a demon forest full of afflictions; and with her hair on end she asks the great sage whether he has seen any of the forms that are hard to see.
event: Neelakesi, feigning fear, asks the sage whether he has seen the spirits of the forest.

tamil: புக்கிருந் தொருமனை யுறைவார் போவதும் வருவதுங் கண்டான்
மக்களுந் தாயரந் தம்முள் மருள்வதும் வெருள்வது முளதோ
மிக்கபல் கதிகளு முயிரின் மெய்ம்மையு முணர்ந்தவர்க் கரிதே
ஒக்குமற் றவையுள வேனு முரைப்பது பொருத்தமின் றெமக்கே.
reading: The sage answers that those who live together in one house see each other come and go, and mother and children do not take fright at one another; for those who know the many states of birth and the truth of souls such fear is rare, and even if these beings exist it is not fitting for him to speak of them.
nuance: The beings he declines to speak of stand before him; his refusal can be read as tact toward one he has already seen through. The housemates image makes all souls kin in one dwelling, across the states of birth.

reading: When the sage has spoken, the tender one asks him to teach her with his whole mind a mantra, if there is one, so that deaths cannot reach her; the ascetic whom even the sky-dwellers worship answers that they will not reach her though Indra himself wished it, so what are demons.
nuance: It is unclear whether அவை (line 3) are the deaths she fears or the spirits; either way the assurance is ironic, given to the demoness herself.
event: Neelakesi asks the sage for a mantra against death, and he tells her no such harm will reach her.

reading: She makes her coral lip tremble, loosens the garment at her hips, draws in her breasts, flashes her rain-dark eyes and sways her slender waist, and as she does all this he asks what any of it is to him.
nuance: The seduction ends in one line of indifference: he does not argue against desire, he finds nothing in it addressed to him.
event: Neelakesi plays every wile of seduction, and the sage asks what these are to him.

reading: Her gold earrings and white bangles slipping, the flowers falling from her head to the ground and tears streaming from her long eyes, she says her anguish is great and cries out that this birth may perish.
nuance: The text does not say whether the grief is one more ruse or the first real turn; the sage answers it as real, with a sermon on birth.
event: Neelakesi breaks down weeping and wishes her present birth would end.

tamil: பிறவியும் பிறவியுட் பிறக்கும் பிணியுமப் பிணியினைத் துணிக்கு
யறவிய மனத்தினை யாகி அலங்கழித் தொழிலொழிந் தடங்கி
reading: The high ascetic tells her that if she wishes to hear of birth, of the diseases born within birth, of the medicine of dharma that cuts them and of that medicine's excellence, she should set her mind on dharma, cease her wavering and her actions, grow still and sit, and she sits.
event: The sage offers to teach birth and its cure, and Neelakesi sits down to listen.

reading: Of the four states of birth he begins with the hell-dwellers: the hell lands, held up by three rings of wind, lie below the nigoda, and are named darkness upon darkness, darkness, smoke, mire, sand, sharp gravel and gems.
nuance: The seven names, read upward from the lowest, match the Jain list of seven hell-earths (deepest darkness, darkness, smoke, mud, sand, gravel, gem). How line 3 should be divided (நிகோதத்தின் இம்பர் இருளின் இருள் இருள்) is my reading.

reading: These seven spread into eighty-four hundred thousand, with the varieties of their pits; the beings below are sexless and of shapes beyond counting, born there as their lot.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 (முழுச்செவி கிண்ணர்கள், முவ்வாதம் அல்லார்) are hard to construe; I read அலிகள் as the hell-dwellers being neither male nor female, which Jain teaching holds, but the line may list other kinds of being.

reading: If she wishes him to tell the kinds of animal life too, he says, they are of two sorts, those that stand fixed in the earth and those that move, and the fixed ones are of five kinds throughout this world.
nuance: Here 'animal' (விலங்கு) covers the whole state of non-human, non-divine, non-hell life, down to the fixed beings.

reading: The moving ones, found in this middle world, have from two to five senses; among them the snail and the like, which lack a nose and have only taste beyond touch, are two-sensed.
Lice, mites, ants and the like, countless millions, have those two senses and smell, three in all; those lacking hearing, like the wasp and the honeybee, have four.

title: தருமவுரைச் சருக்கம் 80-103 (4/6)
theme: Continuing the sermon on the four states of birth, the sage Munichandran describes the five-sensed animals, the five kinds of humans (of the land of enjoyment, of the islands, the divine, the beastlike, and those of the land of deeds, who alone can reach bliss by penance), the five classes of gods, and then, in short lines, the endless pains of hell, where bodies rejoin like water, old enemies fight and killing and flesh-eating are punished in fire; midway he hints to Neelakesi that her own kin are among the demon gods, and she agrees to keep listening.
source_issues: Verse 102 is missing: the core file goes from 101 to 103, so the chapter has 23 verses for the span 80 to 103.
Verse 90, line 2 carries a stray bracketed syllable '(வோர்' at the end, apparently a variant or a misplaced fragment of line 3.
Verse 85, line 1 prints 'கோலமி னோன்றற்', where the sense seems to need கோலமில் தோன்றல்; line 3 prints 'தீண்டலு ரந்தரத்' for தீண்டலர் அந்தரத்.
Verse 95, line 1 was repaired from an old encoding (ேரி for ோ¢); 'வேரியர்' is read as enemies, but the original letter is not certain.
Verse 86, line 1: the name of the land of deeds (ஆவிதையம்) is unclear and may be corrupt.

cast.role: the Jain sage whose penance Neelakesi cannot break and who preaches the dharma to her
the demoness of the burning-ground temple, here in the form of a princess, listening to the sermon

reading: The sage lists the five-sensed animals, those with many legs, eight, and fewer pair by pair, the flyers, walkers, crawlers and creepers, which have hearing as the fifth sense and fill the sea and the islands.
nuance: The verse sorts animals as a Jain classification does, by the number of senses (இந்தியம் ஐந்து) and by legs and gait, not by use to man; the count of legs falls 'two by two' (இரண்டிரண்டே இழிந்த) from eight.

reading: Animals are born from wombs of mixed heat and cold, from membranes, eggs and sprouting, cannot act on what they are told, consume the fruit of the deeds they did, and wander taking one body after another, like and unlike.
nuance: Line 2 (செப்புவ செப்பில் செய்கைகள் ஆற்றம்) is hard to divide: it may say the animals cannot do what they are told, or that they cannot do the deeds that would free them; the reading is not fixed. போர்த்தும், பொடித்தும், பொரித்தும் seem to name the modes of birth (in a membrane, by sprouting, by hatching).

reading: Asked to tell the kinds of humans, the sage names five, the good, the bad, the divine, the base humans and the rest, and says the first of them dwell in the great land of enjoyment.
nuance: சொல்லுக தன்மை என்பாய் எனில் (if you say, tell their nature) shows the sermon as answers to the listener's questions, though she has asked nothing aloud in these verses. The land of enjoyment (போகப் பெருநிலம்) is where pleasure comes without labour; the sage does not praise it, and 86 will place release in the land of deeds instead.

reading: The bad humans live in the small lands of the islands, faulty and lacking in qualities from their kings down, and even if they hold to great penance they do not reach the higher state; so the sage tells the doe-eyed woman.
nuance: The claim limits penance by birth: the same tapas that frees in 86 bears no such fruit here. தன்மை பெறார் may mean they do not gain the state penance gives, or do not gain good nature at all; the first fits the contrast with 86.

reading: The divine humans are those who open the ford, those of heaped-up merit who bear the wheel and their companions, the sky-going Vidyadharas and the unfailing white ones, the sage tells the woman with fresh bangles.
nuance: தீர்த்தம் திறப்பவர் (those who open the ford) is the Tamil form of the Tirthankara title; ஆழியர் (wheel-bearers) are world-ruling kings. Who the ஐயவர் and வெள்ளியர் are, and what பப்பியர் in line 4 means, the verse alone does not settle.

reading: The base humans, ugly of form with tails, horns and curved teeth, live in the islands between and do not touch right conduct or right vision.
nuance: சீலமும் காட்சியும் (conduct and vision) are two of the Jain three jewels; their absence, not the beastlike form, is what makes these men low. The edition prints தீண்டலு ரந்தரத் where the sense needs தீண்டலர் அந்தரத்.

tamil: கானுயர் சோலைக் கரும நிலத்தார் கருவினை போய்த்
reading: Those called humans in the full sense are of the land of deeds, wooded and green, whose nature is that by penance their dark karma departs and they reach the highest bliss.
nuance: கரும நிலம் (land of deeds) is set against the land of enjoyment of 82: release is open only where people must act and can do penance. The name of the land in line 1 (ஆவிதையம்) is not clear and may be corrupt.

reading: The gods are of five kinds, Bhavanas, Vyantaras, Jyotishkas, Kalpas and beyond them Vaimanikas, and in detail the first are ten with the fire-princes; the sage wonders whether telling more to the woman with flowered hair is unfitting.
nuance: The gods appear as one more class of births in the list that began with hell-beings and animals, ranked and numbered, not as objects of worship. The closing doubt (சொல்லல் பொல்லாது கொல்) prepares the turn in 88.

reading: The sage names eight kinds of Vyantara gods, from the sweet-voiced ones to 'your own kin'; at that the woman suffers like wet ghee near fire, and when he says that her nature will be known later and she should hear dharma, she consents.
nuance: நுமர் ஈறா (ending with your kin) is the sage letting her know that he sees what she is: the last of the eight Vyantara classes are the demons, and she is a demoness in a princess's form. Lines 1 and 2 are his words; the narrator speaks from என்றலும். He defers the matter (நின் திறம் பின் அறிவாம்) and keeps to the sermon.
event: The sage hints that her kin are among the demon gods; Neelakesi is stricken, he puts the matter off and bids her hear dharma, and she agrees.

reading: The Jyotishka gods are also five, moon, sun, planets, constellations and stars; some circle Mount Mandara to the right, and others stand shining without moving.
nuance: The sun and moon are here gods of one class among many, ranked below the heaven-dwellers of 90, not supreme lights.

reading: The sixteen Kalpa heavens run from Saudharma to Arana and Acyuta, and above them, take it, dwell the Vaimanikas in groups of three threes, nine and five.
nuance: The verse gives the count of the heavens as plain fact to a listener who is told to take it (கொள் நீ); line 2 of the edition carries a stray bracketed syllable.

reading: Now the sage will tell a little of the great, hard-to-bear suffering of the hell-beings, who are the worst in this round of births.
nuance: The metre changes here to short lines for the account of hell, which runs to 101. The sage promises only 'a little' (சிறிது).

reading: The hell-beings of the dark hells are five hundred bows in stature and are beings of pain that spreads over yojanas.
nuance: ஈரிருள் and the third line are hard to construe; the size of five hundred bows seems to be that of the beings of the lowest hell.

reading: Their black bodies, though cut into many pieces by sword-edges, join again like water.
nuance: The body that rejoins like water is what makes the pain without end: in hell even dismemberment is not an exit.

reading: Even when strong ones do violence to them, their bodies cannot be killed, and there are many such torments that cannot be told.
Seeing their enemies of old, their eyes turn to embers, and they rush on and do great violence beyond counting.
nuance: The torment here comes from the hell-beings themselves, carrying their old enmity into hell, not from a judge. The first word was repaired from an old encoding; வேரியர் is read as enemies (வைரியர்).

reading: They are neuter, and since pain runs through them greatly, no pleasure of union comes to them.
nuance: பேடி (neuter) fits the Jain teaching that hell-beings have no sex; lines 3 and 4 are obscure.

reading: Naming 'the sin of killing' and 'the sin of eating flesh', the tormentors make the hell-beings go into fire and burn, and make them stand inside its mouth and cry out.
nuance: The verse names eating flesh as a sin separate from killing, so one who eats meat he did not kill is not cleared; this is the charge Neelakesi will open the Kundalakesi debate with (163). The tormentors (ஆக்குவார்) are not named, and the verse names no judge. வாயினுள் may be the mouth of the fire or of the hell.

reading: When they long for water to drink, what comes to their eyes and what they can reach is nothing that can be thought pleasant.
Charred, bruised, burnt inside, boiling up, falling, crying, burning: for such great suffering there is no one who relieves them.
nuance: பரிபவரும் இல்லை (there is no one who takes pity or bears it for them) shuts out any rescuer: no god, kin or guru enters this hell.

reading: There, in the hot fire, sinking, rising head over head, with smoke entering, they are gulped and swallowed and so suffer.
Many beings a yojana in size, hard to bring to death, and burning fierce poison: no grace is food for those spoken of, the verse seems to say of hell's last torments.
nuance: The four short lines do not yield a clear sentence; அருளுணா may mean 'grace is not their food' or name a food of hell. The reading is a guess.

reading: After the poison-eating hell-beings in their birth without good, the sage turns to the pains of animals: frightened, each flees from another like the wind, and even standing still in confusion their minds are always afraid.
nuance: The metre changes again. The animal's pain is fear itself, which never leaves the mind, not torment by others.

title: தருமவுரைச் சருக்கம் 104-126 (5/6)
theme: The teacher's sermon to Neelakesi finishes the account of suffering in the four states of birth (beasts killed by nature, war, hunt, sacrifice and medicine; humans pained by their own passions or by harms from elements, beings and disease; even the gods coming to an end), then offers its cure: the threefold medicine of knowledge, clear faith and conduct, with the Jain means of knowledge, the limbs of right faith and the grades of conduct, ending in heaven and then release.
source_issues: 119 line 2: அணுமை, read as அனுமை (inference); the ண may be a misprint.
122 line 2: the word division உலகோடிலிங் காத்த ரொப்பு is doubtful and the line hard to construe.
126 line 2: the division மன்ன ரும்மாய் looks wrong (perhaps மன்னரும் ஆய்).
114 lines 3-4 and 120 lines 1-3 are syntactically obscure as printed.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Jain sage whose penance Neelakesi cannot break

reading: The teacher goes on with the suffering of beasts: they wander ruined by cold heavy rain, are driven into battle to die of wounds, are chased and tormented for the sake of food, and lose their lives in countless nets.
nuance: Most of the harms listed are done by humans (war, the hunt, the net), so the account of the beast's state of birth is also a charge against those who use and kill animals; it leads straight into the next verse's list of killings.

reading: He adds the deaths beasts suffer when Vedic ritualists offer them in sacrifice, when base men kill them for spirits and gods, and when they are prescribed to be fed as medicine for named diseases: the sufferings that come by death are many.
nuance: The verse names the Vedic ritualists (வேதவாதியர்) and their sacrifice outright and counts it from the victim's side, as one more way a beast dies in pain. The Vedic answer is not given here; the charge is argued out with the Vedic disputant in the Veda debate (836-839), where the killing for gods and ancestors is said to bind the killers.

reading: Addressing her, the teacher says that the suffering humans undergo among the four trembling states of birth is of two parts: what falls to those who lack self-restraint, and what is common to all.
nuance: நாற்கதி, the four states of birth (hell, beast, human, god), is the frame of the whole sermon; this verse moves from the beasts of 104-105 to humans and introduces the division that 107-115 work out.

reading: The pains of the unrestrained are the gateway of evil deeds, the mind's fault of hatred, anger with pride and deceit, attachment, grief and fear: all of these are the sufferings of those who lack restraint.
nuance: Anger (வெகுளி), pride (மானம்), deceit (மாயம்) and attachment (பற்று) together match the four passions that Jain teaching names as the binders of karma; the verse treats them not only as causes of later pain but as present pain. The reading of line 3's பற்று as greed or attachment is mine.

reading: Men do not reckon that it will drive them into an evil state of birth, do not care that their noble lineage will be stained, do not see that it is a cover filled with swarms of worms, and so perish for the sake of a filthy body, alas.
nuance: Desire is not named; the object is only அழுக்குடம்பு, the filthy body, and the verse is in the list of the sufferings of the unrestrained, so lust is the likely sense. It sets three deterrents side by side: the next birth, the family's name, and disgust at the body.

reading: Then the common affliction: it divides into two, harm from outside (இடையூறு), which itself branches into two, and bodily disease, which opens into three.
nuance: The sermon now classifies suffering as a physician classifies diseases; the scheme of 109-113 is what the remedy in 116 answers.

reading: He names the two outside harms as those that come from what has life and from what lacks it, and says the first of them, the lifeless, is the four elements.
nuance: Line 3 (அடையா உயிரதுவும் அல்லதுவும்) is compressed; that the 'first' is the lifeless kind rests on 111, which lists the elemental harms and ends உயிரல்ல ஊறே.

reading: Heavy rain and flood, the hurling wind, black rockfall and stone, deadly poison, the many weapons of battle, red fire and thunder striking here: all these are harms that come from no living being.
Spirits that strike and afflict in their anger, men's lasting killing in many ways, and the harm that comes from cruel beasts: these three alike are harms that come from living beings.
nuance: செத்துவங்கள் in line 1 I take as beings or spirits (from sattva) that afflict; the word is rare and the sense is not certain.

reading: The bodily diseases are three: those that can be cured, those that by their nature cannot, and those that, unlike the ones that yield to applied medicine, pass away by subsiding.
nuance: உவசமம் (line 2) looks like upaśama, quieting; the third class may be diseases that settle of themselves, but the contrast with செய்ம்மருந்தின் ஊர்வனவும் is not clear to me.

reading: He tells her that even all the gods he described before come at last to an end, and that apart from this they have no great suffering, and turns to the darkness that the wicked, other than her own kind, enter.
nuance: The sense of lines 3-4 (நுமர் அன்றிப் பொல்லாதவர்கள் உறும் அல்லை) is unsure: நுமர், 'your people', may be the demons of 115, set apart from the other wicked. The gods' end as their only suffering is the clearest point.

reading: Those like her, he says, make pain like fire for all, are called demons everywhere and do what no one would cherish; if it is she herself, she is not such now, but those like her are.
nuance: The teacher turns the account of suffering onto his listener: she was a பேய் who did harm, and the verse marks her change by exempting her from her own kind. The reading of line 4 (நீயே எனின் அல்லை) as 'not you, now' is mine.

reading: These are diseases hard to shake off; the medicine fit to cure them is the triple discipline of understanding, clear faith and conduct, and those who take it are not born again into the disease and come to great joy.
nuance: The three are the Jain three jewels (right faith, knowledge, conduct), here named திரியோகம் and given as medicine after the classification of disease in 109-113; no god administers them, the soul takes them itself (உண்டார், line 3).

reading: Of the three medicines, if she would hear the goodness of knowledge: it is to know well, without defect, the existing realities beginning with the soul; that is its essence.
Means of valid knowledge are perception and what is other than perception; perception comprises knowledge through the five senses and mind, avadhi, the pure manahparyaya and kevala.
nuance: Ranking sense-and-mind knowledge under perception together with the three supersensory kinds (clairvoyance, knowing others' minds, omniscience) is how later Jain logicians arranged the means of knowledge; the older Jain scheme put sense knowledge among the indirect kinds. The verse follows the former. Its perception reaches beyond the senses, which rival schools deny.

reading: Memory, recognition, reasoning, inference and the scripture spoken by the truthful sages: these five, he says, are the means of knowledge other than perception.
nuance: Memory and recognition count here as valid knowledge; schools that treat memory as no means of knowledge would reject that. அணுமை in line 2 is read as inference (அனுமை).

reading: Placing, standpoints and the means of knowledge are the doors of entry, and the soul with its qualities is examined through the categories of search; if one enters through these without straying, knowledge rises to incomparable eminence.
nuance: வைப்பு, நயன், அளவை and மார்க்கணை look like the Jain technical terms nikshepa, naya, pramana and margana; the line division and syntax of lines 1-3 are hard and the reading is tentative.

reading: The kind of right faith, say the victors, is to hold in mind the eight excellent things beginning with God, an unturning longing for the flood of bliss that spreads and surges: that is clear faith.
nuance: The verse cites the victors (வென்றவர், the Jinas) as its authority. Which eight things are meant is not spelled out here.

reading: Having escaped the three follies that come first, not praising others for love, fear, desire, the world or the outward sign, and standing free of the eight prides: this is the nature of those who have joyful right faith.
nuance: The three follies (மூடம்) and eight prides (மயம்) are standard Jain lists of what spoils faith; line 2's division (உலகோடிலிங் காத்த ரொப்பு) is hard and my reading of it is tentative.

reading: Freedom from doubt, desire, disgust and delusion, removing faults, steadying those who have strayed, love without falsehood and showing the peerless dharma: these eight are the limbs of right faith in hand, and its excellence.
Conduct, say those who know the rule of the victors' books, is that which, one with good faith and knowledge, does not leave the heart; and it is of two kinds, the undiminished and the partial.
nuance: The complete and the partial (குன்றாத ஒன்றும் குறைபாட்டதும்) are most likely the full vows of the renouncer and the lesser vows of the householder; the verse itself names only the two grades. Conduct here grows out of faith and knowledge and is not separate from them.

reading: Guarding, restraint, forbearance and the other good virtues, the twofold penance taken up with resolve, enduring hardships and all such things: these are the excellence of the conduct that refuses change.
nuance: இருசார்வு (line 2) I take as penance of two kinds, outer and inner, and பரிசை (line 3) as the hardships to be borne; மாற்றம் மறுக்கும் (line 4) is unclear, perhaps conduct that admits no turning back.

reading: All souls that take this discipline together, good one, live with the dwellers of the high sky as their kings and enjoy their pleasures, and then, with no unfitting deed clinging to them, join the one good bliss, where there is no loss.
nuance: Heaven is a stage, not the goal: the verse puts the gods' pleasures before release and makes release the end of karma's clinging (வினை புல்லல் இன்றி), which 114's word on the gods' end prepares.

title: தருமவுரைச் சருக்கம் 127-149 (6/6)
theme: The sermon ends with the sage's teaching on the body: to the woman who came to tempt him he shows that beauty is in the seer, that adornment covers filth and leads to hell, and that one who lives in the burning ground cannot be moved. Neelakesi casts off her disguise, confesses, is forgiven, hymns the sage's endurance in the burning ground, and, asking for atonement, is told to spread the Jina's path, which sends her into the debates.
structure_note: 127 closes the sermon; 128 to 132 are the sage's words on the body; 133 to 135 her conversion and pardon; 136 to 145 her hymn (four long verses, then five burning-ground verses); 146 to 149 her request, his answer and her departure.
source_issues: Verse 139, line 1: 'உணர்ந்தோய்ந £யுறங்க' has a stray '£' (U+00A3); read உணர்ந்தோய் நீ உறங்க.
Verse 130, line 4: 'நாய்க் கொட்டார்த்தார்' is obscure as divided; the word division may be faulty.
Verses 147, 148, 149: each stanza was printed in eight half-lines and has been joined into four; in 149, line 2 'மாஅ துடைஅடி' is oddly divided.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Jain sage whose penance Neelakesi cannot break

reading: The sage gives Neelakesi the nectar of dharma, teaching how birth comes about, how it is a disease, and how dharma is the medicine that does not fail, so that she may hear, understand and hold it in her heart.
nuance: The verse frames the whole sermon that went before as medicine: birth is the illness (பிணி), dharma the remedy. மறவி தான் இல்லா (line 2) is best taken as 'free of forgetting', a remedy whose effect does not lapse; the phrase is compressed.
event: The sage gives Neelakesi his teaching on birth as a disease and dharma as its cure.

reading: The sage says that hair, teeth, breasts, red lips, shoulders and waist, which the lustful see as beauty, are seen otherwise by ascetics like himself and otherwise again by the pack of jackals, so that, rightly understood, the one body is three different things.
nuance: The argument is about perception, not anatomy: the body has no single nature that lust reads correctly. The jackals, for whom the same limbs are food, are the third witness, and யாம் (we) places the ascetic between the lover and the scavenger.

reading: Like fish that crave the bait on the hook of a low fisherman on the bank and come to harm, those caught by the one wrapped in foam-fine cloth and a girdle meet only deep sorrow.
nuance: The fisherman is கயமகன், a base man, so the bait has a malicious hand behind it; the verse does not say whether that hand is the woman's or desire's own. வரை (line 4) is read as the bounded body girt with cloth and girdle; it could also mean the woman as a 'boundary' or trap.

reading: Flowers in the hair, kohl on the long eyes, silk dress, many bangles and fresh ear-rolls: these adornments lead all who cling to them into hell, the sage says, and the last line likens them to a show put on for a dog.
nuance: Line 4 (நாய்க் கொட்டார்த்தார் செய்யும் கோலங்கள் வண்ணம்) is obscure as divided in the text; the comparison to something done for a dog is a guess at it, and the claim rests on line 3 alone.

reading: You have bathed, put on scent, worn jewels and garlands, sulked as lovers sulk, the sage tells the woman before him, but you have only covered with skin a body full of many things that leak filth, and I will not speak flattering words to it.
nuance: The sage answers her play (ஊடினாய், the lover's sulk) with a refusal of முகமன், courtly flattery: he declines the lover's role as much as the body. The woman addressed is Neelakesi in the borrowed form of a princess, so the body he strips of its cover is not her own.
event: The sage refuses to flatter the adorned woman who has come to tempt him.

reading: You came before me thinking I would delight in a waist like lightning and shoulders like bamboo, the sage says, but I live in the burning ground clothed with poor skin and many bones; would I be deluded by these?
nuance: The sage's defence is his dwelling, not a doctrine: one who lives among skin and bones in the புறங்காடு already sees what her body will become. The burning ground is also Neelakesi's own haunt (the demoness of its temple), so he turns her ground against her.
event: The sage tells the tempting woman that, living in the burning ground among bones, he cannot be moved by her beauty.

reading: As molten gold fills a clay mould once the wax figure inside has been heated out, she put away her evil, having been shown the worm-ridden truth of the body, took on a form of beauty and drank the nectar of dharma.
nuance: The simile is lost-wax casting: the wax (her old nature) melts away and gold takes the same shape, so the change is inward and complete. Line 3 can be taken as 'shown the body as worms' (the sage's lesson) or as her casting off a false body; the reading of line 3 is not secure.
event: Neelakesi casts off her evil and takes in the sage's dharma.

reading: Thinking that the virtuous sage is like a mother who, out of overflowing kindness, nurses her infant with her milk even when it hurts her, she dropped her illusory form, took her own other form, and bowed, saying, 'Lord, forgive all the wrongs I, a demon, have done.'
nuance: கழிகண்ணோட்டம் names the Kural's virtue of kindly regard in excess; the mother suckling a biting child makes the sage's forbearance maternal rather than judicial. Her confession calls herself பேயேன், the first time she names her true nature to him.
event: Neelakesi sheds the princess's form, takes her own, and begs the sage's forgiveness.

tamil: முழங்கு முந்நீர் வையத்து முனிதக் கார்தம் முன்னின்று
reading: The sage tells her not to grieve: in this world the great put away displeasure when those who deserve their anger stand before them and speak, and what is there that such as we cannot bear? She praises his flowering feet and, with joined hands, begins to hymn him as a mountain of virtues.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are compressed; முனிதக்கார் is read as 'those who deserve anger', so that the great forgive the offender who comes before them. It might instead mean the sages themselves, which would leave the sense close but the grammar different.
event: The sage forgives Neelakesi and she begins her hymn of praise.
