reading: Neelakesi praises the sage as the one who bore the flood rains, who closed the gate of karma, who has a glorious mind, who taught the way to be saved, and who, seeing every harm she did him in the dead of night, showed no contempt; she will come to his peerless feet.
nuance: வினையின் வாயில் அடைத்தோய் (closing the doorway of karma) and, in 139, the doorway that burns karma correspond to the Jain pair of stopping karma's inflow and wearing it off; the hymn uses plain Tamil rather than technical names for them.

tamil: மூட மூன்று முரைத்தோய் நீமுரண்செய் தோற்ற முனிந்தோய் நீ
வீடுங் கட்டும் விரித்தோய் நீவினையி னின்பம் வெறுத்தோய் நீ
காடு கிளர்ந்து காட்டியான் கலக்க வொன்றுங் கலங்காத
reading: She hails him as the one who taught the three delusions, scorned the hostile apparition, expounded bondage and release, loathed the pleasure that karma brings, and stayed wholly unshaken when she made the forest rise up to trouble him; she bows to his blameless feet.
nuance: மூடம் மூன்று (the three delusions) is the Jain list that the sermon gave at verse 122. முரண்செய் தோற்றம் can be the hostile shapes she raised against him or 'birth' as the source of conflict; the third line makes the first likelier, since she names her own assault.

tamil: வெல்லற் கரிய வனங்கனைமெய் வெண்ணீ றாக வெகுண்டோய்நீ
சொல்லற் கரிய பெரியோய் நின்றோமில் பாதந் தொழுவல்யாள்.
reading: She hails him as the one who has left painful birth, cut the burning root of desire, angrily reduced the invincible Ananga to white ash, and by his virtues alone made her, who came to kill him, bow; she worships his feet, beyond words to praise.
nuance: Burning the god of love to ash is the deed Saiva hymns give to Siva; the Jain hymn gives it to a human ascetic, and keeps even the anger (வெகுண்டோய்). Line 3 states the turn of the whole chapter: she was conquered not by force but by his qualities.

tamil: யிடங்கொ ளின்னா வினையெல்லா மெரிக்கும் வாயில் விரித்தோய்நீ
reading: She hails him as the one who knew the truth of the body, cut away the longing for sleep, laid open the doorway that burns all painful karma, and in grace rained the rain of dharma on her, who had no restraint; may his broad red-lotus feet be on her head.
nuance: The grace (அருள்) here is the teacher's compassion in giving the dharma, not a god's power that removes karma; the karma itself is burned by the doorway he showed.

reading: As the heavy rain beat down again and again and many poisonous creatures crawled up his body, he stood restrained, knowing that he is other than the body; she will worship his feet with joined palms.
nuance: உடம்பொடு வேறு எனும் ஓர்ப்பு (the realisation that one is other than the body) is the Jain separation of soul and body made a practice: the ascetic endures because he does not take the body for himself.

reading: In the burning ground of thick darkness, when the harsh wind blew enough to melt stone, he stayed and uprooted all his karmas; she will worship his feet every day as a good deed.
nuance: She calls her worship நல்வினை, a good deed, so the hymn itself is placed within the economy of karma the sage is ending.

reading: In the rainy days when clouds poured, through countless nights in the forest that breeds fear, he sat resolved not to move anywhere; she will bow to his lotus-like feet.
In the old burning ground where jackals howl all night as they eat the bodies of the dead, he meditates with all attachment cut; she will circle and worship his two feet according to rule.
nuance: விதியின் (by rule) shows that the convert's first act is worship in prescribed form, the opposite of the blood offerings her own temple received.

reading: In the forest where fierce little demons tear and play with white skulls, he burns away the eight dusts; she will worship his feet with flowers humming with bees.
nuance: எண் துகள் (the eight dusts) is read as the eight kinds of karma of Jain teaching, which cling to the soul like dust; the verse gives only the number and the image.

reading: In the forest where, among the corpses, the pyre fire blazes and spirits dance the thunangai, he whose virtues never wane stays; she will bow at his feet every day.
nuance: The five burning-ground verses (141 to 145) each set the sage in a scene of terror and then name one victory; the terrors are those of Neelakesi's own realm, so the hymn is also her renunciation of it.

reading: Looking now to the fine good path, she praised the sage's feet three times and said, 'I have done sin as great as the cold sea; tell me what I must do now.'
event: Neelakesi praises the sage three times and asks him what she must do to answer for her sins.

tamil: விலங்கு வெந்நர காதிக டம்முள் விளிந்து தோன் றிவிழு நோயொடு முற்றுக்
கலங்கி யெங்குங் கண்ணில வாகிக் கவலைவெள் ளக்கட லிற்குளித் தாழு
நலங்களில் லாவுயிர் தங்களுக் கெல்லா நடுக்கநீக் கியுயர் நன்னிலை யீயுஞ்
சலங்களில் லாப்பெரி யோன்சரண் கொண்ணீ சனங்கட் கெல்லா மவன்சர ணென்றான்.
reading: The sage answers: for all souls that die and are born again among beasts, in fierce hells and the rest, blinded, sunk in the sea of sorrow and without any good, the great one without guile removes their trembling and gives the high state; take refuge in him, for he is the refuge of all people.
nuance: The refuge offered is the guileless great one, the Jina, not the sage himself; the sage turns her worship of him to the one he follows. The 'trembling' removed echoes the நாற்கதி (four states) of the earlier sermon, of which beasts and hell are named.

tamil: உய்தல் வாயுரைத் தாயதன் மேலு முயிருள்ளிட் டபல வுள்பொருள் சொன்னாய்
நைதலில் லாத்தெளி வோடுநன் ஞான நானுங் கொண் டேனுன் னற்குண மெல்லாம்
பெய்துதந் தாய் பிழைத் தேற்கினி தாவோர் பிராயச்சித் தம்பெரி யோயரு ளென்னச்
செய்த தீமை கெடக்கட னாட்டிற் சினவ ரன்னெறி யேதெருட் டென்றான்.
reading: She says: you have told me the way to be saved and the realities beginning with the soul; I have taken clear good knowledge that does not wither, and you have filled me with all your good qualities; great one, give me, who erred, an atonement. He answers: to end the evil you did, make the Jina's path clear in the land.
nuance: The expiation asked for (பிராயச்சித்தம்) is given not as a rite or a penance but as a mission: she is to teach the Jina's path. This sets up every debate that follows. கடனாட்டில் may be read as 'in the sea-girt land' or 'as a duty'; the command is the same either way.
event: Neelakesi asks the sage for an atonement, and he bids her spread the Jina's path.

tamil: யாஅ தடிக ளதருளா லருந்துய ரகல்வகை யதனான்
மாஅ துடைஅடி யிவைதா மறவலெ னெனவலங் கொண்டு
வேஎ தடவியன் மலைமேல் விரிகதிர் மணிவிளக் காதி
தீஇ தடுதலை விலங்குஞ் சினகர முவகையிற் சென்றாள்.
reading: Saying, 'Lord, by your grace, by which hard suffering is removed, I will never forget these feet', she circled him and went joyfully to the Jina's temple on the mountain, bright with gem-lamps.
nuance: The verse is written with lengthened syllables (யாஅ, மாஅ, வேஎ, தீஇ) at the head of each line, and line 3 and 4's description of the temple is only partly clear.
event: Neelakesi takes leave of the sage and goes to the Jina temple on the mountain.

title: குண்டலகேசி வாதச் சருக்கம் 150-170 (1/4)
theme: Neelakesi worships at the Jina's shrine, whose doors open on her oath of right faith, and sings eight hymns that praise the omniscient one by paradox and by his victory over deeds, death and birth; she then chooses the Buddha's teaching as the first mean path to crush, sees by clairvoyance Kundalakesi's unanswered challenge-branch at the gate of Kampili, flies there in a woman's form, learns from the gatekeeper why the gate is barred, and plucks up the branch.
source_issues: 164 line 3: non-Tamil characters in தண்ட¨¡ய (U+00A8, U+00A1), an encoding leftover; probably a grove word such as தண்டலை, not restored.
164 line 1: நோக்குவாள்யடுத்ததன தவதியால் has an odd junction (ள்ய) and doubtful word division.
153 line 3: யாமென றையென is obscure and may be corrupt.
168 line 4: நீயிலையார் புதனடற்கு is hard to divide; the sense of the line is not fixed.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Arhat, the Jain omniscient teacher, worshipped in the shrine and addressed in the hymns
the Buddhist woman debater whose challenge-branch stands at the gate of Kampili
the gatekeeper of the king of Kampili
the king of Kampili, before whose assembly the debate is to be held

tamil: பல்லி தழ்ப்பனிக் குவளை பானல் பாதிரி பிறவு
மெல்லை யின்மல ரேந்தி றைவன திடவகைக் கெழுந்தாள்.
reading: Carrying flowers without limit, from the mullai, konku, kurundham, kanthal, kuravam and jasmine of the garden to the cool many-petalled kuvalai, paanal and paathiri, she rises to go to the Lord's place.
nuance: The sarukkam opens with worship, not argument: the debater's first act is to bring flowers, and the list runs through flowers of forest, garden and water alike.
event: Neelakesi gathers every kind of flower and sets out for the Lord's shrine.

reading: She takes in the shrine's height, length and breadth, circles it, and declares that if her vision does not stray from the lord of great penance every door shall open; they open, and she bows at the feet of the lord who rules the three worlds.
nuance: காட்சி (line 3) is the word for right vision or faith, the first of the three jewels in Jain teaching; the doors open on an oath sworn by it, so the verse makes her right faith, not a priest or a key, the thing that admits her. The verse narrates the oath and its effect; it does not state the efficacy of right faith as a rule.
event: Neelakesi swears by her unswerving faith in the Jina, the shrine's doors open of themselves, and she worships at his feet.

reading: With fine flowers worked into figures of rare skill, elephants, yalis, wild cattle, the eight auspicious signs, rows of images, birds, creepers and trees, she offers worship at the holy feet of the one who gave the good path of the perfected.
nuance: The Jina is named by what he gave, சித்த நன்னெறி, the good path of the siddhas (the released), not by any act of creation or rescue.
event: Neelakesi worships the Jina's feet with flowers arranged in pictures of animals, birds and the eight auspicious signs.

reading: With incense, sandal and scented powder she praises and bows, hangs garlands, and in wonder at the form of the seer of the tattvas strings good songs on the thousand and eight names and sings them to melody.
nuance: ஆயிரத்தோர் எண் நாம (lines 3 and 4) is read as the thousand and eight names, a Jain litany of the Jina as other traditions have theirs; the eight hymns that follow (154 to 161) are presented as these songs. Line 3 (யாமென றையென வியந்து) is obscure in this text and its sense is not fixed.
event: Neelakesi offers incense and garlands and sings hymns on the Jina's thousand and eight names.

tamil: யொன்ற நோய்பகை யொருங்கே யுடைந்து வெங்களத் துதிர
வென்றி ருந்தனை நீயே வீரர்தம் வீரர்க்கும் வீரா.
reading: Neelakesi sings that the Jina passed beyond angry Death, drove off Kama of desire, renounced ancient aging and crossed the great sea of birth, and that disease and enmity broke together on the battlefield while he stood the victor, hero of heroes.
nuance: The victory is told in a battle image (வெங்களத்து, வென்றிருந்தனை, வீரர்தம் வீரர்க்கும் வீரா), but every enemy named is inward or a condition of embodied life; the Jina wins by leaving them behind (கடந்தாய், துறந்தாய், இறந்தாய்), not by striking them.

reading: She sings that for all the souls who suffer in the sea of evil deeds they themselves did, through death, disease, aging and birth, the Jina gave a good path free of harm and made the raft that is hard to find, poet of poets.
nuance: The sea is தாம் செய் தீவினைக் கடல், the sea of the evil deeds the souls did themselves: no one else is blamed for their suffering, and the Jina's part is to make the raft (புணை படைத்தாய்), not to carry anyone. Line 3 (திரைசெய் நீள்கரை ஒருவி) is read as leaving the wave-beaten shore behind.

reading: She sings that after rare wonders, with the gods beating drums and raining flowers, he sat in the shade of the spreading asoka tree within the circle of golden walls and taught the way by which the two kinds of deed part from the soul.
nuance: The setting is the Jain preaching assembly: the golden ring of walls (பொன் எயில் மண்டிலம்), the asoka tree (பிண்டி), the drums and the rain of flowers. What is taught is that both deeds (இருவினையும்) part, so good deeds too must go for release; the Jina states the way and the soul must walk it.

tamil: பொங்கு சாமரை யேந்திப் புடைபுடை யியக்கார்நின் றிரட்டச்
reading: She sings that with yakshas waving whisks on either side, seated on the lion throne under the halo and the three moon-white umbrellas, he proclaimed the Angas and the Purvas so that the gods' assembly understood, knower of knowers.
nuance: அங்க பூவம் names the two classes of Jain canon, the Angas and the Purvas; the verse grounds the scripture's authority in the omniscient speaker, which is the ground the later sarukkams use against the Veda.

reading: She sings a set of paradoxes: he perceives no touch yet tells the kinds of touch, never says 'I will speak' yet has a voice like a drum, has no wish to harm yet sets his feet on flowers; how is she to understand him, god of gods.
nuance: Each line sets a lack beside a power: knowledge without sense-contact, speech without intention, walking on flowers without the will to hurt them. The third paradox concerns ahimsa: the Jina's steps fall on flowers, yet no harm is meant. Line 2 is elliptic, and the reading supplies 'yet speaks'.

tamil: லெண்ணில் யார்நினை யுணர்வா ரிறைவர்தம் மிறைவர்க்கு மிறைவா.
reading: She sings that he sees nothing with the eye yet sees all things at once, joins with no woman yet has undivided great bliss, eats nothing yet has a radiant form, so that no one who thinks can know him, lord of lords.
nuance: Line 3 (உண்ணல் யாவதும் இலையாய்) says the omniscient one does not eat. Whether the omniscient being eats was disputed among Jains themselves, and this verse takes the side that denies it; the hymn states it as praise, not as an argued position. The bliss of line 2 is பிரிதலில் பேரின்பம், bliss that does not part, set against the joy of union with a woman.

reading: She sings that he hears no word yet utters the scripture and its certain conclusions, has learned nothing yet knows endless things, clings to nothing yet has the spread-out eightfold wealth; who can fully know him, first of the first.
nuance: சுதநயம் (line 1) joins the Jain terms for scripture (சுதம், sruta) and standpoint (நயம், naya). The 'eightfold wealth' of line 3 is read as the eight splendours that attend the Jina, such as those 157 lists, held without attachment (பற்று).

reading: She sings that his true knowledge, which he set out in words, proves false what the other teachers each said from what they knew; none of them has discerned it, and who else knows his nature that burns the whole chain of deeds, leader of leaders.
nuance: The last of the eight hymns turns from praise to the rival teachers, and so prepares the debate. The burning of deeds belongs to the Jina's own nature and knowledge (நின் ஞானம், நின் தன்மை); the verse does not say he burns the deeds of others.

tamil: ஆதி யந்தளப் பரிய அருகந்த பகவர்த மறஞ்சால்
reading: Having bowed at the holy feet of the Arhat, who is beyond measure of beginning and end, with great praise in his shrine full of dharma, she sits and asks which of the many mean paths she should crush first.
nuance: She calls the other schools புன்னெறி, mean paths, before hearing any of them; the debates that follow are set up as a campaign (அடர்க்கற்பாலது, to be crushed) begun at the Jina's feet.
event: After worship Neelakesi sits in the shrine and asks herself which rival path to overthrow first.

reading: Neelakesi decides: the Buddha does not call eating flesh a fault, does not say the soul exists, and does not count enduring austerity as a vow; his mean path robs people like courtesans with alluring eyes, and her task is to go and bring it down.
nuance: This is a Jain's summary of Buddhism, and two of its charges are framed as silences (என்னான், he does not say). The work answers them later: on flesh in the Mokkala sarukkam (342, 347), on the soul in Neelakesi's reply to Kundalakesi (194 to 202). The charge about austerity is not answered in the passages read, so it is left as reported. The comparison to courtesans who cut the purse (பொதியறுக்கும்) is polemic; a Buddhist would not accept that the teaching despoils its hearers.
event: Neelakesi chooses the Buddha's teaching as the first she will overthrow.

reading: Looking over the land by her far-seeing knowledge, she sees that at the gate of the king of Kampili a naaval branch has been planted in the cool grove and stands unanswered, and she takes the name of Kundalakesi as her mark.
nuance: அவதி (line 1) is the Jain term for clairvoyant knowledge, one of the grades of knowledge below omniscience. A naaval (rose-apple) branch planted at a king's gate is the debater's challenge; உரைபெறா says no one has answered it.
event: By clairvoyance Neelakesi sees the unanswered challenge-branch planted at the gate of the king of Kampili and takes Kundalakesi as her opponent.

reading: She who never swerves from dharma, so as to do an act of compassion, circles the great city made in the ordained manner, meditates on the perfected ones on the holy pearl seat, and takes the form of a woman like a great pearl.
nuance: The purpose of the debate is given as தயா செய்தல், doing compassion: refuting a school is framed as mercy toward those it misleads. The sentence runs on into 166. 'The city made in the ordained manner' (நிருமித்த வகையினதா நெடுநகர்) and the pearl seat may be the Jina's assembly rather than an earthly city; the reading is not fixed.
event: Neelakesi circles the holy city, meditates on the siddhas and takes a woman's form to go to the debate.

reading: Going by the sky, she reaches the palace of the king who is an Indra among spear-bearing kings and tells the gatekeeper she is a Gandharva maiden who wants to see the king, and that he should announce her quickly.
nuance: She gives the gatekeeper a false identity (கந்திருவ மகளேன், I am a Gandharva's daughter); the narrative lets the disguise stand without comment.
event: Neelakesi flies to Kampili and asks the gatekeeper to announce her to the king as a Gandharva maiden.

reading: The gatekeeper replies that elephants and horses stand crowded at their posts and stalls and cannot go to water, chariots are not yoked, and not even the great army comes to the long gate, because of the sinful woman who planted a tree and sits here; so it is hard for him to let her in.
nuance: The planted branch closes the king's gate itself: until someone answers the challenge, the palace's elephants, horses and chariots cannot pass. The challenger is called பெண்பாவி, sinful woman, by the gatekeeper, not by the narrator.
event: The gatekeeper explains that the gate has been closed and the palace traffic stopped since a woman planted a challenge-branch there.

reading: Hearing him and looking at his face, the sharp-eyed one asks what grievance keeps her from the palace, offers to set things right, and asks whether there is a quarrel, a loss of property or a loss of life here, and what the cause is.
nuance: Line 4 (நீயிலையார் புதனடற்கு நிமித்தம்) is hard to divide; the reading takes it only as a question about the cause.
event: Neelakesi asks the gatekeeper why the gate is barred and what quarrel lies behind it.

reading: The words of the woman who planted the branch are given: wanting someone to argue well with her about the grace the robed ascetics teach, she planted this naaval branch; let the gatekeeper do his duty, and if anyone has the wit, let them bring an answer in the great king's assembly.
nuance: The verse ends எனச் சொன்னாள், she said, after the gatekeeper's answer of 167, so it is read as Kundalakesi's challenge relayed to Neelakesi; it could also be read as spoken directly by a woman present at the gate. இலிங்கியர் (line 1), those who bear a sect's mark, is read as the Buddhist monks whose teaching she defends; the sense of அருள் here is not fixed.
event: The gatekeeper reports Kundalakesi's challenge: she planted the branch to call for a debate before the king's assembly.

reading: Neelakesi tells the gatekeeper that if so, the gate need be barred no longer, elephants and chariots may move as they will, and he should tell his king; saying this, she of the coral-red lips plucks up the naaval branch.
nuance: Uprooting the branch is the formal acceptance of the debate, and it also frees the palace traffic: the debater's first effect is on public order.
event: Neelakesi pulls up the challenge-branch, accepting Kundalakesi's challenge and reopening the king's gate.

title: குண்டலகேசி வாதச் சருக்கம் 171-191 (2/4)
theme: Before the king of Kampili the debate is staked (honour to the winner, expulsion to the loser); Kundalakesi sets out her teacher, the Buddha who suffered only for others, and the five aggregates and momentary perishing, and Neelakesi attacks the teacher first: his greatness 'from the first', his self-ruin, sufferings that by the Buddhists' own law of karma must be his own sin, a compassion that ends at his release, and his eating of flesh.
source_issues: 173 line 2 is corrupt: வென்க்கோர் (for வென்றார்க்கோர்) and பெரந்துயரும் (for பெருந்துயரும்).
174 line 4 begins with a misdivided or corrupt கிறப்பவும் பெருதுவந்தார் (likely இறப்பவும் பெரிது உவந்தார்).
179 line 4 has a masculine என்னென்றான் in a speech by Neelakesi; the reading is doubtful.
189 line 2 has நீயஙரைத்தா, apparently a corruption of நீ உரைத்தால்.
182 line 4 and 188 lines 3-4 carry proverbs whose stories are lost; the lines are left uncertain.
181 line 2 and 186 line 2 carry repaired encodings flagged by show (ஃ; பேரிடர்).

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddhist woman debater who planted the rose-apple branch at Kampili's gate
the king of Kampili, before whose court the debate is held
the king's court that hears the debate

reading: Hearing the message, the king, swelling with joy, bids the two women with wide flower-like eyes come in, gives them seats, and performs the customary courtesies graciously.
event: The king of Kampili admits Neelakesi and Kundalakesi, seats them and receives them with courtesy.

reading: The king asks the two women to make clear to the court their first teacher, his scripture, the final meaning of that scripture, the matters it treats, and their own tenets.
nuance: The king's five heads (முதலவன், நூல், முடிபொருள், நுதலிய பொருள், நுங்கோள்) set the order of the debate: in 178 Neelakesi takes up the first head, the teacher, before the rest.
event: The king asks the debaters to set out their founder, his scripture, its conclusion, its subject and their own tenets.

reading: Kundalakesi praises the king's request but says she will not speak unless he first declares, before his court, a great prize for the winner and great suffering for the losers.
nuance: Line 2 is damaged (வென்க்கோர், பெரந்துயரும்); the sense of a stake for winner and loser is clear from 174, where the king answers it.
event: Kundalakesi refuses to begin until the king sets a prize for the winner and a penalty for the loser.

reading: The righteous king promises to honour the winner well and to drive the losers out that very day with ill treatment, and both women rejoice at this.
nuance: Line 4 is garbled at its start (கிறப்பவும் பெருதுவந்தார்); 'both rejoiced greatly' is the likely sense. The king's word is kept in 228, where the beaten Kundalakesi is drummed out of the city gate.
event: The king pledges honour to the winner and expulsion to the loser; both debaters welcome the terms.

reading: To the wonder of the royal assembly, Kundalakesi announces the doctrine of the teacher she has chosen, and then the dark-haired woman goes on to set it out.
nuance: Line 4's 'the woman of dark tresses swarmed by bees' most likely names Kundalakesi again, since 176 and 177 are her exposition; it could be read as Neelakesi, so the line is marked uncertain.
event: Kundalakesi begins the debate by stating her teacher's doctrine before the court.

reading: Kundalakesi says her lord, the one of the Bodhi tree, was great from the first, knew only what is good for the whole time until he came to his end, taught only true dharma, wanted nothing for himself, suffered only for others, and saves those who come to him.
nuance: The verse restates in the Neelakesi's metre the invocation of the Kundalakesi itself (கு. 1: முன் தான் பெருமைக்கண் நின்றான் ... பிறர்க்கே உறுதிக்கு உழந்தான்), so the Jain poet puts the rival work's own praise into its heroine's mouth. Each phrase is then attacked in turn: 'from the first' (179-180), 'until the end' (181), 'for others' (183-185). The claim is refuted across 179-190.

reading: Kundalakesi says the teacher first taught the three scriptures and their conclusion: the five aggregates (form, feeling, consciousness, perception and formation), and that thoughts going and coming have no permanence, so that things perish of themselves like the tip of a flame.
nuance: Her list matches the Manimekalai's own (30: உருவு நுகர்ச்சி குறிப்பே பாவனை உள்ள அறிவு) except that feeling is named உழப்பு, pain or toil, and formation செய்கை. The flame-tip image gives the doctrine of momentary perishing. Neelakesi answers the five aggregates in 194 and momentary perishing in 195-199.

reading: Neelakesi says she will set aside for now the conclusions on the four heads, and, asking the good assembly to attend, will take up the marks of the leader of boundless virtue placed first among them and show the many great faults in it, point by point.
nuance: நான்மை here seems to be the four heads of 172-177 (teacher, scripture, conclusion, subject), not the four noble truths; the teacher is attacked first.
event: Neelakesi announces that she will refute the account of the teacher before the other heads.

reading: Neelakesi argues that 'the first' can only mean the beginningless round of births: if he was great within that, (his greatness was a fruit of penance, not of a first state); if he became great afterwards, the word of time ('first') goes wrong; either way the claim of greatness turns false.
nuance: The target is the opening word of 176 and of the Kundalakesi's own invocation (முன்). Line 2 (அறங்கொண்ட தவமாகும்) and line 4's masculine என்னென்றான் are hard to construe, so the first half of the dilemma is reconstructed.

reading: If he had greatness before, she asks, what deed was left for him to complete here; and if he had not and you say he became great by reflecting on dharma, then the toiling outcastes and all others who discerned dharma with single mind would be leaders too.
nuance: The second horn assumes that greatness won by learning dharma cannot single out a founder. The outcaste (புலையர்) is the debater's figure for the lowest possible claimant, a social ranking she uses, not one she argues for.

reading: Neelakesi asks whether the teacher who taught the cruelty of flesh did not understand the saying 'even if you are ruined, do not plan the ruin of the worthy', and whether the doctrine he gave while ruining himself to the end must not itself perish utterly.
nuance: Line 1 quotes, as a saying (என்பதனை), the opening of Naladiyar 80 (தான்கெடினும் தக்கார்கேடு எண்ணற்க); it is not entered as an echo because the edition's word division leaves only three written words, under the four-word test. Line 3 turns 176's 'until the end' (அறக்கெடும் அளவெல்லாம்) into 'as long as he was ruining himself'. ஊன் கொடுமை (line 2) is taken as the Jain charge that the Buddha allowed flesh-eating (cf. 163, ஊன் தின்றல் இழுக்கு என்னான்); the quatrain's second line also speaks of ஊன், which may be why it was chosen. How exactly the saying convicts him is not spelled out.

reading: Those who suffer ruin so that the right way may live are the best of men, she says; but would the world heed one who, heedless of blame and sin, lays waste those who cling to him, and call such a sinner its leader?
nuance: Line 4 (கிழியோடு மாறாக் காசு என்றான் சொல்) seems to be a proverb about a coin that will not pass even with its purse; its point is not recoverable.

reading: If one dipped the tip of a fine hair in the wide sea and flicked it off, the births of suffering he lay in were as many as those drops; you say they were all for others, she says, but would he not then have done sin of the same measure?
nuance: The image measures the countless lives of the Buddha-to-be; the Jain debater reads their suffering as a ledger of evil deeds of the same size, which 184 makes explicit.

reading: Your own people always say that suffering comes only from evil deeds, she says; so if he afterwards made births of suffering for the sake of others, was that not the fruit of a hard deed he did earlier out of attachment?
nuance: She takes a tenet her opponent's school holds (நுமர் உரைப்ப) and turns it against the claim of 176: suffering cannot be chosen for others if all suffering is the fruit of one's own past deed. அன்பினான் is read as attachment, the bond she says caused the deed.

reading: When we see a bonded labourer who, gaining nothing for himself, toils carrying great heaps of dung, she says, the one thing to think of is the long sin he once did; would you then praise the greatness of those who daily and gladly put him to work?
nuance: The simile recasts 'suffered only for others' (176) as bonded labour that pays off a debt, and those who live off it as masters, not as the saved; the second half's target (the disciples) is inferred.

reading: Kundalakesi answers that he toils in this way to remove the great suffering others cannot escape, and that this is how his compassion works.
event: Kundalakesi replies that the Buddha's suffering is compassion acting to end the suffering of others.

reading: Neelakesi takes up the claim that he toils for others out of compassion: when his births ended, did he find that compassion was no real thing, or had all beings dried up, she asks, and tells her to explain it plainly before the assembly.
nuance: புற்கலர் (pudgalas, persons) is a striking word in a Jain's mouth against a school that denies the persisting person; the argument needs only that beings still suffer after the teacher's release.

reading: If he who ends the suffering that pierces and kills life has gained release and died out, she says, let his compassion perish: the sinner rescued no one, and is like the man in the saying who made his father toil and then said 'hold my cloth'.
nuance: The closing comparison (தாதையையே உழப்பித்தோன் ஆடை பற்று) is a proverb whose story is lost; its drift is a son who burdens his father and then asks more of him.

reading: If you say from here that two others there will come and end suffering, who will trust this one's compassion, she asks; and even if there are two, assembly, before they come we will wear out our own deeds and go, she says, laughing.
nuance: The 'two there' are not named; they may be later Buddhas the opponent appeals to. The Jain answer is self-reliance: release comes from wearing out one's own karma (நம் கருமம் உலைப்பித்து), not from another's compassion. Line 2 is corrupt (நீயஙரைத்தா).
event: Neelakesi mocks the appeal to future saviours and laughs.

reading: He first killed his own mother, she says, eats corpse-flesh with his whole body wrapped in robes, and when he explains release calls it emptiness; and you say there is no lord like him? Does one who milks the cow while its own calf dies have pity for anything else?
nuance: Polemic in the Jain's voice: the 'killing' of his mother turns the Buddhist story of Maya dying after his birth into a crime, and 'eats corpse-flesh' is the charge of 163; the Buddhists would accept neither. That release is emptiness is stated only to be mocked. The calf simile: one who takes milk while the calf starves shows no pity, so one who ate flesh cannot claim compassion.

reading: Kundalakesi was like a man who calls a woman his darling though she has no eyes or ears, her breasts are shrunken, her teeth, lips and nose are gone and she is diseased: who else would speak of her beauty?
nuance: The simile closes the attack on the teacher: praising such a leader is a lover's blindness. Whether these are the narrator's words or Neelakesi's is not certain; 'ஒத்தாள்' in the third person suggests the narrator.

title: குண்டலகேசி வாதச் சருக்கம் 192-211 (3/4)
theme: The third part of the debate with Kundalakesi: Neelakesi mocks her opponent and her teacher, denies the Buddha omniscience and so scriptural authority, reduces the five aggregates to knowing and form, and argues through a run of images (the self-binding thief, the soldier who reports his own death, the garland thread, the scented pot) that momentariness and continuity without a soul cannot stand; Kundalakesi then turns to the Buddha's birth-stories of giving his eyes, body, wife and child, and Neelakesi answers that such gifts are madness, meet no need, and make the testing god ignorant.
source_issues: 192 line 2: காலனையும் (her husband as 'Death'?) is hard to construe.
194 line 2: சிங்குந்தன் is obscure; the list of three aggregates may be corrupt.
198 lines 2-3: மறைபொருள்கள் வெளிப்பட்டா and வான்வயிற்றால் do not yield a clear argument.
199 line 4: ஆதனாழிநாட் டாகாதோ is obscure, possibly corrupt.
201 lines 3-4: the line break doubles ல் (போல் / லோசனை), a division error of the edition or e-text.
211 lines 1-2: the break doubles க (தனக / கிறுதி), and மறுதி in line 3 is obscure.
207 line 1: நூலு நாரு மிசைத்தன வொத்தலான் is unclear.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddhist woman debater whom Neelakesi answers
those sitting near who hear the debate

reading: Neelakesi laughs that the Buddhists' leader tore open his mother's side at his birth while himself feeling no pain, and that this woman on the dark hill threw down her own husband; who else on earth, she asks, walks so great a path with so great a compassion as these two.
nuance: The praise is mockery: பெருவழியார் பேரருளார் is turned against the two whose compassion the Buddhists would claim. The first half refers to a birth that harmed the mother, the second to Kundalakesi's killing of her husband on the hill; the verse names neither story more than this, and காலனையும் (her husband, 'Death' himself?) is hard to fix. The jibe attacks persons, not doctrine, and so carries no claim.
event: Neelakesi mocks Kundalakesi with her teacher's birth and her own killing of her husband.

reading: Neelakesi tells Kundalakesi that her leader does not know all things without remainder, since he knew only through the eye and the other organs, by seeing, hearing and reasoning, like a man who merely carries a load, and asks whether the word of one without subtle knowledge can be scripture.
nuance: The argument ties a book's authority to its author's omniscience: what the Buddhists count as the means of knowledge (sense and inference) is here made a limit, so a teacher who used them cannot be the all-knower the Jain invocation (verse 1) makes the mark of god. The simile of the load-bearer (இலை சுமக்கும் ஒருவன்) is not fully clear.

reading: Neelakesi argues that to speak of five aggregates is an error: feeling, perception and volition are not other than knowing and are one with it, so with form there are only two, and in saying more Kundalakesi has stopped speaking of aggregates and arrived at real principles.
nuance: The Buddhist list in Manimekalai 30 is form, feeling, perception, formation and consciousness (உருவு நுகர்ச்சி குறிப்பே பாவனை உள்ள அறிவு); the Neelakesi's terms (குறி, உழப்பு, செய்கை) are close but its own, and its reduction to knowing and form mirrors the Jain pair of soul and non-soul. Line 2's சிங்குந்தன் is obscure, so which three are merged is a reading.

reading: Neelakesi calls it great folly to say that each thing first perishes wholly and that another knowledge arises after that total destruction, likening it to saying that a man who came in yesterday at midnight handed himself over, took me, and went away.
nuance: The absurd tale makes one who has ceased the agent of an exchange: if the earlier moment is wholly gone it cannot pass anything to the later one. The joke turns on the same person being both giver and taken.

reading: Like a thief who is also the one who binds himself, Neelakesi says, if the mind perishes utterly together with what it knew and not a sesame seed of it remains, how can perishing itself be known; she bids the clear-minded woman think it over calmly.
nuance: The thief-and-captor image charges the doctrine with needing the perished mind to witness its own end. தெள்ளியாய் ('clear one') is courteous in form and ironic in force.

reading: Neelakesi compares Kundalakesi to a soldier who, while king, general and champion fall and he himself flees, says 'I was killed': she speaks while bound, and the verse asks whether one who has fallen tells his own fall to the fallen.
nuance: A battlefield report serves as a figure for the momentary self reporting its own extinction: speech about total perishing presupposes a speaker who did not perish.

reading: Neelakesi says that if one cites the birth of the crescent moon and the birth of children, hidden things become plain; she asks what is lacking, and whether the birth Kundalakesi described on this earth should be taken as a principle.
nuance: The verse seems to answer an example the Buddhist used for birth without a continuing self (the moon renewed, the child born), but lines 2 and 3 (மறைபொருள்கள் வெளிப்பட்டா, வான்வயிற்றால்) are obscure and the argument cannot be fixed.

reading: Neelakesi says that Kundalakesi has spent long hours expounding two kinds of continuum, the separate and the unseparated, and asks whether, if they serve only to destroy without trace the meaning of all she said, her case does not collapse.
nuance: பின்ன சந்தானம் and பிறிதில் சந்தானம் name the Buddhist series of moments as the Neelakesi reports them; the Buddhist sources here do not use these terms. Line 4 (ஆதனாழிநாட் டாகாதோ) is obscure and the conclusion is a guess.

reading: If the countless aggregates follow without interval, Neelakesi argues, either they never meet and so stay unmixed, or, if their unbroken succession means they touch, two become one; either way the lord's complete extinction becomes hard to hold.
nuance: The dilemma is aimed at release as total cessation (அறக்கேடு): a series that either never joins or fuses leaves no clean end. The reading of line 2 (கண்ணுறாது ஒன்றுதலால்) is uncertain.

reading: Even if knowledge is carried on by traces, Neelakesi argues, if nothing at all of the first moment is in the one that follows, knowing and speaking become impossible; and if something is there, then like the thread inside a great garland she has described a soul stretched longer than a league.
nuance: The garland image is the core of the Jain answer: what runs unbroken through the flowers is the soul the Buddhist denies. The league (ஓசனை) is mockery of a self drawn out across all its moments.

reading: Neelakesi asks whether Kundalakesi's principle is that the scent of the pathiri flower stays undestroyed in the new pot even after the flower decays, and argues that then, as the scent outlasts the flower, the soul too should outlast the perishing body.
nuance: The image of the new pot scented by pathiri flowers was evidently the Buddhist's example for traces that pass on without a substance; Neelakesi turns it to show something that endures. Line 4 (முடிவு உயிர்க்கே ஆகாதோ) can also be read as a question whether the soul too must end, which would reverse the point.

reading: If Kundalakesi says that a power passed across, Neelakesi argues, that power is a sixth thing besides the five aggregates; and if it is nothing besides the five, then, mad one, she has after all spoken of total destruction.
nuance: The dilemma closes the run on momentariness: either something beyond the aggregates (a self in all but name) or total destruction with nothing to carry deeds or knowledge. பித்தியாய் is a direct insult.

reading: As those sitting near think that Neelakesi has raised many waves of argument, Kundalakesi resolves to establish that the faults laid on her leader's scripture, its meaning and his life have no ground, and sets out to tell what her leader did.
nuance: The debate turns here from doctrine to the teacher's life (நிகழ்ச்சி): having lost the argument on momentariness, the Buddhist defends by the founder's conduct. The order of lines 3 and 4 makes the subject of நிறுத்துவன் யான் Kundalakesi speaking.
event: The onlookers judge Neelakesi's case strong, and Kundalakesi undertakes to defend her teacher's scripture and life.

reading: Kundalakesi tells of her teacher's former gifts: he gave his eyes, gave his flesh, gave himself to a tiger, gave his wife, split open his body and gave it to others, gave land and gave his child, and to those who came to him he gave heaven; she bids Neelakesi listen while she tells them in full.
nuance: These are the birth-stories (சாதகம், 206) of the bodhisattva's total giving, offered as proof of compassion. The gift of wife and child is listed with the gifts of the body without comment. Neelakesi answers the catalogue in 207 to 210 by calling such giving madness and its test by Indra empty.
event: Kundalakesi recites the Buddha's gifts in former births.

reading: Saying that these are the birth-stories of 'our lord who removes the distress of strangers', Kundalakesi with long garlanded hair told them one after another for the whole length of a day.
nuance: ஏதிலார் இடர் தீர்க்கும் (who ends the distress of those who are nothing to him) names compassion for strangers as the teacher's mark. Line 3 (யோகினாணின்று) is unclear: perhaps she stood in her practice.
event: Kundalakesi recites the birth-stories for a whole day.

reading: Neelakesi of the long eyes answers that the Buddha's story Kundalakesi told is like the doings of the deluded and the possessed.
nuance: The Jain answer does not deny the stories but judges them: gifts of one's own eyes, flesh and family are not compassion but disorder. Line 1 (நூலும் நாரும் இசைத்தன ஒத்தலால்) is unclear; it may say that her words matched as thread and fibre are twisted together.
event: Neelakesi dismisses the birth-stories as the deeds of the mad.

reading: People who live their lives do not come asking 'give us slices of flesh, eyes, heads and meat at once'; would anyone go to a gruel-seller to get such things, Neelakesi asks.
nuance: The objection is from use: a gift must answer a real need, and no one needs another's eyes or head. கூழன் (the gruel-man) seems to be the ordinary giver of food, set against the giver of his body.

reading: As for the splitting of the body and the rest, Neelakesi says, if Indra came to test the giver he would know the man's heart; if he could not discern another's mind, to speak of him as a god is merely to claim a title.
nuance: The birth-stories in which a god comes in disguise to ask for the bodhisattva's body are attacked from the side of the tester: a god who must test does not know, and the test itself proves nothing a true knower needed. The close (ஓர் கிழமையும் போலுமே) is uncertain.

reading: Whoever the asker may be, Neelakesi argues, since no ordinary man would ask such a thing the giver will see that he is a god; and having seen it, the wish to give will arise with no fear that he will die.
nuance: If the giver recognises the divine asker, the sacrifice is safe and its merit void: the gift is made in the expectation of no loss. Taking அன்னவன் இன்மையின் as 'since no such man exists' is a reading.

reading: Indra does not think that one without firm knowledge reaches an end, Neelakesi says, and since there is no answer to this, she asks the jewelled woman where she will find a way to join the earlier and later parts of her story.
nuance: Line 1 (உறுதி யல்லதுணர்வடையான்றனக) and line 3 (மறுதி) are hard to construe; the verse seems to say the birth-stories cannot be made consistent with the god's testing. The reading is tentative throughout.

title: குண்டலகேசி வாதச் சருக்கம் 212-231 (4/4)
theme: Neelakesi ends her debate with Kundalakesi by mocking the Jataka tales of the Buddha's gifts of body and life as useless, harmful or false; the king rules the tales fictions, Kundalakesi names her teacher Arkkachandran and is driven out of the city, and Neelakesi refuses every reward, asks the king to keep dharma, and leaves through the sky for Ujjain.
source_issues: 212: lines 1-2 (ஆதனாற் குறந்தாங்கெழுவான்றும்ம / வேதமில் சுடரேற்றொருதாமென்றான்) do not divide with confidence.
220: line 1 (யானை யுள்ளா செங்குள தங்கெலாம்) appears corrupt.
225: line 1 has scribal errors (எனெ, இருக்ந்); line 3 கோந்தலி for கூந்தலி. The verse changes metre from the preceding run.
226: lines 1 and 3 carry encoding damage (இட்ஜுசொலவவை, முலூங்க).
227: encoding damage (சும்க்கினை, எளூ, ம்க்கசந்திரன் for அர்க்கசந்திரன், அவாச்சியன்).
228: a stray '(' before வாரலென்று in line 3.
224: the speaker கோன் is read as the presiding king; the verse does not name him.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddhist woman debater who planted the rose-apple branch as a challenge
the king of Kampili who presides over the debate between Neelakesi and Kundalakesi
the people of Kampili who drive the defeated Kundalakesi out of the city
the Buddhist teacher at Ujjain whom Kundalakesi names as her master

reading: Neelakesi sums up against Kundalakesi's catalogue of the Buddha's gifts: the one who proves his compassion by these birth-tales, she says, gives those who recite them only one and the same notion, and the line about a flame being lit seems to refer to one of the tales.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 (ஆதனாற் குறந்தாங்கெழுவான், வேதமில் சுடரேற்று ஒருதாம் என்றான்) do not divide with confidence; only line 3, சாதகம் இவற்றான் அருள் சாதிப்பான், is clear, and it states the position the following verses attack: that the Jataka gifts establish the Buddha's grace.

reading: Neelakesi says the fool who gives eyes and other organs is like one who does not see that an ox has no milk, since those who asked for them never said what lack the gift would meet.
nuance: The argument turns the Jataka's praise of the asker-satisfying gift into a question about need: a gift is judged by what it supplies, not by what it costs the giver. மருதின் வாழ் பகை in line 4 is obscure.

reading: Neelakesi asks whether half a body split off becomes one with another's body: thinking so is folly, for the flesh is eaten only by crows, and an eye given is the same, since a body once broken does not join another.
nuance: The objection is practical, not moral: flesh and eyes cannot be grafted, so the famous gifts could not have helped anyone. பரகாயம் (another's body) is a borrowed technical word.

reading: Since the self is present in both halves of a body cut in two, Neelakesi argues, the one who takes the half is the giver's killer, and if no awareness remains, cutting off a corpse and saying 'take it' is no gift at all.
nuance: The premise that the self (உள்ளம்) fills the whole body, so that both halves are alive, is the Jain view of the soul as coextensive with its body; the verse does not name the school, but it is the doctrine the argument needs. The dilemma leaves the receiver either a killer or the taker of a corpse.

reading: Neelakesi calls it folly to hold that when the body is cut into pieces the life within goes off separately with each, and asks whether any clear-minded person would trust the 'ultimate truth' that comes from a vulture's mouth.
nuance: பரமார்த்தம் is the Buddhist term for ultimate truth; பாறு வாய் (vulture's mouth) mocks it as carrion talk. What the opponent is said to hold about the divided life is inferred from the gift tales, not quoted from a Buddhist text.

reading: Neelakesi points to the tale of the adorned woman who saw the Buddha's beauty and begged him to unite with her: if he would not grant her that grace, to say he split open his own head for a petitioner is a deceit.
nuance: The point is consistency: a compassion that gives the head to one asker but refuses another's desire is not the boundless giving Kundalakesi claimed. Which tale is meant cannot be fixed from the verse.

reading: If dying in vain, knowing that nothing will come of it, is the excellence of your Bodhisattvas, Neelakesi asks, would not the woman who burns on the pyre with the husband who guarded her also have high virtue?
nuance: A reductio: the wife's death on the pyre is offered as the absurd consequence the Buddhists would have to praise. The phrase ஆவது இன்மை அறிந்தும் (knowing nothing comes of it) is the Jain description; a Buddhist would not grant that the Bodhisattva's death achieved nothing.

reading: Neelakesi takes the tale of the patient sage who, while preaching dharma as peace, was cut down by a wicked man with a fierce weapon and gave way to his attacker, and calls it the lie among lies.
nuance: காந்தி (patience, Sanskrit kshanti) and கலகன் seem to name the Kshantivadin tale and its king; the reading of lines 2 and 4 (கலகன்றான், இடம் போந்து கொண்டதும்) is uncertain.

reading: Neelakesi appears to ask why, if the gods are seen worshipping where the Tathagata took the form of an elephant, he did not become fish and other creatures when they too were in pain: is that the nature of the Tathagata?
nuance: Line 1 (யானை யுள்ளா செங்குள தங்கெலாம்) is probably corrupt; the reading of the whole verse as a charge of selective compassion rests on line 4's ததாகதர் தன்மையோ.

reading: Against the tale that, born a monkey, he took pity on his troop when hunters came to kill them and saved them, Neelakesi asks where there are monkeys that cannot leap straight across, since monkeys by nature leap from tree to tree.
nuance: The objection is to the tale's need, not its kindness: a bridge of the monkey-king's body was useless to creatures that leap.

reading: If it is said that those of good conduct stretch themselves far for others, Neelakesi asks whether it is greatness for a monkey to lie stretching out its tail, not seeing that hands and feet are for rising against those who come to kill.
nuance: சீலம் is the Buddhist term for moral conduct. The verse sets resistance or flight, what limbs are for, against the self-offering the tale praises.

reading: If you say that giving the red blood of one's own body to a demon is a great gift, Neelakesi asks, would giving all human filth to dogs then be good dharma?
nuance: Line 1 (தாய்க்கொன்றான்) does not divide with confidence; the reductio in lines 3 and 4 is clear: a gift is not dharma merely because something of the body is handed to a creature that wants it.

reading: The king tells Kundalakesi that a one-sided teacher, saying 'this is what I will do', made up the fictions of the birth-tales, and bids her, doe-eyed one, give up her esteem for them.
nuance: ஏகாந்தன் (one who holds to a single side) carries the Jain charge against other schools of one-sidedness, set against their own many-sided view; கற்பங்கள் here reads as fabrications. The speaker is taken to be the king (கோன்) presiding over the debate, who in 174 promised to expel the loser; the verb சொன்னான் is masculine, so it is not Neelakesi.
event: The king gives his verdict to Kundalakesi that the Jataka tales are inventions and tells her to stop esteeming them.

reading: Those who keep the hare's tale under cover and tell it to outsiders as truth are fools, the verse says; the woman with tresses dark as rain-cloud spoke fittingly, and nothing she said ran against the words of the wise.
nuance: முயல் உரை is read as the hare tale (the Bodhisattva as a hare offering his body), the last of the Jataka gifts; முயல் could also mean effort. The verse changes metre, and the scribal forms எனெ and இருக்ந் in line 1 are corrupt. Whether lines 1 and 2 continue the king's verdict or are the narrator's is unclear.
event: The debate closes with Neelakesi judged to have spoken without contradiction.

reading: The king commands that the victory of the one whose words were dense with meaning be proclaimed quickly through the land, with the drum and the long banner sounding.
nuance: Lines 1 and 3 are corrupt in the edition (இட்ஜுசொலவவை நார்களு, முலூங்க); the gist, a drum proclamation ordered by the king, rests on lines 2 to 4.
event: The king orders Neelakesi's victory proclaimed with drum and banner.

reading: Kundalakesi is asked what remains now and who taught her this doctrine, and is told to say it quickly; she answers that it is the teacher Arkkachandran, who lives in the inner city on the south side of walled Ujjain.
nuance: Who asks is not stated: the address அன்னாய் and the plural நுமக்கு suit Neelakesi questioning the defeated debater. The text is corrupt in places (சும்க்கினை, எளூ, ம்க்கசந்திரன் for அர்க்கசந்திரன், அவாச்சியன் for ஆசாரியன்).
event: Kundalakesi, questioned, names Arkkachandran of Ujjain as her teacher.

reading: The townspeople, after many harsh words, beat the drum, shout many reproaches telling her not to come back, heap many insults on the fair-browed woman who had laughed as she entered the city after planting her rose-apple branch at the guarded gate, and drive her out of the city's gate.
nuance: This is the penalty the king announced before the debate (174): the loser is to be sent out with shame. The நாவல் branch is the challenge Kundalakesi planted at the gate (164, 169). A stray bracket before வாரலென்று in line 3 is an edition mark.
event: Kundalakesi is driven out of the city gate with drums and insults.

reading: The king, like a lion, thunder and a bull, says of Neelakesi, who is beautiful like a flowering creeper in a field, knows many books in their nature and is without fault: what is it fitting for me to do for her now?
event: The king asks what reward he should give Neelakesi.

reading: When the king said this, she of dharma, who wanted no jewels, gave no thought to adornment, and desired none of these, neither land nor great treasure, told the king: from now on, hold to the path of dharma here.
nuance: The reward is refused item by item (jewels, adornment, land, treasure) and replaced by a charge laid on the king; the winner's prize becomes his conduct. வேந்திழை in line 4 is ஏந்திழை with the glide of the preceding உறுக என.
event: Neelakesi refuses jewels, land and wealth and asks the king instead to follow the path of dharma.

reading: Neelakesi tells the king that this is what she came for, and that with a lordship like Indra's he should not scorn the path of dharma; then, leaving him, she rises and sets out through the sky toward the quarter where Arkkachandran lives.
nuance: இந்திரன் அனைய repeats the comparison used of this king when Kundalakesi first arrived (166); the sky road is how Neelakesi travels between debates.
event: Neelakesi takes leave of the king and departs through the sky toward Arkkachandran.

title: அர்க்கசந்திர வாதச் சருக்கம் 232-249 (1/2)
theme: Neelakesi comes to Ujjain, finds the Buddhist teacher Arkkachandra preaching in his monastery, hears his monks recite the Vinaya's rules for eating, shaving and grooming, asks whether that is dharma, and, challenged, opens a catalogue of what she calls the deceits of the Buddhist vows: the bodhisattva's gift of his wives, the denial of a soul alongside a being who wins release, and rules on partners and faults.
source_issues: 234: show flags a repair of கண்டீர் on line 2, but the line has no such word; the flag seems to belong to 247 line 4, which does read கண்டீர்.
233 line 4: அவாச்சியன் is not a regular form; probably a damaged title (ஆசாரியன்?).
237 line 3 (மணலெடுத்), 241 line 1, 245 line 4, 247 lines 2 and 4, and 248 lines 1-2 are obscure or damaged and cannot be construed with confidence.
249 line 3: ஒரு மில்லா looks like a lost letter (ஊரும் இல்லாள்?); the metre is short.

cast.role: the demoness converted to the Jain dharma, now its debater
the Buddhist teacher of Ujjain whom Neelakesi challenges
the shaven-headed Buddhist monks reciting the Vinaya in his monastery

reading: Neelakesi reaches the great city of Ujjain and, once she has looked at its walls, its many great men, its cloud-touching mansions and its streets, the narrative turns to what she found there.
event: Neelakesi arrives at Ujjain and looks over its walls, mansions and streets.

reading: In the city lived Arkkachandra, a teacher honoured by kings with great elephants, matchless in the reach of his reasoning.
nuance: The last word, அவாச்சியன், is not a usual Tamil form; it seems to stand for a title of the teacher (ஆசாரியன் or a like word), but the reading is a guess.

reading: He was counted great in conduct like the bodhisattvas and buddhas, had mastered the threefold scripture as it should be known, and was a lion among debaters.
nuance: நூல் மும்மை, the three-part scripture, fits the Buddhist canon in three baskets; the poet grants the opponent full learning before the debate, so her coming victory is over the best of his school.

reading: In a monastery set in a flowering grove beside high mansions where koels sing, he mounted the seat and was expounding to the assembled worthies release and the deeds that bind.
event: Arkkachandra sits on the teaching seat in a monastery and preaches release and karma.

reading: She goes there, enters, and standing beside a gem-studded pillar, she whose name means blue tresses hears the various recitations being given.
nuance: The poet names her by a paraphrase of her name (நீல ஐம்பால், blue fivefold hair) rather than by நீலகேசி itself.
event: Neelakesi enters the monastery and stands by a pillar listening to the recitations.

reading: What she hears recited are rules: how to receive food in the bowl, how to scoop up gruel, how to bend the back while eating, and how, taking it up in small portions, to swallow it slowly.
nuance: Line 3 (மணலெடுத் திட்டவை) may mean taking sand, which makes little sense of eating; it may be a corrupt or rare word for small handfuls, so the detail of the rule is unsure. The verse runs on into 238 and is completed by its வினைய விதியினால்.

reading: The list goes on with how to wipe the bowl after eating, how to dispose of and share out leftovers, how to shave the head and how to paint the eyes with collyrium, all by the rules of the Vinaya.
nuance: The Jain poet makes the Buddhist rule-book a list of table manners and grooming, which a Buddhist would not accept as its sum; Neelakesi's answer to these rules comes in 239.
event: The monks recite Vinaya rules for eating, cleaning the bowl, shaving and painting the eyes.

reading: When the shaven-headed monks had recited such things to all who marvelled at the Vinaya book, she who had already learned the way of the Jina asked whether that was what they called the path of dharma.
nuance: Her question does not deny that the rules exist but that rules of eating and grooming amount to dharma; முனைவன் தன் நெறி reminds the reader that her standard is the Jain teaching she took in the earlier sarukkams.
event: Neelakesi challenges the monks: is such a rule-book the path of dharma?

reading: Hearing that, the teacher on the high seat, like a mass of fire on a red hill and firm in having withered his opponents' power, demanded what this talk was doing here.
event: Arkkachandra, from the high seat, demands why she speaks so.

reading: She replies that if the name of the Vinaya book means the removal of deeds, it is a fine name indeed, and asks him to set out plainly, as his firm doctrine, what that binding deed is.
nuance: She seems to play on வினயம் and வினை: a discipline whose name sounds like the undoing of deeds should be able to say which deed binds. Line 1 (வீரஞ் செய்து விழியல்) is obscure, and the pun is my reading.
event: Neelakesi asks Arkkachandra to explain what deed the Vinaya removes.

reading: Asking him to unfold for her, even a millet-grain's worth, what it is to become deed, she announces that he should now hear the deceits that come with those vows, and takes them up one by one.
nuance: சலம் (deceit, sophistry) is the frame word: it opens the catalogue here and closes it at 249 (சலமதோ).
event: Neelakesi begins to list the contradictions in the Buddhist vows.

reading: She asks: when one who gave away himself and gave away his wives, and took dharma from hearing its meaning, sees the people of other households, can what he would do next even be spoken of?
nuance: The giver of self and wives is the bodhisattva of the birth stories, though the verse does not name him; she turns the highest Buddhist gift into a sign of a man for whom no bond holds. A Buddhist would read the same gift as perfected giving.

reading: She asks whether it is not the hidden teaching of their 'left' book that, in the town of pleasure among courtesans, one who hid his true form under purity and truth may be sent off with 'go safely'.
nuance: The verse alludes to a story she expects the hearers to know; வாம நூல் may mean a left-handed or crooked book, and the episode cannot be fixed from the Tamil alone. This is a polemical charge, not an account a Buddhist would own.

reading: She cites the elder called Simhadatta, who, when asked in the sangha to show compassion to people, said 'what is this?' and gave some answer to seven ascetics.
nuance: Line 4 (எங்கெங் காமி லெனவுரைத் தானரோ) cannot be construed with confidence; the point seems to be that a Buddhist elder refused or evaded an act of compassion, which would turn the school's own claim of compassion against it.

reading: She reminds them that they said their teacher taught that there is no soul at all, and yet that a sattva, with that soulless one, relieves suffering and is the means to release from deeds.
nuance: The argument is that release and compassion need a someone who suffers and is freed, which the no-soul teaching denies; she does not answer the Buddhist account of a chain without a self, only points to the words.

reading: She points out, to those so sharp in argument, that one who has taken up good penance and reached a state where the mind no longer runs, stirs and wanders may still, by their rules, commit more than ten faults and keep his place in the monastery.
nuance: Lines 2 and 4 (நத்தம், வத்தன) are hard; the reading that the rules tolerate a calmed monk's many faults is a guess from the shape of her catalogue.

reading: She adds that the Pudgalas, whose assembly was set up as kin of the Buddha's, recite something that shows one truth: that there is a person after all.
nuance: புற்கலர் seem to be the Buddhist school that held a 'person' (pudgala) neither the same as nor other than the aggregates; she uses an inner Buddhist dispute to answer the no-soul claim of 246. Lines 1 and 2 are hard to construe.

reading: She closes by asking whether it is not deceit to list as possible wives a hermaphrodite, an animal, a courtesan, a woman, one who has nothing, a lifeless thing and a mute.
nuance: The list may twist a monastic rule that names kinds of partner for the gravest sexual offence into a permission; the Tamil does not show which rule she means, and line 3 (ஒரு மில்லா) looks damaged. A Buddhist would not accept this as his teaching.

title: அர்க்கசந்திர வாதச் சருக்கம் 250-266 (2/2)
theme: The close of the Arkkachandra debate: Neelakesi charges the Buddhist monk with preaching compassion while eating flesh, impermanence while building mansions, and suffering while grumbling over comforts; she refutes his reply that only the mind matters, shows his void release to be no goal at all, teaches him the Jain path of conduct, knowledge and vision, and wins him over, after which he names Mokkalan as his teacher.
source_issues: Verse 253, line 2: மலையோ ரனையந்ன் has a stray ந்ன், probably for அனையநன் (மலையோரனைய நன் மாடம்).

Verse 256: the lines are much longer than the surrounding verses and run words together (பெருமுடுகுநாறுமேற், மணற்சுமையுந்தான்பெரிதாற்); the word division appears faulty, and 256-258 are a different metre (a song with refrain) from the verses around them.
Verse 257, line 4 has an extra refrain phrase (அழல்நரகத் துள்ளேயடுப வாலோ), and 258 has five lines; the refrain may have been written out in full by the editor.
Verse 260, line 1: துத்தலே and தோந்தொடர்ப் பாடு are hard to divide (தோம் தொடர்ப்பாடு?).

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddhist monk (also called சூரிய சோமன்) whom Neelakesi debates and converts

reading: Neelakesi asks the monk whether he, wearing the guise taken from one who held that living on in the house of one's birth is a fault, yet full of unworthy things everywhere, can even speak of the high matter of renunciation.
nuance: The monk is called by the guise word அவாச்சிய (line 2, after sandhi), which 259 repeats as his title; its sense (perhaps 'one not to be spoken of', perhaps a Buddhist monk's title) cannot be fixed from the verse. Line 3 (சிறந்த வல்லன சிங்கின) is obscure, so the charge of unworthiness is read from the frame of the argument.

reading: Neelakesi lists the monks' contradictions: they preach great compassion but eat fish and flesh, spread soft beds yet claim lofty penance, claim to dissolve evil deeds, and what they have found is the void; she asks whether so faulty a path holds together.
nuance: The verse is built as a run of paired verbs (உரைப்ப/உண்பன, திரைப்ப/செய்வ), each pair setting a word against a deed. The void (சூனியம்) is named here as the Buddhist goal; the charge that it is empty is answered at length in 262 and 263.

reading: Neelakesi says they call everything impure, yet bow only at the feet of their own defiled master, call him Sugata though they speak of no bliss, and declare the toil of others' austerities to be worthless.
nuance: சுகதன் (Sugata, 'the one gone well') is played against சுகம் (bliss): the title promises the joy the doctrine is said to deny. Lines 2 and 4 do not divide with certainty (அழுக்குற் றவனடிக் கேத்தலர், பல்லார் வருத்தம்), so the reading is tentative.

reading: Neelakesi mocks them as people who say all things do not last yet accept goods, raise mansions like mountains, and treat life as a thing with a price: such is the understanding of those who sit in baseness.
nuance: The doctrine of impermanence is turned against the monastery: those who teach that nothing stays build as if to stay. Line 2 (மலையோ ரனையந்ன்) and line 3 (விலையே யுயிரென் றிறந்த நினைப) are corrupt or hard to divide.

reading: Neelakesi says they cultivate friendliness toward creatures and then sit eating those very creatures' flesh as if devouring them, and knock their heads before a shrine; the ways of madmen are just like this.
nuance: மயித்திரம் (maitri) and சயித்தியம் (caitya) are Sanskrit-derived Buddhist terms used precisely, and பயித்தியம் (madness) rhymes on them; the mockery is in the sound as well as the charge.

reading: Neelakesi says they set on their heads and worship a copy of a copy of the Buddha's form, and when a creature has died they chew its red flesh: such is the kind of grace their master taught.
nuance: செத்த பொழுதின் (when it has died) points at the defence that flesh of an animal not killed for the eater is allowed; the verse only sneers at it, and 260 gives the argument against it. The image worship is mocked as twice removed from its original (போலிக்கும் போலி).

reading: In a mocking song, Neelakesi has the monk cry 'suffering, suffering' when his lice-ridden robe stinks, when the load is heavy, when he sees a prawn and cannot have it, and conclude that since all his endless tasks are suffering, all is suffering.
nuance: The refrain துக்கம் துக்கம் and the close சருவம் துக்கம் parody the Buddhist teaching that all is suffering by reducing it to a greedy monk's petty discomforts; a Buddhist would not accept this as the teaching (compare Manimekalai 30, where suffering is traced to clinging). Line 2 (மானறா நோக்கி மணற்சுமையுந்) is unclear.

reading: Neelakesi warns that the lies told under cover, the wages taken, the burnings, the felling of living marutham trees, and the quarrels in anger over meat in the hand will without doubt torment them in the burning hell.
nuance: The list joins speech (lies), livelihood (wages), harm to living plants and greed for meat; the killing of trees counts plants as lives, a Jain concern. Line 2 (வையத்தஞ் சுட்டனவும்) is uncertain in its object.

reading: Neelakesi tells them that, swelling attachment and multiplying ties while showing themselves free of it and seizing what was left in their keeping, they will take a demon's body or else be dragged, merciless as they are, into the dark hell.
nuance: அடைக்கலமே வவ்வுநீர் charges the monks with taking deposits entrusted to them; the punishment is graded, a ghost's birth or, more often, hell. The refrain ஈர்க்குமாலோ closes the song begun at 256.

reading: Hearing her teaching, the monk replies to the lady of fragrant hair that there is nothing but the mind, and that our dark-robed Buddhas would not call all that is called evil conduct evil deed.
nuance: The monk's defence of the meat charge is that karma lies in intention alone (சித்தமே அல்லதில்லை). This is the Neelakesi's version of the Buddhist view; Manimekalai 30 lists bodily deeds such as killing and theft among the ten evil deeds, so a Buddhist text itself would not accept that conduct is never evil karma.
event: Arkkachandran answers Neelakesi's charges by saying that only the mind matters.

reading: Neelakesi retorts that he wants only to eat and will not cut off fault and entanglement; if he says the mind is good, who can believe it, and when a butcher with a knife cuts off leg and head and stabs, will karma not attach when he eats?
nuance: This answers 259 and 255: the eater who did not kill still shares the killing. The phrase இல்லில்வாழ்பேய் (the demon that lives in the house) is read here as a figure for the household butcher, but that is uncertain.

reading: Neelakesi says that if the inner mind and outer conduct agree there may be release, but if one takes flesh the fault comes with it and attachment there, and if the two part, the outward guise is just as false: can he prove otherwise by speaking deceit and growing angry?
nuance: பாயிரம் is taken as the outward (Sanskrit bāhya) against உள்ளம், the inward; that reading carries the verse and is not certain. The verse answers 259 by refusing to split intention from deed.

reading: When she tells him that, if on reflection nothing that is stands, the release he dresses up comes to this, that the truth is to become void, the monk, grieving and sighing, asks her, good lady, what he should do.
nuance: The verse turns on என்றாட்கு (to her who said): lines 1 to 3 report her reductio, line 4 his surrender. Line 1 (போகவுண் டாக தந்தே) is hard to divide.
event: Arkkachandran, unable to answer her, asks Neelakesi what he must do.

reading: Neelakesi says that even if the dead went straight among the gods, people would not look to that joy but would fear death; so we grieve for the Buddha who taught a void release without saying there would be anything to hold to, and she bids the lamenting man leave it.
nuance: The argument is from fear: if even death that leads to heaven is dreaded, a release that is only voidness can attract no one. தொத்து (something to cling to) names what the void release lacks. The close (அத்த புலம்பனீ போக) can be read as a dismissal of the Buddha or a bidding to the monk to stop lamenting.

reading: The woman further tells him that, fortunate in having cast off all base paths, if he takes up well the good path, good knowledge and right vision and walks by her word, he will reach unfailing great bliss and abide forever.
nuance: நன்னெறி, நன்ஞானம், காட்சி are the Jain three jewels (conduct, knowledge, vision), given here as the path that replaces the void release.
event: Neelakesi teaches Arkkachandran the path of right conduct, knowledge and vision.

reading: As a rutting wild elephant from the forest is bound hand and foot, mounted and driven with the goad, so Suriya Soman, first among the Buddha's followers, was bound and taken by the rope of the good lady's words.
nuance: சூரிய சோமன் (sun-moon) is a Tamil rendering of the name Arkkachandra (அருக்க, sun; சந்திரன், moon), which 266 gives directly.
event: Arkkachandran is won over to the Jain dharma by Neelakesi's speech.

reading: Having made Arkkachandra take up the dharma, she bade him say quickly who had taught him these things, and he said it was Mokkalan, the Buddha's chief disciple, who had gone to Murukkuvay.
nuance: முருக்குவாய் is taken as a place name; the line could also be read otherwise. The naming of the teacher sends Neelakesi on to the Mokkala debate of the next sarukkam.
event: Arkkachandran, now converted, names Mokkalan, the Buddha's chief disciple, as his teacher.

title: மொக்கல வாதச் சருக்கம் 267-291 (1/8)
theme: Neelakesi, having converted Arkkachandra, flies to Padumapuram and opens the Mokkala debate by mocking the Buddhist monks' outward life (the dyed robe, the begging bowl, bodily cleanness, the crafts of a monastery), arguing that restraint lies in the senses and contemplation needs only food; Mokkalan, proud, disputes her victories, recites the Jain categories and calls them the Jina's own invention, and she answers that the Lord's word is truth.
source_issues: 282 line 4: the edition's '•' for ஃ was repaired by the tool (பஃறொடர்ப்பா).
291: the stanza is printed in eight half-lines and was joined into four by the tool.
273 line 4 (தொட்டைந் பூணியோ) and 286 line 3 (வென்றாள்மள்) look corrupt.
274, 275 line 1, 280 lines 1-2 and 284 line 1 have rare or doubtful forms whose division is not sure.
287: the speaker is not marked; it may be Neelakesi's challenge or Mokkalan's boast.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddhist elder at Padumapuram, named in 266 as the Buddha's first disciple and Arkkachandra's teacher
the robed monks of the Padumapuram vihara

reading: Neelakesi tells Arkkachandra not to come with her, goes to Padumapuram along the sky as swift as thought, and reaches a vihara where old sayings and their reasons are written out in full, its ground strewn with flowers and golden sand.
nuance: The verse runs on into 268 and has no main verb of its own; the place it describes is named as the பள்ளி only in 268. That the vihara's walls carry written sayings with their reasons (மூதுரையும் காரணமும்) fits a Buddhist house of teaching, but that is a reading of a compressed line.
event: Neelakesi leaves Arkkachandra behind and flies through the sky to Padumapuram.

reading: Seeing the vihara with its makara-bannered gateway, high walls, rows of carved pillars and images like heaven's, she remarks with pity that this splendour is the wealth that ships crossing the shark-filled sea have brought in.
nuance: Her first word is a jibe: the monastery's beauty is bought with sea-trade profit, so the renouncers live off merchants' wealth. அளியள் (pitying) sets her tone before any argument begins. குடிஞை (owl, or a carved ornament) is not certain here.
event: Neelakesi sees the vihara at Padumapuram and comments on where its wealth came from.

reading: Seeing the robed monks, whose conduct and learning match what is said of them and who are called faultless in great penance, she stands in the vihara courtyard holding a cluster of branches of the arasu tree, one leg bent.
nuance: இலிங்கிகள் names the monks by their outward sign (இலிங்கம், the mark of an order), which is the theme of her whole attack. The praise in lines 1 and 2 may be ironic. Standing with a hand on the arasu (bodhi) branch inside a Buddhist courtyard is a challenger's pose, as Kundalakesi planted the naaval branch in 228.
event: Neelakesi stands in the courtyard of the vihara, holding a branch of its arasu tree.

reading: She asks the monks what good comes of their busy work: stitching cloth, dyeing it in ochre and beating it, perfuming it with incense, handling food, with no leisure even to scratch their heads.
nuance: The question turns the monks' care for the robe into a householder's chores; the following verses press the same point. Line 3 (தன்னமு மளித்தாய) is not clear; it may refer to giving out food or to something else in the routine.
event: Neelakesi asks the monks what fruit their work on the robe brings.

reading: When the monks have no answer and sit with bowed heads, she takes their silence as their reply and turns to Mokkalan, the good elder, saying she will question him properly and he must answer without deceit.
event: The monks fall silent before Neelakesi, and she challenges Mokkalan to answer.

reading: She asks whether the robe is for release, which would then come without knowledge, or for dignity, in which the wealthy outdo him, and what use covering is; Mokkalan replies that covering has a small use, that the form may be known.
nuance: Her dilemma leaves the robe only two possible ends, release or prestige, and Mokkalan answers with a third, recognition, and concedes the use is small (சிறிது). The next verses attack that answer.
event: Neelakesi asks what the robe is for, and Mokkalan answers that it makes the monk known.

reading: She answers that robes are easy to make and hard to keep from harm and thieves, and that the garb serves mainly to tell flesh-givers who you are, you whose heart delights in meat.
nuance: விடக்கமர்ந்த உள்ளத்தாய் (you whose heart is set on flesh) carries the Jain charge that Buddhist monks accept meat given to them; the Buddhist side would not accept that the robe exists to solicit it. Lines 1, 2 and 4 are compressed, and the last words (தொட்டைந் பூணியோ) are probably corrupt.

reading: She says that a man in such a covering who takes gold will be cornered as a cheat with a low man's hardness, that no one faults his own kind, and asks what he saw that made him take this up.
nuance: The verse is obscure: போர்வை பூச்செனின் and வெண்கண்டு do not divide with confidence, and the reading given is one possibility. Its drift fits the verses around it, that the garb invites suspicion rather than trust.

reading: She tells him that he hides all his limbs calling it penance because his mind is not firm, and builds many enclosures around himself; it is the eyes, looking at women and other things, that stir the mind, so he should guard them.
nuance: Behind the charge stands the Jain (Digambara) practice of going unclothed: covering the body is read as a confession of weak control, and restraint is placed in the senses rather than in cloth. The verse does not name nudity. உண்ணன்மை in line 1 is unclear; it may be 'not eating' or a corrupt form.

reading: If, as he says, women would be disturbed on seeing him, and his penance would crumble through their nature, then people will not say there is dignity in his mind, and his virtue falls under no head at all.
nuance: She turns his excuse for covering (that women would be troubled) back on him: a penance that a woman's look can break is no penance.

reading: She attacks the begging bowl: slip and it is lost, stumble and the same, it is a costly vessel that brings much labour and harm, it is not fit for right conduct and hinders the meal, and if one does penance without fault, what is the bowl for?
nuance: The bowl (மண்டை) is the Buddhist monk's mark of begging. The Jain ascetic of the Digambara rule eats from the hollow of his hands, which is the unstated contrast. Line 2 (வினை பெரிதால் வினைக்கேடாந் தொழில்) may mean much work, or much karma, from the bowl; both fit her charge.
