reading: Water makes the skin clean, betel the mouth, the chewing stick the teeth; if cleaning the outside made the mind pure, she says, then courtesans would have purity of dharma in plenty.
nuance: The reductio picks the figure most given to bathing and adornment to show that bodily care says nothing of the mind. It answers the monks' care for clean, dyed and perfumed robes in 270.

reading: He left home life as a burden and took up penance, she says, yet he splits firewood, gathers pots, boils cloths with dye and beats them; he cooks dye and cooks flowers: was it only cooking rice he gave up?
nuance: The joke is in அடுதி (you cook): the monk still keeps a kitchen, only for dye. சவருடைய in line 1 is unclear; it is taken here as 'troublesome'.

reading: She lists the crafts he has learned in his penance, dyeing, tailoring and others, and says that had he practised so many trades at home he would at least have eaten his fill; of contemplation there is none.
nuance: The names of the crafts in lines 1 and 2 (மச்சிகம், கச்சாரம், சண்ணாரம்) are rare and their sense is not sure. ஓர்ப்பு (reflection) in line 4 sets up 281, where the renouncer's duty is said to be contemplation.

reading: She says that if the renouncer's duty is to bring contemplation to completion, he needs nothing but food, and asks whether he has nothing else to teach the dead, those yet to come, those now living and those born in heaven.
nuance: Line 3 and 4 are hard to construe; one reading is that his teaching for all beings in all times comes down to this robe-work. The first half is clearer: contemplation needs only food to sustain it, not the crafts of 280.

reading: She asks whether he alone does not know what all eight directions proclaim, that the body lives by food and awareness by the body, and tells him that if penance without wasting away is what matters, he should end his many entanglements by the belly alone.
nuance: The chain food, body, awareness is cited as common knowledge, not as a school's doctrine. It concedes that the body must be fed while denying that anything more (the robe's crafts) is needed. பண்டி (belly) and the last line are not certain.

reading: Hearing the compassionate woman, Mokkalan, swollen with pride in his possessions, the intoxication of petty learning and the esteem of the deluded, considers what she intends so as to frame a reply.
nuance: The narrator judges him before he speaks: the three sources of his pride (wealth, petty knowledge, the regard of fools) answer the opening jibe of 268 about the vihara's wealth. ஆங்காரித்து is taken as 'puffed with ahamkara'.
event: Mokkalan, proud, weighs Neelakesi's purpose before answering.

reading: Since what she held to as refuge was the Arhat's teaching and the clash between them was real, Mokkalan answers in anger that she has come here like Hiranya and met with trouble.
nuance: Line 1 (தரணென்று நன்றென்றாடன்றன்மை யுருவென்றாள்) is hard to divide; தரண் may be சரண் (refuge). The comparison with Hiranya, the proud king destroyed for defying a god, is a threat, and one a Buddhist speaker borrows from Vaishnava story.
event: Mokkalan, angered, warns Neelakesi that she has come to her ruin like Hiranya.

reading: She replies that there are two here already defeated by her, whom he will know when she names them: Kundalakesi, with waist like a drum and long spear-eyes, and Arkkachandra, who once taught that woman dharma.
nuance: Arkkachandra is called the one who taught Kundalakesi (அன்னாளுக்கு அறம் உரைத்த), which matches 227, where Kundalakesi names him as her teacher.
event: Neelakesi tells Mokkalan she has already defeated Kundalakesi and Arkkachandra.

reading: Looking her in the face, Mokkalan says this is a great lie: Kundalakesi defeated everyone of opposing creeds in the world, wandering everywhere under the vow of the naaval branch and giving dharma to others.
nuance: சம்புவிரதி names the challenger's vow of the jambu (naaval) branch that Kundalakesi planted in 228. Line 3 has a doubtful form (வென்றாள்மள்) and line 4 is unclear.
event: Mokkalan calls Neelakesi's claim a lie and praises Kundalakesi as undefeated.

reading: She says that after hearing him list those defeated, beginning with the Vedic brahmins, and name the creed of each, if he can tell rightly how the Arhat's followers were defeated in the first hall, she will surely defeat him.
nuance: Who speaks is not marked, and the verse can also be read as Mokkalan's boast; 288 (எனக் கேட்டு) only says that someone heard it. ஆதிகால் ஆவணத்துள் (in the first hall, or at the first time) is unclear.

reading: Hearing this, Mokkalan sets out what the Lord worshipped by the Indras taught: dharma, adharma, time, space, the soul, matter, merit, sin, bondage and release.
nuance: The list is the Jain categories as the Manimekalai's Jain gives them (27:171-182), here put in a Buddhist's mouth so that he can mock them in 289. காயம் stands for space (ஆகாயம்) and உருவு for matter, both as the line reads them.
event: Mokkalan recites the Jain categories.

reading: He spells out what happens in each of these categories and says that the Lord told them as they arose in his own mind, without knowing the things and their workings as they are, like girls building in the sand at play.
nuance: The charge is that the Jina's categories are a mental construction, not knowledge of what is; Neelakesi answers it in 290 and 291.

reading: When Mokkalan has said this, she laughs and says he does not know the Lord's nature: if Indra worships sages and goddesses as is fitting, can they be called his masters?
nuance: Her answer seems aimed at the epithet he used in 288 (worshipped by the Indras): worship by Indra does not of itself make one supreme, so the Lord's authority rests on his nature, which 291 sets out. The construal of lines 3 and 4 is not certain.
event: Neelakesi laughs at Mokkalan and begins her answer.

reading: She tells him that, not knowing her Lord's nature and scripture, he has not shown a single fault in them even in thought; since what the Lord taught is the truth, are not the categories and their workings stated before established as without error?
nuance: The argument rests on the Lord's nature: his teaching is தத்துவம் (truth itself), so the categories need no further proof once no fault is found. Mokkalan's 289 named no fault, only an origin.

title: மொக்கல வாதச் சருக்கம் 292-316 (2/8)
theme: In the second run of the debate with Mokkalan, Neelakesi defends the Jain existents of motion and rest, space and time, the soul of the body's size, its bondage, its passage between births and the persistence of things through change, against Buddhist objections she restates and answers; the run ends, in a shorter metre, with her attack on the Buddhist excuses for eating meat killed by others.
source_issues: Verses 292, 301 and 313: the tool repaired a TSCII leftover on line 3; the repaired readings are plausible but unverified.
Verse 293, line 4: நினக்குப்மாம்புண்ட has a stray ப் before மாம்; read நினக்குப் பாம்புண்ட.
Verse 309, line 4 begins டேயுடம்பு where தேயுடம்பு (the fiery body) is expected.
Verse 310, line 2: புககிடங்கொண் looks like புக்கிடங்கொண் with a dropped pulli.
Verse 312, line 1 carries a stray semicolon (அழித்து;பன்மணி).
Verse 316, line 4 (துதாங்கனத் தொன்றுமே) does not divide into words and appears corrupt.
Verses 313 to 316 are in a shorter metre than 292 to 312, but the core file records no metre change before 313.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddhist teacher Neelakesi debates in the மொக்கல வாதச் சருக்கம்

reading: Neelakesi sets out the charge that the Jain counts do not agree with one another (if the existents are five, the six substances are not they, and neither tallies with the nine categories recited), and closes by asking whether the opponent, who hides and shows his own things at will, has an account that holds together any better.
nuance: The five அத்தி (astikayas), the six substances and the nine categories are three standard Jain lists that overlap rather than compete; the charge treats them as rival totals. The answer is the run of verses that follows (293 to 296), which explains dharma and adharma, two of the five, and turns on the Buddhist's own list. Who frames the charge is not fully clear from the verse alone, though it closes with என்றாள்.

reading: Neelakesi says the opponent twisted the Jain teaching into 'we move by dharma': the Jains say only that where dharma is lacking there is no motion, for dharma lets moving things go as the sea lets a ship go, without pushing it as the wind does, and good teaching turns in him to poison like milk a snake has drunk.
nuance: The refuted claim is the opponent's version of the Jain doctrine, which Neelakesi calls a quibble (சலம்); the Jain view as she gives it separates a condition of motion (the sea) from its cause (the wind).

reading: Neelakesi says the opponent will not accept that adharma stands to rest as dharma stands to motion, and mocks him for wearing out his mouth repeating 'going and making go, staying and making stay' until he rubs his teeth too.
nuance: அல்லதற்கம் stands for adharma (the existent of rest). The pairs செல்லவும் செலுத்தவும், நில்லவும் நிறுத்தவும் are the opponent's confusion of a thing's own going or staying with being made to go or stay.

reading: Neelakesi answers the opponent's question why sea, land and space are not enough, and what is lost if dharma and adharma do not exist: if they did not, the world would have no edge, and the room of souls and matter would spill past every bound.
nuance: புற்கலம் is pudgala, matter. The Jain argument is cosmological: space is unbounded, so something other than space must mark where the inhabited world ends.

reading: Neelakesi says the opponent needs no long speech to be shown short: he admits only the five great aggregates, has no space of measureless extent, needs no conditions of rest and motion, and so, setting out to state the world's limit, only strains his own understanding.
nuance: பஞ்சமா கந்தம் is the Buddhist list of five aggregates. That the Buddhist denies space as an entity is the Jain's report; the answer is that without space and the existents of motion and rest he cannot say where the world ends.

reading: Neelakesi mocks the opponent for denying time while speaking without shame of moments, aeons and ages, and of a man as child, scholar and old ascetic in turn, and asks whether he is deluded or has eaten something that dazes him.
nuance: காலம் here is time as one of the Jain substances, not the Kural's right season. கணிகம், the moment, is the Buddhist's own word for momentariness, so the barb is that his central doctrine presupposes the time he denies.

reading: Neelakesi says that where the Jains, watching the heavenly bodies rise, take them as marking time, the opponent watches the same bodies, sees them only as themselves and says there is no time at all, though he counts and praises years by them; she sees no way to correct such excess by sound doctrine.
nuance: கோள் may mean the planets or the tenets of the two sides; the reading as heavenly bodies fits the counting of years (ஆண்டு எண்ணி).

reading: To the opponent's charge that the Jains fabricate what they neither inferred nor saw, Neelakesi answers that on that rule there could be no medical treatise to cure disease, and tells him to stop speaking in confusion and correct his own want of understanding.
nuance: கருத்து is inference and கண்கூடு perception, the two means of knowledge the Buddhist logicians allow; Neelakesi's counter-instance is a body of knowledge that rests on texts.

reading: Neelakesi takes up the opponent's rule that the soul knows only matter within the senses' range and that what such knowing does not reach cannot exist, and asks him to say, without scripture, whether Indra's queen in his far city is short or tall.
nuance: The taunt works because the Buddhist too speaks of Indra and his heaven, which no sense has reached; Neelakesi turns his own cosmology into testimony he relies on.

reading: Neelakesi takes up the objection that a soul of the body's size cannot be held inside the body, any more than one pot fits inside another of its measure, and answers that the opponent himself holds that consciousness, of the body's extent, is held within the body, so to deny the same of the self is a fool's way.
nuance: The Jain soul takes the size of the body it occupies. ஆதன் (fool) and the pot image (அளவைக் குடம்) are both slightly obscure; the parity argument with consciousness is clear.

reading: Neelakesi says that if the opponent explains consciousness as contained in the body because it is formless, there is no great dispute, since the Jains say the same of the soul, but asks how on his account formless consciousness can have contact, union, mixture or binding with a body that has form.
nuance: திருவாளன் is ironic. The verse turns the opponent's problem (how is a formless soul bound?) back on his own account of consciousness and body.

reading: When Neelakesi says that if there is bondage it is the soul that suffers, the opponent answers that when the body-mass suffers there is no 'I' to lament; she asks whether his doctrine is then that a man struck by an arrow cries 'I am wounded to death' for a pain that belongs to strangers.
nuance: பிண்டம் is the lump of the body, the Buddhist's bundle without a self. Line 3 (ஏதிலர்க்காய்ச் சோமாகி) does not construe cleanly.

reading: Neelakesi says the opponent stumbles on the high road by not seeing that 'by my acts I came to grief' is an error on his own terms, and that those who hold feeling, cognition, perception and action to belong to one being have nothing here to answer for.
nuance: உழப்பு, அறிவு, குறி, செய்கை are four of the five Buddhist aggregates (feeling, consciousness, perception, formations), the non-bodily ones. Neelakesi does not deny the list; she gives all four one owner, which is what the Buddhist denies.

reading: Neelakesi repeats the dilemma the opponent levels at the Jains (a formless soul cannot be bound, and a soul with form would be diminished, so either way fails) and says he has not taken in what was said to him and grasps no comparison however it is put.
nuance: The answer she says he ignores is the parity argument of 302: his own formless consciousness is held in the body.

reading: Neelakesi calls it great folly, not the word of those who know, to say that cognition arises and itself suffers and that as it arises something else is bewildered, says the opponent seizes only on faults, and taunts him to trap the wind in a machine.
nuance: The target seems to be a momentary cognition taken as subject of suffering; what பிறிதொன்று names is unclear, and so is the point of the wind-trap taunt.

reading: To the objection that no one carries the soul, it does not walk, and deeds cannot convey it, so the doer of good can hardly reach the world of the gods, Neelakesi answers that he speaks from outside the doctrine: does not the whirligig turn when the wind strikes it?

Neelakesi takes up the dilemma about the one reborn (if he is the same man his great sorrow has no end, and if he is not, the good he did is wasted) and says the question 'who then becomes?' only states the Jain position, mocking the opponent for hiding himself in broad daylight to escape the laughter.
nuance: The dilemma suits a Buddhist attack on a persisting soul, and the reply that it states the Jain view suggests the Jain answer of a self both same and changed (see 312); but whose dilemma it is and how எமது இட்டமே is meant are not certain.

reading: To the opponent's demand that she say how a body is gained if the soul leaves the dead body with only its karma-body and no body has been laid in the mother's, Neelakesi answers that he fails to see the fiery body, like a shadow, entering another body.
nuance: வினையுடம்பு and தேயுடம்பு are the Jain karmic and fiery (taijasa) bodies that go with the soul between births. Line 4 begins with டேயுடம்பு where தேயுடம்பு is expected.

reading: Neelakesi explains that things give room to one another as heated iron takes in water, and that the soul, embracing the father's seed and the mother's blood, settles within the body like ghee in plaster and grows along with it.

Neelakesi says the Jains need neither of the opponent's alternatives, that a deed bears fruit only while it stands or ripens only when it has wholly perished, because a deed, when explained, has persistence, arising and destruction at once.
nuance: நிலை, தோற்றம், நாசம் is the Jain triad of persistence, origination and destruction. ஐவினை in line 4 is obscure (fine, subtle, or a division error).

reading: Neelakesi gives the example of a gold pot broken and made into a jewelled crown, where the gold persists while one form is lost and another made, and says that men and gods are souls in the same way, so the opponent should not think it idle talk that the Jains repeat daily.
In a shorter metre, Neelakesi tells the Buddhists that if killing is a sin, it reaches the eater too, and rejects their claim that sin goes and joins only where there is intention.
nuance: The verse addresses the Buddhists in the plural (புத்தரே நீவிர்). குறட்கண்ணும் in line 1 is obscure, and the eater is supplied from the argument of 314 rather than named here.

reading: Neelakesi takes up the opponent's rule about eating, after renunciation, what others have cooked, and asks whether he does not count himself an ascetic while eating what a woman he has renounced has cooked.
nuance: சூனை (slaughter, or the place of killing and cooking) and the construction of lines 1 and 2 are uncertain; the argument appears to be that the Buddhist ascetic eats meat cooked by householders and denies any share in the killing.

reading: Neelakesi says that if the opponent claims the sin of killing is undone by raising the hand and saying 'let it perish', he says it as a fool, and tells him to go back and forth into his meditation.
nuance: The last line is sarcasm about Buddhist meditation as a cure for a killing that has already happened. Whether the gesture is a real Buddhist rite or the debater's caricature the verse does not show.

reading: Neelakesi takes up the question what fault there is in holding that pleasure and pain are the effects of the two kinds of deeds, and answers that on that view the suffering of the penance one later undertakes falls under the same rule.
nuance: The verse can be read either as the Buddhist objection that penance's pain is only old karma ripening, which would make penance pointless, or as Neelakesi turning that objection; line 4 (துதாங்கனத் தொன்றுமே) is corrupt and the answer is not given here.

title: மொக்கல வாதச் சருக்கம் 317-341 (3/8)
theme: In the third part of the debate with the Buddhist elder Mokkalan, Neelakesi first defends Jain asceticism against Buddhist mockery (the hardship of the body, the unwashed ascetic, the renouncing death, the vow of silence), then argues that eating meat shares the guilt of killing, using the Buddhists' own worship of the bodhi tree, relics and images to show that acts at a distance bear fruit.
source_issues: 317 line 2 and 339 line 2: ஃ was repaired from the old encoding.
326 line 4: a TSCII leftover was repaired (னென்றல்).
322 lines 3-4: சுந்தமாக and வந்தி தோறும் are obscure.
324: ஆண்வயிற்று and இழவூசி do not yield a clear sense; the verse may be corrupt.
328 line 3: (பற்றிய) is an editorial supply in brackets.
329 lines 2-3: நீங்குமின் ... வீங்கிதற் கெய்தா விடின் is hard to construe.
341 line 2: நான்முலைப் is read as நால்முலைப் (four-teated, the cow).

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddhist elder (தேரன்) of Padumapuram whom Neelakesi debates in the Mokkala sarukkam

reading: Neelakesi tells Mokkalan that no one among her people says an evil deed once done turns into pleasure, and asks whether, base fellow, he reviles them with lies only to have a reason for reviling.
nuance: The verse answers a charge, apparently that the Jains' bodily hardship is itself an evil deed they expect to ripen as bliss; she denies anyone holds it and calls the charge slander (வைதல்). The charge itself is known only from her denial.

reading: Neelakesi turns on Mokkalan's view that tormenting the body to conquer the senses is a fault: then why, she asks, do his own people practise the shaving of the head and the other rules they themselves laid down?
nuance: The answer is a tu quoque, not a defence of austerity on its merits: the Buddhist rejection of self-mortification is met by pointing to the monk's shaven head (தலைமழி).

reading: Neelakesi says the Jain ascetics want no adornment and enjoy no pleasures because they accept these as hindrances to meditation, so if dirt gathers on them it does no harm: that is simply what a human body is like.
nuance: The verse answers the stock mockery of the unwashed Jain ascetic (மலம் ஏறினும்); it does not praise dirt but makes the body's filth a fact not worth correcting. Line 4's மனையதான் is hard to divide.

reading: Neelakesi says her side never claimed to enjoy sin, that Mokkalan has proclaimed that undergoing hardship gains nothing, and that if he says giving it up brings bliss to the soul, he should become a god, go about, and show it.
nuance: The answer is a challenge to show the promised bliss rather than an argument, so the claim is marked reported. ஓவல் (ceasing, giving up) may mean giving up austerity or the final cessation; the reading turns on it.

reading: Neelakesi asks what Mokkalan gains by heaping blame on the noble ones who teach that at the time of dying even every tie to dharma must be given up, and who show that path.
nuance: The verse seems to defend the Jain practice of a chosen, renouncing death, which the opponent blames; it names no fasting, so vadakkiruththal is not tagged. ஒற்றுமை தாங்கொளீஇ in line 2 is not clear.

reading: The verse quotes Mokkalan as saying that the Jains, who hold that evil comes even from thought, allow desire through the five senses, and answers with a question whether one may then strike at every turn, saying the victim will be wiped out without trace.
nuance: The sense is unsure: சிந்தனையினும் தீவினை ஆம் may describe the Buddhist teaching that the deed lies in intention rather than the Jain view, and சுந்தமாக and வந்தி தோறும் in lines 3-4 are obscure, so no claim is recorded.

reading: Neelakesi asks whether, by firmly reviling those whose scripture says they will not eat if they so much as see a கந்தி within the house, though they eat what the women of the house set before them, Mokkalan is not taking on evil karma.
nuance: கந்தி is read here as a woman ascetic, as in Jain usage, but that and the phrase பிறகிட in line 1 are not certain; the rule of alms described cannot be fixed from the verse alone.

reading: The verse takes up a rule of conduct that turns on whether a child is female or neuter, apparently in the womb, and asks by what means one could know that it is not, setting this against Mokkalan's teaching.
nuance: The verse is too obscure to construe with confidence (ஆண்வயிற்று, இழவூசி); which rule is meant and whose it is are not clear, so no claim is recorded.

reading: The verse turns to the vow of silence: if Mokkalan objects that one who took silence for fear of lying spoke when truth was about to be harmed, Neelakesi answers that he himself says giving to everyone is good, and asks what shame there is in that, taunting him whether he will carry the street too.
nuance: The connection between the Jain vow of silence (மோனம்) and the Buddhist praise of giving to all is not clear; the taunt தெருச் சுமக்கிற்றியோ is obscure.

reading: Continuing on the silent ascetic, the verse asks whether a sign of the hand that says 'I will save you', made from the heart without speech, is concealment, and challenges Mokkalan to say what lie it broke, or whether it is fitting to say no lie was told.
nuance: Who makes the gesture is not certain: it may be the silent Jain ascetic answering by signs, or an image of the Buddha with the hand raised in protection. The edition's line 4 needed repair.

reading: Neelakesi announces that she can establish, as a good deed, the teaching that eating flesh is a fault because one fears the deed of killing, and since Mokkalan has drawn his bow to have his truth accepted, she will now speak.
nuance: The verse opens the argument on flesh that runs to the end of the chapter; the bow (வில்லினை ஏற்றி) is the debate itself.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if the Buddhists worship the bodhi tree out of devotion to the Buddhas, they should rather worship the Buddhas' devotees, and if they say the tree breeds devotion to the Buddhas, then the sinner should worship their bowl, umbrella and sandals too.
nuance: The reductio makes any object associated with the Buddhas equally worthy, so tree-worship proves too much. It also prepares the argument of 330-331: if an indirect act toward the Buddha gains merit, an indirect part in killing gains sin. பத்தம் in line 4 is read as the bowl; பற்றிய is the edition's bracketed supply.

reading: Neelakesi says that if Mokkalan holds it right to tell people to leave those who show grace as the Buddhas did, then what his people do teaches only harm, and with that she ends this point.
nuance: The verse ends with என்றாள், closing a turn of the debate. Lines 2-3 (நீங்குமின், வீங்கிதற் கெய்தா விடின்) do not yield a clear argument; தேரமற்று may hold the address தேர (elder), the title of a Buddhist monk.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if Mokkalan establishes that praising, long ago, the one who left a tooth, or worshipping a bodily relic after hearing old stories, becomes a good deed afterwards, then he cannot say that killing and eating are without fault.
nuance: பல்லுடையான் is read as the one whose tooth is kept, a tooth relic; உறுப்பே தொழுதாலும் supports a relic cult. The argument is by parity: the Buddhist cannot accept merit at a distance and deny sin at a distance.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if, when someone makes golden images like the lord so that worshippers may praise him, both the worshippers and the makers gain good, then those who kill and those who eat both fall into cruel karma.
nuance: The Buddhist premise is granted, not answered, and turned into the Jain conclusion: merit shared between maker and worshipper means sin shared between killer and eater.

reading: Neelakesi says that eating the body of a creature that simply died and eating what was killed by the spear both bring evil, and compares it to going to a woman left alone after her companion was struck down: is not that union a fault, fellow?
nuance: The simile seems to say that one who did not do the harm still joins in its gain and so shares the fault; who struck the companion is not said, so the reading of line 3 is tentative.

reading: Neelakesi says that the Jains carry the peacock feather and guard other lives, and what they fulfil is compassion, whereas Mokkalan eats stinking flesh and gnaws bones so that his body grows fat, and asks whether, apart from that, he has any compassion.
nuance: The peacock feather (பீலி) is the Jain ascetic's whisk for brushing small creatures from his path; the contrast is between an ascetic's tool for sparing lives and a monk who eats lives.

reading: Neelakesi says that as peacock feathers drop at a shake and are gathered, so Mokkalan has no thought of eating only flesh that has fallen of itself: he stands craving meat and calls for it, doer of evil.
nuance: The verse meets an implied counter, that the Jains too use what comes from animals: their feathers are shed, while the monk's meat is sought.

reading: Neelakesi asks what evil deed Mokkalan has fallen into, in saying that because those who kill and cook deer, fish and other creatures and those who give the meat are hidden from him, the deed of killing does not reach him.
nuance: This is a Jain's account of the Buddhist rule that meat is allowed when the monk did not see, hear or suspect that it was killed for him; the verse states only the hiding of killer and giver.

reading: Neelakesi says that if the monk claims he does not share in the killing because the animal was not marked out for him, he who plucks it up and eats still sins, and he stands level with highway robbers who go out on the road and waylay travellers.
nuance: பூப்போல் செறிக்கப்படும் உயிர் in line 3, lives crowded like flowers, may mean the many small lives harmed with the meat; the line is not clear.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if Mokkalan says paying a price for meat is like a fair act, then by giving daily to those who live by the net he is always wanting killing, man without virtue.
nuance: Line 2 (வினையாக்க நிலையுமீறு, the growth, stay and end of karma) seems to name a Buddhist concession that the argument uses, but it is not clear how.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if, with money given to the Buddhist monastery, people without understanding go and fetch meat, that is a scandal, and money given for a meat curry joins its giver to the killers in broad daylight.
nuance: எம்பள்ளி in line 2 (our monastery) is odd in her mouth and may be the Buddhists' words quoted.

reading: Neelakesi charges that Mokkalan holds the flesh set on the tongue to be the real gain, since its pleasure is his, and that, not by faith placed in his god, he wipes away the cruel deed by calling the meat pure.
nuance: The claim is the Jain's version of the Buddhist rule of permitted, 'pure' meat, and the school would not put it as a wiping-away of guilt. வேவினை and சிரத்தை செயலன்று are hard to fit together.

reading: Neelakesi says that, like a man of ripened lust who keeps thinking when he will get the maiden of his kin, Mokkalan has agreed to eat the hare and the other creatures already eaten, and those still living too.
nuance: The simile makes craving for meat like lust that cannot wait. முன்தினப்பட்ட முயல் may only mean animals usually eaten, or may glance at the birth story of the hare that gave itself as food; the verse does not decide it.

reading: Neelakesi answers the comparison of meat with the four-teated cow's milk: flesh, made of stinking semen and blood, is not pure like milk, she will say it without fault, and the word of Vaaman is at odds with the world itself.
nuance: வாமன் is taken as the Buddha, as the opponent's teacher; the name is also used of the Jina elsewhere, so the identification rests on the context. The verse assumes, as the world does, that milk is pure food and flesh is not.

title: மொக்கல வாதச் சருக்கம் 342-366 (4/8)
theme: Neelakesi presses Mokkalan on eating flesh, answering his defence by intention with the seller who kills for the buyer's price and the teacher whose permission sustains the killing; worsted, he attacks Jain bodily mortification as profitless self-torment, and she answers with the Buddha's own ten perfections and ascetic rules and the bodhisattva's praised sufferings, then attacks the gift of the body as a killing of the lives within it, and begins to defend the Jain view that plants have life.
source_issues: 343: lines 2-3 (ஈப்பவுங் கொள்பவு நேர்து மவையவை / தூப்பெனு மில்லன) do not construe with confidence.
344 line 3 (ஓவெனு முன்விலை வாணிக ரென்றினர்) is obscure; the word division may be corrupt.
346 lines 2-3 and 348 line 2 (துரந்தனள்) are hard to construe; the speaker's reference is uncertain.
356 line 4 (றுற்றியுய்த்த றன்னொடுதுதாங்கென்றாத்தர்) is run together and partly corrupt; துதாங்கு (dhutanga) and ஆத்தர் can be made out.
357 line 2 (நேருமனையி லுண்மையா னீரும்வேண்டி னீரெனக்) does not scan or construe cleanly.
362 line 1 was repaired from a TSCII leftover; lines 3-4 remain obscure.
364 is largely obscure (வயாத்திரு, மெழு கூனொடு); the opponent's argument cannot be recovered.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddhist elder at Padumapuram, named in 266 as the Buddha's first disciple and Arkkachandra's teacher

reading: Neelakesi argues that the noble, who shun toddy as they shun poison, ought by the same reasoning to shun flesh, and asks where an ascetic firm in truth is to be found when the one who takes flesh and eats it is none other than Mokkalan.
nuance: The argument works from a ban the Buddhists already keep: the monk renounces toddy, so the debater asks why the same judgement stops short of meat. The last line turns the general question into a charge against the elder himself.

reading: She says that if the brahmins' scripture and his own are both claimed to bring benefit, she can grant what each tells one to give up and to take, but since both speak only of things that are not clean, he has never had a sharp judgement.
nuance: The verse pairs the Buddhist scripture with the brahmins' (பார்ப்பனி ஓத்து) as alike in allowing what is unclean, which in context means flesh. The middle lines are hard to construe and the reading given is tentative.

reading: She grants, for argument, his plea that the eater incurs no evil deed because he never thought of consuming the small creatures in the flesh, and answers that the sellers of meat want only the price, not the deed, so the killing is done for the buyer.
nuance: This answers the Buddhist defence by intention: the eater did not will the death. The reply moves the question from the eater's mind to the market, where the merchant's motive is the price the eater pays. Line 3 (ஓவெனு முன்) is obscure.

reading: She recalls his saying that those who join in acts such as pulling out an arrow already lodged in a beast are not touched by the deed, and asks who here shows compassion by eating while pleading such excuses.
nuance: The example of the lodged arrow seems to stand for every share in a death that comes after the blow; the debater treats it as a loophole. Line 3 and the word கடம் in line 4 are unclear, so the sense of the comparison is uncertain.

reading: She turns his own teaching back on him: if, as he says, a demon with a mind set on eating earns a lasting evil deed, then by his own words the will to eat is what binds, and the one who eats is bound.
nuance: The Buddhist emphasis on intention, used in 344 to excuse the eater, is here made to condemn him: the desire to eat is an intention too. The figure of the demon (பேய்) may glance at Neelakesi's own past as a flesh-taking demoness. Lines 2 and 3 do not construe clearly.

reading: She says he knows that whatever is taught as dharma is taken up as dharma, yet does not see that teaching it earns dharma for the teacher; that flesh is a fault is no outsider's slander, and if all renounced it, who would go near killing?
nuance: The verse joins two points: people do what their teachers call dharma, and if all gave up flesh the killing would end. Together they make the teacher, not only the buyer, answerable for the slaughter his permission sustains.

reading: She reminds him that he has even her own word, that she, standing at the head of dharma and joined to grace, drove violence away; what then does holding to cruelty gain him, and is anything more precious than the lasting life of beings? Let him think and see.
nuance: துரந்தனள் யான் is a woman speaking of herself, which suggests Neelakesi cites her own turning from the bloodshed of her shrine (9) as the example of a mind that gave up violence; this is a reading, not certain.

reading: Finding that his defence of eating flesh can no longer stand, Mokkalan, snarling like a dog, turns to argue with the fair-browed woman against the mortification of the body.
nuance: காயக் கிலேசம், torment of the body, names the Jain outer austerities; the debate shifts from meat to penance because the Buddhist now attacks rather than defends. The narrator's simile of the dog shows where the poem's sympathy lies.
event: Worsted on eating flesh, Mokkalan angrily turns to attack the Jain practice of bodily mortification (காயக் கிலேசம்).

reading: Mokkalan tells her that drying in the sun, soaking in the open, giving up food in fasts and forsaking sleep night and day in a hot sea of suffering brings no gain at all, O long-eyed one.
nuance: The list is of the Jain outer austerities: exposure, fasting, wakefulness. The claim is answered in 354 to 358, where Neelakesi shows that the Buddhists' own ascetic practices and their praise of the bodhisattva's sufferings are hardships of the same kind.

reading: He argues that if some good were to be seen in wasting the body away, then burning in fire, throwing oneself from a height and wasting with disease could all be called penance, and bids her say why not.
nuance: A reductio: the Jain must either say what separates his fasting from self-destruction or accept the absurd conclusion. The argument assumes that pain itself is what the Jain values, which the Jain reply in 358 and 359 does not grant.

reading: He adds that cutting one's own wounds and enduring being split, forcing open the eyes with sticks, throwing oneself from a lofty mountain, and the practices of the 'lords' who do such things, are of no use.
nuance: அண்ணலார் (the lords) is likely ironic, aimed at the ascetics who are honoured for such feats. The list mixes known ascetic exploits with plain self-harm to make the line between them vanish.

reading: He says that if tormenting oneself were the old and good dharma, then tearing out tongues, hanging oneself to die, leaping into fire to perish and climbing the cruel red stake would all be excellent.
nuance: The closing image of the impaling stake (கழு) is the death of a criminal, so the argument ranks the ascetic with the condemned man. The verse ends the attack that 354 begins to answer.

reading: Neelakesi replies by naming what his own teacher laid down: giving, conduct, forbearance, fitting vigour, flawless meditation, understanding with skill in means, the firm resolve of compassion, strength and knowledge: these are the ten perfections.
nuance: ஈரைம் பாரமீதை, the twice-five perfections, is the tenfold list in which skill in means, resolve, strength and knowledge follow the six of giving, conduct, forbearance, vigour, meditation and wisdom. Here the Jain debater gives the list fairly, since her point needs it to be the Buddhists' own.

reading: She goes on with the ascetic rules his teacher gave: living at the foot of a tree, dwelling in the open, sitting and standing without lying down, wearing cast-off cloth, sleeping in the burning ground, entering houses in turn without passing any by, and eating with the rest.
nuance: The items match the Buddhist ascetic observances (துதாங்கம், named in 356): the debater lists them to show that Buddhism too has practices of hardship. வருச்சியார் புகுதல் seems to mean going for alms without skipping houses; the last item is unclear.

reading: The list ends with taking only three robes, stopping the meal at the word 'enough', sleeping on whatever place is given, not eating a second time, treating alms as a fault (?) and not going where one had planned: these, she says, are the ascetic practices the Buddha spoke.
nuance: துதாங்கு is the Buddhist term for these voluntary austerities and ஆத்தர் (the trustworthy one) names the Buddha as their author, so the list is presented as his own word. The fourth line is badly corrupted.

reading: With the ten perfections and the ascetic practices come many hardships, she says, yet he declares that when sharp cold, sun and hunger come together, good dharma cannot join the mind.
nuance: She sets the Buddhists' own hard practices beside their claim that hardship keeps dharma out of the mind: the claim is answered by their own rule-book. Line 2 does not construe cleanly.

reading: She says he calls it glorious that the bodhisattva endured having slices of his flesh cut and his body split by the sword in the doing of dharma, yet with a mind that never stays on the good path he speaks against those who do great penance: a fool.
nuance: The bodhisattva is not named; the cutting of flesh and splitting by the sword recall the birth stories of self-giving, which the debate attacks elsewhere (214, 243, 360). Here the stories are used only to show inconsistency: the Buddhist praises bodily suffering when his own hero bears it.

reading: She says that as he holds the ten perfections to be the burden by which bodhisattvas become Buddhas, so the Jains too hold that conduct and vows are what make one a Siddha, the perfected one.
nuance: பாரவட்டம் and the last line are obscure. The parallel is the point: each school has a discipline that leads to its perfected state, so the Buddhist cannot call the Jain discipline mere torment without saying the same of his own.

reading: She asks: if it is good that the bodhisattva gave himself on the great mountain to a beast hungry for flesh, though the many lives within his body die, is it good also to poison the water that many drink, saying 'may the sick man be cured'?
nuance: The birth story of the body given to a hungry beast is alluded to, not told (மா is any beast). The argument rests on the Jain view that a body teems with small lives, so one act of giving is many acts of killing; a Buddhist would weigh the gift by its intent, which the verse does not consider.

reading: If he answers that the giver knew the others would not die, or that poison is plainly not good, she asks how the countless lives in the giver's own body and the flesh that came to be killed are not then counted a fault.
nuance: The verse anticipates two replies and turns both: whatever the giver knew, the deaths in his body follow from his act. Line 1 is hard to read and the first reply is uncertain.

reading: Answering his example of hair and nails, which grow and change yet have no life, she says that hair grows only where the living soul abides in the body, and that the rising growth seen in a tree is of another kind.
nuance: This opens the argument on whether plants have life, a Jain tenet (trees are one-sensed beings) that the Buddhist denies. The text was repaired at line 1, and lines 3 and 4 do not construe cleanly.

reading: You spoke of trees growing, folding up and differing in their spreading leaves, she says; these and the rest are found together in the living beings of this world as well.
nuance: The argument is from shared marks: what grows, closes at night and puts out leaves of different shapes behaves as the animals do. It is an inference by likeness, which the Buddhist answers with lifeless things that change (365, 366).

reading: She takes up the 'craving' (வயா) of the growing pumpkin, a mark of life in plants, and tells him that he erred in his account of it, but the lines that give his account are obscure.
nuance: வயா, the craving of pregnancy, is ascribed to plants to argue that they feel. What the Buddhist said about the pumpkin and the wax and flesh of line 3 cannot be made out.

reading: She recalls that when it was urged that plants wilt at every touch, he answered that the hide one eats also shrinks when brought to the fire, and she asks how the change of a thing without awareness can be the same.
nuance: The hide example is answered again at 369, where the hide is said not to be like the living plant. சேதனை இல்லாய் may address Mokkalan as lacking sense, or describe the hide as lacking awareness.

reading: She sets out his further reply: if trees are said to have life because their budding, flowering and power to cure grave disease show growth from their own cause, then the iron and the magnet drawing together would also be such a change.
nuance: The magnet is the Buddhist counter-example to the Jain argument from plants' responsiveness. Her answer to it lies beyond this chapter, so the claim is left as reported here.

title: மொக்கல வாதச் சருக்கம் 367-390 (5/8)
theme: The middle of the Mokkala debate: Neelakesi argues against the Buddhist teacher Mokkalan that trees and the elements have souls; he turns to attack the Jain view that a thing both lasts and perishes, that substance stands with its qualities and that a thing can be called inexpressible; she answers each and turns his dilemma of identity and difference back on the Buddhist aggregates, and they dispute milk turning to curd and gram to mash as examples of transformation.
source_issues: 372 line 2: the edition's '•' is the old encoding of ஃ (repaired in the core).
383 line 3: a TSCII leftover was repaired in the core (ேரி); the reading பேரிவை is kept.
388 line 1: பயற்றியல்டே is corrupt.
389 line 2: பையைகளேஎன்னும் looks corrupt; the line's sense is doubtful.
390: obscure throughout; the reply falls in the next chapter.
367-374: no speech verb names the speaker; Neelakesi is taken as speaker from the story and the Jain 'we' (யாம், 367).

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddhist teacher, named as the Buddha's chief disciple, whom Neelakesi debates

reading: Neelakesi holds that trees have life by the same mark as we do, since they change with the seasons, and answers that the heat and cold Mokkalan offered to show her reason faulty work on us in just the same way.
nuance: The verse picks up an exchange already under way: Mokkalan has called her reason (ஏது) fallacious by saying heat and cold, not life, make trees change; she turns the objection back on the human body.

reading: If Mokkalan rejects the analogy by pointing to knots and heat in trees as mere alterations, she says, he has thrown down the truth that the changes of an embodied body are felt.
nuance: கிரந்தி is taken as a knot or swelling in the wood; the sense of the second half turns on that and on reading பார்ப்படுத்தாய் as 'cast to the ground'.

reading: She meets the objection that withering does not prove life: a tortoise whose skin is unlike ours also withers, and the taro of the garden comes to its natural end, so withering belongs to the living.
nuance: The tortoise clause (தோலொத்திராமையும்) is hard to divide; the reading that it is an animal unlike us which still withers is a guess.

reading: Neelakesi says that when the Jains argue trees have life because cut trees heal as cut bodies do, Mokkalan calls this an error and lists it among faults, like men risen in madness.
nuance: She reports his charge of fault only to mock it; the comparison to the mad is aimed at him.

reading: She compares his refusal to accept the souls her scripture names, the beings that have earth and the rest for body, to calling a land's people by the land's name, a confusion of the thing with what it lives in.
nuance: The simile of the land and its dwellers is compressed and its direction is not certain; the claim follows the Jain doctrine that earth, water, fire, wind and plants are bodies of one-sensed souls, set out in the sermon (77).

reading: Everyone calls trees the fixed beings (தாவரம்), she says, and he does not know even that; why does he ask 'on whose word do you say it' as if tying his robe?
nuance: The last line's jibe about the Buddhist robe (சீவரம்) and its knot is obscure; it seems to mock his demand for an authority.

reading: If a human-born being had no more than a tree-soul's knowledge of the body, she asks, why would those who revere the Bodhisattva of that nature refuse to make a distinction where he is greater?
nuance: The verse seems to turn the Buddhist's own Bodhisattva, who passed through many births, against his denial that trees have souls, but the syntax of lines 3 and 4 cannot be fixed.

reading: Trees and the rest, even the shy plant that shrinks, live by feeding and die when they are not fed, as plainly as stingy rich men live on gruel.
nuance: நாணமுடைய மரம் is read as the plant that shrinks at a touch; the comparison in line 4 with misers who live on gruel is uncertain.

reading: Shaken in his hold on his view that trees and the deluded alike lack lasting souls, Mokkalan tells her to set out her scripture, and he will search out the faults in its nayas and its means of knowledge.
nuance: The first two lines are hard; whatever their exact sense, the verse marks the debate's turn from the souls of plants to the Jain theory of knowledge.
event: Mokkalan, unable to hold his ground on the souls of trees, challenges Neelakesi to lay out her scripture so that he can attack its nayas and pramanas.

reading: Mokkalan tells her to hear the faults that follow from holding a thing both to stand and to perish, to be and not to be, to be one and to be different, the narrator noting that he did not know her side fully.
nuance: The narrator's remark that he spoke without knowing all her position (முற்ற மவளது பக்க மறிதலில்) is the work's verdict in advance on the attack that follows.
event: Mokkalan announces the faults he will find in the Jain view of things as both lasting and perishing.

reading: Mokkalan argues that if a thing must stay the same it can do no work, and if it perishes then what appears is new each time, so her thing is faulty either way.
nuance: Neelakesi answers in 378 that these faults belong to one-sided views. Line 2 (காயத்தின் றன்மைய) is not clear in its detail.

reading: Neelakesi answers that the faults he listed cannot be charged against those who hold that things both stand and do not stand, are one and then different, have gone and have not gone, each in its own respect.
Mokkalan says that since she calls the lasting qualities eternal and the passing ones non-eternal, a thing standing apart from both kinds of quality cannot be accepted.
nuance: Neelakesi answers in 380 that no one held the substance to stand apart from its qualities.

reading: Neelakesi asks why, having granted that the lasting qualities endure and the perishing ones pass, he will not grant the substance, and who ever said that the substance bearing them was something not joined to them.

Mokkalan presses a dilemma: if there is no thing besides the qualities the thing is only a label; if the qualities are distinct, they are distinct things; if they are one, they are one; she must say which.
nuance: Neelakesi turns the same dilemma back on him in 382 and 383.

reading: Neelakesi replies that his own school lays impermanence, no-soul, endless suffering and impurity on all five aggregates, so her position does not clash with his path.
nuance: தூய்தன்மை is read as தூய்து அன்மை, 'not pure', which makes the four the Buddhist marks the Manimekalai also lists (அநித்தம் துக்கம் அநான்மா அசுசி). Her point is that the Buddhist too ascribes qualities to a bearer.

reading: She turns his dilemma on him: if there is no aggregate besides the noble truth it is a mere name, if they are different they are two things, and if both are names of one they are one; let him say which.
nuance: ஆரிய சத்தை is read as the noble truth (ārya-satya); if it means 'noble existence' the retort is the same in form. The speaker is named by the verb கூறினளே.

reading: Mokkalan argues that if she says she will not say, she contradicts herself in saying it, and if she says it one way the faults already named attach to her.
nuance: The target is the Jain mode of the inexpressible; Neelakesi answers in 385. The second line's turns on சொல்லலன் are hard to follow exactly.

reading: Neelakesi answers that a thing is not in another's nature and is in its own, and that its many qualities cannot be stated at once; that is the only sense in which it cannot be spoken, which those who do not understand words miss.
nuance: Line 4's 'outsiders' speech' (புறத்தீர் உரை) is not clear; it seems to say the charge is the outsiders' misunderstanding.

reading: Mokkalan objects that if her scripture means transformation, then when milk becomes curd and the milk has not perished, the curd ought still to be called milk, which is absurd.
nuance: He addresses her by her eyes streaked red like a fish (சேல்). Neelakesi answers in 387.

reading: Neelakesi says the substance is the mass of form, while milk, curd and buttermilk are names of its stages; the milk perishes and curd arises, so the thing has a threefold nature.
Mokkalan says she holds the change of gram into a cooked mash as her doctrine, and demands that she show plainly some one thing apart in both states, or he will call it a turtle's hair.
nuance: 'Turtle's hair' (ஆமை மயிர்) is the stock example of the non-existent. Line 1's பயற்றியல்டே is corrupt. Neelakesi answers in 389.

reading: Neelakesi says the lump that perished and the paste that arose are both the thing in its modes, which differ from each other, and she too affirms loss and arising for the form.
nuance: பையைகளேஎன்னும் in line 2 looks corrupt; it is read as naming the modes.

reading: Mokkalan retorts that if she wants changing things to become gram and mash by change, then gram poured with charcoal and water should also burn, and asks whether that is the same.
nuance: The verse is obscure and the answer falls in the next chapter, so the claim is marked reported here; the reading of கரியும் as charcoal is a guess.

title: மொக்கல வாதச் சருக்கம் 391-414 (6/8)
theme: In the Mokkala debate Neelakesi and the Buddhist thera argue over whether a quality and its substance are one or different, how atoms join into matter, and the Jain claim that a thing exists and does not exist in different respects; he attacks it with the gooseberry, the elephant, the bull's horn, the hare's horn and right and left hands, and she answers by separating substance from state, real things from fictions, and naming from existence.
source_issues: 391 line 1 (பாவியுண்டா) and 394 line 3 (தியம்) cannot be construed with confidence.
397 line 3 (ஆரிடமாய) and 403 line 4 (கலைக்குண்மை) are obscure; 408 line 3 (குழமண்ணர்களா) is not a word I can construe.
404 line 1 lists கன்று among things that never grow horns, which clashes with the calf of 402; the word may be damaged.
409 line 4 ends with a doubled full stop (ஒத்தாய்..) and 413 line 4 has none.
396 line 4 joins the name as றேரனுமே, so the speaker's form is given as written.

cast.role: the demoness converted to the Jain dharma, now its debater
the Buddhist thera (தேரன்) whom Neelakesi debates in the Mokkala sarukkam

reading: Answering the cooked-pulse example, Neelakesi says the gross pulse changes in its way and the water too passes off as vapour, so that when both are spent together into the mash it is folly to grant a change to one and deny it to the other.
nuance: The verse replies to 390, where the Buddhist mocks pulse and water boiled together into கும்மாயம்; the example is the stock Jain one for a substance that persists through change. Line 1 (பாவியுண்டா) is hard to construe, and the speaker is inferred from the alternation of என்றான் and என்றாள்.

reading: The Buddhist objects that if perishing, arising and persisting are qualities, then the thing that perishes, arises and persists would have to be some further substance, and asks what that could be.
nuance: He takes the Jain triad of origination, persistence and destruction and tries to force it into a split between qualities and a bearer that is never found, which suits his own view that there is no lasting substance behind momentary events.

reading: Neelakesi replies that the quality spoken of is the qualified substance itself and the substance is never apart from its many qualities, so she holds them both different and one, and his confusion is to treat these as contradictory.
nuance: This is the Jain position of difference-in-identity (வேறென ஒன்றென) between quality and substance, stated against the Buddhist demand for one or the other; the Jain refuses the either-or rather than choosing a side.

reading: The Buddhist asks the woman who holds the scripture how matter (புற்கலம்), the primary substance, joining with itself, spreads out as stones, water, earth and fire, and whether the things that meet enter into one another.
nuance: புற்கலம் here is the Jain pudgala, matter, not the Buddhist Pudgalavada person of 248. தியம் in line 3 is not a word I can construe; the sense of the question is clear from 395 to 397.

reading: Neelakesi tells him to hear what the scripture lays down: the atoms have qualities fit for binding, are hard to separate once joined, and, setting aside the classes that do not bind, build up from the two-atom compound onward.
nuance: The appeal is to ஓத்து, the Jain canon; the rule of excluded classes (நீத்த வருக்க நெறிமை) seems to be the doctrine that only atoms of certain degrees of quality bind, but the line is compressed.

reading: The thera argues that if the aggregate (கந்தம்) rises from the dyad upward, then atoms that crowd together and touch must, being round, have an inside and sides, and so are seen to be divisible.
nuance: கந்தம் here is the aggregate of atoms, not the Buddhist five aggregates; the argument, that contact implies parts and parts deny indivisibility, is the Buddhist objection to atoms in general.

tamil: ஓரிட மாய முதற் பொருட் குள்ளும் புடையுஞ்சொல்லிப்
reading: Neelakesi says he prattles in giving an inside and sides to a primary substance that holds one place, enlarging it to split it, and answers that by sharing the same place atoms reach plurality and become form, as happens even with cognition.
nuance: The reply seems to rest on the Jain view that many atoms can occupy one point of space, so that combination does not require parts; the comparison with அறிவு in line 3 is obscure.

reading: The Buddhist, whom the narrator calls great in the dharma that gives away women, mocks her: the hill gooseberry is in her hand, and at that very moment she will say it is not in Uraiyur, as if this were a truth hard for others to see.
nuance: He parodies the Jain claim that a thing exists from its own place and does not exist from another as a truism. The narrator's epithet (பெண்டானம் ஈயும் அறம்) turns Neelakesi's earlier charge about the bodhisattva who gave his wives into a sneer at the speaker.

reading: He goes on that everyone knows fire is hot, water cold and wind thin, and says that if she says these are Buddha's words she will not call them false, yet she has spoiled them like a whole pot of gruel.
nuance: The run of lines 3 and 4 is unclear: who calls what false and what the gruel (முழுக்கூழ்) stands for cannot be fixed from the verse alone.

reading: He adds that she would call the rutting elephant tied to the post non-existent, though when it has come and stands here its existence cannot be denied, and curses her words; the narrator names him as one who has seen a release like a burnt seed.
nuance: The closing epithet (வெந்து ... வித்தின் அனைத்தாகிய வீடு) gives the Buddhist release as a seed burnt so it cannot sprout again; whether the narrator means it as praise or as the Jain view of nirvana as extinction is not said.

reading: Neelakesi answers that she called the thing non-existent there and existent where it is, stating non-existence and existence together, and that he finishes only the arguments he wants and will not also say the same of her Lord whom the gods throng to worship in the golden fort.
nuance: This answers 398 to 400: the Jain claim is not that the gooseberry or the elephant is absent, but that existence and non-existence each hold in their own respect. The point of line 4 about the Lord in the golden fort is unclear.

reading: The Buddhist says that if the horn of the killing bull is non-existent in the young calf, then, since she speaks of existence and non-existence together, she should say the calf is the killing bull at that very time.

Neelakesi replies that a difference of thing is spoken of only when the bull has arisen; for the calf not yet grown, non-existence comes first while the existence of the substance stands firm, and nowhere does either change.
nuance: She separates the persisting substance from its states: the horn is a state not yet arisen, so its absence in the calf is prior non-existence and not the absence of the animal. கலைக்கு in line 4 is unclear.

reading: He counters that a calf, a hare, the beast called donkey and a hill never come to have a horn on the head as a limb, so her distinction fails, and some things are simply non-existent in some respects.
nuance: The hare's and donkey's horns are the stock examples of what never exists; why கன்று (calf) appears in this list, after the calf of 402 that does grow horns, is unclear.

reading: Neelakesi says no one speaks of distinctions by taking up a horn that does not exist as if it did; if he wants distinctions he must learn the existence and non-existence of things that cannot stand without joining, or else he too is granting the donkey a horn.
nuance: Her reply limits the scope of her own doctrine: existence and non-existence in respects are said of real substances and their states, not of fictions.

reading: Mokkalan laughs: there is no right or left hand except by relation, she says the same of that, she of great cunning has quickly understood both to exist, and she is very good indeed.
nuance: The praise is sarcasm; his point is that relational terms like right and left have no being of their own.
event: Mokkalan laughs at Neelakesi.

reading: Neelakesi answers that if a thing exists only by this relation, both sides arise together, so each side becomes void and the limbs too, and tells him to go round now like the shaft of an oil press, which is his safety.
nuance: The oil-press image mocks an argument that goes in circles; the middle of the verse is compressed.

reading: He replies that hands and feet do not get their being from relation, since the body must have the parts named, and says she has made the little humans of the world into lumps of clay.
nuance: குழமண்ணர்களா in line 3 is obscure and the turn of his argument is hard to follow; he seems to concede that limbs are not merely relational.

tamil: னாலாவ தான முடிவி னாயொடு நண்டு மொத்தாய்..
reading: Neelakesi says the hands, which exist by relation to the feet, also come to be by their own former nature, and that if he asks in what way they exist, his conclusion makes him like the dog and the crab.
nuance: The dog and crab comparison is an insult whose point is lost; the doctrine seems to be that a thing has both its own nature and a relational one.

reading: The Buddhist says she demands that the word 'is not' (அல்) in his scripture mean 'does not exist' (இல்), and asks whether one who says 'that is not a dog, it is a jackal' is saying the jackal does not exist.
nuance: He separates negation of identity (அல்) from negation of existence (இல்), a distinction Tamil grammar itself draws.

reading: Neelakesi says that when the cognition 'dog or jackal?' arises he claimed that 'not' is known only after examining both words, that he does not know words or seek the way of those who know, and that prattling many words is what ghosts do.
nuance: Line 2 seems to report his position before she dismisses it; her answer is mostly scorn, not a counter-argument.

reading: The thera, smiling a little at the woman with the chosen garland, says she claims a thing that does not exist has neither name nor cognition, and asks whether dependence, separation, meeting and the absence of a mind are not named so only for want of knowing.
nuance: சார்வு is the Buddhist term for dependent arising; the list in line 2 seems meant as names for absences or relations that have no substance, but the force of line 3 (உணராமையிற்கு) is uncertain.
event: The Buddhist thera smiles at Neelakesi.

reading: Neelakesi asks whether anyone, even a common man, who studied the meaning the Trustworthy One gave in that scripture could fail to know, and says that of all he has dragged in he cannot name one by the scripture's account that has a name and a cognition but no existence.
nuance: ஆத்தன் is the Apta, the trustworthy teacher, the Jain title for the Jina; சாத்தன் stands for anyone at all. The appeal is to scripture, but made as a debating challenge.

reading: The Buddhist says she always holds that the nature of one thing does not belong to another, yet water heated as iron is heated stirs and takes on fire's quality, and if so her long thesis is diminished.
nuance: He turns a Jain thesis against itself with heated water. The reply is not in this chapter: 415 turns to the soul in the body, which may be her answer by analogy, but the text does not say so.

title: மொக்கல வாதச் சருக்கம் 415-438 (7/8)
theme: In the Mokkala debate Neelakesi and the Buddhist elder Mokkalan argue whether the soul that gives and does penance is the one rewarded in heaven, whether a thing can change yet persist, whether a quality leaves its substance (the flower's scent in a pot), what release is and why the freed do not return, and whether the Jina can know all things in all times at once and speak without karma.
source_issues: 417 lines 3-4: the speech-close என்றா/டானத்தின் runs across the line break (என்றாள் தானத்தின்?), and the verse ends with a second என்றாள்.
420 line 1: நூறான் இரும்பாய் is obscure.
422 line 3: show repaired • as ஃ (அஃதால்).
424 line 2: நாயிற்கு is obscure; probably a corruption.
425: no closing என்றாள்/என்றான்; speaker inferred from the alternation; பாக்கனாய் obscure.
429 lines 2-3: யோடுகொடு and கூர்ங்கை are obscure, perhaps for யோகொடு.
431 line 4: என்லை is probably a misprint for எல்லை.
436 lines 2-4 and 437 line 4 (அன்னம்) are hard to construe.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddhist elder at Padumapuram, called the thera (தேரன்)

reading: Neelakesi argues that if the soul stays joined with the body it has taken, seeing and knowing are rightly said to belong to the soul that is there, and calls Mokkalan unlearned: for him, who has only the heap of the body, the working of that heap goes wrong.
nuance: பிண்டம் (the lump or heap) is her word for what the Buddhist puts in place of a soul; the point is that perception needs a perceiver dwelling in the body, not a mere aggregate.

reading: Mokkalan replies that she holds the soul to be not other than the body in place, and objects that then no one can say today that the man who did great dharma, beginning with alms, becomes a god in the course he goes to, so all such deeds would be despised.
nuance: The objection takes the Jain teaching that the soul fills the body it occupies and argues that a soul bound to this body's place cannot be the one rewarded in heaven; 417 answers it.

reading: Neelakesi answers that the same abiding soul is there when it goes about giving without stint, when it leaves pride and suffers to keep its vows, and when it is in heaven, and tells him to take this as the truth of giving.
nuance: She grounds the worth of giving (தானம்) on the identity of the giver across lives: the giver and the one in heaven are one soul. The value of the gift is made to rest on the reward reaching its doer.

reading: Mokkalan says she shows that a thing has no being at a time other than its own, and argues, addressing her as the woman with scented tresses, that then the good soul of a world-famed ascetic would not exist in the time to come, and keeping the precepts would be wasted toil.
nuance: The first line can be construed in more than one way; read here as his statement of her view that each state of a thing exists in its own time, turned against continuity of reward.

tamil: சாற்றி னுயிர்தன் பொழுதே யுண்மை தங்கு மென்றாள்.
reading: Neelakesi answers that whether the soul is suffering in austerity, guarding hard vows, fasting and wasting away, or is called an exalted unblinking god, its being stays with it in each of its times.
nuance: இமையான், the one who does not blink, is a god; the verse places the ascetic and the god he becomes on one line of a single soul's existence.

tamil: தேறார் தெருண்டா ரெனச் சொல்லினன் றேர னும்மே.
reading: Mokkalan charges that she says one thing does not become another, and in the same breath teaches that milk becomes curd, so her words are like those of people who contradict themselves; the thera says those who do not understand think they are clear.
nuance: The first half-line (நூறான் இரும்பாய் நிகழாமை) seems to give her example of what does not become something else; its exact sense is not clear. The charge is against the Jain view that a thing both persists and changes.

reading: Neelakesi replies that she said suitable things become their effects by meeting their own causes, and asks whether she, like a madman, would say anything becomes anything; she tells him to speak along the line of the seed, and calls him a white elephant.
nuance: The seed (வித்து) is the model of change by proper cause. வெள் யானை may be a jibe at the white elephant of the Buddha's birth story, or simply an insult for a dull one; the text does not settle it.

reading: Mokkalan says she holds that a quality cannot exist in a thing other than its own, and counters that the world says the scent which is the quality of the patala flower has passed into the potsherd; she spoke without examining, so let her claim go.
nuance: He appeals to common usage (வையம் உரைக்கின்றது) as evidence that a quality can move from its substance into another.

reading: The narrator tells how the peerless woman ended her answer by giving reasons to the Tathagata's man: even when a flower's scent sits in a new sherd, the wise say the fine scent is the flower's, for the flower's particles stay there and carry it.
nuance: தாதுக்கள் here are read as the flower's fine particles: the scent never leaves its substance, since bits of the flower lodge in the pot. ததாகதற்கு names the opponent by his master.
event: Neelakesi closes her reply on the flower's scent with reasons.

reading: Mokkalan takes up the place of release she desires, and asks, if she calls it good, what went there in the way the burning hell and the bright heaven, which they named together, are places one goes to.
nuance: The second line (நாயிற்கு) is obscure. The gist seems to be that a release located in a place is only one more destination like hell and heaven.

reading: Neelakesi retorts that his teacher spoke of six kinds of destinies and of heaps of aggregates as if they were places, and he shows them; if one says the place of release of those who have destroyed karma's fruit by rule is such, and he asks what it is, is the answer not scripture?
nuance: The verse has no closing என்றாள், so the speaker is inferred from the alternation. ஆகமம் here is the Jain scripture, not the Saiva Agamas. பாக்கனாய் is an obscure term of address.

reading: Mokkalan asks whether, if release is a birth-place from which none come back, the not-coming-back belongs to the place reached; and if she explains it by the absence of karma, he argues that if the freed one is the same who was bound, karma will reach him again.

Neelakesi says she does not call release a birth, nor say the place itself prevents return, nor that karmas cling merely because they exist; she holds that it is the unforgetting yoga activity that brings back the stain, and his words do not reach her.
nuance: யோக பாவம் is the Jain sense of yoga: the activity of body, speech and mind through which karma flows in. With that activity gone, nothing draws karma to the freed soul. Not the Saiva or Siddhar yoga of union.

reading: Mokkalan argues that she calls this the excellent release while the soul still has knowledge that arises, continued being, and a clinging thought that takes outer objects; by such a soul there is no way to give up evil karma, good woman, and he challenges her to answer.
Neelakesi rejects every one of his unprofitable reasons, arguing that harm comes only where the binding activity stands, and that he understands nothing; let his speech end.
nuance: Lines 2 and 3 are obscure (யோடுகொடு, குன்றினில் கூர்ங்கை நாட்டால்); the reading takes them as an image of something that cannot harm where there is nothing to take hold, in line with 427.

reading: Mokkalan says she holds that her Lord knows all endless things by knowledge without any instrument, and objects that endless knowledge itself is an inner instrument; he asks her, nectar to those who join her, to answer.
nuance: The Jain claim of omniscience without sense organs is stated here by the opponent; the objection is his.

reading: Neelakesi tells him to fix his mind on this: what are called instruments are karma and the partial knowledges that karma produces; impurity covers all but the Lord, and to think otherwise is like a crow trying to see the end of the roaring sea.
nuance: விகல ஞானங்கள் are the defective, sense-bound knowings that karma gives; the Lord's knowledge is not of that kind. The crow and the sea mock a limited knower claiming the whole.

reading: Mokkalan sets a dilemma: if the Lord has no organ, he has no speech either and is only like a mountain echo to those who throng and ask; if he has an organ and comes to those who ask, she will be calling good karma done long ago the Lord.

Neelakesi answers that by the instrument called the body the Lord knows and tells what those who come to him ask, and asks whether karma can do that; then, though he may be angry, she tells the thera to go into the fire and wishes never to see his like even in a dream.
nuance: The curse in lines 3 and 4 marks the debate's heat; it is not an event, only speech.

tamil: முறையினா லறிய லன்னேன் மூத்தலே யிளமை சாக்கா
டுறையல வொருவன் கண்ணே யுடனவை யாக வொட்டி
யறைதுநா மன்ன மன்னா யன்னண மாக வென்றான்.
reading: Mokkalan argues that if the Lord knows not in order but all at once, then old age, youth and death, which never dwell together in one man, would be together in his knowledge, and his knowledge would rise upon what does not exist; let it be so then, swan-like one.
nuance: The objection is that knowing past and future at once means knowing what is not now real. The word division of line 4 (அன்ன மன்னாய்) is taken as அன்னம் அன்னாய்.

reading: Neelakesi answers that we see those of virtuous conduct who have won firm divine bodies show forth the three times, and he will not grasp that the Lord, wiser than the three worlds, knows them all the more; he has covered his mind.
nuance: The argument is a fortiori: if gods who reached heaven by virtue can show the three times, the Lord greater than they can.

reading: Mokkalan argues that a knowledge grasping at once all good things of all days in all their aspects would be like a good man with a good sword cutting all the stalks of the wet water creeper at one stroke; only if that can be would her word hold.
nuance: The image seems to be the cutting of many stalks that looks like one act but is a succession of cuts; the lines are hard to construe.

reading: Neelakesi asks who ever learned from anyone that the moon is different in each pool of water or the sun has a different light in each town, and says the wise called the Lord such; what the thera said does not hold.
nuance: The moon one in all waters and the sun one over all towns answer 436: one undivided knowing is present to all things at once. அன்னம் in line 4 is hard to construe.

reading: Mokkalan asks: if the Lord's knowledge grasps the countless things at once through a common quality present in all, then all their differences would be lost; and if their natures are not alike, how could knowledge take them all?
nuance: Neelakesi's reply comes in 439, the first verse of the next run, where she answers that things are grasped by being both alike and unlike.

title: மொக்கல வாதச் சருக்கம் 439-462 (8/8)
theme: The last run of the Mokkala debate: Mokkala attacks the Jain claim of omniscience (infinite objects, past and future things) and mocks the Jain marks of the Lord; Neelakesi answers, declares him defeated with Kundalakesi's old arguments, sings a hymn to the Jina's knowledge, marvels and feet, and explains release as a burnt seed that never sprouts; Mokkala accepts, disowns his teachers, sends her to his own teacher at Kapilapuram, honours her and leaves, and she sets out against the Buddha.
source_issues: 441: show repairs line 4 ('•' read as ஃ); line 3 (களக்கிவர் தன்ன மன்னாய்) remains hard to divide.
442: the repeated ஓதலில் is unclear and may be a corruption.
447: lines 1-2 (கோதியிட்டு, ஆதிசாலாவணத்துள் ஆர்கதர்) are obscure; who defeated whom there is uncertain.
449: line 4 சுகதன, usually the Buddha's name, sits oddly in a hymn to the Jina; possibly corrupt.
455: line 3 (மனையிருள் நெறிபெற மதிகெட அடைவன) is obscure.
459: line 4 (நக்கனனாய்க்கென்று நன்னுதல் என்றான்) is obscure and may be corrupt.
448-455: the metre changes for the hymn; the section is not marked off by any rubric.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddhist elder at Padumapuram, named in 266 as the Buddha's first disciple and Arkkachandra's teacher

reading: Neelakesi says there is no lasting fault in holding that the Lord's knowledge stands and grasps the many different things by the ways they are alike and unlike, and rebukes Mokkala for not taking in, after all he has heard today, the truth of such knowledge.
event: Neelakesi answers Mokkala's objection to the omniscience of her Lord and rebukes him for not grasping it.

tamil: எல்லையில் பொருள்க டம்மை எல்லையி லறிவி னாலே
யெல்லையின் றறியு மெங்க ளெல்லையி லறிவ னென்பாய்
எல்லையில் பொருள்க டம்மை யெல்லையின் றறியி னின்ற
வெல்லையி லறிவு தானு மெங்ஙன மெய்து மென்றான்.
reading: Mokkala objects that if the boundless knower knows boundless things without limit by boundless knowledge, that knowledge could never reach the end of them.
nuance: The verse turns on the word எல்லை, used seven times: an object without end, he argues, cannot be known to its end, so a knowledge that knows it completely contradicts itself.
event: Mokkala objects that infinite objects cannot be known completely.

reading: Neelakesi replies that she has already said the Lord's knowledge lights up the whole nature of the many gathered things at once as the sun does, and calls him a simpleton for repeating the same objection.
nuance: Line 3 is hard to divide (களக்கிவர் தன்ன மன்னாய் ஆத்தனது அறிவும்); the image there is unclear, so only the sun simile and the rebuke are read with confidence.
event: Neelakesi repeats that the Lord's knowledge reveals all things like the sun and rebukes Mokkala.

reading: Mokkala presses a dilemma: if the Lord has no knowledge of what is not present he is defective, if he has it then nothing more is needed, and since the things so known include what does not exist, his knowledge would be working on non-existent things, which is a fault.
nuance: The repeated ஓதலில் is the crux; I take it as knowledge of what is not before him (past and future things), which 443's answer about gone and coming qualities supports, but the word could be read otherwise.
event: Mokkala argues that knowing past and future things would mean knowing what does not exist.

reading: Neelakesi answers that the stainless one knows by his abiding knowledge the qualities that have gone, those that will come and those of today through the nature of the substance itself, so past and future are not lacking in things.
nuance: The answer rests on the Jain view that a substance carries its past and future modes, so the omniscient does not know a non-existent but an aspect of what is; it meets 442 directly.

tamil: னறவியா யுந்த நூலுள் ளாத்தனா மாயி னக்காற்
reading: Mokkala mocks the Jain marks of the Lord: if one is the Aptha in your scripture because he has no birth, no forgetting and none of the four wombs, then the stone that rolls about in the open would be a holy one too.
event: Mokkala argues that the Jain marks of lordship, being absences, would make a stone a lord.

reading: Neelakesi retorts that if being born made one great, children would be greatest; the Lord is great because the eightfold seeds are utterly burnt; and she wishes on those who call the excellent Lord a stone that they become lepers with sores breaking through the skin.
