nuance: The eightfold seeds (அட்டக வித்து) are read as the eight kinds of karma, so lordship is defined by what has been destroyed, not by mere absence of birth. Lines 3 and 4 read as a curse on the mocker, but the syntax is loose and the curse is my reading.
event: Neelakesi rebuts Mokkala's stone argument and curses those who call her Lord a stone.

reading: Neelakesi asks what fault there is in calling Lord the one who has no womb to enter, has no equal, has reached endless knowledge, and is praised on every side by the twelve assemblies under the pindi tree within golden walls, beneath the triple umbrella.
nuance: The golden walls, the pindi (asoka) tree and the three umbrellas are the marks of the Jina's preaching hall; she answers the stone jibe by adding positive marks to the negative ones.

reading: Neelakesi, who won by speaking with justice, tells Mokkala that what he has sifted and put forward is the line by which Kundalakesi once defeated the Jains in the great hall, and that he too has fallen.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 (கோதியிட்டு, ஆதிசாலாவணத்துள் ஆர்கதர்) are hard; I read ஆர்கதர் as the Arhat's followers and the place as a hall or market of debate, which makes Mokkala's arguments a reuse of Kundalakesi's; the verse may instead say Kundalakesi was defeated there.
event: Neelakesi declares Mokkala defeated, saying his arguments were the ones Kundalakesi had used.

reading: Neelakesi tells Mokkala that he has babbled at length only what fools say and has a mind so swollen that men call him a great fool, and announces that she will tell him the worth of the stainless one, the father, the leader, the seer of reality who taught the justice of the path of tapas.
nuance: The metre changes here, and the next seven verses are a hymn to the Jina in short four-syllable feet.
event: Neelakesi begins a hymn on the qualities of her Lord.

reading: The hymn says that wherever the Lord goes, enmity, hunger, disease and the many sorrows perish, trees burst into bud, flower, shoot and fragrance, the land yields its harvest, and all rejoice in every direction.
nuance: The Lord is called சுகதன், a name usually given to the Buddha; either the hymn claims the title for the Jina or line 4 says these marvels are other than the Buddha's, and I cannot settle which.

reading: The hymn says our Lord's knowledge knows wholly, like a gem in the open palm, all the unerring things that combine and separate, that never fail in their permanence, that rise and fall, and whose nature is without end.
nuance: Things are described at once as abiding (நிலையின) and as rising and falling (எழுவன விழுவன): the Jain view that a thing is permanent as substance and changing as mode, set against the Buddhist claim of momentariness.

reading: The hymn says those with full senses know through them and in order, but the Lord is not one whose knowledge goes by order even when things happen in order; hidden things exist but do not hide from his knowledge, and this is how he knows all.

The hymn says the grace of the supreme one to whom all bow shows the sure way to cut the whirlpool of the sea of disease-bringing births, the way our sorrow ends, and the attainment of the jewel-like state of Siva.
nuance: சிவகதி here is the auspicious state of the released soul, not union with Siva; the hymn shares the Saiva words அருள், பரமன், சிவகதி while giving them Jain sense.

reading: The hymn names the signs of the Lord's presence: showers of flowers and drops of fragrance, the deeds of the gods, the praiseworthy qualities, the spreading sound of praise from which the state of Siva follows, and the blazing gem-set seat.
The hymn says that when kings, gods and countless others sit and ask, our Lord's speech thunders like a drum so that all of them, rejoicing, understand in many ways the things that are.
nuance: The speech heard by every listener in his own way is the Jina's divine sound, one of his marks.

reading: The hymn says these are the twin feet of our Lord, which with spreading rays destroy the darkness of deeds, drive away dense darkness, defeat cruel faults, and are reached by those who seek the path.
nuance: Line 3 (மனையிருள் நெறிபெற மதிகெட அடைவன) is obscure; and வினையம் in line 4 may be 'discipline' or a play on வினை, deeds.

reading: Neelakesi ends the hymn: those who, saying this is the Aptha, strew flowers on the place of his feet and praise him with fitting hymns lose both kinds of deed and come to the undivided state of Siva.
nuance: Both kinds of deed (இருவினை), good and bad, must perish; the verse makes worship of the Aptha a cause of that, a stronger claim for devotion than the debate verses make.
event: Neelakesi closes her hymn by telling what reward the Aptha's worshippers receive.

reading: Mokkala grants that if these are the Lord's powers they are fitting and the matters as set out are without error, and asks her to explain, as she has examined it, how release differs from what has simply perished.
nuance: The question seems to be whether Jain release is anything other than extinction; the reading of வீந்த இவற்றின் வேற்றுமை is doubtful.
event: Mokkala concedes the Lord's powers and asks what release is.

reading: Neelakesi answers that as a burnt seed never sprouts, the soul, having become the same in the eight qualities and free of birth, abides permanently in the state of perfection with its eightfold nature intact.
nuance: The burnt seed answers 457: release is not perishing, since the soul remains; what is burnt is only the capacity to be born.

reading: Mokkala, his heart cooled, says this is right, and that the nature of his leaders who ruined this release is unworthy, and he laughs at himself.
nuance: Line 4 (நக்கனனாய்க்கென்று நன்னுதல் என்றான்) is obscure; நக்கனன் may be 'he laughed' or a form of நக்கன், the naked Jain ascetic, so it is unclear whether he laughs or addresses Neelakesi.
event: Mokkala accepts the Jain account of release and disowns his own teachers' doctrine.

reading: Mokkala tells her that the one who first gave him this delusion is in Kapilapuram, the city that bewilders those who see it, teaching his doctrine there, and bids her go and fight him without flinching.
event: Mokkala sends Neelakesi to Kapilapuram to debate the teacher who taught him.

reading: As soon as she declared the excellence of the Jain way, Mokkala said at once that he would never forget her, the jewelled woman who is a raft of dharma with the power to cut off birth and bring bliss, and he circled her and departed.
event: Mokkala honours Neelakesi by circling her and takes his leave.

reading: She who has grace, whose knowledge is dharma, whose only wealth is enlightening those who do not understand, and whose senses are full, rose like a flame that ends darkness and went against him.
nuance: அவன்மேல் at the end points forward to the Buddha in Kapilapuram named in 460, and closes the sarukkam.
event: Neelakesi rises and sets out against the Buddha.

title: புத்த வாதச் சருக்கம் 463-487 (1/8)
theme: The Buddha debate opens: Neelakesi travels to the Buddha's city, finds flesh sold in its market and argues that the buyer and eater share the killing, mocking the Buddha's compassion for leaving flesh unforbidden; she then finds the Buddha teaching the three scriptures and the aggregates, charges his doctrines with contradiction, and makes him set out the aggregates, which he begins to expound down to the octads of form and the four elements.
source_issues: 464 has three lines; a line seems lost, and the speaker of எனலும் cannot be recovered.
478 line 3 reads புந்தியால் where the near-identical 480 line 3 reads போதியால்; one is probably a copyist's slip.
479 line 4 ends in என்னெவெ, apparently a garbled form of a closing word such as என்னவே or என்றலும்.
482 line 3 is divided oddly (எழுந்தவன குடுமி), probably for எழுந்தவன் குடுமி.
470 is printed with almost no word division in lines 1 to 4.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddha, whom Neelakesi debates in person in his city; also called சுகதன், சேடன், தோன்றல்
the people standing in the Buddha's town whom Neelakesi addresses about the meat market
the followers who sit worshipping the Buddha and hear his teaching (தமர்கள், 479)

reading: Naming the fair lands, the rivers, the lands of sickness, the great burning grounds and the jewelled mountains as she passes them, Neelakesi reaches the beautiful city of Sugata, the Buddha.
nuance: The journey is told as her own pointing speech (இவைதாம் repeated), so the land is seen through the traveller's eyes; சுகதன் (line 4) names the Buddha by the title Sugata, which marks the town as his own.
event: Neelakesi travels through lands, rivers, forests and mountains and arrives at the Buddha's city.

reading: Amid the sound of drums and the ringing of bells, someone says that this, greater than its walls, is the place where the lord of the red-robed ones dwells.
nuance: The verse has only three lines and the speaker of எனலும் is not named; whether it is Neelakesi herself or someone on the road who points out the town cannot be fixed. செம்படர்கள் (line 2) seems to name the ochre-robed monks, but the sense of சிறையின் மிகுமால் is unclear.
event: Someone points out the Buddha's dwelling place as Neelakesi approaches.

reading: The description of the city goes on: buildings like rain-clouded mountains, flags on bamboo poles, groves of plantain, and men wearing garlands and women with spread tresses who, if one must name them, are tigers of the caves and peacocks.
The catalogue of the land continues with the coast: fishing boats riding the tall white waves, swift ships moving, groves loud with bees, and fair ponds, mounds and sandy jungle tracts.
nuance: The verse has no main verb; its list runs on into 467, where எனவும் closes it.

reading: It is said too to be a land of rich fields where kayal fish leap and water lilies open, and a land adorned in ways the following lines describe obscurely.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 (முயன்மீ னெறியு முறியுங் கறியா தயன்மே யுறையா தணியிற்று) resist parsing; they seem to praise the land's order or plenty, but no single sense can be fixed.

reading: It is said also to hold a burning ground where flocks of vultures and demons gather, shrouded corpses lie, fat and bodies mingle, and bones are heaped up.
nuance: The burning ground stands in the same list as the coast and the fields, without comment; in a work whose heroine was a demon of the burning ground (the opening sarukkams), the place is part of the ordinary landscape rather than a horror.

reading: Neelakesi says that the very street shows what became of the scriptures that taught the cruel sorrow of wandering through births, and those standing there answer that the Buddhists here do not condemn flesh.
nuance: The verse turns on the reading of ஆனின்றாரும் (line 3) as 'those standing there', which makes line 4 a bystanders' report; it could also be Neelakesi's own sarcasm. The charge that flesh-eating is allowed is answered at once in 470 to 474.
event: In the Buddha's town Neelakesi remarks on the street, and bystanders tell her the Buddhists there do not condemn meat.

reading: Neelakesi asks the bystanders whether they will not call it evil for the robed ones who preached dharma to eat flesh from the market, when creatures living all around have come there as meat.
nuance: The robe is described lavishly (dyed like marutham flowers where bees hum), so the finery of the dress is set against the stall of meat; the charge is about the gap between preaching dharma and buying flesh, not only about diet.

reading: Neelakesi points to the animals in the market, which seem to lift their heads and open their mouths to say that because buyers with money want flesh the netters lay down their lives for that price, so is the killer alone the cruel one?
nuance: The argument is given to the victims: the slaughtered beasts themselves seem to blame the buyer, which turns an economic argument (price draws the net) into an accusation spoken by the dead.

reading: Neelakesi says that the teacher who gave away his own wife and laboured only for others, wanting nothing for himself, had only to say that the one who eats flesh also gathers evil karma, and the many animals on earth would have lived without dying.
nuance: The Buddha's legendary self-giving (the gift of his wife, a former-birth story) is granted in full, and then used against him: his compassion stopped short of the one word that would have saved the animals. The praise is the weapon.

reading: With irony Neelakesi calls the Buddha a knower who would not speak without reflection, and says this too is his kindness, that he will lift all, together with his own children, into the burning hell: truly a most gracious and noble one.
nuance: Every term of praise (பெரிதாம் அளியன், பெருந்தகையன்) is meant in reverse; the verse says the teacher's permission of flesh is a fault of knowledge, not a lapse, since he 'knew rightly'.

reading: Neelakesi says that, like a middleman who neither sells nor buys outright but takes his profit between them, the umbrella-bearing monk who piles up foul meat, recites his threefold excuse and goes off covered in his robe is a very Death to living beings.
nuance: முத்துரைத்து (line 3), 'speaking three', is read here as the threefold test by which meat is pure for a monk (not seen, heard or suspected to be killed for him); that reading is likely but not certain from the verse. The simile matters: the middleman profits from a trade he does not perform, as the eater profits from a killing he does not do.

reading: Saying 'let us go and see the master who, like one who comes up beside dancers and watchers and spins out matching words, sorts out who incurs sin and who does not, the killer or the eater', Neelakesi goes on.
nuance: The teacher is mocked as a talker who fits his words to whoever is listening; the claim she means to test, that the sin is the killer's and not the eater's, has already been answered in 471 and 474.
event: Neelakesi resolves to go and confront the Buddha himself and sets out.

reading: Under the shade of the fair peepal the handsome teacher sits on a flowered seat that sheds the rays of many gems; some praise and worship him, saying he has shown resolve, but he sits wrapped in his robe, moved by nothing.
nuance: பரிவிலன் (line 4) can be read as calm detachment or as coldness to his worshippers; the narrator does not say which, and the robe 'buried' around him (படம் புதைத்து) keeps the picture ambiguous.
event: Devotees worship the Buddha seated under the peepal tree, and he sits unmoved.

reading: To those who sit there sure that he is the trustworthy teacher, the noble one divides his doctrine's meaning many ways, saying this is the Sutra, this the Vinaya, this the other, the Shastra, these three.
event: The Buddha expounds his teaching to the assembled devotees.

reading: He goes on to declare that the five aggregates are momentary, that there is nothing that knows having first examined, and yet joins by reasoning that there is a person (pudgala), and also that apart from what cannot be spoken there is nothing.
nuance: The verse is built to show the doctrines at odds: momentary aggregates and no lasting knower set against a person that is somehow there. Line 4 (மந்திலாற் சொலாப் பாட்டினோடு) is obscure; 'the unsayable' is read from 480's அவாச்சியம். This is the Jain poet's account of Buddhist teaching; a person held to be inexpressible belongs to one Buddhist school, not to all. The claims are answered in 479 to 482.

reading: The dark-haired one comes up to the Buddha as he tells his followers that these are the true principles, and says: you babbled many things like a madman, and I will show that what you babbled agrees in no way.
event: Neelakesi approaches the Buddha and challenges his teaching.

reading: Neelakesi lists the contradictions: he says the five aggregates exist, yet expounds that form with feeling, perception and formation does not exist; he joins a person by reasoning; and he speaks of nothingness and of the inexpressible besides.
nuance: Line 3 repeats 478's line 3 almost word for word but with போதியால் for புந்தியால்; one is likely a copyist's slip.

reading: The Buddha answers that even if many of the things he said of the five do not fit, there is a point in the reality of the aggregates, so the mental states too exist and she should be clear on it; Neelakesi laughs and asks whether he is the one who preached dharma to Nanda.
nuance: The Buddha concedes ground (அமைவில எனினும்) before he holds it, which the poet means as a first retreat. Neelakesi's laugh names Nanda, the Buddha's kinsman whom tradition says he converted, as if to ask how such a muddled teacher won anyone.
event: The Buddha partly concedes and defends the reality of the aggregates; Neelakesi laughs at him.

reading: Neelakesi says that he has spoken many tenets of his choosing, and if all but one were lost and he claimed goodness from that one, it would be like a man covered head to foot in leprosy who touches only his clean tuft of hair: is he pure?
nuance: The simile answers 481's concession: one sound tenet cannot clean a doctrine that is sick everywhere else.

reading: Neelakesi tells him to set out the five aggregates he established as good, and she will make clear that they are not; the elder in the ochre robe then begins slowly to expound them, bidding her listen.
event: Neelakesi challenges the Buddha to state the aggregates, and he begins to expound them.

reading: The Buddha lists the aggregates with their divisions: form; feeling of three kinds; consciousness of six; perception in like number; and formation of twenty in two kinds; these, he says, are our wealth.
nuance: The counts (three feelings, six consciousnesses, twenty formations) are read from compressed lines and line 2 (மருவா தனமாண் குறியத் துணைசெய்) is hard to divide. The list is finer than the bare five names of the Manimekalai; it is answered from 494, where Neelakesi vows to burn the aggregates like a hunter's hut.

reading: The Buddha tells her, fair-browed one with fragrant garland, that of the five in order the first, form, contains within its bounds many octads, each fixed as eight joined together.
nuance: The octad (அட்டகம்) is the smallest unit of matter as eight inseparable things together; 495 answers it, arguing that if the mass is inseparable its parts become mere qualities of one bearer, or else must be separate things.

reading: He names the eight: earth, water, fire and wind, with colour, taste, fine smell and touch; and says that what is left out of the eight can be told, with sound and appearance.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 (இலவே யவையெட் டினும்விட் டதிறம் ...) are hard to construe; the reading that sound is added outside the eight is a guess.

reading: He gives the marks and works of the four great elements: earth is hard, water moist, fire hot and wind brings motion; and their functions are bearing, holding together, drying and stirring.
nuance: Each element has a nature and a function: earth bears, water binds, fire dries or ripens, wind stirs. The reading of அயர்த்தல் as 'holding together' is from the pattern of the list.

title: புத்த வாதச் சருக்கம் 488-512 (2/8)
theme: The Buddha himself sets out the aggregates (feeling, cognition, activity, their momentary arising, the soul as a name for them, and his four truths), and Neelakesi vows to destroy his view and answers that inseparable parts need a bearer, that a thing is known only through its qualities, that the eight constituents of matter put water in fire, and that his accounts of cognition and will contradict themselves or regress into the void.
source_issues: Verse 490, lines 3-4: மயலா மனமே வசிகா யத்தினா / மயலா ரிதாவை are hard to divide; குயலா குயலம் (line 1) stands for குசலம் அகுசலம்.
Verse 493, line 2: நாட்டிலங்காட்டமிலை is hard to divide.
Verse 496, line 1: பூதன்கும் புகுந்தே தெருல்லலுற் றயவற்றுக் is corrupt and cannot be construed; line 4 சாத மாமுயிர் may lack a syllable.
Verse 502, line 4: சொ;லுத has a stray semicolon for சொல்லுத.
Verse 503, lines 3-4 and verse 509, lines 3-4 are obscure in word division.
Verse 510, line 4: the proverb தச்சனஞ் சிச்சா ரகழ்கள்வன் is hard to divide (தச்சன் அஞ்சி?).
Verse 495 cites the Buddha's example as a fist (முட்டி), but 492 speaks of a hand (கை); the example may have stood in a verse now lost or differently worded.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddha, whom Neelakesi debates in person in this sarukkam

reading: The Buddha tells Neelakesi that the feelings are three: pleasure, the pain that brings distress, and a middle feeling that comes from what is neither good nor evil deed.
nuance: This opens the Buddha's own account of the aggregates in the sarukkam, with feeling (வேதனை) first; the neutral feeling is tied here to deed that is neither good nor evil (line 3), a causal link the verse states in passing. Neelakesi answers the separateness of feeling in 505.

reading: The Buddha says that cognitions arise when the five senses and the mind meet their objects, and that perceptions are what is named in these six; this, he says, is his way.
nuance: Cognition (அறிவு) and perception (குறி) are both defined by the six doors, with no knower behind them; 507 to 509 attack exactly this, asking how six cognitions can be counted if only one occurs at a time.

reading: The Buddha says that the activities called wholesome and unwholesome are divided into many kinds by the fruit of deeds and are done by mind, speech and body, and asks who among the deluded could know them.
nuance: குயலா குயலம் is the Pali-Sanskrit pair kusala and akusala, and வசி and காயம் are speech and body; the verse names the formations by the three doors of action. Lines 3 and 4 (மயலா மனமே, மயலா ரிதாவை) are hard to divide, so the closing question is a reading.

reading: The Buddha says the five aggregates arise together and perish within a single moment, as the tip of a flame on a lamp does.
nuance: The flame tip (சுடர் நுதி) is the image Kundalakesi used for the same doctrine in 177 (எரிநுதி). The claim that all five arise at once is what 506 turns against him, by giving the aggregates a causal order.

reading: The Buddha says that as five fingers placed together are called a hand, so the five aggregates together are what is called a living soul.
nuance: The soul becomes a collective name, not a thing; 495 takes the same fingers (there a fist, முட்டி) and argues that what holds them together must be a bearer of qualities.

reading: The Buddha ends his account: the aggregates are impermanent, painful and impure, and no soul is to be established in them; these four are his truth, and those who know them so reach release whatever they do.
nuance: The four named here are impermanence, suffering, impurity (அசுவம், asubha) and no soul, which is a Jain poet's version of the Buddha's 'four truths'; the Buddhist Manimekalai (30) gives the four truths as suffering, its cause, release and its cause. எவையே செய்தும் ('whatever they do') may be the poet's barb that knowledge alone, not conduct, is said to free, the point the monk made in 259. Line 2 (நாட்டிலங்காட்டமிலை) is hard to divide.
event: The Buddha finishes setting out his doctrine of the aggregates to Neelakesi.

reading: Having heard of the many-natured five aggregates and of the false soul that is a mere name for their loose unity, the lily-garlanded Neelakesi says she will destroy his view, like those who burn down a hut.
nuance: பொய்யுயிர் ('false soul') is the narrator's summary of the Buddha's position, and காட்சி ('view', line 4) is the word Jains use for right or wrong faith, so destroying his காட்சி is a matter of doctrine, not only of debate. The simile வேட்டக் குரம்பை சுடுபவர் is unclear: the hut of hunters, or a hut one has cherished.
event: Neelakesi hears the Buddha out and vows to destroy his view.

reading: Neelakesi argues that since he calls the aggregate inseparable, there must be one bearer whose qualities they are; otherwise, split apart, each must be a separate thing, as the five fingers in the fist he cited are.
nuance: The Buddha's example cuts both ways: either the aggregates are one thing's qualities (குணம் of a குணி, the Jain soul) or they are five things and no 'person' at all. The Buddha said 'hand' in 492 and Neelakesi says 'fist', so the example may have stood in a lost or differently worded verse.

reading: Neelakesi argues that things have both their nature and their action, joined yet distinct, and asks what fault there is in establishing the soul from its nature.
nuance: Line 1 is corrupt and the argument is read from lines 2 to 4; தன்மை and கருமம் (nature and function) return in 501.

reading: Neelakesi says that as he gives hardness and support as the marks of earth, she gives knowing and seeing as the marks of the soul; if earth is established, so is the soul, man of great wisdom.
nuance: உணர்வு and காட்சி are the Jain pair of knowledge and perception that define the soul; the argument is one of parity, using the Buddhist's own way of defining an element by its marks. பெரிய பிரச்சையினாய் (great prajna) is ironic.

reading: Neelakesi says he holds there is no earth apart from hardness and no soul apart from cognition, yet says that earth persists and bears things; she calls him the compassionate one who toiled for others through every aeon.
nuance: The address in line 4 repeats the praise Kundalakesi gave her teacher in 176 (அயலார்க்கே துன்புற்றான்), now spoken to the Buddha himself in a verse that charges him with contradiction.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if earth is nothing but hardness he cannot make great earth known, and yet he demands to be shown the soul; has any thing ever been made clear except through its qualities?

Neelakesi says that he claims to accept no contradiction, yet has not given up the eight he took as real, which puts water in fire unchanged, a contradiction plain to sight; is this, Buddha, the wisdom that says only incoherent things?
nuance: அட்டகம் ('the eight') is read as the eight constituents that the Buddhist account holds are always found together in matter, so that water is present even in fire; the verse names the eight only by number. திட்ட விரோதம் is the logician's term for a claim contradicted by what is seen.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if nature and function belong to the elements, then since the four elements are opposites present within one another, each would destroy the other's nature and use.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are obscure (தானென்னைவே றின்மை), so the step from the first half to the conclusion is a reading.

reading: Neelakesi asks why one says 'this is a town, this a forest', and how, if all are present together, one could say 'this is water, this is fire'; if the eight are everywhere, even giving a name goes wrong.
nuance: The town and forest are the ordinary case of naming by what is there; the octad, she argues, leaves no ground for naming one element rather than another.

reading: Neelakesi takes up his answer that though the constituents stand together he names a thing by the one that predominates, and dismisses the reasonings he offers; with this she ends a stretch of her reply.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 (புக்கனதாம் பொறியானின்புலமன்றிப் பொய்யெனத்தா னக்கனர் சாக) are obscure; they seem to say that what enters through the senses is called false, and that others laugh at such methods, but the sense cannot be fixed. என்றாள் closes a speech, though 504 continues in her voice.

reading: Neelakesi says that apart from the eight with form, it is impossible for all that falls within the five aggregates to join, touch and produce one another; deluding the attached with illusions, she says, he drives his chariot through empty space.
nuance: அவகாயத்துத் தேரை ('a chariot in empty space') is read as an image of an argument that moves without ground; the verse is hard and the reading is offered tentatively.

reading: Neelakesi argues that the three feelings remain in him too, and that if the many activities he named before are examined, feeling is only their outgrowth and nothing apart from them.
nuance: She makes the move she made against Kundalakesi in 194, folding feeling into activity, and so denies feeling the standing of a separate aggregate. Line 2 (கரிவே தனையவர் காமுறு காமம்) is obscure.

reading: Neelakesi argues that activity is made by cognition and feeling by activity, and that cognition bears a trace of its object; so the aggregates stand in an order of cause and effect, and things that lose their connection become other and other and cannot be had.
nuance: Read against 491, the causal order cognition, activity, feeling tells against the claim that all five arise in one moment. Lines 3 and 4 are hard to construe.

reading: Neelakesi asks how, when only one of the six cognitions occurs at a time, he knows that the other five exist; and if he says they exist though sunk from view, what fault is there in affirming the soul by the same method?

Neelakesi says that he holds that when one cognition is present the departed ones cannot be perceived even by name, that no two cognitions exist at once, and also that the six exist together; his words, she says, destroy one another.
nuance: ஓருணர்வே உடையீர் ('you who have only one cognition') turns his doctrine into an insult: a mind that holds one thing at a time cannot see its own contradiction.

reading: Neelakesi takes up the answer that cognition occurs as one because the knower stands alone in it, and argues that if the six are distinct by their own existence, going out to their objects and meeting them would suit a knower.
nuance: The verse names a knower (அறிவான், line 2), which is what the Jain wants the Buddhist to concede; the construal of lines 3 and 4 is uncertain.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if he says all things are not known at once for lack of will, then a separate will for each would bring them all together, and one will for all makes will the bearer of qualities; he is, she says, like the carpenter who in fear cries 'thief'.
nuance: A single will that governs every cognition is a soul under another name, which is why the carpenter of the proverb, who cries out and so gives himself away, fits; the proverb itself (தச்சனஞ் சிச்சா ரகழ்கள்வன்) is obscure.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if his will perishes at every arising, knowledge cannot grow from excellence to excellence; if each pot just milked is tasted, how could the vessels be full of milk, curd and buttermilk?
nuance: Milk, curd and buttermilk are one substance through its changes; the image asks for something that lasts through change, which momentary perishing denies. The phrasing of lines 3 and 4 is hard and the image's exact point is a reading.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if every cognition arises by way of will, and his will has no will before it, positing one for it too makes a regress without end; so there is no escaping it: his expansion ends in the void.
nuance: The void (சூனியம்) here is the end of a failed argument, not a goal; it echoes Neelakesi's charge in 263 that the Buddha taught a void release.

title: புத்த வாதச் சருக்கம் 513-537 (3/8)
theme: Neelakesi debates the Buddha himself: she charges that his store of consciousness is the soul under another name, argues that hearing is by contact and that a momentary mind could not understand a word or know anything, presses the difference between perception and consciousness, and then takes the Buddhist ten bad deeds in order, showing that the rules on coveting, anger, view, lying, slander and harsh or gentle speech do not hold as stated.
source_issues: 515 line 3: யாலாக்கிய and ஒருவாப் பாக்கியம் are hard to construe.
517 lines 3-4: முற்றறிவின் றீத்தனை does not yield a clear comparison.
518 line 1: பிரிவின்கணாறாம் பெயர் நுனது is obscure.
521 line 4: கேள ends without its final vowel sign (for கேளாய் or கேண்மோ), probably a slip.
522 line 2: காடின் gives no sense, probably corrupt.
527-530: the e-text's '•' was repaired to ஃ (வெஃகுதல், இஃது, அஃது).
528 line 2: மனமை is probably a slip for அன்மை.
531 lines 1-2: குறள்ளே (for குறளை) and கொனைதல் are probably faulty.
537 lines 1-2: கடுக்கத் தாமடி கள்ளெனக் காய்ஞர்யா ரொடுக்கச் சாம்பிவை is obscure.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddha, whom Neelakesi debates in person in this sarukkam

reading: Neelakesi says that when she argued the consciousnesses other than the one now manifest are gone, since nothing can be grasped of them, the Buddha answered that they rest in a store (ஆலயம்); by that name he has quietly taken back the soul.
nuance: The word ஆலயம் (line 3, doubled) answers to the Buddhist store-consciousness: Neelakesi's point is that a lasting receptacle of past knowings is the soul in all but name, the same move she made against Kundalakesi's carried-over power (203). Whether the Buddhists would accept the store as a soul is exactly what the Jain account denies them.

reading: Neelakesi likens the Buddha to a burglar who, saying he cannot be seen in the dark evening, digs into a rich man's house at broad noon: he keeps as his 'store' the precious soul the compassionate teach, and has lost his dignity in confusion.
nuance: The simile turns doctrine into theft: the soul belongs to அருளுடையார் (the compassionate, line 3, the Jains as Neelakesi presents them), and taking it in daylight under a new name is a theft everyone can see.

reading: Neelakesi takes up the Buddhist rule that nose, tongue and body know their three objects only when they strike against them, and asks how, if the knowing in these three is formless, it can take touches at all.
nuance: The Buddhist position reported is that smell, taste and touch are known by contact; the objection is that a formless knower cannot be struck. Line 3 (யாலாக்கிய, ஒருவாப் பாக்கியம்) is hard to construe, so the shape of the objection is read from lines 1-2 and 4.

reading: Neelakesi says the Buddha teaches that the ear takes sound without its reaching it, but he has not learned the truth: we do not hear a thing at the moment we see it but afterwards, because sound must travel until it reaches its organ.
nuance: The argument is from experience: sight and sound of one event come apart in time, so the ear must wait for sound to arrive. பெருந்தவத்தாய் (line 3), 'man of great penance', is said in mockery.

reading: The Buddha replies that if sound came and touched the ear it could not be heard as far off; Neelakesi answers that sound in the ear may still be known as from afar, and bids him understand.
nuance: Lines 3-4 are obscure: the comparison with the 'fire' of all-knowing knowledge (முற்றறிவின் தீத்தனை) cannot be fixed, so the shape of her answer is uncertain. The verse closes in the narrator's voice (தெருட்டினளே).
event: The Buddha objects that a sound heard as distant cannot touch the ear, and Neelakesi answers him.

reading: Neelakesi asks how, if the mind that grasped the first letter of a word perishes, anyone can understand a word whole and speak it, or learn and put together any reckoning at all.
nuance: The objection to momentariness is tested on the smallest case, a single word heard letter by letter. Line 1 (பிரிவின்கணாறாம் பெயர் நுனது, perhaps 'your name, its letters parted') is obscure.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if the aggregates are called a soul only by their union, then to call him 'Buddha' for his awakening is a lie too, since the awakening belonged only to its first moment; he does not even know what he has attained.
nuance: She turns the Buddhist account of the self as a conventional name against the Buddha's own title: on that account no one persists to be the awakened one.

reading: Neelakesi of the spreading hair, who speaks nothing but winning words, concludes that since the Buddha's words have no real things for their objects, she is now clear that he who spoke them has no knowledge at all.
Neelakesi announces that she will now explain the six perceptions (குறி), their objects and how they take them, and how perception differs from consciousness, without confusing the terms.
nuance: குறி here is the perception aggregate, not a sign: the next three verses press whether it can be told apart from knowing (உணர்வு), the point she made against Kundalakesi in 194.

reading: The woman whose speech outdoes a tune names the six perceptions: of eye, nose, body, ear, tongue and, with the mind, the perception that thinks.
nuance: காடின் (line 2) gives no sense and is probably corrupt; the sixth perception is read as the mind's.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if consciousness and perception have one and the same object they are one thing, and if each takes another object the difference can be shown; so she says.
nuance: The opening horn of a dilemma: two aggregates with a single object collapse into one, as she argued in 194 that feeling, perception and volition are not other than knowing.

reading: Neelakesi presses the dilemma: if perception reaches its real object while consciousness does not, then either their object is one and they are one, or, if consciousness never meets it, consciousness has no object at all.
nuance: Lines 1-2 are compressed and the sense of உண்மைகுறி is not secure; the conclusion in line 4 is clear.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if perception and consciousness arise with their object at one instant and perish together, nothing is known, and if they do not arise together, then since the object arises at once there is still no knowing.
nuance: This is the momentariness objection in its sharpest form: a knowing that lasts no longer than its object has no time in which to know it.

reading: Neelakesi turns to the Buddhists' wholesome and unwholesome deeds, which they class by mind, speech and body, and says she will show that they do not hold even a sesame seed's worth, beginning with the three of the mind.
nuance: குசல அகுசலம் (line 2) are the Buddhist terms. From here to 537 she takes the ten bad deeds in order: the three of the mind (527-530), then the four of speech (531-537), the list the Manimekalai's teacher gives (Manimekalai 30, lines 64-70).

reading: Neelakesi argues that if all wanting is coveting, then the whole garland of verses the Buddha strung together is coveting too, and he does not see even this.
nuance: The target is the first mental fault, வெஃகல். Lines 2-3 (தீண்டல் அன்ன, தீண்டிய வந்தவோ) are hard to construe; the charge read here, that the teacher's own wish to teach is a wanting, rests on line 2.

reading: Neelakesi says that since the Buddha does not declare that coveting the good is good and coveting what is not good is not, he must now state a rule under which his word 'coveting' is free of evil.
nuance: She asks for coveting to be judged by its object. மனமை (line 2) is probably a slip for அன்மை, which the parallel with நன்மை requires.

reading: Neelakesi says deceit, pride and greed, which are of the mind, are as evil as anger, yet the Buddha, though he saw them, did not condemn them; that is his fraud, and once these are admitted others follow.
nuance: மாயம் மானம் உலோபம் with வெகுளி (lines 1-2) make the Jain four passions: anger, pride, deceit and greed. The charge is that the Buddhist list of mental faults (coveting, anger, wrong view) leaves three of them out.

reading: Neelakesi grants that right view is the excellence above all seeing, but argues that whoever wants it, judging it good, wants it from desire, and so by the Buddhist rule falls while assenting to it.
nuance: காட்சி is the third mental item (பொல்லாக் காட்சி, wrong view, in the Buddhist list), and also the Jain right vision. Line 4 (வழித்தனன்) is obscure, so the conclusion is read from the run of argument in 527-528.

reading: Neelakesi recalls that the Buddhists declared lying, slander, harsh words and idle talk to be the four evil deeds of the tongue, and their opposites good.
nuance: The list is the Buddhist one as the Manimekalai gives it, almost word for word (பொய்யே குறளை கடுஞ்சொல் பயன் இல், Manimekalai 30, line 68). குறள்ளே and கொனைதல் (lines 1-2) are probably faulty.

reading: Neelakesi lists composite things: begging bowl, water pot, mansion, monastery, house, topknot, ascetic's vessel, robe, pot, shop, food, bed, body and soul, and all other things made of parts.
nuance: The list runs straight into 533, and mixes the monk's own goods (மண்டை, குண்டிகை, கூறை) with the body and soul, so that his daily speech is caught by the argument.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if all these are only names for collections with no single thing there, yet the Buddhist names them again and again, he cannot establish true speech, and his own rule against lying condemns him.
nuance: This is where the two halves of the sarukkam meet: the doctrine that composites are only names (532) is set against the rule that lying is a bad deed of speech (531). The vocative விளி நாச (line 4) is obscure.

reading: Neelakesi mocks the red-robed one who says earth, water, the great city, vessels, wind, fire, forest and clan are all false, saying that of all this only his own deceit is not false.
nuance: The list of elements and goods called பொய் is the Jain account of Buddhist teaching; the Buddhists would say such things exist by convention, not that they are lies. Line 4 (சலம் பொய் அன்று, சத்தை) is read as sarcasm, but its exact turn is uncertain.

reading: Neelakesi says that besides slander, which the Buddhists call a fault, there are many other unworthy kinds of speech, such as talking alone with a woman and teaching the arts of pleasure, and harsh words must be guarded against as well.
nuance: The objection is that the four-item list is too short; her examples come from a renouncer's code of speech rather than from the Buddhist list.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if speaking gently is a good deed, then those who softly lay plans to wound and kill, and the whispered counsels that urge such deeds, would be upright.
nuance: She refutes the rule that soft speech is good by the gentle-voiced plotter: the goodness of speech lies in what it brings about, not its tone. மந்திரம் (line 3) is counsel, not a sacred formula. Line 2 is compressed.

reading: Neelakesi asks who would condemn as harsh the stern words that restrain, and whether saying 'give' is not wholesome, and calls the Buddhist teaching a wicked lesson that brings its holder down.
nuance: Lines 1-2 are obscure (கடுக்கத் தாமடிகள், ஒடுக்கச் சாம்பிவை); the reading that a harsh word may restrain, as 'give' is good whatever its tone, is tentative.

title: புத்த வாதச் சருக்கம் 538-562 (4/8)
theme: Neelakesi, debating the Buddha in his own city, attacks his account of karma and his first truth: she argues that the rule making killing and theft depend on knowledge and intention would excuse a man who kills, robs or abducts by mistake, while intent without a deed still binds; then she argues that 'all is suffering', 'all is impure' and 'nothing stays' each undo the four noble truths and every reason for conduct.
source_issues: Verse 544 repeats verse 313 (Mokkala debate) word for word.
Verse 538: lines 1 and 4 (களபாவமாம், ஏவனன்றென்றி) are hard to divide and may be corrupt.
Verse 548, lines 1-2 (துப்பினால், வப்பினார்முலை காய்வது வாமனீ) are obscure; the line division may be faulty.
Verse 554, line 4 (பழுக்களே காய்வது ண்டுமுண் டேபிற) has a stray ண்டு and looks corrupt.
Verse 562 is in a longer metre than the verses around it, and its line 3 (யென்றலி னேன் விழவெய்தி) looks corrupt.
Verse 543, line 2: யில்லைனப் probably for இல்லையெனப்.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddha himself, whom Neelakesi debates in his own city in the புத்த வாதச் சருக்கம்; addressed as வாமன் and நாதன்

reading: Neelakesi argues that if the Buddha will not speak of things that have no fruit, then what his followers say about persons (புற்கலர்) dying could count as truth only if something were held to persist, and nothing in his teaching matches that.
nuance: Line 1 (களபாவமாம்) and line 4 (ஏவனன்றென்றி) resist division; the reading rests on புற்கலர் (pudgala, the 'person') and சாவ (dying) in lines 2 and 3, and on the frame of the argument against a doctrine with no lasting self.

reading: Neelakesi takes up the Buddha's teaching that killing, lust and theft are deeds of the body and asks how that can be, when without a mind no one is there in any place to do such deeds.
nuance: The Buddhist grouping is by the door a deed goes out through (body, speech, mind, as 526 set out); Neelakesi reads it as if the body were said to act alone. The same three bodily deeds open the Manimekalai teacher's list of ten evil deeds.

reading: Neelakesi lists deeds that harm without a chosen victim (planting thorns on a path, burning a house, pushing people into a pit, despoiling temple vessels, driving an elephant at people) and asks whether these do not bring blame and sin.
nuance: The list prepares the attack on the five conditions of killing in 541: in none of these deeds does the doer know and intend a particular life. கோயிற் கலஞ்செய்தல் may mean damaging the temple's vessels or something else done to them; the sense of harm is clear from the frame.

reading: Neelakesi restates the Buddha's rule that a killing is a killing only when five things meet: a life joined to a body, the thought 'this is a life', the intention 'I will destroy it', the deed done with that fault, and the death.
nuance: The rule is stated here in order to be answered: 543 to 550 bring cases of mistaken identity in which, by this rule, a man would die or be robbed with no sin incurred. ஐந்தில் (line 4) names the five; their list is read from lines 1 to 4.

reading: Neelakesi tests the intention rule from the side of worship: if a man, thinking 'this is the god', bows in devotion but has in fact bowed to something other than the god, does he incur fault or not?
nuance: The verse is a question whose answer is left for the hearer; தாவனை in line 4 (what was wrongly worshipped) and தூவென மும்மையே தோற்றி in line 3 are hard to fix, so the exact case is uncertain.

reading: Neelakesi recalls that the Buddhists say a man who stabs someone resembling his enemy, taking him for that enemy, incurs no killing-karma, and bids them consider how the person stabbed nonetheless died.
nuance: The answer is the plain fact of line 4 (செத்தவாறு): a man is dead, and the rule of intention cannot make him alive. The verse sets the pattern of resemblance (ஒத்தவன்) that 549 repeats for theft (ஒப்பது).

reading: Neelakesi says that, by the Buddhists' own words, even when someone dies no sin of killing follows, because the doer's mind did not go out and reach that victim.
nuance: Line 1 to 2 (குறட்கண்ணும் ஒன்றுமே ... எப்பாரியார) are obscure; the verse repeats 313 of the Mokkala debate word for word, so the editor or the tradition placed the same argument in both debates.

reading: Neelakesi argues that where the intended enemy did not die, the Buddhist must either deny the sin of the hostile intention or charge it to the other life that was killed, and she bids him hear how karma truly works, citing one who worshipped a wicked man and was ruined.
nuance: பட்டிலன் (line 1, 'he did not die') fixes the case as a failed or misdirected killing; line 3 (துட்டனைத் தொழுதோன் துறந்தான்) alludes to a story the verse does not tell, and the reading of lines 2 and 3 is a guess.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if karma binds only when all five conditions are met, then in a case the Buddhists themselves tell, where no one died, it would be unfitting that the doer went to the fierce Avici hell for splitting Kalakan.
nuance: The verse turns on a story it only names (அவீசி, the hell; காந்தி, பாலி and கலகன், unidentified here); that the case is a Buddhist one in which no death occurs is read from வீய்ந்ததின்மையின் (line 2) and the argument.

reading: Neelakesi says that the man who sets out to kill though his sharp weapon fails, the man who sets out for another's house, and the burglar all carry the dark deed of their intent, and the world and kin are bound with the one who speaks it.
nuance: Here Neelakesi grants intention its weight; her case against the Buddha is not that the mind does not matter but that mind and deed both bind, so a failed intent and an unintended death each carry karma. Line 4 (சொல்லுவானோடு உலகமுஞ் சுற்றமே) is unclear.

reading: Neelakesi presses the Buddha on a case involving contact with women, saying that his claim not to reckon karma from such contact does not survive even being stated.
nuance: Nearly every line is obscure (துப்பினால் in line 1, வப்பினார் முலை காய்வது in line 2); the Buddha is addressed as வாமன் as in 517. The claim is read from the frame of 541 to 550.

reading: Neelakesi states the Buddhist rule on theft: if a man takes a thing that resembles what he once deposited, believing it his own, there is no fault whether he carries it off or keeps it, for even when seen it is not theft.
nuance: The rule is answered by the satire of 550, which applies the same reasoning to another man's wife.

reading: Neelakesi mocks the rule: let a man carry off a householder's wife asleep at home, telling himself 'this is she' (his own wife, whose soft feet ached from walking by day), and take her by deceit, crying 'long live the Buddha'.
nuance: The verse is a reductio: it adds nothing to the rule of 549 but its consequence. The cry வாழ்க புத்தன் puts the Buddha's name on the abduction.

reading: Neelakesi says that, having laid waste the aggregates by showing them to be as unreal as a crow's teeth since nothing binds them into one, she will now shatter with a few words the noble truths he taught and the mind as well.
nuance: காகதந்தம் (crow's teeth) is a stock example of a thing that does not exist. ஆரிய சத்தை (line 3) names the noble truths, which 553 to 562 take up.
event: Neelakesi turns from the aggregates to attack the Buddha's noble truths.

reading: The verse gives the Buddhist account that the body-heap, though one, is viewed apart as five, and a challenge to show here the truth that was seen; Neelakesi answers that she will speak of suffering and of awareness.
nuance: The speaker of lines 1 to 3 may be the Buddha (கொண்டுநின்றாம், கண்டநா மெய்ம்மை, 'we held', 'the truth we saw') and line 4 Neelakesi's reply (கூறுவோம்); the verse has no speech marker but எனின், and ஆகுலம் in line 4 is read as distress.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if all is suffering, then good things too become worthless the moment one says so; the teaching is therefore faulty, and since suffering admits no plurality, the fool was wrong to say there are four truths.
nuance: The argument needs the Buddhist to hold that the third and fourth truths, cessation and the path, are themselves suffering; the Manimekalai's teacher gives release as joy (இன்பம் வீடே), which the reductio does not meet.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if the flawless truth is to see the three kinds of suffering together, then the Buddha, having spoken that truth, erred in saying he gave joy to others.
nuance: உழப்பு மூன்றும் (line 1) is read as the three kinds of suffering; line 4 (பழுக்களே காய்வது ...) is corrupt or obscure and is left unread.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if all is suffering, every deed is one and its fruit must be equal, so the Buddhists cannot say that others have fallen into low births while their own people rise, or that their path is the highest.

Neelakesi tells the Buddha that if the end of everything is only suffering with no joy, he should stop giving counsel and guarding conduct, go a little into fire, and not seek shade, since every act only adds to endless suffering.
nuance: The verse drives 'all is suffering' to its practical end: if there is no joy anywhere, fire and shade are alike, and so are virtue and vice.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if his word that nothing at all is pure is true, then all who wear garlands and sandal paste have failed to find the safe good path.
nuance: The verse does not say whose garlands are meant; it may point at the Buddhists' own worship with garland and sandal, or at all householders, so the force of the consequence is uncertain. Naladiyar 48, a Jain quatrain, says just this of those who praise sandal and garland.

reading: Neelakesi points out that the Buddhist says his recitation, conduct and food are flawless and pure, and asks what, then, he calls impure; the Lord, she says, knew other things very well.
nuance: நாதன் நீ பிற நன்கறிந்தாய் (line 4) is irony.

reading: Neelakesi, whose shoulders surpass the bamboo, says that the bowl-carrying monkeys who ignore the truth the Buddha spoke burn with anger, saying 'we are pure and others are impure'.
nuance: கவி மண்டைகள் (line 3) joins monkey and begging bowl as an insult to the monks; the narrator's line names Neelakesi as the speaker by her shoulders.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if even those who saw the right path long ago gain no purity afterward, then for one who takes whatever arises day by day as its nature, there is nothing that could have made things impure.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 (இன்றுமின்று மியல்வது வாக்கொள்வாய்க்கு இன்றித் தூய்தன்மை) are hard to divide; the reading joins the momentariness of 562 to the purity argument of 557 to 561.

reading: Neelakesi tells the fools who said all is impure to smear themselves with rot, bathe in the gutter, and gulp the filth that vultures and pigs eat, since by their teaching none of it differs from anything else.
nuance: தூய்தன்மை in line 4 is தூய்து அன்மை, 'not being pure'. Line 3 (மெழுகுமின்னிடை மெச்சியமல்லதின்) is obscure.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if he says things do not stay, the saying itself does not stay, and if he says 'we are not', his own happy thesis is spoiled; since all is the same as itself, she asks, good one, how will he establish the four truths he spoke.
nuance: The verse is in a longer metre than its neighbours. நல்லாய் (line 4) addresses the opponent as 'good one', ironically. Line 3 (எல்லாந் தானே யென்றலினேன் விழவெய்தி) is not secure.

title: புத்த வாதச் சருக்கம் 563-586 (5/8)
theme: In the fifth part of the debate with the Buddha, Neelakesi mocks his former-birth gifts (the rain for worms, the body split open, the wife and children given away), argues that denying the soul refutes itself, and then answers his account of karma without a doer, the seed-and-sprout continuity and the lac-stained pomegranate seed, by pressing that nothing beyond the five aggregates carries a deed to its fruit.
source_issues: 564 line 3: மெய்தல் ரேயின் is damaged; perhaps மெய் தேரின்.
570 lines 3-4: தாம சீவன் and வாம சீவன் are obscure and may be corrupt.
577 line 4: காடம்டுவ is not a word; the line is corrupt.
581 lines 2-4 and 584 line 2 (தப்படையான்) are hard to construe and may be corrupt.
585 line 2: the first letter is the non-Tamil character ¦ (U+00A6), an encoding error; perhaps செம்மை.
563 line 3 and others: the old encoding • for ஃ was repaired by the build.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddha, whom Neelakesi debates in person in the புத்த வாதச் சருக்கம்

reading: Neelakesi asks the Buddha, whom she hails as the one famed for sending rain so that worms might live, to explain how gifts of great wealth made by farmers, merchants and others to the faultless are said to turn out differently, since faultless people are to be seen too.
nuance: The closing epithet turns a former-birth tale of compassion (rain sent for worms) into mockery; the sense of lines 1-3, whether the fruit of a gift is said to differ by its receiver, rests on a compressed construction.

reading: Neelakesi asks whether worship paid by those convinced that something is a god, and giving mixed with the wish to be rid of what is in one's hand, are not all faults when examined, addressing the Buddha as the noble one who split his own body to give to those who asked.
nuance: Line 3 (மெய்தல் ரேயின்) is damaged; reading it as 'if one examines truly' makes the verse a charge that the Buddha's body-gifts fall under faults his own side names.

reading: Neelakesi asks whether jewelled women are goods fit to be given as alms, and whether those who take charge of them once they are handed over can be shown not to be thieves, mocking the Buddha's greatness in giving to others out of compassion while his own children wailed.
nuance: The objection shifts ground from earlier attacks on the body-gifts: here the wrong is that persons are not the giver's property, so the gift turns the receiver into a thief. The word கருணையால் is used against the compassion it names.

reading: Neelakesi says that the Buddha made the teaching that nothing endures his path, and that if after ruining everything in many ways he then offers a remedy he cannot keep to the truth he declared, hailing him as the one whose virtue stopped the murderous wrathful elephant.
nuance: The epithet in line 4 recalls the taming of a raging elephant; the argument that a remedy presupposes something lasting is a reading of the compressed lines 2-3.

tamil: ஓதி யாது முயிரில்லை யென்ப துரைத்து நின்றாயேற்
வேதி லார்சொல் பரிகற்ப னையி னாலின் மைசொல்லி
னீதி யாநின் கருத்தினா லுண்மை யுந்நேர்ந் தாயன்றோ.
reading: Neelakesi argues that if the Buddha holds there is no soul at all, then admitting even one faultless mark as soul destroys his thesis, and if he denies the soul only through a constructed fiction (பரிகற்பனை) he has by his own view conceded that it exists.
nuance: Line 3's ஏதிலார் சொல் may mean 'the word of strangers' or 'unrelated words'; either way the move is that a denial made by mere construction admits the thing denied.

reading: Neelakesi asks the Buddha, who said the soul is nothing, who then he is that accepts being and non-being standing as they are as the path, and says that since the nine heads he spoke of before cannot hold by any means, he has today taken her Lord as the Lord.
nuance: The question நீ யாவனோ turns the no-self thesis on the speaker. What the nine (நவத்திறம்) are is not said in this verse.

reading: Neelakesi asks whether, if there is no knower who recollects, the Buddhist can explain knowing by any of seven ways: by likeness, by unlikeness, by construction, by 'nothing other than it', by the strength of deeds, by yoga, or by the moment of clear understanding.
nuance: The list is compressed and the reading of some items (புனைவு, யோகு) is tentative; the point is that recollection (மீட்டுணர்வு) needs one who knows across time.

tamil: நாம சீவன் முதலாய நான்மை களின்முன் மூன்றிலுந்
தாம சீவன் முழுவது மென்று தருக்கு கின்றாய்
வாம சீவ னிவற்றினா லுண்மை மறுக்க லாகுமோ.
reading: Neelakesi appeals to the four ways of designating the soul that begin with the soul-in-name, says the Buddha's word changes if purity belongs to the soul in the first three, and asks whether by these he can deny the soul's existence.
nuance: நாம சீவன் முதலாய நான்மை looks like the Jain fourfold placing of a word (by name, by representation, by substance, by state); தாம சீவன் and வாம சீவன் in lines 3-4 are obscure and may be corrupt.

reading: Neelakesi says she has shattered the knower, truth, the five aggregates and everything else by showing that none of them stands, and bids the Buddha name anything left; the Buddha answers that he will subdue her by his own path, and bids her consider.
event: Neelakesi declares the Buddha's categories refuted and challenges him to name another; the Buddha says he will subdue her by his own path.

reading: Neelakesi says she will not accept a path without reason except from those who teach the wide wandering that has no beginning, the means that cuts off birth, and the fit between a deed and its fruit.
nuance: The verse sets her terms for the reply that follows: any account the Buddha gives must show how a deed's fruit reaches its doer. That ஒப்பு means the deed-fruit correspondence is a reading.

reading: The Buddha says that as sprout and branch appear in succession from a seed, he calls the continuity arising by potency a change, that release is not other than this, and bids Neelakesi take it as the truth.
nuance: Neelakesi answers the seed image in 579-583, where she argues the analogy carries nothing across for the aggregates. The account is given in a Jain work.

reading: The Buddha says that the deed exists and its fruit exists, but there is not a millet-grain's worth of a doer, and that none of the aggregates stands for even a moment.
nuance: Neelakesi answers at once in 575 and again in 584. The thesis matches the Buddhist teacher's own words in Manimekalai 30 (the chain has no maker), so here the polemic attacks a view the school holds.

reading: Neelakesi answers that the Buddha calls virtue a real thing and giving a real thing, yet says there is no one who knows, acts and enjoys, and that if the aggregates last only a moment even his own name quarrels with him.
nuance: The jab at his name is a reading of பிணங்குவது ஒக்கும் நின் பேர்: the 'awakened one' cannot be a knower if there is no knower.

reading: The Buddha says an evil mind brings the suffering of burning and a mind of worth brings bliss hereafter, as when a pomegranate seed is steeped in lac its red is seen in the flower.
nuance: The lac-and-pomegranate image is the Buddhist answer to how a deed reaches its fruit without a lasting self; Neelakesi takes it apart in 579-585.

reading: The Buddha goes on that the seed and the lac are each made of eight constituents, and that the red and the other marks appear in the flower's eye and colour, and so it is here.
nuance: எட்டின் இயன்ற reads as the Buddhist octad of matter; line 4 (காடம்டுவ) is damaged and the second half of the verse is hard to construe.

reading: The Buddha gives his parallel: two youths made of the five aggregates, one of wholesome and one of unwholesome deeds, so that from the good-minded one comes a god and from the one of cruel deeds a hell-dweller.
nuance: The terms குசல and அகுசல are the Buddhist words for wholesome and unwholesome action; Neelakesi answers the parallel in 579-580.

reading: Neelakesi says the seed is only the eight and nothing else, and the five aggregates are likewise, so she asks how his example fits and bids him hear while she takes it up and rebukes it.
Neelakesi argues that the lac is something added to the eightfold seed, but he shows no such further thing for the five aggregates, and tells the deluded Buddha to stop showing the pomegranate.
nuance: This is the same dilemma she put to Kundalakesi in 203: whatever carries the deed across is a further thing beyond the five, which is what the Jain calls a soul.

reading: Neelakesi says that showing the colour in the flower does not fit, since a man's deed bears fruit in the god he becomes, and asks whether the Buddha has set aside that the act too perishes when the pomegranate dies.
nuance: Lines 2-4 are compressed (மாவின்கண் may be 'in the mango' or a place-word); the reading that the flower is the wrong place for the fruit of a deed is tentative.

reading: Neelakesi says that even if he shows a difference between seed and flower, he must speak of the infant and the old man, and that babbling like the mad he cannot join a deed to its fruit in any way.
nuance: The infant and the old man are one person at two times: Neelakesi moves the question from a plant's series to the life of one human, where the doer and the enjoyer should be the same.

reading: Neelakesi asks: if the seed's form, faded with the lac, skips the sprout and settles in the flower, what would he say of Angulimala?
nuance: Angulimala, the killer who became the Buddha's disciple, is named without his story; how his case bears on the argument (whether his killings bore fruit) is not spelled out here.

reading: Neelakesi asks whether, if he says the lac comes to be like that by such a course, he will also say that one man toils at the deed while another, born a god, enjoys its fruit.
nuance: The objection is that without a lasting self the one who acts and the one who enjoys are two; line 2 (தப்படையான் உழப் பெய்வழி) is obscure and the reading rests on the sense of the whole.

reading: Neelakesi argues that his flower example cannot carry a deed's sweet fruit from one birth to the next, so by his account there would be neither this birth nor the next.
nuance: Line 2 is damaged (a non-Tamil character stands for its first letter), and line 1 is hard to construe.

reading: Neelakesi draws a consequence: if the fruit of many flowers is reckoned as eaten because they were seen as its cause, then deer flesh and fish meat in the begging bowl could pass for bees' food.
nuance: The construction is obscure; that the absurd consequence aims at the Buddhist monk's eating of meat (மண்டை, the bowl) is a reading.

title: புத்த வாதச் சருக்கம் 587-610 (6/8)
theme: In the Buddha debate Neelakesi argues against the Buddha that karma cannot lie in the mind alone, since wherever mind is action is, and dismisses his seed-and-flower analogy; the Buddha restates that a deed's power passes hidden through the continuum to its fruit though the doer perishes, and Neelakesi answers that a continuum cannot cross from a dead man to a god, since every example of transmission needs its cause present or an unbroken link.
source_issues: 588 line 2 and 603 line 4: the edition's '•' is the old encoding of ஃ (repaired in the core).
591 line 3: செர்தலிற் is read as சேர்தலின்.
595 line 1: சித்திமுடைச் is read as சித்தமுடைச்.
607 line 1: யற்றுழிக் தோன்றுக has a doubtful க் before தோ (expected த்).
592, 594, 597, 598 (பலிசையி), 603 line 2 and 610 line 3 are obscure; their readings are tentative.
587-599 and 603-610: no speech verb names the speaker except என்றாள் (596, 598, 603); Neelakesi is taken as speaker from the story. 600 to 602 are the Buddha's (இருந்தான், என்றான்).

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddha himself, whom Neelakesi debates in the Buddha sarukkam (named புத்தன் in 571)

reading: Neelakesi takes the Buddha's own account of the evil deed as what brings burning pain and turns it on him: all his own deeds that were pain endured for others he must himself suffer, since he laboured only for others.
nuance: The last words, பிறர்க்கே உழந்தாய், repeat the praise of the Buddha in Kundalakesi's invocation and in Neelakesi 472 (பிறர்க்கே உழந்தான்); here the praise becomes the charge. வாயுழப்பாம் வழி (line 2) is compressed, and whether the pain meant is the giver's own or that of those he gave away (his wife and children, 472, 565) is not settled by the verse.

reading: If the Buddha teaches that the mind is the deed, Neelakesi asks how he can hold that bodily action is not karma even to the size of a sesame seed, and says he never states a quality without deceit.
nuance: The Buddhist position under attack is that karma is intention (உள்ளம் வினை); Neelakesi answers it in this verse and the next seven by arguing that action cannot be left out of karma.

reading: If mind and action are one for the Buddha, Neelakesi asks where he got the merit and demerit that arise within the doer, since it contradicts what he agreed before.
nuance: தரும அதருமி (line 2) is read as merit and demerit settling in the self; the verse uses the Buddhist's earlier concession (முன்னுடம்பாடு) against him, a debate move rather than a doctrine of its own.

reading: If instead the Buddha says mind and action are different, Neelakesi says that without an agreed account of the deed he cannot say from what the eating of its fruit follows, and he speaks what does not fit.

If the Buddha grants that action arises from seeing, knowing and desire, Neelakesi says he has conceded several qualities to one bearer, and asks what fault there is in his view now that he has come to the great dharma of the one under the pindi tree.
nuance: பிண்டி நீழலவன் is the Jina under the asoka tree: Neelakesi claims that the Buddha's own chain of seeing, knowing, desire and action presupposes one lasting bearer, and so lands him in the Jain teaching. செர்தலிற் (line 3) is read as சேர்தலின்.

reading: Neelakesi asks why the words of those who say a deed makes karma by what it brings about should trouble him, and says that if his teaching were dharma, it would be good to bind a person in fetters and handle all their senses.
nuance: The second half is read as a reductio: if only the mind makes karma, an act done to a bound and unwilling body would carry no fault. Whose senses are meant (தம் பொறி) and who is bound (என்னை) are not certain.

reading: If the Buddha says karma is made by desire, Neelakesi asks who would call desire the mind, and says that action too arises from the experience that desire has joined, a link he does not know.
nuance: ஆர்வம் (desire) and சித்தம் (mind) are kept apart here; துப்பு, used through 593 to 596, is read as experience or enjoyment of objects.

reading: If the Buddha calls awareness desire, Neelakesi says, then desire for other men's women would be awareness; and if he says such desire is pain and not awareness, the experience inseparable from it would no longer be karma.
nuance: The example of desire for others' wives (பிறர்கள் தம் பொற்றொடியார்) tests the Buddhist equation of desire with awareness; line 4 (இணர் பிரியாத் துப்பு) is obscure and the conclusion is reconstructed.

reading: Neelakesi argues that since action done with mind is a deed, experience done with mind is a deed too, and since the Buddha calls mind karma, wherever there is mind there is also action.
nuance: The argument turns the Buddhist premise into its opposite: if intention is karma and intention never comes without doing, action can never be left out. சித்திமுடை (line 1) is read as சித்தமுடை.

reading: Neelakesi says she has made the Buddha state how action produces experience and experience action, and tells him to set aside his tale of seed and flower, made up as a lie.
nuance: பொய்கை செய்து (line 3) puns on பொய் (a lie): the seed-and-flower analogy of 576 is called an invention. The poet names the speaker by an epithet, the young woman with flower-like eyes.
event: Neelakesi closes her argument on mind and action and dismisses the Buddha's seed-and-flower analogy.

reading: Neelakesi says that, having destroyed the nature of both kinds of seed and broken his two kinds of god and his flower, the sweetened mango he offers will break in the same way if he brings it.
nuance: The two seeds and the two kinds of deva look back to the Buddha's analogies in 576 to 578 (the lac-stained pomegranate seed; the good and evil sons who become god and hell-being); the sweetened mango is a further analogy she pre-empts. The lines are compressed and the reading is tentative.

reading: Neelakesi says she has by force stripped the seed of its worth and left it barren, and that she will crush one by one, judging fairly, all the texts he cites in his boasting.
nuance: அலிசெய்து (made sterile) completes the seed image. பலிசையின் (line 3) is obscure; 'boasting' is a guess. நடுவுணர்ந்து claims impartiality for the Jain side.
event: Neelakesi declares the seed analogy defeated and promises to refute the Buddha's other texts.

reading: Neelakesi says that the aggregate that was born perished there along with its deed, so it cannot eat its fruit afterwards; then reaching that excellent heaven does not hold, and doing dharma is itself in vain.
nuance: The argument is the Jain charge that momentariness destroys moral reward: if the doer ends with the act, heaven earned by merit has no recipient and virtue loses its point. பிண்டம் is read as the aggregate person of the Buddhist account.

reading: The Buddha, unable to hold back his strength, sits hearing the many faults she pours out, and then says he will show her how she has hidden the truth in all the many paths she has laid out, and bids her listen.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are the narrator's; lines 3 and 4 are the Buddha's speech. This is one of the few places the narrator shows the Buddha's state of mind, and it is not flattering.
event: The Buddha listens to Neelakesi's charges and begins his reply.

reading: The Buddha says, addressing her as the woman of fresh bangles, that he meant the fruit is like the power of a seed treated with lac: it hides between, hard to see, passes through the tree and appears and spreads in the flower.
nuance: This is the Buddha's restatement of the lac-and-seed analogy of 576, answering Neelakesi's objection in 583 that the lac's colour is not seen even in the sprout. Neelakesi answers it in 603 to 610 (the gap in the branch, 610).

reading: The Buddha says that, in the same way, though the doer and his deed have perished, the continuity of the continuum that runs on from him later receives the fruit, so the good path he saw is hard for her to know.
nuance: The Buddha concedes that the doer perishes (அறங்கெட்டவன், line 1) and puts the fruit in the continuum (சந்தானத் தொடர்ச்சி); Neelakesi attacks this continuum in 603 to 610.

reading: Neelakesi asks what, once all the aggregates have perished without remainder, a feeble continuum arising among them could do, and bids the Buddha answer.
nuance: வாம (line 4) is read as a vocative of வாமன், a name of the Buddha (Manimekalai 30 calls him வாமன்): 'answer, Vaman'. Line 2 (அந்தமிலாக் குற்றமாம் எனச் சொல்லும்) is obscure: it may report a Buddhist saying that the aggregates' total perishing would be an endless fault.

reading: Neelakesi asks how, when the man who did the deeds perished, there can be an appearing among the gods, and why the ascetic is said to have become a god in the Tushita palace, and tells the Buddha to show the continuum he proclaims by joining the two.
nuance: துடித விமானம் is the Tushita heaven, where Buddhist tradition places the Bodhisattva's last birth before he came down as the Buddha; Neelakesi turns the Buddha's own story into a test case for rebirth without a self.

reading: Neelakesi says there is a vast empty space between a human body and a god's body, so no connection enters across it, and the side the Buddha has taken perishes with that; what a pity, she says.

If the Buddha says that examples like the tamarind, the seal, the shadow of a living thing and the cool moon make plain how transmission ends, Neelakesi asks whether the radiant god who eats the deed exists while the dying man still exists.
nuance: The four examples are read as the Buddhist illustrations of a cause producing an effect without passing into it (sourness felt at the sight of tamarind, a seal and its impression, a body and its shadow, the moon and its reflection); Neelakesi's point is that in each the cause is present while the effect arises, so the dead man would have to coexist with the god. The identification of புளி and பொறி is a reading.

reading: If nothing travels across and the effect simply appears where there is a gap, Neelakesi asks whether that is ever seen here, for then light and many other things would stand filling the whole world.
nuance: The reductio is that an effect arising across a gap with nothing crossing would let anything appear anywhere. Line 1 (யற்றுழிக் தோன்றுக) has a doubtful consonant, and the sense of lines 3 to 4 is reconstructed.

reading: Neelakesi says that if the cool moon perished and its reflection still came, she would accept his word; what the eye does not see is no business of hers, and who could stop one so simple-minded.
nuance: வெண்மதியாய் (line 4) puns on the white moon of the example and a blank mind: the Buddha is mocked with his own image.

reading: Neelakesi says that if the moon is not there, its light is not there either, and the new thing is empty once the old has perished; she bids the one who set up the destinies of rebirth show how that is said.
nuance: ஆத்தா (line 4) is read as a vocative of ஆப்தன், the trustworthy teacher, used here with irony; கதியினை நாட்டிய refers to the Buddha's teaching of the destinies into which beings are born.

reading: Neelakesi asks whether the Buddha has forgotten the long branch that joins root to flower without a gap, since in calling a man's becoming a god the work of the unwearying he has left an emptiness in between.
nuance: She grants his seed-to-flower analogy only to show what it needs: an unbroken branch. Between death and the god's birth there is none. மானுயர் தெய்வப் படி (line 3) is read as the pattern of a human become a god; மடியிலார் may be the Buddhas or the Buddha himself.

title: புத்த வாதச் சருக்கம் 611-634 (7/8)
theme: In the Buddha debate Neelakesi attacks the Buddhist account of continuity: she rejects the flame, wind and stream as examples of a series, presses the Buddha on how a deed bears fruit across moments, dismantles his doctrine of the trace (vasana) carried like flower scent into a pot, argues that total perishing would make release automatic, and reduces his balance-beam image of simultaneous arising and perishing to nothing.
source_issues: 629 line 3: the edition's '•' is the old encoding of ஃ (repaired in the core).
617 line 4: சடருடை before வாசனை is doubtful, perhaps corrupt.
626 line 2: இல்லற்க is an odd form; the sense of the line is doubtful.
628 line 3: யேலுந் before சவறது looks miswritten (expected யேனும் or யேலும்).
624 lines 3-4: the word division of சுவாகதம் போந்ததென் றேவன் றிருந்தடி is uncertain.
613 line 3 and 634 lines 1-2 (அட்டகம்) are obscure.
Most verses have no speech verb; Neelakesi is taken as speaker from the story, from என்றாள் (618, 628, 629, 624) and from the vocatives to the Buddha (612, 613, 631).

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddha himself, whom Neelakesi debates in this sarukkam

reading: Neelakesi takes up the Buddha's plea that his school too speaks of an unbroken continuity of arisings, called santana, and answers that the wind, the flame and the stream poured from a water-pot will not serve as examples of it, since in each two things are real.
nuance: The 'two' of line 4 is taken as a lasting stuff and its passing states (air, oil or water beside the gust, the tongue of fire, the falling stream), so each of the Buddhist's own examples is turned into a case of something that persists; the verse does not spell the two out.

reading: She puts a dilemma: if the continuity is only a notion, it is like the knowing of the mad, the dreamer or the possessed, which does not answer to anything; if it is a real thing, then, Buddha, his words have no meaning.
She asks the Buddha how, on his account, he can show the stages of ageing, the fine smallness of a thing's beginning, the growth that opens out moment by moment, and its decline.
nuance: Ageing and growth by degrees need something that grows and ages; the point is implied by the question rather than stated. The third line (சாத்திரத்தால் அத் தவிரன்கட் டாழ்ச்சியும்) is obscure and its sense is guessed.

reading: What use, she asks, is telling of the many aeons and the merit of the unblinking one, if he says the fruit comes in the very moment a thing arises; and if he says it comes down the line afterwards, then the deed goes on and on and exists.
nuance: The aeons (கப்பம்) are the Bodhisattva's long striving told in the birth stories; she makes them pointless under momentariness, or else makes the deed a lasting thing.

reading: Even if he calls the earlier moment a cause, she says, it is no cause, since nothing of it goes into the next; mocking him as a god of logic who speaks folly, she asks whether the village tank fills when no water comes down the channel.

What has arisen perishes utterly without staying, and the wholly non-existent cannot arise, she says, so his endless talk of continuity is only words, and she calls him one whose way is to lay many low and feed on them.
