nuance: The last line is abuse: it charges the Buddhist teaching with deceiving people for a living, not only with error.

reading: The narrator tells that when the Buddha had argued the continuity of arising by the flame and she had shown each point faulty and pressed him hard, he searched for an answer and set out to establish the doctrine of vasana, the trace that carries over.
nuance: The word before வாசனை (சடருடை) is doubtful; the sense that he now turns to the trace is clear from the verses that follow.
event: Pressed on the flame example, the Buddha turns to defend continuity by the doctrine of the trace (vasana).

reading: Neelakesi states his new claim, that after a moment perishes all its powers cling to what follows as the scent of fragrant flowers is found in a pot, and says that the tenet he holds does not fit these examples.
While the earlier moment exists the later does not yet, and when the later is had the earlier is gone, she argues, so in what way can a trace join the two.

If he answers that pot and flower exist together and so the scent can join them without fault, she replies that perishing and birth are never together, which is just why she said the moments do not join.
Something that goes whole from within the perishing moment into the arising one cannot be called a mere trace, she says; posited so, it is a firebrand that burns his whole side.
nuance: If whatever crosses over crosses entire, it is a lasting thing, which is the Jain's point; the firebrand turns the Buddhist's own device against him.

reading: He speaks of the pollen's smell that came from the blossom into the new pot as passing to the cool water, she says; but if the scent perishes along with the flower, whose would the trace be? She tells him, as one who does not know, to answer with understanding.
nuance: The image is the old one of the new pot that perfumes the water put in it. ஓதன in line 3 is unclear; it is read as 'the scent that is spoken of'.

reading: He keeps saying 'trace, trace' along the line, she says, and assenting to it achieves nothing; let him come and show what thing it is that the pathiri flower, kept in the vessel, smeared with its scent.
nuance: பாசனம் is taken as the vessel (Sanskrit bhajana): she demands the lasting receiver that a scent needs.

reading: If he says the trace, perishing in the flower and arising in the new pot, is found everywhere, she says in mockery, then let him hail it as an auspicious arrival and think on the fine feet of his god.
nuance: The second half is hard: சுவாகதம் is taken as 'welcome' and the line as sarcasm that a trace found everywhere would be a lasting, all-pervading thing fit to be worshipped; the word division of தேவன் or ஏவன் is not certain.

reading: If the trace too perishes utterly, she argues, it must have a trace of its own and the series runs on without end; if he says no such reckoning applies to it, then none applies to the first either, and the faults she named at the start stand.

If he says the scent went over, it did not perish; if he says it did not go, the smell too is absent; and she boasts that when she, knowing the good, declares this right, no one can say before her that it is not.
nuance: The second line's ending (இல்லற்க) is odd; the dilemma of the first two lines is clear.

reading: Since he makes perishing total, she argues, the release he speaks of must be that very perishing, so nirvana would come alike, and briefly, to those who join in great austerity and to those without virtue.
nuance: The argument makes Buddhist release a by-product of momentariness, which the Buddhist would deny: the Manimekalai's teacher places release in seeing impermanence and the cessation of craving, not in the perishing of moments. நீடலதே is read as 'not lasting'.

reading: If he declares that, since arising follows down a line, this reply is the excellence of his path, she says she will make plain that it is faulty, and bids him listen with a clear head.
nuance: The first two lines are compressed and the exact claim she quotes is uncertain; சவறு is taken as 'fault'.

reading: Does a moment bring forth its successor and then perish, she asks, or does the later arising come when it perishes; of the two, which is his way of arising? Let him say it plainly, without darkness.

If a moment produces the next and then perishes, she says, there is contact between them, as with a woman who bears a child and dies; if he says the perishing one never meets what follows, let him show a son to a maiden who has died.
nuance: A dead virgin has no son: the image makes a cause that never meets its effect as impossible as a child without a mother.

reading: Both ways fail, she says, perishing after giving birth and perishing as the next arises, so he is made to give up both; she then asks him, as Vaman, whether he ever spoke of perishing so as to make it forgotten.
nuance: வாம is read as the vocative of வாமன், a name for the Buddha. The second half is obscure.

reading: She tells him not to spin round with many evasions: if he shows the rising and sinking of the two ends of a balance as the arising and perishing of moments, both ends must be there, and if the end that is gone does not exist, the image does not hold.
nuance: The balance-beam is the Buddhist's figure for a cause perishing at the same instant as its effect arises; her reply turns on both pans being present together. The third line is read loosely.

reading: For what does not exist there is no perishing, she says, just as no one speaks of the size or fineness of a crow's tooth; the narrator adds that she, whose tongue moves only for the good, asked him whether any word could be said of such a thing.
On his view there is no balance, she concludes: the beam too is absent, the two ends have no way to stand, rising and falling are mixed everywhere, and what is seen at the end is void.
nuance: அட்டகம் is taken as the beam or frame of the balance; if it too is momentary, the image collapses. The verse turns the Buddhist figure into emptiness (பாழ்) as a reproach, not a doctrine.

title: புத்த வாதச் சருக்கம் 635-658 (8/8)
theme: The end of the debate with the Buddha: Neelakesi takes apart his balance-beam image of cause and effect and the claim that wholes are only names, asks who reaps a deed's fruit, meets his answer that the reaper is neither the doer nor another but another in the doer's line, like paddy and cane, and argues that what is not the same is other, that his own gifts in former births would then be fruitless, and that the doers reap; he falls silent, assents to the Jain account of things as perishing in one respect and not in another, and she leaves saying that any being who understands the Lord's scripture reaches release.
source_issues: 636, 650, 652, 655, 656 line 2: the old encoding • for ஃ was repaired in the core.
639 line 4 and 654 line 4: a TSCII leftover was repaired (ேரி); 639 line 1 சொன்னேற்கு (first person) sits oddly in the sense.
655 line 3: புத்த£ர் carries the non-Tamil character £ (U+00A3); probably புத்தர் or a vocative புத்தீர்.
655-658: many TSCII leftovers were repaired by the build (ி, ா); readings follow the repaired text.
657 line 4: a stray space before the final full stop (என்றான .).
658 line 4: நோழையும் is not a known name or word; it may be a corruption of a name for Neelakesi (as நீலையும்).
647: in short lines, unlike the four-foot lines around it; it may be a quoted saying or a damaged verse.
648 lines 2-3 and 651 line 4 (உலங்கருவாமே) are obscure and may be corrupt.
636-640 and 645-656: no speech verb names the speaker; Neelakesi is taken as speaker from the run of the argument, the Buddha in 642-644 from என்றான் and the vocative நறுநுதலாய்.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddha, whom Neelakesi debates in person in this sarukkam; here named by his former gifts (641)
the Buddhists as a body, whom Neelakesi challenges to come in companies (655)

reading: Neelakesi tells the Buddha that to anyone who enters into it, all his scripture is like a children's nonsense rhyme about a wasp and a blind oil-woman who poured out her oil for fear her looks would be spoiled.
nuance: The rhyme is quoted as a sample of nonsense, not for its content; the insult opens the last round of the debate by calling the whole scripture incoherent rather than one tenet false.

reading: Neelakesi takes up the Buddha's image of the balance beam, whose two ends sink and rise at once, and says that if he granted arising and perishing to one gathered whole in the same way she would call it fitting.
nuance: The beam is the Buddhist image for a cause ceasing as its effect arises; her point is that the image needs one beam, a single thing that bears both motions, which is what the doctrine of momentary aggregates denies.

reading: If he answers that the beam has no standing of its own apart from the sinking and rising of its ends, and that its oneness is only a name given by convention, she tells him to hear the many faults that follow.
nuance: இடுகுறி, an assigned name, is the Buddhist account of every whole as a label for parts; the faults are given in 638 and 639.

reading: If beam and ends do not exist together, she says, she has answered that already, and a further fault follows: he would have to say there is a cow that gives milk without tail, head or middle.

If he says compounded things are unreal yet grants that the awareness of them is real, she argues, he falls into the tangle of quality and bearer, part and whole, and has brought that great trouble on himself.
nuance: Line 1's சொன்னேற்கு is first person and does not fit the sense well; the reading takes the line as stating his position.

reading: Two masses, three masses, countless masses, and more to come: she bids him leave them, take one whole and set the soul's good in it, and so act as one blessed.
nuance: பிண்டம் is a lump or aggregate; she mocks the multiplying of momentary heaps and urges a single bearer of the self's welfare. The last line is hard to construe.

reading: When Neelakesi asks whether the doer of a deed enjoys its fruit, or another, or all, or no one, the one who had given his eyes more times than the sea has grains of sand begins to answer.
nuance: The Buddha is named only by his gifts in former births (eyes given beyond counting), the very gifts she will turn against him in 649 and 653.
event: Neelakesi asks the Buddha who reaps the fruit of a deed, and he begins his answer.

reading: The Buddha says he does not call the reaper the doer, nor another, nor both, nor can it be said no one reaches the fruit, and bids her hear who it is.
nuance: A fourfold denial; Neelakesi answers it in 645 to 651 by holding that what is not the same must be other.

reading: He says it is neither that, nor other, nor both, nor like it, but another thing arising in its line, and offers an example.
nuance: The key words are அதன் வழியின் மற்றொன்று, another in its line: the doctrine of a continuity without identity, which 646 and 651 attack.

reading: It is not the seed sown, nor the sprout, nor what came from those two, he says, but as with tall sweet sugarcane and paddy; and he bids the fair-browed woman look at it from the middle.
nuance: நடுவாக நோக்காய் asks her to look from the middle, the Buddhist middle between identity and difference; Neelakesi takes his own paddy and cane apart in 650 and 651.

reading: Neelakesi says that if it is not the same it is other, and she sees nothing he has established; as a horse that is not male is a mare, can he prove anything that both is and is not so?
nuance: She presses the excluded middle against his tetralemma; the first two lines are hard to divide.

reading: Whether by resembling the doer, by not being him, by coming in his line, or by being called other, she asks, is there any way the reaper ceases to be another?
Though a carp is like an eye, though a thicket is not a forest, though things multiply through the female, all of them are other things.
nuance: Three examples answer his three ways in 646: likeness (the carp and the eye), being less than the whole (thicket and forest) and descent (offspring); each still yields another thing. The verse is in short lines, unlike its neighbours.

reading: She says he holds that a stranger reaps and the doer does not, and calls this a heaping up of impossible things, like describing a creature that is no hare, faintly like one in the face, like a field-tortoise.
nuance: The run of comparisons in lines 2 and 3 is obscure (மக்குளி is not clear); their sense as a list of impossibles is taken from line 4.

reading: If the reaper is neither another nor himself, and so is another after all, she asks the Buddha who took birth as a hare: if the one who did the deed gets no fruit of it, what is that fruit but waste?
nuance: The hare birth is the tale of the hare that gave itself as food; she does not deny the tale here but uses it: on his doctrine its fruit could never have reached the Buddha. Line 2's address to a woman of cloud-dark tresses suggests line 1 quotes his formula back at her.

reading: He likened it to paddy, other than itself yet not other, but then said something else; when he tells of those in heaven, she asks, is not the one who gains heaven another than the one who earned it?
nuance: Line 1 is hard to construe; the force is that his own preaching of heaven as a reward needs the one rewarded to be the one who did well.

reading: Let him say that sugarcane comes in the line of paddy and paddy from cane; if he cannot, his example fails, and if he says the son in the line of the father who did the deed is not the father, his account comes apart.
nuance: She turns his paddy against him: paddy gives only paddy, so the example shows a kind that persists, not a 'neither same nor other'. The last words (உலங்கருவாமே) are obscure.

reading: The Buddha says the doer is the doer and the reaper the reaper and that this is how his truth lies; Neelakesi asks whether others reach the fruit, saying the fruit of both kinds of deed belongs to the doers themselves, and he sits silent in thought.
nuance: His new formula keeps doer and reaper as two terms, which grants her the separation she has been pressing; her answer, செய்தார்கள் தாம், makes the doer the reaper. His falling silent is the turn of the debate.
event: The Buddha restates that doer is doer and reaper is reaper; Neelakesi answers that the doers reap, and he falls silent.

reading: She reminds him that in former times he toiled only for others, giving eyes, head, flesh and wife, and asks whether, even now, he has failed to teach any way by which the doers of a deed come to eat its fruit.
nuance: The gifts Kundalakesi praised (205) become evidence against the Buddha: they were made in hope of fruit, and his teaching leaves no one to receive it.

reading: However much he strains and however long he ponders, she says, if he claims by his own vision to explain how a deed joins its fruit, let him see that it comes to not even a millet grain.
nuance: காட்சி may mean his view or doctrine as well as his seeing; either way the verdict is that the doctrine cannot join deed to fruit.

reading: Unless he wants total destruction, what stood before must continue, and if it slips away that contradicts his own word; she challenges the Buddhists, however many, to gather in their companies and defend their tenet.
nuance: The choice she gives is annihilation or persistence; the challenge to all Buddhists widens the debate from the Buddha to his order.
event: Neelakesi challenges all the Buddhists to come together in companies and defend their tenet.

reading: Quoting his objection that a thing which stays is eternal, one which ceases is not, and one called both has the faults of both, she asks whether by saying so he makes himself a one-sided thinker.
nuance: ஏகாந்தன் is the Jain word for one who holds a single-sided view; the charge turns his objection to the Jain 'both' into evidence of his own error. The answer is given in 657.

reading: When she asks whether he will not praise a conclusion in which a thing is cut off in one way, not cut off in that way too, and both, a conclusion that is no false cutting, the Buddha says he will praise it.
nuance: உச்சேதம் is annihilation; the Buddha here assents to the Jain many-sided account he attacked in 656. Whether line 4 gives her question and his assent, or his challenge and her assent, turns on the masculine என்றான், which favours the Buddha as speaker.
event: The Buddha agrees to praise the Jain conclusion that a thing perishes in one respect and not in another.

reading: Neelakesi says that those of any form who understand the Lord's scripture reach in due order the release they seek; bidden to go on with steadfastness, by scripture or another way, she departs.
nuance: எவ்வுருவினாரும், those of any form, includes the speaker herself, a demoness converted (4). முறையினால் makes release gradual, by order, not sudden. Who says செல் in line 4 is not stated; the Buddha is the likeliest.
event: Neelakesi tells the Buddha that anyone who understands the Lord's scripture reaches release, and having won, she leaves.

title: ஆசீவக வாதச் சருக்கம் 659-682 (1/3)
theme: Neelakesi, leaving Kapilapuram after defeating the Buddha, sings a hymn claiming that all faultless scripture and every true god belong to the Jina and that he knows without reckoning; she reaches the Ajivikas at Samadandam, where Puranan names Makkali as their silent omniscient Lord, the nine Kathir books as scripture, and five categories of atom (earth, water, fire, wind and soul) that never enter one another; she undertakes to show this contrary to perception and reason, and begins by arguing that a Lord who never spoke left no scripture and that silence cannot make a Lord.
source_issues: 665: line 4 (அந்திணையில் பேராற்றல்) is hard to divide; the sense of what the feet bestow is uncertain.
671: காழ்ப்பாடு is rare; it recurs at 694 and 699 as an Ajivika term, but its exact sense is not fixed by the text.
673: line 4 புகழ்பூ ரணனே is divided across பூ / ரணனே; it may name the speaker பூரணன் or call the Lord the Full One.
674: line 4 உணு is probably அணு.
675: line 3 (புலமா கொலியொன் றொழிய முதற்காஞ் சலமாய்) is hard to divide; the quality assigned to earth is unclear.
677: line 2 குணமே யிலவாம் seems to deny the atoms qualities just after 676 assigns them; possibly corrupt.
681: ஒக்கலி and யோகலி, named as two gods, are otherwise unknown; the forms may be corrupt.
682: lines 3-4 are compressed and the turn of the argument is a reading.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the most learned of the Ajivika ascetics at Samadandam, their spokesman in the debate
the Ajivika ascetics gathered in the grove at Samadandam

reading: Leaving Kapilapuram behind, Neelakesi travels by the sky path, vast as a mountain, and begins to praise the one of shining body who shed the inner four deeds and knows without having to reckon.
nuance: எண்ணாது உணர்ந்தான், 'he who knew without reckoning', is the mark she earlier denied the Buddha, who she said knew by seeing, hearing and reckoning (193). உண்ணால் வினை is read as உள் நால் வினை, the four inner deeds, which fits the Jain account of the omniscient but is a reading of a joined form.
event: Neelakesi leaves Kapilapuram by the sky and begins a hymn to the Jina.

reading: She asks whether any word of the other schools free of fault lies outside the ocean of scripture told by the one who gave the Angas, any more than there is a flower that does not come to rest at the Lord's red feet.
nuance: The verse turns on a rhetorical question whose force can be read two ways: that no rival school speaks without fault, or that whatever is faultless in them is already in the Jina's scripture; the parallel with the flowers that all end at the Lord's feet favours the second.

reading: She asks whether there is any penance-path that ends birth not found in the scripture-ocean of the one who gave the Purvas, and likewise whether there is any god who does not bear the Tirthankara's holy name.
nuance: The second half folds every god of every school into the Jina: whatever is rightly worshipped as a god is a name of the Tirthankara.

reading: She asks where there is any scripture the world recites that does not draw on the learning the Poet uttered, and says that the world's scriptures and much else besides were born of what he said.
Adorned with flowers and sandal, she says she knows nothing but her Lord's flower feet, and asks that those feet bring her, who knows nothing else, through to the end.
She has no joy except in the paired feet of the Lord who was first in the world, and trusts those feet to bring her, who has no other joy, to birth in the state where suffering is put away.

Nothing is in her mind but the holy feet of the one who knows without approaching, like a fine gem shining in the night, and she trusts those feet to give her, whose mind holds nothing else, great power.
nuance: அண்ணாது உணர்ந்தான, 'who knew without coming near', repeats the claim of 659 that the Lord's knowing does not go through the senses' contact with things.

reading: Praying that the old deeds gathered on her may end, she worships the feet of the Lord of the triple umbrella in thought, word and body, and from the great city of Kukkuta goes like a flag of lightning into Samadandam.
nuance: The convert who once begged the sage to quench her cruel deeds (62) now asks the Jina's feet for the same thing; the prayer is hers, and the verse does not say how the feet are to end the deeds.
event: Neelakesi worships the Jina's feet, praying to be rid of her old deeds, and goes from Kukkuta city to Samadandam.

reading: To the ascetics gathered there she says that the grove of fragrant flowers is lovely to see and asks who these are that dwell in it.
event: Neelakesi comes on the Ajivika ascetics in their flowering grove and asks who they are.

reading: From that throng of godlike ones who want no cause, Puranan, greatly learned and greatest of them, speaks so that the woman may know.
nuance: காரணம் வேண்டாக் கடவுட் குழாம், 'the god-throng that needs no cause', may be a Jain's barb at the Ajivika teaching that things come about without cause; the phrase can also be plain praise of ascetics who want nothing.
event: Puranan, the most learned of the Ajivikas, steps forward to answer her.

reading: Puranan tells her that these are not strangers but Ajivikas, great ascetics of undeluded vision at whom all the wide world marvels.
event: Puranan names his company as the Ajivikas.

reading: Neelakesi, unequalled in every science, tells him that much is gained by setting out in order the teacher, the scripture, the categories and how they come about, and asks him to state his scripture here.
nuance: Her four heads (ஆத்தன், நூல், பொருள், நிகழ்ச்சி) are the questions the king of Kampili put at the first debate (172), now in her own mouth: she has become the examiner.
event: Neelakesi asks Puranan to set out his teacher, scripture, categories and their workings.

reading: Puranan answers that Makkali himself is the Lord, that their scripture is the nine books called Kathir, that the subtle categories are five, and that their working is fixedness (காழ்ப்பாடு).
nuance: Neelakesi answers each head in turn: the authority of the books in 680-681, the five categories in 687-693, and the காழ்ப்பாடு in 694, where she calls it a fixity of bewilderment. காழ்ப்பாடு, 'hardening', is read as the fixed course of things; the word is rare and its exact sense is not secure.
event: Puranan names Makkali as the Ajivikas' god and states their scripture and categories.

reading: Puranan says the Lord is Lord because he knew, and kept himself closed; were he to speak without restraint, he would be like one who has thrown something and would fall back, bewildered, into the round of wandering.
nuance: This is the Ajivika ground for a silent omniscient: to speak is to be moved, and to be moved is to fall back into birth. Neelakesi takes the verse up almost word for word in 682 to answer it. The simile எறிந்தான் அனைய (like one who threw) is compressed and its exact point is not certain.

reading: Puranan describes the Lord as one who neither speaks nor eats, has no wrinkle or grey hair, and has a form that cannot be seen, like a rainbow in the sky that no bound contains.
nuance: The last words, புகழ் பூரணனே, may close the speech with the speaker's name or may call the Lord the Full One (பூரணன்); the division of line 4 allows either. Neelakesi turns the rainbow simile against him in 684.

reading: Puranan says the matters spoken of in the Kathir, beginning with restraint and the goal, when gathered come to this: there are atoms, and they are of five forms.
nuance: உணு in line 4 is read as அணு.

reading: Puranan names the five as earth, water, fire, wind and soul, each with its many qualities, and says that, sound apart, coolness is the first quality of water.
nuance: Soul counted as the fifth beside the four elements is the same five the Manimekalai's Ajivika gives. Line 3 is hard to divide, and which quality is assigned to earth is not clear.

reading: Puranan says burning and the like belong to fire, compacting and feeding to wind, turning back and knowing to soul, and that these are the qualities of the substances named.
nuance: Knowing is listed as one quality among the others, the soul's as burning is fire's; Neelakesi's attack on the five classes begins at 687.

reading: Puranan says the five kinds of atom all combine and separate, but that one does not enter into another, not even for an instant.
nuance: Neelakesi answers this in 698, where she presses him that, if nothing gives room to anything else, ghee cannot become flame. Line 2's குணமே இலவாம் seems to deny the atoms qualities just after 676 gave them; the reading is unsure.

reading: Puranan says these are the categories and he will tell something of their nature for the assembly, warns her not to scorn the Ajivikas as caring only for taste, and claims the categories cannot be overthrown by others.

When he has named the Lord, scripture, categories and their working, Neelakesi, of skilled speech, sets out before the learned company to show that all of it is contrary both to sight and to reason, and speaks again.
nuance: கண்ணினும் அன்றிக் கருத்தினும் வேறு: she will test his account by perception and by inference, the two means both sides grant, not by her own scripture.
event: Neelakesi begins her answer, undertaking to show the Ajivika account contrary to perception and reason.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if the one who knew everything kept silence and never spoke, then the books were spoken by souls full of hatred and other faults, so they are not scripture, and she asks him, fool, how he came by them.

She goes on that if he says the two gods Okkali and Yokali told the books, then had they known as Makkali knew they too would have kept silent, and to speak of the truth without knowing it is unfit, so what these teachers said is faulty.
nuance: Okkali and Yokali are otherwise unknown in the corpus; the verse treats them as the Ajivika's fallback authors. இக்கலியாளர் may pun on Makkali's name and on கலி, the dark age.

reading: Taking up his words, she says that if a knower who speaks what he knows becomes subject to longing and anger and falls back into wandering by that fault, then, by his own reasoning, he too would become a lesser Apta by sitting silent.
nuance: The verse reuses the words of 672 (அறிந்தான், எறிந்தான் அனைய, மறிந்தான், தடுமாற்று) to turn them: if silence is what makes the Lord, any silent man is one. The last line is compressed and its turn is a reading.

title: ஆசீவக வாதச் சருக்கம் 683-706 (2/3)
theme: The middle of the Ajivika debate: Neelakesi argues that a Lord who knows all and keeps silent is lesser than any speaker, that silence proves nothing and a moving body betrays desire, and that a rainbow is a caused thing; she then attacks Puranan's five atom-kinds (earth alone holding the sensible qualities, darkness outside the five, kinds and substances both one and many), his god's freedom from disease, his denial of merit in giving and of sin in killing, and the identity of quality and substance (the ripening date, the plate made a pot, the classes of words), and opens her attack on the doctrine that every outcome is fixed with the example of an infant girl.
source_issues: 693: lines 4 and 5 had '•' for ஃ (old encoding), repaired by the build.
706: the edition prints the verse number as 7096; it is 706 (the next verse is 707).
693 line 4 ends வேண்டூம் where the refrain in line 5 has வேண்டும்; probably a misprint.
Several lines in 685, 689, 690, 691, 692, 698 and 702 resist word division (e.g. னற்ற மகலவென் றானீ, பிறப்பிறவா, பெறவேலா, கல்லாந் தயிர்த்தோடி); readings there are marked uncertain.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Ajivika teacher at Samadandam who expounds Makkali's doctrine (668)

reading: Neelakesi argues that if the Ajivika Lord did not tell all that he knew, then any common man and she herself, who wag their tongues to tell others whatever good they see, are greater than he and stand free of fault in this world and the next.
nuance: சாத்தன் in line 2 is the stock name for any man at all; the argument ranks the silent omniscient below the most ordinary speaker. The silence answered is the one Puranan claimed for his Lord in 673 (உரையான் இறைவன்).
event: Neelakesi answers the claim that the Ajivika Lord keeps silent and says that ordinary speakers would then surpass him.

reading: Taking up Puranan's comparison of the Lord to the rainbow, Neelakesi says that one with a body and senses is a born being, and that a rainbow is no uncaused marvel but what appears when the sun's rays fall on the rain-cloud: that is its whole nature.
nuance: The word சாதகன் in line 2 is read here as 'one who is born'; it could carry another sense, and the division of line 4 (தனுவாம் as 'becomes a bow') is my own.
event: Neelakesi turns the rainbow simile for the Ajivika Lord against him.

reading: Neelakesi asks how Puranan knows that his Lord, who said 'I know all' and then kept silent, really knew; if the proof is that he did not speak, then infants, this tree and the mountain have the same greatness.
nuance: Line 2 (னற்ற மகலவென் றானீ) is hard to divide; the sense taken is that the Lord fell silent so that fault would leave him, which matches 682's claim that speaking would bring passion.
event: Neelakesi mocks the Ajivika proof of the Lord's omniscience from his silence.

reading: Neelakesi argues that the Lord who bends and stretches his limbs, breathes, walks and sits has not stilled his body, so by Puranan's own reasoning he acts from desire; and if he did none of these, who would grant he had life at all?
nuance: The verse turns the Ajivika defence of 682 (that to speak would make the Lord a man of desire and anger) back on him: silence of the tongue leaves the rest of the body in motion.
event: Neelakesi argues that the silent Lord's bodily movements betray desire as much as speech would.

reading: Neelakesi declares that since the Ajivika has spoken what should not be spoken, the earth-kind, water-kind, fire-kind, the wind-kind and the kind of life, she will not stop harrying him until all who sit near have seen it.
nuance: The metre changes here to five-line verses whose last line repeats the fourth with a varied opening; the refrain carries the taunt. The five பால் are the five atom-kinds Puranan set out in 674-677.
event: Neelakesi announces before the onlookers that she will confute the Ajivika's five kinds.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if colour and the other sensible qualities all belong to the earth-kind, the other three elements, having none, could never be seen by eye or any sense, and so could never be known by any means at all.
nuance: The target is 675's claim that every sense-object but sound is earth's; water keeps only its coolness, fire its burning. The objection is that this leaves water, fire and wind unseen.
event: Neelakesi attacks the Ajivika assignment of the sensible qualities to earth alone.

reading: Neelakesi says the Ajivika has multiplied the kinds of water, fire and restless wind by holding only to their names, without examining anything, and so his doctrine, the five he brought forward, collapses.
nuance: பிறப்பிறவா in line 2 is not clear to me; it may mean 'without passing beyond birth' or be a corrupt reading.
event: Neelakesi declares the Ajivika's doctrine of five kinds overthrown.

reading: Neelakesi asks, if things are only these five, to which of the five darkness belongs, and if to none, to which the state the Ajivika himself abides in belongs; and are not the compounds made of atoms beyond number?
nuance: அருடாழ்ந்து in line 4 may be அருள் தாழ்ந்து, 'sunk in grace' or 'fallen from compassion'; the jibe is unclear. கந்தம் here is the atom-compound of Jain usage, not the Buddhist aggregate.
event: Neelakesi challenges the Ajivika to place darkness among his five kinds.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if the many kinds he named do not mix and yet are all one substance, he has both oneness and difference at once, and says he has shown no shame at all before the assembly.
nuance: சலவாதி may be 'deceitful debater'; சமழலையே is read as 'not ashamed' (சமழ்). Both readings are mine.
event: Neelakesi charges the Ajivika with holding both identity and difference of his kinds.

reading: Neelakesi presses: if the one substance becomes the many kinds and there is nothing besides, he must explain how the earth-kind that has turned to ash gives off no smell, and if he is cornered he must establish the same for the other substances.
nuance: Line 3's பெறவேலா is unclear; the challenge read is that ash, still earth, has lost earth's smell, so the quality cannot be the substance itself.
event: Neelakesi asks the Ajivika why ash, though of the earth-kind, has no smell.

reading: Neelakesi says that if kinds and substances are not different, listing 'these are kinds, these are substances' as many is like calling one thing hill, mountain, peak and crag: a mere arrangement of words.
event: Neelakesi mocks the Ajivika's lists as synonyms for one thing.

reading: Neelakesi recalls that the Ajivika said the god has no disease, yet one day a sickness hotter than fire came upon him; even dying, she says, Puranan will not come to the truth, so full is his doctrine of wavering and fixed dogma.
nuance: The 'sickness hotter than fire' may recall the tradition that Makkali died of a burning fever; the verse names neither the god nor the occasion, and whether கடவுள் here is the founder or the ascetics (கடவுட் குழாம், 668) is not certain.
event: Neelakesi cites the burning sickness that struck the Ajivika god against the claim that he is free of disease.

reading: Neelakesi argues that as the hidden planets, though outshone by the sun, still yield their effects at rising and setting, so if all is fixed the beings that have stood through long ages of many births must roam grazing and eating without end, and the Ajivika must accept even fruitless feeding.
nuance: The planet simile and the force of உதவாத ஆர்தல் are hard to fix; the reading that the verse attacks the fixed course of births is mine.
event: Neelakesi draws an absurd consequence from the Ajivika's fixed course of births.

reading: Neelakesi asks what this low act of the sinner and fool is: he says that what exists never perishes and what is not never comes to be, yet he says the pure rice he eats in the alms hall has sunk to impurity.
nuance: The charge is that calling pure food impure admits a change that the doctrine of 'nothing arises, nothing perishes' forbids; அளி in line 2 is read as the hall where food is given.
event: Neelakesi points out the Ajivika's inconsistency over impure food.

reading: Neelakesi says the Ajivika wants no merit for those who give in every manner, standing, receiving or eating, and holds both that a gift bought by killing is evil and that killing carries no sin; she asks what one who denies the fruit of his own gift has found, and what he has found in austerity above the household life.
nuance: Line 3 sets two Ajivika sayings side by side (கொன்றீகை தீது, கொல்பாவம் இல்) as a contradiction. The Neelakesi gives the Ajivika a denial of the fruit of acts; whether the school would accept that account the verse does not show. Line 5 may instead ask what he saw in household life rather than austerity.
event: Neelakesi charges the Ajivika with denying the merit of giving and the sin of killing at once.

reading: Neelakesi recalls that when she asked him how ghee turns to flame and burns, if what is not cannot arise and what is cannot perish, he answered only that stones sink and other things float; then, she says, nothing gives room to anything, and he has no cause for sinking and rising.
nuance: என்றேனுக்கு in line 2 makes the verse a report of an exchange: her question and his answer. Line 3 (கல்லாந் தயிர்த்தோடி யாழ்மிதப்பு) is hard to divide; the sense of stone sinking and things floating is a guess.
event: Neelakesi reports the Ajivika's answer about sinking and floating and rejects it as giving no cause.

reading: Neelakesi says that if the running horse and the horse that eats grass at feeding time are one unchanged thing, let him show her that marvel and she will accept his view and every dogma of his band of 'gods'.
nuance: கடவுட் குழாம் is Puranan's own name for the Ajivika ascetics (668), used here in mockery. The point of காநாட்டிய வீதி is not clear.
event: Neelakesi challenges the Ajivika to show a thing unchanged through its states.

reading: Neelakesi says that if colour and all the qualities are the substance itself, he should show the greenness seen in the young date-fruit still firm in the ripe fruit; she would call him wise if he could, and a god if he can do it with a thing that has changed.
event: Neelakesi tests the identity of quality and substance with the ripening date.

reading: Neelakesi says that since he holds that shape and the like are the substance itself and nothing else, he should show the old shape still present when a plate is broken down and made into a vessel, and show all its changes.
event: Neelakesi asks the Ajivika to show the plate's shape in the pot made from it.

reading: Neelakesi says that when she asks for the things that float and sink, he concludes a plurality of four categories; but if what floats is what sinks and there is nothing else, his words serve nothing, and he has broken his own side at once.
nuance: பதப்பொருள் நான்கு in line 2 may be four categories of meaning; what they are is not stated. உதப்பேனும் in line 4 is obscure.
event: Neelakesi argues that the Ajivika's own distinctions break his doctrine of identity.

reading: Neelakesi says that words of action, quality and form are seen distinct when words are separated without error, and joined with their sense they are seen combined by sandhi, but the Ajivika's words fit no rule of grammar.
nuance: The argument from grammar is that the three classes of word stay distinct even when joined, as the qualities stay distinct in a thing; the Ajivika's speech is said to break that rule.
event: Neelakesi appeals to grammar against the Ajivika's denial of distinct qualities.

reading: Neelakesi announces that she will say a few words on the Ajivika claim that what comes to be, the way it comes, the measure to which it comes and the time when it comes are all fixed, and on how that claim falls.
nuance: The metre changes again to short four-line verses. The refutation follows in 705 to 707 (the infant girl).
event: Neelakesi turns to the Ajivika doctrine that everything is fixed.

reading: Neelakesi sets up her case: take up with proper care the infant girl who is to become a woman, and consider her when she is three cubits tall and when the years stated in their order have passed.
nuance: The verse only sets up the example; its point comes in 706 and 707, where the woman's breasts, child and hair would have to be present already in the infant if all is fixed.
event: Neelakesi begins an example of a girl child to test the doctrine of fixed outcome.

reading: Neelakesi says that, on his view, the nature of the child and the woman she will be, the whole of the seed, already exist without sprouting, and tells him not to hurry, for she will undo his view before it can complete its course.
nuance: துறவாளவளும் in line 1 is unclear (perhaps 'she who will not leave it' or 'the renunciant'); the reply is in 707, where breasts, child and hair absent from the infant overturn the view.
event: Neelakesi presses the infant example against the fixed-outcome doctrine.

title: ஆசீவக வாதச் சருக்கம் 707-729 (3/3)
theme: Neelakesi ends her debate with the Ajivika Puranan: she refutes the fixed order (niyati) by the parts a body gains after birth and by the regress of daughters in the womb, attacks the Ajivika account of souls (their colours, numbers, extent and form) and the natural motions of fire, soul, wind and water, then offers him the cure of births as a physician would; he asks to be taught, she shows by a bent finger that a thing both is and is not, he accepts, and she sets him to ascetic penance and gives him the nine categories.
source_issues: 722 line 4: the opening வாமத்துணீயும் does not divide cleanly (perhaps வா மற்று நீயும்); the sense is uncertain.
723 line 4: கூயத்தின் is unclear and may be corrupt.
711 lines 2-4: அயதி, வியதி, பயதி are puns on நியதி whose senses cannot be fixed from the text.
716 line 2: அகன்றடுமாற்றம் may stand for அகன்ற தடுமாற்றம்; line 3 is obscure.
719 and 723 line 2: the old encoding of ஃ was repaired by the build.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Ajivika teacher whom Neelakesi debates in the Ajivika sarukkam

reading: Neelakesi argues that breasts, children, smiles (the teeth), the hair of the head and the nails appear only later; if they had no standing existence before, the Ajivika's doctrine that what does not exist cannot arise is shaken.
nuance: The verse continues the test begun at 704-706, where the Ajivika's fixed order (நியதம்) was set against a woman and the infant she bears; the parts named are exactly those a newborn lacks. Line 3's நிலையில்லாமை is read here as 'not existing beforehand', which is the sense the argument needs.

reading: If the Ajivika answers that these things do exist in the infant already, Neelakesi says, his talk of a fixed later time is a sham, and he cannot keep saying they come at the end, for the infant he spoke of is a cubit long while the things to come are many.
nuance: களவே (line 2) is taken as 'deceit': if everything is already there, calling its appearance 'fixed for later' only hides the problem. The division of lines 2-4 is hard to fix.

reading: Neelakesi draws the regress: this woman holds a girl in her womb, that girl in the same way holds her own, and so on without end, so that endless infants would lie one within another by nature, which is laughable.
nuance: This is a reductio of preformation: the generations to come must all be packed in the first womb. The Ajivika claim answered is that of 707-708.

reading: Neelakesi says that even if the Ajivika states how things will come to be, his doctrine trembles once the fixed order is made the cause, for if a separate effect also exists it is a fault, and one man's time and end would then be settled.
nuance: The line division (நனிகாரணமாய் நடுக்கு நினகோட்டனிகாரியமும்) allows several readings; the gist taken here is that a fixed order leaves nothing for a person's own deeds to cause.

reading: Neelakesi plays on the Ajivika's word niyati: to say every occurrence is fixed is niyati; if he says 'ayati' he settles in falsehood, if 'viyati' his anger is foolish, and if 'payati' that too gives him something.
nuance: அயதி, வியதி and பயதி look like Sanskrit-sounding variations on நியதி used to mock the opponent, but what each means here cannot be fixed from the Tamil alone.

reading: Neelakesi mocks the Ajivika's account of souls, which gives them colours like ripe fruit and counts them in great numbers rising like smoke through the world, asking whether there can be so many delusions and whether he is not greatly confused.
nuance: The colours seem to answer to the Ajivika grades of birth by colour (the Manimekalai's Ajivika gives six, black to white); the numbers in lines 1-2 (எத்துணையும் அகன்று ஐந்து நூறாம்) are unclear.

reading: Neelakesi turns the Ajivika's claim that no soul enters another and that each has its own breadth and length against him: when we sit crowded together, souls would have to press one upon another, and he has no answer to that.

Neelakesi argues that a thing's nature is in itself where it exists: as the soul's extent within the flesh perceives, so if the soul knows nothing once it has gone above, she would not call it existent at all, and none could then establish it.
nuance: பிரதேசம் (line 2) is the Jain term for the soul's spatial units spread through the body. Which Ajivika claim the verse answers (a released soul without knowledge, perhaps) is not stated.

reading: Neelakesi says that if the one soul has form, it would take many slices like a pumpkin until it perished; if the Ajivika denies that, his own scripture is contradicted; and if he gives up both, it becomes very easy to show the soul does not exist.
nuance: The trilemma leaves the opponent three exits, each fatal: a cuttable soul, a contradicted scripture (ஆகமம்), or no soul at all.

reading: Neelakesi says the Ajivika, who counts souls by a number, sets out their places and their end and makes a great circle that brings them round again, has not seen the truth; if souls are of fixed count, the wandering would not be endless.
nuance: மண்டலம் (line 2) is read as the Ajivika's great cycle of births after which all reach the end; the text's அகன்றடுமாற்றம் may be அகன்ற தடுமாற்றம் (the wide wandering). Line 3 is obscure.

reading: Neelakesi sets out the Ajivika teaching of natural motions: fire and the soul move upward, wind moves sideways, water and earth move downward, each falling or rising by its kind, and asks what follows even if that is so.
nuance: The answer follows in 718-720: a soul that rises by nature could not stay in a body, and wind and water change direction.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if fire and soul go by their own direction, it is not fitting that the soul should stay here at all; yet the Ajivika himself holds that dying and the working of deeds exist.

Neelakesi says that the wind which went south until it reached its quarter will one day turn back, and asks the ascetic whether he can now state in daylight the truth of his doctrine of fixed direction.
nuance: வடந்தை (line 3) is the north wind; the point seems to be that the same wind blows from south and from north. Lines 3-4 are obscure, and line 2 has a repaired letter.

reading: Neelakesi says, mocking, that the Ajivika has explained well how water, which first falls to the ground and then comes down again as drops from the clouds, reaches where it goes.
nuance: நன்றே (line 4) is read as irony: water that has gone up into the cloud breaks the rule that water only sinks.

reading: Neelakesi says the Ajivika does not give the times of the categories that are recited everywhere, yet guards precepts while proclaiming that there are no qualities, and asks whether any medicine can cure such madness.
nuance: மால் (line 4) turns the debate toward the medical images of 722-724. What 'times' and 'qualities' refer to is not settled by the Tamil.

reading: Neelakesi tells the Ajivika that she too was once like him, sick and without any good quality, so that those who saw her called her a demon, until a great one gave her dharma saying 'take this' and she grew bright; there is no medicine like it.
nuance: She speaks of her own past: the demoness of the burning ground whom the sage Munichandra taught (ch. 3-7). The debater offers the opponent the cure she herself received. The opening of line 4 (வாமத்துணீயும்) is unclear.
event: Neelakesi tells the Ajivika how she, once a demon, was cured by the dharma a great teacher gave her.

reading: Neelakesi says the teachers' instruction is like a physician's: it settles what the disease is, searches out its root, knows the medicine fit for it and gives it, and so cuts away the suffering of many beings.
nuance: The order of line 1 (நோய், நோய்முதல் நாடி) is the order of Kural 948, but the shared run is under four words, so it is linked, not marked as an echo. கூயத்தின் (line 4) is unclear.

reading: Neelakesi names birth and the rest as the diseases; their cause, known rightly, is the eating of bad deeds; sinking in them comes from the threefold fault; and what ends the suffering is true understanding.
nuance: திரிதோடம் (line 3) is the physician's three humours, carried over to the soul; the Jain triple fault is probably meant, but the verse does not name its members.

reading: The Ajivika answers Neelakesi, praising her deer-like gaze and long eyes: he will not forget; if she will state without fail how this true understanding, best of all, stands, he too will look at things the way she does.
event: The Ajivika Puranan asks Neelakesi to teach him true understanding and promises to see things her way.

reading: Neelakesi shows him a finger: if the straight finger bends and he says 'that finger has gone', then by his own words that one finger both is and is not; this, she says, is the point.
nuance: The finger that remains a finger while its straightness ends is the Jain way of holding that a thing persists and changes at once, against the Ajivika's 'nothing arises, nothing perishes' (698).
event: Neelakesi bends a finger before Puranan to show that a thing both is and is not.

reading: The narrator says that hearing her words, that a thing sinks in one respect and not with others, and rises in one respect, the Ajivika, with a humbled mind, said 'this is the truth'.
nuance: ஆழ்ச்சி and ஏழ்ச்சி (sinking and rising) take up the natural-motion debate of 717-720 in the new key of respects.
event: Puranan, humbled, accepts Neelakesi's teaching as the truth.

reading: Neelakesi tells Puranan that he has cleared away all falsehood and come to know the truth; beyond this, eating from the hand and taking the last resting place, he should do the penance proper to him.
nuance: கைந்நின்று உண்டும் is read as the Jain ascetic's eating from the palms, and கடைப்பள்ளி as the last bed, the vowed death; both readings are probable but not certain.
event: Neelakesi tells the converted Puranan to take up ascetic penance.

reading: Neelakesi gives Puranan the true scripture of the god who knew without learning, the three-times-three categories and the nature of all things, bids him put off the wrong paths, and sends him away.
nuance: மும்மூன்று (lines 2-3) is read as the nine categories the Jains recite. Line 2 (சொல்லானும் அல்லன்) seems to say the lord is not a mere speaker but the source whose word it is; the sense is not secure.
event: Neelakesi gives Puranan the nine categories and dismisses him.

title: சாங்கிய வாதச் சருக்கம் 730-748 (1/3)
theme: Neelakesi goes to Hastinapura to the Sankhya teacher Parasaran, draws out his twenty-five principles and his doctrine of a soul that does nothing yet experiences, then attacks it: a non-acting soul could not teach, speak, enjoy, be bound or be carried between births, and his defence of a second, acting soul destroys his own thesis.
source_issues: Verse 738 is missing from the core file: the chapter has 18 verses for 730-748, and 739 follows 737 without a break in sense being evident.
731 line 4 (ஒன்றா வகையால் உரைகளை ஒட்டா) ends without a finite verb and seems incomplete.
733 line 2: பருங்கினன் is an unusual form, possibly corrupt.
736 line 2: இன்பன பேதனலே பகன் is hard to divide.
734 lines 1 and 3: the e-text's '•' was repaired to ஃ (இஃது, அஃது).
740 lines 1-2 and 744 line 2 are hard to construe.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Sankhya teacher of Hastinapura who has planted a challenge flag
the Ajivika teacher Neelakesi has just defeated, who directs her to the Sankhya

reading: When the defeated Ajivika had told her of him, Neelakesi went to Hastinapura to confront the Sankhya teacher who had planted a tall challenge flag there and was held by everyone as their authority.
nuance: ஆங்கவன் சொல்ல picks up the end of the Ajivika sarukkam (729), where she sends Puranan away; the flag planted to dare all comers (கொடி நட்டு) is the formal opening of a debate. எவர்க்கும் மறை என்று இருந்த is read here as 'regarded by all as their scripture or authority'; it could also mean he was hidden from or closed to everyone.
event: On Puranan's word Neelakesi goes to Hastinapura to meet the Sankhya teacher who has planted a challenge flag.

reading: Arriving, she saw his devotion and stood to hear him recite, and he set out his path, then the coming forth and the drawing back of things at the world's dissolution.
nuance: பிரளையத்து ஆக்கமும் பேர்ச்சியும, the emergence and the withdrawal, is the Sankhya cycle of manifestation and reabsorption into nature. Line 4 (ஒன்றா வகையால் உரைகளை ஒட்டா) breaks off and seems to run on into 732; its sense is not clear.
event: Neelakesi listens as the Sankhya teacher expounds his path and the cycle of emergence and dissolution.

reading: The narrator sums up what he expounded: the supreme self, root nature and the nature that is not the root, with the rules and divisions that belong to them, the subtle matters laid down in his treatise.
nuance: மூலப் பகுதி and அல்லாப் பகுதி render the Sankhya distinction between primal nature and its evolutes. பாலொத்து நின்ற is obscure; it may liken the self to milk, or mean 'standing on its own side'. The supreme self (பரமாத்துமன்) returns in 746-747, where she asks how it relates to the many souls.

reading: He laid all this out before the gathered assembly, and she, the foremost in knowledge, questioned Parasaran as if she too longed for the truth.
nuance: விரும்பினள் போல, 'as though she desired it', tells the reader her questions are a debater's feint: she plays the eager pupil to draw out his doctrine before attacking it. பருங்கினன் in line 2 is an unusual form, perhaps for a verb of setting out or teaching.
event: Before the assembly Neelakesi questions the Sankhya teacher Parasaran, feigning a learner's eagerness.

reading: She asks him, as a disciple asks the one who begot her, what this teaching is; he says it is his path, she asks to be taught it, and he begins: hear these things.
nuance: என்னைப் பயந்தீர், 'you who gave me birth', is the address of a pupil to a teacher as spiritual parent, and continues the feint of 733; நன்னுதலாய், 'fair-browed one', is his condescending address to a woman.
event: Neelakesi, posing as a pupil, asks to be taught the Sankhya path, and the teacher begins.

reading: The Sankhya teacher lists his twenty-five categories: the abiding soul, the unmanifest, the great principle, the sense of self, the five and five senses, the one mind, the five subtle elements and the five gross elements.
nuance: The count works out: soul, the unmanifest (தெற்றென இல்லது, 'what is not clearly there'), மான் (mahat), செருக்கு (ahamkara), ten senses, mind, five மாத்திரை (tanmatras) and five பூதம் make twenty-five. Neelakesi pronounces these categories faulty in 739 and attacks the soul among them from 740 on.

reading: He describes the soul: it does nothing in any way, has none of the qualities, is a principle of its own, unstained, eternal, present everywhere, the far-seeing witness, and yet the one who experiences.
nuance: Line 2 (இன்பன பேதனலே பகன்) is hard to divide; அலேபகன், 'unstained', can be made out, but the rest is uncertain. The pairing in line 4 of the non-acting soul with துத்தல் உடையன், 'one who experiences or eats', is the joint Neelakesi presses in 740-745: how can what does nothing enjoy?

reading: He describes the unmanifest as standing, spread out and formless, with no sense organ and no action, and from it the great principle, from the sense of self the sixteen, and besides them the five elements.
nuance: ஈரெட்டு, 'twice eight', are the sixteen products of the sense of self (the eleven organs with mind and the five subtle elements), with the five gross elements beyond them, the classical Sankhya order of evolution. Line 1's இக்கு and line 2's division are unclear.

reading: Like one throwing a stone before a raging rutting elephant she declared his categories faulty, and he, swollen with pride, turned to the woman and told her to name the fault.
nuance: மதம் is both an elephant's rut and a school's doctrine, so மதத்தினின் மிக்கவன் is the man swollen with rut and with his creed; the simile makes her challenge brave rather than rash. உதப்பு is a rare word, taken here as the fault or flaw he demands she show.
event: Neelakesi declares the Sankhya categories faulty, and the angry teacher demands that she name the fault.

reading: Neelakesi argues that if he says the soul does not act, then his speaking cannot be his own: these words, being the work of something else, are flawed, and the path is not even his.
nuance: The argument turns the doctrine on the speaker: a teacher whose self does nothing cannot claim the teaching he is uttering. Lines 1-2 (நின்னை வையாய் ... உளது அன்றெனின்) are hard to construe, and the reading of their steps is tentative.

reading: She goes on: since he holds the soul does nothing in any way, even his standing as the master who teaches the principles fails, and contradiction with what is seen and falsehood cling to the doctrine.
nuance: Line 1 repeats 736's own words (எத்திறத்தின்னுஞ்செய்யான்) so the refutation quotes the thesis. திருட்ட விரோதம், contradiction with what is seen, is a named fault of the debate manuals: everyone sees the soul acting.

reading: The Sankhya replies that the soul is of two kinds, and that apart from the soul that does nothing there is a soul bound up with action, from which the work of the world proceeds.
nuance: This is his escape from 740-741: action belongs to a karmic soul (கரும உயிர்), not to the pure one. Line 1 (பெருமை உயிர்க்குரையேன்) and the middle term in line 2 (இடை ஒன்றும்) are obscure. Neelakesi answers at once in 743.

reading: She replies that if acting souls and non-acting souls both truly exist, his thesis is destroyed and falsehood and the other faults come upon it; what will he do now?
nuance: மேற்கோள் is the formal thesis of a debate; to grant an acting soul is to contradict the thesis that the soul does not act, so the defence of 742 sinks the position it defends.

reading: She asks what an idle soul without qualities, hidden and unmanifest, actually does: if it only enjoys, how does it come to enjoy, and if everything goes on without it, what is it for?
nuance: சோம்பன், 'the idler', is her mocking name for the inactive soul. Line 2 (ஓம்பற்கு அருமையின் உண்ணுமாற்றான்) is hard to construe; the question 'how does it eat' answers to the experiencer of 736.

reading: She asks how a soul that is formless and does nothing, and that on examination neither touches nor joins nature with its forms and modifications, can be the cause of its own seeing and experiencing.
nuance: விகிர்தி விகற்பொடு names nature's modifications and their varieties. The objection is the one she pressed against the Buddhist on how formless consciousness can be joined to a body (302); a Jain soul, of the body's size, is in contact with what it knows.

reading: She asks whether, if the soul stands pure, conscious, pervading everything and unchanging, nature makes it whirl in the round of births out of hatred for the released soul or love of the bound ones.
nuance: முத்தாத்துமன் and புத்தாத்துமாக்கள் are the released and the bound souls (புத்த for baddha, 'bound', not the Buddha). The mock alternatives, hatred or desire, are her point: a changeless pure soul gives nature no reason to bind it, so Sankhya bondage has no cause.

reading: She demands that, instead of saying the supreme soul takes on the souls' modifications only as crystal takes colour from what is beside it, he state properly what the one soul is.
nuance: பளிங்கு அடை போல, 'like crystal by what lies near it', is the Sankhya image of a soul that only seems coloured by nature's changes. She treats the image as an evasion. மாத்திரை in line 3 may mean 'a mere measure' (only an appearance) and is uncertain.

reading: She closes with a dilemma: if he says the soul goes from birth to birth, his doctrine breaks; if he says it does not go, the earlier objections return; what accompanies the soul is its twofold deeds, and his speech is mere fluency of teeth and tongue.
nuance: Line 3 (பல்லும் நுன் நாவும் பதையாது உரை) mocks talk that runs on without the tongue faltering. எல்லும் துணையும் இருவினை is read as 'the twofold deeds are its light and companion', the Jain answer to what carries a soul between births; the line is compressed and the reading is tentative.

title: சாங்கிய வாதச் சருக்கம் 749-765 (2/3)
theme: In the middle of her debate with the Sankhya teacher Neelakesi attacks his chain of principles: she asks whether mahat comes from prakriti, mocks the count of eleven organs and the organs of action, sets out the Jain view that the four elements are built of atoms and that space is one formless thing reaching beyond the world, denies that sound belongs to space, and argues that an unchanging soul and an unknowing nature can neither join anew nor produce anything.
source_issues: 761 line 1: the edition's '•' was repaired to ஃ (இஃதினு மஃதில்லை).
755 lines 1 and 2 (தந்திர மாவன ... வந்தர வாத்துவன்) are obscure and may be corrupt; the reading is a guess.
762 line 2 (பொருடம் தாக்கமும் போத்தந் துரைப்பிற்) has an odd word division and is hard to construe.
765 line 1 opens with இல்லுளி, which I cannot construe with confidence.
Chapter 33's span (730-748) lacks a verse 738 in the core file; noted here only as seen in the neighbouring show output.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Sankhya teacher at Hastinapura whom Neelakesi debates in this sarukkam (named சாங்கியன் in 730)

reading: Neelakesi takes the Sankhya's mahat, the principle said to give birth to the pride of 'I' and 'mine', and argues that whatever brings a thought into being must be a sentient thing, which her opponent never considered.
nuance: The Sankhya puts mahat on the side of unconscious nature; the objection turns that against him: producing the sense of self is a work of thought, and thought belongs to the sentient. The reading of சேதனை twice (lines 2 and 3) as the sentient is mine and the lines are compressed.

reading: She asks whether mahat comes forth from prakriti or is a separate thing in its own right, says there is no third possibility, and bids him answer so that the learned may judge.
nuance: A dilemma: each horn is answered in the verses that follow (751 and 761). சான்றார் appeals to the assembly of the wise who judge a debate.

reading: She presses the dilemma: if the quality is the first substance itself, nothing new has come forth, and if it is other than it, a further thing exists; she, skilled in speaking on scripture, asks what he can say to this.
nuance: Line 2 (அதற்பிறி தென்னி னதுமனனு முண்டா) is hard to construe; the sense that a distinct product would be a new thing beside prakriti is my reading. சுதப்பொருள் (line 4) praises her command of scripture.

reading: Neelakesi says that if the formless, unmanifest cause can bring forth its opposite, the world with form, he may as well say that empty space by itself creates gross things, and calls his words incoherent.
nuance: A reductio: the Sankhya's unmanifest (அவ்வியத்தம்) is formless, and if formless can yield form, any formless thing, space included, could. In 759 she gives the Jain view of space as formless and producing nothing.

reading: She says prakriti made of mutually hostile qualities, and products in which one quality comes to exceed the others, destroy his own thesis and leave all his classes empty, so his doctrine is only laughable and she will not believe it.
nuance: பகைக்குணம் (line 1) names the three qualities as enemies of one another; the point is that opposed qualities cannot form one stable cause, and if a product comes by one exceeding the rest, the balanced cause is already lost.

reading: Mocking the count of organs, she says he made five organs of knowing and five of action, ten and one more, yet left out an organ of madness, an organ of possession and an organ of punching.
nuance: The joke rests on the Sanskrit names புத்தேந்திரியம் and கம்மேந்திரியம்: if every power of acting counts as an organ, there is no end to the list. The 'one' added to the ten is the mind.

reading: She turns to the five subtle elements that he says arise in between, and says that if he counts thought and the rest as qualities of the soul, not even Indra could match him.
nuance: The sarcasm of line 4 suggests that counting thought as the soul's quality would give away the Sankhya case, for which thought belongs to nature, and take the Jain side. Lines 1 and 2 (தந்திர மாவன ... வந்தர வாத்துவன்) are obscure and the reading of தந்திரம் as the subtle elements is a guess.

reading: She asks: if hands, feet, the two organs of excretion and speech are organs, then let him show, having understood it, what sense object they act on and what knowledge they know.
nuance: A sense organ, for her, is defined by an object and a knowing; the five organs of action have neither, so calling them organs is a misuse of the word.

reading: If he says they are counted as organs because they act, she asks what fault there would be in adding the suckling breast, the lips, the eyebrows, the moving cheeks, the chewing teeth and the throat.
nuance: The reply to a defence the opponent might give (acting, கருமம்): the criterion of action would make every working part of the body an organ.

reading: She sets out the Jain account: the five subtle qualities, smell and the rest, belong to matter bound up in atoms; they are what the senses grasp, and as atoms come together and grow in order they make the four kinds of elements, as reason shows.
nuance: Against the Sankhya's five elements unfolding from subtle elements, she counts four elements built of atoms, with smell and the other qualities as their sensed properties; space is kept apart and treated in 759. The construal of lines 1 and 4 is mine.

reading: Space, says the lady of beautiful long eyes, is one, extends through this world and the non-world beyond it, and is non-sentient and without form.
nuance: உலகு and அலோகம் (line 1) are the Jain world and non-world: space alone runs on beyond the world into the empty non-world, which is why space cannot be one of the elements that unfold from prakriti.

reading: She says sound has form and so cannot rest in space, which is formless; in making sound belong to space he spoke against true teaching, says she of the deer-like gaze.
nuance: In the Jain view sound is matter, and so it has form; the Sankhya derives ear and sound from space. The epithet of line 4 is read as மான் மருவா வந்த நோக்கு, a gaze that came as a deer's.

reading: She sums up: mahat does not come from prakriti, nor the next principle from mahat; the many qualities that would compose them have no arising, and since the elements gain no reality, his principles are unfit.
nuance: This answers the dilemma of 750 by denying both horns: the chain of principles fails at its first link. அத்த (line 4) addresses the opponent as master, likely with irony.

reading: She says that if he joins the blind man and the lame man together to explain how soul and nature combine, the comparison does not make it clear, for those two act by their own understanding, while here the work is said to happen with no knower in it.
nuance: The blind man carrying the lame is the Sankhya's own image for nature that acts without seeing and the soul that sees without acting. Her objection, as I read lines 3 and 4, is that both men in the image are conscious and agree, which nature cannot do. The lines are terse and the reading is not secure.

reading: She asks what good it does to set out these classes of principles for a soul that never changes in any way, and says that if the comparison is pressed truly, his thesis and every part of his proof collapse.
nuance: If the soul is wholly unchanging (விகாரம் இலா), knowing the principles cannot change its state, so the teaching of the twenty-five loses its purpose; மேற்கோள் is the thesis of a formal proof.

reading: Laughing, the lady of fair brow tells him to look and see: the soul and prakriti he praised, being of a kind that cannot produce even when joined, are like eunuchs who bear no child however they consort.
nuance: The image answers the Sankhya union of soul and nature: one does not act and the other does not know, so their joining yields nothing. Line 1 (குணத்தின் நீயவட்) is unclear; அவள் may be prakriti spoken of as female.

reading: She argues that if soul and nature were joined everywhere even before, calling their union new means nothing, and the many things to be produced would have existed before as well.
nuance: Both soul and nature are said to pervade all, so they were never apart, and a first union that starts the world cannot happen; and if effects already exist in their cause, nothing is newly produced. The opening இல்லுளி is obscure.

title: சாங்கிய வாதச் சருக்கம் 766-782 (3/3)
theme: The close of the Sankhya debate: Neelakesi refutes a Lord who is all things and creator, then the pre-existence of effects and the twenty-five principles, and Parasaran concedes and receives right vision.
source_issues: 772 line 2: the e-text's '•' was repaired to ஃ (அஃதும்).
769 lines 1-2: என்னை யொழித்து ... சொன்ன முறைமையன் is hard to construe.
775 lines 1-2: வெந்துநெஞ் சாண்டிடத் தாடி தவஞ்செய்த is obscure; the episodes alluded to cannot be fixed.
778 line 4: செருவோ டுரிமையிற் சேர்பவு மன்றே is obscure.
779 lines 3-4: எண்முறை யறிமற் றீண்டுபு நன்றன வீறா is obscure, perhaps corrupt.
781 line 3: பண்டே லறியெனப்பராசர runs words together and பண்டேல் is doubtful.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Sankhya teacher whom Neelakesi debates in the Sankhya sarukkam

reading: The opponent holds that because his Lord has the five qualities (dancing, destroying, creating, withdrawing, and the state that shines when release is won), none of the faults Neelakesi has examined touch him.
nuance: The five named here are the Saiva five acts, with the dance (ஆடல்) first, though the sarukkam is named for the Sankhya; the verse does not say whether Parasaran now speaks for a lord added to the Sankhya scheme or the debate has turned to a theist. The view is answered at once in 767-775, which is why it is marked refuted.

reading: Neelakesi answers that if everything spoken proceeds from one being by a single rule, then even the debaters who come forward as others are he, and there is no gain in the dispute; give it up, she says.
nuance: The objection turns the debate itself against the doctrine: if the one Lord is all, Parasaran is arguing with himself.

reading: She asks: if elephants, horses, armies, subjects and everything else are he, then he forever rules only himself, so who could ever say 'this one is our king'?
She argues that if all but herself is he, and he destroys, fights and consumes himself, people would have to call him a madman.
nuance: பித்தன் (line 4), 'madman', is also a common name of Siva; the verse may be turning the epithet against its bearer, though it does not say so.

reading: She compares such a god to a man who stabs his own eye with his own hand, where there is no one else even to ask why, and demands the reason.
nuance: The repeated line (1 and 3) makes the image the argument: harm done to creatures by a god who is the creatures has no motive at all.

reading: She argues that the creator could not have made himself, since before the making he was not, and if another made him there is no end of makers; 'who made you, fool?' she asks.
She says that penance done after killing upon killing perishes, so that too is unfitting, and a god who makes things after destroying them has no understanding at all and is utterly foolish.
nuance: The verse assumes the Jain rule that killing undoes penance and applies it to the god himself; line 3 (இன்றிதின் றிட்டுப் படைப்பின்) is read as destroying before creating.

reading: She lists what the one god must be: thinker and speaker, flesh and food, healer and disease, the angry one, the killer and the one who dies, giver and receiver, the one who removes; and asks what he gains by any of it.
Neelakesi concludes that the god who bites as the dog, kills as the jackal, beats and eats as the demon, gores as the bull, torments as the fly and stings as the ant is everywhere one evil god.
nuance: The catalogue of small cruelties is the Jain's moral test of the doctrine that God is all: whatever harms a living thing would be God harming.

reading: She asks whether, if this god who burns, dances and destroys with his foot is also the one who creates with his hand, the confusion of fools could ever end.
nuance: Lines 1-2 seem to recall deeds told of Siva (a burning, the dance, a foot that destroys, one who did penance), but the words are compressed and the episodes cannot be fixed from them.

reading: Turning to his doctrine that things are eternal, she says he must hold that the tall palm is already in its seed; then however large it is, why not say that much is also in the hand that holds the seed, fool?
nuance: The verse attacks the Sankhya teaching that the effect already exists in its cause; the reductio is the Jain's, and Parasaran's own wording of the doctrine is not given.

reading: When he says the tree is not there now but will be later, she answers that he then makes it non-existent at one time and existent at another, and so all things are both; thus the red-streaked-eyed one set out the truth.
nuance: The opponent's retreat ('not now, but later') is taken as granting the Jain position that a thing is existent and non-existent in different respects; the verse ends the satkarya argument by absorbing it.

reading: She says he has spread three things (the formed, the formless and space) into twenty-five, while the formless, the non-world and the insentient are three that belong together of their own right.
nuance: அலோகம் (line 3), the space beyond the world, is a Jain category, so she sets her own scheme against his count; line 4 (செருவோ டுரிமையிற் சேர்பவு மன்றே) is hard to construe.

reading: She recalls that he said the person who pervades the whole world is real and that primal nature endures, and tells him to learn by the right count that here earth and the other three come first.
nuance: Lines 3-4 are obscure; the sense that the four elements are taken as basic is a guess from நிலமுத னான்கே.

reading: She tells him that he, a bound soul, should not take his supreme self alone to be perfected while denying that state and knowledge to souls, since he himself said that self enjoys and sees.
nuance: Sankhya's person is inactive yet a seer and enjoyer; Neelakesi takes the two verbs (துய்த்தல், காண்டல்) as admitting what the Jain soul has, knowledge and experience, and so as giving every soul the perfected state.

reading: Parasaran says he has taken this from the jewelled one whose name is her bee-filled hair, and when he says it she tells him he did not know before and now sees, and gives him right vision.
nuance: குழற்பெயர் (line 1), 'named for her hair', plays on Neelakesi's name (the dark-haired one). காட்சி is the Jain jewel of right vision, which she gives the defeated as in the earlier sarukkams.
event: Parasaran concedes that he has taken Neelakesi's teaching, and she gives him right vision.

reading: She tells him to give up the thought that there is no principle beyond the twenty-five, to worship the red feet of the Jina, and to live well.
event: Neelakesi bids Parasaran leave the twenty-five principles and worship the Jina's feet.

title: வைசேடிக வாதச் சருக்கம் 783-803 (1/2)
theme: Neelakesi reaches Ulokan, the follower of Kanada, who sets out the Vaisheshika's six categories and nine substances; she answers that the four elements are one stuff changing into each other, that sound does not prove ether, that direction is space named relative to an observer, that mind and time are not single substances, and that qualities cannot be separate from their bearer nor joined to it by inherence, offering at the end the Jain triad of arising, perishing and lasting.
source_issues: 783 line 4: the run மீட்டினா னுலோகன திடத்தை is read as ஈட்டினான் உலோகனது இடத்தை; the opponent's name rests on this division.
792 line 3: the text was repaired from a TSCII leftover (flagged by show); the line's sense is uncertain.
793 line 3 (ஒலியொடு முதறம்முட் புல்லல்) is obscure, probably corrupt.
802 line 3: உதனமு is not a word I can identify; possibly corrupt.
803 line 2: மதற்குநி is read as அதற்கு நீ.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Vaisheshika ascetic, follower of Kanada (கணாதன்), whom Neelakesi debates in the வைசேடிக வாதச் சருக்கம்

reading: Having won over the previous opponent as well, Neelakesi goes on and, among the many ancients who taught their ways as the path to release, reaches the place of Ulokan, who had stored up the teaching that Kanada is the master.
nuance: The sarukkam opens by naming Kanada (கணாதன்) as the founder whose teaching the opponent holds; the opponent himself is called உலோகன், a name that recalls the school's other title for its founder, though the verse uses it of the debater. The word division of line 4 (ஈட்டினான் உலோகனது இடத்தை) is the reading assumed here.
event: Neelakesi, having converted her last opponent, travels on to the dwelling of Ulokan, the follower of Kanada.

reading: The great ascetic sees the beautiful woman, takes her for one come in a contentious mood, and tells her to listen while he sets out, for her to take to heart, the truth that stands on the right path.
event: Ulokan sees Neelakesi, judges her ready to argue, and offers to expound his doctrine.

reading: The Vaisheshika says the path is the abiding truth, and that the categories, hard to know, are six: substance, quality, action, the general, the particular, and the joining of them.
nuance: The six are given in Tamil and Sanskrit mixed: திரப்பியம் for substance, குணம், தொழில், then பொது and சிறப்பு, and inherence only as the act of joining (புணர்ப்பது). Neelakesi answers the substances in 791 to 797 and the separation of quality from substance and the joining in 798 to 802.

reading: He names the substances as nine, the five elements with direction, mind, time and soul; qualities are their nature, and action is the moving of the substances from place to place.
nuance: Action is defined as புடைபெயர்ச்சி, shifting position, so action is motion only. Each of the nine is attacked in turn from 791: the elements, ether (793), direction (794 to 796), mind and time (797).

reading: He defines the general as the higher and lower sameness that gathers things into their kinds, the particular as what makes a thing known as distinct, and the joining as what lets one say that these qualities and actions belong to this thing.
