nuance: The joining is defined by what it licenses one to say (கிளத்தல், line 4), and that is where Neelakesi presses in 800 to 802: if a quality is other than its bearer, nothing makes it 'its'.

reading: The narrator sums up: the Vaisheshika taught that of the six the first three have being and the last three do not, and that substances, qualities and actions are each separate from one another.
nuance: The verse says the last three reached இன்மை, non-being; this is the Jain poem's wording, and the school would more likely say that generality, particularity and inherence lack the universal of being rather than that they do not exist. The separateness of substance, quality and action is the claim the rest of the chapter attacks (798 to 802).

reading: When he lifts his head and asks whether these principles are not right, Neelakesi answers that to practise penance on such principles would be false penance, and she will go.
nuance: The verse runs his question and her answer together; the division assumed here gives lines 1 and 2 (to ஒத்ததன்றோ, with உரை நல்லாய் as his address to her) to him and lines 3 and 4 to her.
event: Ulokan asks proudly whether his principles are not sound; Neelakesi says penance on them is false and makes to leave.

reading: He tells her that since she heard him expound the true path and calls it unsound, she must prove it a false path before she leaves; she stops him with a raised hand and bids him listen while she shows it.
event: Ulokan challenges Neelakesi to prove his doctrine false before leaving, and she halts him and begins her refutation.

reading: Neelakesi says the four elements from earth onward are one if their origin and form are considered, though he recites them as separate primary substances, and offers to show how they pass into one another in either order.
nuance: Her point is that the four are not four kinds of stuff but one stuff in four states, which turn into each other forwards and backwards (வலமுறை இடமுறை); the examples follow in 792.

reading: She gives examples of the elements turning into one another: water joined to the right thing becomes salt, ghee blazes up as fire, wind roars from agitation, and a great hailstone is a lump of water that came from water layer by layer.
nuance: Each example is a change across the Vaisheshika's boundaries between elements: water to earthy salt, a liquid to fire, water to a solid. Line 3 was repaired in the text (see source_issues) and the details of lines 2 and 3 are uncertain.

reading: She says that since he makes sound the quality of ether, and no element stands firm on its own or is joined with sound among the primary ones, he should give up the clamour of his ether.
nuance: What she dismisses is 'your' ether (நின் காயம்), the one defined by sound; in 794 she herself folds direction into space (காயம்), so the attack is on the Vaisheshika's proof of ether, not on space as such. Line 3 is obscure and the middle of the argument is uncertain.

reading: She says direction is only pointing: from where the sun set and rose people make four, eight or many quarters and use them by convention, and even so it comes down to space.

She proposes setting many people in a circle with one in the middle and asking him to name the directions: if the eight directions are born from where he stands, she sees no thing of his called direction, and asks him to show it.
nuance: The thought experiment makes direction relative to an observer: the same spot is a different quarter for each person in the ring.

reading: She says that if a quarter is that direction for one person and not for another, and people at every point can say the same, he should go, now devoted, and live holding the feet of the Supreme as attainment and the end.
nuance: The verse closes the case on direction with an appeal to conversion; the Supreme (பரமன்) is in the Jain poem the Arhat. The syntax of lines 2 and 3 (ஏக நீ, இனி என்னை) is uncertain.

reading: She says what is called mind is the union of the soul with bodily form, and that time is of two kinds, so his time does not stand as a substance there.
nuance: She does not deny mind or time outright: mind is placed in the soul's union with the body, and time is split in two (இருமைத்து), against the Vaisheshika's single substance. What the two kinds are the verse does not say.

reading: She asks that if qualities and actions are other than their substance, how a corpse ever came to be a living soul; if the soul in itself neither knows nor speaks, nothing ever reached it and we were never joined to it.
nuance: The target is the separation of knowing from the knower: if awareness is only a quality added to the soul, the soul by itself is as inert as a corpse.

reading: She argues that if a thing has no quality of its own, it is other than any quality, and as surely as fire cannot be shown by its coldness, such things would never appear at all.
nuance: The simile of line 3 (fire and cold in a vessel) is compressed and its exact turn uncertain.

reading: She says that if, having called quality and bearer separate, he needs a further thing to join them, that is false: since quality and bearer have no joining apart from each other, neither can be made known and neither exists.
nuance: This is the answer to the joining of 787: a link between two things that are never apart is either needless or, if they are truly apart, unable to make either known.

reading: She says the nine substances are many by their own being, and that their number, their hardness and each quality are known only because they belong to the thing.
nuance: The verse could also be read as the Vaisheshika's reply that qualities are known through their relation of belonging; the reading here takes it as Neelakesi's, leading into 802.

reading: She asks how, if a thing's quality is other than it, he can slip into calling it this thing's quality; and if the soul is one thing without knowing, it could not even suffer, and that would have to be true.
nuance: Line 3's உதனமு is obscure; the reading of lines 3 and 4 as an absurd consequence (no knowing, so no suffering) is a guess.

reading: She says that if he grants that a thing perishes when its state perishes, then destruction is admitted, and there is nothing to regret: if he also admits its arising and takes in the three together, that would be very fine.
nuance: The three (மும்மை) are arising, perishing and lasting, the Jain triad she set out against Mokkalan (387). Here she offers it as the settlement for a school that held the substances eternal.

title: வைசேடிக வாதச் சருக்கம் 804-823 (2/2)
theme: Neelakesi ends the debate with the Vaisheshika teacher Ulokan: she holds quality and action to be both one with and other than their bearer, argues that karma, merit and guilt could not bind or be shed if they were separate from the soul, takes apart generality, particularity and inherence, wins him over by the method of standpoints, and leaves him to worship at the Lord's shrine.
source_issues: 811 line 1 reads பாதுவெலா, evidently for பொதுவெலா; line 4's செதுவலாம் is obscure.
810 line 2 reads குழுமிக கெட்டன without the doubled consonant (for குழுமிக் கெட்டன).
814 line 4 reads பொருள ளெண்ணலே with a doubled ள.
819 line 4 துருநெறி and 815 line 4 முனிவு போக்கிதோ are hard to construe and may be corrupt.
823 line 2 நக்கனளாகிய can be divided as நக்கனள் ஆகிய or நக்கன் ஆகிய; the speaker division in 818 and 822 is not marked.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Vaisheshika teacher of Kanada's school whom Neelakesi debates in this sarukkam

reading: Neelakesi states her own position: the saying that the qualities are the qualified thing also holds, without contradiction the qualities are found in the substance, and the being and not-being of their twoness (one and different) together make a doctrine worth revering.
nuance: Line 3's இருமைய தின்மை உண்மையும் is the Jain both-ways answer: the quality is one with and other than its bearer. Against the Buddhist in 393 she defended the bearer; here, against a school that makes quality a separate category, she defends the oneness.

reading: Neelakesi says the many uses things have come through their qualities, by knowing and by closeness, as clay and gold serve through the qualities that stand in them; nothing works except through that intimate union.
nuance: Line 2's செண்பினான் is obscure; the clay and gold of line 3 are the stock examples of a substance that keeps its kind through changing forms.

reading: Neelakesi argues that the goodness that fetches a price, the evil that is loathed, and the guilt of killing and theft stay as qualities in the person who bears them, a settled oneness; call them separate and nothing would follow.
nuance: The metaphysical point is pressed through ethics: if virtue and the guilt of killing and stealing were not the doer's own qualities, praise and blame could not reach the doer.

reading: Neelakesi says that falling into good deeds and bad, and reaping fruits as many deeds ripen, belong to the soul as its qualities; if those qualities were ever separate from it, the round of births and release would be empty words.
nuance: The stake of the whole quality debate is named here: if karma's fruits do not inhere in the soul, nothing is bound and nothing is freed. Both good and bad deeds (நல்வினை, தீவினை) are counted as binding.

reading: Neelakesi argues that the dancer's dancing and the running horse's running belong to the one combined thing, so action too must be granted to be one with its bearer.
nuance: This answers the Vaisheshika category of action (கருமம், தொழில்) as she answered quality: the dance is not a thing that could be found apart from the dancer.

reading: Neelakesi says the dancers' dancing, the horse's running, recitation of scripture and every other act that has stopped are not lost; they persist in their bearer and come forth again when called for.
nuance: Action is treated as a capacity that stays latent in the substance, not as an event that perishes when it ceases; this is how she can call it one with its bearer.

reading: Neelakesi tells Ulokan that he has not grasped how qualities and actions, distinct yet not at odds, gather, pass away and come to reside together in the substance, and that the fault lies with him.
nuance: Line 2 reads குழுமிக கெட்டன without the doubled consonant, and line 4's அதுவும் நின்னுடையதே பிற is hard to construe; the reading follows the drift of the argument.

reading: Turning to generality, Neelakesi argues that if the universal stands joined to every thing it would be a oneness making all things one, and if it does not join them, saying that it went into them is empty.
nuance: Line 1 is printed பாதுவெலா, plainly for பொதுவெலா (the universal, பொது); line 4's செதுவலாம் is obscure. The dilemma itself (all one, or not joined at all) is clear.

reading: Neelakesi presses further: since he says the universal has entered endless things, it must be scattered into many, shrinking, joining and staying, and going without any use; what then has it become?

Neelakesi says that what is called the universal is only likeness, so the things called common are simply things that resemble one another; and she asks why, if he counts such a thing again among six categories, he does not add this one and make seven.
nuance: போலி (line 1) gives the Jain account of the universal as similarity among things, not a separate entity. The jibe about counting seven turns on the Vaisheshika list of six categories (ஆறு, line 3).

reading: Neelakesi says that particularity, examined, is just the quality that stands fully in the thing itself, so it too has no being of its own, and she will throw out his count of categories.
nuance: Line 4 reads பொருள ளெண்ணலே with a doubled ள.

reading: Neelakesi argues against inherence: if there is no joining except by a joiner, then the inherence that goes to join must itself be joined by another, and so on; she asks whether he piles up many useless things as if reciting verses.
nuance: The regress is clear in lines 1-2; line 4's முனிவு போக்கிதோ is hard to construe, and the sense of பாட்டினால் (line 3) is a guess.

reading: Neelakesi dares Ulokan to make the heron take blackness and dry ginger take astringency, and so do away with difference once and for all, and laughs that this learned man is to be pitied.
nuance: If inherence could join any quality to any substance, nothing would stop black from inhering in the white heron; the absurd test shows a quality belongs to its own bearer by nature.
event: Neelakesi challenges Ulokan to join blackness to a heron and laughs at him.

reading: Neelakesi concludes that since things and their natures always arrive together as one, they are one, and since the twoness he needs is not found, there is nothing left for inherence to join.

An exchange: Ulokan asks why she calls substance one and qualities many and yet says they are both one and different; she answers that if a quality perishes it perishes for the substance too; and it is said that the reality of the quality is now established.
nuance: The verse is a run of quoted speeches each closed by என; who says the last (நன்று...) is not stated, and the reading of line 3 is tentative.
event: Ulokan questions Neelakesi's one-and-different thesis and she answers him.

reading: Neelakesi explains that seen from the side of the bearer there are no qualities apart, and seen from the side of the qualities the same holds; so one may join or separate them, and with the fourfold reckoning so gained one may decide, and the good of the path is reached.
nuance: Lines 1-2 set the two standpoints, of the substance and of the quality, from which the same thing is called one or many; நான்மை (line 3) and துருநெறி (line 4) are not clear, and the fourfold may be the four alternatives of one, different, both and neither.

reading: The narrator tells how Ulokan, through the method of standpoints, came to the conclusion that the quality has no reality apart from its bearer, that the bearer is one with its quality, and that the qualities are those things themselves, and judged it good.
nuance: எய்தினான் (line 4) is masculine: the opponent himself reaches the conclusion, by நயம், the standpoint method. The defeat is recorded as a conversion of judgment, not a rout.
event: Ulokan accepts Neelakesi's conclusion by the method of standpoints.

reading: Neelakesi bids Ulokan to understand that substance, quality and action have one reality, to make it clear in the threefold path, and to meditate on the red feet of the lord of the path of compassion so that darkness perishes, and so to be.
nuance: மும்மை (line 2) is most likely the three jewels of right faith, knowledge and conduct. Darkness ends by the disciple's own understanding and remembering of the lord, not by the lord's act.
event: Neelakesi instructs the defeated Ulokan in the Jain path.

reading: Having given Ulokan her parting charge, Neelakesi says she will cross the bamboo-filled forest road, and he answers by asking the sweet-spoken one to think of the pain of parting.
nuance: The division of speakers is inferred from the two என்னவே; பேம்படுப்பவரொடும் (line 3) is hard, perhaps parting even from those who once caused fear.
event: Neelakesi takes leave of Ulokan, who speaks of the pain of parting.

reading: Neelakesi smiles that his words are fitting and true, and tells him that steadily praising the Lord's shrine is the best course; when he says it is right, she leaves.
nuance: சேதியம் (line 2) is the caitya, the shrine of the Jina. நக்கனளாகிய may be read as 'she smiled' or as நக்கன் (the unclothed one) with the Lord; the reading takes the first.
event: Neelakesi tells Ulokan to worship at the Lord's shrine; he agrees and she departs.

title: வேத வாதச் சருக்கம் 824-853
theme: In the Vedic debate Neelakesi goes to the Brahmin Bhutikan's Veda school at Kakandi, answers his taunt that a Sudra woman cannot judge the Veda, argues by inference that the Veda was made and contradicts itself on killing and birth, and attacks sacrifice by holding that each deed falls on its doer and not on the gods or ancestors it is offered to; the text breaks at 845-851 and resumes with Bhutikan's concession.
source_issues: Verses 845 to 851 are missing from the core text: the chapter runs 824-844 and then 852-853, so the end of the attack on sacrifice and Bhutikan's turn are lost.
825 line 3: எர்த்துரைத்தான் is probably a slip for எடுத்துரைத்தான்.
826 lines 1 and 4: முன் நான் பயந்த and போத்தந்தியோ are hard to divide.
828 line 2: குவகொடும் is unclear and may be corrupt.
829 line 2: ஒருஐறயுள் is garbled (perhaps ஓர் உறையுள்); lines 3-4 carry repairs of TSCII leftovers.
832 line 1: கதியவர் is unclear.
834 line 3: சூதித்த தோற்றமும் பிழைப்பென is obscure.
835 line 2: பெறுதலை யென்னைகொ றத்துவந்தனையன்று பறுமுண்டே is badly corrupt.
840 line 3: றுதலிய is probably a slip for நுதலிய.
841 lines 2-4: றின்றவர்க கியாவையும் and கொன்றுவி யேனல னோ are hard to divide; the sense is uncertain.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Brahmin teacher of the Veda at Kakandi whom Neelakesi debates
an elder seated in Bhutikan's Veda school, perhaps Bhutikan himself
the people of Kakandi who watch the debate

reading: After crossing many kaathams Neelakesi enters the guarded city of Kakandi and goes into the Veda school of the Brahmin Bhutikan, known in the world for teaching and expounding the Veda, its limbs and the other sciences to all who seek them.
event: Neelakesi reaches Kakandi and enters the Veda school of the Brahmin Bhutikan.

reading: When she asks what their subject is, an old man seated there, taking this to be the lady's errand, sets out gently and in order the rare Veda from the beginning and the works that came after it.
nuance: Whether the elder (முதுமகன்) is Bhutikan himself is not said; the next verse has Bhutikan answer her in anger. எர்த்துரைத்தான் in line 3 looks like a slip for எடுத்துரைத்தான்.
event: Neelakesi asks what is taught there, and an elder of the school lists the Veda and the works that follow it.

reading: Bhutikan, flaring up, tells her that if all she speaks is unbelief, the scripture brought forth of old is the Veda, which is self-existent, and that she, a Sudra woman, talks so only because she has no competence in it.
nuance: The Brahmin answers her with her birth before her argument: the charge of being a Sudra woman (சூத்திரி) is the point she takes up in 827 and that 830 and 834 answer. Line 1 (முன் நான் பயந்த) and line 4 (போத்தந்தியோ) are hard to divide; the sense 'the scripture of old is the Veda, self-born' is clear from சயம்பு.
event: Bhutikan angrily calls her an unbeliever and a Sudra woman unfit to judge the Veda.

tamil: நீதியி னாலுரை நீயினி யானது நேர்வ னென்றான்.
reading: Neelakesi, unshaken, says she is able in all of it and that he has looked only at her birth, and bids him state his case; he answers that if the Veda has any beginning or any end she should show it by reasoning, and he will concede.
nuance: The terms of the debate are set here: the Brahmin stakes the Veda's authority on its having no origin, and the next five verses are her inferences that it was made. Read with the division சாற்றுக என்றாட்கு ஆதி: lines 1-2 are hers and lines 3-4 his.
event: Neelakesi rejects the slur on her birth, and Bhutikan challenges her to prove the Veda has a beginning or end.

reading: Neelakesi argues that the Veda is a made thing, since it involves action and novelty, goes against what is seen, mixes falsehood with sense, and is bound up with confusion, contradiction and killing, and so surely drives its followers to an evil birth.
nuance: She stacks several reasons (ஏது) in the form of a formal inference, the logicians' own method turned on the Veda. Line 2 குவகொடும் is unclear and may be corrupt.

reading: To the question who made it, if anyone knows, she answers that when a man defiles a room in the middle of the town and slips away, no one concludes on inquiry that nobody did it merely because his name and form cannot be found.
nuance: The coarse example is chosen to insult as well as to argue: the authorless Veda is likened to filth left by a man who hid. Line 2 ஒருஐறயுள் is garbled (perhaps ஓர் உறையுள்).

reading: She argues that when appearance, smell, taste and touch are examined in full, the claim that some are of high birth and others low does not hold true, as those versed in the two Vedas, the makers of treatises and the penetrating know.
nuance: The argument against caste is from perception: no sense can find the difference that birth is said to make. It also answers the taunt of 826. The force of இரு வேதம் (two Vedas) and of line 1's list is not certain.

reading: She argues from reasons that the Veda is not a thing of nature, since it is completed by the effort of utterance in letters and words, has the character of something produced, and its makers give their names to its parts; so speaks the learned one whose name tells of hair that rivals the rain-cloud.
nuance: The poet names Neelakesi here by a gloss on her name (நீல-கேசி, dark hair) joined to புலமை, learning, just after Bhutikan has called her an incompetent Sudra.

reading: She adds that since the Veda names particular persons and matches the present age rather than the days of the ancients, and since it is a body of injunctions, we call it new like the songs we sing, and that is fitting.
nuance: Line 1 கதியவர் is unclear; the sense 'it names persons' rests on பெயர் இன்னவை சுட்டின.

reading: She lists the Veda's contradictions as its own reciters state them: it says killing is evil yet sets no limit to what may be killed in sacrifice for gain, says to give up sexual union and that a heaven is reached by it, and says the holy fords are the path and also that they are evil.
nuance: The sacrificial claim is answered in 836 to 844. The account of what the Veda teaches is the Jain debater's, and a Vedic school would not grant that its rules contradict each other.

reading: She goes on: they say birth yields nothing and austerity yields fruit, yet they set out with approval the order of the four classes from the beginning and will not grant a Sudra birth; to the clear-sighted these are confusions on confusions.
nuance: She does not argue that either Vedic teaching is false here, only that they cannot both stand. Line 3 சூதித்த தோற்றமும் பிழைப்பென is obscure.

reading: Because it has made contradictions within itself and caused confusion, she asks what is gained by it, and says that a teaching that is firm and worthy, true in all it says, has no conflict within, and that such a teaching is what makes people do excellent things.
nuance: Line 2 (பெறுதலை யென்னைகொ றத்துவந்தனையன்று பறுமுண்டே) is badly corrupt and cannot be divided with confidence; only the drift of lines 1, 3 and 4 is clear.

reading: She charges that for the Vasus, Rudras, ancestors and many others they kill cows, buffaloes, horses, tigers, dogs and more without pity, and that even if they behave as mere eaters of what others killed, the heavy deed is theirs.

If he says that in killings meant for the gods and ancestors he wishes the evil deed to fall on them, she answers that whoever is intended, what each did comes to each, and that deed reaches him in ways he cannot know.

She argues that just as one who sets up a feeding-hall for his kin cannot know how its merit stands, so the gods for whom killing is done do not even show that the deed has reached them, and have no reckoning by which to know it.
nuance: The comparison in lines 1-2 is compressed and its point is not certain.

reading: If merit done with the wish that it reach the eminent goes to them rather than the doer, she says, then a deed aimed at renouncers who have already won release would drag them back into this birth: what folly is that.
nuance: A reductio: the doctrine of transferred merit would let anyone's deed bind even the liberated, which neither side will grant.

reading: Who would say, she asks, that nectar or poison eaten with a friend or an enemy in mind goes to them rather than to the eater; so the many deeds of killing aimed at the gods ripen in many ways in you, faithless one.

If he says the evil deed joins only the killers and not those for whom the killing was done, nor the eaters, as it does not join the gods, she calls it foolishness and says the deed falls alike on those who eat the flesh with pleasure.
nuance: Lines 2-4 are hard to divide (றின்றவர்க கியாவையும், கொன்றுவி யேனல னோ), so the exact shape of the objection is uncertain.

reading: Can gods who rejoice when killers of flies and dogs give to them, and who do only evil, remove that evil deed; and if they say the rite drives off diseases and demons, she answers that when death comes they will learn how hard karma is to remove.
She mocks: we cannot end our own sufferings and others' are harder still to remove, and these gods likewise cannot end their own, yet they are said to bring every kind of disease on others.
event: Neelakesi mocks the gods of the sacrifice.

reading: If the gods were hungry beings who tormented the beast we kill and give, she says, they would kill and eat it themselves and none could stop them; so speak no ill of them: the gods take their food from afar and have no bellies that eat rice with flesh.
nuance: She turns piety against the rite: to say the gods eat flesh is itself to slander them (தீங்கொன்றும் உரையன்மின்).

reading: Telling Bhutikan that no good comes of speaking falsely and bidding him speak the truth, she hears him speak it too, and the people say that he also is fit to be praised by all quarters, men of the nature called true who stand in the truth.
nuance: Verses 845 to 851 are missing from the text, so the turn between her attack on sacrifice and his concession is lost; 852 opens on her last plea.
event: Bhutikan, urged to speak the truth, concedes, and the onlookers praise him.

reading: After she has expounded to him and the citizens, to their delight, which teachings are good and prepares to leave, those bound to her in love, eager because she made the path of dharma known, follow her a little way, circle her and turn back.
event: Neelakesi teaches Bhutikan and the townspeople, then leaves; her new followers escort and circumambulate her.

title: பூத வாதச் சருக்கம் 854-874 (1/2)
theme: The materialist Pisasakan rises after the Vedic debate and, before King Madanasittan's assembly, holds that the five elements combined yield the senses, awareness and pleasure as liquor yields intoxication, and that nothing survives their parting; Neelakesi restates his view and answers that he has no omniscient teacher or scripture, that his own debating presupposes fruit and a debater, that awareness, moral traits, the unity of the senses, memory and a newborn's instinct cannot be effects of the elements.
source_issues: 855: line 1 நில்லப் பாவினி can be divided நில் அப்பா இனி or நில் பாவி நீ; who speaks the challenge is unclear.
856: the materialist is பிசாசகன் here but பிசாசிகன் in 892 and 894.
857: line 1 தண்ணென் றீ is an odd epithet of fire; the division may be corrupt.
858: line 3 (அந்தி நாளுங் குடஞ்சுடர் நாட்டம்போல்) is obscure; the comparison is a reading.
863: கட்டில் (line 1) and சுதத்தி (line 4) are doubtful forms.
866-867: compressed lines (ஒளித்து நின்ற வுணர்வுரு; மேலவா காயக்காம்) make the turn of the cause-effect argument uncertain.
864, 865, 871: ஃ restored from the old encoding '•' (flagged by show).

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the materialist (பூத வாதி) who challenges Neelakesi after the Vedic debate; called பிசாசிகன் in 892 and 894
the king with a great army and elephants before whose assembly the materialist debate is held
the king's court that hears the debate

reading: After Neelakesi has left the Vedic debater pale, a materialist rises in anger to go against her, reckoning that to subdue so practised a debater would be no small gain.
nuance: பூத வாதி names the opponent by his doctrine, that only the elements are; his motive is the prize of beating a famous debater, not a question he wants answered.
event: A materialist rises to challenge Neelakesi after her defeat of the Vedic debater.

reading: When someone bids the man stop and state here the truth he has seen, the king Madanasittan, with his great army, stone-like shoulders and rutting elephants, is about to speak.
nuance: Line 1 can be divided நில் அப்பா இனி (a courteous 'stay now, sir') or நில் பாவி நீ ('stop, sinner'); the first fits a presiding king inviting the materialist to state his case, the second Neelakesi challenging him. The description of line 3-4 is of a king, and he seems to be the one who then opens the hearing (856).
event: The materialist is called on to state his doctrine before King Madanasittan.

reading: Told to let the royal assembly hear, the materialist Pisasakan, of the diseased face, says he will make no talk of substance and quality but will set out, as settled, only the workings of the five elements.
nuance: பிசாசகன், a name that sounds like பிசாசு (a demon), is given with an insult (பிணிகொள் மூஞ்சி); the end of the sarukkam turns the name into a joke (892: 'your very name is Pisasikan'). Refusing the substance-quality frame that the Vaisheshika and Jain debates turned on is his first move.
event: Pisasakan begins his case before the king's assembly.

reading: Pisasakan says that from fire, earth, water, wind and space come eye, nose, tongue, body and ear, and colour, smell, taste, touch and sound, which arise where the elements are joined.
nuance: He counts five elements, space (காயம்) among them; the materialists are usually said to count four. Each sense and its object is derived from the elements; nothing is left over for a soul.

reading: He says that when the five come together, knowing, pleasure and the rest appear, as the power to intoxicate appears in liquor and as a lamp's light in a pot, and that when the combination scatters each part goes back to join its own kind.
nuance: Consciousness is a new power of the mixture, as drunkenness is of fermented liquor, and it ends with no remainder when the parts return to their elements. Neelakesi answers the liquor figure in 866 and the claim that a mixture yields what its parts lack in 868. The lamp-in-a-pot comparison of line 3 is compressed and its point is a reading.

reading: He says the whole world is these elements alone, and that those who stand convinced by the clever talk of a soul only make many fruitless quarrels and end up as mere scholars.
nuance: The sting is that belief in a soul produces argument and nothing else; Neelakesi turns the same charge back in 864, asking what his own debating is for if nothing bears fruit.

reading: He ends that in time past, present and to come this combining alone is what happens, the world is always of this nature, and those who say otherwise are deluded.
nuance: Answered in this chapter's arguments for the soul (865-874) and conceded by him at the sarukkam's end (893).

reading: Having heard that this is his settled tenet, the carp-eyed Neelakesi repeats it for the learned and for everyone sitting there until they hold it clearly, and then takes up her reply.
nuance: She restates the opponent's case to the whole audience before answering it, the debate's rule that the view refuted must first be granted and understood.
event: Neelakesi restates the materialist's position to the assembly and begins her refutation.

reading: Neelakesi says that since he has no teacher shining with knowledge freed from deeds, he has no first book, and lacking scripture of that worth his words are invention and false.

She says that if there is no soul besides the elements, then the forked staff, the bowl and the other gear fit for penance, and the ascetic's state itself, are wasted, and guiding people by teaching is a cheat.
nuance: The argument is that ascetic practice only makes sense if something survives the body; it may also hit the materialist's own ascetic garb, which the verse implies he wears. கட்டில் in line 1 and சுதத்தி in line 4 are doubtful forms.

reading: She asks why he labours in debate to prove that only the elements are and other books are false, when on his view there is no Lord's good path, no good deed and no good fruit, so that the effort itself is waste.
nuance: A performative objection: arguing to win presupposes that some outcome is worth reaching, which his denial of fruit undercuts. It returns the 'fruitless quarrel' charge of 859.

reading: She asks: if nothing is soul and only what he calls elements exist, then which of the five is the element that has come and sits debating with her, and which is that debate?

She says he has offered the intoxicating power of liquor to show how the five yield knowing and pleasure, and asks whether, since in liquor both cause and effect are material, he means that awareness lay hidden as a material form.
nuance: The reply to 858: drunkenness is a change in matter produced by matter, so the comparison either makes awareness material or fails. Lines 3-4 are compressed and the turn of the argument is a reading.

reading: She says the effect of what has form is form and the effect of the formless is formless, as with space, yet he says awareness is not the effect of any one thing; what then is its matching cause?
nuance: The principle is that an effect shares the kind of its cause, so formless awareness cannot be the product of elements with form. Line 2's ஆகாயக்கு ஆம் is a division of a joined form.

reading: She asks whether straw, earth, hair and dung put in a bag will yield crystal, and whether the claim that the five false elements joined make awareness and pleasure deserves a thought.
She says there is no thieving element, lusting element or generous element, so to say that some mind-element produces these traits is false: they are not qualities of the elements.
nuance: Moral character is her evidence that mind is not material: no element carries theft, desire or bounty as a quality, so these must belong to something else.

reading: She asks him to mark the matter and say one thing: are the five knowings that come through the five senses, made of the five elements, the property of those five, or of something other?

She says that even if one grants that each element's effect is its own sense-knowing, all of them would then be sentient; and if instead they all make up one product, the argument arrives at the soul.
nuance: A dilemma: either every element is conscious (which he denies of dead matter) or the unity of knowing needs a single subject, which is the soul. The second horn's wording (யாக்கம் ஒன்றே) is compressed.

reading: She says that if he makes all the elements into knowing, he must still posit another element for the mind; let him think it over or search it out, for that is all he can do against her now.
She asks whether, when beings born in a body later recall what they ate, saw, understood and did, he will say that this recollection is the effect of an element that can be seen.
nuance: Memory is the evidence here: recollection carries the past into the present, which no perceptible element is seen to do.

reading: She asks how, in the first days after birth, the infant and other young know to run to the mother's breast and not to other food, since the five elements just come together in those days cannot do that.
nuance: Instinct as proof of a prior knower: the newborn's seeking of the breast is knowledge it was not taught in this body. The verse does not say 'former birth', but the argument points there, and the materialist concedes birth at 893.

title: பூத வாதச் சருக்கம் 875-894 (2/2)
theme: The end of the debate with the materialist Pisasikan: Neelakesi argues that differences of karma, missing senses, memory, feelings and omens cannot come from the elements and that a soul exists; then, to the man who trusts only what he sees, she shows part of her demon form, comforts him as a mother, and he takes the Jain dharma before a marvelling court.
source_issues: 877 line 3 was repaired from a TSCII leftover (தேரி); line 2 (ஊர் மச்சி மூக்சில) has an unclear word division.
875 line 1 (புத்தி யானின்றி) is hard to divide.
883 line 2 has கீழவு where கிழவு (old age) seems meant; lines 3 and 4 are obscure.
886 line 3 reads இல்லுயு ரென்றி, apparently for இல் உயிர் என்றி.
887 line 4 (அறங் கோடலை) is obscure.
888 line 2 (உணர்விலா முட்டை காண்கென முனகை முறுக்கியே) is obscure and may be corrupt.
890 line 1 has a stray space in கண் புதைத்துக் and an unclear வழவே.
894 line 1 (பேந்தரு தோற்றம்) is obscure.
The opponent is spelt பிசாசகன் in 856 and பிசாசிகன் in 892 and 894.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the materialist (பூதவாதி) who debates Neelakesi in the last sarukkam; called பிசாசகன் in 856 and பிசாசிகன் in 892 and 894
the king before whose court the materialist debate is held (named in 855)
the king's court that hears the debate

reading: Neelakesi argues that if beings came from the elements alone, with no knowing principle, the many pups of one litter of pigs or dogs would all be alike; their differences come from deeds, as from a seed.
nuance: Same parents, same food, same elements, yet the litter differs: the Jain answer puts the difference in each soul's own karma. The materialist's view is given as the Jain poem states it, not in a materialist's own words. The construal of புத்தி யானின்றி (line 1) as 'without a knowing principle' is mine.

reading: She presses that if an aggregate of elements can form with some elements lacking, and awareness is only the elements' own, then where the five she names are not all present the materialist must bring in a hidden element to supply the awareness.
nuance: A reductio: the doctrine that admits only the seen elements would need an unseen one. The verse is compressed and the steps are my reconstruction.

reading: Neelakesi asks how creatures such as the crawling conch, which have earth, water and wind in their bodies and fire too since they eat, still lack the eye and the ear, if each sense were made by an element.
nuance: She turns the Jain grading of beings by the number of their senses against the materialist's scheme in 857, where each element yields its sense: the lower creatures have the elements but not the senses. Line 2 (ஊர் மச்சி மூக்சில) is hard to divide; 'lacking the nose' is a guess.

reading: She asks what cause brings the elements together one by one in the order of awareness, and says mockingly that if they can shrink and all merge into one another she will grant that his truth stands.
nuance: The objection is that combination needs a cause the materialist does not name; the closing concession is ironic.

reading: Telling him to give up the thought that the five senses each arise from one of the five elements, Neelakesi establishes the reality of the soul that lives on.
nuance: The narrator's ஒட்டினாள் (line 4) reports the outcome as won: the soul's existence is set up against the materialist's reduction of sense to element in 857.

reading: She says that if awareness and pleasure are granted even to the one-sensed beings, the claim that they are a mere aggregate is false: wherever awareness and pleasure are, a soul is joined there.
nuance: ஓரறிவு (line 1) is the Jain term for the one-sensed beings, plants and the like; awareness in the lowest form of life is made the mark of a soul.

reading: If the body comes from wind, she argues, what work is left for the aggregate in making the soul; but if he says the soul is something apart from these five, that would be worth accepting.
nuance: Taking மாற்றி (line 3) as 'apart from' makes the verse an opening for the opponent to concede; the sense of line 2 is uncertain.

reading: She calls faulty his claim that, since the five elements are real and separate and there is no soul without end or origin, everything falls apart and comes to nothing when they part.
nuance: This is the materialist's account of death: the elements disperse and nothing survives. Here the reply is only 'it has a fault'; the following verses give the reasons.

reading: She argues that what is heard in infancy is remembered in old age, so there is a knower that never loses it, and asks who else would make men bow in worship.
nuance: The argument from memory: the body's elements change from childhood to old age, but what was learned stays, so the one who holds it is not the elements. Lines 3 and 4 are obscure and the second half of the reading is a guess; கீழவு (line 2) reads as கிழவு, old age.

reading: She challenges him to stand before her and insist that pain, purity, fear and dread, love, honour, deceit, courage and pleasure are made by fire.
nuance: The list mixes feelings with moral qualities (purity, honour, deceit): the point is that the moral life cannot be credited to an element.

reading: She asks whether dream, mantra, thought, the span of life, the astrology people consult and the omen of bird cries are his elements, and bids him say if he knows.
nuance: She counts omens, astrology and mantra as real things the elements cannot explain: the debater argues from what the world already trusts, not from Jain doctrine alone.

reading: She says the world accepts it when one reborn leads his kin to the thing he had laid away in his former life, and that though he says there is no soul in any form, the dead come back and do mischief.
nuance: The reborn man finding his own hidden treasure is offered as evidence outside the claimant's own mind. Line 4 (செத்து வம்மெய்திற் சில்லைமை செய்பவால்) is hard to construe; 'the dead come back' is my reading. உலகு ஒட்டும் (line 2) makes common acceptance the test.

reading: She asks the man who says there are no ghosts and no rebirth why then a possessed person pinches his mouth and beats himself, and tells him to grant that a deity called by mantra, and not by trickery, comes and seizes.
nuance: Possession is offered as a public sign of unseen beings. The phrase அறங்கோடல் (line 4) is unclear; reading it as the deity's seizing is a guess.

reading: When he says he will accept it, she points and bids him look, and putting aside her assumed form she shows him her power of transformation.
nuance: The materialist who trusts only the seen is given something to see: the demoness who has argued all the debates in a woman's form reveals what she is. விகுர்வணை (line 4) is the Jain word for this power of changing form. Line 2 (உணர்விலா முட்டை காண்கென முனகை முறுக்கியே) is obscure.
event: Pisasikan says he will accept the claim if shown; Neelakesi points and, dropping her assumed form, shows him her transformation.

reading: Knowing that even spirits and the people of the wide world weep and die at that sight, and that he would die if he saw it whole, she shows him only her mouth and her curved teeth.
nuance: Her restraint is the first act of care in the scene: she measures out the proof so as not to kill the man she is converting.
event: Neelakesi, judging that the full sight would kill him, shows Pisasikan only her mouth and curved teeth.

reading: He covers his eyes and falls face down; she lifts him, seats him, speaks fitting gentle words, tells him she is his friend, and calms his trembling.
nuance: Line 1's வழவே is unclear; the gesture sequence is plain.
event: Pisasikan covers his eyes and falls; Neelakesi raises him, speaks kindly as his friend, and stills his fear.

reading: Asked to tell what the ghost he saw was like, he says he saw its mouth, begs not to be pressed, and says he is sick with it; she tells him not to fear, that she is a mother to him, and that there is never any death.
nuance: என்றும் சாதலில்லை (line 4) carries the doctrinal point of the scene into comfort: what he fears ends nothing. Who says each phrase is fixed from the dialogue, and the reading of line 3's அவள் தாய் as 'a mother to you' is a guess.
event: Neelakesi asks Pisasikan to describe the ghost; he says he saw its mouth and is ill with fear, and she reassures him.

reading: She tells him that the very name he bears, Pisasikan, makes him without question the ghost's son, and that if he takes the faultless dharma he is kin to her and her own, and bids him speak; and he speaks.
nuance: A pun: பிசாசிகன் means 'the ghost's one', so the denier of ghosts was named for them; the demoness adopts him through dharma. Taking the dharma makes him kin (சுற்றம்) of those who keep it.
event: Neelakesi tells Pisasikan his name makes him her son and that taking the dharma makes him her kin, and asks him to speak.

reading: He says he has understood and holds firm all she told him, birth, ghosts and the rest, has taken the dharma as it should be taken, and will not forget it now.
nuance: The convert names first what he had denied (பிறப்பு, பேய்): the debate ends not with silence but with assent to its two disputed facts.
event: Pisasikan accepts rebirth and ghosts and takes the dharma.

reading: The narrator says that when Pisasikan was thus won, the king and all that royal assembly marvelled, and all the people honoured the woman of searching learning as their lady.
nuance: This closes the last debate of the work. பேந்தரு தோற்றம் (line 1) is obscure; it may describe the fear-struck look of the converted man.
event: The king and his assembly marvel at Pisasikan's conversion, and all honour Neelakesi.

title: பாயிரம் 1-6
theme: The prologue praises the god who conquered the sum of his deeds and frees those who bow at his feet, announces the story of the red-eyed tall one who tore the lion, and asks the good to take the poet's lapses as the moon's spot is taken, naming his patron of the assembly and the old purana whose account he will follow.
source_issues: Verse 2 line 1: the word கணிவான்சுடர் may be a misprint for அணிவான்சுடர்; the sense taken is a light of the world above.
Verse 4: whose assembly the king's assembly is (கோமான் அவை) is not settled by the text.

cast.role: the Jain god the invocation praises as conqueror of the sum of deeds
the red-eyed tall one who tore the lion, hero of the story the poet begins

tamil: நின்றா னடிக்கீழ் பணிந்தார் வினை நீங்கி நின்றார்.
reading: The poet praises the one who conquered the whole sum of his deeds, whose knowledge spread wide, filled everything and lost nothing, and who now stands as a shining form in a ring of light; those who bowed at his feet were freed of their deeds and stand released.
nuance: The verse says that the devotees' deeds left them after they bowed (வினை நீங்கி நின்றார்) but does not say whether the bowing or the god's example does it; the god is praised for what he conquered, not for any giving. The verse does not name him; the Jain Arhat is read from வென்றான் வினையின் தொகை and from the next verse's link to the story's hero.

tamil: வெங்கண் வினைபோழ்ந் திருவச் சரண் சென்ற மேனாள்
reading: The poet says the god stood as a light of the world above, having split fierce deeds, and that he begins the story of the red-eyed tall one, who in an earlier day went for refuge to him and who tore open the green-eyed lion with gaping mouth.
nuance: Line 1 அணிவான்சுடர் reads கணிவான்சுடர் in this text and may be a misprint. The grammar that joins the refuge (சரண் சென்ற மேனாள்) to the red-eyed tall one in line 4 is loose, so the hero's earlier refuge is the likely reading, not a fixed one. The hero is named only by epithet here; the Jain Vasudeva of the story is Tivittan.
event: Tivittan, the red-eyed tall one, tears open the lion (recalled as a feat of his past); the poet announces that he will tell his story.

reading: The poet says that, to tell the qualities of the tall one with the victorious discus, a desire has risen in him to spin a Tamil work here, and that if a flaw should come, great ones of knowledge are those who guard the lapses of people like himself.
nuance: நேமி நெடுமால் is the discus-bearing tall one, taken as the same hero as the செங்கண் நெடியான் of verses 2 and 5, and not as a god of worship; the Tamil does not say so here. அற்றங்கள் காப்பார் is guard the lapses, which is a different act from the Cintamani's washing of the flaw.

reading: The poet asks what fault there is in this speaking of excellence, since it was accepted by the discerning in the assembly of the king, Tirumal Nedunjendan, called lord of pure Tamil, with his victorious spear and cool garland.
nuance: Whether Tirumal Nedunjendan is the poet's patron, the king in whose assembly the work was first heard, or both is not fixed by the verse; கோமான் அவை may be his assembly or a king's assembly he belongs to. No claim rests on the identity.

reading: The poet says that even his fault, in the thought that told the story of the red-eyed tall one, is no fault before the good, as the moon's spot does not stop some from raising hands to it when it rises through the dark sky.
nuance: The moon's spot is used as an excuse in the same way in Neelakesi 6 and Civaka Cintamani 4; here it is the moon's rising before worshippers that matters, so the blemish is overlooked and not cleaned off.

reading: The poet says that he will go by the account of the Purana of fair words, which came about because of the daughter of the Vidyadhara king, who is like a vanji creeper with anklets on her feet.
nuance: The verse gives the poem's source as an older purana and not as a tale of his own invention; the Vidyadhara king's daughter is the figure through whom that purana is said to have arisen, and is not an agent here. The verse names no purana.

title: நாட்டுச் சருக்கம் 7-21 (1/2)
theme: The first verses of the Naattu sarukkam describe the land as a place where hills, farms, pastures and shore each give their own sounds and flowers: a country of festival, bees and honey, whose women's beauty and perfumes reach even ascetics.
source_issues: Verse 7 line 4: TSCII leftover letters repaired (நிதியது); the reading of the last line stays doubtful.
Verses 10: one repaired letter in line 2.
Verse 12 line 2 reads திணையுந தேரல்சேர் and line 4 ends oddly, probably misprints.

cast.role: the women of the land
the cowherds
the children of the shore

reading: The country is a city set round with a jewelled hill, rivalling the Vidyadhara world in festival, and its wealth is said never to sleep; the name Surumai ends the verse.
nuance: The last line's wealth-that-sleeps and the name சுரமை are hard to construe after the edition's repair of line 4.

reading: Lotus beds, shoals of red carp and the women's faces and eyes are set side by side, so the land's waters and its women share one beauty.
Women's swan-like walk and soft speech make the cool fields ring, and the villages ring in turn with the anklets on their small feet.
Bees and parrots fill the groves while the houses are full of the speech and lutes of women.
nuance: Line 2 has a repaired letter; the sense is plain.

reading: Scented water-flowers and women's perfumes are so heavy that they weaken even the ascetics who stand in good austerity.
nuance: The poet lets the land's sweetness reach the austere: a quiet admission that the senses test the renouncer, in a work whose later sarukkams praise renunciation.

reading: Mountain, forest, farmland and shore, the four regions, are all found together in this one land.
nuance: Line 2 reads திணையுந தேரல்சேர் in the edition (a likely misprint) and line 4 ends oddly; the four-region claim is clear.

reading: Festival drums, falling streams and the roar of elephants together fill the air on one side of the land.
On one side of the land the cowherds' drums, their sweet konrai-flutes and their shouting fill the pastures.
On another side the sound of festival drums, flocks of birds and the plough-song of the fields is joined.
On the coast the music of the fishers, the children's play, the shore's noise and the surge of waves are all heard.
Kandal, blue lilies and vengai flower on the hills, and the honey of the high slopes runs thick like ghee.
Konrai, kurundu, kotal and the jasmine bowers fill the village commons with scent and drip honey.
The seashore's lilies, red lotus beds and the bees on them pour out honey that flows everywhere on one side of the land.
The seaside groves, with their screwpine, blue lilies and parrots, look like a wishing-tree forest.
On the high hills, peacocks dance whenever the great clouds roar over the peaks.

title: நாட்டுச் சருக்கம் 22-35 (2/2)
theme: The country description of the Soolamani's opening section continues with birds on sand banks, lotus ponds and swans, hill-flanks with sleeping elephants, buffaloes and crocodiles, the stored grain and pods of the cropland, the sea-shore's pearls and toddy, the flowers in the women's hair, the music of drums and flutes, and ends by calling the fragrant land like heaven.
source_issues: Verses 23, 24, 30 and 34 each had a modern heading printed on the line above them in the edition; it was removed and not taken as verse.
Verse 23 line 4 reads புள்ளறது, probably a misprint for புள் அறாது; verse 27 line 4 (புனலபுலங்களே) and verse 28 line 1 (மேய்ந் து) are badly divided in the text.
Verse 25 ends with a comma, not a full stop, which may mark a verse run on from line 4 or a misprint.

reading: On the sandy banks the jasmine and the young konrai drop their pollen thick under ceaselessly humming bees, and in every such spot the birds scratch the damp sand and look to their young mates beside them.
nuance: Pure scene-setting inside the country description (நாட்டுச் சருக்கம்): the birds are shown as pairs with their young mates, a quiet picture of ease with no event or claim.

reading: A pond lies thick with red lotus whose honey never fails, and with bees and birds crowding its thicket the water-birds cry out over it without pause.
nuance: The first two lines are hard (துள்ளிறாக்கவுட்கொண்டு, உள்ளறாதுதைந்தோகை) and line 4 reads புள்ளறது, which looks like a misprint for புள் அறாது 'the birds without ceasing'; the general picture of a bird-filled lotus pond is clear, the word-by-word sense is not.

reading: Young swans, stirring angrily among the white-shooted green lotus and its thorny stems, churn the roots and make the backwaters of the tank seem to sprout eyes.
nuance: The sense of the last line (கண்முளைத்த தடத்த கழியெலாம்) is not fixed: it may say the backwaters are full of the bud-eyes of the lotus, or that they are alive with the swans' sprouting wakefulness; the angry swans (முனிந்து) are the one sure action.

reading: On the hill-flanks, where bees hum over the kanthal clusters and the she-elephants fan their herd, great elephants with raised trunks drink the sandal-scented flow and stand asleep.
nuance: Line 3 and the grammar linking the elephants to the sandal and to the fanning are obscure (ஏந்து சந்தனச் சரல் இருங்கை), and the verse ends in a comma in the text; it is the fullest hill-country picture of the chapter but its syntax is partly guessed.

reading: On the cool outskirts of the hills the herds drink the cool honey that the konrai garlands drop, then in the rainy season browse the tender dark leaves of the young tamarind, while the mango blossoms.
nuance: The subject of கறித்தொறு and of போர்செய் மாவினம் (fighting herds of beasts, or of cattle) is not named; the verse may be about grazing cattle and deer or about fighting animals, and the sense given here is the likelier of the two.

reading: Black buffaloes graze the kuvalai pool until they tire, then wade in so that their milk runs into the water, and the birds are driven off the pools of the fields.
nuance: The last line (புள்ளலைத்த புனலபுலங்களே) is corrupt or badly divided in the text, and the verb for the milk (உள்ளலைத்தொழுக) is uncertain; only the buffaloes grazing in the kuvalai pool and the milk flowing into water can be read with confidence.

reading: The crocodile that has fed on the spawn of the carp returns to the lotus ford, and the herd of great makara on the silty bank glare at it in anger along the whole backwater.
Heaps of bamboo seed, of the long-eared millet, and of numberless other grains rise high in the houses, and do not grow less however much is eaten.
nuance: The verse is about yield at rest: grain is already gathered and stored, with no farmer in sight, and the last clause (உண்ணிலாங் குலவாமை) says the store does not shrink as it is eaten, which is the poet's way of calling the land inexhaustible. The reading of line 1 (கண்ணிலாங்கழை) is uncertain.

reading: The mullai tracts seem overspread with the large pods of sesame in shining clusters, the hanging cool pods of the avarai, and the pods of the tuvarai crowded on their climbers.
nuance: The mullai here is a farmed land of pod-crops, not the wild forest of the herdsmen's land; the verse names no person.

reading: The wide lands are full of tall sugarcane rising in clumps, groves thick with shrubs, and red paddy bending under its green-filled ears.
The cool sea-lands are full of conches, pearls and pearl-oysters, the sweet toddy that wells in the coconut spathe, and the goods that ships and waves bring in.

The flowers of each tract are seen in the women's hair: the hill women by the millet field, the herdswomen selling ghee, and the farm women who weed out the kuvalai, with garlands strung in the shore grove.
nuance: The three kinds of women (கொடிச்சியர், இடைச்சியர், கடைச்சியர்) are named by the tract they belong to, so the verse sorts the country by its peoples as well as by its plants; the syntax of the second half is loose, so which flower belongs to which woman is only partly clear.

reading: The small drum of the craftsmen swells the kuravai dance of those drinking honey-wine, and the herdsmen with their crooks play sweet konrai flutes, so that, they say, the long-bodied asunam beast falls asleep.
nuance: The asunam (அசுணம்) is the animal the tradition says sleeps to sweet music; the verse uses it to show the flute as soothing. கலவர் in line 1 is a doubtful word for the people who beat the small drum, and whether the following kuravai belongs to the same group is not clear from the text.

reading: Mango vines, jasmine arbours, the dark-leaved mullai creeper, mallikai thickets and golden naazhal all breathe such strong fragrance that the land is like heaven.
nuance: This last verse of the country description ends in a comparison (துறக்கம் ஒக்குமே, 'is like heaven') that no earlier verse of the section makes; the poet offers the land's scent as proof of its excellence, with no doctrinal claim.

title: நகரச் சருக்கம் 36-52 (1/2)
theme: The poet's praise of the city of Podanam, the capital of the Surama country, as a serpent's-world rival, a lotus on the earth, a heaven come down, a city of drums, anklets, bees and plenty, ending with the introduction of its king Payapati, gentle to those who approach and hot to foes.
source_issues: Verse 36 line 3: a stray space before a dead consonant was repaired by the build.
Verse 38 line 3 has a stray comma inside a word; the sense of lines 1-3 is not fixed.

cast.role: the king of the city of Podanam

tamil: சொன்னநீர் வளமைத் தாய சுரமைநாட் டகணி சார்ந்து
மன்னன்வீற் றிருந்து வைக நூலவர் வகுக்கப் பட்ட
பொன்னவிர் புரிசை வேலிப் போதன மென்ப துண்டோர்
நன்னகர் நாக லோக நகுவதொத் தினிய தொன்றே.
reading: The city called Podanam stands inside a golden wall on the throne-ground of the Surama country, a fine town that seems to laugh at the world of the serpents.
nuance: Line 1 is a loose construction (the land's fame and the capital seated in it); the sense is the praise of the country before the city, and the comparison is with the Naga world below.

tamil: சங்கமேய் தரங்க வேலித் தடங்கடற் பொய்கை பூத்த
அண்கண்மா ஞால மென்னுந் தாமரை யலரி னங்கேழ்ச்
செங்கண்மால் சுரமை யென்னுந் தேம்பொகுட் டகத்து வைகும்
நங்கையர் படிவங் கொண்ட நலத்தது நகர மன்றே.
reading: The sea is a pond and the wide earth a lotus in it; in the lotus's honeyed centre lives red-eyed Tirumal in Surama, and the city takes the beauty of women's forms.
nuance: The poet builds the comparison in three nested steps (sea as pond, earth as lotus, Surama as its seed-vessel), and the last line turns the city into a woman's body, the poem's usual measure of beauty.

tamil: செஞ்சுடர்க் கடவு டிண்டே ரிவுளிகா றிவள வூன்றும்
மஞ்சுடை மதர்வை நெற்றி வானுழு வாயின் மாடத்
தஞ்சுட ரிஞ்சி , யாங்கோ ரழகணிந் தலர்ந்த தோற்றம்
வெஞ்சுடர் விரியு முந்நீர் வேதிகை மீதிட் டன்றே.
reading: The city's sky-reaching mansions, where the sun's horses graze and the clouds are caught on the frontage, seem a flower opened by the sea and set on the altar of the great ocean.
nuance: Lines 1-3 are hard to construe; the image of the city as a flower laid on the ocean's altar rests on line 4.

tamil: இரும்பிடு தொடரின் மாவி னெழுமுதற் பிணித்த யானைக்
கரும்பிடு கவள மூட்டும் கம்பலை கலந்த காவின்
அரும்பிடை யலர்ந்த போதி னல்லியுண் டரற்று கின்ற
கரும்பொடு துதைந்து தோன்றுஞ் சூழ்மதில் இருக்கை யெல்லாம்.
reading: Beyond the groves, elephants chained at the roots of mango trees are fed sugar-cane, and bees drink pollen from the buds, all around the city's walled dwellings.

tamil: மானளா மதர்வை நோக்கின் மையரி மழைக்க ணார்தம்
தேனளா முருவக் கண்ணிச் செல்வர்தோ டிளைக்கு மாடங்
கானளாங் காம வல்லி கற்பகங் கலந்த கண்ணார்
வானளாய் மலர்ந்து தோன்று மணிவரை யனைய தொன்றே.
reading: The mansions rise like a jewelled mountain, where women with rain-dark painted eyes and lords in honeyed garlands play, and the creeper of desire is mixed with the wishing tree.
nuance: The mansion's pleasure is shown as love meeting wealth, with the creeper and the wishing tree the poet's own figures for desire and its fulfilment.

reading: The mansions are said to rival the mountains: incense smoke is the cloud, drums rumble like thunder, and women like banners show up like lightning.
nuance: Each part of the mansion has a mountain's counterpart (smoke-cloud, drum-thunder, banner-lightning); the poet is showing the whole built city as a weather.

reading: The golden halls, the silver bamboo-like pillars and the jewelled floors that gleam under the moon are said not to be made of earth.
nuance: The closing claim that the mansions are not earthen is praise by exaggeration, not a doctrine about the city.

reading: The jewelled drums, the anklets of dancing women and the songs of singers, all heard from the mansions, make the city sound like a hall of many instruments.
The bees, drawn by the water-lilies and by the women's long eyes, mistake the eyes for flowers and, bewildered, grow weary buzzing among the dwellings.
nuance: The mistake of bees for flowers is the poet's stock image for the women's eyes, and the verse is praise of their beauty, not a scene.

reading: The crystal-slabbed benches along the shop-lined streets, with swaying garlands and bees, look like a grove of wishing trees.
The sound of anklets of dark-eyed women echoing in the mansions makes the swans in the ponds restlessly wonder whether their mates have left them.
nuance: The swans' fear of parting is the poet's own touch, an image of separation set inside a description of plenty.

reading: The royal streets, stained with the red lac that women's anklet-sounding feet leave, look like lotuses blooming in a field.
Lotuses, pearl strings that gleam like moonlight and jasmine garlands are not rare in the great city, so the speaker says there is no scarcity of such adornments.
nuance: The verse closes on the negative (not rare), so the sense is that adornments are plentiful; line 4 is short of a clear subject.

reading: The city's white mansions overflow with ripe fruits, the sweet water of three kinds, jackfruit, mango heaps and honey, as if the whole place were ripened.
Its men and women, caught up in joy, know no difference between evening and morning, so that the golden city seems an Indra's heaven come down to earth.
nuance: The unawareness of time is praise of the city's pleasure; it contrasts with the Jain teaching of impermanence that the epic later brings in, but this verse does not make that contrast.

reading: The king of that great city, the single protector of the world under one white parasol, is the crowned, victorious king of kings called Payapati.
nuance: Line 2 is the common figure of a single parasol shading the world; the verse names the king only here, so who he is must come from the lines that follow.
event: Payapati, the city's king, is named and praised as sole protector under the white parasol.

reading: He is a king beyond reckoning in his works, whose command holds even the distant, gentle to those who come near and hot to enemies, with a great army.
nuance: The king is described as cool to those who come to him and fierce to foes, a double character that the praise treats as kingly, not as a flaw.

title: நகரச் சருக்கம் 53-69 (2/2)
theme: The city's king is praised for a reign in which only Kama's arrows are abroad, who takes his sixth share only as grace and keeps learned counsellors; the verses then turn to his two chief queens, Mikapathi and her sister Sasi, who bind his mind until the work of ruling is set aside and the world sleeps under his one umbrella.
source_issues: 58 lines 2-3 and 57 line 4 (பொதுமை நீக்கினான்) are hard to construe; the readings given are tentative.
66 line 3-4 (the way the first one joined them) is obscure, and the first one is taken as Kama.

cast.role: the king of the city, unnamed beyond நரபதி and மன்னவன்
the king's queens, a thousand in all and two above the rest
the chief queen
Mikapathi's younger sister, the king's other chief queen

reading: In the days this king guarded the world nothing but Kama's arrows mingled in the land; no fierce, fire-like killing force of spear-bearing warriors troubled his sea-bounded realm.
nuance: The praise of a bloodless reign names Kama's arrows as the only weapon abroad, which sets up the verses that follow, where the same arrows work inside the palace.

reading: The king takes his sixth share only as a duty of grace, rejoices in no harm done to the world, and brings even enemies low by making them bow, never by slaying them in anger.
nuance: The reading takes ஆறிலொன்று as the royal share of the produce and அறம் as its name; the verse says nothing of a rival measure.

reading: Kings find shelter in the shade at the king's feet, sages find refuge in the shade of his crown, and the world stands cool under the shade of his umbrella.
With neither lasting foes nor a ring of hostile neighbours, the king guards himself and the earth, so there is nothing here to puzzle over.
The king takes as kin men great in the books that unfold the truth and, like the swan that parts milk from water, keeps the world free of the common.
nuance: பொதுமை நீக்கினான் is the hard phrase; it may mean he put aside what is common, or what is shared, in his rule, and the sense is not fixed.
event: The king chooses learned counsellors as his kinsmen.

reading: Whatever the king does not hint at, none of the countless strangers dares to propose, and the speakers around him stay unafraid; his divisions follow in orderly array.
nuance: Lines 2 and 3 are hard to construe; the verse seems to say that nothing is said at court except at the king's hint, and that his forces fall in as he arranges.

reading: His queens appear to light the royal clans, with swelling breasts whose weight bends their waists and a mastery of the arts.
The queens are slender-waisted, broad-hipped women with reddish spots of beauty on the breast, bending like a vanci creeper with a bough of five bright flowers.
The queens are full of desire and of shining chastity, with dark hair heavy with flowers, shoulders bright as smoke-lit flame and broad dark eyes.
Besides the thousand wives, two stand above the rest, said to have come down from the sky and to be like lotus goddesses, beyond any words.

tamil: நீங்கரும் பமிழ்த மூட்டித் தேனளாய்ப் பிழிந்த போலும்
ஓங்கிருங் கடலந் தானை வேந்தணங் குறுக்கு மின்சொல்
வீங்கிருங் குவவுக் கொங்கை மிகாபதி மிக்க தேவி
தாங்கருங் கற்பின் றங்கை சசிஎன்பாள் சசியோ டொப்பாள்.
reading: The chief queen Mikapathi, sweet of speech, is joined by her younger sister Sasi, whose chaste constancy matches Indra's queen Sachi.
nuance: தங்கை marks Sasi as the younger sister, and the verse praises both for a chastity hard to bear; the poet's own voice carries the praise.

tamil: பூங்குழை மகளிர்க் கெல்லாம் பொன்மலர் மணிக்கொம் பன்ன
தேங்குழல் மங்கை மார்கள் திலகமாய்த் திகழ நின்றார்
மாங்கொழுந் தசோக மென்றாங் கிரண்டுமே வயந்த காலத்
தாங்கெழுந் தவற்றை யெல்லா மணிபெற வலரு மன்றே.
reading: The two women shine as the diadem of all flower-eared women, like the mango sprout and the asoka that bloom together in spring.

tamil: பெருமக னுருகும் பெண்மை மாண்பினும் பேணி நாளும்
மருவினும் புதிய போலும் மழலையங் கிளவி யாலும்
திருமகள் புலமை யாக்குஞ் செல்விஎன் றிவர்கள் போல
இருவரு மிறைவ னுள்ளத் தொருவரா யினிய ரானார்.
reading: Cherished by the king and fresh in their prattle every day, the two become single in his heart, as dear as the goddess of wealth and the goddess of learning are to a great man.
event: The two queens come to hold one place in the king's heart.

tamil: மன்னவ னாவி யாவார் மகளிரம் மகளிர் தங்கள்
இன்னுயி ராகி நின்றா னிறைமக னிவர்க டங்கட்
கென்னைகொ லொருவர் தம்மே லொருவர்க்கிங் குள்ள மோட
முன்னவன் புணர்த்த வாறம் மொய்ம்மலர்க் கணையி னானே.
reading: The king is the life of the women and they are his; the poet asks what makes one heart run toward another, and gives the answer in the way the flower-arrowed god had ordained.
nuance: The verse treats the love among the three as set by Kama's design, and does not say whether the poet holds it a bond to be praised or one that binds.

tamil: சொற்பகர்ந் துலகங் காக்குந் தொழில்புறத் தொழிய வாங்கி
மற்பக ரகலத் தானை மனத்திடைப் பிணித்து வைத்தார்
பொற்பகங் கமழப் பூத்த தேந்துணர் பொறுக்க லாற்றாக்
கற்பகக் கொழுந்துங் காம வல்லியங் கொடியு மொப்பார்.
reading: Setting aside the work of speaking justice and guarding the world, the queens bind the king's mind, like a kalpaka sprout and a creeper of desire that cannot bear their load of flowers.
nuance: The verse says the king's ruling work is pushed outside; the narrator does not blame the queens or the king here.
event: The queens draw the king's mind from the work of ruling.

tamil: மங்கைய ரிருவ ராகி மன்னவ னொருவ னாகி
அங்கவ ரமர்ந்த தெல்லா மமர்ந்தருள் பெருகி நின்றான்
செங்கயல் மதர்த்த வாட்கட் டெய்வமா மகளிர் தோறும்
தங்கிய வுருவந் தாங்குஞ் சக்கரன் றகைமை யானான்.
reading: Two women, one king: he gives himself wholly in each, taking the form of Indra among goddess-like women.

tamil: முற்றுநீர் வளாக மெல்லா முழுதுட னிழற்று மூரி
ஒற்றைவெண் குடையி னீழ லுலகுகண் படுப்ப வோம்பிக்
கொற்றவ னெடுங்க ணார்தங் குவிமுலைத் தடத்து மூழ்கி
மற்றவற் கரசச் செல்வ மின்னண மமர்ந்த தன்றே.
reading: His sea-girdled earth sleeps under the shade of one white umbrella, while the king bathes in his queens' breasts, and such was the wealth of his rule.
nuance: The closing verse sets the single umbrella of rule beside the delight of the palace and lets them stand together as the king's 'rule-wealth' (அரசச் செல்வம்), without comment.

title: குமாரகாலச் சருக்கம் 70-94 (1/2)
theme: The two princes Vijayan and Tivittan are born, grow into youth and set the city's women aflame, and the king rises, is blessed and goes in state to the assembly hall.
source_issues: 77: line 2 repaired in the source, TSCII leftover ு + U+0BA1 read as ூ.
88: line 1 தவழழொளி தடாவி has a doubled letter and may be corrupt.
92: line 2 நஞ்சிவர் வேனர பதியை is hard to construe.
94: line 3 begins டுளொங்கொளி, probably a misprint for துளங்கொளி.
73: line 2 இயன்ற வேற்பவர் is unclear.

cast.role: the elder prince, born to the first queen
the younger prince, born to the second queen
the queen who bears Vijayan (unnamed in these verses)
the queen who bears Tivittan (unnamed in these verses)
the gods who rain flowers at the birth
the love-god
the two princes, together
the city's young women who love the princes
the king, father of the two princes
the armed young guards who come to the king
the women attendants who praise and fan the king
the brahmins who bless and crown the king
the sword-bearing chamberlains who guard the king

reading: Two beings come down together from the heaven of the kalpa into the queens' wombs and are born, shining like the sea's deep water.
nuance: The two are heavenly beings born here, so the story opens their human lives with a rebirth, not a beginning; line 1's திருவயிற்று (holy wombs, plural) shows two mothers.
event: Two beings descend from a heavenly kalpa and are born as the two sons of the king.

reading: The great queen's joy overflows as Vijayan is born, bright as a white moon that fills the cool world.
event: Vijayan is born to the queen.

reading: In due time the second queen bears Tivittan, whose radiance outshines the jewel-lights, and the gods rain flowers.
nuance: Line 3 has the sea's conches swelling, so earth and heaven both mark the birth.
event: Tivittan is born to the second queen, and the gods shower flowers.

reading: At their birth the quarters grow clear, the gods' city rings with praise, wishes are fulfilled and the clinging moisture of afflicting evil deeds dries up for many, the poet reports.
nuance: The closing என்பவே (they say) gives the claim as report. தீவினைப் பசை pictures karma as a moisture that makes deeds stick; the verse does not say whose deeds, only that it dries for many.
event: At the princes' birth the quarters clear and the hold of evil karma is said to dissolve.

reading: The two grow up in their splendid city and reach the age of princes, and the love-god sets his arrow-buds in the hearts of dark-eyed women.
event: The princes come of age and Kaman plants his arrows in the women's hearts.

reading: A prince is described: fragrant with conch-white, lotus-petal eyes, a crest like dark night, gold earrings swinging at his ears.
nuance: The sequence of 75 and 76 describes the elder, as 78 later names the other as his younger.

reading: The elder prince has an unwithering garland, broad chest, long arms, shining body, shoulders like hill peaks and a stately walk.
The younger prince is described: body like a fresh flower, eyes surpassing lotus, red lips like the ambal, and the holy mark on his chest.
nuance: திருமறு is the mark on the chest; the verse gives it as a feature of the person without comment.

reading: The younger prince bears the emblems of conch and discus on his palm, walks like a splendid elephant, and is the younger of the one just described.
nuance: Conch (சங்கு) and discus (திகிரி) on the palm are given as body marks. 109 later has the court declare Tivittan a guardian of the whole world, which makes these marks read as signs of rule.

reading: As the princes enter a youth that sets fire in the hearts of bangled women, their splendour dulls their rivals' wealth.
event: The princes reach an age that kindles love-sickness in women.

reading: The coral-lipped women turn glances at them, as if the love-god's flower-arrows had taken shape in sidelong looks.
nuance: அவர்கடம் மருள்கொலோ (is it their bewilderment?) leaves open whether the glance is love or the princes' charm striking them.
event: The women show their love by glances, which the poet likens to Kaman's arrows.

reading: The women swoon with fear: the dark-gemmed one has come in a dream, taken their hearts and will not let go; will he take their lives?
nuance: The dark one of the sea's colour (81) and the conch-coloured one (82) are likely the two princes, as 106 later calls the younger கடல் வண்ணன்; the verse itself names neither.
event: The women, dazed, say a prince seen in dream has taken their hearts.

reading: One woman says the conch-coloured prince is in her heart and not a target for other women's eyes; the poet asks who raised this heart-sickness, and answers that it is their age.
nuance: Lines 1-2 are the woman's thought, lines 3-4 the poet's question, so the speaker changes within the verse; 82's assignment is uncertain.
event: A woman declares that the fair prince lives in her heart.

reading: For the women the fire of desire rises within for these radiant youths and burns with countless flames, and no creature but shame-bound women bears it more heavily.
nuance: காம வூழெரி joins desire and ஊழ், a fire from fate; the last line reads as a claim that women bound by shame suffer most, but its sense is unsure.

reading: Because the heart-sickness that goes out to the wealthy lords grows stronger in each woman than the other, the princes reach the age that makes a fire burn in their hearts.
nuance: This verse repeats 79's closing line, now attaching the fire to the lords' wealth (திருவளர் செல்வர்) as well as to their youth.

reading: On another day the crowned king, his head ringed with flowers and bees, passes his rest among the young women of his court.
nuance: The sense of இளையவர் குழைய (the young [women/men] drooping) is not clear from the verse.
event: The king rests in his palace among the young women.

reading: In the garland-hall amid the smoke of aloe and honey, the king on a cotton-stuffed couch gives himself to rest until the red light changes.
nuance: செஞ்சுடர் இரிவதோர் திறத்தனாயினான் is hard; it is read here as the king stirring as the red light moves.
event: The king sleeps in the garland-hall until dawn.

reading: The king wakes and signals, and young attendants, in gold clothes, tight girdles and with bows in hand, come to take their post at his feet.
event: Armed young attendants come to guard the awakened king.

reading: Ceremonial articles gather by him, he washes his eyes, and the lotus-faced women call out their wish for him to live many years.
nuance: Line 1's தவழழொளி தடாவி is a doubtful reading.
event: The king washes his eyes and the women wish him long life.

reading: Brahmins bless him, set the flower-crown on his head, and he bows to the gods and praises them like Indra.
nuance: The verse puts brahmin blessing and the king's worship before the day's rule begins, as part of the morning rite.
event: Brahmins bless and crown the king, who then worships the gods.

reading: Women with garlands and staves go before the king through the palace gate, with the drum's roar, and he plans to reach the assembly hall.
event: The king, escorted, sets out for the assembly hall.

reading: Girls praise his golden feet, fan him with chowries and clothing, and the king reaches the great outer court.
event: The king, praised and fanned by girls, reaches the outer court.

reading: Chamberlains with swords and girdles guard the king, lord of the Naga-poisoned (poison-spear-bearing) city, as he goes.
nuance: நஞ்சிவர் வேனர பதியை in line 2 is hard; it is read as an epithet of the king.
event: Chamberlains guard the king as he passes.

reading: The king passes the three gates, scented with water and strewn with flowers, and reaches the pavilion outside.
event: The king passes three gates and reaches the outer pavilion.

tamil: பளிங்கொளி கதுவப் போழ்ந்த பலகைகண் குலவச் சேர்த்தி
விளங்கொளி விளிம்பிற் செம்பொன் வேதிகை வெள்ளி வேயுட்
டுளொங்கொளி பவளத் திண்காற் சுடர்மணி தவழும் பூமி
வளங்கவின் றனைய தாய மண்டப மலிரப் புக்கான்.
reading: The king enters the great hall of crystal, gold and coral pillars that shines like heaven's wealth.
nuance: Line 3 begins டுளொங்கொளி, an apparent misprint for துளங்கொளி.
event: The king enters the assembly hall.

title: குமாரகாலச் சருக்கம் 95-118 (2/2)
theme: In the court of the lion throne the poets praise the king, an astrologer is admitted and reads a night's dream as the coming of a Vidyadhara king's daughter and a messenger with a letter, the court affirms it and names Tivittan, and in the council hall the ministers speak of his lordship of the discus and plan a guarded garden for the day.
source_issues: 108 line 2 நானேளு looks like a misprint for நா னேழு; the unit counted is not named.
103 line 1 அலகின் மெய்ந்நூல் அபவு சென்று is obscure.
115 line 4 அஞ்சிநின் றவ்வுலகாட்சி செல்லுமே is hard to construe.
