cast.role: the reigning king on the lion throne (Prajapati by tradition)
the young lord of the dream, named at 109
the king's priest
the king's counsellors, who give counsel in the council hall
the kings who attend the court
the poets who sing the king's praise
the doorkeeper of the court
the astrologer who reads the dream
those seated in the court
the guard posted in the garden

tamil: குஞ்சரக் குழவி கவ்விக் குளிர்மதிக் கோடு போலும்
அஞ்சுட ரெயிற்ற வாளி யணிமுக மலர வூன்றிச்
செஞ்சுட ரணிபொற் சிங்கா சனமிசைச் சேர்ந்த செல்வன்
வெஞ்சுட ருதயத் துச்சி விரிந்த வெய் யவனோ டொத்தான்.
reading: The throne is described, with a fanged beast carved on it gripping an elephant calf, and the lord who takes his seat on it is likened to the fierce sun spreading over the top of the rising hill.
event: The lord takes his seat on the lion throne.

tamil: பூமரு விரிந்த நுண்ணூற் புரோகிதன் பொறிவண் டார்க்கும்
மாமல ரணிந்த கண்ணி மந்திரக் கிழவர் மன்னார்
ஏமரு கடலந் தானை யிறைமகன் குறிப்பு நோக்கித்
தாமரைச் செங்கண் டம்மாற் பணித்ததா னத்த ரானார்.
reading: The priest, the garlanded counsellors and the kings of the sea-like army take the places assigned to them, watching the sign of the lord and at the order of the lotus-eyed one.
nuance: இறைமகன் (line 3) and தாமரைச் செங்கண் தம்மான் (line 4) are not named; they may be one person, the prince, or the lord on the throne, so who sets the seating is not fixed here.
event: Priest, counsellors and kings take their appointed seats at the lord's sign.

tamil: முன்னவ ரிருந்த பின்னை மூரிநீ ருலகங் காக்கும்
மன்னவன் கழலைத் தங்கண் மணிமுடி நுதியிற் றீட்டிப்
பின்னவன் பணித்த தானம் பெறுமுறை வகையிற் சேர்ந்தார்
மின்னிவர் கடகப் பைம்பூண் வென்றிவேல் வேந்த ரெல்லாம்.
reading: After the elder one is seated, the victorious kings touch their crowns to the king's anklets and take the places that the younger one assigns them in due order.
nuance: முன்னவர் and பின்னவன் are not named; they read as the elder and younger prince, and the younger is likely Tivittan, who is named at 109, but the verse does not say so.
event: The kings bow their crowned heads at the king's feet and take the seats the younger prince assigns.

tamil: வழிமுறை பயின்று வந்த மரபினார் மன்னர் கோமான்
விழுமல ரடிக்கண் மிக்க வன்பினார்; வென்றி நீரார்;
எழுவளர்த் தனைய தோளா ரிளையவ ரின்ன நீரார்
உழையவ ராக வைத்தா னோடைமால் களிற்றி னானே.
reading: Men of hereditary line, loving the king's feet, proud in victory and strong of arm, are what the king of the frontleted war-elephant keeps at his side.
nuance: இளையவர் (line 3) may mean young warriors or the younger princes; the sentence is read as describing the king's attendants.
event: The king places loyal men of old families beside him as attendants.

tamil: காவல னென்னுஞ் செம்பொற் கற்பகங் கவின்ற போழ்தில்
நாவல ரென்னும் வண்டு நகைமுகப் பெயரி னாய
பூவலர் பொலிவு நோக்கிப் புலமயங் களிப்ப வாகிப்
பாவல ரிசையிற் றோன்றப் பாடுபு பயின்ற வன்றே.
reading: When the king stands in full bloom like a golden wishing tree, the poets, like bees, gather to his bright face and begin to sing in measured melody.
event: The poets gather and begin to sing the king's praise.

tamil: பண்ணமை மகர நல்யாழ்ப் பனுவனூற் புலவர் பாடி
மண்ணமர் வளாக மெல்லாம் மலர்ந்ததின் புகழோ டொன்றி
விண்ணகம் விளங்கு திங்கள் வெண்குடை நிழலின் வைகிக்
கண்ணம ருலகம் காக்கும் கழலடி வாழ்க வென்றார்.
reading: The poets, skilled in the books of the lute and song, sing that the king's fame fills the earth, and wish long life to the feet that guard the world under the moon-like white umbrella.
event: The poets sing and wish the king long life.

tamil: மஞ்சுடை மலையின் வல்லி தொடரவான் வணங்க நின்ற
அஞ்சுடர்க் கடவுள் காத்த வருங்குல மலரத் தோன்றி
வெஞ்சுட ரெஃக மொன்றின் வேந்துகண் ணகற்றி நின்ற
செஞ்சுடர் முடியி னாய்நின் கோலிது செல்க வென்றார்.
reading: The poets praise the king as the one who rose from a line guarded by a bright god, who turned rival kings' eyes away with one fierce spear, and bid his rule go on.
nuance: The verse credits the line's survival to a god of bright lustre; who is meant is not named.

tamil: இன்னணம் பலரு மேத்த வினிதினங் கிருந்த வேந்தன்
பொன்னணி வாயில் காக்கும் பூங்கழ லவனை நோக்கி
என்னவ ரேனு மாக நாழிகை யேழு காறும்
கன்னவி றோளி னாய்நீ வரவிடு காவ லென்றான்.
reading: The king, seated among the praise, tells the doorkeeper to lift the guard and let in whoever comes until seven nazhikai have passed.
nuance: காவல் வரவிடு can mean opening the gate or letting the guard down; either way the order is that the court is open to any caller for seven nazhikai.
event: The king orders the doorkeeper to admit anyone for seven nazhikai.

tamil: ஆயிடை யலகின் மெய்ந்நூ லபவுசென் றடங்கி நின்றான்
சேயிடை நிகழ்வ தெல்லாஞ் சிந்தையிற் றெளிந்த நீரான்
மேயிடை பெறுவ னாயின் வேந்துகாண் குறுவன் கொல்லோ
நீயிடை யறிசொல் லென்றோர் நிமித்திக னெறியிற் சொன்னான்.
reading: A learned astrologer, who knows by thought what happens far off, tells the doorkeeper that if he finds an opening he would see the king, and bids the man judge the moment.
nuance: Line 1 அலகின் மெய்ந்நூல் அபவு சென்று is obscure; the sense that he is a master of an exact science and waits at the gate is clear.
event: The astrologer asks the doorkeeper whether he may see the king.

tamil: ஆங்கவ னரசர் கோமான் குறிப்பறிந் தருளப் பட்டீர்
ஈங்கினிப் புகுமி னென்றா னிறைவனை யவனுஞ் சேர்ந்தான்
வீங்கிருந் தானை யானும் வெண்மலர் பிடித்த கையால்
ஓங்கிருந் தானங் காட்டி யுவந்தினி திருக்க வென்றான்.
reading: The doorkeeper, knowing the king's mind, tells the astrologer he has leave to enter; the king, a white flower in his hand, shows him a high seat and bids him sit at ease.
event: The doorkeeper admits the astrologer and the king offers him a seat.

tamil: உற்றத னொழுக்கிற் கேற்ப வுலகுப சார நீக்கிக்
கொற்றவன் குறிப்பு நோக்கி யிருந்தபின் குணக்குன் றொப்பான்
முற்றிய வுலகின் மூன்று காலமூ முழுது நோக்கிக்
கற்றநூற் புலமை தன்னைக் காட்டுதல் கருதிச் சொன்னான்.
reading: Having laid aside worldly courtesies as his discipline asks, the astrologer, who has looked fully at the three times, waits for the king's sign and then speaks, wishing to show the mastery of the books he has learned.
nuance: The narrator gives his motive as showing his learning (line 4), which colours the prophecy that follows; Naladiyar 52 treats the study of astrology as folly.
event: The astrologer, after waiting on the king's sign, begins to speak.

tamil: கயந்தலைக் களிற்றி னாயோர் கனாக்கண்ட துளது கங்குல்
நயந்தது தெரியி னம்பி நளிகடல் வண்ணன் றன்னை
விசும்பகத் திழிந்து வந்தோர் வேழம்வெண் போது சேர்ந்த
தயங்கொளி மாலை சூட்டித் தன்னிட மடைந்த தன்றே.
reading: The astrologer tells the king that a dream was seen in the night: an elephant came down from the sky, set a shining garland of white flowers on the sea-hued young lord, and went to its own place.
nuance: The Tamil does not say whose dream; 111 suggests the king's. The identification of the sea-hued young lord with Tivittan rests on 109.
event: The astrologer relates the night's dream of the sky-descending elephant that garlands the young lord.

tamil: மன்மலர்ந் தகன்ற மார்ப மற்றதன் பயனுங் கேண்மோ
நன்மலர் நகைகொள் கண்ணி நம்பித னாம மேத்தி
மின்மலர்ந் திலங்கு பைம்பூண் விஞ்சைவேந் தொருவன் வந்து
தன்மக ளொருத்தி தன்னைத் தந்தனன் போகு மென்றான்.
reading: The astrologer gives the dream's fruit: a Vidyadhara king in shining jewels will come, praise the young lord's name, give him one of his daughters and go.
event: The astrologer foretells that a Vidyadhara king will give his daughter to the young lord.

tamil: கட்பகர் திவலை சிந்துங் கடிகமழ் குவளைக் கண்ணித்
திட்பமாஞ் சிலையி னாய்! நீ தெளிகநா னேளு சென்றால்
ஒட்பமா யுரைக்க வல்லா னொருவனோ ரோலை கொண்டு
புட்பமா கரண்ட மென்னும் பொழிலகத் திழியு மென்றான்.
reading: The astrologer adds that when seven have passed, a man able to speak well will come down with a letter into the garden called Pushpakarandam.
nuance: நானேளு (line 2) looks like a misprint for நா னேழு; the unit of seven is not named and may be the seven nazhikai of 102.
event: The astrologer foretells the arrival of a messenger with a letter in the Pushpakarandam garden.

tamil: என்றவ னியம்பக் கேட்டே யிருந்தவர் வியந்து நோக்கிச்
சென்றுயர் திலகக் கண்ணித் திவிட்டனித் திறத்த னேயாம்
ஒன்றிய வுலக மெல்லா மொருகுடை நீழற் காக்கும்
பொன்றிக ழலங்கன் மார்ப போற்றிபொய் யன்றி தென்றார்.
reading: Those seated marvel and answer that Tivittan is indeed of this kind, the one who will protect the whole joined world under one umbrella, and say the prophecy is not false.
nuance: The vocative in lines 3-4 addresses the one who will rule under one umbrella, and the court is taken to speak of Tivittan; they confirm the astrologer without any test.
event: The assembly names Tivittan as the one foretold and affirms the prophecy.

tamil: உரையமைந் திருப்ப விப்பா லோதுநா ழிகையொன் றோட
முரசமொன் றதிர்த்த தோங்கி யதிர்தலு முகத்தி னாலே
அரசவை விடுத்த வேந்த னகத்தநூ லவரை நோக்கி
வரையுயர் மாடக் கோயின் மந்திர சாலை சேர்ந்தான்.
reading: After about one nazhikai a drum sounds; the king dismisses the court with a look, turns to his counsellors and goes to the council hall of his tall mansion.
nuance: அகத்தநூலவர் is read as those learned in the counsel-books, the ministers (compare மந்திரத்துளார் in 113).
event: The king ends the audience and withdraws to the council hall with his counsellors.

reading: In the council hall the king recounts the night's dream as the astrologer interpreted it and the fortunate fruit he assigned, and lifts his crowned head.
nuance: தூக்கினான் is read as raising his head; it could also mean weighing the matter.
event: The king repeats the dream and its fruit to his ministers.

reading: The ministers answer the king that he whom the whole encircled world will worship and lie down in the shade of will bloom as lord of the discus, which they had heard before.
nuance: பண்டுங் கேட்டுமே says they had heard this before; an earlier prophecy about the prince is not shown here.

reading: The ministers, knowing the king's mind and saying the young lord must have good austerity, begin their counsel.
nuance: The verse does not say that the austerity was of a past birth, and no school's doctrine of merit is named.
event: The ministers begin to give counsel.

reading: The ministers say that the conch-line and the discus-line are on the young lord's palm, so he will hold the discus weapon in his hand like the conch-handed lord.
nuance: The comparison borrows the image of Vishnu, the conch-handed; the verse does not call the prince Vishnu.

reading: The ministers say that if the Vidyadhara king's slender, peacock-gaited daughter comes down without fail, the rule of that world will follow.
nuance: Line 4 அஞ்சிநின் றவ்வுலகாட்சி செல்லுமே is hard to construe; the sense that the Vidyadhara realm's rule is tied to the bride's descent is not certain.

reading: The ministers propose that, for the day the astrologer named, they set the fragrant stone platform in order and post Turumakanthan as guard in the lovely garden.
event: The ministers propose to prepare the stone platform and set Turumakanthan to guard the garden.

reading: The king approves the plan as very good, orders Turumakanthan to go and guard daily, and goes to the palace of his dear consorts.
nuance: இன்றுணையவர் கடங் கோயில் is read as the palace of his consorts.
event: The king approves the plan, charges the guard and goes to the consorts' palace.

reading: Turumakanthan bows at the king's feet and goes to the flower garden where bees hum and honey drips from the long branches.
event: Turumakanthan goes to the garden to keep watch.

title: இரதநூபுரச் சருக்கம் 119-142 (1/5)
theme: The sarukkam turns from the kings of the plain to the Vidyadhara ridge: a hill of gods, groves and lovers, then its golden city Ratanupura-Chakravalam and its king, who has every virtue and learning but lacks grace toward the lowly.
source_issues: Verses 120, 124-127, 131-133, 135, 137, 139, 141-142: several lines are hard to construe because of the edition's word division and compressed grammar; flagged uncertain.
Verse 137 line 3: the name-riddle is left unresolved.

cast.role: king of the Vidyadharas of the southern ridge

reading: The poet leaves the kings' talk where it stands and promises to tell of the Vidyadhara country on the ridge.
event: The poet turns from the kings of the plain to the city of the Vidyadharas.

reading: The Vidyadhara hill, pale as moonlit ground, stretches to the sea and rises so high that the jewelled mansions of the sky stand aside for it.
nuance: Lines 3-4 are hard to construe; the sense of the hill outreaching the sky's mansions is the likely one.

reading: Gods gather with their women to play in the groves, and the sparks that fall from their jewels make the groves look like the red evening sky.
Heavenly women and their loving mates drink the coral-lipped nectar and embrace, so crushed garlands scent the wishing-tree groves.
Kinnara gods dwell with their women in the sandal groves, which are full of a cool divine fragrance.
A cool wind stirs the mandara grove and the tulasi, and pollen and flower-honey spill over the breasts of the heavenly women like water.
nuance: The verb in line 4 can also mean the scent leaps upon them; the image of pollen and honey as bath-water is the likelier.

reading: In the sandal bowers beds of leaves are set; those who still bear flesh delight in pleasure there, while those of the sky stay day after day.
nuance: The contrast between the fleshly and the sky-dwellers in lines 3-4 depends on a rare compound and may be read as two groups of lovers or as men against gods.

reading: Women of fine hair play with the hill's youths, and the scented powder of their play falls and stains the sleeping rocks.
nuance: The edition's word division in lines 3-4 is doubtful.

reading: The red dye of women's feet, learning a walk of their own, marks the rocks and draws the eyes of their lovers.
nuance: Lines 1-2 are uncertain in wording; the footprint-dye is certain from line 3.

reading: Streams run down golden rocks where naga maidens bathe, mixing with the rut of the elephants and smelling of jasmine.
The flowers are golden lotuses and the groves are wishing-tree gardens, so the poet asks what more need be told of the Vidyadhara ridge.
nuance: The question of line 4 is a figure of speech that cuts the description short; its exact force is not settled.

reading: On the southern ridge of the Vidyadharas, where the moon rests on the hill, a golden city called Ratanupura-Chakravalam is said to stand.
nuance: The city's name is given here for the first time; the title of the sarukkam comes from it.

tamil: அம்பொன் மாலையார்க ளித்த லத்தெ ழுந்த ரத்தவாய்க்
கொம்பா னார் கொடுத்த முத்த நீர வாய கோழரைப்
பைம்பொன் வாழை செம்பொ னேப ழுத்து வீழ்ந்த சோதியால்
வம்பு பாய்ந்து வந்தொ சிந்து சாறு சோர்வ மானுமே.
reading: Gold plantains ripen red-gold, and their gleam seems to drip as juice on the garland-wearing women's pearl-lipped talk.
nuance: The wording of lines 1-2 is corrupt or very compressed; only the gold fruit and its glow are firm.

tamil: வேய்தி ழன்னி லாவி லங்கு வெள்ளி விம்மு பாளைவாய்ப்
பாய்நி ழற்ப சுங்க திர்ப்ப ரூஉம ணிக்கு லைகுலாய்ச்
சேய்நி ழற்செ ழும்பொ னாற்றி ரண்ட செம்ப ழத்தவாய்ப்
போய்நி ழற்பொ லிந்து வீழ்வ போன்ற பூக ராசியே.
reading: Heaps of areca nut under the moonlit silver spathes look like fallen gems and ripe gold clusters.
nuance: The sense of line 1 turns on a doubtful word; the image of the nuts as fallen jewels is clear.

tamil: காந்தி நின்ற கற்ப கந்தி ழற்க லந்து கையறப்
பாய்ந்தெ ரிந்த போல்வி ரிந்து பாரி சாத மோர்செய
வாய்ந்தெ ரிந்த பொன் மாட வாயி லாறு கண்கொளப்
போந்தெ ரிந்த போன்ம ரம்பு றம்பொ லிந்தி லங்குமே.
reading: The wishing-trees' radiance and scattered parijata flowers look like scattered fire, and the golden mansions' doors shine behind the trees.
nuance: Lines 1-2 are hard to construe.

tamil: மாசில் கண்ணி மைந்த ரோடு மங்கை மார்தி ளைத்தலில்
பூசு சாந்த ழித்தி ழிந்த புள்ளி வேர்பு லர்த்தலால்
வாச முண்ட மாரு தந்தென் வண்டு பாட மாடவாய்
வீச வெள்ளி லோத்தி ரப்பொ தும்பர் பாய்ந்து விம்முமே.
reading: Lovers sport together, ruining their sandal paste and sweating, and a wind scented with the groves and bees makes the flowers sway.

tamil: ஆந்து ணர்த்த மால மும்ம சோக பல்ல வங்களும்
தாந்து ணர்த்த சந்த னத்த ழைத்த லைத்த டாயின
மாந்து ணர்ப்பொ தும்பர் வந்து வைக மற்ற தூன்றலால்
தேந்து ணர்ச்சு மந்தொ சிந்த சைந்த தேவ தாரமே.
reading: Mango, ashoka and sandal sprouts in flower let their honey drop, and the swaying devadaru drops it too as the wind bears the scent.

tamil: தெய்வ யாறு காந்த ளஞ்சி லம்பு தேங்கொள் பூம்பொழில்
பெளவ முத்த வார்ம ணற்ப றம்பு மெளவன் மண்டபம்
எவ்வ மாடு மின்ன போலி டங்க ளின்ப மாக்கலால்
கவ்வை யாவ தந்த கர்க்கு மார னார்செய் கவ்வையே.
reading: The divine river, groves and flowering bowers of this place are such pleasant haunts that all the noise they make is the love-god's own tumult.
nuance: The place is made an arena of Kama's play, so the setting prepares the later court scenes of desire among the Vidyadharas.

tamil: மற்ற மாந கர்க்கு வேந்தன் மான யானை மன்னர் கோன்
அற்ற மின்றி நின்ற சீர ழற்பெ யர்ப்பு ணர்ச்சியான்
முற்று முன்ச டிப் பெ யர்சொன் மூன்று லஃகு மான்றெழப்
பெற்று நின்ற பெற்றியான் பீடி யாவர் பேசுவார்.
reading: The king of that city, lord of war-elephant kings, is faultless and named by a riddle of fire and syllables that the poet leaves to the reader; who could describe him?
nuance: The name is given as a puzzle in lines 2-3 and cannot be fixed with certainty from the verse alone.

tamil: இங்கண் ஞால மெல்லை சென்றி லங்கு வெண்கு டைந்நிழல்
வெங்கண் யானை வேந்தி றைஞ்ச வென்றி யின்வி ளங்கினான்
கொங்கு கொண்டு வண்ட றைந்து குங்கு மக்கு ழம்பளாய்
அங்க ராக மங்க ணிந்த லர்ந்த வார மார்பினான்.
reading: His white umbrella's shade reaches the world's end, fierce-eyed elephant kings bow to him, and he shines in victory with a saffron-smeared, garlanded chest.
event: The Vidyadhara king receives the homage of rival elephant kings.

tamil: றிச்சை யாய வெய்தினா னேந்து செம்பொ னீண்முடிக்
கச்சை யானை மானவேற் கண்ணி லங்கு தாரினான்
வெச்ச னுஞ்சொ லொன்றுமே விடுத்து மெய்ம்மை மேயினான்.
reading: He has mastered every branch of knowledge, the Vidyadharas fear him, his wishes are met, and he lets no false word pass but keeps to truth.
nuance: The word வெச்சனும் in line 4 is obscure; the claim of truthfulness rests on மெய்ம்மை.

reading: In the days when this Vidyadhara king guards the world under his one sceptre, there is a single fault among his virtues: he lacks grace toward the lowly lives beneath him.
nuance: The poet praises the king's virtues in the previous verses and then names one flaw; compassion toward lower creatures is the Jain test of a ruler's goodness, though the verse itself names no school.

reading: While the golden-crowned spear-bearing Vidyadhara king rules the realm, the plantain-like banners tremble.
nuance: Whether the trembling banners are an omen of the fault just named or simply a sign of his might is not clear in the Tamil.

reading: In the days when his bright old crown shines, the brows of the women press on the men like bent bows.
nuance: Lines 1-3 are hard to construe; the closing bow-like brow image is firm.

title: இரதநூபுரச் சருக்கம் 143-166 (2/5)
theme: The Vidyadhara king's long reign gives him a queen, a son Arukkakirti and a daughter Sayampavai, whose beauty is praised verse by verse until kings bow to her; then, as she comes of age, spring opens over the grove with a few sayings on the wealth of the worthless.
source_issues: Verses 143-145, 147, 151, 153-158, 160-162: several lines are hard to construe because of the edition's word division and compressed grammar; flagged uncertain where the sense could not be fixed.
Verse 166 line 4 reads பிஇன்றை in the edition, perhaps for பின்றை.

cast.role: king of the Vidyadharas of the southern ridge
the king's queen
the king's son
the king's daughter
a woman who tells that the season has come
the women who tend the young princess
the Vidyadharas, subjects of the ridge
the kings who bow to the princess
bees of the spring grove, drawn as bards and guests
the cuckoo of the grove

reading: Under his white umbrella the king of endless fame rules happily, and the days of his reign run to many, spent among loving women and the ornaments of desire.
nuance: Line 4 is hard to construe: the word division makes it unclear whether the women and the love-ornaments are the days' company or something counted among them.

reading: While the king keeps the wide earth gladly under the shade of his feet, the young girls' swelling breasts are bound by their mothers.
nuance: Lines 3-4 are compressed; the binding of the girls' breasts by their mothers is the likely sense, shown as a sign of peace in his time.

reading: His keen sword is feared; kings who submit in dread of it find even the honey-dripping groves turned harsh to them.
nuance: The sense of line 4 turns on a word division; the reading is uncertain.

reading: His queen Vayuvegai, a young vine of pure birth, shines on his chest like the flower-goddess on the chest of the dark Lord.
nuance: The simile compares the king with the Lord who carries Lakshmi on his chest, which a Jain poet uses for royal splendour, not worship.
event: The king takes Vayuvegai as his queen.

reading: The king whose elephant wears a golden frontlet becomes the adornment of his queen, who is dressed in golden silk.
event: The king dotes on his queen.

reading: The vine-like queen with lotus eyes becomes nectar to the king and, matching his nature, a feast to him.
event: The queen becomes the king's delight.

reading: While the king lives with her many days, a son is born, Arukkakirti, wearing a garland and anklets.
event: A son, Arukkakirti, is born to the king.

reading: A daughter, Sayampavai, is born, as if come down from the good world; she is so lovely that even the vine of love desires her.
nuance: The verse says she came down (இழிந்து) from the good world, which gives her birth a heavenly origin; it does not say which birth came before.
event: A daughter, Sayampavai, is born to the king.

reading: The red evening sky and the young moon are set beside her as measures of her radiance, and other women bow before her.
nuance: Lines 1-2 and the verb in line 4 are hard to construe; the sense that her radiance outdoes the moon and the sky is the likely one.

reading: Her hair is like a flower swarmed by bees, her eyes like carp, her brows like bows, and her waist so slight that one asks whether it is there.
Bees feed on the wishing-tree flowers at her ear while the vines of her brows seem to bend as if pained.
nuance: The sense of lines 3-4 is not secure.

reading: Sky and earth marvel at the radiance of her eyes, as though a goddess had been born; the maiden is gazed upon with awe.
nuance: The verb அணங்க is doubtful here; it may mean 'stand in awe' or 'ache'.

reading: Her fragrance rises beyond the body-paste she wears, and her grace and modesty make the honey-dripping flower-vine droop in shame.
Tended by her attendants, who hail her as the lady of the hill-king's ancient line, she grows, her breasts a little heavy.
nuance: Whether மங்கை in line 3 names the attendants or describes her is not clear from the word division.
event: Sayampavai grows up in her attendants' care.

reading: Her sidelong looks and shining teeth are called love's own guard, and her curling hair hangs loose as she looks and moves.
Awed by her grace, the Vidyadharas think of her and long to serve her, bringing flower-clusters without stint.
nuance: Line 3 is hard to construe.
event: Vidyadharas long to serve Sayampavai.

reading: Once she is born, the kings with fierce-eyed elephants bow with their long crowns and take up service at her feet, won by the lance of her smile.
nuance: Her smile is likened to a spear, so kings who bow to the father's sword in verse 145 bow here to the daughter's beauty.
event: Kings submit to Sayampavai's beauty as if to a conqueror.

tamil: நங்கையாள் வளர்ந்து காம நறுமுகை துணர வைத்து
மங்கையாம் பிராய மெய்தி வளரிய நின்ற நாளும்
பைங்கண்மால் யானை யாற்குப் பருவம்வந் திறுத்த தென்றாள்
வங்கவாய்ப் பவழச் செவ்வாய் வயந்தமா திலகை யென்பாள்.
reading: As she grows to a woman, love's bud swelling in her, Vayantamatilakai says that the season has come for the elephant-lord.
nuance: The elephant-lord is not named; whether he is a suitor or the king is not clear. Whether பருவம் means the spring or the girl's age is left open; verse 161 gives spring.
event: Vayantamatilakai tells that the season of love has come.

tamil: தேங்குலா மலங்கன் மாலைச் செறிகழன் மன்னர் மன்ன!
பூங்குலாய் விரிந்த சோலைப் பொழிமதுத் திவலை தூவக்
கோங்கெலாங் கமழ மாட்டாக் குணமிலார் செல்வ மேபோல்
பாங்கெலாஞ் செம்பொன் பூப்ப விரிந்தது பருவ மென்றாள்.
reading: Vayantamatilakai tells the king of kings that the season has come, and the golden kongu flowers bloom as the wealth of the worthless does, which spreads no scent.
nuance: The king of kings addressed is not named in the Tamil; he may be the Vidyadhara king. The simile faults wealth that lacks worth, not wealth itself.
event: Vayantamatilakai tells the king of kings that spring has come.

tamil: வேய்ந்திண ரொசிந்த சோலை வேனிலான் வென்றி யோகைத்
தேந்துணர் கொடுப்ப மூழ்கித் தேறல் வாய் நெகிழ மாந்தித்
தாந்துணர் துணையோ டாடிச் சாறுகொண் டூறு மேரார்
மாந்துண ரொசிய வேறி மதர்த்தன மனிவண் டெல்லாம்.
reading: Honey-drunk bees in the flowering grove dive into the nectar, bathe in it and play with their mates in the spring king's victory.
event: Bees feast on nectar in the spring grove.

tamil: கடிமலர்க் கணையி னான்றன் கழலடி பரவிக் காமர்
படிமலர்த் தும்பி யென்னும் பாண்படை தொடர்ந்து பாடக்
கொடிவளர் மகளிர் பூங்கட் குடைந்துநீர் குடிமி னென்று
வடிமலர் வள்ளத் தேந்த வாய்மடுத் திட்ட வன்றே.
reading: Bees are shown as bards singing at the feet of the god of love, while flower-vines like women hold out honey cups and bid them drink.
nuance: The flowers pour as women do, so the grove acts out a feast of the god of love.
event: Bees praise Kaman and drink nectar offered by blossoms.

tamil: அஞ்சுடர் முருக்கி னங்கே ழணிமல ரணிந்து கொம்பர்த்
துஞ்சிடை பெறாது தும்பி துவன்றிமேற் றுகைக்குந் தோற்றம்
செஞ்சுட ரிலங்குஞ் செந்தீக் கருஞ்சுடர்க் கந்துள் சிந்தி
மஞ்சுடை மயங்கு கானம் மண்டிய வகையிற் றன்றே.
reading: Bees swarm over the flame-red murukku blossoms, and the sight is like fire fallen upon a dark smoky forest.

tamil: அந்தழை யசோகம் பூத்த வழகுகண் டவாவி னோக்கி
வெந்தழற் பிறங்க லென்று வெருவிய மறுவி றும்பி
கொந்தவிழ்ந் துமிழப் பட்ட குளிர்மதுத் திவலை தூவச்
செந்தழற் பிறங்க லன்மை தெளிந்துசென் றடைந்த வன்றே.
reading: A bee afraid that the red ashoka blossom is a blaze finds when pollen drops that it is no fire, and goes to it.
nuance: The bee's fear and relief show a mistaken seeing set right by a nearer look.
event: A bee fears a blossom as fire, finds out it is not, and goes to it.

tamil: மாஞ்சினை கறித்த துண்டந் துவர்த்தலின் மருங்கு நீண்ட
பூஞ்சினை முருக்கஞ் சோலைப் பூக்கள்வா யார மாந்தித்
தீஞ்சுவை மிழற்று கின்ற சிறுகுயில் செல்வ ரேனும்
தாஞ்சுவை திரிந்த பிஇன்றைச் சார்பவ ரில்லை யன்றே.
reading: The cuckoo, whose mouth is sour from nibbling mango, drinks murukku flowers and sings; even the rich, once their sweetness turns, find none to come near them.
nuance: The likeness (செல்வரேனும்) is drawn only in the last two lines; whose sweetness turns, the wealth or the person, is not said.
event: A cuckoo leaves sour mango for sweet murukku flowers.

title: இரதநூபுரச் சருக்கம் 167-190 (3/5)
theme: The king rides out to the spring groves, which flatter his women and are drawn as copies of their bodies, then goes to the shrine of the Arhat where he and the descending charanas sing hymns of a god who needs no praise and is loved all the same.
source_issues: Verses 168, 178: the word வயந்தம் and the phrase வயந்தமாட்டருளி are hard to construe from the edition's word division; flagged uncertain.
Verse 174 line 3: 'வரியணி ந்து' has a stray space in the edition.

cast.role: the king who goes to the spring groves, then to the shrine
heavenly sages who descend and sing to the Arhat
the Arhat worshipped in the shrine and in the charanas' song

tamil: கோவைவண் டூது கின்ற குரவெனுங் குரைகொண் மாதர்
பாவைகொண் டாடு கின்ற பருவத்தே பயின்ற காமன்
ஆவிகொண் டிவளிக் கைவிட் டகலுமோ வென்று தத்தம்
பூவையுங் கிளியுங் கொண்டு புலம்பின பொழில்க ளெல்லாம்.
reading: Girls at doll-play, already touched by love's god, fear he will take their lives and leave; they carry their parrots and mynas and wail through all the groves.
nuance: The syntax of lines 1 to 3 is compressed in the edition's word division; the sense of the girls' fear is held with some doubt.

tamil: வயந்தமாங் குணர்த்தக் கேட்டே மன்னவன் மக்க ளோடு
முயர்ந்ததன் னுரிமை யோடு முரிமைகாப் பவர்க ளோடும்
கயந்தலைக் களிருந் தேரும் வையமுங் கவின வேறி
நயந்தன னகரி னீங்கி னோவன நண்ணி னானே.
reading: Told of spring, the king leaves the city with his children, his household and the keepers of his household, riding elephant and chariot, and comes to the pleasure groves.
nuance: The first line's வயந்தம் may be spring personified as the announcer; the edition's division leaves this open.
event: The king sets out from the city with his children and retinue for the spring groves.

reading: As the king arrives, the groves greet him: flowers scatter, koel birds sing a blessing, and slender creepers lift their buds in salutation like women who speak good omens.
The woodland honours him further: creepers pour pollen as scented powder, boughs wave like fly-whisks, and the kongu buds open as umbrellas.
Bees hum like bards singing his virtue, and parrots shake down cool flowers as though strewing the tokens of homage before the spear-bearing lord.
A breeze bathes in the creepers' honey and the stream, sets the bees singing, and loosens flowers on the king's crown.
With spring thus welcoming him, the king of the earth takes pleasure in showing his women the groves and bids them play till their waists ache.
nuance: The poet names him with the sceptre (செங்கோன்) in passing; the verse makes no claim about justice and links no sceptre to the play.
event: The king shows the groves to his women and bids them play.

reading: The mango and the flaming ashoka, the punnai with its scattered pollen, and the bee-hummed banks show spring shining like the wealth of the women addressed.
nuance: The comparison of spring's bloom to the women's wealth (செல்வம்) turns the scene's praise toward the women, not the season.

reading: The shoots of the ashoka and the young creepers are said to have taken their forms from the women's hands and waists, so nature is made to borrow from the body.
Mango shoots take the women's colour, koels learn their speech, and flowering trees gather their lips' red: spring is drawn as a copy of women.

tamil: காவியுஞ் செங் கழுநீருங் கமலமுங் கண் விரிந்துநளி
reading: Lotus and water-lily ponds and pavilions would dazzle even the love-god, but women without mates, with sweet parrot speech, will hardly live through this spring.
nuance: The verse turns the season's beauty into a danger for the unpartnered, as the Kural's love chapters do for the parted.

reading: Having thus delighted the young women, the king takes leave of the spring, and goes with flowers to the golden city of the temple shrine.
nuance: மன்னவன் வயந்தமாட் டருளி is difficult; the sense of taking leave of spring is a reading, not fixed.
event: The king leaves the spring grove and goes to the city where the god's shrine stands.

reading: Glad, the king walks round the shrine of the clan's god from right to left, and its gem-set doors burst open with bright light.
event: The king circles the shrine and its jewelled doors open.

reading: The shrine of the god of unmeasured might shines: it is said to drive out ills, end births, and give boons to heaven.
nuance: The verse credits the shrine and its god with ending births (பிறவி தீர்ப்பன) without saying whose own effort does it; Jain doctrine elsewhere leaves release to the self's own work.

reading: The king, with hair standing on end and radiant, joins his hands and praises well the red lotus feet of him who conquered the harsh dust of karma.
event: The king bows in worship before the conqueror of karma.

reading: They say the god of pure body and bright limbs is called the knower of all; yet even called so, the world-holder is hard to truly know.
nuance: The refrain repeats the line, an old pattern of hymn that turns each epithet back on itself; the claim is about the limits of naming.

reading: They say the god who has no bird-borne weapon and has conquered all strife is the Lord; yet even so named, he is hard to know.
nuance: The unarmed god may be set against gods who bear weapons; the verse does not name any rival.

reading: They say the god with the auspicious mark on his right is without any blemish; even so told, the one who unfolded the great scripture is hard to know.
Having praised the Lord thus, the king bows his head with the flower of the offering, shuts the gem doors, and walks to the courtyard of his shining palace.
event: The king ends his worship, closes the shrine doors and goes to his palace courtyard.

reading: The charanas, heavenly sages, come down from the sky as the scripture's flame burns, circle the father's rich city and bless him with bells ringing.
event: The charanas descend and circle the city, singing.

reading: Their song addresses the one who walked above a lotus, saying that though he is not pleased by their praise, they will not give up love for him who stood so that all the world rejoiced.
nuance: The pattern repeats in 187 to 189; each time the praise concedes that he feels no delight, then keeps the love anyway.
event: The charanas sing to the Arhat.

reading: They say again that though he does not take joy in being worshipped beside the lotus, they will not give up love for him who stood in a state that cannot be reversed, so the path rejoices.
They say a third time that he is not glad when the heavens bow and they praise, yet the cool world rejoices at his standing, so they will not leave their love.
The sweet song of the lovers of the sage's lord ends, and all lives that heard it were freed from sorrow, as long as it lasted.
nuance: The poet closes the hymn with the claim that hearing it soothes lives; the bound of the verse's last two lines is hard to fix.

title: இரதநூபுரச் சருக்கம் 191-214 (4/5)
theme: Sages teach the Vidyadhara king that deeds sprung from a lack of true knowledge bind beings through births until they take refuge at the Lord's feet and hold true seeing, knowledge and conduct, whose end is a state of unfailing bliss; the king goes home, and his young daughter takes the Chakravalam vow and worships the Lord on the hill.
source_issues: Verse 202 line 4 reads மற்ரவை, probably a slip for மற்றவை.
Verse 212 line 1 reads சுடொரொளி and line 2 நோன்புயர, likely letters misread; the sense is clear.
Verse 214 line 3 repeats போதியங் கிழவனை from line 2 and is short in sense; the verse may be damaged, and 'சேதியஞ் செல்வ' is unclear.
The cast id sayampavai for the king's daughter may differ from the id used in chapters 9 and 10, which were marked in parallel.

cast.role: king of the Vidyadharas of the southern ridge; here called by his land and arms, not by name
the group of sages who come to the king and teach him
the chief of the sages, who speaks the sermon
the sky-travelling sages called Jagadabhinandana, probably the same sages
the women attending the king
the people who hear the sermon
the Vidyadhara king's young daughter who takes the vow
the Jain god, here addressed in the girl's hymn

reading: The sages, their own duties fully done and now mountains of virtue, look to the war-proud king and are eager to pour the rain of dharma on him.
nuance: The rain-of-dharma image has the teaching fall on the hearer unasked by any gift from him; the sages' eagerness, not the king's request, begins the sermon (the king asks in 197).
event: The sages, having finished their rite, turn to the king wishing to teach him dharma.

reading: Wherever these sages sit there appear the south wind, a fine drizzle of honey, an ever-fresh cool ashoka tree and a shining disc of moonstone.
nuance: The verse lists the signs that mark a sage's seat; the ashoka (பிண்டி) is the Jain holy tree in the other Jain epics, but the verse itself does not name any faith.

reading: When the sages take their place on the three-tiered platform of the Victor's shining city, the spear-bearing king goes to them and sets their feet upon his head.
event: The king goes to the sages on the three-tiered platform and lays their feet on his crown.

reading: The sages bless the lord of the water-rich land and bid him sit, and he takes his seat amid women in fine cloth and jewelled girdles.
nuance: The king is called by his land (பழன நாடன்) and not by name; line 4 calls him faultless (ஏசிடை இலாதவன்) just as he comes to hear teaching on faults.
event: The sages bless the king and tell him to be seated; he sits among his attendant women.

reading: The sword-bearing king bows his jewelled crown to the sages and blesses them.
nuance: Lines 1-3 compare his shoulders to the lotus-seated goddess and a long necklace; the construction is hard and the sense of the comparison is a guess.
event: The king bows his crown to the sages and gives praise.

reading: The king looks at the chief of the sages and says he has one sweet thing to ask of him, and the sage answers him kindly.
nuance: Who says 'அடிகள்' and who asks the favour in lines 1-2 is not marked in the text; reading the king as the one who speaks first fits the sage's reply in 197.
event: The king addresses the chief sage, who replies gently.

reading: The sage says what is in the king's mind: he wants the old sweet word that cuts the bond of deeds, and the king folds his hands in eager assent.
event: The sage names the king's wish for the teaching, and the king joins his hands.

tamil: மெய்யறி விலாமை யென்னும் வித்தினிற் பிறந்து வெய்ய
கையறு வினைகள் கைபோய்க் கடுந்துயர் விளைத்த போழ்தில்
மையுற வுழந்து வாடும் வாழுயிர்ப் பிறவி மாலை
நெய்யுற நிழற்றும் வேலோ யினைத்தென நினைக்க லாமோ.
reading: From the seed of lacking true knowledge there spring cruel helpless deeds which, when they ripen into harsh pain, leave living beings weary through a garland of births too long to reckon.
nuance: The verse names the seed as absence of true knowledge (மெய்யறிவிலாமை), not craving; lines 3-4 are tightly packed and the exact construction of the last line is uncertain.

tamil: வீழ்வினை பிறிது மாக்கி வெய்துற விளிந்து தோன்றி
ஆழ்துய ருழக்கு மந்தோ வளியற்ற வறிவில் சாதித்
தாழ்வினை விலக்குஞ் சார்வு தலைப்படா வளவு மென்றான்.
reading: Driven by their deeds, beings do further deeds from the fruit of the first, die in pain and are born again, and sink in suffering until they reach the refuge that bars the low births.
nuance: The refuge (சார்வு) is not yet named here; the next verse supplies it. The word is not the Buddhist சார்பு (dependent arising) of the Manimekalai.

tamil: காதியங் கிளைகள் சீறுங் காமரு நெறிக்குங் கண்ணாய்ப்
போதியங் கிழவர் தங்க டியானத்துப் புலங்கொண் டேத்தி
யாதியந் தகன்று நின்ற வடிகளே சரணங் கண்டாய்
மாதுய ரிடும்பை தீர்க்குஞ் சரணெனப் படுவ மன்னா.
reading: The sage names the refuge: the feet of the one who stands beyond all beginning, whom the lords of enlightenment praise in meditation, as the cure for great suffering.
nuance: Lines 1-2 are hard: காதியம் looks like the four destroying deeds of Jain teaching, and போதியங் கிழவர் is a phrase other traditions use for those of the bodhi tree, here read as masters of enlightenment.

tamil: மெய்ப்பொரு டெரிதல் மற்றப் பொருண்மிசை விரிந்த ஞான
மப்பொருள் வழாத நூலி னருந்தகை யொழுக்கந் தாங்கி
யிப்பொருள் ளிவைகள் கண்டா யிறைவனால் விரிக்கப் பட்ட
கைப்பொரு ளாகக் கொண்டு கடைப்பிடி கனபொற் றாரோய்.
reading: The sage tells the king to hold fast to what the Lord laid out: discerning true things, the knowledge that grows on them and conduct kept faithful to the text.
nuance: The verse names three things in turn; whether the poet means the Jain triad of right faith, knowledge and conduct is a reading, as the verse does not number them. Verse 203 speaks of three nectars.

tamil: உற்றடு பிணியு மூப்பு மூழுறு துயறு நீக்கிச்
சுற்றிநின் றுலக மேத்துஞ் சுடரொளி யுருவந் தாங்கிப்
பெற்றதோர் வரம்பி லின்பம் பிறழ்விலா நிலைமை கண்டாய்
மற்ரவை நிறைந்த மாந்தர் பெறப்படு நிலைமை மன்னா.
reading: The end of these is a state free of disease, age and the pain of births, with a shining form the world praises and a limitless, unfailing bliss, which those who are full of these things reach.
nuance: The verse says the released keep a form (உருவம்) and bliss; it does not say they join a god. Line 4 reads மற்ரவை, likely a slip for மற்றவை.

tamil: அருந்துய ரறுக்கு மாண்பி னாரமிர் தவைகண் மூன்றும்
திருந்தநன் குரைப்பக் கேட்டே தீவினை யிருள்கள் போழும்
விரிந்தநல் லறிவின் சோதி விளங்கலிற் சனங்க ளெல்லாம்
பரிந்தகங் கழுமத் தேறிப் பாவம் பரிந் தவர்க ளொத்தார்.
reading: Hearing the three nectars that cut hard suffering taught well, the people, lit by wide knowledge that tears the darkness of evil deeds, grow clear in heart as if freed from sin.
nuance: The 'three nectars' (அமிர்தவைகள் மூன்றும்) most likely refer back to the three things of verse 201, but the verse does not say so. The verse says the people were as if without sin (ஒத்தார்), not that they were.
event: The assembled people hear the teaching and are cleared of heart as if of sin.

tamil: மன்னிய முனிவன் வாயுண் மணிகொழித் தனைய வாகிப்
பன்னிய பவங்க டீர்க்கும் பயங்கெழு மொழிக டம்மால்
கன்னவில் கடகத் தோளான் காட்சியங் கதிர்ப்புச் சென்றான்
பின்னவ னுரிமை தானும் பெருவத மருவிற் றன்றே.
reading: The sage's jewel-bright words, which end the sins they tell of, bring the king to right vision, and his own one too takes up a great vow.
nuance: காட்சி (sight, vision) is read here as the right seeing of the Jain triad. உரிமை (one's own, dear one) is taken as the daughter of 205, but the verse does not say who it is.
event: The king reaches clear sight through the sage's words and a dear one of his takes a great vow.

reading: The king's young daughter bows, rises shining after drinking their sweet word, resolves on a vow and thinks how to finish it with greatness.
nuance: The verse does not name her; she is the girl born as Sayampavai in verse 150, which this chapter does not repeat.
event: The king's young daughter bows to the sages and takes a vow.

reading: Wearing a garland of honeyed cool flowers, the king bows to the sages' feet, circles the god's shining city in the right-hand way and goes.
event: The king bows to the sages, circles the shrine city and leaves.

reading: The king, guarded by young men with spears, goes back to his own city.
nuance: Lines 1-2 say something of women's minds and the love-god's place in them, but the construction is not clear and the link to the king's return is a guess.
event: The king goes back to his own city.

reading: After the king and the lords of the inner city have gone, the sky-travelling sages called Jagadabhinandana praise the Lord again and leave through the sky in a blaze of light.
nuance: The sages named here are likely the same ones who taught the king, but the verse does not say so.
event: The sky-travelling sages worship the Lord and depart through the sky.

reading: By the vow she has taken, the creeper-haired girl comes to a flame-like glow that shines, like a banner of fire on a mansion.
nuance: Lines 1-2 pile images (a flame-banner, the shadow of mansion banners) and the comparison is hard to resolve; the main sense, that the vow makes her glow, is clear.
event: The king's daughter shines with a new glow from her vow.

reading: Though the girl is as soft as she is, a vow set out as it should be is high, and nothing is hard for those who are spotless within.
nuance: The verse says it of her tenderness: a delicate girl can bear a hard vow, because what holds it up is a clean mind, not strength of body.

reading: Honoured even by Indra's world, her vow sheds its light and she grows, nourished as if by mantra and sweet ghee, into something like a spotless flame-banner in the sky.
nuance: The mantra and ghee image can be read as a figure for her glow rather than a literal rite; the verse does not describe a fire-offering.
event: The king's daughter keeps her vow and glows like a flame-banner.

reading: After she has kept the vow named Chakravalam well, the sweet-voiced girl comes to wish a great special worship of the god.
nuance: The vow's name matches the city's in verse 130, and the text does not link them. Line 1 reads சுடொரொளி, probably for சுடரொளி.
event: The girl completes her vow and sets out to hold a great worship.

reading: On the moonlit hill, over the crest, the king's daughter worships the god's shrine and praises it so that the gods' world marvels.
event: The king's daughter worships at the hilltop shrine and praises the god.

reading: The hymn addresses the Lord as the primal god who gave the rare scripture, the lord of the bodhi, who stood on the flower, and bows to his holy feet.
nuance: Line 3 repeats line 2's போதியங் கிழவனை and breaks the metre of the sense; the line may be damaged. The words பூமிசை ஒதுங்கினை are close in sense to Kural 3's மலர்மிசை ஏகினான், but share no words with it, so this is a link, not an echo. The speaker is taken to be the girl, from 213.

title: இரதநூபுரச் சருக்கம் 215-238 (5/5)
theme: In the Ratanupura palace the princess hymns the god and brings his flower remnant to her father, who praises her in images of mango, moon and Ganga, then is troubled over whom to give her to and, after weighing love against the treatise, sends for the ministers learned in policy.
source_issues: Verses 215 and 216: line 3 repeats line 2 word for word in the edition (a doubled line).
Verse 219: the words ending line 2 and starting line 3 and the subject of the final verb cannot be resolved; flagged uncertain.
Verses 223, 230, 231, 233, 235: lines hard to construe in the edition's word division; flagged uncertain.

cast.role: the Vidyadhara king's daughter, unnamed in these verses
the Jain god the princess hymns
king of the Vidyadharas of the southern ridge, her father

reading: The king's daughter hymns the god as the one who cut off desire and was wrathful at Death, the lord with the bright mark on his breast, whose flower-like feet she and her women bow to.
nuance: Line 3 repeats line 2 word for word in the edition; the repetition is kept as a text problem rather than a second statement.

reading: The hymn goes on: the god gave grace, ended deep sorrow, is the one lord of the wheel and of the world, and she bows at his feet to speak of his graceful words.
nuance: Line 3 repeats line 2 in the edition, as in the verse before.

reading: The spear-eyed girl, having praised the god in such words that keep off the fearsome enemy of deeds, wears the remnant of his holy feet's flowers.
event: The princess ends her hymn and puts on the flower remnant from the god's feet.

reading: Having taken the honey-rich flower remnant from the god's feet, the girl walks, praised by her doe-eyed companions, to the temple-like palace of her father's rich city.
event: The princess, praised by her companions, goes to her father's palace.

reading: Someone tells the king, goes gently up with feet that praise, and holds out the flower remnant in a red palm whose soft fingers turn red.
nuance: The final verb is masculine (நீட்டினான்) though the princess has been the actor in the two verses before; the sense of who offers the remnant, and the words ending line 2 and starting line 3, cannot be fixed.
event: The god's flower remnant is held out to the king in a palm.

reading: The king smells the crown of the hair of his daughter, who bows like a creeper while bees leave her lily-like flowers, and begins to say these things.
event: The king smells his daughter's hair-crown and begins to speak to her.

reading: The king tells her that though many bunches of nectar flowers stand, only the mango cluster makes spring appear, and he shines because she was born to him.
nuance: Her birth is praised as what lights the father and the house, a view of a daughter that the following four verses repeat in other images.

reading: The king says that where Ganga water flows even the sea becomes sacred, and that since her birth his family has been made known to the world and the seas' neighbours bowed.
The king says that, as the base creatures do not touch a lotus pool, the whole region has fallen away from lowness since her birth.
nuance: Lines 2 to 4 are hard to construe; the king's claim may be that lowly people stay clear of the realm because of her.

reading: The king says that as the young moon growing in the sky makes the world glad and dispels darkness, so her growth dispels the darkness in the house.
The king says that as a bee comes in love to the jasmine and the lone champak grove, she is a fortune among women, whose house makes the whole earth glad.
Having said such praise of her ornaments to the red-lipped girl, the king tells her to go into her mother's house and eat the meal.
event: The king bids his daughter go to her mother's house and eat.

reading: Telling her to wear anklets, not heavy ornaments, and walk gently, the golden king looks fondly on his daughter.
event: The king sends her off wearing anklets and watches her go.

reading: The king reflects that even if mortals seized every earthly jewel by force and won every heavenly one by fate, a girl as a jewel is hard to come by, a thing past counting.
nuance: The edition's word division makes the speaker's own judgement of her worth hard to separate from the narrator's report that he thought so (line 4).
event: The king ponders his daughter's worth beyond all treasure.

reading: The king asks which youth among the spear-bearing sons of the ancient mountain-kings is fitted by quality for her, which marked hero of the body and brave.
event: The king wonders who among the Vidyadhara youths is worthy of his daughter.

reading: The king reasons that though fine jewels may be set with soft flowers, and elders may join girls where families do not mingle, women with sad curls would not say no.
nuance: The sense of lines 3 and 4 turns on குலம் கலந்தில்வழி and on the sandhi of அன்றென்கிற்பவோ; the verse may mean that a daughter would not refuse an ill-matched union.

reading: The king thinks that if parents give girls away with only the groom's side's gain in mind, girls whose hearts are not in it can only grieve and speak otherwise.
nuance: The word அந்தை (line 1) is rare and the grammar compressed; the reading of lines 1 and 2 is provisional.

reading: The king concludes that love is known only through love, outsiders cannot weigh a woman's desire by their own judgement, so in her matter he should follow the words of those who recite the treatise.
nuance: The verse gives two guides in tension: the girl's own love, which no outsider can judge, and the treatise's ruling, which the king chooses to follow; it does not say whether her love will be asked.

reading: The king reasons that a ruler's life is of two kinds, his own senses and those joined to others', and so ministers urge him to act on his own judgement.
nuance: The syntax of lines 1 and 2 is compressed, and whether the ministers urge the king or are urged by him cannot be fixed from the Tamil.

reading: The king reflects that though lotuses stand in cool pools they open by the sun's rays, and kings dwelling among virtue's groves likewise open by those who consider with learning.
The king says that a boat on the great flower-sea reaches its shore if it sails true to the five times, and that those who enter with the learned's skill will find the sea of the elders' conduct.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are hard to construe in the edition's word division, including the 'five' of line 2.

reading: The king notes that what one takes for good another finds not so, but one thing stands: the world accepts what accords with the treatise of policy.
The king says that brahmin conduct and kings' lives, without counsel, do not flower, and that even Indra's lordship is borne up by the thousand masters of the treatise.
nuance: The Indra and the thousand 'masters of the treatise' (ஈரைஞ்ஞாற்றுவர் தந்திரக் கிழவர்) are brought in as a Vedic and Brahmanical example in the king's own argument; the verse makes no Jain claim.

reading: Having so reasoned in his mind, the king sends his men to summon the ministers who are masters of the treatise of policy, and they go to say what he has commanded.
event: The king sends messengers to bring his ministers learned in policy to counsel him on his daughter's marriage.

title: மந்திரசாலைச் சருக்கம் 239-262 (1/8)
theme: The king calls his ministers into the sealed council hall and tells them that kings rule through counsel and the learned, then asks who could match his daughter's worth; the ministers bow, and Sachchutan and others begin to answer in turn with images of gem and sun and sandal.
source_issues: Verses 239-240, 244, 246, 249, 251-253, 255, 259-260, 262: several lines are hard to construe because of the edition's word division and compressed grammar; flagged uncertain.
Verse 262 has no closing என்றான் and its speaker is not stated; verse 255 does not name the marriage.

cast.role: king of the Vidyadharas of the southern ridge, who holds council
the Vidyadhara king's counsellors, summoned to the council hall
the minister who first answers the king

reading: The king's word reaches the learned counsellors, who tremble at it and come to his feet.
nuance: The words that open the verse name the king only by an epithet, and the poison-bright spear in line 4 names him again; that both are the same king, who spoke at the end of the last section, is the likely reading.
event: The king's summons reaches his ministers, who come in fear to the king.

reading: The poet describes the council hall as a closed place with a silver-rimmed platform, where no sound leaves and neither bird nor anything else comes in.
nuance: Line 2 names only birds and 'what are not birds' as barred; the poet gives no reason, and the closing of the hall to sound is the plain point.

reading: The king and his ministers go into the fragrant hall and sit, and the king, earrings flashing, begins to speak.
event: The king and his ministers enter the hall and sit, and the king begins to speak.

tamil: மண்ணியல் வளாகங் காக்கு மன்னவர் வணக்க லாகப்
புண்ணிய நீர ரேனும் புலவராற் புகலப் பட்ட
நுண்ணிய நூலி னன்றி நுழை பொரு ளுணர்த்த றேற்றா
ரெண்ணிய துணிந்து செய்யுஞ் சூழ்ச்சியு மில்லை யன்றே
reading: The king says that even kings of good nature can grasp subtle meanings only through the fine treatises the learned have composed, and that none decides on his own thought.
nuance: The verse ranks the treatise above the king's own discernment; it does not say that books alone suffice for acting.

tamil: வால்வளை பரவி மேயும் வளர்திரை வளாக மெல்லாம்
கோல்வளை வுறாமற் காக்குங் கொற்றவ னெடிய னேனும்
மேல்விளை பழியும் வெய்ய வினைகளும் விலக்கி நின்றார்
நூல்விளை புலவ ரன்றே நுணங்குபோ தணங்கு தாரீர்
reading: The king says that though he guards the whole sea-ringed earth with an unbent sceptre, it is the learned of the books who stand to keep later blame and fierce deeds away from him.

tamil: சுற்றுநின் றெரியுஞ் செம்பொன் மணிமுடி சுடரச் சூட்டி
வெற்றிவெண் குடையி னீழல் வேந்தன்வேற் றிருக்கு மேனு
மற்றவன் மனமுங் கண்ணும் வாழ்க்கையும் வலியுஞ் சால்பு
மற்றமி லரசுங் கோலு மாபவ ரமைச்ச ரன்றே
reading: The king says that though he sits crowned under the white umbrella, his mind, his eye, his living, his strength, his worth and his rule and sceptre belong to his ministers.
nuance: Line 4 gives the ministers an epithet, மாபவர், that can be read as 'of great penance' or as 'great ones'; either way the weight falls on their share in his rule.

tamil: வீங்குநீர் ருலகங் காக்கும் விழுநுக மொருவ னாலே
தாங்கலாந் தன்மைத் தன்று தளையவிழ் தயங்கு தாரீர்
பாங்கலார் பணியச் சூழு நூலவர் பாக மாகப்
பூங்குலா மலங்கன் மாலைப் புரவலன் பொறுக்கு மன்றே
reading: The king says a single yoke cannot carry the whole watery world, but it can be borne when learned counsellors, who plan how rivals will bow, share the load with the ruler.

tamil: அற்றமின் றுலகங் காக்கு மருந்தொழில் புரிந்து நின்றான்
கற்றவர் மொழிந்த வாறு கழிப்பது கடன தாகு
மற்றவற் குறுதி நோக்கி வருபழி வழிகள் தூரச்
செற்றவர்ச் செருக்குஞ் சூழ்ச்சி தெருண்டவர் கடவ வன்றே
reading: The king says that a king who has taken up the hard work of guarding the world must pass it as the learned direct, and that those who see his good, keep blame far off and break proud foes are the wise in counsel.
nuance: The last two lines are compressed and the link between the 'good' sought for him and the foes' pride is not spelled out.

tamil: செறிந்தவர் தெளிந்த நூலார் சிறந்தவை தெரிந்து சொன்னால்
அறிந்தவை யமர்ந்து செய்யு மமைதியா னரச னாவான்
செறிந்தவர் தெளிந்த நூலார் சிறந்தவை தெரிந்து கூறி
அறிந்தவை யியற்று கிற்கு மமைதியா ரமைச்ச ராவார்
reading: The king says he is a king who calmly acts on what well-read learned men choose and tell him, and that ministers are those who tell him so and then carry it out.
nuance: Lines 1-2 and 3-4 say nearly the same in the same words, one for the king and one for the minister; the poem sets the two offices side by side.

tamil: வாள்வலித் தடக்கை மன்னர் வையகம் வணக்கும் வாயில்
தோள்வலி சூழ்ச்சி யென்றாங் கிருவகைத் தொகையிற் றாகும்
ஆள்வலித் தானை யார்கட் காதிய தழகி தேனும்
கோள்வலிச் சீய மொப்பீர் சூழ்ச்சியே குணம தென்றான்
reading: The king says that kings win the world by two powers, strength of arm and counsel, and that though the armed host is fine, he tells lion-like ministers that counsel is the quality that counts.

tamil: ஊழ்வர வன்ன தேனு மொருவகைக் கரும மெல்லாம்
சூழ்பவர் சூழ்ந்து சூழுஞ் சூழ்ச்சியுட் டோ ன்று மன்றே
யாழ்பகர்ந் தினிய தீஞ்சொ லமிர்தனா ரேனுஞ் சூழ்ச்சி
வாழ்பவர் வல்ல ராயின் மன்னராய் மலர்ப வன்றே
reading: The king says that even what comes like fate shows itself within the counsel of those who take counsel, and that those who live by counsel, if skilled, flourish as kings.
nuance: ஊழ் வர அன்னது is condensed. The sense may be 'even an act that fate has set is shown through counsel', not that counsel overturns fate; the verse does not say a former deed is meant.

tamil: ஆற்றறான் சூழ்ச்சி யென்ப தாதலா லதனை யாயும்
ஆற்றலா ரமைச்ச ராக வமைச்சரோ டமர்ந்து செல்லும்
ஆற்றலா னரச னாகி னரியதொன் றில்லை யன்றே
reading: The king says that of the three powers taught for kings, counsel is the highest, so a king who sits and goes with able ministers meets nothing hard.
nuance: The verse does not name the three powers.

tamil: வடந்திகழ் முலையி னார்தங் காமத்தின் மதர்த்த மன்னர்க்
கடைந்தவர் மாண்பு மாங்கொன் றில்லையே லரசர் வாழ்க்கை
கடந்தவழ் கடாத்த வேழங் களித்தபின் கல்வி மாணா
மடந்தவ ழொருவன் மேல்கொண் டன்னதோர் வகையிற் றாமே
reading: The king says that kings maddened with love of the women who wear necklaces, if they have no learned men to join them, are like a rutting elephant flushed with pride and ridden by a fool without learning.
nuance: Line 4's image is hard to construe: the rider is read here as a fool who has mounted the elephant.

tamil: சுந்தரச் சுரும்புண் கண்ணிச் சூழ்கழ லரசர் வாழ்க்கை
தந்திர மறிந்து சூழ்வான் சூழ்ச்சிசார்ந் தமையல் வேண்டும்
மந்திரம் வழுவு மாயின் வாளெயிற் றரவு காய்ந்து
தந்திரந் தப்பி னாற்போற் றன்னையே தபுக்கு மன்றே
reading: The king says that kings must lean on counsel, and that if counsel slips, it turns on the king like an angry fanged snake whose charmer's art has failed.
nuance: தந்திரம் in line 4 could be the charmer's art or a rule of statecraft; the snake image fits the first better.

tamil: எடுத்தன னிலங்கு சாதி யெழிலொடு திகழு மேனு
மடுத்தன நிறத்த தாகு மணிகிளர் பளிங்கு போல
வடுத்தவ மலர்ந்து நுண்ணூன் மதியவர் வினையின் மாட்சி
கொடுத்தவா நிலைமை மன்னன் குணங்களாக் கொள்ப வன்றே
reading: The king says that a jewel of fair birth takes the colour of what it lies on like a crystal, and that so the good deeds of the learned are counted as the king's own virtues.
nuance: Lines 1-3 are knotted; the verse is read here as a crystal taking its hue from what lies beside it, not as a claim that the ministers are flawless.

tamil: மன்னுநீர் வளாக மெல்லாம் வணக்குதல் வல்லீ ராய
பன்னுநூற் புலவீர் முன்னர்ப் பலபகர்ந் துரைப்ப தென்னை
யென்னைநீ ரிறைவ னாக்கி யிராப்பக லியற்ற வன்றே
யின்னநீ ரின்ப வெள்ள மியைந்தியா னுயர்ந்த தென்றான்
reading: The king tells the ministers it is useless to say more, since they made him king by their daily work, and that through them he has risen into a flood of joy.
event: The king thanks the ministers and says he owes his kingship and his joy to their work.

tamil: கொங்குடை வயிரக் குன்றின் கொழுஞ்சுடர் விளக்கிட் டாங்கு
நங்குடி விளங்க வந்த நங்கைதன் னலத்திற் கொத்தான்
தங்குடி விளங்க நின்ற தன்மையா னெவன்கொ லென்றான்
சங்குடைந் தனைய தாழைத் தடமலர்த் தொடைய லானே
reading: The king asks who could match the worth of the maiden born to light his house like a lamp on a diamond hill, and in what way he must stand so that his own house shines.
nuance: The verse names no marriage; the question of who is her match is read here from the lamp image and the word நங்கை, 'the woman', and the poem's turn to a Vidyadhara match elsewhere in the section.
event: The king puts to the ministers the question of the fit husband for the maiden who lights their house.

tamil: இறையிவை மொழியக் கேட்டே யிருந்தவ ரிறைஞ்சி யேத்தி
யறைகழ லரவத் தானை யணிமுடி யரச ரேறே
நிறைபுக ழுலகங் காத்து நிலாகநின் னிறைமை யென்று
முறைமுறை மொழிய லுற்று முன்னிய முகத்த ரானார்
reading: The ministers hear the king, bow and praise him, wish him a long, widely praised rule over the earth, and each in turn prepares to speak.
event: The ministers bow, praise the king and prepare to speak in turn.

tamil: பணிந்துமற் றேனை யார்பாங் கிருப்பநூல் பலவு நோக்கித்
துணிந்துதன் புலைமை தோன்றச் சச்சுதன் சொல்ல லுற்றான்
இணந்துநின் றுலவுந் தும்பி யிடையிடை யிருண்டு தோன்ற
அணிந்துநின் றலரும் பைந்தா ரணிமணி முடியி னாற்கே
reading: One minister, Sachchutan, bows while the others sit aside, studies the many treatises, and begins to speak with humility before the king in his gem crown and green garland.
nuance: Line 2 says he speaks out of 'his own lowliness'; the humility is a convention of address.
event: The minister Sachchutan bows to the king and begins to speak.

tamil: பொற்கதிர் பரப்பி வந்து பொங்கிருள் புதைய நூறுந்
தொழிற்கதிர்க் கடவு டோ ன்றச் சூரிய காந்தமென்னும்
எழிற்கதிர்ப் பிறங்கல் வட்ட மெரியுமிழ்ந் திடுவ தன்றே
அழற்சதி ரிலங்குஞ் செவ்வே லதிர்கழ லரசர் கோவே
reading: Sachchutan tells the king that the sun-gem spits fire when the sun appears and scatters the night's dark, and addresses him as the king of kings with the blazing spear.
nuance: The verse gives only the image; the application to the king and his ministers is drawn in verse 259.

tamil: கோணைநூற் றடங்க மாட்டக் குணமிலார் குடர்க ணைய
ஆணைநூற் றடங்கக் காக்கு மரசர்த மருளி னாலே
பேணுநூற் புலவர் மாண்பும் பெருகுவ துருவத் தார்மேல்
பூணுநூற் பொலிந்து தோன்றும் பொன்வரை மார்ப வென்றான்
reading: Sachchutan says that by the grace of kings who guard the order of command and treatise, the worth of the learned poets grows, as the sacred thread shows bright on the chest of the golden-chested king.
nuance: Lines 1-2 are dense; the sense taken is that kings who keep the rule of treatise draw out the worth of those who follow it, as the sun draws fire from the sun-gem in 258.

tamil: சூழ்கதிர் தொழுதி மாலைச் சுடர்பிறைக் கடவு டோ ன்றித்
நாழ்கதிர் சொரிந்த போழ்திற் சந்திர காந்த மென்னும்
வீழ்கதிர் விளங்கு வட்டம் வெள்ளநீர் விரியு மன்றே
போழ்கதிர் பொழிந்து பொங்கிப் புலானிணம் பொழியும் வேலோய்
reading: A minister tells the king that the moon-gem pours a flood of water when the moon god rises and sheds cool rays, and addresses him as the spear-bearer who pours out flesh and fat.
nuance: Line 4 turns from the cool image to the spear that sheds the flesh and fat of foes. The speaker is the next minister in the turn announced in 256, and is not named.

tamil: கண்ணளித் துலக மெல்லாங் கவின்பெறக் காவல் பூண்டு
தண்ணளித் தயங்கு செங்கோற் றாரவர் தவத்தி னாலே
மண்ணளித் தினிய நூலோர் மந்திர மலரு மென்றான்
விண்ணளித் திலங்கும் வெள்ளி விரிந்தவெண் குடையி னாற்கே
reading: The minister says that by the merit of kings who guard the world with a gracious straight sceptre, the counsel of learned men blossoms, and he speaks it to the king under the white umbrella.
nuance: தவம் here may mean the austerity or merit of the king, not a former deed; the verse does not say.

tamil: கண்ணிய கடாத்த வேழங் கவுளினா னுரிஞப் பட்டுந்
தண்ணிய தன்மை நீங்காச் சந்தனச் சாதி போலப்
புண்ணிய கிழவர் கீழோர் பிழைத்தன பொறுப்ப வாயின்
மண்ணியல் வளாக மெல்லாம் வழிநின்று வணங்கு மன்றே
reading: The speaker says that as sandal keeps its coolness though a rutting elephant rubs against it, so if the virtuous masters bear the lapses of the lowly, the whole earth follows and bows to them.
nuance: This verse has no closing என்றான் and may belong to a third minister's speech; the speaker is read here as the same unnamed minister as 260-261.

title: மந்திரசாலைச் சருக்கம் 263-286 (2/8)
theme: In the council hall a counsellor presses the king with a theory of kingship: the king's heat or grace is the world's, the king and learning are its eyes, and austerity and rule are two hard burdens. Then, asking leave to speak of a maiden's lord, he turns to a long praise of the Vidyadhara realm as a heaven on the ridge.
source_issues: Verse 274 reads என்ணுவ for எண்ணுவ, a plain misprint.
Verse 285 line 4 begins with a stray ணி (ணிரத்தின), apparently a broken initial of தண் or the like.
Verse 271 line 3 reads செய்கையிர் றிரியு where செய்கையின் றிரியு is expected; this edition's sandhi is uneven.
Verses 263 and 282 carry an edition's question mark inside the verse.
Verses 278 to 286 are in shorter-lined quatrains in a different metre from 263 to 277, and the speaker is not marked as changing; they are read here as the counsellor's own description.
Verse 278 calls the hill the northern mountain (வடமலை), where verse 130 places the city on the southern ridge.

cast.role: a counsellor in the council hall, speaking to the king; unnamed in these verses
the king addressed in the council hall, called lord of kings and bearer of the spear

tamil: நிறந்தலை மயங்க வெம்பி நெடுங்கடல் சுடுவ தாயின்
இறந்தலை மயங்கு நீர்வா ழுயிர்க்கிட ரெல்லை யுண்டோ ?
மறந்தலை மயங்கு செவ்வேன் மன்னவன் வெய்ய னாயின்
அறந்தலை மயங்கி வைய மரும்பட ருழக்கு மன்றே
reading: The counsellor says that if the sun scorched the great sea there would be no end to the misery of the creatures that live in its water, and so, when a king grows cruel and fierce, aram goes astray and the world suffers hard pain.

tamil: மண்குளிர் கொள்ளக் காக்கு மரபொழிந் தரசர் தங்கள்
விண்குளிர் கொள்ள வோங்கும் வெண்குடை வெதும்பு மாயிற்
கண்குளிர் கொள்ளப் பூக்குங் கடிகயத் தடமுங் காவும்
தண்குளிர் கொள்ளு மேனுத் தாமிக வெதும்பு மன்றே
reading: If kings give up the old way of guarding the earth's coolness and their white parasols grow hot, then even the cool ponds and groves, which flower to please the eye, will be scorched with them.

tamil: தீயினர் படர்ந்து வேந்தன் செறுவதே புரியு மாயிற்
போயினம் படர்ந்து வாழும் புகலிட மின்மை யாலே
வேயினம் படர்ந்த சாரல் வேங்கையை வெருவிப் புல்வாய்
மாயினம் படர்ந்த தெல்லாம் வையகம் படரு மன்றே
reading: If the king bent on evil will do nothing but destroy, the people have no refuge to go to; as the deer of the bamboo slopes fear the tiger, so the whole world is driven out.
nuance: The last two lines compare the people to deer driven from a tiger-haunted hill; the exact turn of line 4 is hard to fix.

tamil: மறந்தலை மயங்கி வையத் தொருவரை யொருவர் வாட்ட
விரந்தலை யுறாமை நோக்கி யின்னுயிர் போலக் காக்கும்
அறந்தலை நின்ற வேந்த ரடிநிழ லன்றி யார்க்கும்
சிறந்ததொன் றில்லை கண்டாய் திருமணி திகழும் பூணோய்
reading: When men wound one another, the only best thing for anyone is the shade at the feet of a king who stands in aram and guards the people like his own sweet life, watching that they not come to begging.

tamil: ஒருமையாற் றுன்ப மெய்து மொருவனை யும்மை யாலே
திருமையான் முயங்குஞ் செல்வச் செருக்கொடு திளைப்ப நோக்கி
இருமையு மொருமை யாலே யியற்றலி னிறைவன் போலப்
பெருமையை யுடைய தெய்வம் பிறிதினி யில்லை யன்றே
reading: The counsellor says that, as the king orders a man's lot for both worlds in one act, there is no god so great as he, and calls him god-like on that ground; how the man's suffering and wealth are meant is not clear.
nuance: The word உம்மை (a former birth) is in line 1, so the verse seems to set a king's power beside the working out of earlier deeds, but the grammar of lines 1-2 allows more than one construction.

tamil: கண்ணெனப் படுவ மூன்று காவலன் கல்வி காமர்
விண்ணினைச் சுழல வோடும் வெய்யவ னென்னும் பேரார்
எண்ணினுட் டலைக்கண் வைத்த கண்ணஃ தில்லை யாயின்
மண்ணினுக் கிருளை நீக்கும் வகைபிறி தில்லை மன்னா
reading: The counsellor names three eyes, the king, learning and the sun that circles the sky, and says that without the one set first among them nothing else could drive the darkness from the earth.
nuance: Which eye is meant by the one 'set at the head' (line 3) is not stated; the speaker's praise of the king in the preceding verses suggests the king, but it may also be learning.

tamil: குடிமிசை வெய்ய கோலுங் கூற்றமும் பிணியு நீர்சூழ்
படிமிசை யில்லை யாயின் வானுளயார் பயிறு மென்பார்
முடிமிசைத் திவள வேந்தர் முறைமுறை பணிய விம்மி
அடைமிசை நரலுஞ் செம்பொ னதிர்கழ லரச ரேறே
reading: The counsellor asks what the dwellers of the sky would say if the harsh rod, death and disease did not lie upon the people of the earth, and addresses the king as the lord of kings whom rulers bow to in turn.
nuance: The question in lines 1-2 is cut short and the sense of பயிறும் (practise, serve) is not fixed, so the point of the question is unclear.

tamil: தண்சுடர் கடவுள் போலத் தாரகைக் குழாங்க டாமே
விண்சுடர் விளக்க மாக விளங்கல வேந்தர் போல
மண்சுடர் வரைப்பின் மிக்க மக்களு மில்லை கண்டாய்
கண்சுடர் கனலச் சீறுங் கமழ்கடாக் களிற்று வேந்தே
reading: Not even the stars, shining like the cool moon in the sky, outshine men as kings do; no people in the world's bright round are greater than kings, says the counsellor to the angry elephant of a king.

tamil: அருந்தவ மரைச பார மிரண்டுமே யரிய தம்மை
வருந்தியு முயிரை யோம்பி மனத்தினை வணக்கல் வேண்டும்
திருந்திய விரண்டுந் தத்தஞ் செய்கையிர் றிரியு மாயிற்
பெருந்துயர் விளைக்கு மன்றே பிறங்குதார் நிறங்கொள் வேலோய்
reading: The two burdens of a king, hard austerity and the weight of rule, are each hard to bear and must be borne by hardship to himself, guarding life and bowing the mind; if either strays from its own work it brings great sorrow.

tamil: அந்தரந் திரியுஞ் செய்கை யமரர்தம் மரசு வேண்டி
இந்திர வுலகங் காணு நெறியவை யாவை யென்னின்
மந்திரம் வழாத வாய்மை மாதவம் முயற லன்றேல்
தந்திரந் தழுவிச் செங்கோ றளர்விலன் றரித்த லென்றான்
reading: Asked what ways lead to the rule of the gods and the sight of Indra's world, the counsellor says that the true word that never fails the mantra and great austerity are the ways, or else a king holding the sceptre in policy without slackening.
nuance: Two roads to the same world are put together: the ascetic's and the king's. The verse gives no word of grace; both depend on the doer's effort.

tamil: மரந்தலை யிணங்கி வான்றோய் மணிவளர் வயிரக் குன்றம்
உரந்தனக் குயர வேந்தி யுய்த்திடு மொருவற் கேனும்
அருந்தவ மரசை பார மவைபொறை யரிது கண்டாய்
இரந்தவர்க் கீட்டப் பட்ட விருநிதிக் கிழவ வென்றான்
reading: Even a man who could lift a diamond hill on his strength to carry it far would find the two burdens, austerity and rule, hard to bear, the counsellor tells the lord of the great treasures given to beggars.

tamil: உரிதினி னொருவன் செய்த வூழ்வினை யுதயஞ் செய்து
விரிதலி னதன துண்மை விளங்கினாற் போல வேந்தர்
கருதிய கருமச் சூழ்ச்சிப் பயத்தினாற் கருதும் வண்ணம்
எரிதவழ்ந் திலங்கும் வேலோய் என்ணுவ தென்ண மென்றான்
reading: The counsellor says that, as a deed done by a man in an earlier birth rises into fruit and shows that it was real, the fruit of the counsel kings take comes out as they intend, and asks the king to say what he is thinking.
nuance: Karma is used as a comparison for counsel, not argued; the speaker treats it as known.
event: The counsellor asks the king to tell the plan he has in mind.

tamil: பஞ்சிநன் றூட்டப் பட்ட மாதுளம் பருவ வித்து
மஞ்சிநின் றகன்ற சாகை மலரிடை வடிவு காட்டும்
அஞ்சிநின் றனலும் வேலோய் சூழ்ச்சியு மன்ன தேயால்
வெஞ்சொலொன் றுரைக்க மாட்டா விடுசுடர் விளங்கு பூணோய்
reading: Counsel, says the speaker, is like a pomegranate seed fed with cotton, whose form shows again in the blossom of its branch; he adds that he cannot say one harsh word.
nuance: The comparison is clear in outline, but how the seed's form returning in the flower fits counsel, and who is the subject of line 4, is not certain.

tamil: கொற்றவேன் மன்னர்க் கோதுங் குணமெலாங் குழுமி வந்து
முற்றுநின் றுருவு கொண்ட மூர்த்திநின் முன்னர் யாங்கள்
இற்றென வுரைக்கு நீதி யோதுநூ லெல்லை காணக்
கற்றவர் முன்னை யேனோர் கதையொத்துக் காட்டு மன்றே
reading: The counsellor says that all the virtues told of kings gather and take form in the king before him, so whatever the counsellors say of the ways of policy will seem to men who have learned the books to their end like an old tale.

tamil: தேன்மகிழ் தெரிய லாய்நின் றிருக்குலந் தெளிப்ப வந்த
பான்மகிழ்ந் தனைய தீஞ்சொற் பவழவாய்ப் பரவை யல்கும்
வான்மகிழ் மணங்கொண் மேனி யணங்கினுக் குரிய கோனை
யான்மகிழ் துணர்த்தக் கேட்பி னிடைசிறி தருளு கென்றான்
reading: The counsellor asks the king, if he will hear what he tells gladly of the lord fit for the maiden, to grant a little time.
nuance: Lines 1-3 name a maiden of sweet speech and coral lips and a lord fit for her; who is meant is not stated until later verses, and the reading of the clause is therefore open.
event: The counsellor asks for a little time to speak about the lord fit for the maiden.

reading: The counsellor begins to describe the northern hill, adorned for festival, where the Vidyadharas live, and says it is like a heaven in which the gods are never gone.
nuance: The speaker calls the hill the northern mountain (வடமலை); verse 130 places the city on the southern ridge.

reading: The counsellor says this realm is like the sky-world to the people of earth but hard for those without merit to enter, full of wishing-tree groves, and rich in heaven's pleasures.
The groves of the realm bear fruit in every season, wealth of every kind is gathered in it, and all troops of gods can enjoy all the senses there day and night.
Lotuses with golden petals bloom in its ponds, golden garlands open in its groves, golden pollen covers its jewelled ground, and golden dust shines in the air.
The groves are wishing-trees, the lovers' places are sandal bowers and the perfumes are musk and civet; the counsellor asks whether anything else could be called heavens.
No hall there lacks jewels, its golden streams are past counting, and its gem hills cannot be numbered; the counsellor asks who would not be bound if he got them.
Above it, the counsellor says, sixty great cities touch the sun's bright disk, and among the cities that cannot be left one shines like a crest-jewel under spreading moonlight.
nuance: சூளாமணி, the crest-jewel, is the name of the whole work; here the word is a comparison for one city.

reading: None of the mansions of that golden world is built of wood or clay, and a golden city called Ratna-pallavam surpasses the city of the old gods.
nuance: The initial of line 4 is garbled, and the identity of the city named (and its relation to the city of verse 130) is not clear.

reading: Women with bangled hands play with their men, desire sprouts endlessly in them, and the city seems a gods' world come down in joy, loud with its noise.

title: மந்திரசாலைச் சருக்கம் 287-310 (3/8)
theme: The sarukkam's council scene continues. The minister Sachchutan first shows the Vidyadhara king the pleasure-city of Asvagriva, then names Asvagriva's parents, brothers and counsellors, his strength, the tribute he took and gave up, and urges that the girl be given to him; Bhavachutan then rises to speak and begins to name a fault.
source_issues: 299 has three lines (the edition's own count); one line is probably lost.
300 line 4 நடையவன் is hard to construe; reading is held loosely.
The speaker of 287 to 306 is named only at 307 (சச்சுதன்); the addressee is fixed from 277 in the previous chapter, where the speaker offers to tell the king of the girl's suitor.

cast.role: the Vidyadhara king's minister who speaks 277 to 306 in favour of giving the girl to Asvagriva
the second minister, who answers Sachchutan from 307
the Vidyadhara king, father of the girl, to whom both ministers speak
the discus-lord, son of Mayurakandan and Nilanganai, suitor for the girl
the Vidyadhara clans who fear Asvagriva
the kings who pay Asvagriva tribute
women who carry love-messages through the garland street
the lovers in the grove
the astrologers who set down the girl's horoscope

reading: Young women, creeper-slender to men and praised for their small anklet-feet, have a custom of touching those feet to the flower-garlanded hair of their lovers, which tells of the lovers' quarrel.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are hard to construe: தோய வைத்து ஊடல் உணர்த்தும் தொழில் may mean the woman sets her foot in the man's hair to show or to end her sulk. The reading follows the nearer sense and is held loosely.

reading: The broad chests of strong-armed men, smeared with red sandal, are pressed by the breasts of dark-eyed women, and the bees caught in the crushed paste cling and cry out.
nuance: முடவண் டிலைத்தடத் தேங்கும் இரக்கம் (line 3-4) is obscure; முடவண்டு could be a bee with a crushed wing, and the pity it draws is read here as a figure for the crushed paste.

reading: Women of full breasts, wearied, taste with their lovers the ripe fruits of love's joy, and many lift a curved brow in mock anger as desire mingles within them.
nuance: The ripe fruits (இன்பக் கனிகள்) are the pleasure itself, and the frowning brow is the sulk of lovers' play, not a real quarrel.

reading: Many men have drunk the nectar of coral lips and cannot match the women's appetite, so they tire, and the dark long-eyed women's languor is great.
nuance: The verse says men tire because they are not equal to the women (ஒவ்வாது இளைப்பர்), which turns the usual picture of the weary woman about.

reading: Waists seem to ache and droop, bees wander eating the fresh scent of buds in the women's wreathed hair, and a breeze moves through.
A gem-dark bee, dyed by the red sandal of the women's breasts, sees its growing mate in the cloud-high grove and, unafraid, hides nearby.
nuance: The last two lines are compressed: அஞ்சா ஒளிக்கும் அயலது அதுவே is taken as the bee hiding unafraid beside its mate, a pairing that echoes the lovers.

reading: On beds of soft leaves in the grove, strings of gems slipped from the women's clothing, sandal paste and garlands lie in a heap over which swarms of bees press.
event: Lovers leave their gems, paste and garlands scattered over the leaf beds of the grove, and bees swarm over them.

reading: Go-between women with love-letters and wishing-tree garlands in jewelled caskets roam the garland street, and the speaker bids the king see how many there are.
nuance: கண்டாய் (line 4) is the speaker's own pointing-out: the sight is offered to the king as proof of the city's life.
event: Go-between women carry love-letters and garlands through the garland street.

reading: Garlands snap and golden vessels ring out as anklet-wearing men churn the sea of desire among the women; their doings are marked as wicked.
nuance: தீமைத் தொழிலவை தேர்ந்துள வன்றே (line 4) can be read as an aside that these doings are faulty, or as the poet's tag for such deeds being ready to hand; the sense is not fixed, and no claim is built on it.

tamil: பொன்னகர் தன்னை யாள்வான் புரந்தர னணைய மாண்பின்
மன்னவன் மயூர கண்டன் மற்றவன் தேவி மாருள்
மின்னவிர் மருங்கு னீலாங் கனையென விளங்கி நின்றா
ளன்னவள் புதல்வன் கண்டா யச்சுவக் கிரீவ னென்பான்
reading: The speaker names Asvagriva's line: his father Mayurakandan, a king as majestic as Indra over the golden city, and his mother Nilanganai, a chief queen who shines among the wives.
nuance: This opens the minister's turn from the city to its lord; the earlier verses of the sarukkam give no speaker name, and the speaker is Sachchutan only from 307.

tamil: அதிர்கழ லலங்கல் வேலோ யச்சுவக் கிரீவ னென்னும்
பொதியவிழ் பொலங்கொள் பைந்தார்ப் புரவலன் றிகிரி யெய்தி
மதிதவழ் குன்ற மெல்லாம் வணக்கிய பின்றை மண்ணும்
கொதிதவழ் வேலி னான்றன் குறிப்பொடு கூடிற் றன்றே
reading: Asvagriva, lord of the garlanded spear, took up the discus, bowed the mountains that moon-skim, and the earth fell in with his will.
