event: Asvagriva wins the discus and brings the hill-kings, and then the land, under his will.

tamil: சுற்றமாண் புடைமை யாலுஞ் சூழ்கதிர்த் திகிரி யாளுங்
கொற்றமாங் குடைமை யாலுங் குலத்தது பெருமை யாலுங்
சுற்றமாண் விஞ்சை யாலுங் கருதிய முடித்த லாலும்
வெற்றிவே லவனோ டொப்பார் வேந்தர்மற் றில்லை வேந்தே
reading: No king is his equal in strength of kin, in the discus he rules by, in the parasol of victory, in lineage, in learned vidya and in finishing what he plans.

tamil: தம்பியர் நீலத் தேரோன் றயங்குதார் நீல கண்டன்
வம்புயர் மகரப் பேழ்வாய் வயிரமா கண்டன் வண்டும்
தும்பியுந் துவைக்குந் தொங்கற் சுகண்டனென் றிவர்கள் கண்டாய்
reading: The speaker names Asvagriva's three younger brothers: Nilakandan, Vairamakandan and Sukandan.
nuance: The edition gives this verse three lines; a fourth is lost or was never cut.

tamil: படையின தமைதி கூழின் பகுதியென் றிவற்றின் பன்மாண்
புடையவ ரவனொ டொப்பா ரொருவர்மற் றில்லை வேந்தே
விடயமொன் றின்றி வென்ற விடுசுடை ராழி யாளும்
நடையவ னுவப்பின் ஞாலம் பிறருழை நடப்ப தென்றான்
reading: In the army, its calm order and the share of food, and in other manifold things, none equals him; the discus he rules by is held without a country to answer to, and the speaker says that if he is pleased the world would pass to others.
nuance: The army and the food are two of the limbs the Kural counts (381). நடையவன் உவப்பின் ஞாலம் பிறருழை நடப்ப தென்றான் (line 4) is hard to place and may mean that the world will go over to others' side if he is pleased.

tamil: ஆணைநூ லமைச்ச னாவா னரிமஞ்சு வவன தற்றல்
கோணை நூற் பவரைத் தன்சொற் குறிப்பின்மே னிறுத்த வல்லான்
பேணுநூ னிமித்தம் வல்லான் சதவிந்து பெரிய நீரான்
reading: Arimanju is his minister of the law-treatise, able to bring learned men round to his word; Satavindu, great-natured, is skilled in the omen-books; no learned man sees his equal.
nuance: The minister's mastery is told wholly in books (ஆணைநூல், நூல், நிமித்தம்), with no word for native wit.

tamil: தன்னலாற் றெய்வம் பேணார் சார்ந்தவர் தானுஞ் சார்ந்தார்க்
கென்னலா லிவருக் குற்றா ரில்லையென் றிரங்கு நீரான்
பொன்னெலா நெதிய மாரப் பொழிந்திடு கின்ற பூமி
மன்னெலா மவனை யன்றி வணங்குவ தில்லை மன்னா
reading: A man of pity says that those who lean on him honour no god but him and have no kin but him; the earth rains wealth for him, and all kings bow to none other.
nuance: The subject of lines 1 and 2 is unclear: it could be Satavindu of 301 or Asvagriva himself, and தன்னலால் தெய்வம் பேணார் (line 1) may mean they honour no god other than him.

tamil: குளிருவா ளுழுவை யன்னான் குமாரகா லத்து முன்னே
களிருநூ றெடுக்க லாகக் கற்றிரள் கடகக் கையால்
ஒளிறுவா ளுழவ னேந்தி யுருட்டிவட் டாட வன்றே
வெளிறிலாக் கேள்வி யானை விஞ்சைய ரஞ்சி யிட்டார்
reading: In his youth the sword-bearer lifted and rolled like a toy a heap of rock that two hundred elephants might have raised, so that the faultless-learned Vidyadharas took fright.
nuance: The subject is named only by the title of the sword-bearer, குமாரகாலம், his youth; the verse is read as about Asvagriva.
event: The young Asvagriva lifts and rolls a mass of rock that two hundred elephants could raise, and the Vidyadharas fear him.

tamil: முற்றவ முடைமை யாலே மூரிநீ ருலக மெல்லாம்
மற்றவ னேவல் கேளா மன்னவ ரில்லை மன்னா
செற்றவ னலித லஞ்சித் திறைகொடுத் தறிவித் தன்றே
நற்றவ நங்கை தோன்றா முன்னநா மாண்ட தெல்லம்
reading: Because of his full austerity no king of the sea-girt earth fails to heed his command; fearing his anger they paid tribute and sent word, and all that was ours was lost before the girl of good austerity appeared.
nuance: நாம் மாண்டது எல்லாம் (line 4) may mean everything we lost, or all that passed before her birth; the sense is not fixed. The claim in line 1 is a courtier's, put to win the king, and the work does not here answer it.
event: The kings, fearing Asvagriva's anger, pay tribute and send word to him.

tamil: ஈங்குநங் குலக்கொம் பொப்பாள் பிறந்தபி னினிய னாகித்
தேங்கம ழலங்கல் வேலோன் றிறைகொள லொழிந்து செல்லு
மாங்கவன் றிறங்க ளெல்லா மறிதியா லாணை வேந்தே
தீங்கியா னுணர்த்திற் றுண்டோ திருவடி தெளிக வென்றான்
reading: Since the girl, the creeper of the speaker's own family, was born, Asvagriva has grown kind and stopped taking tribute, and the speaker asks the king to say whether he has told anything untrue.
nuance: The speaker's own reckoning is that the girl's birth is why Asvagriva softened; the verse does not say whether the girl's beauty or her line is the cause.
event: After the girl's birth Asvagriva gives up taking tribute from the Vidyadharas.

tamil: மற்றவற் குரிய ணங்கை யென்பதன் மனத்தி னோடு
முற்றுவந் துளது சால வுறுதியு முடைய தொக்கும்
வெற்றிவேல் விஞ்சை யாரு மஞ்சுவர் மின்செய் பைம்பூண்
கொற்றவ குறிப்புண் டாயிற் கொடுப்பது குணங்கொ லென்றான்
reading: The speaker says the girl is fit for Asvagriva, that his mind is set and firm, that the Vidyadharas fear him, and asks whether, if the king is willing, giving her would not be good.
nuance: Bhavachutan answers in 308 to 310, but the argument is not finished in this chapter, so the claim is left as reported, not refuted.
event: The minister urges the Vidyadhara king to give his daughter to Asvagriva.

tamil: சுடர்மணி மருங்குற் பைங்கட் சுளிமுகக் களிதல் யானை
யடர்மணிக் கதிரும் பைம்பொன் மாலையு மணிந்த சென்னித்
தொடர்மணிப் பூணி னாற்குச் சச்சுதன் சொல்லக் கேட்டே
படர்மணிப் படலை மாலைப் பவச்சுதன் பகர லுற்றான்
reading: When Sachchutan, whom the king of the golden-mounted elephant honours, has spoken, Bhavachutan rises to speak.
nuance: This verse names the two ministers, and so fixes that the speaker of 277 to 306 was Sachchutan.
event: Bhavachutan takes up the debate after Sachchutan has spoken.

reading: Bhavachutan says that Sachchutan, learned and quick to judge, wise in sifting and strong of tongue, says nothing that is not true, and that nothing he has said is excess.
nuance: He first grants his colleague's learning and truthfulness, and turns in 309.

reading: Bhavachutan says he too saw Asvagriva's worth, but he saw one fault in this proud warrior, and he will not join in without speaking it out.
nuance: The fault itself is named only after this chapter. ஒட்டினும் ஒட்டேன் (line 4) is read as refusing to join the colleague's view while holding back this point.
event: Bhavachutan declares that he has found a fault in Asvagriva and will state it.

reading: When the lady of the wreath was born, those who know the excellence of the sky's planets, faultless in their craft, laid the birth-horoscope leaf in the place of the giving-planet.
nuance: தானக் கோளிற் சாதக வோலை தலைவைத்தார் (line 4) is read as placing the leaf under the planet of giving; the horoscope's content is not told here.
event: On the day the girl is born, astrologers draw up her birth horoscope.

title: மந்திரசாலைச் சருக்கம் 311-334 (4/8)
theme: In the council hall the counsellors name the princes who might win the maiden, and the sarukkam closes on Pavachchuthan's judgment, the gifts of Suthasagaran and a warning about the danger of the match.
source_issues: Verses 311-317: the Tamil gives no clear speaker and the verses are written in compressed grammar; the speaker is taken as a counsellor and every verse is flagged uncertain.
Verse 320 line 3 repaired; verse 333 line 2 repaired (stray space before a dead consonant).
Verse 329 ends with an exclamation mark that the edition added.

cast.role: the counsellors who name the suitors; the speaker of most verses is read as one of them
the king who names his heir to the city
a learned counsellor whose word settles the choice
the man who brings the gifts to the chosen prince
those seated in the council

reading: The speaker says the woman who takes the queen's crown beside the lord of the flowered shore is like Lakshmi herself, praised by all the others sent to wear the title.
nuance: The grammar of lines 1-3 is compressed and the queen meant is not named; the verse is read as praise of a chief queen at a court.

reading: The speaker says the son who came as the good child of our lord and, by his lord's order, became the young king, is praised by the world as a lord of the just sceptre who enjoys its pleasure.
nuance: Who the young king is cannot be fixed from these lines; the 'just sceptre' praise is the speaker's.

reading: The speaker says that a palm-leaf horoscope was written for the maiden, and that, now she has reached the age of desire, the prince who will be her helper stands near.
nuance: The leaf is the first sign in the chapter that her match is fixed by a written fate and not by choice; whether the leaf names a man is not stated.
event: A horoscope leaf written for the maiden is recalled, and the one who is to be her partner is said to be at hand.

reading: The speaker says that, by the saying that the aeon's time has run out for Achuvakandan the lord of the sea-girt earth, the maiden with the flowery eyes will not be found for any other.
nuance: ஊழிக் காலம் ஓடின can be read as a foretelling of the king's end; it returns at 333 where the words said of him are matched with old saying. The sense is held open.

reading: The speaker names the king's beloved Sittirai as the maiden of golden fame, who holds the queen's crown with the grace of her gentle beauty.
nuance: 'Sittirai' is read as a woman's name; the line is compressed.

reading: The speaker says that among the five hundred sons of the king, Ratnakandan stands before them and is the young king of all the others, bright as a shining spear.
nuance: The last line is tangled; the praise of Ratnakandan is the sure part.
event: Ratnakandan is named the chief among five hundred princes.

reading: The king declares that this one is who he will be to him and rules this city, and so he makes known to the whole city who the heir is.
event: The king announces the heir to the whole city.

reading: A speaker addressing the chief of the great hill asks that the lady be given to the one among the youths with sharp spears who is truly worthy of her.
nuance: Verses 318-329 are a list of names and lands: the speaker is read as a counsellor, but the Tamil gives no word for his office.
event: The speaker begins to name the princes and asks that the maiden be given to the worthy one.

tamil: கேடிலிம் மலையின் மேலாற் கின்னர கீத மாளும்
தோடிலங் குருவத் தொங்கற் சுடர்முடி யரசன் செம்மல்
பாடல்வண் டிமிரும் பைந்தார்ப் பவனஞ்ச னென்ப பாரித்
தாடலம் புரவி வல்ல அரசிளங் குமர னென்றான்
reading: The counsellor names Pavananjan, son of the king on the Kinnara hill and a master of horses, as a young prince for her to consider.
event: A prince of the hill, Pavananjan, is put forward.

tamil: அளந்தறி வரிய செய்கை யமிழ்தமா பதியை யாளும்
வளந்தரு வயிரப் பைம்பூண் மன்னவன் சிறுவன் வண்டார்
விளங்கொளி யுருவத் திண்டோள் வேகமா ரதனை யன்றே
இளங்களி யுழுவை யாக விருநிலம் புகழ்வ தென்றான்
reading: The counsellor puts forward the son of the king of Amirthamapati, Vegaman of firm shoulders, whom the whole earth praises as a young lion.
event: Vegaman is put forward.

tamil: வேழத்தாற் பொலிந்த சோலை மேகமா புரம தாளும்
ஆழித்தே ரரவத் தானை யரசர்கோன் புதல்வ னந்தார்ப்
பாழித்தோ ளுருவச் செங்கட் பதுமத்தேர்ப் பெயரி னானை
ஊழித்தீ யென்று வேந்த ருட்குவ துருவத் தாரோய்
reading: The counsellor names the son of the king of Megamapuram, Pathumatheran, whom kings fear as the fire of the aeon.
event: Pathumatheran is put forward.

tamil: உலங்கெழு வயிரத் திண்டோ ளொளிமுடி யரசன் செம்மல்
அலங்கலம் புரவித் தானை யருங்கலத் தேரின் பேரன்
குலங்கெழு குரிசில் கண்டாய் கொண்டல்வா னுருமோ டொப்பான்
reading: The counsellor names the grandson of the king of Rathinapuram, a noble youth who is like thunder under cloud.
event: A grandson of the king of Rathinapuram is put forward.

tamil: நங்கண்மால் வரையின் மேலோன் நன்னகர் கீத மென்னும்
திங்கண்மால் புரிசை வேலிச் செழுநக ரரசன் செம்மல்
அங்கண்மா ஞால மாளு மரிகண்ட னவனை விண்மேல்
செங்கண்மான் முனியு மேனுஞ் செய்வதொன் றில்லை கண்டாய்
reading: The counsellor says that Arikandan, son of the king of the city Keetham, rules a great earth, and not even the red-eyed Tirumal in anger could do him harm.
nuance: செங்கண்மான் is the epic's own epithet for its hero (verse 2, the red-eyed tall one), so the boast sits beside the story's turn.
event: Arikandan is put forward and said to be unassailable.

tamil: சேந்தெரி செம்பொன் வீதித் திரிபுர மதனை யாளும்
வாய்ந்தெரி வயிரப் பைம்பூண் மன்னவன் புதல்வன் மல்லா
டேந்துதோ ளரசர் போரே றிவனளி தாங்க னென்பன்
காய்ந்தெரி கனலின் வெய்யோன் கல்வியாற் கடலோ டொப்பான்
reading: The counsellor names the son of the king of Thiripuram, Alithangan, as a bull among warrior kings, hot as fire and deep in learning as the sea.
event: Alithangan is put forward.

tamil: செந்தளிர் புதைந்த சோலைச் சித்திர கூட மாளும்
அந்தளி ரலங்கன் மாலை யரசர்கோன் சிறுவ னந்தார்
இந்திரன் புதல்வ னன்னா னேந்தலே மாங்க தற்கிம்
மந்திர வுலகின் வாழு மன்னர்மா றில்லை மன்னா
reading: The counsellor says the son of the king of Chitrakuta is like Indra's son, so that the kings who live in this world of mantra are no match for him.
nuance: The name of the prince in line 3 is read from compressed grammar; the Indra comparison is clear.
event: Mangathan is put forward.

tamil: அருமணி யடுத்த வீதி யச்சுவ புரம தாளும்
திருமணி திகழும் பூணான் பெருமகன் சிறைவண் டென்னும்
கருமணி துதைந்த பைந்தார்க் கனகசித் திரனை யன்றே
ஒருமணி திலத மாக வுடையது நிலம தென்றான்
reading: The counsellor names Kanakachitran, son of the king of Achuvapuram, and says that the earth owns him as its one jewel for the forehead.
event: Kanakachitran is put forward.

tamil: சீரணி முழவ மோவாச் சிரீநிலை யதனை யாளும்
காரணி தடக்கை வேந்தன் கான்முளை கனபொ னார்ந்த
தேரணி யரவத் தானைச் சித்திரத் தேரின் பேரான்
தாரணி மார்ப னன்றே தரணிக்கோர் திலத மாவான்
reading: The counsellor names the grandson of the king of Sirinilai, Chitrattheran, as one who will be the single mark of beauty on the whole earth.
event: A prince of Sirinilai is put forward.

tamil: கற்றவர் புகழுங் சீர்த்திக் கனகபல் லவத்தை யாளும்
கொற்றவன் சிறுவன் கோலக் குங்குமக் குவவுத் தோளான்
செற்றவர்ச் செருக்குஞ் செய்கை செருவல்லான் சிங்க கேது
மற்றவன் பிறந்த பின்னா மண்மகள் மகிழ்ந்த தென்றான்
reading: The counsellor names Singakethu, son of the king of Kanakapallavam, who crushes the pride of his foes, and says the earth rejoiced after his birth.
event: Singakethu is put forward.

tamil: இஞ்சிசூழ் ழெரிபொன் மாடத் திந்திரன் மிசைந்த நாமச்
சஞ்சய முடைய கோமான் றாண்முளை தரணி யெல்லாம்
அஞ்சுநீ ரலங்கல் வேலா னருஞ்சய னவனை நங்கண்
மஞ்சுசூழ் மலைக்கோர் சூளா மணியெனக் கருது மன்னா!
reading: The counsellor names Arunjayan, son of Sanjayan, before whom all the earth trembles, and says he is to the hills as the crest-jewel.
event: Arunjayan, son of Sanjayan, is put forward; the roll of suitors ends.

tamil: எங்கிவர் தம்முள் யாவ ரிலங்கிரும் பவழச் செவ்வாய்க்
கோங்கிவர் குவிமென் கொங்கைக் கொம்பினுக் குரிய காளை
ஆங்கவன் றன்னை யாராய்ந் தறிந்தருள் செய்க வென்றான்
வாங்கிரும் பரவை முந்நீர் மணிகொழித் தனைய சொல்லான்
reading: A speaker asks that the young man worthy of the maiden be sought out from among these princes, examined and told to him, in words like gems cast up by the sea.
nuance: The speaker is not named; he may be the king or the one who has just read the roll.
event: The speaker asks that the worthy prince be examined and chosen from the list.

reading: Pavachchuthan of wide learning speaks briefly to the one whose feet are served by kings' crowns, and all present agree that it is so.
nuance: What Pavachchuthan said is not given in the verse.
event: Pavachchuthan gives the judgment and the whole company agrees to it.

reading: Suthasagaran brings a flower garland, a string of pearls, a fruit-bearing creeper and sandal paste, and says something to the wrestler of the broad chest.
nuance: The words are not quoted; that these are betrothal gifts is likely but is the reader's inference.
event: Suthasagaran speaks to the chosen man and gives him garlands, pearls and sandal.

reading: The speaker tells the lord with the crested elephant that the words said about Achuvakandan, who rules the sea-girt earth, and Pavachchuthan, the strong-shouldered, are like the old words of the aeon.
nuance: ஊழியார் உரை recalls 314 (ஊழிக் காலம் ஓடின). Whether it means the elders' fate-lore or a prophecy is not fixed.

reading: The speaker says there is a little knowledge in what he reports, but that even the soft arms of the flower-garlanded girl would turn to enmity if others touched them, and so the bright-speared one should take care.
nuance: This verse ends the section on a warning that undoes the praise of the list; the line has hard compounds.

title: மந்திரசாலைச் சருக்கம் 335-358 (5/8)
theme: The council of the Vidyadhara king: a first counsellor praises a line of lords and women, then Sumantiri speaks, naming Achuvakandan, a youth firm in austerity and the sage's prophecy that he will reach heaven and then liberation, and ends by saying fate may overturn all plans.
source_issues: Verses 335-346: the identity of the speaker, of the persons named (Megavahana, Megamalini, Vichuvan, Jothimalai) and their ties to one another are not fixed by the verses; many lines are hard to construe, so most are flagged uncertain.
Verse 344 line 1 and 345 line 2: the word division makes the sense doubtful.
Verses 348-349 and 357: the argument about Achuvakandan and the maiden's hand is not clear from the Tamil alone.

cast.role: the first counsellor of the Vidyadhara king, who speaks in 335-346 (unnamed, identity uncertain)
the fourth of the Vidyadhara king's four counsellors, who speaks from 348
king of the Vidyadharas of the southern ridge
the youth, son of Jayasenan of Bhavagiri, firm in austerity
king of Bhavagiri, the youth's father
the avadhi-knowing sage at Chitrakuta

reading: The speaker begins by saying that, among the crowned kings, one has no one to turn aside his rod, and that he will tell the king a little of what now presses on them.
nuance: Who 'he' is in lines 1-2 is not fixed by the verse; the sense is left open.
event: The first counsellor opens his speech to the king.

reading: The speaker names a lord of the golden city of the ridge, Megavahana, who rules it in comfort with his proud rutting elephants and bright spear.
nuance: The ridge city is the Vidyadhara realm of the sarukkam before; the verse names the lord and his elephants only.

reading: A woman with curling hair like a peacock's tail, hummed over by bees, is named Megamalini.
nuance: Her tie to Megavahana is not stated in the verse; a daughter is the likely sense.

reading: A man named Vichuvan, of old renown, is said to have come to worship her goddess and to rule happily, even commanding Death.
nuance: The verse says he 'came to worship her god' (தெய்வம் வழிபட மேவி வந்தனன்) without saying where; the last line's claim that he commands Death is boast-like praise.
event: Vichuvan comes to worship.

reading: The speaker says that one born to rule the sky-world and be a door of rescue for earthly beings has appeared, and the world grows once its griefs have gone.
nuance: The person praised is not named; the lines are hard to construe.

reading: The same lord, having ruled the sky-world by a boon, came here, gave long grace, and then became a light bright as the moon and fit for the world above.
event: He gives grace and then takes his place above.

reading: The speaker says that, with the thought of ending others' darkness through himself, he is such a one that no other would think ill of him.
If the girl's lover comes to the chest of the garland-wearer, then evening, moon and daylight all seem to meet in one.
nuance: The lines are in the style of lovers' praise; the exact comparison is hard to fix.

reading: The sister of the lord is praised as a wishing-tree branch with fragrant hair and carp-long eyes.
A woman wearing bright jewels, whose hair is hummed over by kinnara bees, is named Jothimalai.
A lord whose name joins the sun's is set beside a long-eyed woman whose breast is likened to the whole earth.
nuance: Lines 2-4 are hard to construe; the lord's name is not spelled out.

reading: The speaker ends by asking the king, if grace is in him, to weigh what he has said and act on it.
event: The first counsellor closes his advice and asks the king to act.

tamil: கொங்குவண் டலைந்த தாரான் குறிப்பறிந் திவைக ளெல்லாம்
அங்கவன் மொழிந்த பின்னை யவனையு மமைதி கூறி
நங்கைதன் றாதை தோழர் நால்வரு ணால்வ னாவான்
தொங்கலந் துணர்கொள் மார்பிற் சுமந்திரி சொல்ல லுற்றான்
reading: The poet says that the garland-wearer, having heard all this and understood the intent, spoke calming words to the first speaker, and Sumantiri, the fourth of the girl's father's four companions, began to speak.
nuance: Whose heart 'the garland-wearer' is understood to read is not quite clear from the lines.
event: The first counsellor finishes, and Sumantiri, the fourth counsellor, takes up the counsel.

tamil: அண்ணலங் களிகொள் யானை யச்சுவ கண்டன் மூத்தாற்
கெண்ணலுந் தகுவ தன்றா லிவன்பணி யகற்ற லாற்றாக்
கண்ணலங் கவரும் வேலோர்க் கீயினுங் கரும மன்றால்
பெண்ணலங் கனிந்த பேதை யிருப்பதும் பெருமை யன்றே
reading: Sumantiri says it is not right to weigh the claim of the elder Achuvakandan, whose order none can turn aside, nor to give the maiden to spear-bearers, and that she stay unwed is no honour.
nuance: The chain of reasons in lines 1-4 is hard to follow; whether he refuses or urges Achuvakandan's claim is uncertain.
event: Sumantiri begins by naming Achuvakandan and the maiden's unwed state.

tamil: தாழ்கதி ரார மார்பிற் றமனியக் குழையி னான்றன்
போழ்கதிர்க் கடவுள் போலும் புதல்வனுக் குரிமை செய்ய
தாழ்கதிர் விலங்க லாளு மரசவஃ தரிது கண்டாய்
reading: Sumantiri says that for the son, bright as the sun-god, of the golden-eared ruler of the walled city of Surendra, ruling the hill-realm by right would be a hard thing.
nuance: The ruler and the son are unnamed; it is unclear which side the verse favours.

tamil: மங்கையர் முகத்தி னீண்டு மைகடை மதர்ப்ப மாந்தி
அங்கயல் பிறழ்வ போலு மையரி யடர்த்த வாட்கண்
பங்கயச் செங்க ணான்மேற் படைத்தொழில் பயின்ற போழ்தும்
தங்கிய மனத்த னாகித் தளர்விலன் றவத்தின் மிக்கான்
reading: Though the sword-like glances of women, dark-lined and flickering like carp, strike at him as weapons, the young man keeps a steady mind and stands high in austerity.
nuance: The youth is not named until verse 353; verses 350-353 are read as describing Vijayapathiran. The weapons are the women's eyes, read as a figure.

tamil: மண்கனி முழவச் சீரு மடந்தையர் தூக்கு மற்றும்
பண்கனி பாட லாடற் பாணியும் பயின்று மேவான்
விண்கனிந் தனைய வின்ப வெள்ளமும் வெறுத்து நின்றான்
கண்கனி யுருவக் காளை கடவுளர் தகையன் கண்டாய்
reading: The youth does not take to the beat of drums, the songs and dances of women, and turns from heavenly pleasures, a handsome man like one of the gods.
nuance: The Jain frame is inferred from the later naming of the sage Asodharan; the verse itself only describes the youth's distaste.

tamil: செறிகழ லவற்குத் தாதை சித்திர கூட மென்னும்
அறிவரன் கோயி லெய்தி யணிவிழ வயர்த்த காலை
இறுதியி லவதி ஞானி யசோதர னென்னும் பேர
உறுவனை வணங்கிக் கேட்டான் மகன்றிற முலங்கொ டோ ளான்
reading: His father, in a festival at the shrine of the sage of Chitrakuta, bows to the avadhi-knower named Yasodhara and asks about his son's future.
nuance: The father is named Jayasenan only in verse 353.
event: The father goes to Asodharan at Chitrakuta and asks about his son.

tamil: பங்கயப் பழன வேலிப் பவகிரி யரசன் பைந்தார்
தங்கிய தடங்கொண் மார்பன் சயசேன னவற்குத் தேவி
செங்கய னெடுங்கட் செவ்வாய்ப் பிரீதிமதி பயந்த காளை
வெங்களி யானை வல்ல விசயபத் திரனென் பானே
reading: Sumantiri names the youth: Vijayapathiran, son of Jayasenan, king of Bhavagiri, and his queen Pritimati.

tamil: மந்திரத் தரசர் கோவே மற்றவன் வையங் காக்கும்
தந்திரந் துறந்து நோற்று மறைந்தசா சார மென்னும்
இந்திர வுலக மெய்தி யேழொடீ ரைந்து முன்னீர்
அந்தர காலந் தேவர்க் கரசனா யாண்டு வந்தான்
reading: The youth will give up the rule that protects the world, practise austerity, reach Indra's world Sasara, and rule there as lord of the gods for seventeen oceans of time.
nuance: The lines are the sage's prophecy as Sumantiri reports it; the later 'we heard' (355) shows it is reported speech.
event: The sage foretells the youth's rebirth as a god.

tamil: ஆதலா லமர போக நுகர்ந்தவ னரைசர் செல்வம்
போதுலா மலங்கன் மார்ப பொருளென மருளல் செல்லான்
தீதெலா மகல நோற்றுச் சிவகதி சேரு மென்றக்
கோதிலா முனிவன் சொன்ன வுரையிவை கூறக் கேட்டாம்
reading: So, Sumantiri says, having enjoyed divine pleasures he will not be dazzled into taking kings' wealth for substance, and will reach Sivagati by austerity that ends all evil: this was the sage's word.
nuance: Sivagati here is the Jain word for liberation; it need not mean Siva's grace.
event: Sumantiri closes his report of the sage's words.

tamil: அம்மையாற் றவங்க டாங்கி யலர்ந்தநல் லறிவி னாலும்
இம்மையா னுடம்பு நீங்கி யிகந்துபோ மியற்கை யாலும்
செம்மையாற் கடவுட் டானஞ் சேர்வதே சிந்தை யாற்கு
மெய்ம்மையாற் கருமச் சுற்றம் வேண்டுவ தில்லை வேந்தே
reading: Sumantiri says that through austerity, wide knowledge and the body's nature of leaving in this life, the thoughtful reach the place of the god, and truly have no need of kin of karma.
nuance: கருமச் சுற்றம் is read as kin bound by deed or duty; the sense turns on that phrase.

tamil: வாரணி முரச மார்ப்ப வயிரொடு வளைக ளேங்கத்
தாரவர் குழாங்க ளீண்டச் சயமர மறைது மேனும்
ஆரவி ராழி யனை யஞ்சுது மறிய லாகா
காரவி தடக்கை வேந்தே கழலவர் கரும மென்றான்
reading: Sumantiri says that even if a swayamvara were proclaimed with drums and conches and crowds, they cannot tell whether they dare face Achuvakandan, king, for that is a matter for the brave.
nuance: Lines 2-3 are hard; the swayamvara is read as a conditional.

tamil: ஒன்றுநாங் கருதிச் சூழி னூழது விளைவு தானே
கன்றிநாங் கருதிற் றின்றி மற்றோர்வா றாக நண்ணும்
என்றுநாந் துணிந்த செய்கை யிதன்றிறத் தென்ன மாட்டாய்
இன்றுநாந் துணிது மாயி னினிச்சிறி துரைப்ப னென்றான்
reading: Sumantiri says that when they plan one thing, fate decides the result, and a plan pressed hard may end otherwise, so none can say the course is certain; if they decide today he will say a little more.
nuance: The fate claim is used as a counsellor's caution, not as a reason to give up counsel; he still offers to speak further.
event: Sumantiri warns that fate may overturn their plans and offers more counsel.

title: மந்திரசாலைச் சருக்கம் 359-382 (6/8)
theme: After the council settles that the king should ask about his daughter, he withdraws through a day of palace pool-play, offerings, time-keeping and music, then walks with his guards to the astrologer's mansion, where the astrologer begins to take up the girl's matter.
source_issues: Verses 359-361: the speakers are not named; Satavindu's role and the identity of the man addressed as wearer of the shining thread are given in earlier verses not read here.
Verses 363-371, 378, 380-382: several lines are hard to construe because of the edition's compressed grammar and word division; flagged uncertain.
The king is identified as the Vidyadhara king by verse 363 (king of the hill-dwellers) and by the sarukkam's context; the verses do not name him.

cast.role: king of the Vidyadharas of the southern ridge, named in this chapter as king of the hill-dwellers (verse 363)
the king's counsellors, who give counsel in the council hall
the women who fan the king and shower him with garlands, like celestial women
the young people who bathe in the palace pools
the women who play in the palace pools and set out offerings
the court's time-keepers who read the water-clock and report the hours
the Vidyadhara guards who surround the king
the astrologer whose mansion the king visits, learned in the book of omens (not the astrologer of the dream in the earlier city)

tamil: வீழ்புரி விளங்கு நூலோய் மேலுநங் குலத்து ளார்கட்
கூழ்புரிந் துறுதி கூறு முயர்குல மலர நின்றான்
தாழ்புரி தயங்கு நுண்ணூற் சதவிந்து மொழிந்த வாற்றால்
யாழ்புரி மழலை யாள் கண் ணாவதை யறிது மென்றான்
reading: A counsellor says that, by what Satavindu said, the council will learn what is to befall the girl of the yazh-soft voice, while the king stands for the good of the high clan.
nuance: The speaker and the one addressed as wearer of the shining thread are not named in the verse; Satavindu is named but his role is left to the sarukkam's earlier verses.
event: The council opens on the question of the king's daughter.

tamil: என்றவன் மொழிந்த போழ்தி னேனையா ரினிதி னோக்கி
மின்றவழ் விளங்கு வேலோய் மெய்யினு மேவல் வேண்டும்
சென்றவன் மனையு ணீயே வினவெனச் சேனை வேந்தன்
நன்றவர் மொழிந்த வெல்லா நல்லவா நயந்து கேட்டான்
reading: The others look on kindly and tell the king the matter must be true and he should go to the man's house and ask himself, and the king listens gladly to all they say.
event: The counsellors urge the king to go and ask in person, and he agrees.

tamil: இந்திர னனைய நீரோ யினிப்பிறி தெண்ணல் வேண்டா
மந்திர நீளு மாயின் வருவன வறிய லாகா
சந்திரன் றவழ நீண்ட தமனியச் சூல நெற்றி
அந்தரந் திவளு ஞாயிற் கோயில்புக் கருளு கென்றார்
reading: The counsellors tell the Indra-like king to think of nothing else, since delay in counsel hides what is coming, and ask him to enter the palace that touches the sun.
event: The counsellors press the king to enter the palace at once.

tamil: மந்திரக் கிழவர் தம்மை மனைபுக விடுத்து மன்னன்
சுந்தரச் சுரும்புந் தேனுஞ் சூழ்கழ னிரையு மார்ப்ப
வந்தர மகளிர் போல்வார் வரன்முறை கவரி வீச
அந்தரக் கடைக ணீங்கி யகனக ரருளிப் புக்கான்
reading: The king sends his counsellors to their homes and walks into the great city's palace past the outer gates, fanned by women like celestials while bees and anklets sound.
event: The king dismisses the counsellors and enters the palace.

reading: As the king of the hill-dwellers climbs into the hall, the honey-broken, sun-bright rays shine and a ring of light stands in the hall's middle.
nuance: Lines 3-4 are compressed; the ring of light is read as a sun-bright disc on the floor.
event: The king mounts the radiant hall.

reading: Elephants with face-plates, fed cane and betel, ring their bells at their sides while swarms of bees and bangles sound.
nuance: The grammar of lines 1-2 is dense; the elephants' feeding is the likely sense.

reading: The hall of divine offerings fills with festival: humming bees, honey-dripping garlands, scented paste, offering-banners and singers.
nuance: கடவுட் டானம் is read as the place where offerings are made; the compound is not fixed.

reading: Young bathers dip in pools of blue lilies and emerald-stepped ponds, and bees fall mingled with the drops.
Waves of the lotus-pollened ponds strike the women's breasts, and the pools grow thick with washed face-paste and saffron paste.
As women with long hair bathe, they crush the lotus and ambal beds and the bright light of their moon-faces mingles with the water.
nuance: Lines 1-2 are hard to construe.

reading: Women whose kohl has washed off in the great cool pool have eyes as red as long flowers and bow before the lily pollen and honey that spray over them.
nuance: The sense of line 3 (hiding from nurses, or the flowers hiding the girls) is uncertain.

reading: On wet sand under a pavilion the women hang fans and set up spray from machines, sprinkle sandal drops and paste and scatter blue lilies on the seed-pots.
nuance: The device in line 3 is read as a spray-machine; the sprinkling and scattering are the likelier sense.

reading: Women like jewelled twigs lay out a flower offering on a gem seat carved to look like a lotus-pod, bright as crystal.
nuance: The rare compounds in lines 1-3 leave the exact offering uncertain.
event: Women set out a flower offering on a jewelled seat.

reading: Skilled time-keepers who know the books of the hours tell the king, at his feet, how many ghatikas have passed and bless him.
event: The time-keepers report the passing hours to the king and bless him.

reading: With women praising him the king enters his twin-adorned chamber, where he enjoys the nectar to the sound of fine music.
nuance: அமிர்தம் can be a drink or simply sweetness; the verse does not say which.
event: The king retires to his chamber for music and pleasure.

reading: Bright in his white-threaded body and a jasmine garland, the king walks on foot along a street strewn with fresh flowers.
event: The king walks along the flowered street.

reading: His golden anklets ring, bees and honey-drops follow his garland, and at every step his shark-shaped earrings throw lightning-like gleams.
Vidyadhara guards with oiled spears, lances, drawn swords and girded belts close round the king.
event: The Vidyadhara guards encircle the king.

reading: Women pour garlands and powder over him with folded hands as the king reaches, in his grace, the high gate of the astrologer's mansion.
event: The king reaches the astrologer's mansion.

reading: The learned man blesses the king as the clan's glory who has come, bidding him take victory, while the auspicious articles are spread.
event: The astrologer greets the king with a blessing.

reading: The king enters a gem-floored hall thick with aloe smoke and fallen honey as bees hum.
event: The king enters the hall.

reading: Seated in the hall, as the attendants read his sign and leave, the bright-eared one says the matter is the girl's affair.
nuance: Which of the two is meant by 'the bright-eared one' turns on the sarukkam's context, not on the line.
event: The attendants withdraw and the king states his errand.

reading: Bright with bracelet and garland, the astrologer thinks, then begins to speak from his flawless book what he foresees.
event: The astrologer prepares to read the omen.

reading: Looking at the gold-bright, bending-waisted girl, the astrologer says that the jewelled daughter's matter has come to be weighed.
nuance: The verse gives only the opening of his words; the content of the reading is not yet stated.
event: The astrologer takes up the king's question.

title: மந்திரசாலைச் சருக்கம் 383-406 (7/8)
theme: A teacher tells the king the woman's fortune by reciting the ancient purana: the middle world, the ages, the first lord and the wheel-king Bharata, then the lord's foretelling to Bharata of the line of great persons down to the Kesava Marici, who is the younger prince of the court.
source_issues: Verse 402 line 3: the rival's name (ஆசரவச்சுவக்கிரீவன்) is corrupt in the edition; read as Ashvagriva.
Verses 383-387: the speaker and addressee are not named, so the teacher and the king are taken from verse 386.
Verse 398 line 3 and verse 394 line 3 carry stray spaces in the word division (ஊ ழியா, தோ ன்றினாய்).

cast.role: the noble teacher who tells the king the woman's fortune and recites the purana
the king the teacher addresses; not named in these verses
the Vidyadhara king's daughter, unnamed in the verse
the first lord, who speaks to Bharata in the purana
Adinatha's son, the first wheel-king, to whom the lord speaks
Bharata's son, foretold as the first Kesava
the younger prince of Podanapura, the Kesava of the purana

reading: A woman shining like a garland spread out as moonlight, her eyes unlike any other, walks round the king in the street and reaches him, as fortune was meant to meet him.
nuance: Lines 3-4 are compressed; the verse does not name the woman, and she is taken here to be the Vidyadhara king's daughter of the opening verses.
event: The woman circles the king in the street and comes before him.

reading: A speaker says he cannot tell in words the beauty of the slender woman with golden jewels, and addresses a king whose sword gleams widely.
nuance: The speaker is not named in the verse; the teacher of verse 386 is taken as the voice, and the one addressed as a king by the sword epithet.

reading: The speaker says that what shines forth will make clear the holy word of the light who once bore the wheel of dharma, and calls the youth the rightful lord of the woman's breasts.
nuance: Who is called மைந்தன் (youth or hero) is not fixed; he may be the king's son whom the woman is meant for.

reading: Hearing the noble teacher's account of the woman's fortune, the king, whose fame has no falsehood in it, shone with the radiance of one who had seen the truth.
event: The king hears the teacher's account of the woman's fortune and is lit with joy.

reading: When the king asks how the woman's lot spreads in the holy word of the one who sent his eyes over the whole world, the teacher recites the ancient great purana to him.
event: The king asks how the woman's fortune lies in the lord's word, and the teacher answers with the old purana.

reading: The purana begins with the shape of the middle world: a continent in the great sea and a ring of ocean around it, each double the last, in numbers past counting.
nuance: The verse gives measures only as doubling; no figure is stated, so the structure is all it teaches.

reading: At the centre stands the long mountain Mandara, ringed by a fair terrace; the great jambu tree stands in the midst of the earth-disc, which hangs in the air.
The disc is told as six great mountains, seven lands and fourteen rivers, a world ringed by the sea's nets of waves.
In this disc, by the turning of ages, two lands rise and fall; of the two, the southern one is Bharata-khanda.
nuance: The turning ages are only named by ஊழி here; the doctrine of a rising and a falling half-cycle is read from line 2 and the later verses.

reading: That southern land, jewelled and with wish-giving trees and golden groves, was an enjoyment land for three ages, and in the following age the first patriarchs were born.
nuance: பிரமர் is read here as the patriarchs of the following age; the word is not glossed in the verse.
event: In the age after the three enjoyment ages, the first patriarchs are born.

reading: The patriarchs began the sun, the cool moon's ring and the other things the age lacked; so the enjoyment age ended.
nuance: Line 3 says these ones 'made' (படைத்தனர்); whether the sun and moon were newly set or newly seen is not decided by the Tamil.
event: The patriarchs appear and set up the sun, moon and other things of the new age.

reading: When the third age ended, the lord appeared as a form of light to end the many sorrows of living beings, to be praised by the seven worlds.
event: At the end of the third age the first lord is born to end beings' sorrow.

reading: The first lord's red feet drove out the dark, and the world took refuge in his grace as the eyes opened.
nuance: The verse uses the wheel's name ஆழி for the first lord's emblem; the dark is darkness of the eyes, and the eyes' opening is the gain.

reading: The lord, free of the senses' enjoyment and full of merit, opened the doors that ease the hunger of the afflicted, and set up the orders of men and their qualities.
nuance: The verse is cautious: it closes with 'they say', so the account is given as a received tradition, not as the poet's own report.
event: The first lord ends the hunger of the afflicted and establishes the orders and qualities of men.

reading: By that lord's grace a king of the sea-bound earth, with a single great umbrella, became Bharata, the king of the spear.
nuance: The verse closes with 'they say', so the sovereignty is told as received tradition.
event: By the first lord's grace Bharata becomes the sole king of the earth.

reading: Bharata, who bowed the earth with his wheel and ruled it, one day came to the first lord's feet, worshipped and praised them.
nuance: Bharata rules by a discus of war yet bows at the feet of the lord of the dharma-wheel; the verse sets the two wheels side by side without comment.
event: Bharata, ruler by the wheel, worships and praises the first lord.

reading: Bharata bowed his crowned head and asked what lay ahead; the lord answered, his voice like thunder that sheds nectar rain from a rain-heavy cloud.
event: Bharata asks the lord what is to come, and the lord answers.

reading: The lord tells him the count: twenty-four lords beginning with himself, twelve wheel-kings beginning with Bharata, and nine each of the Kesavas and their rivals.
nuance: The verse lists three classes of great persons (lord, wheel-king, Kesava with rival); the text only names them in the classes and counts, not by name.

reading: The lord says to the king that his son Marici will be born in the family of the hero of the golden anklet and be the first of the Kesavas.
nuance: The identification of Marici's line with Podanapura is not in this verse; read with 406.
event: The lord foretells that Bharata's son Marici will be born as the first of the Kesavas.

reading: Telling of that Kesava: the lord says that because of a girl of silver-hill beauty he will take the life and the discus of Ashvagriva.
nuance: Line 3's spelling of the rival's name is corrupt (ஆசரவச்சுவக்கிரீவன்); it is read as Ashvagriva.
event: The lord foretells that the Kesava will take Ashvagriva's life and discus.

reading: The lord says that the Kesava, going afterwards with his sea of an army, will become the lord of the wheel and conquer.
nuance: The verse does not name the Kesava; the vocative பரத makes the lord's address to Bharata plain, and line 4's final word is read as a closing epithet.
event: The lord foretells the Kesava's march with his army and his lordship of the discus.

reading: The lord says that beginning, end and middle are theirs, the sea-ringed world's right; the king of kings rejoiced, and the teacher closes: such is the way of the purana.
nuance: Lines 1-2 read as the lord's words; line 3 narrates Bharata's joy; line 4 is the teacher closing the story to his own king. The break between voices is uncertain.
event: Bharata rejoices at the lord's words about the sea-ringed world.

reading: So, as the purana's book tells, the bull-armed hero came down from the shining sky and was born on the earth ringed by the swelling sea.
nuance: The hero is not named; he is taken as Tivittan whose rise Marici's line foretold in verses 401-403.
event: The purana's hero descends from the sky and is born on earth.

reading: Of the two sons, born in golden Podanapura of Surama land, the younger is the youth, named Nambi, whom the teacher has been describing.
nuance: This verse ties the purana to the two princes of earlier chapters: the elder is Vijayan and the younger Tivittan, who bears the discus marks of verse 78.
event: The teacher names the younger of the king's two sons as the hero of the purana.

title: மந்திரசாலைச் சருக்கம் 407-430 (8/8)
theme: The Vidyadhara king's astrologer foretells that Tivittan will split a lion and that the king will gain both rows of the ridge by giving his daughter; the king tells his queen, the queen answers, the ministers choose Marusi as envoy, and Marusi flies to the grove outside Tivittan's city.
source_issues: Verses 407, 408, 411, 414, 416, 417, 419, 422, 424, 427, 428: several lines are hard to construe because of the edition's word division and compressed grammar; flagged uncertain.
Verses 413 to 419: the speaker is taken to be the king speaking to Vayuvegai on the strength of 412 and 420; the verses do not say so.

cast.role: king of the Vidyadharas of the southern ridge, father of the girl
the Vidyadhara king's astrologer, who foretells Tivittan's deed and the marriage
the Vidyadhara king's queen, mother of the girl
the priest whose word the king reports
the king's ministers
the learned envoy sent with the letter

reading: The speaker says that the woman is fit to come and rest on the breast of the god-like lord who guards the sea-girt earth in a human body, wearing a honeyed garland.
nuance: The grammar is clipped and the speaker is not named here; line 410 calls the whole run the astrologer's words, which is the basis for the speaker given.

reading: After the girl is given to the discus-bearer, the speaker says, one daughter goes to him and the two Vidyadhara rows of the ridge, with their wealth, come to the king; at this word the king swells with joy and becomes sovereign.
nuance: The wording of line 2 is compressed; the sense that one is given to the lord and two rows come to the king is the likely one.
event: The Vidyadhara king, told that giving his daughter wins him both rows of the ridge, is filled with joy.

reading: The speaker says that the sign taken about the garlanded one needs nothing more than this: within a month's days Tivittan will split a lion's mouth.
event: The astrologer foretells that Tivittan will tear open a lion within a month.

reading: The astrologer's words sink the radiant king in a joy beyond bearing; he does not blink for a long while and lifts his crowned head so that it blazes.
event: The Vidyadhara king receives the astrologer's word with joy.

reading: The king gives the learned astrologer a golden rain of treasure and a bright garland, speaking of Jyotimalai, so that he might rule his land with the rare wealth.
nuance: Lines 1 to 3 are hard to construe. It is not certain whether Jyotimalai is the daughter's name or a garland of light, whether the astrologer or another man receives the gift, or who rules the land.
event: The king rewards the astrologer with wealth.

reading: The king goes to Vayuvegai's golden city as the day wears on and tells her, so that she of the swan gait will know, the girl's greatness and the plan to be carried out.
event: The Vidyadhara king travels to Vayuvegai's city and tells her of the girl's greatness and the plan.

reading: The king says that a house without children is like a grove with no blossom, a pool with no young lotus, and an evening with no crescent moon.
The king says that when a first daughter is born, wives become the branches, children the flower clusters and elders the honey of the wishing-tree of the family, which then stands cool and fair.
The king says that for women, bearing children is harder to gain in this sea-girt world than elephants with trunks or gold and gems.
The king says that as a lamp in a dark place makes the cave shine, so the daughter now shines in every direction, and he calls her mother, rich in jewels, to see it.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are corrupt or lean in their word division; the lamp comparison is the likely sense.

reading: The king calls the daughter born to her, like a gem from a right-whorled conch, a pure and flowering creeper who will be the glory of the whole family that bears her.
nuance: Line 2 is unclear.

reading: The king reminds her of the saying that the childless are like trees, and says she has now gained a wealth like the red evening sky of the waxing crescent.
nuance: The king gives the saying as a common one and does not argue for it; he uses it to praise what she has gained.

reading: The king tells her that the priest, learned in lore, said that her daughter, with a look that dazzles deer, will be the lotus-goddess to the god, a nectar to him.
nuance: The priest here is reported by the king; he does not speak in the scene.
event: The priest, in the king's report, declares that the daughter is destined for Tivittan.

reading: At the king's words the queen hides her wide smile in great joy and speaks, bowing with garlanded hair.
event: The queen suppresses a smile and bows to answer the king.

reading: The queen tells the king of kings that the girl was valued through his grace, and that if kings are without grace, children have no worth among later folk.
The queen says that by the grace of the feet of the elephant-riding kings, whose crowns bear the bees of strewn flowers, the girl gained her beauty and fair hair.
nuance: Which kings the grace belongs to is not stated; the sense is that the match with a king's son is what gives the girl standing.

reading: The king, pleased at the queen's few sweet words, lies with her until his jewelled garland is crushed against her breast.
event: The king and queen lie together, pleased with each other.

reading: The next day the king calls his son and his ministers, tells them his plan and tells the tale of the learned astrologer.
nuance: The king's agent form here is pointing to the ministers; no word names him on the line, so he is marked unnamed.
event: The king summons his son and ministers and recounts the astrologer's prophecy.

reading: When the king speaks of the girl's wealth and the lord's due, the garlanded ministers, joyful, understand it and answer him.
event: The ministers, once told the plan, reply with joy.

reading: The ministers tell the king that doubt about the girl's marriage is gone and that a messenger should now be sent to Tivittan's father, the king of the burning spear.
event: The ministers advise sending an envoy to Tivittan's father.

reading: The ministers name Marusi, a learned man who can carry what he has been taught and say what is fit, as the one to send, since he can put kin and the matter in words.
When the ministers have spoken the king calls Marusi and gives him a fine letter with honour; Marusi blesses the king's feet.
nuance: The Vidyadhara king, as the passage's one king, is understood to be the giver of the letter; the verse does not name Marusi by the word at line 4.
event: The king gives Marusi a letter for Tivittan's father, and Marusi blesses him.

reading: At the king's order Marusi crosses the sky, past the roaring clouds, and reaches the edge of a grove outside the golden city of the Surumai land.
event: Marusi flies to the land of Surumai and reaches a grove beside its golden city.

reading: The poet describes the grove, Pushpakarandam, where bees murmur and drip honey and pair with fresh blossoms.

title: தூதுவிடு சருக்கம் 431-454 (1/6)
theme: Wandering through a flowering grove, a garlanded man reaches an asoka and a gem slab, where its keeper explains a priest's foretelling that a prince will come, and the king then sends four women, drawn in their ornaments and killing glances, to attend him.
source_issues: Verses 431-436: the edition's word division runs words together, and several tree names are doubtful.
Verse 444 line 3-4: the priest's name is garbled (பொன்னருவி and an unclear second name).
Verses 440-447: the speakers are not named in the verses; the keeper, the descender and the priest are inferred from the sequence.

cast.role: the garlanded man who enters the grove and reaches the slab
the keeper of the asoka and the gem slab
the learned priest whose foretelling the keeper reports
the king who sends the four women
the four goddess-like women sent to attend the guest

reading: A catalogue of grove trees in bloom: bakula and mango with honey-drinking bees, naga and punnai dropping flowers on the ground beside them.
nuance: The verse is a list in the edition's compressed word division, with its words run together; the trees are named by their usual Tamil names but several identifications are held with doubt.

reading: The grove list continues: shady sandal, champak, kurava and asoka, each described by what it spreads, its cool and its bees.
nuance: Continues the list of 431; the repeated verb endings give a litany of trees rather than a sentence.

reading: More trees of the grove are named by the look of their shoots and flowers: iluppai, madhuka, kaithai and punnai among them.
nuance: Two or three tree names here are doubtful in the edition's word division.

reading: Creepers and climbing flowers are listed: jasmine, mullai, madhavi and kokudi with buds and clusters, and a flowering pond among them.
The grove's open flowers are listed again: kongu, punnaga, ilavam and patiri, whose petals open beyond counting.
In the grove's flowers bees, koels and mynas take their pleasure, and the verse ends by saying the grove's blossoming was such as to delight those who delight in fate and mind.
nuance: The last line, which seems to say the sight pleased minds that delight in fate, is read with doubt; விதி மகிழ்பவர் is not clear from the edition's division.

reading: A garlanded man, pleased at the sight, hears birds call him to come here, and enters the bank of a pond where flowers open.
nuance: The man is named only by his garland (அலர்தாரவன்) and by the verb; the story elsewhere gives him a name this verse does not.
event: The garlanded man enters the bank of the flowering pond.

reading: The pond's bank, wet with spray, is heavy with flowers and rising bees, and the south wind comes to meet the place.
Where the water, the pearl-strewn sand, a gold-bright altar and bright fire-like flowers meet, the man sees an asoka tree.
event: The man sees an asoka tree beside a shining altar.

reading: As he reaches its shade, the keeper of it tells the flowers to scatter and bloom, and shows a gem-bright slab, saying many things in wonder at what it is.
nuance: Who is meant by the one who says 'what is this' (line 4) is not settled by the verse.
event: The keeper welcomes the man and shows him the gem slab under the asoka.

reading: The keeper tells him, wearer of the garland, that this gem-stone, made to be a shaded seat for him, is pleasing to climb, and bids him sit gladly.
nuance: The speaker is taken from the keeper of 440 and the addressee from the vocative 'wearer of the garland' (தாரோய்); the verse does not name either.
event: The keeper offers the garlanded man the gem slab as his seat.

reading: The one who came down from the shining sky says he cannot think how a tree of fire-bright flowers could cast a shade, and asks whose golden place it is in the grove-god's precinct and how he came to enter it.
nuance: Whether the descender is the garlanded man of 437 or another is held open by the edition's compression.
event: The man who has come down from the sky asks what the place is and how he came to enter.

reading: The keeper answers that the slab is not to be thought of as a god's; no one but the anklet-wearers addressed is fit for it.
nuance: The plural 'you with anklets' (கழற்றகையினீர்) shows more than one hearer; the verse does not say who they are.
event: The keeper says the slab belongs by right to those he addresses.

reading: The keeper begins to say how the slab came to be, and reports that a learned house-priest of the city's lord had once spoken of it.
nuance: The priest's name is garbled in the edition's division (பொன்னருவி and an unclear second name).
event: The keeper reports that the king's priest foretold the slab.

reading: The priest had said that a fierce, spear-carrying lord of the Vidyadhara world would come seeking a bride for the king's son and descend here this very day.
nuance: The report is relayed by the keeper and the speaker of 'என்றான்' is the priest only by the story so far.
event: The priest foretells a Vidyadhara lord's coming to seek a bride for the king's son.

reading: The priest added that the youth would destroy him, the foe of a lion-slaying man, when he came blazing in anger with his discus, so that the one he faced would tremble.
nuance: The enemy and the youth are not named; the identification with the story's hero and his foe is from the larger book, not this verse.
event: The priest foretells the youth will overcome the discus-bearing enemy.

reading: After he has killed his enemies, the youth will make this shaded slab, and when he descends is to be received, so the priest said; the keeper has stayed to wait.
nuance: The line 'நீங்கலன் இருந்தனன்' makes the keeper's waiting part of the fulfilment.
event: The keeper has waited at the slab as the priest foretold, to greet the one who descends.

reading: When the keeper has finished, the king sends four goddess-like women after the man who has eaten and sits there, to ease his journey's weariness.
nuance: Whether the guest has eaten what the keeper offered or merely rested is not clear from அருந்தனன் in line 1.
event: The king sends four women to attend the seated guest.

reading: The four women walk like swans, their gem girdles and anklets ringing, ear-ornaments glinting, and flowers slipping loose in their hair.
event: The four women walk toward the guest.

reading: As the women walk, their arm-garlands swing, their brow-bows rise in alarm and their sword-sharp eyes outdo the deer's in pride.
nuance: The brow-as-bow and eye-as-sword images are the poet's description of the women's bodies, not an event.

reading: The women's red-dyed feet and ringing anklets, their girdled hips, pearl-hung breasts and gait confuse the peacock in the hills.
nuance: The comparison is written as if nature were baffled by them; the grammar of lines 3 and 4 is read with doubt.

reading: Their peacock-tail girdles, spotted pairs of breasts and bending waists make a busy sight, and bees cry out and rise from them.
nuance: The verse is a compressed description of the women's bodies; its last line reads as the bees' lament.

reading: The power of their breasts and brows, of their lives' undoing and of every art of love is said to be marked in the killing look of their sword-like eyes.
nuance: The verse treats the eyes as the sign of the love-god's whole equipment, at which breasts and bow-brows are only instruments.

reading: Their lips tremble and their pearl-teeth smile, sweat beads their foreheads, earrings shine and their curled hair meets their brow-marks, as they shape their faces' work with a thin glance.
nuance: The verse ends the chapter on the women's approach, with the message they are sent to deliver not yet spoken.
event: The four women shape their faces' play toward the guest.

title: தூதுவிடு சருக்கம் 455-478 (2/6)
theme: In the envoy sarukkam the young women of the city plague the men with the arts of desire, then turn to serve the Vidyadhara guest, and at the king's bidding Vijayan and Tivittan ride out in procession while the women swoon on the terraces.
source_issues: Verse 474 line 1 reads as a rubric, not a line of the metre, and its words are damaged.
Verse 463 line 1 reads வளைர்ந்த for வளர்ந்த.
Verse 472 line 4 splits அம்பரசரன் across the word break.
Verse 469 line 4 shows a doubled line break in துகளில் விஞ்சையன்.
Verse 462 ends with a full stop and is the only verse of the run to do so.

cast.role: the young women of the city who plague the men and then serve the guest
the young men who suffer and speak to the women
the Vidyadhara guest, taken to be the envoy of the sarukkam
the king who bids the princes ride out
the conch-coloured elder prince
the younger prince

reading: The poet says that in the smoke of incense bees take the women's bright eyes for blue lilies and their hands for kanthal flowers and swarm at them, and the women are sorely pained.
nuance: The grammar of lines 1-2 is compressed; the women are taken as the sufferers, but the verse could also be read of the men pained at the sight.
event: Bees mistake the women's eyes and hands for flowers and the women are pained by them.

reading: The poet pairs the women's looks with things that delight: hair with bees, hands with sugar cane, sweet songs with lute strings, the nectar of the lips with the bud-like teeth.
As men in fragrant garlands bow their hearts to the women, the women's wide eyes, struck by desire, dry within and wilt, and they bow back as if before a goddess.
nuance: The pairing of bowing in line 4 is hard to place; it may be the men who bow to the women as to a goddess.
event: The men bow to the women and the women bow back, both pained by desire.

reading: The poet says the men, saying the oiled hair of the women would burn them like fire and their long dark eyes can kill, worship them and break down, begging to be spared if the women should scorch them with their breasts.
event: The men worship the women and collapse, saying their hair burns and their eyes kill.

reading: The poet says these women were reared as the living pattern of the lore of love, with trailing hair and the forms of garlanded creepers, and shown as proof of the Kama manual.
nuance: The first line names the lore and the arts of learning as a good path; line 4 makes the women its example.

tamil: கனிப வேலிவர் கடல்விளை யமிர் தெனக் கனிவார்
reading: The poet says the women, reared with swelling breasts, bloom like cool flowers for those they love, melt like fruit sweet as sea-ambrosia for them, and turn in anger like Kama's five arrows.
The poet says their sulks call for union and their unions breed sulks, so that these young women with red lips go about holding Kama's five arrows.
nuance: The play of sulk and union is the stock pairing of love poetry; here it is cast as the work of Kama's arrows.

tamil: பின்னை யாங்கவன் பிறவிக்கு முதல் கண்ட வகையே.
reading: The men, seeing the bodiless Kama only through these women, say they will somehow bear him, and cry out in wonder at what sin the Creator committed in making them, since here they have found the root of his birth.
nuance: The speaker of lines 3-4 is not named; they are read as the men of the scene, and the Creator is only exclaimed against, not argued with.

tamil: தூம லேகைகள் பொடித்தன துணை முலை யுறவே
reading: The poet says that as the fire of desire blazed within them, fine lines of hair rose from the girdle across the belly, like smoke-lines, toward the breasts.
nuance: The body is read as the women's; the 'smoke' is the line of fine hair, which the verse makes the sign of fire within.

reading: The men ask the women why their faces darken, and say that if they were gone to the forest to bear small austerities then to be angry at others would be understood, but they linger in sandal paste.
nuance: The verse is a question put to the women; its first lines are hard to construe and the sense of vanavar or ascetic guardians is read loosely.

tamil: தூம மென்புகை துழாவிவண் டிடை யிடை துவைக்கும்
reading: The men say that when they see Kama's long bow, with arrows, bent on the faces of these women, it is hard to say why they should still hold on to their sweet lives.
nuance: The bow is read as the women's brows set on their faces; the poet leaves the image unexplained.

reading: After the men's cry the women go off like creepers drawn on cloth to the Kalpaka grove, hurrying to tell Kama of their victory over the army of lovers.
event: The women leave the men in pain and go to the Kalpaka grove to report their conquest to Kama.

reading: The poet lists what the women carry: one a cloth, one a jewelled vessel, the attendants strings of gems, others garlands of cool gems in their hands.
event: Women carry cloths, jewel vessels and garlands.

reading: The poet lists what the women bear: caskets of colour, flower-garlands, perfumed powder and trays of gems, with all that was wished, and the young women go in step.
event: The young women carry colours, garlands and powders in jewelled caskets.

tamil: டுகளு மான்பிணை யனையவ ருழைச் செல வொளிர்தார்த்
reading: As the women with golden vessels of omen go to the man, followed by others, the faultless Vidyadhara in his bright garland decides that this must be heaven.
nuance: That the guest is the Vidyadhara envoy of the sarukkam's title is read from the sarukkam, not stated in the verse.
event: The women go with auspicious vessels to the Vidyadhara, who judges the place to be heaven.

reading: The Vidyadhara sits and thinks these are what those who reach heaven gain; the young women set aside their sidelong looks and little smiles and devote themselves to the guest-duty owed to the man in the room.
nuance: The women keep their looks for the lovers of verse 466 and turn them off for the guest; the verse makes hospitality a duty that cuts across the arts of desire.
event: The women put away their glances and smiles and serve the guest.

reading: The women bathe him, anoint him with sandal paste, garland him and feed him a meal of six tastes, so that he shines as one of the gods.
event: The women bathe, anoint, garland and feed the guest.

reading: Women named Tilakai, Kalyanikai, Senai and Kamalamalai, who are like moving flower creepers, attend him, and the old-famed lord of the sky is glad.
nuance: The four names are clear from the Tamil but the word ambarasaran at the end is split in the text and read as the guest.
event: Four named women attend the guest, who is pleased.

reading: At the king's bidding Vijayan, called the conch-coloured one, mounts the great trunked elephant together with Tivittan, ready for battle.
nuance: Whether the verse sends the princes to war or to a procession is not stated; the sarukkam's theme of sending an envoy points to a march out.
event: At the king's order Vijayan and Tivittan mount a war elephant.

reading: The poet says the elder brother mounts the elephant with a golden brow-band and a gem on its neck, and sits there like a white moon rising with a dark cloud above the red-gold mountain.
nuance: Line 1 reads as a headline for the verse, not as a line of the metre, and is damaged.
event: Vijayan and Tivittan mount the elephant.

reading: The poet lists the crowd that gathers: musical instruments, elephants, chariots with warriors, people, fly-whisks, white banners, kings in sweat and the women with flowing hair.
nuance: The verse is a single run of nouns with no verb; it describes the procession.

reading: Singers, bowers, those who bless with long life and dancers join the throng, and women in the mansions faint, their garlands slipping and their breast-ornaments falling.
event: The women on the mansion terraces faint as the princes pass.

reading: The women with cloud-like hair, faces like the full moon, earrings and golden ear-leaves lean out, with garlands swaying, and then are hidden in the mansion windows.
event: The women look out from the mansion windows and withdraw.

reading: The women on the upper storeys, hair clustered with bees and garlands slipping, look like dancing peacocks.

title: தூதுவிடு சருக்கம் 479-502 (3/6)
theme: The princes ride through the city while its women, shedding shame, pour out their longing, and in the grove under the Ashoka the Vidyadhara envoy Maruci rises, bows, studies the two princes and begins his address.
source_issues: Verse 479 line 3 and 480 line 1: the edition's word division is uneven and one letter looks wrong in ந்ன்றலைந்த (479 line 4); read as நின்றலைந்த.
Verses 492, 498, 501 and 502 are in compressed grammar and are read only for their general sense.

cast.role: the city's young women who love the princes
the two princes, together
the learned envoy sent with the letter

reading: The poet shows the coral-lipped women of the city on its many-storeyed terraces, their bright faces and carp-like eyes playing among clusters of lotus.
The women stand along the garlanded terraces with long spear-like eyes slanting, so that the roofs look like a lotus pool in which blue lilies have opened together.
The women with their companions shower perfumed powder, bow with bangled forearms, lose their shame and go before the princes to beg for a garland and a glance.
nuance: The word கண்ணிதம்மின் is read as a plea for the princes' garland; the verse does not say it is given.
event: The city's women scatter perfumed powder and beg the princes for their garlands.

reading: In their longing the women sing and forget the tune, dance and forget the beat, leave their hair garlands unworn, and stand shy in the shade.
event: The women sing and dance in confusion before the princes and then draw back, shy.

reading: The poet praises the women's brows like two strung bows, eyes like two carp, red lips and jewelled forehead bands, and says their beauty is not only in these.
The women gather at the long gate with lac-reddened soles and slipping girdles, so that the terraces look like a mountain where fire has scattered.
nuance: The comparison of the terraces to a fire-scattered mountain is hard in lines 3 and 4 and is read loosely as an image of their glow.
event: The women gather at the gate of the mansions, their girdles slipping.

reading: With anklets ringing, gold ear-rolls shining and others praising them, the women move about the gate and perform a dance for the princes.
event: The women dance before the princes at the gate of the mansions.

reading: Wearing garlands, scattering gold powder and sandal paste, the blue-eyed women give up their hearts and join the princes who rule the earth in a mist of infatuation.
event: The women, giving up their hearts, come to the princes.

reading: The women's shoulders grow pale, they sigh, their clothes slip and flowers fall from their hair, and they begin to languish as jasmine pollen scatters.
nuance: The verse pictures the languor of love at first sight, with no absence or parting yet; the women pine for men who have only passed.
event: The women, in love, grow pale and sigh.

reading: The troop of the princes, whose chests hold the women's eyes, bees, garlands and minds, arrives at the grove.
event: The troop of the princes reaches the grove.

reading: The women follow in heart as the kings and heroes enter the sky-high grove of flowers, and the bees, drunk on honey, rise in a swarm.
event: The princes and their heroes enter the grove, with the women's hearts following.

reading: After the elephants with golden brow-plates and white tusks are left, the bees and beetles hum at the princes as if asking whether these are the spear-bearing lovers.
nuance: Whether the princes dismount or the elephants simply stop is not clear from இழிந்த; read here as the princes alighting.
event: The princes leave their elephants and the bees gather round them.

reading: In the grove the madhavi creepers, as if with soft hands, show the princes the places among the flowers, while bees scatter pollen-water over them.
The poet says the grove's colour cannot be told: flowers rain honey, bees hum, and clouds of blossoms hide the sky.
nuance: Lines 2 to 4 are in compressed grammar and are read only for their general sense of a grove thick with bloom.

reading: As the southern breeze blows through the flowering grove the vines clasp the trees, like women with garlanded hair embracing the young men they love.
The princes pass the jasmine bowers and the madhavi arbours and reach the Ashoka tree beside the lotus bower.
event: The princes walk through the grove's bowers and reach the Ashoka tree.

reading: While the women call blessings, the princes reach the Ashoka shade and the Vidyadhara rises gladly, joins his hands and bows to them in eager love.
nuance: The verse says only the Vidyadhara; he is taken as Maruci, the envoy the king chose at 427 and who reached the grove at 429.
event: Maruci, the Vidyadhara envoy, rises and bows with joined hands to the princes under the Ashoka.

reading: At his bow a bright-faced prince in earrings and garland asks him why he bows to them, since they should be the ones to bow to elders of faultless virtue.
nuance: The verb is singular, so one prince speaks, and the verse does not say which; the id princes is used for the pair.
event: A prince asks Maruci why he has bowed to them.

reading: The Vidyadhara, come by the sky road, looks glad-eyed at one prince of milk-white radiance and one with a body like the dark sea, matching what he sees to the rules of his lore.
nuance: நூல்நெறி is read as the lore by which marks of a person are judged; the verse does not name the marks.
event: Maruci looks closely at the two princes, one fair and one dark.

reading: The Vidyadhara gazes at the spear-bearing heroes again and again, from their feet up to their garlands, his heart sunk in love like that of one who is lovesick.
nuance: The reading of காலன்கால்கள்கொண்டு கண்ணிகாறும் as 'from the feet to the garland' is uncertain; the simile of the lovesick is the poet's.
event: Maruci stares at the two princes from feet to garland.

reading: With garlands and jewels gleaming so that the eye cannot take them in, the Vidyadhara draws near the princes and, sitting on a rock beside them, begins to speak.
event: Maruci sits on a rock near the princes and begins to speak.

reading: Maruci addresses the worthy princes who came down from the golden heights, hiding the divine elephant, to humble the sea-girt earth, and says those who bow at their feet have done hard penance.
nuance: The speaker names no school; the claim is the envoy's courtesy. Its logic, that reaching the great is a fruit of earlier tapas, is the epic's own karma-thought, but the verse does not use the word for karma.

reading: Maruci praises the princes' radiance and the way it makes the world's beings feel gladly drawn to them, saying it cannot be matched, and goes on to hymn them.
nuance: Lines 1 to 3 are in compressed grammar; the sense of praise is plain but the words that carry it are not fixed.

reading: The princes, their gaze bright, say that talk is enough, that they will go to see their lord, and tell him to mount the elephant.
nuance: The word அடிகள் may name the princes' father or another lord; the verse does not say which, and the one invited to ride is read as Maruci.
event: The princes tell Maruci that they will go to see their lord and ask him to ride.

title: தூதுவிடு சருக்கம் 503-526 (4/6)
theme: Tivittan and Vijayan ride with the Vidyadhara envoy into Podanam; in the hall the envoy's letter offering a daughter to the younger prince is read, and when the king sits silent the envoy argues angrily that men of the earth cannot win what is above them, until the king answers that he cannot frame a reply and takes it all as a dream.
source_issues: Verses 503, 505, 510, 512, 513, 514, 515, 519, 522, 523, 524, 526: several lines are compressed or hard to construe; flagged uncertain.
Verse 514 line 2: the name written as the writer of the letter reads like a corrupt word; read as the Vidyadhara king who rules Rathanupura.
Verse 522 line 2: the word களபக்கு for the animal is unclear.
Verses 518 to 523: the speaker is taken to be the envoy of 517; 524 to 526 are taken to be the king, on the strength of 516 and 524 line 4.

cast.role: King Payapati of Podanam, who receives the letter
the Vidyadhara envoy carrying the letter, read as Marusi of 427 to 429
the Vidyadhara king whose letter is read
the learned counsellor who takes the letter and reads it
the younger prince, to whom the girl is offered
Tivittan's elder brother
the women of the city who welcome the princes
the gatekeepers who announce the arrivals

reading: The two princes, with the Vidyadhara beside them, ride the neck of a rutting elephant in a flood of splendour that holds every eye, and shine like gods.
nuance: Who sits where on the elephant turns on a compressed second line, so the sense is the likely one only.
event: Tivittan and Vijayan ride a rutting elephant with the Vidyadhara envoy toward Podanam.

tamil: கதிர்நகைக் கபாட வாயிற் கதலிகைக் கனக நெற்றி
மதிநக வுரிஞ்சு கோட்டு மாளிகை நிரைத்த வீதிப்
புதுநக ரிழைத்து முத்து பொலங்கலத் தொகையும் பூவும்
எதிர்நகைத் துகைத்து மாத ரெதிர்கொள நகரஞ் சேர்ந்தார்
reading: The city has been decked with gates, plantain-flags, gold-topped mansions that rub the moon, and the women meet the princes with pearls, gold vessels and flowers as they enter.
event: The princes enter the decked city while women welcome them with pearls, gold vessels and flowers.

tamil: விரைக்கதி ரலங்கற் செங்கேழ் விண்ணியங் கொருவ னோடும்
வரைக்கெதிர்ந் திலங்கு மார்பின் மன்னவ குமரச் செல்வர்
எரிக்கதி ரேற்றைக் கால மெழுநிலாப் பருவ மேக
நிரைத்தெழு மிருது மன்று நிரந்ததோர் சவிய ரானார்
reading: With the one who travels the sky, the sons of the kings, broad-chested and garlanded, take on a radiance that spreads like the bright season of the rising moon and the rows of clouds.
nuance: The comparison in the last two lines is compressed and its season-words are hard to fix.

tamil: வார்கலந் திலங்கு கொம்மை வனமுலை மகளி ரிட்ட
ஏர்கலந் தெழுந்த தூம வியன்புகை கழுமி நான
நீர்கலந் துகுத்த மாலை நிறமதுத் திவலை சிந்தக்
கார்கலந் திருண்ட போலுங் கண்ணகன் தெருவுட் சென்றார்
reading: The princes pass down the broad street where incense smoke from women's bowls and drops of honey from garlands soaked in perfume make the air as dark as a gathering cloud.
event: The princes ride down the wide street through incense smoke and dripping garlands.

tamil: தெளிர்முத்த மணலுஞ் செம்பொற் சுண்ணமுஞ் சிதர்ந்து தீந்தேன்
ஒளிர்முத்த முறுவ லார்த முழைக்கலங் கலந்து மாலைக்
குளிர்முத்த நிழற்றுங் கோயிற் பெருங்கடை குறுகச் சென்றார்
reading: Over pearl sand, gold powder, flowers and sandal strewn by bright-toothed women, they come close to the great gate of the palace, which is hung with cool pearl garlands.
event: The princes reach the palace's great gate.

tamil: மற்றவை ரடைந்த போழ்கின் வாயிலோ ருணர்த்தக் கேட்டு
கொற்றவ னருவி தூங்குங் குளிர்மணிக் குன்றம் போல
முற்றிநின் றிலங்குஞ் செம்பொன் முடிமிசை முத்த மாலைக்
கற்றைகள் தவழச் சென்றோர் கனககூ டத்தி ருந்தான்
reading: When the gatekeepers announce them, the king, like a jewelled mountain crowned with a falling stream, goes in with strands of pearl lying over his gold crown and sits in the golden hall.
nuance: The king is not named here; he is read as Payapati from 509's 'king who gave kindness to the world' and the sarukkam's earlier verses.
event: The gatekeepers announce the arrivals and the king takes his seat in the golden hall.

tamil: மன்னவ குமர ரோடும் விஞ்சையன் மகிழ்ந்து வையத்
தின்னருள் புரிந்த வேந்த னிடையறிந் தினிதி னெய்திக்
கன்னவில் தோளி னான்றன் கழலடி தொழுது நின்றான்
அன்னவர்க் கிருக்கைத் தான மரசனு மருளிச் செய்தான்
reading: The Vidyadhara, glad, enters with the princes at the right moment and bows at the king's feet, and the king graciously gives them places to sit.
event: The envoy bows to the king, who offers seats to the envoy and the princes.

tamil: வீரியக் குமர ரொடும் விஞ்சையஞ் செல்வ னோடும்
காரியக் கிழவர் சூழக் கவின்றுகண் குளிரத் தோன்றி
ஆரியன் னலர்ந்த சோதி யருங்கலப் பீட நெற்றிக்
தாரகை யணிந்து தோன்றுஞ் சந்திர சவிய னானன்
reading: The king shows himself with the brave princes, the Vidyadhara and his counsellors around him, as the moon gleams among stars on the top of the jewelled seat.
nuance: The simile of line 4 makes the king the moon; the rest of the verse is a compressed list of those who sit around him.
event: The king takes his place among princes, envoy and counsellors.

tamil: அலகையில் தானை வேந்த னம்பர சரனை நோக்கி
உலகுப சார மாற்ற முரைத்தலுக் குரிய கூறி
விலகிய கதிர வாகி விளங்கொளிக் கடகக் கையான்
மலரகங் கழுமப் போந்து மனமகிழ்ந் திருந்த போழ்தின்
reading: The king, looking at the sky-goer, speaks the courtesies that fit the occasion, and the bracelet-armed envoy sits in joy as the grove of the hall fills with his presence.
event: The king greets the envoy with courtesies and the envoy sits pleased.

tamil: விஞ்சைய னெழுந்து தங்கோன் வெள்ளிவே தண்ட நோக்கி
அஞ்சலித் தடக்கை கூப்பி யரக்கிலச் சினையின் வைத்த
எஞ்சலி லோலை காட்ட விறைமகன் குறிப்பு நோக்கி
வஞ்சமில் வயங்கு கேள்வி மதிரவன் கரத்தில் வாங்கி
reading: The envoy rises, faces his own lord's ridge, folds his hands and shows the letter laid in a lac seal; reading the prince's sign, a learned counsellor takes it from his hand.
nuance: Whether 'the lord's son' of line 3 is Tivittan, whose sign the counsellor reads, or another prince is not fixed by the verse.
event: The envoy shows the sealed letter and the counsellor Mathiravan takes it.

tamil: நிகரிகந் தழகி தாகி நெரிவடுப் படாத வேழப்
புகர்முகப் பொறிய தாய புகழ்ந்தசொல் லகத்துப் போகா
மகரவாய் மணிகட் செப்பின் மசிகலந் தெழுதப் பட்ட
பகரரும் பதங்கள் நோக்கிப் பயின்று பின் வாசிக் கின்றான்
reading: The counsellor studies the ink-written words from the jewelled casket, lines that are fair, unmatched and unbroken by creases, and then reads them aloud.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are hard to construe; the description of the leaf and the casket is the likely sense.
event: Mathiravan examines the letter's writing and begins to read it aloud.

tamil: போதனத் திறைவன் காண்க விரதநூ புரத்தை யாளும்
காதுவேன் மன்ன னோலை கழலவன் றனக்கு நாளும்
ஆதிய வடிசி லொண்கே ழஞ்சன முள்ளிட் டெல்லாம்
தீதுதீர் காப்புப் பெற்றுச் செல்கென விடுத்த தன்றே
reading: The letter of the king who rules Rathanupura addresses the lord of Podanam, and sends for the one of the warrior anklets food and ointment and the rest, free of harm, as his protection for the journey.
nuance: The name of the writer in line 2 and the sense of line 4 are doubtful; the verse is read as the opening of the letter's words.
event: The Vidyadhara king's letter, read aloud, greets the lord of Podanam and sends gifts.

tamil: வல்லக னிளைய நம்பிக் குரியளா வழங்கப் பட்டாள்
மல்லக மார்பி னன்றான் மருமக ளிவளைக் கூவி
வல்லிதிற் கொடுக்க மன்னன் வாழ்கதன் கண்ணி மாதோ
reading: The letter says that the girl is given as the younger prince's own and asks the strong-chested king to call her his daughter-in-law and take her, wishing him and his garland long life.
