nuance: The offer is in the letter's voice, and the letter is the speech of the absent Vidyadhara king; who 'gives' and who 'takes' in line 4 is not made plain.
event: The letter offers the Vidyadhara king's daughter to the younger prince.

tamil: வென்றியம் பெருமை விச்சா தரரென்பா ரெம்மின் மிக்கார்
இன்றிவன் விடுத்த திவ்வா றென்கொலோ வென்று சிந்தித்
தொன்றுமற் றுரைக்க மாட்டா திருந்தன னுரங்கொ டோ ளான்
reading: The reading done, the king, thinking that Vidyadharas are greater than his own kind, wonders what lies behind this message and sits unable to say a word.
event: The king, puzzled, sits silent after the letter is read.

tamil: தீட்டருந் திலதக் கண்ணிச் செறிகழ லரசர் கோமான்
மீட்டுரை கொடாது சால விம்மலோ டிருப்ப நோக்கி
வாட்டரும் பெருமை யெங்கோ னோலையை மதியா வாறென்
reading: Seeing the king sit sighing without a reply, the envoy, unstoppable in his anger, begins to say that he cannot see why a letter of his unquenchable lord is not honoured.
nuance: The envoy is named by the sky-goer's title; the identification with Marusi rests on 427 to 429 and on the envoy's arrival at 505 and not on a name in this verse.
event: The envoy angrily asks the silent king why he does not honour his lord's letter.

tamil: முன்னமோர் கருமம் வேண்டி மொழிபவேல் மனிதர் தம்மால்
என்னவ ரேனு மாக விகழ்ந்திடப் படுப போலாம்
அன்னதே யுலக வார்த்தை யாவதின் றறியும் வண்ணம்
மின்னவின் றிலங்கும் வேலோய் நின்னுழை விளங்கிற் றன்றே
reading: The envoy says that the world's saying is shown true in the king: when a man speaks wanting something, whoever he may be, he is slighted.

tamil: பூவிரி யுருவக் கண்ணிப் பொலங்குழை யிலங்கு சோதித்
தேவரே யெனினுந் தோறச் சில்பகல் செல்ப வாயில்
ஏவரே போல நோக்கி யிகழ்ந்துரைத் தெழுவ தன்றே
மாவிரி தானை மன்னா மனிதர தியற்கை யென்றான்
reading: He adds that even gods, once they fall and a few days pass, are looked on and scorned like anyone, and calls this the way of men.
nuance: Line 2's wording is hard, so the sense of falling and slighting is the likely one; the envoy speaks this as an accusation of the king's manner, not as a rule he lays down.

tamil: வரைமலி வயங்கு தோளாய் வியாதியான் மயங்கி னார்க்குச்
சுரைமலி யமிர்தத் தீம்பால் சுவைதெரிந் துண்ண லாமோ
விரைமலி விளங்கு பைந்தார் விஞ்சையர் செல்வந் தானும்
நுரைமலி பொள்ளல் யாக்கை மனித்தர்க்கு நுகர லாமோ
reading: The envoy asks whether a man sick with disease can taste the sweet milk-nectar, or men whose body is a frothy hollow can enjoy the wealth of the Vidyadharas.
nuance: The body-as-froth image is the one the Naladiyar uses to teach detachment; here it is used as an insult in a rank argument, and no doctrine of release is stated.

tamil: அறவிய மனத்த ரன்றி யழுங்குத லியல்பி னார்க்குப்
பிறவியை யறுக்குங் காட்சிப் பெருநிலை யெய்த லாமோ
வெறிமயங் குருவக் கண்ணி விஞ்சையர் விளங்கு தானம்
மறவியின் மயங்கி வாழும் மனித்தர்க்கு நிகழ்த்த லாமோ
reading: He asks whether those who lack a mind of dharma and are bent on wasting can reach the great state of insight that cuts birth, and whether Vidyadharas' place can be told to men living in forgetfulness.
nuance: The birth-cutting vision is used only as an analogy for what men cannot reach; the verse does not say which school's insight it means, and it is spoken by a Vidyadhara in an argument about rank.

tamil: அருங்கடி கமழுந் தாரை யழிமதக் களிற்றி னாற்றல்
மரங்கெடத் தின்று வாழுங் களபக்கு மதிக்க லாமோ
இரங்கிடு சிறுபுன் வாழ்க்கை யிந்நிலத் தவர்கட் கென்றும்
வரங்கிடந் தெய்த லாமோ மற்றெமர் பெருமை மன்னா
reading: He asks whether a young elephant that lives by eating trees can be set beside the strength of a rutting elephant, and whether men of this earth, of a pitiable small life, can win by waiting the greatness of his people.
nuance: The word in line 2 for the animal is not clear (களபக்கு); the comparison is the likely sense.

tamil: உள்ளிய மரங்கொள் சோலை மண்மிசை யுறையு மாந்தர்
ஒள்ளிய ரேனுந் தக்க துணர்பவ ரில்லை போலாம்
வெள்ளியஞ் சிலம்பி னென்கோன் விடுத்தே யேது வாக
எள்ளியோ ருரையு மீயா திருந்தனை யிறைவ வென்றான்
reading: He says that men who live on earth, even the clever, seem not to know what is fitting, and rebukes the king for not giving even a word of answer after his lord on the silver ridge sent the letter.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are compressed; the rebuke is for the king's silence.

tamil: ஆங்கவ னுரைப்பக் கேட்டே யம்பர சரனை நோக்கித்
தேங்கம ழலங்கன் மார்ப சிவந்துரை யாடல் வேண்டா
ஓங்கிய வோலை மாற்றக் குரியவா றுரைக்க மாட்டா
தீங்கியா னிருந்த தென்றா னெரிசுடர் வயிரப் பூணான்
reading: The king, hearing him, turns to the sky-goer and asks him not to speak in anger, saying that he has stayed here because he cannot say what a fitting reply to so grand a letter would be.
nuance: The speaker is not named in the verse; the diamond-ornamented man of line 4 is read as the king whose silence is the cause of 516 and 517.
event: The king asks the envoy not to be angry and says he cannot frame a fitting reply.

tamil: வெஞ்சுடர் தெறுதீ விச்சா தரரென்பார் மிக்க நீரார்
செஞ்சுடர்த் திலதக் கண்ணித் தேவரே தெரியுங் காலை
மஞ்சிடை மண்ணுள் வாழும் மக்களுக் கவர்க டம்மோ
டெஞ்சிய தொடர்ச்சி இன்ப மெய்துதற் கரிது மாதோ
reading: The king says that the Vidyadharas are fiery, great, and no less than gods when examined, so that for men who live under the clouds on the earth a bond and joy with them is hard to gain.
nuance: The king grants the premise of the envoy's pride without agreeing to the match; the work leaves the claim unanswered here.

tamil: ஈட்டிய வூன்செய் யாக்கை யெம்முழை யின்ன வாறு
வாட்டமில் வயங்கு கண்ணி மணிமுடி மன்ன னோலை
காட்டிநீ யுரைத்த வெல்லாங் கனவெனக் கருதி னல்லான்
மீட்டது மெய்ம்மை யாக வியந்துரை விரிக்க லாமோ
reading: The king says that this body made of flesh is as it is, and that he would take all that the envoy has said, showing the letter of the garlanded king, to be a dream, since he cannot rightly marvel at it and speak it out as true.
nuance: The dream is used for what is too good to be believed, though the court has just treated a dream as a true sign (106 to 112).
event: The king tells the envoy he can only take the offer as a dream.

title: தூதுவிடு சருக்கம் 527-549 (5/6)
theme: Prajapati meets the envoy's claim with the saying that earlier deeds alone decide a man's wealth; Marusi, abashed, answers the doubt that Vidyadharas and men do not marry by saying they are all men, names himself, and tells the story of Nami of Kasi, who sang to a yogi, was given the Vidyadhara lore and the silver mountain by Dharanan, and from whom the Vidyadhara king descends.
source_issues: Verses 527, 528, 529, 530, 532, 535, 537, 538, 540, 541, 545, 546, 548: word division and compressed grammar leave lines hard to construe; flagged uncertain.
Verse 538: அரசு வேண்டான் conflicts with Nami's request for wealth in 547; both readings noted in the verse.
Verses 527 to 531: the king and Marusi are not named in the verses, and who speaks is taken from 529 and 531; the earlier words that angered the king lie before this chapter.

cast.role: the king of Podanam who receives the envoy; Prajapati by tradition, unnamed in these verses
the Vidyadhara king's envoy
the prince of Kasi who sings to the yogi
the yogi in meditation and the first lord of the lineages; by tradition Adinatha, unnamed in these verses
the thousand-hooded king of the serpent lords who gives Nami his wish
the beasts and birds that bow to Nami's song

tamil: இன்னவ னின்ன நீரா னின்னவே யெய்து கென்று
முன்னவன் செய்த மொய்ம்பின் வினைகளே முயல்வ தல்லால்
பின்னவன் பிறந்து தன்னாற் பெறுதலுக் குரிய வாய
துன்னுவ தென்றுக் கான்று துணியுமோ சொல்ல வென்றான்
reading: The king says that only the strong deeds a man did in an earlier birth strive to bring each person his lot, and asks whether one born later could by his own doing gain what is not due to him.
nuance: The king's use of karma here is a way to hold the Vidyadharas' wealth out of reach of men; Marusi gives way in 529, and then argues in 531 that Vidyadharas are men, so the objection is met by another route and not by denying karma. Speaker taken from 529, which names the king's words; lines 3 and 4 are hard to construe.
event: The king answers Marusi by saying that earlier deeds alone decide what each man reaches.

tamil: மெய்ப்புடை தெரிந்து மேலை விழுத்தவம் முயன்று நோற்றார்க்
கொப்புடைத் துங்கள் சேரி யுயர்நிலைச் செல்வ மெல்லாம்
எப்படி முயறு மேனு மெங்களுக் கெய்த லாகா
தப்படி நீயு முன்னர் மொழிந்தனை யன்றே யென்றான்
reading: The king says that the high-state wealth of the Vidyadhara quarter belongs to those who understood the truth and practised higher austerity, that no effort of ours could reach it, and that Marusi had said so himself earlier.
nuance: The reference to Marusi's own earlier words points to verses before this chapter's first; they are not in this chapter, so what he said is not checked here. The word எங்களுக்கு is read as men in general.

tamil: இறைவனாங் குரைத்த சொற்கேட் டென்னைபா வம்பொ ருந்தாக்
கறையவா மொழிகள் சொன்னேன் காவலன் கருதிற் றோரேன்
பொறையினாற் பெரியன் பூபன் சிறியன்யா னென்று நாணி
அறிவினாற் பெரிய நீரா னவிந்தன கதத்த னானான்
reading: Hearing the king's words, Marusi is ashamed that he spoke unfit words without grasping the king's mind, calls the king great in forbearance and himself small, and his anger dies down.
nuance: Who it is that is angry and whose words are called unfit are not stated outright, and the sentence in lines 1 to 2 is compressed; the reading follows 527 and 528 as the king's rebuke and Marusi's yielding.
event: Marusi, abashed by the king's reply, gives up his anger.

tamil: கிளர்ந்தொளி துளும்பும் மேனிக் கேசர ரோடு மண்மேல்
வளர்ந்தொளி திவளும் பூணோர் மணவினை முயங்க லில்லென்
றளந்தறி வரிய சீரோற் கையமீ தகற்று கென்றாங்
குளர்ந்துன னுணர்வி னூக்கி யுரைக்கிய வெடுத்துக் கூறும்
reading: The doubt is stated that Vidyadharas of shining bodies and the ornamented men of the earth do not join in marriage, and that this doubt be removed for the one of unmeasured glory; Marusi, stirring his understanding, sets out to answer.
nuance: The claim is put in order to be answered, and 531 answers it by saying that Vidyadharas are men. The verse does not say who holds the doubt; the king is the likely holder, since it is he who must be won over.
event: The objection that Vidyadharas and men do not marry is raised, and Marusi begins his reply.

tamil: மஞ்சிவர் மணங்கொள் சோலை மணிவரைச் சென்னி வாழும்
விஞ்சையர் விச்சை யாலே விழுமிய ரென்ப தல்லால்
அஞ்சலில் தானை வேந்தே மனிதரே யவரும் யாதும்
வெஞ்சுடர் விளங்கு வேலோய் வேற்றுமை யின்மை கேண்மோ
reading: Marusi tells the fearless king that the Vidyadharas of the jewelled mountain are excellent only by their lore, and are otherwise just men, so that there is no difference between them and the king's people.
nuance: The verse says where the difference lies, in lore, and that lore is not a difference of birth; it does not say what makes the claim true beyond Marusi's word, and the work later has the marriage go forward.
event: Marusi answers the doubt by saying Vidyadharas are men, set apart only by their learning.

tamil: மண்ணவில் முழவின் மாநீர்ப் பவபுர முடைய மன்னன்
பண்ணவில் களிதல் யானைப் பவனவே கற்குத் தேவி
வண்ணவிற் புருவ வாட்கண் வாயுமா வேகை யென்பான்
reading: Marusi begins to name his own king's house: the lord of the drum-sounding, water-ringed city of Pavapuram, his queen and a woman of dazzling beauty whose name is given as Vayuvegai.
nuance: The word division makes it unclear which name belongs to the king, which to the queen and which to the daughter; the same name Vayuvegai is the queen's in the earlier chapters.
event: Marusi introduces the Vidyadhara king's city and royal house.

tamil: மற்றவ ளோடும் வந்தேன் மன்னன்யான் மருசி யென்பேன்
அற்றமில் கேள்வி யெந்தை யஞ்சுமா னென்னும் பேரான்
பெற்றதா யருசி மாலை பெருமக னருளினால் யான்
கற்றநூல் பல்ல வாகுங் கருமணிக் கடகக் கையான்
reading: Marusi says that he came with her, gives his name, his learned father Anjuman and his mother Arusimalai, and says that by the great lord's grace the books he learned are many.
event: Marusi names himself and his parents to the king.

tamil: அலகைசா லாதி காலத் தரசர்கள் தொடர்ச்சி யெல்லாம்
உலகநூல் பலவு மோதி யுணர்ந்தன னுரைப்பக் கேண்மோ
விலகிய கதிர வாகி விடுசுடர் வயிரக் கோலத்
திலகம்வீற் றிருந்த கண்ணித் திருமுடிச் செல்வ என்றான்
reading: Marusi says he has read in many world-books the whole succession of kings of the earliest times, and asks the crowned king to hear it.
nuance: The account that follows is his own recital of what books tell, so its traditions are reported through him.
event: Marusi announces that he will recount the descent of kings from the books he has studied.

tamil: ஆதிநா ளரசர் தங்க ளருங்குல மைந்து மாக்கி
ஓதநீ ருலகின் மிக்க வொழுக்கமுந் தொழிலுந் தோற்றித்
தீதுதீர்ந் திருந்த பெம்மான் திருவடி சாரச் சென்று
நீதி நூற் றுலகம் காத்து நிலத்திரு மலர நின்றான்
reading: Marusi says that in the first days the first lord set up the five great royal lineages, made known their conduct and occupations, then went to the feet of the faultless lord and guarded the world by the book of justice.
nuance: The verse does not name the first lord; it is taken as the same figure the earlier chapter calls the first lord, and the sentence does not make clear whether the faultless lord to whom he goes is the same person or another.
event: The first king establishes the five lineages, with their conduct and occupations, and then rules justly.

tamil: முசிநாச் சுரும்பு பாய முருகுடைத் துருக்குஞ் சோலைக்
காசிநாட் டரசன் செங்கோற் கதிர்முடிக் கச்ச னென்பான்
மாசினாற் கடலந் தானை மன்னவற் றவற்குத் தேவி
தூசினாற் றுளும்பு மல்குல் சுதஞ்சனை சுடரும் பூணாய்
reading: Marusi names Kachchan, the Kasi king of the just sceptre, whose queen is Suthanjanai of the jewelled ornaments.
event: Marusi names the king of Kasi and his queen.

tamil: வேய்ந்தக நிழற்றுங் கோதை மிளிர்மணிக் கலாப வட்டம்
போந்தகந் திகழ்ந்து மின்னுப் பூந்துகில் பொலிந்த வல்குல்
வாய்ந்தகங் கமழுங் கோதை யவள்பெற்ற வரச சிங்க
நாந்தகக் கிழவர் கோவே நமியென்பான் நலத்தின் மிக்கான்
reading: Marusi says that their son was Nami, a prince of the Nandaka-sword line, excelling in goodness.
nuance: The phrase நாந்தகக் கிழவர் is read as the swordsmen's line; the sense is clear but the epithet is rare.
event: Marusi names Nami as the son of the king of Kasi.

tamil: அங்கவ னரசு வேண்டா னற்கடல் படைத்த நாதன்
பங்கயங் கமழு மேனி பவித்திர பரம யோகி
தங்கிய தியானப் போழ்தி றாழ்ந்துதன் றடக்கை கூப்பிப்
பொங்கிய காதல் கூரப் பாடினன் புலமை மிக்கான்
reading: There Nami, who is said not to want a kingdom, bowed his head in the pure supreme yogi's steady meditation, joined his broad hands and, swelling with love, sang, being rich in learning.
nuance: The line அரசு வேண்டான் says he did not want a kingdom, yet in 547 he asks for wealth; either the first words mean he did not ask the kingdom of the yogi, or the line is not sound. The yogi is not named.
event: Nami bows before the meditating yogi and sings to him.

reading: Nami sings that the Lord took in the whole world within his unlimited knowledge, hid it and is its guardian and protector, eyes to all lives, and that he is the king of dharma.
nuance: The hymn's refrain is நீயே, you yourself; its second and third lines repeat each other's words.

reading: Nami sings that the Lord stood so that the hot-rayed sun was put to shame, that he has gone to the limit of all things and conquered, and that he is Tirumal.
nuance: The name Tirumal is used in praise of the Jain Lord, as the epic uses it for Tivittan elsewhere; the verse does not equate the two. Line 1 is hard to construe.

reading: Nami sings to the one of full kevala knowledge that he gives his servants unfailing bliss, and that he put away and cast off the cruel spear and every desire.
nuance: The Lord is praised as having no wish and yet as the giver, which Kural 4 does not allow its lord; the phrase எங்குற்றவேல் in line 3 is obscure.

tamil: என்றவன் பாடக் கேட்டே யிறஞ்சின குறிஞ்சி யேகா
நின்றன விலங்கு சாதி நிலங்கொண்ட பறவை எல்லா
மன்றுமெய் மறந்து சேர்ந்தார் கின்னர ரமரர் தாழ்ந்தார்
வென்றவன் றியானத் துள்ளான் வியந்திலன் சிறிதும் வேந்தே
reading: At Nami's singing the hills bowed, the animals and birds and the Kinnaras and gods gathered and bent, but the victor in meditation was not at all astonished.
nuance: The yogi does not answer the song; the reply to Nami comes from Dharanan, the serpent king, in the verses that follow.
event: All creatures and the gods bow to Nami's song, while the yogi stays in meditation unmoved.

tamil: மணநிரைத் திலங்குந் தாரோய் மற்றவ னுலோக நாதன்
குணநிரைத் திசைத்த கீதங் கேட்டலு மணிகொள் கோவைக்
பணநிரைத் திலங்கப் புக்கான் பணதர ரரச னன்றே
reading: On hearing the song of Nami to the lord of the world, Dharanan, the king of the serpent lords, came with his thousand hoods in a gleaming row.
event: Dharanan, drawn by the song, comes in with his thousand hoods.

tamil: பன்னக ருலகங் காக்கும் பாய்கதிர்ப் பசும்பொன் மேனி
மின்னவிர் வயிரச் சூட்டு விடுசுடர் மணிப்பொற் பூணான்
தன்னிக ரிகந்த தோன்றல் சரணெனப் பரமன் பாதம்
மன்னர்கட் கரசன் முன்னை வலங்கொடு வணக்கங் செய்தான்
reading: Dharanan, ruler of the serpent world, of body like fresh gold and with a crest of diamond and gems, circled the Lord's feet to the right and made his reverence, saying that he took the Lord as his refuge.
event: Dharanan circles the Lord's feet to the right and bows.

tamil: தேந்துண ரிலங்கு கண்ணித் தேவனத் தேவர் கோனைத்
தீந்தொடை நரம்பின் றெய்வச் செழுங்குரல் சிலம்ப வேத்தப்
பூந்துணர்க் கற்ப லோகம் புடைபெயர்ந் திட்ட போற்றா
வேந்துடை மான மெல்லாம் வேலினால் விடுத்த வேந்தே
reading: Dharanan says to Nami that his song to the lord of the gods, in the strings' divine voice, set the kalpa heaven shaking, and calls him the king who by his spear cast down the pride of kings who did not worship.
nuance: The lines are difficult; it is not certain that Dharanan is speaking or that the vocative at the end is Nami, though 546 and 547 make this the likelier reading.

tamil: தூண்டிய சுடரி னின்ற தியானத்தைத் துளங்கு வாய்போ
லீண்டுவந் திசைக்குற் றேவ லெம்மிறை யடிக்கட் செய்தாய்
reading: Dharanan asks Nami what he wants, having come and done service at the Lord's feet, like a flame that shakes in meditation.
nuance: The first two lines are obscure, and the simile of the lamp may describe Nami's meditation or his song.
event: Dharanan asks Nami what he wishes.

tamil: பண்மிசைப் படர்ந்த சிந்தைப் பணதரற் பணிந்து மாற்றத்
துண்மிசைத் தொடர்பு நோக்கி யுறுவலி யதனைக் கேளா
விண்மிசை யவர்கள் போல வேண்டிய விளைக்குஞ் செல்வ
மண்மிசைப் பெறுவ னாக மற்றிதென் மனத்த தென்றான்
reading: Nami bows to Dharanan and says that what is in his mind is to obtain on the earth the wealth that gives every wish, as the dwellers in the sky have it.
nuance: Nami asks the serpent king, not the yogi he has praised, and asks for wealth rather than release; the verse offers no judgment of the wish.
event: Nami asks the serpent king for wealth that grants every wish.

tamil: இச்சையங் குரைப்ப கேட்டாங் கிமைய வரியற்கை யெய்தும்
வீச்சையுந் துணையும் வெள்ளி விலங்கலுங் கொடுத்து வேந்தாய்
நிச்சமு நிலாக வென்று நிறுவிப்போய் நிலத்தின் கீழ்த்த
னச்சமி லுலகஞ் சேர்ந்தா னாயிரம் பணத்தி னானே
reading: Hearing his wish, Dharanan gives him the sky-going lore, a companion and the silver mountain, tells him to be king always, sets him there and goes down to the fearless world below the earth.
nuance: The word துணை is read as a companion, who is not named; the silver mountain is taken as the ridge on which the Vidyadharas live, as in earlier chapters.
event: Dharanan gives Nami the lore of the sky-dwellers, a companion and the silver mountain, and returns below the earth.

tamil: ஆங்கவன் குலத்து ளானெம் மதிபதி யவனோ டொப்பா
யோங்கிய குலமுஞ் செல்வப் பெருமையு முடைய நீயு
மீங்கிரு குலத்து ளீர்க்குங் கருமம்வந் திசைத்த போழ்தி
னீங்கரு நறுநெய் தீம்பால் சொரிந்தோர் நீர்மைத் தென்றான்
reading: Marusi closes: the one of Nami's line is our overlord, and for the king, of high lineage and wealth like his, a matter that joins the two houses will be like pure ghee and sweet milk poured together.
event: Marusi ends by saying the Vidyadhara king descends from Nami and that a union of the two houses would suit them.

title: தூதுவிடு சருக்கம் 550-572 (6/6)
theme: At the court of Podanam, the priest answers the Vidyadhara envoy's recital of his king's clan with the Podanam line, telling of the first lord's grace, of the ancestor who gave rule to his son and stood in meditation until anthills and creepers grew round him, and of the kevala he gained; then the king praises Marusi, names the envoy as the king's mouth, defers to the Vidyadhara king's wish, honours him and sends him back.
source_issues: 552, line 4: கற்ப தெல்ல்லம் has a doubled ல்; read as கற்பதெல்லாம்.
554, line 4: செங்சுடர் stands for செஞ்சுடர்.
564, line 2: ரன்னை stands for தன்னை.
572, lines 1 to 2: உலனல ... சலநல சடி என்பேர் is garbled and probably hides a name; the unit is flagged uncertain.
550 to 572: the speakers of 563 to 569 are fixed from the surrounding verses (549, 562, 564, 570), not from any line that names them.

cast.role: the Podanam king's priest, who recites his lord's line
the learned Vidyadhara envoy, also called Kesaran
the Podanam king, father of the princes, who receives the envoy
the ancestor of the line who gave his rule to his son and stood in austerity on Kailasa
the kings seated at the court who hear the two recitals

tamil: தங்குலத் தொடர்ச்சி கூறித் தானவ னிருந்த போழ்தி
னுங்குல நிலைமை யெல்லா நூலினீ யுரைத்த வாறே
எங்குல நிலைமை யானு முரைப்பனென் றெடுத்துக் கொண்டு
பொங்கலர்ப் பிணைய லான்றன் புரோகிதன் புகல லூற்றான்
reading: When the envoy has finished telling the line of his own king, the priest says he will give the line of his own lord in the same manner and begins.
nuance: The exchange of clan recitals before any message is delivered is the epic's way of staging the envoy's first test; the priest speaks 551 to 561.
event: Marusi ends the recital of his own clan, and the priest of Podanam begins to recite his king's clan in return.

tamil: யாவனாற் படைக்கப் பட்ட துலகெலாம் யாவன் பாத்த
பூவினாள் பொறியொன் றானாள் புண்ணிய வுலகங் கான
ஏவினான் யாவ னம்மை யாவன துலக மெல்லாம்
reading: The speaker asks in a run of questions by whom the world was ordered, whom the gods bowed to, and whose is the whole world, leading into the account of the clan's first lord.
nuance: The verb for what the first lord did is 'created' (படைக்கப்பட்டது), but the lines are a rhetorical build-up and the next verse names only a descendant by his grace; the Jain tradition's first lord is a founder of the order of life, not a creator, and the verse does not decide this.

tamil: மற்றவ னருளின் வந்தான் மரகத மணிக்குன் றொப்பச்
சுற்றி நின் றிலங்கு சோதித் தோள்வலி யெனும்பே ரானக்
கொற்றவ னுலகங் காத்த கோன்முறை வேண்டி யன்றே
கற்றவ ரின்று காறுங் காவனூல் கற்ப தெல்ல்லம்
reading: By the first lord's grace there came one named Tolvali, like an emerald hill, whose guarding of the world is the reason the learned still study the books of protection.
nuance: The verse names only 'arm-strength' (தோள்வலி); the traditional identification with Bahubali, the Podanam king of the old line, is not in the Tamil here.

tamil: கொடிவரைந் தெழுதப் பட்ட குங்குமக் குவவுத் தோளான்
இடிமுர சதிருந் தானை யிறைத்தொழில் மகனுக் கீந்து
கடிமண் மனுக்குந் தெய்வக் கழலடி யரசர் தங்கள்
reading: A king of the line gives the work of rule to his son, while kings crowd at his feet, and sets his mind on the sage's way.
nuance: Nothing in the line says the king of 553 is the same as Tolvali of 552, but 554 to 560 run on as one life and are read so.
event: The king hands the kingship to his son and goes out to renounce.

tamil: விண்ணுயர் விளங்கு கோட்டு விடுசுடர் விளங்க மாட்டாக்
கண்ணுயர் கதலி வேலிக் கார்க்கயி லாய நெற்றிப்
புண்ணியக் கிழவன் போகிப் பொலங்கலம் புலம்ப நீக்கித்
திண்ணிய தியானச் செந்தீச் செங்சுடர் திகழ நின்றான்
reading: On the Kailasa hill's brow the holy king puts off his gold ornaments and stands, his firm meditation shining as a red flame.
nuance: Meditation is imaged as a fire, so the ornaments left behind and the flame within are set against each other.
event: The king strips off his ornaments and stands in meditation on Kailasa.

tamil: கழலணிந் திலங்கு பாதங் கலந்தன கருங்கட் புற்றத்
தழலணிந் தெழுந்த வைவா யருமணி யாடு நாகம்
பொழிலணிந் தெழுந்த வல்லி புதைந்தன பூமி நாதன்
குழலணிந் தெழுந்த குஞ்சி குடைந்தன குருவிக் கூட்டம்
reading: As he stands, serpents rise from the anthills round his feet, creepers cover the earth-lord's body, and flocks of small birds nest in his hair.
nuance: The stillness is shown by what the forest does to the standing man; the verse says nothing of his pain.

tamil: அருமுடி யரசர் தாழ்ந்த வடிமிசை யரவ மூரக்
கருவடி நெடுங்க ணல்லார் கலந்த தோள் வல்லி புல்ல
மருவுடை யுலகம் பாடல் வனத்திடைப் பறவை பாடத்
திருவுடை யடிக ணிண்ற திறமிது தெரிய லாமோ
reading: The speaker says that kings bow to his feet with snakes crawling over them, the vines clasp his arms as women would, and the forest birds sing for him, so that his state cannot be known.
nuance: The kings who bow are the rank he left; the verse sets their worship beside creeper and serpent.

tamil: வெண்டவாங் குவளைக் கண்ணி மன்னர்தம் மகுட கோடி
விண்டவாம் பிணைய லுக்க விரி மதுத் துவலை மாரி
உண்டவான் கழல்கள் சூழ்ந்த திருவடி யரவ மூரக்
கண்டவா றிங்க ணார்க்குங் கருதுவ தரிது கண்டாய்
reading: In the same tableau the garlands of bowing kings drip honey on his feet, and the speaker says that what is thought of those who watch this is hard to say.
nuance: Line 3 reads the serpents as moving over the feet already crowded by kings' crowns, so the passage presses worship and the wild together.

tamil: அடுக்கிய வனிச்சப் பூவி னளிமே லரத்தச் செவ்வாய்
வடிக்கயல் நெடுங்க ணார்தம் வளிக்கையால் வளித்த மார்பில்
தொடுக்கிய தொடுத்த போலுந் துறுமலர்க் கத்தி மாதர்
கொடிக்கையா லிடுக்க றன்மேல் கொற்றவன் குலவப் பட்டன்
reading: A king reclines, his chest fanned by women of fish-like eyes and red lips and bound by their flowered arms, in the setting of a garland-wearing sensual life.
nuance: Whether this describes the same king before he renounced or a separate sensual figure set beside the ascetic is not fixed by the Tamil.

tamil: புல்லிய பொலங்கொம் பொப்பார் புலவியுட் கலவி சென்று
மெல்லிய மாலை தம்மால் விசித்தலை விடுத்து மீட்டு
மல்லுய ரலர்ந்த மார்பின் மாதவிப் பேதை யார்த்த
வல்லிகள் விடுக்க மாட்டா மனத்தினன் மன்ன னானான்
reading: The women free the king's chest of the garlands they had tied in love's quarrel, but the king's mind cannot let go of the vines of a girl called Madhavi.
nuance: The word மாதவி may be a flower (the madhavi creeper) or a girl's name; both readings keep the picture of a mind that will not release its hold, set against the clasp of 556.

tamil: ஓவலில் குணங்க ளென்னு மொளிர்மணிக் கலங்க டாங்கித்
தேவர்க ளுலக மெல்லாஞ் செழுமண மயர்ந்து கூட்டக்
கேவலப் பெண்ணென் பாளோர் கிளரரொளி மடந்தை தன்னை
ஆவியு ளடக்கிப் பின்னை யமரர்க்கு மரிய னானான்
reading: He wears a set of jewels called his unfailing virtues, and when the gods of all the worlds hold a rich wedding he takes the lady called Kevala, the woman of rising light, into his soul and then becomes rare even to the gods.
nuance: The ornaments are his own virtues and the bride his own full knowledge; the marriage image of the poem is turned inward.
event: The king takes in the maiden Kevala, whom the gods wed to him, and rises above the gods.

tamil: எங்கள்கோ னிவன்க ணின்று மிக்குயர் குலத்து வேந்தர்
தங்களோர் புறஞ்சொல் வாராத் தன்மையா லுலகங் காத்தார்
அங்கவர் வழிக்கண் தோன்றி யகலிடம் வணங்க நின்ற
reading: The speaker says that the line of high clan guarded the world so that no reproach ever came on it, and that the man who stands honoured among them now carries the same greatness.
nuance: It is the priest's own king who is praised through descent; the unit is the end of his recital.

tamil: குடித்தொட ரிரண்டுங் கேட்டே குறுமயி ரெறிந்து கண்ணுள்
பொடித்தநீர்த் திவலை சிந்தப் புகழ்ந்தன ரிருந்த வேந்தர்
அடுத்தெரி யலர்ந்த செம்பொ னணிமணி முடியி னானங்
கெடுத்துரை கெடாத முன்னக் கேசர னிதனைச் சொன்னான்
reading: Hearing both lines recited, the seated kings weep and praise them, and Marusi, called Kesaran, speaks before the moment fades.
nuance: The envoy is named Kesaran, the sky-goer, here, and Marusi elsewhere; the same man is meant.
event: The kings who hear the two clan recitals weep and praise them, and Marusi answers.

tamil: இப்படித் தாயிற் பண்டை யிசைந்தது சுற்ற மென்னை
அப்படி யரிய செய்த வடிகளெம் மரச னாய
கைப்புடை யிலங்கு செவ்வேற் கச்சற்கு மருக னாரென்
றொப்புடைப் புராண நன்னூ லுரைப்பதியா னறிவ னென்றான்
reading: The envoy says that so old a bond must be fitting, that the lord who did those rare deeds is the king of his own people and the grandson of Kacchan with the red spear, and that the old purana tells it.
nuance: Kacchan's name is traditionally that of the father of Nami and Vinami, the Vidyadhara line's founders; the verse itself gives only the name and the purana as authority.

tamil: மன்னவன் மனத்தி னாற்ற மிறைவனை வணங்கி வாழ்த்திப்
பின்னவன் ரன்னை நோக்கிப் பேசினன் பிறங்கு தாரோய்
முன்னிய வுலக நூலுங் குலங்களு முறையு முள்ளிட்
டின்னவா றறியு நீரோ ரில்லை நின் போல வென்றான்
reading: The king worships the lord, turns to the envoy and says no one is like him in knowing the world's books, the clans and the right order.
nuance: This praise follows the recitals just given, so the praise is of his measured performance there.
event: The king worships the Arhat and then praises the envoy's learning.

tamil: மந்திரக் கிழவர் கண்ணா மக்கடன் றாள்க ளாகச்
சுந்தர வயிரத் திண்டோ டோ ழராச் செவிக ளொற்றா
அந்தர வுணர்வ நூலா வரசெனு முருவு கொண்ட
எந்திர மிதற்கு வாயாத் தூதுவ ரியற்றப் பட்டார்
reading: The king says that ministers are his eyes, children his feet, strong shoulders his friends, spies his ears, and the book of knowledge his sense, and that for the voice of this machine called king the envoys are made.
nuance: The king is called a machine (எந்திரம்); the limbs of the state are its parts, and the envoy is the mouth.

tamil: ஆதிநூ லமைச்சர்க் கோது மாண்பொலா மமைந்து நின்றான்
தூதனாச் சொல்லிற் சொல்லாச் சூழ்பொரு ளில்லை போலா
மேதிலார்க் காவ துண்டோ வின்னன புகுந்த போழ்திற்
கோதிலாக் குணங்க டேற்றிக் கொழித்துரை கொளுத்த லென்றான்
reading: The king says the envoy has all the virtues the old book gives for ministers, that nothing in policy lies beyond the envoy's speech, and bids him show faultless virtues in sifted words when such a matter comes.

tamil: மற்றிம்மாண் புடைய நின்னை யுடையவம் மன்னர் மன்னன்
எற்றைநூற் றெய்த மாட்டா னிதன்றிற நிற்க வெம்மைச்
சுற்றமா நினைந்து நின்னைத் தூதனா விடுத்துச் செல்லப்
பெற்றியாம் பிறவி தன்னாற் பெறும்பயன் பெற்ற தென்றான்
reading: The king says that the Vidyadhara king, who has such a man, needs no other text, and that sending him as envoy shows that king counted Podanam as kin, so that the birth's fruit has been gained.
nuance: Line 1 to 2 can be read two ways, as praise of Marusi's king for owning him or as the Podanam king's own claim; the first is taken.

tamil: இன்றியா னின்னை முன்வைத் தினிச்சில வுரைக்கல் வேண்டா
ஒன்றியா னுரைக்கற் பால வுரையையு முணர்த்தி நீயே
வென்றியால் விளங்கு தானை விஞ்சையங் கிழவன் கண்ணா
நின்றியான் வாழ்வ தல்லா னினைப்பினி யில்லை மன்னோ
reading: The king says that with the envoy before him he needs no further words, that Marusi should speak what must be said, and that he has no thought but to live with the Vidyadhara king as his own eye.
nuance: The king puts himself in the Vidyadhara king's care in a way that reads as consent, but he does not yet name the girl or the match.

tamil: கொற்றவன் குறிப்பி தாயிற் கூவித்த னடியன் மாரை
உற்றதோர் சிறுகுற் றேவற் குரியராய்க் கருதித் தானே
அற்றமி லலங்கல் வேலோ னறிந்தருள் செய்வ தல்லான்
மற்றியா னுரைக்கு மாற்ற முடையனோ மன்னற் கென்றான்
reading: The king says that if this is the Vidyadhara king's wish, the lord of the flower garland will know and grant it, since he himself has no standing to speak to that king.
nuance: The king answers the envoy as if he were a servant of the Vidyadhara king, and the verse stops short of saying yes.

tamil: தூதன்மற் றதனைக் கேட்டே தொழுதடி வணங்கிச் செங்கோல்
போதுசே ரலங்க லானும் பொலங்கலம் பொறுக்க லாகாச்
சோதிய சுடரச் சேர்த்திப் பெருஞ்சிறப் பருளிச் செய்தான்
reading: Hearing this, the envoy bows at his feet and says he will walk round the feet of the king of the faultless sceptre and fame, and the garlanded king rewards him with a gold ornament and great honour.
event: Marusi bows and offers to circle the king's feet, and the king honours him with an ornament and gifts.

tamil: அற்றைநா ளங்குத் தாழ்ப்பித் தகனகர்ச் செல்வந் தன்னோ
டுற்றவ னுவப்பக் கூறி யுரிமைநா டகங்கள் காட்டிப்
பிற்றைநாட் குரவர் தம்மைப் பின்சென்று விடுமி னென்று
மற்றவர்க் கருளிச் செய்தான் மருசியுந் தொழுது சென்றான்
reading: The king keeps him there for the day, speaks to please him of the city's wealth, shows him the court plays, and orders that he be sent on next day with the elders, and Marusi bows and goes.
nuance: The lines on the city and the plays are compressed; the guest-rite of a day's welcome is the likely sense.
event: The king detains Marusi a day with talk of the city and plays, arranges his sending off, and Marusi leaves.

reading: Marusi reaches the old, crowded city of a lotus-eyed king whose strong arms and war-elephants are praised, the city where those like the king live.
nuance: Lines 1 to 2 are garbled, so which city and which king are meant is a guess; it is read as the Vidyadhara king's city.
event: Marusi arrives at the old city.

title: சீயவதைச் சருக்கம் 573-596 (1/11)
theme: Marusi returns to the Vidyadhara king, who reads the success of the embassy in his face, and reports in order what he saw in Prajapati's grove, palace and court, how the match was settled and what manner of king the host is.
source_issues: Verses 573, 582, 583, 584, 586, 587, 589, 593: the word division and compressed grammar make some lines hard to construe, and 573 reads எழுது where தொழுது is likely; flagged uncertain.
Verses 578 to 591: the speaker is Marusi, taken from 577 (he says he has returned) and from 591 line 4; the verses between do not name him.

cast.role: the learned envoy returned from Tivittan's father
king of the Vidyadharas of the southern ridge, who sent the envoy
the king of the city of Podanam, father of the two princes and host of the embassy
the elder prince, the moon-hued one
the younger prince, the sea-hued one, who is to wed the Vidyadhara girl
the guard posted in the garden, the likely man who met the envoy
the women the host king sends to serve the envoy a meal

reading: After Marusi has entered the great city he passes the three outer gates of the spear-bearing king's palace and comes close to the king, worshipping at his anklets.
nuance: The word before the last in line 4 reads as எழுது in the text; தொழுது (worshipping) is the likely sense, and the palace is the Vidyadhara king's because verse 577 has Marusi report his errand done.
event: Marusi returns to the Vidyadhara palace and approaches the king.

reading: The king, with swaying earrings, gem-set bracelets and a garlanded spear, directs with his hand that Marusi sit on the broad floor.
event: The Vidyadhara king bids the returned envoy sit.

reading: Marusi sits composed on the gem floor the king has laid out, and the king reads from his face how the errand ended.
event: The king reads the outcome of the embassy from the envoy's face before he speaks.

reading: From the brightness of the envoy's face the king grasps, like a sage, that the task is done, and the faultlessly learned Marusi bows and speaks.
event: Seeing success in Marusi's face, the king waits as Marusi bows and begins his report.

reading: Marusi greets the king, wishing his victorious anklets to live, evil to leave and his fame to grow, and says he has finished the king's errand and returned.
event: Marusi announces that the errand is done.

reading: Marusi promises to tell the circumstances of his descent from here, how he came before the king there, and the words the army-bearing king spoke.
event: Marusi undertakes a full report of the embassy.

reading: Marusi tells how he entered the grove of jackfruit whose ripe, thorny fruit split and let their juice and honey run.
event: Marusi enters the grove outside the city.

reading: Marusi tells how he came to a pool where bees swarm the lotuses and flocks of birds hunt the water.
event: Marusi reaches the pool in the grove.

reading: Marusi tells how he saw an asoka tree set about with jewelled and silver-patterned platforms, looking like the love-god's own weapon.
nuance: The asoka's flower is one of the love-god's arrows, which is why the tree is called his weapon.
event: Marusi sees the asoka tree.

reading: Marusi tells of a white stone slab ringed by gold that shines of itself, and of the sight it made to the eye.
nuance: The word division of lines 1 to 3 is run together and the construction is hard, so the sense of the slab's light is only the likely one.
event: Marusi sees the stone slab in the grove.

reading: Marusi tells how a man with curled forelock, shining body, blazing ornaments and a tight girdle came while the bees scattered, and bade him climb up.
nuance: The man is not named. Verse 116 posted Turumakanthan as guard in this garden for the day the astrologer named, and he is the likely figure.
event: A man of the garden comes to Marusi and bids him come up.

reading: Marusi tells what was said to him there, and how at the king's sending some women with auspicious vessels finished serving him a meal.
nuance: The king named is the host, Tivittan's father, taken from the sending of the envoy in verses 426-428.
event: The host king sends women who serve the envoy a meal.

reading: Marusi tells how the moon-hued prince with red lotus eyes and the sea-hued prince in long golden earrings came there, and what they said.
nuance: The princes are named by colour only; moon-hued is taken as Vijayan and sea-hued as Tivittan, the two sons of Pirasapathi.
event: The two princes come to the envoy and speak with him.

reading: Marusi tells of the host king's court, with the great elephants and the roaring army drawn up outside, and how the others came to the assembly.
nuance: Line 1 and 2 are compressed and the number in the first line is hard to place, so only the general picture of the court is safe.
event: Marusi enters the host king's crowded assembly.

reading: Marusi tells how he bowed at the king's anklets, received a seat through the younger prince, and how the horoscope with its golden marks was praised and the letter taken with reverence.
nuance: Whose hand takes the letter is not stated; the king is the likely receiver.
event: Marusi bows to the host king, is seated at the younger prince's word, and the horoscope and letter are received.

reading: Marusi tells how the king, hearing the letter of the lord of the army, was struck with wonder and sat silent, giving no other word.
event: The host king hears the letter and falls silent without replying.

reading: Marusi tells of words raised against the seated king, of how someone grieved and refused, of what the old clan said, and of the rare kinship that was finally joined.
nuance: The speakers of the objection and the refusal are not named and the grammar of all four lines is compressed.
event: An objection to the match is raised and answered and the kinship is settled.

reading: Marusi tells how the king then spoke kind words, became kin, and bestowed gifts and honours as the gold-adorned clans looked on.
event: The host king accepts the match and gives gifts.

reading: Marusi tells what the king's queens and great kin saw as they came forward and what the others said, and then, bowing, goes on to speak further.
event: Marusi finishes his account of the court and bows to add a further word.

reading: Marusi says that beyond all that has been told there is one more thing: he has gladly seen many kings and none is of such a nature.
Marusi says that all the books the king has learned stand against those learned by others and are complete beyond them, so that the books he has gained are the measure of his character.
nuance: The clauses of lines 1 and 2 are hard to divide and the comparison is read as the king's learning outstripping all others.

reading: Marusi describes the king as fiery in command and cool in giving, great by nature yet modest in friendship, hard for kings to reach, easy for those who serve him.
Marusi says that if the king's gentle grace were absent the world itself would be absent, so good is he.
Marusi says that those who live in the shade of the king's umbrella are men of learning joined by love who give their lives when the time comes.

title: சீயவதைச் சருக்கம் 597-619 (2/11)
theme: The Vidyadhara envoy praises the princes and the match before the Podanam king, who rewards him, sends him off and, on his counsellors' word of the month-end prophecy, resolves to send a learned man in return; the poet then turns to the rival king Acuvakanthan, wholly given to pleasure.
source_issues: Verses 597 to 600, 607 to 610 and 616: the word division and compressed grammar leave the sense uncertain; flagged.
Verses 597 to 604: the speaker is the envoy only by inference from 604 and 605; the verses do not name him.
Verse 610: the rival is not named until 619; verses 611 to 618 are taken as his.

cast.role: the learned Vidyadhara envoy, taken as the speaker of 597 to 604
the king of Podanam, called by the epithet of the swift elephants
the king's counsellors
the two princes, Vijayan and Tivittan
the Vidyadhara king's daughter, unnamed here
the rival king of the discus, named only at the close

reading: The speaker says that among children of faultless clans none counts as a stranger, so kin and others alike have no fault in them.
nuance: The compressed grammar and the doubled word for children make the sense uncertain; the speaker is taken to be the envoy opening his address to the king.

reading: The speaker tells the king that when the world is glad the king is glad, and when something harsh touches it he too suffers, as the lord of the garland's grace shows.
nuance: The last two lines are clipped and the speaker is not named; the envoy is assumed from 604 and 605.

reading: The speaker says that because kings are the life of those who live within the sea's fence, the king of kings with the great army cannot sleep, wondering whether protection will fail.
nuance: Set against verses 611 to 619, where the rival king sleeps and wakes in the women's company, this verse gives the standard those verses fall short of.

reading: The speaker says the king, generous as rain-cloud and fond of his sons, is the sort who would tell of them as a lion among deer before the other kings.
nuance: Whether the verse asks the king to speak of his sons or says that he will is not settled by the grammar.

reading: The speaker says the love-god's bow has shown itself in the two bodies and that the sons of the world's ruler, bright with long anklets, are the beauty of their line.
The speaker says the conch-hued elder and the younger, dark as a swelling cloud, bear the auspicious mark set for ruling this world, which the king may see for himself.
nuance: The mark is read as a sign of rule over the world; the verse gives no other detail.

reading: The speaker asks what austerity the vine-slender woman did to be joined with the red-eyed one on whose divine breast the lotus-lady already rests.
The speaker says the woman equals the lord in beauty, that nothing is wanting between them, and that their growing merit joined them, so the king should marvel.
nuance: The verse says merit joined them but not the kind of former birth; the Jain frame is the work's, not stated here.

reading: On hearing this the crowned king of the swift elephants graciously gives the speaker a flood of shining wealth.
nuance: The king is named by the epithet for swift elephants; he is taken to be the same Prajapati who sits on the throne in the earlier chapters.
event: The Podanam king rewards the envoy with great wealth after the praise of his sons.

reading: The king sends the envoy off to his house and, with the counsellors who have joined him, asks what is now to be done.
event: The king sends the envoy to rest and asks his counsellors what to do next.

reading: The speaker, calling the king lord of the red-eyed crown, reminds him that the astrologer said earlier that within a month Tivittan would split a lion's mouth.
nuance: The verse names the reporter only as one of settled learning; whether the counsellors or the astrologer speak is not shown, and the counsellors are taken for the speaker.

reading: Therefore, the speakers said, it is right to send a man of learned excellence who knows the matter, and the king is told so.
nuance: The reply envoy is not named here; the verse says only that one is to be sent to the Vidyadhara king.

reading: The king, who rested his trust on spies and on the counsel thoughtful men had given, accepts it and rejoices with his kin.
nuance: The wording that makes the king one trusting spies rests on a compressed line and may be read otherwise.
event: The king accepts the counsel and rejoices with his kin.

reading: The poet says that as days go on thus, the feared discus-bearer stays in the other quarter, and he now turns to tell of the fierce one set first before them.
nuance: The verse moves the telling from Podanam to the rival king without naming him; only verse 619 gives his name.

reading: The ruler who could not bear to tread on cotton bed for the coolness of it is shown lying on the breasts of delicate women, so absorbed in them that he never wearies.
event: The ruler spends his hours lying with women of the palace.

reading: The ruler holds in his mouth the red-coral-like lips and the sweet nectar of the women, and sinks into their hearts.
event: The ruler takes the women's lips and sinks into love with them.

reading: When the garlanded man and the women mingle, the garlands and breasts strike one another and the bees on them hum together.
The women gather honey from the garlands and offer it, and the ruler takes it and also enjoys the sweetness of the lips of the red fruit.
event: The women give the ruler honey and he drinks it with the taste of their lips.

reading: The women's flower-hung hair and eyes are the honey-drenched lilies, desire is the toddy they offer, and the ruler is lost in it through day and night.
nuance: The poet makes desire the drink, and so turns the women's eyes into the cup; the verse reports it without comment.
event: The ruler, drunk on desire, loses track of day and night.

reading: Whether he is plunged in the women's soft clothes or called awake by a sage, he never, at any other hour, behaves as a king.
nuance: The first lines of the verse are hard to read, and the sage's part is uncertain; the sense taken is that his only role is as lover.

reading: He takes his pleasure in the women's dance on the drum-filled floor, in their song of sweet notes, and he longs to be in heaven's company.
event: The ruler takes pleasure in dance and song.

reading: He takes his play in pools, wine-halls, gardens, peacock hills, white sand and water-sport.
event: The ruler spends his time in pleasure grounds and water-play.

reading: He is so given over that he knows neither the sun's heat nor the moon's cool, and the verse names him Acuvakanthan.
nuance: Only here is the rival king named; the earlier verses of the chapter, about a discus-bearer, are read as his.
event: Acuvakanthan loses all awareness in pleasure.

title: சீயவதைச் சருக்கம் 620-642 (3/11)
theme: The poet turns to the rival king Acuvakanthan, whose temper and pleasures are named; his astrologer Satavintu warns him of pride and neglect and of the younger Podanam prince, and the king, boasting of his own strength, waves the warning away and tells his counsellors to speak.
source_issues: Verse 620 lines 2 and 3 (தேறின் யாரையும் தேறும்): the sense of the king's overconfidence is a best reading.
Verse 625: the phrases கோசிறண்டத்தன் and மாசிறண்டத்தன் are doubled and clipped; the sense is uncertain.
Verses 631 to 640: the verses do not name their speakers; the astrologer is taken as the speaker of 623 to 632 and the king of 634 to 640, from the story and the closing verbs.
Verse 639: the person addressed is not clear.
Verse 633 lines 1 to 2 and verse 642 lines 2 to 3 are corrupt or badly divided in the text.

cast.role: the rival king of the discus, taken as the one the astrologer addresses
Acuvakanthan's astrologer (நிமித்திகன்), who counsels and warns him
the learned counsellors of the rival king

reading: The poet says that a king who destroys in anger without weighing a matter and cannot bear an opposing word, and who, whenever his mind clears, thinks he can see through everyone, is carried along by his pride.
nuance: The poet opens the rival's portrait with his temper, ahead of the scene that shows it; the closing phrase of the verse is read as the poet's own name for such a king.

reading: While the king plays with the garlanded women in the pond, the goddess of fortune, left unembraced, takes offence and looks for a place to go.
nuance: The verse says only that she looks for a place, not that she has gone; it is read as a forecast of loss, and sets the pond scene against the sleeplessness the envoy praised in 599.
event: The king's pleasure in the pond costs him the favour of the goddess of fortune, who begins to look elsewhere.

reading: One day the king's astrologer Satavintu, a sea of learning with unfading fame, speaks to the king of the strong anklets.
nuance: This is the second court in the poem to hear an astrologer; in 103 to 109 the Podanam king's astrologer reads a dream, and here the rival's astrologer reads the same fortune from the other side.
event: Satavintu, the astrologer of the rival king, begins to speak to him.

reading: The astrologer addresses the king and says that among those who rule the sea-ringed land there are said to be six hostile groups, which must be conquered first.
nuance: The verse does not say whether the six are outer rivals or inner faults; the next verse, which speaks of one who has conquered himself, is the only hint that the poet means the latter.

reading: The astrologer says that a king who has conquered himself is hard for others to conquer, and that gold rains in the land where he rules.
The astrologer says that if the king stays with a sceptre without fault he will rule gladly, and the other kings, praising him, will serve under him.
nuance: The words for the sceptre and the rod are doubled and the grammar is clipped, so the sense of the condition is a best reading.

reading: The astrologer says the learned man who keeps what he has earned, draws in what he has not yet, guards the great wealth and gives it away becomes the guardian of others.
The astrologer says that pride is the dense frost which, if it falls, destroys the lotus of wealth that blooms in the water of one's own understanding.
nuance: The sun in the first line is the king's own knowledge, so the image makes understanding both the cause of wealth and the thing pride darkens.

reading: The astrologer says the king should think of those ruined by negligence, and be watchful in the hour of his own strength, as the books of praise say.
nuance: The counsel keeps close to Kural 539 in sense and in the pairing of joy and ruin, but the words are not those of the couplet, so no echo is marked; the verse names its source as the books of praise.

reading: The astrologer says the king already knows the even-handed justice of the right way, but that, though the king may be angered, he will speak what is for the king's good.
On hearing him the king, wreathed in flowers, says he should speak well and bends his ear, the earring on his strong shoulder shedding light.
event: The king tells the astrologer to speak and bends his ear to listen.

reading: The astrologer tells the king to look at the sons of the king who rules the great city of Podanam, men like the god of love.
nuance: The verse names the princes' beauty and not yet the danger; the warning is in 632.
event: Satavintu points the king to the princes of Podanam as the matter of his warning.

reading: The astrologer says the youngest of those strong-shouldered princes will become our ancient enemy, and asks whether a petty word of omen should make him weaken at heart.
nuance: Who speaks the second half, and whether the closing question is the astrologer's own or his report of the king's coming mood, is not clear from the Tamil.
event: Satavintu names the younger Podanam prince as the foe the omen points to.

reading: The crowned king, told to weigh a fit course, waves the matter away with the shining palm of his hand.
nuance: The first two lines are hard to parse; the gesture of the palm is clear, and the rest is read as the astrologer's urging.
event: The king waves off the astrologer's advice with his hand.

reading: The king smiles and says that his shoulders have conquered the whole host of Vidyadhara kings, so what can other foes do against him.
nuance: The boast is the very pride that 627 warned of, spoken by the one warned, and 635 to 640 continue it.

reading: The king asks whether Mount Meru would shake at the fanning of a palm leaf, and so whether the strength of mere humans can disturb his faultless shoulders.
nuance: The boast holds that his own strength is what stands in the way, and that mortal men are the leaf beside the mountain.

reading: The king asks whether a great elephant's tusk blunts on a plantain stem, and so whether his shoulders, which slew the armies of the Danavas, would bend to men.
The king asks whether a handful of small clouds can march against a fast wind, and so whether men, as his foes, could stir against his fury.
The king says that if Indra's thunderbolt were set against him it would still fall short, and that if he turned his mind to his fierce shining discus he could cut down the shoulders of the gods.
nuance: The discus is the weapon 402 says Tivittan will take from him with his life; the boast is placed so that the reader hears that prophecy beneath it.

tamil: யச்ச மின்றி நிற் பாரந் நிமித்த நூல்
reading: The king asks whether, if he wished to send a spell against them, anyone could stand fearless, unless the book of omens is a deceit, and he calls the speaker one of angry nature.
nuance: The grammar of the question can be read as a challenge to the astrologer or as the king's wavering over the omen; the second reading is the more cautious.

reading: The king says he has not been one to obey the word of the learned, and that he would fear only a petty word; even if the whole world rose together in anger he would fight it, and he does not value such an omen.
nuance: The verse is the king's refusal to be warned, and his own claim that the sages' word counts for little; the epic does not endorse it.

reading: The narrator says that the king, who saw no fault in any good man's deed, told fit counsellors to speak and let it be understood.
nuance: He calls counsel only after saying in 634 to 640 that he would fight regardless, so the order may be formal; the last two lines are read in this way.
event: The king orders his counsellors to speak and give their counsel.

reading: When the king of the garland and discus had said this, his learned counsellors, skilled in the work of the books, spoke to him with their own plans and gave him understanding.
nuance: The phrase for the counsellors' learning is hard to read, and the content of the advice is left to the following verses.
event: The counsellors answer the king with their own advice.

title: சீயவதைச் சருக்கம் 643-665 (4/11)
theme: Acuvakanthan's frightened counsellors urge that a small foe be put down before he grows, Arimanju counsels testing him first by a tribute demand, and the four envoys of the discus-bearer fly to Podanam, are admitted by the gatekeeper and deliver a letter demanding wealth, a thousand dancing women and the marks of a king.
source_issues: Verse 647 line 2: the word for the ill-hearted one (தாமரை) looks corrupt.
Verse 662 line 4: the last word (உரைத்தர்) is short of a syllable.
Verses 650, 653 and 663: several words are obscure and the readings are partly guessed.
Verses 643 to 649: neither king is named; the rival is read as Acuvakanthan from verse 619 and the arrival at Podanam in 651.

cast.role: the rival king of the discus
the frightened counsellors who spoke before Arimanju, read as the rival king's
the counsellor who proposes testing the foe by a tribute demand
the four envoys of the discus-bearer sent to Podanam
the gatekeeper of the palace of Podanam
the king of Podanam
the reader who reads out the letter

reading: The speaker warns that a fire, however small its spark, blackens what it touches, and that a foe of old, though small, can win once he is allowed to spread.
nuance: The speakers are not named; they are read as the frightened ones whom verse 646 says spoke before Arimanju. The rival king is not named in the verse.

reading: The speaker says a poisonous thorny tree can be killed at the sprout, even with a nail, but once it has grown tall neither axe nor hatchet will master it.
nuance: The first line is compressed (the words for the poisonous thorn tree run together), and the sense of the second line is taken from the whole image.

reading: The speaker urges the king not to despise the foe as small but to go again and again and learn of him, a king with a honeyed garland and a crown of red gold.
nuance: The syntax is thin: whether the last line names the foe or only addresses the king is not fixed by the words, and it is read here as the foe.

reading: After the frightened speakers have spoken, a man named Arimanju says that if the foe proves truly an enemy, the king should first examine and see, and only then take counsel.
nuance: The name is read as Arimanju because the end of line 1 runs into it; the verse opens as the poet's link and passes into his speech.
event: Arimanju steps in after the frightened counsellors and urges the king to examine the foe before he plans against him.

reading: Arimanju says that making enemies of those who are not enemies, and counting as friends those of an ill heart, will both torment later through excess.
nuance: This sets Arimanju's caution against the counsellors' haste in 643 and 644. The word in line 2 for the ill-hearted one is corrupt and is read as the ill-hearted person.

reading: Arimanju proposes to learn the foe's mind by sending to him for tribute: if he gives it in due order with courteous words, well; if he falls short, no fault will lie with the king.
nuance: The test is built to fail: a king who pays acknowledges the overlord, and one who does not has put himself in the wrong. The last line is compressed.

reading: On hearing this the crowned king calls it good and sends messengers to the spear-bearing king with the order to take the tribute.
nuance: Neither king is named; the crowned king is read as Acuvakanthan and the spear-bearer as the king of Podanam, from the arrival in 651.
event: Acuvakanthan accepts Arimanju's plan and sends envoys to the victorious-spear king to demand tribute.

reading: Four envoys in bright dress, bearing letters pressed with an unbroken seal, set out together along a path through the clouds.
nuance: Several words in lines 1 and 3 are obscure (the ones for the red-lac staves and for their knowledge of the dance), so the description of the four is partly guessed.
event: Four envoys with sealed letters set out through the clouds.

reading: The envoys make for the southern quarter and its hills and, speaking on and on, enter the great city of Podanam that rises high.
event: The envoys enter the great city of Podanam.

reading: The mansions, lit like lightning among the clouds, block the sun's street, and seeing them the envoys turn in disgust from the wealth of their own Vidyadhara kind.
nuance: The envoys are taken as Vidyadharas because the verse speaks of the Vidyadhara wealth they leave behind; the verse does not call them so.
event: The envoys, seeing the mansions of Podanam, come to disdain the wealth of their own people.

reading: The swelling sound of drums, the peacocks that dance to it as to thunder and the festive streets give the envoys, as they pass, a glow of splendour.
nuance: The wording is dense and the last two lines are read only for their general sense, the subject of the verb for glory being supplied.

reading: Cascades fall from the clouds that the mansions' spire-tops cleave, and the envoys see the many streets of the city.
event: The envoys walk the streets of Podanam under mansion-cascades.

reading: The long streets lie covered with the gem girdles of lovers and the garlands flung by those in sulks, so that the envoys find passage hard.
nuance: The picture of lovers' quarrels is read from the words for the girdles and garlands; the sentence is long and compressed.
event: The envoys struggle to pass through streets strewn with ornaments.

reading: The street is mired with the rut and spittle of the great elephants, so that the envoys take it for a field of fragrant toddy-mad ground.
event: The envoys see the streets of rut-wet ground.

reading: The envoys come to the walled city that lies behind a rushing moat, where bees cluster on lilies and swans cry out.
event: The envoys reach the walled royal town.

reading: Standing before the palace gate with its high turrets, they speak to the guard.
event: The envoys, at the palace gate, address the guard.

reading: The envoys tell the gatekeeper to go before the king and say that the men of the bright discus-bearer, come from the silver ridge, stand at the gate.
nuance: The envoys name only their master's discus and do not name him; the ridge of silver is read as the Vidyadhara ridge.
event: The envoys have the gatekeeper announce them as the men of the discus-bearer.

reading: At their words the gatekeeper bows to the king's feet and tells him, and the king says that they may come in.
event: The gatekeeper reports the envoys, and the king bids them enter.

reading: The gatekeeper tells the envoys to come in, and they approach the king, bless his anklets and, with folded hands, give him the letter they had folded.
event: The envoys enter, bless the king and give him the folded letter.

reading: After the reader has read the letter before the king, the discus-king's men repeat in matching words what it says.
nuance: The last word (உரைத்தர்) is short of a syllable and the sense of line 3 is clipped; the verse is taken as a link to the demand in 663 to 665.
event: A reader reads the discus-king's letter aloud and his men repeat its demand.

reading: The speaker begins the list of what must be given: gleaming mansions by the thousand crore and a thousand dancing women with bangled arms and ear-rolls.
nuance: The sentence runs on through 664 and 665 and ends there. The word in line 2 for the first thing demanded is obscure, and 'mansions' is a guess.

reading: The list goes on: conches thrown up by the sea, coral, heaps of pearl, aloe wood, silk and the many goods that come with the waters.
The list ends with white-rayed pearls, aloe, elephant tusks, whisks of white yak-hair and the cool white umbrella, all of which must be given, says the speech of the bright-discus king.
nuance: The white umbrella and the yak-hair whisks are the marks of a king, so the demand goes past tribute toward giving up his standing. The verse does not say Podanam yields or refuses.
event: The envoys finish reading the demand for wealth, women and royal insignia.

title: சீயவதைச் சருக்கம் 666-688 (5/11)
theme: Podanam's king, hearing Asvagriva's demand for tribute, reasons from fate and precedent to submit and gives the envoys women and gifts, until Tivittan learns of it, flares at the word tribute and answers in scorn.
source_issues: Verse 679 line 2: a stray space before a dead consonant was repaired in the text.
Verse 681 line 3: a leftover TSCII character was read as a vowel sign and repaired.
Verses 666 to 670: the verses give no speaker; they are taken as the king's thoughts because 671 ends them with he thought thus.
Verses 681 to 688: the prince is not named in these verses; he is taken to be Tivittan from 679.

cast.role: the king of Podanam, called by the epithet of the swift elephants
the sceptre-bearing sky-goers sent by Asvagriva for tribute, the Vidyadharas of 678
the women of the hall, dancers and singers whom the king gives away
the red-eyed tall one, the younger prince and hero
the dwarf who tells the prince what has happened
the discus-lord, son of Mayurakandan and Nilanganai, whose demand brings the envoys

tamil: வேந்தன்மற் றதனைக் கேட்டே வெற்றுவ னெறிந்த கல்லைக்
காந்திய கந்த தாகக் கவுட்கொண்ட களிரு போலச்
சேந்தவ ருரைத்த மாற்றஞ் சிந்தையு ளடக்கி வைத்து
நாந்தகக் கிழவர் கோமா னயந்தெரி மனத்த னானான்
reading: The king, having heard the envoys' demand, keeps their angry words inside his mind as an elephant keeps a stone thrown by a vain man in its cheek, and turns to a mind that weighs gentle courses.
nuance: The simile is hard: the thrown stone and its being held in the cheek as if it were a scent-ball are read as swallowed insult; the verse does not say outright that the king hides his anger.
event: The king hears the demand and swallows the insult without showing it.

tamil: கருத்துமாண் குலனுந் தேசுங் கல்வியும் வடிவுந் தம்மில்
பொருத்தினாற் பழிக்க லாகாப் புலைமைமிக் குடைய ரேனு
திருத்தினா னிறைவ னேகாண் செய்வினைக் கிழவ னென்பான்
reading: The speaker says that, however a man's birth, learning and form stand, each is made to hear another's word, act on it and live by it by the lord called master of deeds.
nuance: The first three lines turn on a hard clause about baseness that cannot be blamed; the sense of the verse as a whole is held loosely. The king is taken as the one reflecting, from 671, where his thought is said to end.

tamil: மதியினை மலரச் சூழ்ந்து வருந்தித்தாம் படைக்கப் பட்ட
நிதியினை நுகர்ந்து மென்று நினைத்தினி திருந்த போழ்திற்
பதியினைக் கலக்கிச் சென்று பறித்துத்தாம் பிறர்க்கு நீட்டும்
விதியினை விலக்க மாட்டா மெலிபவால் வெளிய நீரார்
reading: The speaker says that men who plan to enjoy the wealth they gained with effort are weakened by fate, which upsets the city, takes what they hold and hands it to others, and no one can bar it.
nuance: Set beside 680 to 683, the king's fate-talk is a reason offered for giving way; the verse does not say that the loss has already come, only that fate can cause it.

tamil: ஓளியினாற் பெரிய னாய வொருவனுக் குவப்பச் செய்தோ
ரளியினால் வாழ்து மென்னும் மவாவினு ளழுந்து கின்றாம்
தெளியநா மிதனைக் கண்டும் செய்வினைத் திறங்க ளோரா
மளிய மோ வளியஞ் சால வறிவினாற் பெரிய மேகாண்
reading: The speaker says that those who live by the favour of a man great in splendour sink in the wish to live by his grace, and though they see it plainly they do not weigh the workings of deeds.
nuance: The speaker takes the knowledge of deeds as the knowledge he and his own lack; the verse blames desire for favour, not the overlord.

tamil: அன்றுநா முயலப் பட்ட வினைகள்மற் றனைய வானா
லின்று நா மவலித் தென்னை யினிச்செய்வ தெண்ணி னல்ல
வென்றியான் விளங்கு மாழி யவர்கட்கு மேலை வேந்த
ரொன்றியாங் குவப்பித் தாண்ட துரைப்பக்கேட் டுணர்ந்தா மன்றே
reading: The speaker says that since the deeds done earlier are of this kind, there is nothing to gain by fretting now, and that he has heard how the earlier kings of the sea-ringed earth joined and pleased the overlord and ruled.
nuance: This is where the king's reasoning from deeds becomes a decision: the fruit of deeds is read as a reason to pay. Verse 685 gives the opposite answer to the same demand.

tamil: என்றுதன் மனத்தி னெண்ணி யிலங்குகோற் கைய ராகி
நின்றகே சரரை நோக்கி நிலமன்ன னனைய சொன்னர்க்
கொன்றியா மிங்க ணுள்ள தொருப்படுத் துய்ப்பக் கொண்டு
சென்றுறு மிறவர்க் கெம்வா யின்னுரை தெரிமி னென்றான்
reading: Having thought thus, the king looks at the sceptre-bearing sky-goers and tells them that he will gather what is here and send it with them, and bids them carry his courteous word to their lord.
nuance: The envoys are called by a name for the sky-goers; taking them to be Asvagriva's Vidyadhara envoys rests on 678 and 680.
event: The king tells Asvagriva's envoys he will gather what is due and send it back with them.

tamil: ஆளிகட் கரச னன்ன வரசர்கோ னதனைக் கூறி
வாளிவிற் றடக்கை வெம்போர் மணிவரை யனைய மார்பிற்
காளைக ளிதனைக் கேட்பிற் கனல்பவா லவரை யின்னே
மீளுமா றமைப்ப னென்று வேண்டுவ விதியி னீந்தான்
reading: The king says to himself that the young men will burn if they hear this and that he will send the envoys back at once, and then gives them what they ask by custom.
nuance: The young men are taken to be the princes Vijayan and Tivittan; the verse says only that fierce youths would flare at the news.
event: The king hides the matter from the princes and gives the envoys what they ask, to send them away quickly.

tamil: செய்யவாய்ப் பசும்பொ னோலைச் சீறடிப் பரவை யல்கு
லையநுண் மருங்கு நோவ வடிக்கொண்ட குவவுக் கொங்கை
வெய்யவாய்த் தண்ணெ னீலம் விரிந்தென விலங்கி நீண்ட
மையவா மழைக்கட் கூந்தன் மகளிரை வருக வென்றான்
reading: The king calls for the women of the long dark hair, slender-waisted and full-breasted, to come.
event: The king summons the dancing women.

tamil: அணிமுழா வனைய தோளா னருளிய தறிந்த போழ்தின்
மணிமுழாச் சிலம்பக் கொண்ட மண்டல வரங்கி னங்கண்
குணிமுழாப் பெயர்த்த பணி குயிற்றுத லிலயங் கொண்ட
கணிமுழ மருங்குற் பாடற் கலிப்பிவை தவிர்த்துச் சென்றார்
reading: On hearing the king's grace the women leave the drum, the dance-ground and the songs they were practising and go.
event: The women leave their dance practice at the king's word.

tamil: மஞ்சிடை மதர்த்த மஞ்ஞை வான்குழா மென்ன வாங்கண்
வெஞ்சுடர் விளங்கு மாடத் திடைநிலை விரவித் தோன்றி
வஞ்சிநன் மருங்கு னோவ மணிநகைக் கலாவ மின்னச்
செஞ்சுடர் சிலம்பு பாடத் தேன்றிசை பரவச் சேர்ந்தார்
reading: The women come, bright like a flock of peacocks in a cloud, into the lamp-lit hall, their waists aching under the girdles and their anklets sounding as bees follow them.
event: The women arrive in the lit hall.

tamil: மாடெலா மெரிந்து மின்னும் வயிரக்குண் டலத்தோ டம்பொற்
றோடுலாந் துளங்கித் தோன்றுஞ் சுடிகைவாண் முகத்து நல்லார்
பாடலா னரம்பின் தெய்வம் படிவங்கொண் டனைய நீரா
ராடலா லரம்பை யொப்ப ரவரிலா யிரரை யீந்தான்
reading: The women, whose singing is like the lute-goddess and whose dancing is like Rambha's, are described, and the king gives a thousand of them away.
nuance: The giving is part of the tribute, as 678 shows, where they are put into the flying car with the other gifts; the verse itself says only that he gave them.
event: The king gives a thousand of the dancing women to the envoys.

tamil: காய்ந்தொளிர் பவழச் சாதிக் கடிகைகள் காண மின்னுப்
யேந்தொழிற் காக துண்ட மருப்பிணை கவரிக் கற்றை
யாய்ந்தொழின் மகரப் பூணா னுவப்பன வனைத்து மீந்தான்
reading: The king gives all that pleases the envoys: coral, strings of pearl, tusks and bundles of yak-tail whisks.
event: The king gives gems and fine things to the envoys.

tamil: அஞ்சுடர் வயிரப் பூணா னருளினான் விடுப்ப வாங்கண்
விஞ்சையர் விமானத் தோற்ற மேலருங் கலங்க ளேற்றிச்
செஞ்சுடர் திலகச் செவ்வாய் மகளிரை விமானஞ் சேர்த்திக்
கஞ்சிகை மறைக்கும் போழ்திற் காளைக ளதனைக் கண்டார்
reading: At the king's leave the Vidyadharas load the gifts into their flying car and put the women in, and the princes see this as the curtain is lowered over it.
nuance: The curtain hides the load only as it closes; the princes see the departure and ask in 679.
event: The envoys load the gifts and the women into their flying car and the princes see them go.

tamil: என்னிது விளைந்த வாறித் தூதுவர் யாவ ரென்று
கன்னவில் வயிரத் திண்டோட் கடல்வண்ணன் வினவ யாரும்
சொன்னவின் றுரைக்க மாட்டார் துட்கென்று துளங்க வாங்கோர்
கொன்னவில் பூதம் போலுங் குறண்மக னிதனைச் சொன்னான்
reading: Tivittan asks what has happened and who these messengers are, and all stay silent in fear until a dwarf like a great ghost tells him.
nuance: The sea-hued one is taken to be Tivittan, by his colour in the earlier chapters; the verse does not name him.
event: Tivittan asks what is happening and a dwarf answers when no one else will.

tamil: அறைகழ லரவத் தானை யச்சுவக் கிரீவ னென்பா
னிறைபுக ழாழி தாங்கி நிலமெலாம் பணிய நின்றான்
திறைதர வேண்டும் என்று விடுதரச் செருவந் தானை
யிறைவனு மருளிச் செய்தா னிதுவிங்கு விளைந்த தென்றான்
reading: The dwarf says that Asvagriva, lord of the discus whom the earth bows to, sent word that tribute must be given, and that this is what has happened here.
event: The dwarf tells Tivittan that Asvagriva has demanded tribute from the king.

reading: At the word tribute-duty the anger he has long held in a full heart kindles in him as a fire rising from a grudge.
nuance: The subject of the burning is taken to be Tivittan, the prince who asked in 679; 683 later calls him the younger youth.
event: Tivittan is lit with anger on hearing the word tribute.

reading: His forehead beads with small drops of sweat like pearls dropped from his crown, and his red eyes shed hot tears like ghee falling into the fire.
nuance: The verse describes the body's signs of anger and has no event of its own.

reading: He looks with the glare of a cobra whose jewelled hood is touched, laughs a fiery laugh and gives the younger one's reply.
nuance: The word for the younger youth is read as Tivittan, the younger prince; the line takes up his own reply in 684 to 688.
event: Tivittan laughs in anger and answers the demand.

reading: Tivittan says that to live by paying written tribute, like men who plough, pay their debts, eat and serve kings, would make a fine royal life.
nuance: The tone is scorn: the verse praises what it means to mock. Its claim is set against the king's reasoning in 670.

reading: Tivittan says they would pay tribute daily and rule the land only if their shoulders, their warrior's anklets and their sword were of no use, and asks what use they are otherwise.
nuance: The addressee is taken to be Asvagriva's envoys or the deluded people of the court; the verse does not decide which.

reading: Tivittan calls the king who demands the tribute a fool who thinks to take the jewel from the hood of a fire-breathing, venom-eyed cobra.
nuance: The cobra is Tivittan's own side; the image makes the demander the victim of his own greed.

reading: Tivittan says that whatever the armies of strife have not won in the places that are his could at best be got by women with great vessels.
nuance: The verse is compressed and its reading of the third and fourth lines is very uncertain; it is taken as a barb at the women sent as tribute in 676 to 678.

reading: Tivittan tells the poor ones that they seem to have frightened the weak in the past with the discus from their stronghold, and bids them leave that, live rightly and guard their lives.
nuance: The addressees are the envoys or the court; the verse also answers Asvagriva through them. The final plea to live rightly belongs to Tivittan's speech.

title: சீயவதைச் சருக்கம் 689-711 (6/11)
theme: Acuvakanthan's envoys return from the princes, and his minister conjures a magic lion to rouse and ruin the prince; the envoys then taunt Tivittan with the lion, and he vows to split its mouth and goes out alone with Vijayan.
source_issues: Verse 689: the opening word leaves open whether the verse is a conditional; the speaker is inferred from 683 to 688.
Verse 692 and elsewhere: அரிமஞ்சு ல வன் is split by the word division and taken as one name.
Verse 703: line 2 reads விளையை; taken as a misprint for இளையை.
Verses 708 and 710: line 3 is obscure; the sense is taken loosely.

cast.role: the red-eyed tall one, hero of the tale; the younger prince, called sea-hued
the elder prince, called conch-hued
the two princes, together
the rival king of the discus, who laughs at the prince's refusal
the envoys the rival king sends to demand tribute and, later, to taunt the prince
the rival king's minister who plans the trap (Arimanjulavan, taken as a name)
the Vidyadhara commissioned to take the shape of a lion

reading: The speaker tells the tribute-seeker that nothing is to be gained from coming to the mountain, since the arrows of victory will fall to fill his heart.
nuance: The grammar is clipped and the opening word may turn the verse into a conditional; it is read as the prince's defiance continuing the speech begun at 683, with the speaker inferred, not named.

reading: The speaker bids the envoys go and tell their lord that, if a rule exists for dealing with those who refuse tribute, he may try it, and that he need not be scolded as women scold.
nuance: The speech is the prince's open invitation to a test; the next scenes show the minister taking it up by a trick.
event: Tivittan sends the envoys back with a defiant message for their king.

reading: After the threat, the envoys are given gold and a company of fragrant-garlanded women, and, ashamed and shaken, leave thinking the foe too strong for their king.
event: The envoys receive gold and women, then depart in fear of the strong enemy.

tamil: போகிய தூதர் தங்கோன் பொலங்கழ றெழுத லஞ்சி
யாகிய தறிந்து சூழு மரிமஞ்சு லவனைக் கண்டே
யேகிய புகழி னானைக் கண்டது மீயப் பட்ட
தோகையஞ் சாய லார்தங் குழாங்களு நெதியுஞ் சொல்லி
reading: The envoys, afraid of what their king's rising anger will bring, find the minister and report both what was said and the women and wealth they were given.
nuance: Whether அரிமஞ்சுலவன் is a name or a title is not fixed by the verse; it is taken as the minister's name because 693 and 700 call the hearer the minister.
event: The envoys report to the minister Arimanjulavan.

tamil: மீட்டிளங் குமரர் கண்டு விடுசுட ரிலங்கு நக்கு
மோட்டிளங் கண்ணி தீய முனித்தழன் முழங்க நோக்கி
யூட்டிலங் குருவக் கோலோர் தங்களுக் குரைத்த வெல்லாம்
தோட்டிலங் குருவத் தொங்க லமைச்சற்குச் சொல்லி யிட்டார்
reading: The envoys repeat to the minister everything the red-hued princes had told them, and the verse gives the princes' laughter and fiery looks.
nuance: The syntax of lines 2 to 3 is tangled; it is read as the envoys reporting the princes' mocking reply.
event: The envoys tell the minister the princes' words.

tamil: பெரும்பகை யதனைக் கேட்டாற் பெரியவன் சிறிது நோனா
சுரும்பிவர் தொடையன் மார்பன் சூழ்ச்சி கொண் மனத்தனானான்
reading: The wise minister, hearing of the great quarrel, thinks that his king will not bear it for a moment and turns his mind to a way of turning the quarrel aside.
event: The minister weighs how to meet the quarrel.

tamil: மின்றொடர்ந் திலங்கு பூணான் விளைவுறா விளைமை தன்னா
னன்றுதீ தென்னுந் தேர்ச்சி நவின்றில னாத லால்யா
னொன்ற வோர் மாயங் காட்டி யுளைவித்துக் குறுக வோடிக்
reading: The minister, judging the young prince not yet schooled to tell good from ill, resolves to show him a trick that will enrage him and drive him to run into a lion on the mountain.
nuance: The minister's judgement of Tivittan is his own and is not confirmed by the verse; the story goes on to test it.
event: The minister plans to lure Tivittan into the path of a conjured lion.

tamil: அன்னண மனத்தி னாலே யிழைத்தரி கேது வென்னு
மின்னணங் குருவப் பைம்பூண் விஞ்சையன் றன்னைக் கூவிக்
கன்னவி றோளி னாற்குக் கருமமீ தென்று காட்டி
மன்னுமோர் மாயச் சீய மாகென வகுத்து விட்டான்
reading: The minister calls the Vidyadhara Arikethu, shows him the task and commissions him to take the form of a lasting magic lion.
event: The minister commissions Arikethu to turn himself into a magic lion.

tamil: ஒள்ளெரி நெறிப்பட் டன்ன சுரியுளை மலைகண் போழும்
வள்ளுகிர் மதர்வைத் திங்கட் குழவிவா ளெயிற்றுப் பைங்க
ணுள்ளெரி யுமிழ நோக்கி வுருமென வதிரும் பேழ்வாய்க்
கொள்ளரி யுருவு கொண்டான் கொடியவன் கடிய சூழ்ந்தான்
reading: The commissioned man takes the shape of a lion whose claws split mountains and whose fiery eyes and gaping mouth thunder.
event: Arikethu takes on the fierce form of a lion.

tamil: இலைத்தடஞ் சோலை வேலி யிமவந்த மடைந்து நீண்ட
சிலைத்தடந் தோளி னார்தஞ் சிந்துநா டதனைச் சேர்ந்து
மலைத்தடம் பிளந்து சிந்த மாண்புடை பெயர முந்நீ
ரலைத்துடன் கலங்கி விண்பா லதிரநின் றுரறி யிட்டான்
reading: The lion-shape goes to the Himalaya and the land of the Sindhu people and roars until mountains split, the ocean churns and the sky echoes.
event: The false lion roars over the Himalaya and Sindhu land.

tamil: பொடித்தலை புலம்பிக் கானம் போழ்ந்துமா நெரிந்து வீழ
வடித்தலை கலங்கி வேழம் பிடிகளோ டலறி யாழப்
புடைத்துழிப் பதடி போலத் துறுகற்கள் புரண்டு பொங்க
விடித்தலின் மனித்த ரெல்லா மெயிறுற விறுகிச் சோர்ந்தார்
reading: The roar flattens the forest, makes elephants cry out with their mates, sends boulders rolling and leaves people clenched and fainting.
event: The lion's roar spreads terror among animals and people.
