tamil: அப்படி யவனை யவ்வா றமைத்தபி னமைச்ச னாங்கண்
மெய்ப்படை தெரிந்து சொன்ன தூதுவ ரவரை மீட்டே
யிப்படி யிவைகள் சொல்லிப் பெயர்மினீ ரென்று வென்றிக்
கைப்படை நவின்ற வெம்போர்க் காளையைக் கனற்ற விட்டான்
reading: When the lion has been made ready, the minister recalls the envoys with a message and sets them to inflame the battle-trained youth.
event: The minister sends the envoys back to enrage Tivittan.

reading: The envoys descend by the river's path and tell their message to the sons of the Podanam king, where they walk with their host.
event: The envoys reach the princes and deliver their message.

reading: The envoys tell the prince that when they reported the tribute word, the refusal and his message, their king, fragrant-haired, said 'good, good' and laughed.
nuance: The envoys, not the narrator, say the king laughed; the laugh is their report of his contempt.
event: Acuvakanthan laughs on hearing the prince's refusal.

reading: The envoys say that when their king heard from their mouths that the prince had called him young, he did not weigh his own light and strength, called it the talk of a child of grace, and sat unangered.
nuance: Line 2 reads விளையை, taken as a misprint for இளையை. The king's calm is belittlement of the prince, not the self-command the Naladiyar praises.
event: Acuvakanthan, told he has been called young, shrugs the word off.

reading: The envoys carry their king's word: the proud little one who set out to take tribute and land cannot kill the thunder-voiced lion in the cave, if he knows his strength.
nuance: The words are the enemy king's own, put in his envoys' mouth; the reader knows from 696 to 699 that the lion is a magic shape sent for the purpose.
event: The envoys relay the king's taunt about the lion.

reading: The envoys end their report, and the younger prince asks in astonishment whether a lion in the land's mountain peak kills its creatures with a roar that splits the hills.
nuance: Line 1 is the envoys' own closing words; lines 2 to 4 are the prince's question, which the verse frames in the narrator's voice.
event: Tivittan hears of the lion and questions the envoys.

tamil: அளவி ணீன் முழை யுறைகின்ற தடிகளென் றுரைத்தார்
reading: The envoys answer that in the prince's own Sindhu land the lion cannot be removed by anyone, and that it lives in a long cave of the gem hill, drinking life with its thunder.
event: The envoys confirm to Tivittan that a lion terrorises the land.

tamil: னேயிப் பெற்றியே விளை த்தில னாயினும் வேந்தன்
reading: The prince answers that he will split the lion's mouth and tear its body in two, and that if he fails the king is a child who talked like a ghost; he sets out.
nuance: The vow is conditional: Tivittan stakes the king's reproach as a child on his failure, and turns the insult of 703 back on him.
event: Tivittan vows to kill the lion and leaves.

reading: The prince swears that the tusked elephants should return to their stalls and the fire-eyed warriors who ply weapons should hold back from the fight.
nuance: The second half of line 3 is obscure and the sense of the oath is taken from the narrator's closing word.
event: Tivittan swears the elephants and armed men must stay.

tamil: இவரு மாமணிக் கொடுஞ்சிய விவுளித் தேர் காலாட்
reading: The prince adds that the chariots, horses and foot soldiers should also stay in camp, and none may come with him.
event: Tivittan orders the chariots, horses and foot to stay behind.

reading: After the city's noise is hushed, the sea-hued prince goes forth, and the conch-hued prince resolves to go with him.
nuance: Lines 2 and 3 are hard to construe; the two princes are read from the epithets sea-hued and conch-hued.
event: Tivittan sets out and Vijayan resolves to go with him.

reading: The two reach the haunt where the lion kills, with the fiery dust of the hill path settling on the trodden path of the elephant-necked riders' feet.
event: The princes reach the place where the lion kills.

title: சீயவதைச் சருக்கம் 712-734 (7/11)
theme: On the mountain Tivittan rouses the lion that has hidden in its cave, tears it apart, and tells Vijayan the harm is gone; then Vijayan, pleased, names for his brother the crystal, lotus pools, elephants and gems that the mountain's beauty offers.
source_issues: Verses 713, 715, 719, 727, 728, 729, 730, 733, 734: compressed grammar or broken word division make the sense uncertain.
Verses 717 and 718: a lion flees into a cave in 717, and a lion king sleeps in a pit in 718; the text does not say whether it is one lion.

cast.role: the younger prince, called the dark-hued one and the younger
Tivittan's elder brother, called the conch-hued one
the two princes who have come to the mountain
the lion that hides in the cave and is killed
the gods of the sky who watch

reading: The fire-maned lion, seeing the heroes who have come, roars like thunder, and the rocks of the mountain split, crumble and turn to powder.
event: The lion sees the two princes arrive and its roar shatters the rocks around.

reading: The dark-hued prince binds on his anklets, bracelets, crest and curled hair, and the lion is broken by one whose strength is like the lion's own.
nuance: The last line is compressed and the word division doubtful: it can be read as the prince's cry and the lion's fall, or as the lion splitting something, so the sense is not fixed.
event: Tivittan arms himself for the fight with ornaments tied on and hair bound.

reading: With the cliffs crumbling and no place left to flee, the green-eyed lion takes its fierce shape and springs on him, and the red-eyed dark tall one prevails by his speed while Death and the quarters of the sky shake.
nuance: The Tamil says the lion 'took a form' (உருவுகொண்டு), which hints at more than an animal; these verses do not say what.
event: The lion leaps on Tivittan and he overcomes it by his swiftness.

reading: In his leap his feet do not touch the ground, the bracelet-hung arms swing, and his hair, garland and chains rise off his shoulders and neck.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are compressed and the nouns hard to join to their verbs; the sense is the speed of the leap and is held loosely.
event: Tivittan leaps so that his feet leave the ground and his ornaments fly up.

tamil: முரங்கொ டோ ளவன் விரனுதி யுறவுடைந் தொழிந்த
reading: Trees are torn up by the roots, deer and birds that had run along fall to the ground in terror, and the crests of the mountain break at the touch of his fingertips.
event: The force of the hero's blows uproots trees, scatters beasts and breaks the peaks.

reading: Clouds close in, rocks of the crest pile together, the forest deity dances for joy, and the one in the lion's form flees into a cave of the bright mountain and hides.
nuance: The forest deity's dance is read as joy at the lion's flight; the verb is clipped.
event: The lion flees into a cave and hides.

reading: The younger prince, great in praised fame, moves fast, the earth shakes and the great mountain trembles, and the lion king who lives in the pit stirs from his sleep.
nuance: Verse 717 had the lion fleeing into a cave; here a lion king sleeps in a pit. The text does not say whether one lion or two is meant.
event: Tivittan's speed shakes the mountain and wakes the lion in the pit.

reading: Angered that the lion hid in the dark cave, the strong one bids it live long and split the great mountain, and stands at the cave-mouth roaring until the world shakes and the hill's echo answers with open mouth.
nuance: The first two lines are the taunt, its sarcasm heard in 'live long' (வாழிய); the word division at line 3 joins the speaker's name to the verb.
event: Tivittan taunts the hidden lion and roars at the mouth of its cave.

reading: At the roar the lion, enraged, blazes at fang and eye, answers in a counter-roar, and the cave and the great mountain split and burst.
event: The lion answers the challenge with a roar that bursts the cave.

reading: With burning eyes, gaping mouth, bright claws, thick feet, curled mane and gleaming curved fangs, the lion rises out of the darkness of the cave.
event: The lion comes out of the cave.

reading: Its fearless nature swells with its great strength and fame, as if it were a lion that had scooped up the world, and the gods of the sky tremble.
event: The lion comes forth in full might and the gods tremble.

reading: As the furious lion rises to drink the blood running from his chest, he treads on its mane, seizes it by the curved fangs in his big hand, and the lion lies torn to strips.
event: Tivittan treads on the rising lion, grips its fangs and tears it apart.

reading: The gods, with fingers on their lips, marvel that this one has destroyed in anger a lion able to kill a thousand lions, or thousands upon thousands of beasts.
nuance: Line 3 is a cry of wonder (ஏ) that the gods use, not a statement by the narrator.
event: The gods stand amazed at the killing of the lion.

reading: The slain lion's blood runs down the rock with rut-water, broken white tusks and bright pearls, like the Ganga washing down vermilion mud.
nuance: The pearls and tusks are the lion's spoil: it had killed elephants.

reading: The famed one, neither glad nor amazed, goes to his brother and says that he has put away this harm and they should now go to Podanapuram.
nuance: His lack of exultation is the point of line 1; the word is 'harm' (ஏதம்), so the lion is treated as a fault in the land to be removed, not as a rival.
event: Tivittan tells Vijayan the harm is removed and proposes returning to Podanapuram.

reading: Glad at his younger brother's strength, Vijayan answers that before the flow of this blood is left, they must first see the mountain's low slopes.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are clipped and the exact reason for staying is not clear.
event: Vijayan, pleased at Tivittan's strength, asks to see the mountain before leaving.

tamil: வாங்கு நீரணி வளை வண்ண னுரைக்கிய வலித்தான்
reading: Seeing the mountain's beauty, the younger prince, whose anklets kings praise, marvels with wide eyes, and the conch-hued one begins to answer, kindly, that these are works of great merit.
nuance: Line 3 may be Vijayan's own words; the break between narration and speech is not marked.
event: Tivittan marvels at the mountain and Vijayan begins to explain what he sees.

reading: Vijayan tells the hero that what shows white in the grove, where the wind brings flower-dust and honey-drops and the bees do not stop humming, is no pool but a chamber of crystal.
nuance: The word division of the first line and the verb 'kollena' are hard to fix, so the sense is a loose one.
event: Vijayan names the crystal walls that look like water.

reading: Vijayan says that the pools where bees dark as a bull hum over lotus on stalks, and where silvery fish leap and tear the flowers, are no pools.
nuance: Line 3 is the hardest in the passage: its words for the fish and the broad leaf are guesses.
event: Vijayan names a mirage of lotus pools on the mountain.

reading: Vijayan says that where the hill-side darkens under long drops and men shiver with a roar, the dark shapes in which lightning flashes are no clouds but elephants.
event: Vijayan names the elephants that look like clouds.

reading: Vijayan says that the white-haired beasts that graze the bean-fields and drink the stream, and drift like young clouds on the great hill, are the yaks moving about.
nuance: The addressee is the sea-hued prince, 'kadalvanna' in line 4, which fits Tivittan.
event: Vijayan names the yaks that look like clouds.

reading: Vijayan says that the bright gems lying where mountain water leaps in the rock hollows glow like a young crescent moon shining in the night sky.
nuance: The word division of lines 1 and 2 is broken.
event: Vijayan names the gems that glow like moons.

reading: Vijayan says that in the dark of the plantains, bamboo and hard-to-see caves, the gems seem to burn with the gold glow of the prince's own ornaments.
nuance: Lines 2 and 3 are broken by word division.
event: Vijayan likens the mountain's jewels to the prince's ornaments.

title: சீயவதைச் சருக்கம் 735-757 (8/11)
theme: A stretch of sustained description of the mountain where the lion lives: first its perils (cloud, tangle, serpents, bears), then its gem rocks and a long catalogue of flowering trees, ending in lovers' comparisons. No event occurs; it prepares the lion hunt.
source_issues: Verses 735 to 741, 744 to 749 and 752 to 753: word division and compressed grammar leave the sense uncertain; flagged.
Verses 745 to 749 are word-play (yamaka) verses; readings give only the overall picture.
Verses 738 and 742 to 744 address a hearer; the speaker and hearer are not named and are inferred.

cast.role: unnamed speaker who points out the mountain to a hero, inferred from the second-person words in 738, 742 to 744
the unnamed hero addressed (a prince, by inference); 743 calls him broad-chested

reading: Cloud banks cover the mountain so thickly that day seems eaten by night, and torrents and seeping wet make the broad slopes impassable.
The slope is choked with tangled creepers, cane and bamboo, dark and many-kinded, and is said to be unfit to approach.
Great snakes with cave-wide mouths lie sleeping among boulder heaps, having swallowed the elephants that roamed there.
The speaker points out hissing snakes, growling beasts and elephant dens, and says these troubles are for all who are not 'ours'.
nuance: Whether the hearer is the same hero as in 742 and 743 is inferred; the verse itself only says 'see' (கண்டாய்).

reading: Clouds pour flood-water on the groves while the addressee is urged to go swiftly; the sense of the first lines is unclear.
Ground that looks sound hides pits or mire where elephants sink beyond saving, while a far glow flickers; the sense is doubtful.
Gem-studded rocks give off a glow like many moons, so bright that it dazzles those who look.
The speaker tells the hero that, since the seasons do not change here, this mountain can hardly be told apart from the heaven of the scriptures.
nuance: The heaven is called by the word for scripture (சுருதி); the verse compares scenery to it and makes no doctrinal claim.

reading: Jewel-rocks and stone chambers, mixed with fragrant kongu flowers, shine like old lamps against the sky.
A very short, compressed verse addressing a garlanded one with a question about rows or waves; its sense is unsettled.
In a word-play verse, mango trees rise on the slope, flowers spread, seepage never dries and the place turns dark as night.
In a word-play verse, young women with bangles and their companions pass the time in games in the broad groves.
The groves ring with bees and spread with opening flowers, where bangled women play and let petals fall, so that every place looks like their play.
Lotus and champak bloom spread over the slope; the fine second half of the verse is hard to parse.
A word-play verse on one word (elephant, snake, mountain, tree) describes sandal groves, humming bees, pollen and gem-spitting snakes, and says the place mocks the nagas' own world.
The verse lists the flowering trees of the slope, naming nirava, duruka and asoka among them.
The list of slope flowers goes on, with kodal, thondri, ingi and maruthu named.
Sandal and cool leaf-garlands stand ready for the women of the wild, and the branches hold out blossom garlands.
Kinnaras take pleasure here and mandara trees shine; the third line speaks of fear and the fearful.
Gold-bright kongu and vengai blooms spread among the rocks, like Indra's bow broken and fallen among dark clouds.
Heaps of blue-gem rock are half hidden by fallen blossom, like the hair-knots of women in fire-red cloth.
Sun-lit rock slabs strewn with pollen look like the red-cloth beds where young lovers lie.

tamil: அழலணி யசோகஞ் செந்தா தணிந்துதே னரற்ற நின்று
நிழலணி மணிக்கன் னீல நிறத்தொடு நிமிர்ந்த தோற்றம்
குழலணி குஞ்சி மைந்தர் குங்குமக் குழம்பு பூசி
எழிலணி திகழ நின்றா லெனையநீ ரனைய தொன்றே
reading: Red ashoka blossom hums with bees against blue rocks, and the sight is compared to youths smeared with saffron paste and adorned.

title: சீயவதைச் சருக்கம் 758-780 (9/11)
theme: Vijayan shows Tivittan the gods' hill and its play, points to the blood of the lion Tivittan has killed and praises the prince's duty to risk his body for the world's creatures and the form of fame that outlasts it, and the two then enter a scorching desert.
source_issues: Verse 767: line 2 had a stray space before a dead consonant, repaired in the core text.
Verse 778: line 3 reads நீர்ககடல் with a doubled letter, taken for the sea-hued prince's epithet.
Verses 758 to 776: the speaker is Vijayan, taken from 767 and 768, where the poet says the conch-hued one showed these sights and spoke; none of these verses names him.
Verse 777 reads தங்கதை, taken as தம் கதை (their mace); doubtful.

cast.role: the elder prince, called the conch-hued and the white-wave-hued, who shows and speaks
the younger prince, called the sea-hued, who killed the lion
the two princes, together

tamil: இணைந்துதேன் முழங்க விண்ட வேழிலம் பாலை வெண்பூ
மணந்துதா தணிந்து தோன்று மரகத மணிக்கற் பாறை
கணங்கெழு களிவண் டாலப் பாசடை கலந்த பொய்கை
reading: The speaker points to a hill-rock of emerald hung with white flowers and pollen, humming with bees, beside a pool thick with white lotus.

tamil: காரிருட் குவளிக் கண்ணிக் கதிர்நகைக் கனபொற் றோட்டுக்
கூரிருள் சுரிபட் டன்ன குழலணி கொடிறுண் கூந்தல்
பேரிருள் கிழியத் தோன்றும் பிறையெயிற் றமர நோக்கிற்
சூரர மகளிர் வாழு மிடமிவை சுடர்ப வெல்லாம்
reading: The speaker says these shining places are where the dark-haired, crescent-toothed women of the sura race live.

tamil: வாரிரு புடையும் வீக்கி வடஞ்சுமந் தெழுந்து வேங்கை
யேரிருஞ் சுணங்கு சிந்தி யெழுகின்ற விளமென் கொங்கைக்
காரிருங் குழலங் கொண்டைக் கதிர்நகைக் கனகப் பைம்பூண்
நீரர மகளிர் கண்டாய் நிறைபுனற் றடத்து வாழ்வார்
reading: The speaker says the high-breasted women with gold ornaments who live in the brimming pool are the water-women.

tamil: மேகமேற் றவழ்ந்து வேய்கண் மிடைத்துகீ ழிருண்ட தாழ்வர்
ஏகமா மலையி னெற்றி யிருஞ்சுனைத் தடங்க ளெல்லாம்
நாகமா மகளி ரென்னு நங்கையர் குடையப் பொங்கி
மாகமேற் றரங்கஞ் சிந்தி மணியறை கழுவு மன்றே
reading: The speaker says the nagas' women bathe in the mountain pools, which swell and wash the gem rocks.

tamil: ஆவிவீற் றிருந்த காத லவரொடு கவரி வேய்ந்து
நாவின்வீற் றிருந்த நாறு நளிர்வரைச் சிலம்பின் மேயார்
காவிவீற் றிருந்த கண்ணார் கந்தர்வ மகளிர் கண்டாய்
பாவிவீற் றிருந்த பண்ணி னமுதினாற் படைக்கப் பட்டார்
reading: The speaker says the lotus-eyed women who live with their lovers on the cool slopes are gandharva women, made of the nectar of song.

tamil: அலங்கிண ரணிந்த விஞ்சை யரிவைய ரிடங்கள் கண்டாய்
விலங் கலின் விளங்கு கின்ற வெள்ளிவெண் கபாடமாடம்
இலங்கொளி மகரப் பைம்பூ ணியக்கிய ரிடங்கள் கண்டாய்
நலங்கிளர் பசும்பொற் கோயி னகுகின்ற நகர மெல்லாம்
reading: The speaker says the silver mansions of the hill are the dwellings of Vidyadhara women and yakshis, and the whole town laughs in gold.

tamil: போய்நிழற் றுளும்பு மேனிப் புணர்முலை யமிர்த னாரோ
டாய்நிழற் றுளும்பு வானோ ரசதியா டிடங்கள் கண்டாய்
சேய்நிழற் றிகழுஞ் செம்பொற் றிலதவே திகைய வாய
பாய்நிழற் பவழச் செங்காற் பளிக்கு மண் டபங்க ளெல்லாம்
reading: The speaker points to the crystal halls with coral pillars where gods play with their consorts.

tamil: எழின்மணிச் சுடர்கொண் மேனி யிமையவ ரிடங்கள் கண்டாய்
முழுமணிப் புரிசை வேலி முத்தமண் டபத்த வாய
கழுமணிக் கபாட வாயிற் கதிர்நகைக் கனக ஞாயிற்
செழுமணிச் சிகர கோடிச் சித்திர கூட மெல்லாம்
reading: The speaker says the gem-bright mansions and picture halls with jewelled gates are the dwellings of the gods.

tamil: தும்பிவாய் துளைக்கப் பட்ட கீசகம் வாயுத் தன்னால்
வம்பவாங் குழலி னேங்க மணியரை யரங்க மாக
உம்பர்வான் மேக சால மொலிமுழாக் கருவி யாக
நம்பதேன் பாட மஞ்ஞை நாடக நவில்வ காணாய்
reading: The speaker says the hill itself plays a drama, with wind through beetle-bored bamboo as flute, clouds as drum and peacocks as dancers.
nuance: கீசகம் is taken as bamboo that wind makes a flute of; the line is hard to construe and the sense of the first two lines is a guess.

tamil: பொன்னவிர் மகரப் பைம்பூட் பொலங்குழை யிலங்கு சோதிக்
கன்னவில் வயிரத் திண்டோட் கடல்வண்ண னுவப்பக் காட்டி
மன்னவின் றிறைஞ்சுஞ் செய்கை வளைவண்ணன் மலையின் மேலால்
இன்னன பகர்ந்து சொல்லு மெல்லையு ணீங்க லுற்றார்
reading: The poet says that after the speaker had shown the sea-hued prince these sights and said such things, they went on.
nuance: Grammar of lines 2 to 3 is loose; the conch-hued one is taken as the speaker and the sea-hued as the one shown, as the brothers are named in 778.
event: Vijayan shows Tivittan the sights of the hill and the two move on.

tamil: பாசிலைப் பாரி சாதம் பரந்துபூ நிரந்த பாங்கர்
மூசின மணிவண் டார்க்கு முருகறா மூரிக் குன்றம்
காய்சின வேலி னான்றன் கண்களி கொள்ளக் காட்டி
யோசனை யெல்லை சார்ந்து பின்னையிஃ துரைக்க லுற்றான்
reading: The poet says that, having shown the hill of bees and flowering trees for the spear-bearer's delight, the speaker reached the end of a league and began to speak.
nuance: Who is meant by the one with the angry spear is not fixed; he is taken as Tivittan.
event: Vijayan shows Tivittan another hill, walks a league and begins to speak.

tamil: வலிகற்ற மதர்வைப் பைங்கண் வாளொயிற் றரங்கச் சீயங்
கலிகற்ற களிறுண் பேழ்வாய்க் கலிங்கினா னிழிந்து போந்து
குலிகச்சே றலம்பிக் குன்றங் கொப்புளித் திட்ட தொப்ப
ஒலிகற்ற வுதிர நீத்த மொழுகுவ தின்ன நோக்காய்
reading: The speaker points to the stream of blood running down from where the lion had come out of its cave, like red clay that the hill has vomited.
nuance: The verse is the fruit of the astrologer's word of soolamani 409, that within a month Tivittan would split a lion's mouth; here the deed is already done and seen only as blood.
event: Vijayan points out the blood of the lion that Tivittan killed.

tamil: வெம்பவேங் குயிரை யெல்லாம் விழுங்கிய வெகுண்டு நோக்கிச்
கம்பமா வுலகந் தன்னைக் கண்டிடுங் களிகொள் சீயம்
நம்பநீ யழித்த தல்லா னகையெயிற் றதனை நண்ணல்
வம்பறா மகரப் பைம்பூண் வானவர் தமக்கு மாமோ
reading: The speaker says the lion that swallowed lives and saw the world as trembling was beyond even the gods, so none but Tivittan could have destroyed it.

tamil: ஆங்குநீ முனிந்த போழ்தி னரிது வகல நோக்கி
வாங்குநீர் வண்ண கேளாய் மாயமா மதித்து நின்றே
னோங்குநீண் மலையின் றாழ்வா ரொலிபுன லுதிர யாறு
வீங்கிவந் திழிந்த போழ்து மெய்யென வியப்புச் சென்றேன்
reading: The speaker says that when Tivittan raged he watched from afar and took it for illusion, and wondered when the roaring stream of blood came down the slope and proved it real.
nuance: மாயமா மதித்து நின்றேன் may mean he took it for illusion, or for a marvel; the first is followed.
event: Vijayan watches Tivittan's rage and the stream of blood after he kills the lion.

tamil: குன்றிற்கு மருங்கு வாழுங் குழூஉக்களிற் றினங்க ளெல்லா
மன்றைக்கன் றலறக் கொன்றுண் டகலிடம் பிளப்பச் சீறி
வென்றிக்கண் விருப்பு நீங்கா வெங்கண்மா விதனைக் கொன்றா
யின்றைக்கொண் டுலக மெல்லா மினிதுகண் படுக்கு மன்றே
reading: The speaker says Tivittan killed the lion that had eaten the herds of elephants, so that from this day the whole world sleeps in peace.
nuance: The Jain work praises a killing; the verse justifies it by the lion's own killing and the safety it brings, and does not weigh it against non-killing.
event: Tivittan killed the lion that preyed on the elephant herds.

tamil: உரைசெய்நீ ளுலகின் வாழு முயிர்களுக் குறுகண் கண்டால்
வரைசெய்தோண் மைந்தர் வாழ்க்கை மதிக்கிலார் வனப்பின் மிக்கார்
திரைசெய்நீ ருலகங் காக்குஞ் செய்கை மேற் படைக்கப் பட்ட
அரசர்தம் புதல்வர்க் கையா வறம்பிறி ததனி லுண்டோ
reading: The speaker says that when living beings are in danger, strong-armed princes do not weigh their own lives, for the king's sons have no duty beyond guarding the world.

tamil: கற்றவர் கடவுட் டானஞ் சேர்ந்தவர் களைக ணில்லா
ரற்றவ ரந்த ணாள ரன்றியு மனைய நீரார்க்
குற்றதோ ரிடுக்கண் வந்தா லுதவுதற் குரித்தன் றாயில்
பெற்றவிவ் வுடம்பு தன்னாற் பெறுபய னில்லை மன்னா
reading: The speaker says that if the body cannot help the learned, the pious, the helpless, the ascetics and the brahmins when trouble falls on them, it brings no fruit, king.
nuance: மன்னா is the address; whether it names Tivittan or turns to a general king is not clear. The first line's list of kinds of people is also hard to divide.

tamil: மன்னுயிர் வருத்தங் கண்டும் வாழ்வதே வலிக்கு மாயி
லன்னவ னாண்மை யாவ தலிபெற்ற வழகு போலா
மென்னையான் கொடுத்தும் வையத் திடுக்கணோய் கெடுப்ப னென்னும்
நின்னையே போலு நீரார் நிலமிசை நிலவி நின்றார்
reading: The speaker says a man who lives on while watching beings suffer has the manliness of a eunuch's beauty, and that people like Tivittan, who offer even themselves to end the world's pain, stand on earth.
nuance: அலிபெற்ற அழகு is the verse's own measure of the man who lives on; line 3 reads எனையான் as 'myself' and line 4 as praise of Tivittan.

tamil: ஒருவன திரண்டி யாக்கை யூன்பயி னரம்பின் யாத்த
உருவமும் புகழு மென்றாங் கவற்றினூழ் காத்து வந்து
மருவிய வுருவ மிங்கே மறைந்துபோ மற்ற யாக்கை
திருவமர்ந் துலக மேத்தச் சிறந்துபின் னிற்கு மன்றே
reading: The speaker says a person has two forms, the one of flesh and sinew that vanishes here and the other of fame that outlasts it and is praised by the world.
nuance: யாக்கை in line 3 is taken as the other body of fame; ஊழ் காத்து வந்து may mean the body is kept by fate until its time, but the clause is hard to construe.

reading: The poet says that, having said this, the two went with the mace through a cloud-hill forest of flowers into a fierce desert, where the sun stood at noon and scorched the earth.
nuance: தங்கதை is taken as தம் கதை, their mace, the line is not secure.
event: The two princes enter a scorching wasteland at noon.

reading: The poet says that after they reached the desert, the white-wave-hued prince bade the sea-hued one see how this fierce forest was.
nuance: Line 3 has a doubled letter in நீர்ககடல், taken for the sea-hued prince's name; the content of Vijayan's words is not given in these lines.
event: Vijayan speaks to Tivittan after they reach the desert.

reading: The poet says that in the desert the bamboo splits and drops pearls, the rocky ground breathes fire from cracks, and the water the clouds should give is gone.
nuance: The desert description is hard to divide into words; the pearl-bamboo and the sense of dried water are read from lines 2 and 3 only roughly.

reading: The poet says the tall bamboo ripens and sparks, scattering parched grain over the rocks, which seethe all around.
nuance: உக்க நெற்பொரி is taken as parched rice grains fallen from the bamboo; the verse is a picture of heat and the grammar is unsettled.

title: சீயவதைச் சருக்கம் 781-803 (10/11)
theme: On the road to the lion's forest, Vijayan names the wilderness and the guards of the forest, then shows Tivittan the flowering woods, hill-fields and marutham country one by one, in a long series of landscape verses with no action.
source_issues: Verses 781 to 785: the speaker is taken as Vijayan from 778, which says he spoke of the fierce forest; the verses do not name him.
Verses 781 to 789, 797, 799, 801 to 803: the word division and compressed grammar leave the sense uncertain; flagged.
Verse 786: the epithets are heavy and the line division is rough.

cast.role: the elder prince, the moon-hued one who shows the country to Tivittan, so taken from 778 and 800
the younger prince, the red-eyed dark one addressed as 'kazhaloy' (801) and 'aaramaarba' (797)

reading: With the red sun beating down, the omai trees stand tall and sound like a house of mourning kin, as the elephants hide from the heat in their shade.
nuance: The mourning-house simile gives the dry forest a grief of its own; the grammar of the third line and the word division are rough.

reading: In the dry season the nelli's withered branches creak, and the sun's glare drops its shade as though fire were falling from the branches all around.
nuance: The lines are compressed and the first line's sense of weeping or drought is not settled; read with caution.

reading: The snake rages while the gloriosa climbs, and the lily flowers on the cloud-fed shoots stand like a bow-wielding deer-hunter's hand, so the rain seems about to return.
nuance: The picture of cloud-sent rain and gloriosa blossoms is hard to construe; the verse may turn on a simile of the flower as a hand.

reading: Seeing the white chariot rush past, the thirsty deer herd droops like a noble who begged from a worthless man's eyes and met blame.
nuance: The simile ranks begging of the base as a stain on the high-born, which the narrator accepts as common ground; the first two lines are loosely worded.

reading: The drummers and bowmen who do cruel deeds and eat the border land's spoil guard the forest, and none stand there but the addressee's own servants.
nuance: The guards are the king's own hunters, so the wild place is held by men who live by violence on his behalf.

reading: Naming the lands that the lion-conquering red-eyed one and the king of the white-tusked elephant hold, the moon-hued prince praises them and says these are the addressee's.
nuance: The epithets are heavy and the line division is rough; the identification of the moon-hued one with Vijayan comes from 778 and 800.
event: Vijayan, praising the country, begins to show Tivittan the lands that are his to hold.

reading: The land of our lord abounds in water that rises in all seasons, in the grace of the monsoon and in floods that swell in the rivers.
nuance: The grammar is compressed; the speaker is taken as Vijayan, 'our lord' being the king.

reading: The east wind dances, the bees sing, and the creeper-woman watches the play while the konrai drops gold and the gloriosa turns its hand away.
nuance: The whole verse is a play with the wind as dancer, the flowers as audience and the bees as singers.

reading: The gloriosa that opens its hand, the dark water lilies, the wide-open eyes of the flower rounds, the smiling jasmine and the curled clusters bend and bear fruit.
nuance: The syntax runs on into 790; the verse is a list whose verb comes in the next verse.

reading: Fruit that reddens like a lip, vines slim as a waist and everything seen catching the eye, so the forest looks like a garland of women.
nuance: The forest is likened to women, which is the poet's usual way of praising a land's loveliness.

reading: Jasmine spread under the moonlight, bees singing on the sandbank and the places of white sand look to one side as though the moon had spread.
The bees circling the nectar-rich blossoms in the jambul grove make the forest look dark, as if a lump of night were sleeping there.
The ripe tondai fruit and the thorny coral-red flowers of the thonri make the forest glow like an evening sky.
The golden konrai, the aghil creeper and the pollen-laden blossoms make the whole country look like molten gold.
nuance: The images of gold and the flowers' dust are heaped on one another, a way of praising the country's wealth.

reading: The peacocks dance and the green crops move with the wind like a sea of water in the monsoon-glad forest.
At the sound of the cowherds' and bards' drums the peacocks dance and the deer herds delight in the festival of the land beside the hill.
nuance: The festival is imagined, with the peacocks as dancers and the deer as spectators.

reading: The riverbank, where sand-banks, creepers and the pollen of flowers lie, looks like a sacrificial hall, and the addressee is said to wear a garland on his chest.
nuance: The sacrificial-hall simile (யாகசாலை) is the poem's picture of orderly beauty; it says nothing for or against the rite, and the Jain poet uses it as a plain figure.

reading: The cows' milk streams from udders as the calves suck, the birds feed and sing, and the jasmine opens as if to taste the flow.
nuance: Milk, flowers and birds are given human mouths and gestures.

reading: The clouds drip water on the hills, the jasmine opens in the fields, and the guests go on to the wide stretches where fish and water-birds dwell.
nuance: The last line shifts to the farming country, so the verse marks the travellers' passage from forest to field.

reading: The rain-fed nectar flows from the fresh-opened flowers into the marutham water, and the moon-bright prince tells his companion to look at this.
nuance: The last two lines name the speaker's glory, which makes this verse a turning point from the forest to the farm country.
event: Vijayan, pointing, tells Tivittan to look at the water of the farming country.

reading: The addressee is told to look at the fish that dart away and the young swans that rise from the shallows as the water swells, turning cloudy and bright.
nuance: The word division is broken; the sense of the first lines is only roughly clear.

reading: The jackfruit segments, the plantain's fruit and the heaps of mangoes in the orchard have become the places of the meeting of lovers and guests.
nuance: The sense of the last line is uncertain; 'kalavi' is taken as mingling or union.

reading: The monkeys eat the fruits of the mango, groan with fullness, and the male langur hides under the plantain leaf while the hill-field she-monkeys wail.
nuance: The picture of monkeys' wailing is played for comedy; the verse closes the series of 'look at this' verses.

title: சீயவதைச் சருக்கம் 804-826 (11/11)
theme: The two princes are shown the country and the city on the road, ride into Podanam by night amid the king's army, bow before the king who embraces them, and are asked by him about the forest dust in their hair, which Vijayan answers with a lion's ravage and Tivittan joins in.
source_issues: Verses 804 to 813: the speaker, hearer and sense of the descriptive verses are inferred; the yamaka word play and run-together words hide the syntax of 805 and 807 to 811.
Verse 821 line 1 has சிழ்ருவர் and line 2 களிதல், slips for words not recoverable from the text alone.
Verse 824 line 3 வேற்றுவன் தமர்கள் is obscure, and 811 ஒருமாதவளும் is doubtful.

cast.role: an unnamed speaker who shows the sights of the road and city to one hearer, 804 to 813
the elder prince, who answers the king
the younger prince, who speaks in 825
the two princes, Vijayan and Tivittan
the king of Podanam who receives his sons
the king's army that rides out to meet the princes
the maidens who hold lamps and bow to the princes
the fierce lion that came to ruin the king's forest

reading: The speaker points out honey dripping from the tips of young plantains and the shed buds of jasmine falling among the cool lotuses of the ponds.
nuance: The verses 804 to 813 point at things to look at (காண், கேள்) and are taken as the speech of an unnamed guide to one hearer (814 says it was told to 'him'); the Tamil does not name speaker or hearer. The yamaka word play and run-together words make the exact picture doubtful.

reading: The speaker points to lilies and lotus blooms among the paddy, the lotus flowers shaming a smile.
nuance: The grammar of lines 1 to 3 is broken by the word division; only the lotuses that outdo a smile are sure.

reading: The speaker shows the smoke of boiling sugar-cane juice rising and mixing with the high groves nearby, so that the place looks like a mountain with clouds.
nuance: The cane-boiling smoke is the one concrete sign of the countryside's work; the rest of the verse is simile.

reading: The verse describes a woman whose cheek, eyes and dark hair carry the dark-blue lily and the sheen of sapphire.
nuance: The repeated word கருநீல is the poet's play on sound; whether the woman is a particular one or a type of the country women is not shown.

reading: The verse describes a woman's forehead, lips, bangles and hair against the flowering செங்கிடை plants of the fields.
nuance: The repeated word வளர்செங்கிடை and the compressed syntax leave both the plant and the sense of each line uncertain.

reading: The verse describes a woman dressed in leaves and garlanded with the flowers of the water lily, set in a field rich with them.
nuance: The refrain வயலாம்பல் is word play and the clauses are hard to attach to a subject.

reading: The verse pictures a woman of the grove, in a place thick with lotus petals, gladdened as if by the blooming lotus.
nuance: The refrain வளர்தாமரையல்லி is word play; the sense is only roughly fixed.

reading: The speaker bids a hearer listen to what rises as a woman of shining hair, in search of fame, lets fruit and honey run.
nuance: The words ஒருமாதவளும் and கிளர்பார்வையுற are corrupt or obscure, and the verse's subject is not clear.

reading: The speaker shows the gem-lit city rising, its wall tops, tower tops and flags blending with the sun's rays.
nuance: From here to 813 the guide turns from the country to the city ahead, which sets up the arrival in 814.

reading: The speaker shows the altars of the city's sacrificers, where the smoke of the oblations of righteous Vedic brahmins rises over the groves.
nuance: The poet lets the Jain epic's own travellers see Vedic fire-offerings as a mark of a well-ordered city; he gives no view of the rite itself.

reading: The speaker's telling ends as the princes come to the golden city at nightfall, while the city sounds, and their want is gone.
nuance: வறுமை நீங்கினார் is taken as the end of the road's hardship; the line does not say whose want or of what kind.
event: The two princes reach the king's city, Podanam, at nightfall.

reading: The king's wide army of young elephants and bridled horses comes in a ring of dust to circle the princes, its extent beyond measure.
nuance: The verse says 'we could not measure' (அளந்தறிந்திலம்), a poet's voice in the plural that is not a character's.
event: The king's army rides out and circles the princes to bring them in.

reading: The princes appear in the king's golden city like a creeper of red flowers in a wood, while maidens hold lamps in their hands.
event: Maidens line the way with hand-lamps as the princes ride into the city.

reading: The poet describes the city's high houses, dim with the smoke of perfumes, as if they were hills of cool snow.
nuance: The simile of snow mountains is the poet's only comment; no person acts.

reading: The poet describes the city at night, the rays of the young moon falling on garlands and ornaments as if the ancient city slept.
nuance: The jasmine garlands and the moon-lit gems carry the sleep image; no event is given.

reading: As the princes reach the palace, maidens bow at their feet and the king in his gem crown bids the youths come in.
nuance: The words நம்பிமார் வருக are the king's, in the poet's telling.
event: The king orders the princes brought before him in the palace.

reading: The princes, afraid of what the king will do, bow so that their locks touch his feet while he stands uneasy at heart.
nuance: The verse says the princes fear (அஞ்சி) and the king's heart is bewildered (மருளுறு). It does not say why, so the setting is probably that the king had been anxious about them.
event: The princes bow low to the king, who is troubled in mind.

reading: The king calls both strong-armed sons to him and holds them close with both his arms.
nuance: Line 1 and 2 hold what look like slips of the text (சிழ்ருவர், களிதல்); the embrace itself is clear.
event: The king calls the two princes forward and embraces them both.

reading: The king looks gladly at his sons as the dust of forest flowers falls from their hair.
nuance: The pollen from the forest is the first sign, which 823 turns into a question, that the princes have been in the wild.
event: The king, glad, sees flower pollen from the forest fall from the princes' hair.

reading: The king asks why the dust of forest blooms clings in the hair of the two, and Vijayan replies.
nuance: The question itself is carried in lines 1 to 3 in broken syntax; its sense is taken from what Vijayan answers.
event: The king asks how forest dust came into the princes' hair, and Vijayan answers.

reading: Vijayan says a fierce lion came to ruin the forest round about the city's edge, and that when it was reported, this mighty servant drove it away.
nuance: The words வேற்றுவன் தமர்கள் and இவ்வாற்றல்சால் அடியன் are obscure; the verse is read as Vijayan crediting his brother (the 'mighty servant') with removing the lion, which 825 appears to support, but the Tamil of 824 does not name him.
event: Vijayan reports to the king that a lion had come to ravage the forest and was removed.

reading: Tivittan adds that he too went with him to the mountain side, and the king's life flowers back as he hears it.
nuance: The speaker is named only as 'the son of the garlanded lord' (சிறுவன்), taken as the younger prince; the verse leaves open what exactly the lion's end was.
event: Tivittan tells the king he went along too, and the king is gladdened.

reading: By the king's order the youths in their anklets reach their lodging behind the long gate under the sun-lit tower.
nuance: This closes the sarukkam; the last line's words பள்ளி பம்பலங்கள் are obscure and are taken as their resting place.
event: On the king's order the princes go to their lodging in the palace.

title: கல்யாணச் சருக்கம் 827-850 (1/13)
theme: After the lion's death the Vidyadhara king resolves to give his daughter to Tivittan, names the eight lords who guard his city, and raises a host of elephants, horses, chariots and foot to escort the bride, as a vimana of gems is conjured at the gate.
source_issues: 835 line 3: a pulli after a vowel sign was removed by the text repair.
827 line 2: பெர்ந்த looks like a misprint for பெயர்ந்த.
843 line 1: பேகொண் is probably for பேர்கொண்.
848 line 3: ஞான்ல is probably for ஞான்ற.
830, 831, 836: the lords' names are irregular or unclear (பிரீதிதிமா வர்த்த தனன், விருகவெல், கருடன்...அங்கதம்); the cast ids are the nearest readings.
841 line 1 has a stray split in மணித் தொழில்; the sense holds.

cast.role: the bride's father, the Vidyadhara king, named here only by epithets
the red-eyed hero who killed the lion
the moon-bright companion of Tivittan
the spy who brings the news of the lion
the king's kinsmen who take counsel with him
the king's troops, unnamed as a body
men of the host who announce the arrival
the king's younger brother, whose chariot bears the name of blazing fire
the lord of Aripuram
the king Arkakirti
one of the eight lords of the Vidyadhara king: lord of the city of Vardhamana, bright-limbed and lotus-eyed
one of the eight lords of the Vidyadhara king: lord who guards the Gandharva city, fair of form
one of the eight lords of the Vidyadhara king: lord who guards the fort called Gandhamadhanam, with a golden chariot
one of the eight lords of the Vidyadhara king: king of Chakravalam, named for an elephant-like strength
one of the eight lords of the Vidyadhara king: lord of the Devaravanam, whose chariot outshines the sun's
one of the eight lords of the Vidyadhara king: king of Vijayakoodam, likened to a young elephant lord
one of the eight lords of the Vidyadhara king: guardian of Kirutha Madhanam, whose name joins Garuda and the golden armlet
one of the eight lords of the Vidyadhara king: lord of a city ringed by water and lotus, who bears the earth with his strength

tamil: செங்கண்மால் சிங்கம் வென்று செழுமலர்த் திலகக் கண்ணித்
திங்கள்வாள் வண்ண னோடுந் திருநகர் பெர்ந்த பின்னை
அங்கண்மாற் குரிய நங்கை யரும்பெற லவட்குத் தாதை
வெங்கண்மாற் களிறன் னான்றன் றிறமினி விளம்ப லுற்றேன்.
reading: The poet says that after the red-eyed Tivittan, having beaten the lion, went back to the great city with the moon-bright Vijayan, he will now tell of the father of the maiden destined for him.
nuance: Line 2 reads பெர்ந்த where the sense wants பெயர்ந்த; the verse is a hinge that closes the lion episode and opens the wedding section.
event: Tivittan, having killed the lion, returns to the city with Vijayan, and the poet turns to the bride's father.

tamil: உற்றவான் குழவித் திங்க ளொளிமுழை யகட்டுப் போந்து
முற்றுவான் முளைத்த போலு மெயிறுடை மூரிச் சிங்கம்
மற்றம்மா லழித்த தல்லாம் வானமா றாகச் சென்ற
ஒற்றனா லுணர்ந்து வேந்த னுவகையங் கடலு ளாழ்ந்தான்.
reading: A spy brings the king word that the lion has been destroyed, and the king sinks into a sea of joy.
nuance: The lion is likened to a young moon coming out of a cave, so the beast's death is praised through the image of its own beauty.
event: A spy reports the lion's death to the Vidyadhara king, who rejoices.

tamil: கரியவாய் விலங்கி நீண்டு களிக்கய லிரண்டு தம்முட்
பொரியபோ கின்ற போலும் பொங்கரித் தடங்கட் பேதைக்
குரியமா லவற்குச் சென்று கொடுப்பனென் றுலகங் காக்கும்
பெரியவன் றமரோ டெண்ணிக் கடிவினை பெருக்க லுற்றான்.
reading: Thinking the maiden with dark long eyes fit only for the one who killed the lion, the king takes counsel with his kin and begins the wedding rites.
nuance: The daughter is given as a reward for the deed; her own wish is not spoken of, only the father's decision with his kin.
event: The Vidyadhara king resolves with his kin to give his daughter to Tivittan and begins the wedding preparations.

tamil: கிளரொளி மாடக் கோயிற் கின்னரர் கெழுவ லோவா
வளரொளி வயங்கு தோன்றல் வருத்தமா னத்து மன்னன்
உளரொளி யுமிழும் பூணான் பிரீதிதிமா வர்த்த தனனென் றோதும்
தளரொளி தயங்கு மேனித் தாமரைச் செங்க ணானே.
reading: The poet names one of the eight Vidyadhara lords, the lord of the city of Vardhamana, bright-limbed and lotus-eyed.
nuance: One of eight verses (830 to 837) that list the lords by city, each praised through his city, chariot or ornament. The name is written in an irregular form here, with a doubled syllable.

tamil: மண்ணலங் கனியுஞ் சாதி மணிமுழா வதிரு மாடக்
கண்ணலங் கனியுந் தோன்றல் கந்தருவ நகரங் காப்பான்
விண்ணலங் கனியுஞ் சீர்த்தி விருகவெல் கடிகொள் பேரான்
பெண்ணலங் கனியு நீர்மை பெருகிய வுருவத் தோளான்.
reading: The poet names one of the eight Vidyadhara lords, the lord who guards the Gandharva city, fair of form.
nuance: One of eight verses (830 to 837) that list the lords by city, each praised through his city, chariot or ornament. The name விருகவெல் is not clear and may be corrupt.

tamil: பூமரு பொலங்கொள் சோலைப் பொன்னணி புரிசை வேலிக்
காமரு கபாட வாயிற் கந்தமா தனத்தைக் காப்பான்
தேமரு திலதக் கண்ணித் திவாகர தேவ னென்பான்
தாமரை தயங்கு சோதித் தாரணி துரகத் தேரான்.
reading: The poet names one of the eight Vidyadhara lords, the lord who guards the fort called Gandhamadhanam, with a golden chariot.
nuance: One of eight verses (830 to 837) that list the lords by city, each praised through his city, chariot or ornament.

tamil: சுந்தரப் பொடியும் பூவுஞ் சுரும்பொடு துதைந்து வீசிச்
சந்திரன் றவழு மாடச் சக்கிர வாள மன்னன்
மந்தர மலைக்கும் யானை வச்சிர தாட னென்பான்
அந்தரத் தமரர் கோமா னணிந்துபோந் தனைய நீரான்.
reading: The poet names one of the eight Vidyadhara lords, the king of Chakravalam, named for an elephant-like strength.
nuance: One of eight verses (830 to 837) that list the lords by city, each praised through his city, chariot or ornament.

tamil: காரணங் குருவ மேகங் கருவு கொண் டதிர்ந்து வெய்யோன்
தேரணங் குறுக்கு மாடத் தேவர வனத்துச் செல்வன்
ஏரணங் குறுக்கும் பைந்தா ரிரமிய தரனென் றேங்கும்
சீரணங் குறுக்குஞ் செய்கைச் செஞ்சுடர்த் திலகப் பூணான்.
reading: The poet names one of the eight Vidyadhara lords, the lord of the Devaravanam, whose chariot outshines the sun's.
nuance: One of eight verses (830 to 837) that list the lords by city, each praised through his city, chariot or ornament.

tamil: கண்ணிலாங் கனக மாடக் கதலிகை முகிலோ டாடி
விண்ணிலா விருண்டு தோன்றும் விசய கூடத்து மன்னன்
வெண்ணிலா விரிந்த பூணான் வேகமா ரதனீண் முந்நீர்
மண்ணெலாம் வணங்க நின்ற மழகளிற் றரசோ டொப்பான்.
reading: The poet names one of the eight Vidyadhara lords, the king of Vijayakoodam, likened to a young elephant lord.
nuance: One of eight verses (830 to 837) that list the lords by city, each praised through his city, chariot or ornament.

tamil: மென்னரம் பனுக்குந் தீஞ்சொன் மெல்லிய லவர்கள் பாடல்
கின்னரம் பிணிக்குஞ் செய்கைக் கிருதமா தனத்தைக் காப்பான்
கைந்நவின் றிலங்குஞ் செவ்வேற் காவலன் கருடன் சேர்ந்த
மெய்நவின் றிலங்குஞ் செம்பொ னங்கதம் விளைந்த பேரான்.
reading: The poet names one of the eight Vidyadhara lords, the guardian of Kirutha Madhanam, whose name joins Garuda and the golden armlet.
nuance: One of eight verses (830 to 837) that list the lords by city, each praised through his city, chariot or ornament. The name is not stated whole; the reading garuda-angadan joins words of the third and fourth lines.

tamil: ஓங்குநீர்ப் புரிசை வேலி யொண்டுறைக் குவளை வேய்ந்த
தூங்குநீ ருடுத்த பாங்கிற் சோபன முடைய தோன்றல்
தேங்குநீர்க் கடலந் தானைச் சித்திர தரனிவ் வையம்
தாங்குநீ ரொளியோ டொன்றித் தண்ணளி தயங்க நின்றான்.
reading: The poet names one of the eight Vidyadhara lords, the lord of a city ringed by water and lotus, who bears the earth with his strength.
nuance: One of eight verses (830 to 837) that list the lords by city, each praised through his city, chariot or ornament.

tamil: என்றிவ ரெண்மர் தம்மை யிரதநூ புரத்து ளானா
நின்றுநீர் காமி னென்று நிறீஇயபின் னீதி மன்னன்
ஒன்றிய வுலக மெல்லா மொருங்குடன் விழுங்க லுற்றுச்
சென்றுயர் கடலோ டொக்குஞ் சேனைபண் ணமைக்க வென்றான்.
reading: After posting these eight to guard the city of Rathanupuram, the just king orders a host raised that is like a sea swallowing the whole world.
nuance: The host is raised to escort a bride, yet it is pictured as a conquering sea, so a marriage procession borrows the image of war.
event: The king leaves eight lords to guard Rathanupuram and orders his army made ready.

tamil: வெண்ணிலாக் குழவித் திங்கண் மேகத்துப் பதித்த போலும்
ஒண்ணிலா வுருவக் கோட்ட வோடைமால் களிற்றின் மேலோர்
பண்ணெலா மணிந்து தோன்றப் பருமித்துக் கருவி யேற்றிக்
கண்ணிலாம் பதாகை சேர்த்திக் காழகில் கழும விட்டார்.
reading: The troops arrayed elephants like the new moon set in cloud, with ornaments, gear and banners, and burned aloe wood over them.
event: The troops deck the war elephants with ornaments, banners and incense.

tamil: கட்டிய கம்மச் செய்கைக் கதிர்மணிக் கனகச் சூலம்
பட்டமொ டிலங்கப் பண்ணிப் பக்கரை பதைப்ப யாத்து
மட்டவி ழலங்கல் வீரர் சேர்தலும் வலத்து முன்னாற்
கொட்டிய குரத வாலித் தெழுந்தன குதிரைச் சேனை.
reading: Garlanded warriors gathered, and the horse host rose raising dust from its hooves, the horses bound with ornamented tridents and cloths.
event: The warriors gather and the cavalry is made ready and advances.

tamil: மணித் தொழில் வளைந்த சூட்டின் மறுப்பறுத் தியற்றப் பட்ட
அணித் தொழி லாரக் கோவை யாடகக் கொடிஞ்சி யம்பொன்
துணித்திடை பதித்த தட்டிற் சுடர்மணித் துரகத் திண்டேர்
கணித்தளப் பரிய நீர கல்லெனக் கலந்த வன்றே.
reading: The poet describes the sturdy chariots, with gem-set tops, golden pillars and gem-inlaid floors, mingling in numbers beyond counting.

tamil: ஒட்டிய கலிங்கந் தாண்மேற் றிரைத்துடுத் துருவக் கோடிப்
பட்டிகை பதைப்ப யாத்துப் பரட்டைய நரல வீக்கிக்
கட்டிய கழலர் தாரர் கதிரொடு கனலும் வாளர்
மட்டுய ரலங்கல் சூடி மறங்கிளர் மள்ளர் சூழ்ந்தார்.
reading: The fighters came round the host, bound in cloth, anklets and garlands, with bright swords, ready for fight.
event: The foot soldiers gird themselves and gather around the host.

tamil: இன்னிசை யமரர் பேகொண் டியன்றமா நகரங் காக்கும்
பொன்னவில் கடகப் பைம்பூட் புரந்தர னனைய மாண்பின்
மன்னவற் கிளைய வேந்தன் வயங்கெரிப் பெயர்கொ டேரான்
கன்னியைக் காக்கு நீர்மைக் கடற்படை பரப்பிச் சென்றான்.
reading: The younger brother of the king, in a chariot named for blazing fire, goes with a sea-like host to guard the bride.
nuance: The relation is read from மன்னவற் கிளைய வேந்தன், and the word பேகொண் in line 1 looks corrupt.
event: The king's younger brother sets out with his army as the bride's guard.

tamil: அங்கல மலர்ந்த தோன்ற லரிபுரத் தவர்கள் கோமான்
பொங்கல ரணிந்த பைந்தார்ப் புலிப்பெயர்ப் பொலங் கொ டேரான்
மங்கலக் களிற்றி னான்றன் மருமகன் மகர முந்நீர்த்
தங்கொலி மிகுத்த தானை யொடுகதி ரெறிப்பச் சார்ந்தான்.
reading: The lord of Aripuram, in a tiger-named golden chariot and kin to the king of the auspicious elephant, arrives with a roaring host.
nuance: The word மருமகன் can mean son-in-law or sister's son, so the tie to the king of the auspicious elephant is not fixed.
event: The lord of Aripuram arrives with his army.

tamil: வாரணி முரச மார்ப்ப வரிவளை வயிரொ டேங்கத்
தாரணி மறவர் சூழத் தமனியக் கலங்க டாங்கி
ஆரணி யுருவத் திண்டே ரானைமே லருக்க கீர்த்தி
நீரணி கடலந் தானை நிலநெளி பரப்ப நின்றான்.
reading: Arkakirti stands on an elephant, with drums sounding and warriors around him, as his sea-like host makes the ground ripple.
nuance: The verse leaves unsaid whose son he is; the name is the poem's own.
event: Arkakirti stands ready with his army on the field.

tamil: சேனைபண் ணமைத்துச் சென்று திருக்கடை செறிந்த போழ்திற்
றானையுள் படுநர் மாண்பிற் றாரவற் றொழுது கூற
வேனவிற் றடக்கை வேந்தன் விண்ணியல் விமான மொன்று
வானவில் லுமிழ்ந்து மின்ன மனத்தினா னிருமித் திட்டான்.
reading: When the army reached the great gate, men of the host bowed and told it to the king, who created in mind a heavenly vimana shot with rainbow light.
nuance: The king is taken to be the Vidyadhara king, since a vimana made by mind is a vidyadhara power, but the verse does not name him.
event: Men of the host announce the arrival at the gate; the king raises a vimana by thought.

tamil: மற்றதன் வடிவு கேட்பின் மரகத மணிக்க றன்மேல்
பெற்றதன் னிலையிற் றாகிப் பெருகிய வளமை தோன்றிச்
சுற்றிய பசும்பொற் சோதி சொரிந்துபோய்த் துறக்கங் காண
முற்றிய முகட்டு நீலக் குவட்டிடை முடிந்த தன்றே.
reading: The poet describes the vimana as standing on an emerald stone, shedding green gold light and ending in a blue peak that reaches heaven.

tamil: பாரித்த பவழத் திண்காற் பளிங்குபோழ் பலகை தன்மேற்
பூரித்த சுடரின் செம்பொற் போதிகைப் புடங்க டோறு
மூரித்தண் சுடர்வெண் முத்தின் பரூஉத்திரண் முயங்கி ஞான்ல
வேரித்தண் டுவலை கால மாலைகள் விசித்த வன்றே.
reading: The vimana has coral pillars, crystal slabs, gold capitals and strings of pearls and flower garlands hung in its curves.
nuance: Line 3 has ஞான்ல, probably a misprint for ஞான்ற, 'hanging'.

tamil: தடுத்துவில் லுமிழுஞ் செம்பொற் றண்டிகைத் திரள்க டாங்க
மடுத்தன வயிரத் தம்ப மாடநீண் மதலை தோறும்
தொடுத்தன சுரும்பு பாயுந் துணரணி தயங்கு மாலை
அடுத்தன நிறத்த வாக வழுத்தின மணிக ளெல்லாம்.
reading: Gold litters, diamond pillars and garlands hung from every post light the vimana, and all its gems shine in their own colours.

tamil: ஊன்றிய மகரப் பேழ்வா யொளிமுகந் தெளிப்ப வீழ்ந்து
நான்றன மணிசெய் தாம நகைமுக நிறைந்த சோதி
கான்றன கனக சாலங் கலந்தன கங்க ணீகம்
தோன்றின பதாகை சூழ்ந்து சுடர்ந்தன சூல நாயில்.
reading: Garlands hang from the mouths of carved sea-monsters, gold nets and windows gleam, and banners and tridents shine on the roof.

title: கல்யாணச் சருக்கம் 851-874 (2/13)
theme: The wedding hall is dressed in gems, the lord of the city calls his daughter Sayambavai, who goes through the palace to her mother, is adorned, and sets out on the vimana with her guard, her goods and the king's army.
source_issues: Verses 872, 873 and 874 are printed as eight half-lines and were joined into four; verse 862 had a pulli after a vowel sign removed.

cast.role: the lord of the city, father of Sayambavai
the king's daughter, who is sent out to her wedding
the maidens who keep the gate
armed maidens who guard Sayambavai
the queen, her mother
the learned men who judge the hour

tamil: அஞ்சிறைப் பறவைச் சாதி யாவிப்ப வணிந்து மேலால்
விஞ்சையர் மிதுனத் தேவர் விண்ணியங் குருவ மெல்லாம்
செஞ்சுட ரெறிப்பச் சேர்ந்து செங்கதிர்ப் பரவை சிந்தி
வெஞ்சுடர் விலங்க நீண்டு விண்ணிடை விரிந்த தன்றே..
reading: Winged birds and the Vidyadhara and Mithuna gods crowd above the wedding hall, whose red sparks fill the sky and keep the fierce sun off.
nuance: The first two lines are clipped and the subject of the verbs is not clear; the verse is read as the opening picture of the hall.

tamil: வாரணி பசும்பொன் வாழை மரகதக் கமுகொ டோங்கித்
தோரணத் தூண்க டோறுஞ் சுடர்மணி சிலம்ப நான்று
நீரணி நிழல்கொண் முத்த மணன்மிசை நிரந்து தோன்றிப்
பூரண குடங்கள் செம்பொற் கொழுங்கதிர் புதைந்த கீழால்..
reading: The hall is dressed with gold banana trees and emerald areca palms, gem-hung gate pillars, pearls strewn on the sand and full pots.

tamil: கொழுந்திரள் வயிரக் கோடிக் கூர்முளை செறித்துச் செம்பொற்
செழுந்திரட் புடகஞ் சேர்ந்த திருவளர் கபாட வாயிற்
பொழிந்ததண் சுடர வாகிப் பொலந்தொடர் புலம்பத் தூங்கி
எழுந்தொலி சிலம்ப விம்மி யிணர்கொண்ட மணிக ளெல்லாம்..
reading: Gate-leaves bound in gold and pinned with diamond-tipped studs hang with gold chains and rows of ringing gems.

tamil: பாய்கதிர்ப் பளிங்கிற் கோத்துப் பருமணி வயிரஞ் சூழ்ந்த
வாய்கதிர்ச் சால வாயி லகிலயா வுயிர்த்த வாவி
மாயிரு விசும்பின் மான்று மழைதவழ் குன்றம் போலச்
சேயவர்க் குருவங் காட்டித் தேநிரை கொண்ட வன்றே..
reading: Gem-strung crystal doorways and steps shine like cloud-skimming hills and show their forms to those who come before them.
nuance: The last line, with its word for honey-rows, is obscure.

tamil: செம்பொனங் களியிற் செய்து சித்திரந் தெளிப்பத் தீட்டி
வம்பவெண் முத்தச் சாந்தின் மட்டித்து மணிக ளெல்லாம்
தம்புலந் தெரிந்து தோன்றுந் தடத்தின தலங்க ளெல்லாம்..
reading: The floors are painted with gold dye, smeared with pearl paste and set with gems so that every corner shows clearly.

tamil: பாடக மிலங்கச் செங்கேழ்ச் சீறடிப் பரவை யல்குல்
நாடக மகளி ராடு நாடக வரங்கு நன்பொன்
மாடகந் தெளிப்ப வேய்ந்த மண்டபத் தலமும் வண்ண
ஆடக மணிந்த கூட நிலைகளு மயல வெல்லாம்..
reading: The stage where dancing women perform, the pavilion floor and the gold door-frames beside it are likewise fitted out.

tamil: மரகத மணிக ளீன்ற கதிரெனுந் தளிர்கள் வார்ந்து
புரிகதிர் முத்த மென்னும் புதுநகை யரும்பு பம்பி
விரிகதிர்ச் செம்பொன் பூத்து விண்ணணங் குறுப்ப வீங்கி..
reading: The hall's gems are told as a flowering tree: emerald as sprouts, diamond as shoots, pearl as buds, gold as blossom.
nuance: The image makes the building a wishing-tree, which verse 858 names outright.

tamil: கதிர்நகைக் கனபொற் சோதிக் கனகசா லங்க ளென்னு
மதுநகப் பருகி மான்ற மணிவண்டு மயங்கி வானோர்
விதிநகு விமான மென்னுங் கற்பகம் விரிந்த போழ்திற்
பதிநகர்க் கிறைவன் பாவை சயம்பவை வருக வென்றான்..
reading: The hall opens like a wishing-tree among the gods' own vimanas, and the lord of the city says that his daughter Sayambavai should come.
nuance: Only the last line is speech; the first three still describe the hall, and the verse joins the two.
event: The city's lord summons his daughter Sayambavai to the hall.

reading: Told by the girls who keep the gate, the princess comes down like a flowering creeper from her crystal chamber and couch, as a peacock descends.
event: Sayambavai comes down from her upper chamber when the gate-girls announce the summons.

reading: The king's daughter, wearing the victory garland, walks out from the tall mansion like lightning among cloud.
event: Sayambavai walks out of the mansion.

reading: Armed women and others with unripe breasts guard her sides and wish her long years, as she walks with a stately gait.
nuance: The guard here is of arms and numbers, set round a girl who is being sent out to be chosen.
event: Maidens guard Sayambavai and bless her as she walks.

reading: Passing the gates of the girls' city and its scented pool-stair, she goes straight to the palace where the queen sits.
event: Sayambavai goes to the queen's palace.

reading: With the women who guard her fragrant body she reaches the feet of the first mother.
nuance: The word for the first mother is read as the queen, since the house is the city lord's.
event: Sayambavai reaches the queen and bows at her feet.

reading: The lady of the house takes the bowing girl into her arms, smells her scented hair and sinks in a sea of joy.
nuance: The lady is taken as the queen; the sea of joy is hers.
event: The queen embraces Sayambavai.

reading: Thinking heavy gold would hurt her waist, Sayambavai is dressed in light gold, flowers and eye-paint, and made cool like a creeper in the shade.
nuance: The last words are obscure and who dresses her is not named.
event: Sayambavai is adorned for the vimana.

reading: The hour and its signs are looked over, learned men speak, and the speaker says that she may now climb the vimana.
nuance: Who says the last words is not named; the lord of the city is the likely speaker.
event: On the learned men's word of the hour, the king bids Sayambavai board the vimana.

reading: With women, nurses and chamberlains guarding her, she goes to the shining vimana like a goddess of the world above.
event: Sayambavai goes to the vimana in escort.

reading: Two thousand maidens learned in magic arts, loyal to her, guard the girl on all sides with drawn swords.
nuance: Verses 861 and 868 set a guard of arms round the girl.
event: Two thousand maidens take guard round Sayambavai.

reading: Her playthings, balls, parrots, dolls and mynas, are carried to the vimana.
event: Her toys are carried to the vimana.

reading: Garlands, cloth, chests, sandal and boxes of paste are loaded with them.
event: Her garlands, cloths and perfumes are loaded.

reading: Chests and treasure fill the chambers of the vimana, and it moves off with its light around it.
event: The vimana, loaded with her goods, sets out.

tamil: முரச மார்த்தன முரன்றன முரிவளை முகிலிடை வயிரேங்க
அரியொ டாகுளி யாலித்த வதிர்ந்தன யணிமுழ வரு கெல்லாம்
விரைசென் மாவொடு விரவின களிறும்தண் மிடைந்தன கடுமான் றேர்
புரைசை யானையி னெருத்திடை யரசனும் புகழொடு பொலிவுற்றான்.
reading: Drums, conches and war-horns sound, horses and elephants crowd in, and the king rides an elephant's neck in glory.
nuance: The lines are printed as eight half-lines and were joined.
event: The king rides out at the head of the procession.

tamil: சிகர யானையின் கவிழ்மணி சிலம்பின சிலம்பின பணிலங்கள்
முகர வாயின பணவங்கண் முரன்றன முரன்றன முகிலெல்லா
மகர மால்கடல் வரைமிசை யெழுந்தனெ வெழுந்தது படைமாற்ற
நகர வாயிலின் புறம்பணை நடந்தது நடுங்கின கொடியெல்லாம்.
reading: Elephant bells, conches and horse-drums roar like the sea as the host leaves by the city gate, with banners trembling.
nuance: The lines are printed as eight half-lines and were joined.
event: The army sets out through the city gate.

tamil: ஒளிறு வாட்படை யுளர்ந்தது கிளர்ந்தன ருழைக்கல வுழையோர்கள்
களிறு காத்திர முறுத்தலி னெறித்தலை கருமுகி னெரிவுற்ற
குளிறு மின்னியங் குழுமலிற் செழுமலைக் கொடுமுடி யுடனார்த்த
வெளிறில் கேள்வியான் பெரும்படை விசும்பிடை நிரந்தொளி விரிந்தன்றே
reading: Swords gleam, elephants are held back, and the learned king's great host spreads shining through the sky.
nuance: The subject of the last line is taken as the king 'of faultless learning'.
event: The army fills the sky around the vimana.

title: கல்யாணச் சருக்கம் 875-898 (3/13)
theme: The guide shows the maiden the hills, rivers, elephants and women of the Vidyadhara host as it crosses the sky, after which the party lands at Podanam, and the poet lays out the camp, its elephants, chariots, palaces and the allied kings around the royal banner.
source_issues: Verses 877 to 888: the printed stanza ran into eight half-lines and was repaired to four lines; the word division stays broken in places.
Verses 875 to 888: the speaker is not named; the guide is taken from the feminine verb of 875 and the address to the maiden.
Verses 890 to 898: the verses are short metre with clipped grammar; several readings are held loosely.

cast.role: the woman who points out the sights to the maiden, taken as her companion; named only by a feminine verb
the Vidyadhara king's daughter, addressed as 'nangai' and 'paavaai', unnamed here
the Vidyadhara king's host, in the sky and then at camp
the elephants of the hills and of the camp
the host's jewelled chariots
the women who travel with the host
the allied kings who camp beside the host

tamil: அமித மாகிய பெரும்படை யகன்கட லகல்விசும் பழகெய்த
அமித மாகிய பெருவரை நிமிர்சிகை யதனய லமர்ந்தேக
அமித மாகிய நிலைத்தலை மலையணி யருவிக ளவையெல்லாம்
அமித மாபவை சயம்பவைக் கடிதொழு தவையவை யறிவித்தாள்.
reading: The poet says that, as the vast host passes through the sky over seas, great peaks and hill-top streams, she makes all of them known to the maiden, who bows to each.
nuance: The verse opens the tour of the land below and rests on the repeated word அமிதம், used four times; the guide is only a feminine verb here and is taken to be the maiden's companion.
event: The guide names to the maiden the seas, mountains and streams that the Vidyadhara host passes over in the sky.

tamil: நங்கை காணிது நம்மலைக் கும்பரப் பொன்மலைப் புடைவீழுங்
கங்கை யாறிதன் கரையன கற்பகக் காவுகளிவை கண்டாய்
இங்கு நாமிரு விசும்பிடை யியங்கலிற் சிறியவொத் துளவேனும்
அங்க ணார்க்குநம் முலகினை யளப்பவொத் துளவவை யறியுங்கால்.
reading: The guide tells the maiden to look at the golden mountain's falling Ganga and its wishing-tree groves, which seem small from the sky yet would measure the earthly world for those who dwell there.
nuance: The tour shows the land by setting two worlds against each other, ours and the upper one, each measured by the other.
event: The guide points out the heavenly river and groves to the maiden from the moving host.

tamil: இரைக்கு மஞ்சிறைப் பறவைக ளெனப்பெய ரினவண்டு புடைசூழ
நுரைக்க னென்னுமக் குழம்பு கொண்டெதிர்ந்தழெ நுடங்கிய விலையத்தாற்
றிறைக்க ரங்களிற் செழுமலைச் சந்தனத் திரள்களைக் கரைமேல்வைத்
தரைக்கு மற்றிது குணகடற் றிரையொடும் பொருதல தவியாதே.
reading: The guide describes a river whose foam is like sandal-paste and whose bees are its birds, bringing sandal logs to the bank and breaking against the eastern sea's waves without rest.
nuance: The poet turns the river into a person: foam as ointment, waves as hands, bees as birds. The word division of this verse is broken and several words are rare, so the sense is held loosely.

tamil: முந்து மற்றிதன் முதன்மலைப் பிறந்துநம் மலையது முழைப் பேருஞ்
சிந்து வென்பது வலத்தது செழுங்கலஞ் சிதர்கின்ற திகழ்யாறு
நுந்து பொன்னொளித் திரையெனுங் கரதலப் புடங்களி னுரையென்னும்
பந்து பொங்கநின் றடித்திடத் திளைப்பதொத் துளததுப கருங்கால்.
reading: The guide says a river called the Sindhu, born at the foot of that mountain and flowing to the right of their own hill, plays like a girl striking a ball of foam with the palms of its gold waves.
nuance: The only river named in the tour is the Sindhu; the sense of the last line rests on a rare word and is held loosely.

tamil: உயருஞ் சந்தனப் பொழிலலைத் தொளிர்மணிக் கலங்களை யுமிழ்ந் திட்டுப்
பெயருந் தெண்டிரைப் பிறங்கலுட் பிணங்கிய பெருவரை யகிறேக்கி
வயிர வேதிகை மலைவது கோபுர வாய்தலின் படிதீண்டி
அயிரை வார்கரைக் குடகடற் றிரையொடு பொருதல தவியாதே.
reading: The guide shows a river that throws up jewels from the sandal groves, runs through hills in the waves and beats against the shore like the eastern sea, never ceasing.
nuance: The verse repeats the closing refrain of 877 about the waves of the eastern sea. The word division of this verse is broken and several words are rare, so the sense is held loosely.

tamil: தேனெய் பாலொடு கலந்தன சின்மொழிச் சிறுநுதற் றிருவேநஞ்
சேனை மாமுகிற் படலங்கண் மிசைச்செலச் சினைமுகில் முரலக் கேட்
டேனை யானைக ளிணையென விருந்திட விருங்கைமா வினங்காக்கும்
கான யானைகள் கருவரை யனையன கனல்வன விவை காணாய்.
reading: The guide bids the maiden see the wild elephants, mixed with honey and milk, that rage at the thunder of clouds drifting over the host and take it for a rival elephant.
nuance: The epithet 'the elephant-like mountain' casts the clouds and the herd as rivals; the lines 2 to 3 are clipped.
event: The guide points to the forest elephants raging at the clouds above the host.

tamil: பேய்மை யானங்கொண் டிருந்தன்ன பெருவரை நெரிதரத் திரைசிந்தித்
தீமை யானைகள் செவிபுகு செறிகடாந் திளைத்தலிற் றிசைநாறிப்
போய்மை யானங்கொண் டிழிதரும் பெருந்திசைப் புடையன புனல்யாறு
சேய்மையா னமக்கொளிர் முத்தின் பருவடந் தெளிப்பவொத் துளபாவாய்.
reading: The guide shows rivers coming down from the great hills, bearing the smell of rutting elephants' must, which seem to scatter a string of pearls for the maiden to see.
nuance: The verse is a continuing scene of the tour; the word division is broken.

tamil: கருவிவா னத்தி னகடுதொட் டனவென நிலத்திடைக் கவின் செய்ய
மருவிநங் கட்கு மணிவட்டுச் சிதர்ப்ப வொத் துளசில மலை யெல்லாம்
அருவி வெண்டிரை சொரிகின்ற வருவரைக் குவடுக ளவை முன்னாற்
பரவை வெண்கொடி யெடுத்துநம் படைக்கெதி ரெழுவதொத் துளபாவாய்.
reading: The guide describes the hills with falling streams that look like white banners raised against the host and like hands that scatter pearls and gems at the passers-by.
nuance: The streams are made the banners of a rival army raised before the host; the conceit makes the landscape an opponent that yields.

tamil: அலங்கல் வார்குழ லிமிர்தன்ன சின்மொழி யரிவைநம் மருங்கெல்லாம்
விலங்கல் போல்வன வெண்மருப் பிரட்டைய வேழங்கள் விளையாடி
இலங்கு மால்வரை யிறுவரைத் தடங்குத்தி யிடந்திட விருபாலும்
கலங்கொள் பேழைகள் கவிழ்ந்தனெக் கதிர்மணி சொரிகின்ற வவை காணாய்.
reading: The guide points to tusker pairs playing like hills, goring the hillside so that jewels pour out like chests overturned on both sides.
event: Pairs of elephants gore the hillside and spill gems.

tamil: அங்கண் மால்வரை யருவிதந் தடக்கையிற் புடைத்துநின் றமர்ந் தாடிப்
பைங்கட் செம்முகப் பரூஉக்கையம் பகடுதம் பிடிக்கணம் புடை சூழச்
செங்கற் றூளிதஞ் செவிப்புறத் தெறிதலிற் சிகரங்க ளிடையெல்லாம்
பொங்கிக் குங்குமப் பொடியொத்துப் பொலிகின்ற பொலங்கொடி புடைநோக்காய்.
reading: The guide describes female elephants circling a bull that sports under a hill stream, whose raised red dust looks like saffron powder over the peaks.
nuance: This verse and the next two are the guide's remarks to the maiden at a point where the tour turns to the host's own life.
event: A bull elephant plays in the stream among his herd of cows.

tamil: துளங்கு வார்குழைத் துவரிதழ்த் துடியிடைச் சுடர்நுதற் சுரிகோதாய்
விளங்கு வெங்கதிர் விலங்கிய விசும்பிடை யியங்குதல் புலன்கொள்ளாப்
பளிங்கி னொள்ளறைப் பரப்பிடைப் பாய்வித்த பருமணி நெடுமான்றேர்
வலங்கொ ணம்படைக் கடலிடை மறித்தவை சுழல்கின்ற வகை நோக்காய்.
reading: The guide shows how the jewelled chariots in their ranks turn about in the ocean of the host, moving so smoothly across the clear crystal sky that the eye cannot catch their going.
event: The Vidyadhara chariot horses wheel in the host's ranks in the sky.

tamil: எடுத்த மாருத மெறிதலி னெகிழ்ந்தன சிகழிகை யிணரோடும்
தொடுத்த மாலைகள் துணர்கொளப் புனைவன துகிலிடை புடைசோர
உடுத்த காஞ்சியி னொளிமணிக் கதிர்நகைப் பட்டங்க ளுடையாக
அடுத்து வீழுமொ ரணியிழை யிளையவள் படுகின்ற ததுகாணாய்.
reading: The guide points to a young woman of the host whose loosened hair and wind-blown garlands and robe let fall her girdle, the sparkling ornaments dropping about her.
nuance: The poet draws the woman's unwinding dress as an unconscious show; the verse carries no reproof.
event: A young woman of the host loses her robe and ornaments in the wind.

tamil: மல்கு மும்மத மதகளி றுழக்கலின் மயங்கிய மழைமேகம்
பில்கு நுண்டுளி யுறைத்தலிற் பனித்தநம் பெரும்படை மடவார்கள்
நல்கு காதல ரகலத்து ளொடுங்குதல் பலர்முன்னை நனிநாணி
மெல்கு பூந்துகில் விரித்தவா வருகின்ற விதலைகண் மிகநோக்காய்.
reading: The guide shows women of the host trembling from the mist of fine drops from clouds and the must of elephants and hiding in their husbands' arms, spreading their robes from shyness before many.
nuance: The shyness here is playful and shown as seemly; the verse is the one in the tour that sets desire against modesty.
event: The women of the host hide in their lovers' chests and draw their robes against the drizzle and the crowd.

tamil: இலைய நாடகத் தெழில்கெழு விமானமஃ தியல்கின்ற விசைதன்னான்
மலையி னம்மொடு வருவவொத் துளவவை வரவில மடனோக்கி
உலைவில் வையகத் தொளிசெயும் பகலவ னுறுசுடர் சொரிகின்ற
வலையங் கையல வருவது மற்றிதன் சலத்தது வலிகண்டாய்.
reading: The guide says the aerial cars of the host, moving to a song of play, come like a troop of hills, and bids the maiden look at their power under the sun's glare.
nuance: The last two lines turn on rare words and the sense is a guess.

tamil: இன்ன போல்வன விளையவட் குழையவ ளினியன பலகாட்டிப்
பன்னு மாயிடைப் பழனங்கள் வளாவிய படுகலி நெடுநீத்தம்
துன்னு நீர்வயற் சுரமியத் தகணியுட் சுடரணி நகர்சார்ந்து
தென்னென் றேனிமிர் திருநிலை யகமெனுஞ் செறிபொழி லதுசேர்ந்தார்.
reading: Having shown the young woman many such sights, the party crosses flooded fields and a lovely city and comes to a grove called the lord's seat, where they reach their stopping place.
nuance: The verse closes the tour and passes from the maiden's view to the host's camp.
event: After the tour the Vidyadhara party arrives at a grove beside Podanam.

reading: The host of the maiden's lord settles in a thick flower-grove; the bees swarming over the women's garlands spoil the honey.
nuance: Lines 1 and 4 are clipped and the sense is held loosely.
event: The Vidyadhara king's host makes camp in a flower grove.

reading: Bees that fed on the rut of angry elephants wheel away as if falling from the beasts' bound necks.
nuance: This is a pure picture of the camp's elephants.

reading: The rutting elephants burn against the sandal trunks they lean on, as the bees sing a slow note, like a post that blazes.
nuance: The last line compares the bull to a burning post and the comparison is hard to place.

reading: Steeds in tumult roll over saffron dust and flowers, and the rows of the great stables come with many gleaming hands spread out.
nuance: The sense turns on rare words.

reading: Chariots with banners and the king's royal lodgings are laid out in a circle at the camp, as if heaven itself had come down.
event: The camp's lodgings and chariots are set out in a ring.

reading: The camp has golden mansions, halls of diamond, gold dancing-halls and aloe-wood beds, all full of new richness.
Silver pavilions set with coral, scented sleeping-halls and day-palaces fill the generous king's town.
Tanks like drawn water, gardens that smell divine, small hills and jasmine bowers with sand slopes are all found in the camp.
nuance: The closing word என்பவே is the poet's formula for hearsay and sets the whole camp as report.

reading: The host surrounds the king's banner-hall and the fields beyond it, and the other kings, wearing pearl garlands, make for the outskirts of the forest.
nuance: The verse leaves unclear which king's flag-hall it means and where the forest lies.
event: The host rings the royal camp and the other kings pitch beside the forest.

title: கல்யாணச் சருக்கம் 899-922 (4/13)
theme: The maiden-city is built and the Vidyadhara maiden enters it; Maruci reports to the king of Suramai, who orders the city dressed and, on his counsellors' word that the Vidyadhara lord is an equal, has elephants, chariots, horses and soldiers made ready while the prince orders gifts of cloth, jewels, drink and food sent to the Vidyadhara city.
source_issues: Verse 914: the printed stanza ran into eight half-lines and was repaired to four lines.
Verses 902 to 910: the speakers are not named in the text and are taken from the story so far.
Verses 911 to 922: the garland-chested prince is taken to be Tivittan; the verses never name him, and the speaker of 912 to 917 could be the king.
Verses 903, 904, 906, 907 and 921: several rare words and a broken word division leave the sense held loosely.

cast.role: those who raise the maiden-city; named only by a plural verb
the Vidyadhara king's daughter, called only 'maiden' here
the learned Vidyadhara envoy who goes to the king
the king of the Suramai land and Podanam, named only by royal titles here
the king's counsellors
the garland-chested prince, taken to be Tivittan, who orders the procession and gifts
the elephant-drivers who ready the war-elephants
the firm jewelled chariots
the soldiers who say life is taken only by fate
the official told to send cloth, jewels, drink and food to the Vidyadhara city

reading: In the guarded grove round the old fort the builders raise a great maiden-city for the girl, with many maidens keeping its gate.
nuance: Every line opens with the same word கன்னி, in a yamaka that plays on 'maiden' and 'city of the maiden'; the exact sense of each use is held loosely.
event: Builders raise a great city for the Vidyadhara maiden in the guarded grove.

reading: The maiden steps down from her lightning-bright aerial car while golden women praise her and, by her father's grace, enters the jewelled mansion of the maiden-city.
event: The Vidyadhara maiden descends from the aerial car and enters the maiden-city.

reading: Once the party is settled, Maruci goes to the king of the river-watered Suramai land, bows at his feet and tells him, and the victorious king swells with gladness.
nuance: The king of Suramai is taken to be Pirasapathi of Podanam; the verse does not name him.
event: Maruci reports the Vidyadhara party's arrival to the king, who is delighted.

reading: The king orders the jewelled ornaments worn, the drums sounded through the city, arches raised in every direction and full golden pots set out.
nuance: The speaker is not named in the verse and is taken from the king's joy in 901.
event: The king orders the city dressed and drummed for the wedding.

reading: The king orders that the needy seize two treasures, that neighbouring kings be summoned by envoys, and that the temples of the Jina's wealthy city hold a festival.
nuance: The wedding is made a public gift-day for beggars and a political summons to neighbouring kings together; the closing words about rain are obscure.
event: The king orders wealth given out, kings summoned and a festival held.

reading: The king orders the women to adorn the bright-jewelled girl for her going into the jewelled grove, with bright ear-rings, ornaments and finery.
nuance: Whether the one to be adorned is the Vidyadhara maiden or the bride-to-be of the line is held loosely; the verse says only 'the woman of the gem-grove'.
event: The king orders the maiden dressed for her entry into the grove.

reading: The king orders the elephants with their women to go in, the young cow-elephants to be made ready, and the fire-armed troops to enter and keep guard.
event: The king orders elephants, women and guard troops to take their posts.

reading: Having ordered the attendants so, the king speaks to Maruci in words meant to bewilder him and bids him enter a golden-city mansion.
nuance: The sense of the king's words to Maruci turns on one rare word and a doubtful construction.
event: The king speaks to Maruci and sends him to lodge in a golden mansion.

reading: The king, gracious to the envoy's side, asks his gathered counsellors how the capable Vidyadhara lord is to be met, and they answer in a way the king understands.
event: The king asks his counsellors how to receive the Vidyadhara lord and they answer.

reading: The counsellors tell the king that the Vidyadhara lord was born in a great sea of noble kin, that his link to Nami's line also draws near, and that there is no fault in him to count.
nuance: 'Nami' in line 3 is taken to be the ancestor of the Vidyadhara line whose song is told in an earlier sarukkam; the verse's grammar is clipped.
event: The counsellors vouch for the Vidyadhara lord's lineage.

reading: The counsellors add that he matches the king in clan, character and beauty, is strong beyond challenge, and has the build of a wrestler with pillar-like shoulders.
event: The counsellors praise the Vidyadhara lord's equality with the king.

reading: Therefore, say the counsellors, whatever the king does for him brings no blame; they speak as men who are a sea of the treatise on conduct.
nuance: The counsellors are called a sea of the treatise on conduct (நீதிநூல்) in the narrator's voice; the verse does not say whom the treatise belongs to.
event: The counsellors advise that no fault attaches to any honour done to the Vidyadhara lord.

tamil: ஆங்கவர் மொழியக் கேட்டே யறிவினுக் கரச ரென்று
வாங்கிருங் கடலந் தானை மன்னவன் மகிழ்ந்து மற்றப்
பூங்குழை மகளிர் காக்கும் பொன்னணி வாயில் போகித்
தேங்கம ழலங்கன் மார்பன் றிருநகர் முற்றஞ் சேர்ந்தான்.
reading: Hearing them, the king rejoices that his counsellors are men of wisdom and goes through the gold gate kept by flower-eared women to the courtyard of the garlanded prince's fine palace.
nuance: The garlanded prince is taken to be Tivittan, the groom; the verse names him only by his garland.
event: The king goes to the prince's palace courtyard.

tamil: அடுகடா மாவி நாறு மழிமதங் கருவி வீழத்
தொடுகடா வயிரத் தோட்டி யுடையன தொடர்க ணூன்ற
விடுகொடா வியாள நிற்ப மெல்லவன் பணிகள் செய்யும்
படுகடாக் களிறுந் தேரும் புரவியும் பண்ணு கென்றான்.
reading: He orders ready the war-elephants, whose rut falls like rain, with diamond goads and chains planted firm, and the chariots and horses.
nuance: The speaker is taken to be the prince, but the king is also a possible subject of 'என்றான்'.
event: The prince orders elephants, chariots and horses made ready.

tamil: பணித்தசொல் லதனைக் கேட்டே பகைநிலைக் கந்தி னோடும்
பிணித்தபொற் றொடர்கண் விட்டுப் பெயர்ந்தகா னிகள நீக்கி
மணித்தொடர் மருங்கின் வீழ்த்து வரிபுரிக் கச்சை வீக்கி
அணித்தகைப் பாகர் பண்ணிக் கொடியெடுத் தருகு சேர்ந்தார்
