nuance: The simile sets the sun as a king whose command makes petty rivals draw back; it is one of the poet's royal comparisons for nature.
event: The sun rises and the other lights recede.

reading: At daybreak the white conches call, lotuses revel in honey, bees that slept hidden in the flowers hum, and honey-rain falls on the dense grove.
event: The morning wakes the conches, lotuses and bees.

reading: The sun climbs in a crowd of rays, saying that he would see the bride, bright as a lit lamp, circling the fire with her bridegroom.
nuance: The sun is given a wish: to see the fire-circling of the wedding. This ties the sunrise to the wedding that the chapter's name and the next verses lay out.
event: The sun rises to watch the marriage rites.

reading: As the sun drinks the water, snow melts from the rocks, hot rays burn the lilies on the pools and the quarters grow wide, as if the face of the world turned.
event: Day grows hot and the pools wither.

reading: The poet says that the rites of the wedding were completed by good law, and leaves the account of what happened to the groom and bride to those who can tell it.
nuance: The verse is a narrator's turn: the marriage is done and he declines to describe its detail. The word division is damaged.
event: The wedding rites are completed, and the poet leaves the telling of them.

reading: On the day of worship of the feet of the lord who has three umbrellas, drums were beaten on dark elephants carrying heavy gold.
nuance: Whom the 'lord of three umbrellas' (the Arhat) is, is taken from the epic's setting; the verse gives only the title and the drums.
event: Drums are beaten on elephants to announce the worship day.

reading: The streets of the royal city fill with drums, crowds of drummers, incense, smoke, flowers and the food of the offering.
event: The city's streets fill with festival sounds and offerings.

reading: Mares, elephants and others crush together, flags, parasols, whisks and crown-light cover the sky, and there is no room even to tread.
event: Crowds, animals and standards fill the streets.

reading: The people of the city, kept in the road without fault, adorn it for the festival, and drums rise at once for the wedding day.
event: The city is adorned for the wedding day.

reading: The procession lines move by stages, from the Nandi face to the holy water, the afternoon, the chants and the guard's duty.
nuance: The verse works as a list of the day's stages named by the word மாலை; the exact sense of each stage is held loosely.
event: The wedding ceremony proceeds in set stages through the day.

tamil: முரைசங் கொலியோ டுமுழங் கியெழசங் கொலியோ டுணரா வகையால்
reading: Sounds of the sea, of drums and of the court rise together in so great a din that none can tell the one from the other.
nuance: The verse has only three lines in the printed text, so a line may be lost; the sense is held loosely.
event: Sea, drums and court rise in one noise.

reading: Young women with pearl-white laughter and red lips shed pearls from their eyes, which mix with the sand and fill the streets.
event: Young women's pearls fill the sand of the street.

reading: Banners rise, incense smoke fills the air, and night joins day so that night and day agree in the city.
event: Incense and flags turn night to day.

reading: Songs and dances stood together, and kings of the earth and kings of ancient clans slept in the cool on the great mountain.
event: Kings sleep on the mountain after the songs and dances.

reading: Sky-dwellers and Vidyadharas descend in crowds from the heavens, and the golden city shines like stars scattered with the sun.
event: Sky-dwellers and Vidyadharas come down to the golden city.

reading: The Vidyadharas look with joy at the golden lotuses opening on the northern peak and in the pond.
event: The Vidyadharas look at golden lotuses.

reading: The streets spread with goods for the festival: jewels laid out for those who wish them, gems cut for those who wish them, and gifts of cloth.
event: Goods are laid out in the streets for the festival.

reading: Some drink toddy and laugh, others take in the food of the gods, others dwell with kin; so the streets filled with such groups.
event: Different crowds feast and gather in the streets.

reading: Vidyadharas pour down from every quarter, a rain of gold falls, and in the rain a whirl of ancient crowds rises, which is not told here.
nuance: The last line says the speaker does not tell more; it ends the chapter on a promise that the full account is omitted.
event: Vidyadharas come down and a rain of gold falls on the festival.

title: கல்யாணச் சருக்கம் 1085-1107 (12/13)
theme: The Vidyadhara wedding: the groom and bride are bathed, the priest lays the hall and tends the fire, the bride is given and led round the fire, the priests are paid and the onlookers go away amazed or to the forest.
source_issues: Verses 1085 to 1107 have broken word division in many lines (for example the splits in 1089, 1095 and 1098).
Verse 1098: the figures named in lines 1 and 2 and the speaker of line 4 are doubtful.
Verse 1106: the speaker and the star's name are inferred from context.

cast.role: the kings who gather at the wedding, with their elephants
the women who ride in to the wedding on cow-elephants
the youth who weds; named by epithets and unnamed in these verses
the bride, the Vidyadhara king's daughter; unnamed in these verses
the Vidyadharas who bring holy waters for the bride's bath
the people who watch the wedding
the sacred-thread priest who prepares and tends the wedding fire
the hill-king, the bride's father, who gives her to the groom
the kin of the bride and groom who give wealth to the priests

reading: Kings with lotus-bright faces gather in numbers, riding war elephants whose fly-whisks and flower-wreathed foreheads are splashed by the waves of water thrown over them.
event: Kings come to the wedding in crowds on their elephants.

reading: Women with rain-cloud eyes and flower garlands crowd every direction on their cow-elephants, leaving no room, and look like dark peacocks spread over those who see them.
event: Women ride in to the wedding and fill the roads.

reading: The lord sits on a gem seat under the lion-throne in front of the jewelled mansions, with warrior kings around him, like the full moon among stars.
nuance: The word காளை, the youth, is taken to name the groom as in the earlier chapters; the verse does not name him.
event: The groom sits enthroned among kings before the wedding bath.

reading: The youth bathes as auspicious pots are lifted and the water poured over him, and looks like a great mountain over which rain-clouds have emptied.
nuance: The word division is broken in line 1 and the edition's தம் உடன் reading is held loosely.
event: Pots of water are poured over the groom in the wedding bath.

reading: After the kings' pouring of jewelled water and a rain of flowers from the sky, the youth puts on gold ornaments and enters the new city of the sacrifice.
event: The groom finishes his bath, dresses and enters the wedding city.

reading: The Vidyadharas come down from the heights with water from the Ganga and other streams for the bride's bath, so thickly that the sky has no room, and the poet asks what more need be said.
event: Vidyadharas descend with holy waters for the bride's bath.

reading: Water from the six great mountains' streams bathes the delicate bride, and then a rain of flowers of every kind is made to fall on her.
event: The bride is bathed with mountain water and flowers.

reading: A sandal rain pours and a wind carries drops of honey, so that the people are bewildered whether this is a king's world or another age and some are amazed and some glad.
event: Sandal-rain and a scented breeze fall as the bride is dressed.

reading: Dressed in the gifts of the sky-dwellers and praised with songs, the red-eyed bride reaches the sacrifice city.
nuance: Her title is only நங்கை and the red-eyed one, as elsewhere in this chapter; the verse never names her.
event: The bride, adorned, comes to the wedding hall.

reading: Before the bride arrives, the sacred-thread priest adorns the wedding hall and the rest arrange to tend the fire there.
event: The priest and the others prepare the hall and the fire before the bride arrives.

reading: The priest has the gem floor smeared with sandal and wax, marks it with a golden rod, has it smeared again with fragrance, and learns its measure by reciting the Veda.
nuance: The edition's வுலகு/அதனாரிடம் word division is broken in line 4, so the reading of ஆரிடம் is held loosely.
event: The priest prepares and marks the ground for the fire.

reading: He lays out a square of pearl-sand, ringed with raised ground, and spreads darbha grass on it with the tips toward the north and east, and performs a rite over it.
event: The priest lays out the square of sand and spreads darbha.

reading: The priest sets guards for the four-faced one's right and the quarters, spreads the sacrificial sticks and, in the due order, sits to recite and tend them.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are hard; the lines about the four-faced Brahma's right side may belong to the rite's layout and the sense is not fixed.
event: The priest sets the sacrificial sticks and begins the fire-rite.

reading: The lord of the gods, the minister of the asuras and the moon are said to enter the sky, and the astrologer declares that this is the hour with the garland of the ocean.
nuance: Line 1 names நடுக்கடலுளான், the one in mid-ocean, and அமரராசான், but the identity of each figure and the speaker are only inferred from context.
event: The auspicious hour is declared.

reading: Before the fire the hill-king gives the bride to the groom with water, and the lotus-born lady comes with her.
event: The bride's father gives her to the groom, pouring water, before the fire.

reading: With kusa grass braided and held at his right side, the spear-bearing youth sits before the fire beside the maiden, like the radiant moon beside the maid.
event: The groom sits beside the bride at the fire.

reading: Smoke from the fire rises like a dark cloud as the priest tends it and offers into the flame, while the youth in his own mind offers himself to the girl.
nuance: The verse pairs the priest's burning offering with the groom's desire; the same word வேட்டான் is used of both, once for the sacrifice and once for the wish.
event: The priest feeds the sacrificial fire as the groom longs for the bride.

reading: Once the fire-rite has been honoured, the youth rises, takes the soft fingers of the girl and walks with her on his right, like the dark sea joined with the Ganga.
event: The groom takes the bride's hand and walks around the fire.

reading: As the hero takes her flower-hand she trembles with hair on end and sweat on her brow and cannot set her red feet down, and the poet asks who can tell the shyness of the peacock-like girl.
event: The bride shakes and perspires as the groom clasps her hand.

reading: More rites go by and many things are said, and the kin of the girl and of the youth, mingled together, pour out heaps of gold and gems to the priests who keep the fire.
event: The two families give gold and gems to the fire-priests.

reading: The chief priest, skilled in the six limbs, four Vedas and countless ritual books, is made to receive a rain of wealth like the conch treasure.
event: The expert priest is given a rain of wealth.

reading: One shows the peacock-like bride the Vadameen star shining in the sky, and she scorns herself, asking whether she, shameless and lowly, can look at the world as that star does.
nuance: The speaker is taken to be the bride from இகழ்ந்தாள், and the meaning of the self-reproach is not settled; the star is Arundhati only by the ritual's usual order, not by the verse's word.
event: The bride is shown the star and reproaches herself.

tamil: எனமண வினைகள் செல்ல வின்னண மெய்து கென்று
புனவரை கான முன்னி மாதவம் போகு வாரும்
இனமலி செல்வ மற்று மிப்படி வருவ துண்டோ
கனவினு மென்ன மாந்தர் கண்டுமீள் வாரு மானார்.
reading: As the wedding rites go on, some who see such wealth go off to the forest to practise great penance, and others, wondering whether it ever comes even in a dream, turn back.
nuance: The verse stops at the departures and does not say that the penance is a judgment on the wedding; the 'dream' phrase is a spoken wonder, not a doctrinal claim.
event: Onlookers either leave for the forest to do penance or turn home amazed.

title: கல்யாணச் சருக்கம் 1108-1130 (13/13)
theme: On the wedding night the groom goes up to the mansion with the maid, is drawn to her shy beauty, and speaks his wonder and servitude to her, before he goes down into the play grove where young women sing warnings to the plants about her beauty, and then climbs back up.
source_issues: Verses 1110, 1127 and 1128 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four lines.
Verse 1110 had a stray pulli on a line repaired.
Word division is broken in many verses of this chapter, and several readings in 1119 to 1125 are held loosely.

cast.role: the young lord who saw the picture and fell in love and is now the groom; the epithets காளை, விடலை and வேலான் are taken to name him
the bride, the Vidyadhara king's daughter, unnamed in these verses
the bees he tells to keep away from her hair
the young women who sing warnings to the plants, named only at 1129
the sweet mango tree addressed in the song
the kurukkatti creeper addressed in the song
the fragrant kurava tree addressed in the song
the attendants who bow at his feet

tamil: இடிபடு முரசிற் சாற்றி யேற்பவ ராசை தீரச்
சுடர்விடு மணியின் மாரி பொன்னொடு சொரிய வேவிக்
கடிபடு நெடிய மாடங் கன்னியோ டேறி னானால்
முடிவுகொ ளுலக மெய்து மின்பமா மூர்த்தி யென்பான்.
reading: At the drum's proclamation he has jewels and gold showered on petitioners until their wishes are filled, then climbs the tall guarded mansion with the maid, and the poet calls him the form of the joy the world at its end attains.
nuance: The giving comes first and the climb to the bride's bed second, so the wedding night opens with the king's bounty before it turns private; the last line's praise of the youth is compressed.
event: He has gold and jewels rained on petitioners at a drum's proclamation, then climbs the tall mansion with the maid.

tamil: கழுமிய காக துண்டங் கமழ்தொறுங் காள மேகம்
குழுமிய தனைய மாடக் குவட்டிடை யமளி சேர்வார்
விழுமலர்ப் பிணைய லாளும் விடலையு மேரு நெற்றிச்
செழுமணிச் சிலைசென் றேறுந் தெய்வமா மிதுன மொத்தார்.
reading: The garlanded woman and the youth take their couch at the top of the mansion, where the smoke of burning fragrant wood gathers like dark cloud, and they look like a divine pair mounting a jewelled peak.
nuance: Reading காக துண்டம் as a burning aromatic wood is my inference from the verse's cloud and fragrance images.
event: The couple go up to their couch on the mansion's roof.

tamil: பொன்னியல் கொடியி னொல்கிப் பூவணைப் பொருந்தும் பாவை
கன்னிநா ணொடுக்கங் காளை கண்களி கொள்ள நோக்கிப்
பின்னவ ளொடுங்க வாங்கிப் பெருவரை யகலஞ் சேர்த்தி
இன்னகை மழலை கேட்பா னென்கொலோ வென்று சொன்னான்.
reading: The shy girl lies down on the flower bed, he gazes till his eyes are glad, draws her as she shrinks and presses her to his broad chest, and says he longs to hear her sweet laughing lisp.
nuance: The spoken words are given only as 'என்கொலோ என்று', so what he asks is only half stated.
event: The youth draws the shrinking girl to his chest and asks to hear her voice.

tamil: நின்றநா ணென்னுங் கன்னிச் சிறைவிண்டு காளை திண்டோட்
குன்றினாற் செறிக்கப் பட்ட குமரிநீ ரமிர்த யாறு
சென்றுதேன் பகர்ந்து செம்பொற் கலஞ்சிந்தித் திளைத்து விம்மி
அன்றவ னார்வ வெள்ளக் கடலிடை யழுந்திற் றன்றே.
reading: The cage of her shame breaks open as his mountain-like arms close on her, and she, like a nectar-river, sinks in the sea of his ardour.
nuance: Shame is made a cage (சிறை) from which she is released, and the one who sinks is the river, not the sea; the figure of river and sea is compressed and several details are read loosely.
event: The maiden's shame gives way and she is taken into the youth's embrace.

tamil: பருவத்தா லரும்பிப் போதாய்ப் பையவே யலர்ந்து முற்றி
மருவித்தேங் கனிகொண் டுள்ளான் மனங்கொள வளிந்த காமத்
திருவொத்த களியின் றீஞ்சா றாரவுண் டார மாட்டார்
உருவத்தா லிருவ ராகி யுள்ளத்தா லொருவ ரானார்.
reading: Like a bud that by its season opens, ripens and bears fruit, they come to the sweet food of desire and cannot take enough of it, and are two in body but one in heart.
nuance: The ripening bud-flower-fruit image makes the union a growth over time and not an event of one night; the last line states the oneness of heart as the result.
event: The couple consummate their love and are joined in heart.

tamil: உலவிய வலங்கன் மாலை யொளிமல ருடைய மார்பிற்
குலவிய மணிமுத் தோடுங் குவிமுலைக் குவடு பாயக்
கலவியுங் களிப்புங் காமப் புலவியுங் கலந்து சால
நிலவிய மதுவுண் டார்போ னெஞ்சுண மயங்கி யிட்டார்.
reading: His garland and her pearl strings tangle on his chest, and union, delight and playful sulking blend until they fall into a daze like drinkers of honey-wine.
nuance: புலவி is named in one list with union and delight, with no quarrel and no cause given, so the sulk here is part of the pleasure and not a breach.
event: The couple lose themselves in union and play.

tamil: அடிக்கலந் திருத்தி யம்மென் புரிகுழற் சுருளை நீவி
முடிக்கல ரணிந்து காதன் முகிழ்நகை முகிழ்ப்பப் புல்லிக்
கடிக்கணி யாய காளை கவான்மிசை யிருத்திக் காமர்
குடிக்கணி யாய கொம்பு கேட்கமற் றிதனைச் சொன்னான்.
reading: He sets her ornaments right, smooths her coiled hair, crowns her with a flower, embraces her as her smile buds, seats her on his lap and speaks the words that follow so she may hear.
event: The youth adorns the bride, seats her on his lap and begins to speak to her.

reading: He says her body smells of the red lily and her red mouth of the same and of the water lily, and that the god who first made her made his life her servant.
nuance: The maker (தேவன்) as the cause of his bondage is a lover's way of speaking, a small echo of fate in a verse of praise; no claim about karma is made.

reading: He says the doe-eyed doll lit the fire of melting love that burns his bones, and that she is the sweet nectar the old sea bore, taken as a slim form.
nuance: Fire and nectar are said of the same woman, the paradox that verse 1118 develops.

reading: He says her long eyes are the arrows with which the lord of the hot season won, that Kama must have done austerity for his victory, and that he himself has done austerity for this long to touch her fragrant body.
nuance: நோற்றான் and நோற்றேன் are the words of vows and penance; here a lover turns them to the wish to touch his bride, which a Jain reader would hear against the epic's own austerities. Verse 986 already gave Prajapati's words that the winner of such a bride must have great earlier austerity.

reading: He says the dark-eyed girl has become the nectar he eats as a guest, his very life and his rare medicine, while he, a sinner, has become servant to a doll.
nuance: பாவியேன் is the lover's self-reproach in play and not a charge of wrongdoing; the same woman is feast, life and medicine at once.

reading: He says it would be enough to look at her coral-red small feet and worship them, but at the sight of her red mouth and curl-crowded brow he loses himself and cannot say why it is his sin.
nuance: வழிபடுவது, the word of worship, is used for her feet; the last line is hard and its sense is uncertain.

reading: He tells the bees that sat in her braided hair and troubled her slim waist not to come to her tender body's fragrance as before.
nuance: The middle lines are compressed, and who is hurt by whom is read from the context of a bridegroom guarding his bride.

reading: He says the sly-eyed girl has hidden herself, and when he tries to hold her in his heart he cannot see her form, and he does not know what his unsatisfied longing has come upon.
nuance: Even with her in his arms he looks for her in his heart; the closing lines are corrupt or compressed.

reading: He says that even when she sits lovingly on his lap she looks like a stranger each time he blinks, so he will gaze unblinking at her flower-like face, and he knows not how he will live while his beloved is shy.
nuance: Her shame still stands after the embrace of 1111, and he reads it as a distance he fears.

tamil: குலம்பா ராட்டுங் கொம்புமொர் முல்லைக் கொடி யொத்தாள்.
reading: He, with shoulders like a rock, praises her beauty and is like a monsoon storm that makes the young jasmine open, and she like the jasmine vine that is the pride of her line.
nuance: The two similes cast the couple as storm and flower, with the storm as the active one.

tamil: கானார் சோலைக் காவகப் புக்கான் கமழ் தாரான்.
reading: Her flower-garlanded, carp-like eyes take him captive, and the spear-bearing youth, his mind lost, no longer behaves with his attendants as before and goes into the pleasure grove.
event: The youth, lost in her eyes, enters the play grove.

reading: Under the red asoka whose tender leaves hang with bees, he climbs onto a jewelled round seat, plays with his beloved and hears the music sung by the women.
nuance: பிண்டி, the asoka, is the tree under which the Jina is said to have won omniscience in Jain tradition, so the play takes place in the Jina's own shade; the last line's relation of the women to him is unclear.
event: In the grove he plays with the bride and listens to the singing women.

reading: The singers tell the sweet mango not to put out sprouts that borrow the colour of the mountain king's daughter, for in the spring wind it will bear scars and rows of fruit and be plucked.
nuance: வடு means both young fruit and scar, and the warning may play on both; the speakers are named only in 1129.
event: The young women sing to the mango tree, warning it not to rival the bride's colour.

reading: The singers tell the kurukkatti creeper, long may it live, not to take the grace of the vine-waisted chief queen of the wheel-ruler whom kings bow to, for if it does many will pluck it and it will not bloom in the guarded garden.
nuance: The bride is called the great queen of the lord who rules the wheel, so the song already gives her the title Prajapati's words at 986 foretold.
event: The singers warn the kurukkatti creeper not to match the queen's grace.

tamil: வணங்கி வையந் தொழநின்ற மன்னன் காதன் மடமகள்போல்
மணங்க ணாறும் பூம்பாவை வளரல் வாழி நறுங்குரவே
மணங்க ணாறும் பூம்பாவை வளர்த்தி யாயி லிளையராற்
கணங்க ளோடு பறிப்புண்டி கண்டாய் வாழி நறுங்குரவே.
reading: The singers tell the fragrant kurava tree not to grow as lovely as the loving daughter of the king whom the world bows to, for if it does the young men will pluck it in crowds.
event: The singers warn the kurava tree that being as fragrant as the bride will bring it plucking.

reading: Hearing the young women sing, a smile like moonlight flashes for a moment on the king's daughter's face, and the youth's eyes drink it in.
nuance: The smile is not said to answer the song, only to follow it.
event: The bride smiles at the song and the youth's eyes take it in.

reading: As attendants bow at his feet and the bright-earringed bride's radiance holds his mind, the lion-like youth climbs the cloud-brushing pillared mansion.
event: The youth goes back up to the tall mansion.

title: அரசியற் சருக்கம் 1131-1155 (1/17)
theme: The spy's news reaches Acuvakandan, the discus-lord of the Vidyadhara world, that Tivittan has killed the lion and that the maiden has gone to earth as wed; his rage breaks a diamond pillar and ends in boasts, and he summons his kings, who arrive trembling and wonder at whom the anger is aimed.
source_issues: Verses 1132, 1135, 1138, 1145, 1147, 1150 and 1152 were printed as eight half-lines and repaired to four lines.
Verse 1154 had a stray pulli after a vowel sign removed in line 1.
Verse 1138 line 3 and verse 1143 are broken or leave the subject unnamed; verse 1148 does not say who the adorned maiden is.
Verse 1136 may still be the spy's report rather than the poet's own voice.

cast.role: the spy who comes down from the sky to the Vidyadhara king on earth
the Vidyadhara king on earth, the bride's father, addressed as lord of the chariot
the rival discus-lord of the Vidyadhara world, whose rage fills the chapter
the Vidyadhara who took the lion's shape and now reports the lion's death to the king
the minister who hides the news and sends Arikethu to tell it
the Vidyadharas of the sky and of the king's court
the kings seated around Acuvakandan when Arikethu tells his tale
one of the king's own people who brings word of the maiden and of Chakravalam
the messengers sent with drums to summon the kings, named only by a plural verb
the kings called in by drum, who arrive and wonder at his anger

tamil: நாவியே கமழுந் தொங்க னகைமணி வயிரப் பூணான்
ஆவியி னகத்து ளாளு மருவரை யகலத் தாளுந்
தேவியே யாக வன்ன திருவொடு மிருவ ராவான்
பூவினுண் மடந்தை வந்து புகுந்தவா றுரைக்க லுற்றேன்.
reading: The poet opens the sarukkam by saying he will tell how the lady of the lotus, Fortune, came to enter the lord who has both the woman who rules his life and Fortune on his mountain-broad chest.
nuance: The sentence is compressed: இருவராவான் can mean the lord of two consorts or one who becomes a pair with Fortune, and the lord is not named in the verse; Tivittan is the natural reading from the story so far.

tamil: கண்மிசை கனிந்த ஒற்றன்கூற்று காதற் களிப்படு செல்வ முந்நீர்
உண்மிசை யுக்கோர் நச்சுத் துள்ளிவந் துறைப்ப தேபோல்
விண்மிசை யிழிந்து வந்த வொற்றனோர் வெஞ்சொன் மாற்ற
மண்மிசை யிருந்த விஞ்சை மன்னனை வணங்கிச் சொன்னான்.
reading: A spy comes down from the sky and bows to the Vidyadhara king who sits on earth, and his harsh word falls on the king's joy as a drop of poison leaps into one drinking from a sea.
nuance: The first half-line (கண்மிசை கனிந்த) does not parse cleanly after the repair of the eight half-lines; the simile of the poison in the sea of joy is clear.
event: A spy descends from the sky and, after bowing, tells the Vidyadhara king on earth bad news.

tamil: விரைசெல லிவுளித் தேரோய் விஞ்சைய ருலக மாளும்
அரைசர்க டிகிரி யாளும் அச்சுவ கண்ட னோடும்
திரைசெல வுரறி ஞாலந் தின்னிய கடல்க ளேழுங்
கரைசெல வருவ போனம் மேல்வரக் கருது கின்றார்.
reading: The spy tells the lord of the chariot that the kings who rule the Vidyadhara world, with the discus-lord Acuvakandan, mean to come upon them as the seven seas would break over their shores.
event: The spy reports that Acuvakandan and the Vidyadhara kings are planning to march against Tivittan's side.

tamil: அரைசர்கள் வருக போக வதுபண்டே யறிந்து தன்றே
வரைசெறி சிங்க வேறு மணிவண்ண னழித்த ஞான்றே
விரைசெறி பொழில்கொள் சோலை விஞ்சைய ருலகிற் பட்ட
துரைசிறி தென்ன லோடு மொற்றனு முரைக்க லுற்றான்.
reading: The king answers that the kings may come or go, he knew it long ago, from the day the dark-hued one destroyed the mountain lion, and the spy begins to tell what befell the Vidyadhara world.
nuance: The first three lines are the king's words and the fourth is the poet's; மணிவண்ணன் (the jewel-hued one) is taken as Tivittan, who is called dark-hued elsewhere.
event: The Vidyadhara king shrugs off the threat, saying he foresaw it from the lion's death, and the spy starts his account.

tamil: அருளுமா றடிகள் கேண்மோ வரியர சதனை யாரு
மருளுமா றிளைய காளை வாய்பிளந் திட்ட வார்த்தை
தெருளுமா றொருவன் சொல்லக் கேட்டலுஞ் சேணில் வாழ்வார்
வெருளுமா றுள்ள மெல்லாம் வெருண்டுமெய் விதலை கொண்டார்.
reading: The spy bids the lord hear how, when one man told the word that the younger bull had split the lion's mouth, the sky-dwellers were so frightened that their whole bodies shook.
event: The Vidyadharas of the sky tremble on hearing that Tivittan has split the lion's mouth.

tamil: விஞ்சைய ருலக மெல்லாம் வெய்துற விரிந்த மாற்றம்
அஞ்சினன் மறைத்துச் சின்னா ளமைச்சரி மஞ்சு வென்பான்
வஞ்சனைச் சீய மாய வார்கழ லவனைக் கூவி
எஞ்சலில் புகழி னானுக் கின்னண மிசைப்பித் தானே.
reading: The news of the lion's death spreads and scorches the whole Vidyadhara world; the minister Arimanju fears it, hides it for some days, then calls the one who had become the cunning lion and has him tell it to the glorious king.
nuance: The voice may still be the spy's report. வஞ்சனைச் சீயம் is taken as Arikethu, who took the lion's shape at 696 and 697; 1137 names him.
event: Arimanju, after hiding the news, calls Arikethu to report the lion's death to Acuvakandan.

tamil: சொரிகதிர் வயிரப் பைம்பூ ணரசர்கள் பலருஞ் சூழ
எரிகதி ராழி யாள்வா னினிதினங் கிருந்த போழ்தின்
அரியது கேட்க வென்ன வரிகேது வென்பா னாங்குப்
பெரியதோர் வியப்புச் சென்று பட்டது பேசி னானால்.
reading: While the discus-lord sits happily among kings in diamond jewels, Arikethu says he has something rare to tell and reports that a great marvel has befallen.
event: Arikethu reports the lion's death to Acuvakandan before his kings.

tamil: கரியவன் வளைந்த வெள்ளை யெயிற்றவன் காள மேகம்
பெரியதொன் றிரண்டு கொம்மைப் பிறைகவ்வி யிருந்த தன்னான்
உரையெதிர் கபில வட்டக் கண்ணெரி யுமிழ்ந்த மாதோ.
reading: As Arikethu tells of the black lion with curved white fangs, like a dark cloud gripping two crescents, Acuvakandan's tawny round eyes spit fire in answer.
nuance: Line 3 is broken (அரியதங் கென்னை யென்னை) and may be Arikethu's cry of wonder; the sense of line 4, the king's fiery eyes, is clear.
event: Acuvakandan's eyes blaze as Arikethu describes the lion and its end.

tamil: மடித்தவா யெயிறு கவ்வி மருங்கினோர் வயிரக் கற்றூண்
அடித்தலி னசனி வீழ வருவரை நெரிவ தேபோற்
படித்தலை நடுங்க மற்றப் பரூஉத்திரள் வயிரத் தம்பந்
தொடித்தலை சிதைந்து நுங்கத் துகளெழுந் தொழிந்த தன்றே.
reading: With his lip folded over his fangs he strikes a diamond pillar beside him, and like a thunderbolt on a great mountain the thick pillar's head shatters and dust rises as the earth shakes.
event: Acuvakandan smashes a diamond pillar with a blow.

tamil: விஞ்சைய ரதனைக் கண்டு மெய்பொதி ரெறிந்து விம்ம
வெஞ்சினங் கனன்று மீட்டும் விஞ்சைய னவனை நோக்கி
வஞ்சனை மனத்த ராய மனிசரை வலிய ரென்பாய்
அஞ்சினை பெரிது மேடா வென்றன னசனி யொப்பான்.
reading: The Vidyadharas see the pillar broken and shudder with bristling hair; the king, blazing again, turns on the Vidyadhara and says that he who calls treacherous men strong is greatly afraid.
event: Acuvakandan taunts Arikethu for fearing men.

tamil: நிலத்திடை மக்க ளாற்ற னின்னைப்போ லஞ்சு வார்க்கு
மலைத்துணை பெருகிக் காட்டு மற்றதிங் கெம்ம னோர்க்கோர்
இலைத்தது மில்லை மன்னோ வென்றன் னிரண்டு திங்கள்
பிலத்திடை பொடித்த போலும் பிறழ்ந்திலங் கெயிற்றி னானே.
reading: Acuvakandan says the strength of men on earth swells to a mountain only for the timid, and that to his own kind it counts for not even a leaf, his curved fangs flashing like two moons broken out of a pit.
nuance: The claim is the rival king's pride; the lion's death just told is already the evidence against it, but this verse itself does not answer it.
event: Acuvakandan scorns the strength of earth-men.

tamil: கனைகதிர்க் கடகக் கையாற் கற்றிர ளுதிர வெற்றிச்
சினவழ லெறிப்ப நோக்கிச் சிவந்தனன் றெழித்த லோடு
மனநனி மயங்கி மற்ற விஞ்சைய ரஞ்ச நின்ற
நனைமல ரலங்கற் கேது நகைகொண்ட மனத்த னானான்.
reading: At his bracelet-bright hand the stones fall in a heap and a flame of victory-wrath flashes, he reddens and roars, the Vidyadharas lose heart, and Arikethu in his wet-flower garland is left with a mind that has taken on a smile.
nuance: Line 4 gives no reason for Arikethu's smile: forced courtesy, inward scorn or relief are all open.
event: Acuvakandan roars and breaks the stones while the Vidyadharas fear and Arikethu smiles inwardly.

tamil: அடுகுர லரச சீய மதனையோ ராம்பற் றாள்போல்
நொடிவரை யளவிற் கீறி நுனித்தது வியத்தல் செய்யாக்
கடிவரை யலங்கன் மார்பிற் காளையே பெரிய னென்று
தடவரை யனைய தோளான் றன்னுளே வியந்து நின்றான்.
reading: Arikethu, mountain-shouldered, marvels within himself that the youth who tore the roaring lion-king in a snap, as one tears a lotus stalk, is the truly great one.
nuance: The verse does not name who marvels; 1142 ends on Arikethu and 1144 has him join his hands, so he is read as the one thinking.
event: Arikethu privately admires Tivittan's feat.

tamil: இன்றிவ னனலும் போழ்தி னெதிர்நின்று கனற்றி யென்னை
சென்றவ னாற்ற றானே கண்டபின் றேறு மன்னறே
என்றுதன் மனத்தி லெண்ணி யியைந்தவா முகமன் சொல்லிக்
குன்றுடை யரசன் முன்னைக் கூப்பிய கைய னானான்.
reading: He thinks there is no use standing against the king as he blazes today, since the king will understand only when he has seen the youth's strength himself; so he speaks fitting courtesies and stands before the lord of the hill with joined hands.
event: Arikethu holds back, flatters and stands with folded hands before Acuvakandan.

tamil: அமர்நனி தொடங்கு மேனும் ஆர்த்துநீர் கொணர்மி னென்று
தமருளங் கொருவன் வந்து சக்கிர வாளந் தன்னுள்
நமரது நிலையு நங்கை போந்தது நடுங்கச் சொன்னான்.
reading: As Acuvakandan finishes his harsh command that the prince be brought with a shout even if war breaks out, a man of his own people comes and, trembling, tells of their state in Chakravalam and that the maiden has gone.
nuance: நமரது நிலை (the state of our people) is left vague, and நங்கை போந்தது is read with the next verse as the maiden's going to Tivittan.
event: A kinsman interrupts Acuvakandan's command to report the maiden's departure and the state of Chakravalam.

tamil: அடிகளிவ் வவனி தன்மே லிழிந்தது மணங்கோ டொப்பாள்
கடிவினை நிலையு மன்றே கண்டுவந் தொருவன் கூறச்
சுடுசொலிஃ தொழிக வென்று துணைச்செவி புதைத்து வல்லே
முடிமுத றுளங்கத் தூக்கி முனிவினை முடிவு கொண்டான்.
reading: A man who has seen it says the maiden has come down to this earth as one wed; the king, crying that these burning words must stop, stops both ears, shakes his crown and settles on his anger.
nuance: The wording of the news (மணங்கோடு ஒப்பாள், கடிவினை நிலையும்) is compressed; the sense that the rival has the girl he once sought is taken from 306 and 348.
event: Acuvakandan, told that the maiden is wedded on earth, stops his ears and resolves on wrath.

tamil: பெருகினான் வெகுளி கண்ணுட் பிறந்தது பிறங்கு செந்தீ
உருகினான் போன்று தோன்ற மயிர்த்துளை யுகுத்த தெண்ணீர்
திருகினா னெயிறு செவ்வாய் கறித்தனன் றிசைக ளோடும்
அருகினோர் நடுங்க நோக்கி யழனகை டுத்து நின்றான்.
reading: His rage swells: red fire seems to be born in his eyes, water streams from every hair-pore, he twists his fangs, bites his red lip and looks round so that all near him tremble, laughing like fire.
event: Acuvakandan's rage shows in his body.

tamil: மலைகளை மறித்து மற்றோர் மறிகட னடுவ ணிட்டவ்
வலைதிரை மகர முந்நீ ரதுவிது வாக்கு வேன்கொல்
உலகினை யுள்ளங் கைக்கொண் டுருளையா வுருட்டி யிட்டென்
பலபுனை மடந்தை தன்கீழ்ப் பதித்திடு வேன்கொ லென்றான்.
reading: He boasts that he might turn the mountains over and cast them into the sea to make it something else, or roll the world in his palm like a ball and set it beneath his much-adorned maiden.
nuance: Who the 'many-adorned maiden' is, the girl he wanted or another, is not stated.
event: Acuvakandan voices boasts of overturning mountains and rolling the world.

tamil: அனன்றனன் றவைகள் பேசி யமையுமவ் வரசர் தீமை
சனங்களைத் திரட்டிப் பின்னைத் தக்கதொன் றறிவ னென்றான்
சினங்கெழு காலன் மற்றோர் காலன்மேற் சிவந்த தொப்பான்.
reading: Still blazing, he says that if the kings' wrong is to be taken to heart he will gather the people of the gem-mountain world and only then decide what fits; the angry king glows like Death angry at another Death.
nuance: Which kings' wrong is meant by அரசர் தீமை is not fixed; it is read as the rival side's.
event: Acuvakandan decides to assemble his people before deciding his course.

tamil: சிறந்தெரி யனலோ டொப்பான் பணிகொண்டு திசைக ளோடி
அறைந்தனர் முரசிற் சாற்றி யறைதலு மரச ரெல்லாம்
மறைந்தன வுலக மென்ன மாய்ந்தன திசைக ளென்னப்
பறந்தனர் விசும்பு போர்ப்பக் கடற்படை பரப்பி வந்தார்.
reading: Blazing like fire, he sends messengers to every quarter; they proclaim the call by drum, and the kings, as if the world and the quarters had vanished, fly in with the sea-armies they have spread to cover the sky.
event: Acuvakandan's heralds summon the kings, who arrive with their armies.

tamil: மற்றவ ரடைந்து வெய்யோன் மலரடி வணங்கி நின்று
செற்றவ னிருந்த வாறுஞ் செங்கண்டீ யுமிழ்ந்த வாறும்
எற்றிய வயிரத் திண்டூ ணெரிந்திடை கிடந்த வாறும்
உற்றன பிறவு நோக்கி யுள்ளங்க ணடுங்கி யிட்டார்.
reading: The arrived kings bow at the sun-like lord's flower feet, and as they look at how the angry one sits, how his red eyes spat fire and how the struck diamond pillar lies burned, their hearts shake.
event: The summoned kings see Acuvakandan's rage and the ruined pillar and tremble.

tamil: சுரியுளைத் துளைக ளாவி விடுகின்ற சுழலுஞ் செங்கண்
கருமுகி னுடங்கு மின்போற் புருவங்கண் முரிந்து நீங்கான்
பெரியதோர் முனிவு கொண்டான் பிறையெயிற் றரியோ டொப்பான்
எரியினுள் விளிய லுற்றார் யார்கொலோ வளிய ரென்பார்.
reading: Seeing his red eyes spit fire and his brows knotted like lightning in a black cloud, never loosed from wrath like a fanged lion, the kings ask who the wretches are who are to die in the fire.
event: The kings murmur about whom his anger will burn.

tamil: ஞாலமேற் றிரிந்து நாளு முயிர்களை நடுங்கப் பார்க்குங்
காலனைக் கதம்பட் டான்கொ லன்றெனிற் கற்ப மாள்வார்
மேலெனக் கிருப்பார் போலு மெனவெகுண் டனல்கின் றான்கொல்
வேலைநீ ருலகின் மற்றிவ் வெகுளிக்கு முதலென் னென்பார்.
reading: They ask whether he is enraged at Death, who roams the earth making creatures tremble, or at those who rule through the ages and who he thinks are above him, and what the root of this anger is in the sea-girt world.
event: The kings guess whether his anger is aimed at Death or at the lords of the ages.

tamil: ஊழிகள் பெயர்க்க லுற்றிவ் வுலகினைப் பிறிதொன் றாக்கி
வாழுயி ரொருங்கு வாரி மறிகட னடுவட் பெய்வான்
சூழிய தொடங்கு கின்ற தாங்கொலோ சொல்லி னீடொன்
றாழியான் வெகுளிக் குண்டோ யாரிரை யாவ தென்பார்.
reading: They ask whether he has begun to move the ages, make the world something else and sweep all living things into the churned sea, and whether the discus-lord's anger has any prey worth so great an end.
nuance: Line 1 has a stray pulli repaired; the kings' picture of an age-ending flood is their guess, not the poet's.
event: The kings fear his anger portends the world's end.

tamil: தானவ ரரக்கர் பண்டே தஞ்சமா மிவற்கு மண்மேல்
ஊனவர் மனித்த ரேக வுவனுக்கோர் துகளு மாகார்
வானவ ரிவற்கு மாறாய் வருபவர் மதிப்பி னில்லை
ஏனவர் முனிவு செய்வார் யார்பிற ருரைமி னென்பார்.
reading: They say the danavas and rakshasas have long been his refuge, flesh-eating men on earth are not even dust to him, the gods are not worth counting as his rivals, and ask who else he can be angry with.
nuance: The courtiers' flattery is the rival camp's picture of him, set in the story before the war that tests it.
event: The kings fail to find any rival for his anger.

title: அரசியற் சருக்கம் 1156-1180 (2/17)
theme: In the council of the angry king, whose rage over a rumoured pledge of the Rathanupura maid to a human sets the court to talk of war, the soldiers, kin and ministers speak in turn, some urging war and some counselling scheming or restraint.
source_issues: Verse 1173 has three lines instead of four and its first word is damaged.
Verses 1157, 1158, 1159, 1166, 1174, 1177, 1178, 1179 and 1180 had a line repaired from eight half-lines or a stray pulli.
Verse 1180 line 3 ends in a full stop that cuts the sense; verses 1163, 1170, 1171 and 1176 have word division that makes the sense uncertain.

cast.role: the frightened people of the city who talk of the end of the world
the angry king of the strong rutting elephant (கச்சையங் களிநல் யானைக் காவலன்) in 1157, taken as Asvagriva; not named in this chapter
the kings of the court who roar in answer to the king's rage
the soldiers who speak as 'those who say' in 1160 to 1163
the unnamed man who brings back the report of the council, in the first person in 1174; taken as a spy
an unnamed warrior who speaks in council in 1165 to 1169, 1172, 1178 and 1179; may be several voices
the warrior Kanakachitran who speaks in council
the king's younger brother Vajrakandan, in the Tamil வச்சிர கண்டன்
the king's brothers and sons who cool his anger
the minister Arimanju who asks the king what he intends
the ruler of Megakuta who speaks in council
the king of a fire-mountain city who speaks in council
the king's dear friend Arisenan, a spear-bearing warrior

tamil: இற்றதிவ் வுலக மென்பா ரெரிந்தன திசைக ளென்பார்
அற்றன மகர முந்நீ ரகம்புலர்ந் தொழியு மென்பார்
மற்றினி மொழியல் வேண்டா வருவன வறிய லாகா
உற்றபி னறிது மென்றாங் குரையொழி வாரு மானார்.
reading: The people first say the world is broken, the quarters burned and the ocean dried, then fall silent: what is coming cannot be known and they will learn it when it arrives.
nuance: The verse closes the run of crowd dread that begins at 1153; the speakers are the frightened citizens, not the war party.
event: The people of the city, dreading the king's rage, trail off into silence.

tamil: அச்சமோ டுலக மின்றே யவிந்தன போன்று மென்பார்
நச்செரி நகையி னாலே நடுங்கின திசைக ளென்பார்
இச்சைகள் பிறந்த வாற்றா லினையன நினையும் போழ்திற்
கச்சையங் களிநல் யானைக் காவலன் கனன்று சொன்னான்.
reading: Some say the world will be lost in fear and the quarters tremble at his poison-laughter; at these thoughts the lord of the strong rutting elephant burns and speaks.
nuance: The king is named only by his epithet (the lord of the elephant); the story so far makes him the discus-lord Asvagriva, so the cast takes that name.
event: The elephant-lord king, in a rage, begins to speak to the court.

tamil: இரதநூ புரத்தை யாள்வான் புதல்வியை யுனைவஞ் சித்துப்
புரிமனு சர்க்கீ வாக்கே புகன்றனன் போலு மென்ற
உரைதனக் குரைத்த வாறே யுரைத்தன னுலக மெல்லாம்
இரைதனக் கென்று மாற்றா வெரிபடு வெகுளித் தீயான்.
reading: What the king says in anger is that the ruler of Rathanupuram has deceived him and, it is said, has promised his daughter to a human; he repeats the news as it was brought, and his fire of wrath cannot be quenched.
nuance: The verse reports a rumour (போலும் என்ற உரை) that the king repeats as fact, so his rage rests on hearsay.
event: The king repeats the report that the Rathanupura ruler has given his daughter to a human.

tamil: முரைசொலி முழையி னுள்ளான் முழங்குகின் றதனோ டொப்ப
விரையொலி விளங்கு தாரான் விளம்பிய வெகுளி மாற்றம்
அரைசர்க ளதனைக் கேட்டே யிதனுக்கோ வடிக ளிவ்வா
றுரைசெல முனிவ தென்றோ ரொல்லொலி யெழுந்த தன்றே.
reading: The king's angry words roar like a drum in a cave; the kings who hear them rise in a loud cry asking whether he should be so angry over this.
nuance: The assembled kings' cry reads as a question put to him, but its tone (protest or agreement) is not fixed by the Tamil.
event: The assembled kings answer the king's rage with a roar of protest.

tamil: செழுமல ரலங்கன் மார்பன் செங்கண்டீ யுமிழக் கண்டும்
எழுமலர்ந் தனைய திண்டோ ளிவைசுமந் திருப்ப தென்னே
கழுகுபோற் களத்து வென்று கதலிகை நடுது மன்றேல்
விழவயர் விசும்பி னார்க்கு விருந்தின மாது மென்பார்.
reading: Soldiers say: why carry these strong arms idle when the king spits fire; if we do not win on the field like eagles and plant the banners, we shall be a feast for the sky-dwellers.
event: The soldiers urge going to war and say they will win or die.

tamil: ஏவது செய்து வாழும் யாமுள மாக வெங்கோ
நோவது செய்து வேந்தர் நுனித்துயிர் வாழ்ப வாயிற்
சாவது போக வாழ்க்கை தவந்தலை நிற்ற லொன்றோ
வீவது செய்த லொன்றோ நமக்கினி விளைவ தென்பார்.
reading: Other men, who live doing the king's bidding, ask what is left for them if kings live by tormenting others: their life is bound to death, so is austerity the only resort, or is it ruin?
nuance: தவம் here is austerity as the only alternative to dying in the king's cause; the verse does not endorse it as a path, only lets the soldiers name it.
event: Some of the king's men voice doubt about being ruled by the king's anger.

tamil: நாண்டொழின் மகளிர் முன்னும் நகைக்கிளை யாயத் துள்ளும்
வீண்டொழில் விளம்பி யென்னை வீரங்கள் வெறிய வாக
ஆண்டொழில் புகுந்த தம்மா வதோவினி தாயிற் றென்று
தூண்டொழில் வளரத் தத்தந் தோள்களை நோக்கு கிற்பார்.
reading: The soldiers say that after idle boasts before women and kin their heroism will be empty unless the work of men now comes; they look at their own shoulders, restless for war.
event: The soldiers, shamed by their boasts, look to their shoulders and long for battle.

tamil: நாள்வடுப் படாமை நம்மைப் புறந்தந்தாற் குதவி நங்கள்
டோள்வடுப் படாமை மன்னன் புகழ்வடுப் படுத லுண்டோ
வாள்வடுப் பிளவு போலுங் கண்ணியை மகிழ்ந்த காளை
கேள்வடுப் படரும் பூசல் கேட்டிரா நாளை யென்பார்.
reading: The soldiers say that the king who guarded them must not have his fame wounded, and that those who delighted in the maid will hear the din of the youth's kin tomorrow.
nuance: Line 1 to 2 are hard to read in the word division, so the sense that the king's fame must not take a scar is held loosely.
event: The soldiers pledge themselves to protect the king's fame and promise a clash tomorrow.

tamil: இனியிருந் தென்னை பாவ மெழுமின் போய்ப் பொருது மென்பார்
முனிவன செய்த வேந்தன் முடித்தலை கொணர்து மென்பார்
கனிவளர் கிளவி யாளைக் கைப்பற்றித் தருது மென்பார்
பனிவரை யரசர் மாற்றம் பற்பல பரிதி வேலோய்.
reading: The speaker, turning to the sun-spear lord he addresses, says the kings say: why stay, go and fight, bring the head of the offending king, seize the maid; many such words came from the mountain kings.
nuance: Here the speaker first addresses a listener (பரிதி வேலோய்); the chapter ends with a first-person line (போந்தேன், 1174), so from here the verses are read as a report brought back to the listener, a reading not fixed in the Tamil.
event: The speaker relays the kings' calls to fight and to seize the girl.

tamil: சினமெனப் பட்ட தீயுட் பிறந்தது செருக்கு நன்னீர்
மனவுண வுண்டு மானப் பூநின்ற வயிர வொள்வாள்
அனலதொன் றகத்த தாக வாரமர் குருதி வேட்டுக்
கனல்வதோர் கால வொள்வாள் கடைக்கணித் தொருவன் சொன்னான்.
reading: One born of the fire called anger, whose pride feeds on blood, looks at his diamond sword and speaks: pride feeds on the heart and the sword thirsts for blood.
nuance: சினம் is made the source of செருக்கு, so pride is presented as anger's offspring; the warrior does not condemn either.
event: An angry warrior speaks of his sword and pride.

tamil: தோள்களைத் தகர்த்து வீக்கித் துணைக்கரங் கொட்டி யார்த்து
வாள்களைத் துடைத்து நோக்கி வகைசெய்வ தெளிதி யார்க்கும்
நீள்கதி ரிமைக்கு மொள்வாண் முகம்பெற நெருப்புச் சிந்தித்
தாள்களை வெதுப்பும் வெம்போர் தாங்குவ தரிய தென்றான்.
reading: He claps his shoulders, wipes his sword and says anyone can prepare for war, but to bear the fierce war whose sparks scorch the foot is hard.
event: The warrior boasts of the hardship of war and his readiness to bear it.

tamil: தானவ ரெனினு மிப்போ ரிழந்து போய்த் தரணி வாழும்
ஊனம ருலக மாளு மூழியொன் றிதுவன் றாயில்
வானவ ருலகு மண்ணும் வந்துநின் வாயில் பற்றி
ஈனமொ டுறங்கக் காட்டி யிடுவன்யான் றெளியிய தென்றான்.
reading: He swears that unless this war is won, even gods and earth-dwellers will come to the king's gate and sleep in shame, which he will show them.
event: The warrior vows to make both gods and humans sleep in disgrace if he does not win.

tamil: வாளினாற் செருவுண் டேனு மாயமற் றாகு மேனுந்
தோளினா லாகு மேனுஞ் சொல்லெலா மொழிக மற்றக்
காளைதன் னுயிரி னோடுங் கன்னியைக் கொணர்ந்து தந்து
தாளிலே யிட்ட பின்றைத் தவிர்கநின் சீற்ற மென்றான்.
reading: Whether by sword, by trick or by shoulder, he says, let all talk end: he will bring the maid together with the youth's life and lay her at the king's feet, and only then should the king's anger cease.
nuance: The warrior offers any means (sword, trick or shoulder) to win; he places no limit on method.
event: The warrior offers to bring the maid and the youth's life to the king's feet.

tamil: ஆளிகட் கரச னாங்கோர் குறுநரி யறிவில் லாத
மீளிமை பொறாது வெம்பி வெகுண்டெழு கின்ற தென்றால்
நாளினு நங்கள் போல்வார் நகைசெயப் படுவ தன்றே
வாளொளி வயிர மின்னு மணிமுடி மன்னர் கோவே.
reading: A speaker says: if a little jackal, with no understanding, rose in rage against lions, such as we would be laughed at daily, O lord of kings of shining crowns.
nuance: The comparison (lions and jackal) assumes the foe is low; the story's later battles test that assumption.
event: The speaker warns that anger against a lowly foe will make the great a laughing-stock.

tamil: ஆதலா லெங்க ளாலங் காவதொன் றில்லை யாயிற்
போதுலா மலங்கன் மார்ப பொருவது பொருந்திற் றென்னும்
காதலான் கனக சித்திரன் கட்டுரை யதனைக் கேட்டே
கோதிலா மாரி பெய்த கோடையங் குன்ற மொத்தான்.
reading: Kanakachitran, who loves the king, says that since they cannot guard against it there is nothing for them but to fight; on hearing it the king is like a summer hill after rain.
nuance: The words of the two clauses are hard to join (ஆலங்காவது ஒன்றில்லை), and whether the rain-cooled hill means the king's anger is cooled or his wrath is fed is not clear in the Tamil.
event: Kanakachitran urges fighting and the king's rage cools.

tamil: மற்றவ னுரைத்த போழ்தின் வச்சிர கண்ட னென்பான்
கொற்றவற் கிளைய காளை கோத்தொழிற் பாகம் பூண்டான்
இற்றதா லெங்க ளாண்மை யாங்களு மிழிந்து நிற்பச்
reading: Vajrakandan, the king's younger brother, red-eyed, says that their manhood is broken and they themselves stand lowered now that a foe has risen against them.
nuance: Line 3 is hard to read, so the specific cause of the lowered manhood is held loosely.
event: Vajrakandan, in anger, says the foe has lowered their manhood.

tamil: மகரமால் கடலை யல்லாற் சிறுகய மதலை சேரா
சிகரமால் யானை வேந்தே தானவர் செருவன் றாயின்
நிகரலா நீசர் தம்மேல் நீசெலற் பால தென்று
புகரெரி யவிக்க லுற்றான் பொழிமழை பொழிவ தொத்தான்.
reading: One tries to put out the fire like rain: a small pond does not take the great sea's young, so, if this war is not against demons, the king of great elephants should not march on lowly foes.
nuance: The speaker of 1172 is not named; it follows Vajrakandan's speech but may be another voice.
event: A speaker argues that a great king should not fight lowly men.

tamil: கேறனான் றம்பி மாரு மக்களு மின்ன போல்வ
கூறினார் கூற லோடுங் குரையழ லவிவ தேபோல்
ஆறினா னென்னை செய்யு மாயபண் பதுவ தானால்.
reading: His brothers and sons say such things, and at their words the roaring fire seems to die: he cooled, and what can be done, such is his nature.
nuance: The verse has three lines instead of four and the first word is damaged, so the sense that the king cools on his kin's words is held loosely.
event: The king's kin speak and his anger dies down.

tamil: அரசர்க ணெறியிற் கண்டீர் யாம்பிழைப் பிலாமை யென்று
முரசென வதிரும் பேழ்வாய் முழங்கிசை மொழியிற் சாற்றி
வரைசெறிந் தனைய தோளான் மந்திர சாலை சேர்ந்தான்
உரைசெறிந் தங்குப் பட்ட சூழ்ச்சியு முணர்ந்து போந்தேன்.
reading: The king says, 'Look, by the way of kings we are without fault,' thunders his answer and goes into the council hall; the speaker says he came away having learned the counsel made there.
nuance: The last line is in the first person (போந்தேன்), the only mark in the chapter that the narration is a report from a speaker who was present.
event: The king thunders that he is without fault and enters the council hall; the speaker returns with what was planned.

tamil: கன்னிதன் றிறத்துச் சீறிக் காவலன் கனலக் கண்டீர்
என்னினிக் கருது கின்ற தென்றன னெரியு மாழி
மன்னவற் குணர்வுங் கண்ணு மாற்றலும் வலியுந் தோளும்
அன்னவ னமைச்சர்க் கேறா மவனரி மஞ்சு வென்பான்.
reading: The king burns with anger over the maid; the minister Arimanju asks him what he now thinks, a man whose understanding, eye and arm other ministers cannot match.
event: Arimanju asks the angry king what he plans.

tamil: அணிநகர் மேக கூட மதனையாண் டரிய செய்கை
துணிபவன் றூம கேது சொல்லுவா னென்ன சொன்னான்
மணிவரைப் பிறந்து மாண்ட வருங்கல மன்னர் கோமான்
பணிவரை யன்றி யாரே பெறுபவர் பகர்மி னென்றான்.
reading: Dhumakethu, who rules the city of Megakuta and dares hard deeds, says: the rare jewels born of the gem mountains, who but those who bow to the king of kings will gain them, tell me.
nuance: The jewel image is probably the maid and the speaker's point that only those who bow to the overlord deserve her, but the Tamil does not say so.
event: Dhumakethu speaks in council about who deserves rare jewels.

tamil: வரைதன்மேற் றழலின் பேரார் வளநக ரதனை யாளும்
அரசனங் கார வேக னதனைக்கேட் டழன்று சொல்வான்
இரதநூ புரத்தை யாள்வா னிகழ்ந்தனன் பெரிது நம்மைப்
பொருதவன் கிளையை முந்நீர்ப் புறங்கரைப் படுத்து மென்றான்.
reading: Angaravegan, ruler of a city in a fire-capped mountain, says that the ruler of Rathanupuram has slighted them and that they will drive the kin of the man who fought them to the sea shore.
event: Angaravegan proposes to drive the foe's kin from his land.

tamil: மல்லினான் மலர்ந்த மார்பீர் மறைந்துநா மிருந்து வல்ல
சொல்லினால் வெல்ல லாமேற் சொல்லுமி னின்னு மன்றி
வில்லினால் விரவு தானைச் செருவினுள் வீரந் தன்னால்
வெல்லலா மென்னி னென்னை விடுமின்போய்ப் பொருவ லென்றான்.
reading: A warrior says: if we can win by hidden words, tell me; if we can win with bow and army by valour, let me go and fight.
event: A warrior asks whether to win by words or by war and offers to fight.

tamil: பூவினும் பொருதல் வேண்டா சூழ்ச்சியே பொருந்த நோக்கி
யாவது காண்ட லாகு மரசர்க்கு நீதி யென்று
சாவதை யஞ்சு வார்க்குந் தகைமையில் லவர்க்கு மன்றே
ஓவுத லின்றி யோதி வைத்ததங் கொருவ னென்றான்.
reading: One says there is no need to fight even a flower; kings' justice is to look closely at scheming and see what can be gained, which is taught constantly for those who fear death and lack worth.
nuance: நீதி here is the rule of statecraft, not justice in the sense of a fair verdict.
event: A counsellor argues for scheming over open war.

tamil: அழலவி ரலங்கல் வேலோ னவ்வரி சேன னென்பான்
கழலவன் காதற் றோழன் கனன்றவன் கருதிச் சொன்ன
மொழியெதி ருலக மாள்வா னுவந்தவன் முகத்தை நோக்கிப்.
பழிபெரி தொழியச் சொன்னான் படைத்திற லாள னென்றான்.
reading: Arisenan, the king's dear friend and bright-spear warrior, listens to the king's angry words and calls him a man of army's might who should leave behind the great blame.
nuance: Line 3 ends in a full stop, the verse is hard to read and the sense of the last line is held loosely.
event: Arisenan answers the king's rage by speaking of his army's might.

title: அரசியற் சருக்கம் 1181-1205 (3/17)
theme: Under the threat of the discus-lord's army, the Vidyadhara king's council debates what kind of war to fight and the warriors boast in turn; Tivittan takes the war on himself, is given the last art, and receives the envoys' ultimatum for the maid.
source_issues: Many verses (1181, 1182, 1185, 1191, 1196, 1197, 1201, 1202, 1204) were printed in eight half-lines and repaired into four.
Verses 1186, 1188, 1198 and 1199 had a stray pulli repaired.
Verse 1205 has a short last line pattern (about three feet), and verses 1183 and 1184 are compressed and loosely read.
Speakers of 1189 to 1195 are unnamed groups of warriors marked only by என்பார்.

cast.role: king of the Vidyadharas, here named by his banner
the council of counsellors
Srisenan, ruler of Tirunilai, the counsellor who speaks of the kinds of war
the kings of the southern hills who march against the city
the spy whose report is repeated
the unnamed warriors and kings of the council who boast in turn
the young warriors of the host
Asvagriva, the discus-lord whose army is feared
Arkakirti, who speaks to his bow ('red-ray namesake')
Vijayan, the plough-bearing elder brother of the dark-hued Tivittan
Tivittan, the king's son-in-law and the young hero
the Vidyadhara king, Tivittan's father-in-law
the gods of the air called by the mantra
the two envoys who arrive
the envoys of the golden-discus king

tamil: பொருவதோ வெளிதி யாங்கள் பொருந்திற முரைமி னென்னை
மருவிய மனிதப் போரோ வான்கெழு தெய்வப் போரோ
இருமையி னியன்ற போரோ யாதுநாந் துணிவ தென்றான்
விரிசிறை யுவணஞ் சேர்ந்த வென்றிநற் கொடியி னானே.
reading: The king whose banner bears the great bird asks his council whether the coming fight should be a war of men, a war of gods, or one of both kinds, and what they resolve.
nuance: The speaker is named only by his banner (the line-4 epithet), so the identification with the Vidyadhara king rests on the council scene of the preceding verses.
event: The Vidyadhara king puts to his council the question of what kind of war to wage against the discus-lord.

tamil: செப்பிய மாற்றங் கேட்டே திறற்சிரீ சேன னென்பான்
திப்பியர் புகழுஞ் செல்வத் திருநிலை யகம தாள்வான்
அப்படித் தாயிற் கேண்மி னறிந்தவ ரறைந்த வாறென்
றிப்படை நிலைமை யோரா னெடுத்தெடுத் தியம்பு கின்றான்.
reading: Hearing the king's question, the ruler of Tirunilai, named Srisenan, says that he will set out what the wise have laid down and then lays out the army's state in order.
event: Srisenan rises to answer the king's question about the kind of war.

tamil: பொருப்படைத் தொகையோர் மூன்று போர்த்தொழி றானு மூன்றே
மருவுடை மனுடந் தெய்வ மிருமையு மென்ன மற்ற
வெருவுடைப் படையின் குப்பை மேலது நான்கு வீற்ற
திருபடை யொழிந்து நின்ற விவையும்பாங் குடைய வென்றான்.
reading: Srisenan divides the forces and the work of war into three, human, divine and both, and says the host and its kinds follow from this.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are hard to construe (the counting of 'four' and the leftover 'two forces'); the sense of a threefold division is firm, the further split is held loosely.
event: Srisenan classes war and armies into human, divine and mixed kinds.

tamil: அத்திர மாதி யாக வோதிய நான்கு விஞ்சை
தொத்தெரி சுடரு மொள்வா ளெனவிரண் டாகு முன்னாம்
வைத்தவுட் கடைய தேனை யொழிந்தது பரம மாயை
இத்திறத் தினைய வென்றா னெரிமணி யிமைக்கும் பூணான்.
reading: Of the four kinds of vidya (art), beginning with the missile art, he says there are two, a blazing flame and a bright sword, and that the last of what was set down is the great illusion.
nuance: The list is compressed and the words for the arts are partly obscure; only the opening and the closing 'great illusion' (பரம மாயை) are clear.
event: Srisenan lists the arts of the Vidyadhara war: missile, flame, sword and illusion.

tamil: படைக்கல விகற்பும் போரின் பகுதியும் பரப்பி னாங்கண்
இடைப்புகுந் துரைப்பிற் சாலப் பெருகுமஃ திருக்க வென்று
நடப்பது மக்க ளோடு மக்கட்போர் நல்ல வேனும்
புடைப்பில புகுது மாயிற் புறனுரை புணர்க்கு மென்றான்.
reading: Srisenan breaks off the long account of weapons and war's kinds, since telling it all would run on, and says that what will happen is man against man, which is the better course, and that outside matters can be told later.
event: Srisenan cuts short his lecture and settles on a war of men against men.

tamil: விஞ்சையர் பொருவ ராயில் விஞ்சையிற் பொருது மன்றி
வஞ்சனை யின்றி மக்கள் பொருபவேன் மக்கட் போரே
எஞ்சுத லின்றி யேற்ற பொருதுமென் றின்ன சூழ்ந்து
நஞ்சனாற் குரைப்பக் கேட்டு நன்றது துணிமி னென்றான்.
reading: The plan stated is that if the Vidyadharas fight with their arts, men will fight them with theirs; but men will fight men, with no trickery, and the king is told to carry this to the enemy and decide.
nuance: Whether the 'telling' of line 4 is the king's message to the enemy or the council's advice to the king depends on a doubtful word at the end of line 4.
event: A war of men without deceit is proposed and the king is asked to decide.

tamil: ஆய்ந்தவ ரோடு போதந் தாழியா னருவிக் குன்றிற்
காய்ந்துவந் திறுத்த பின்றைக் கடிநகர் நமது தன்மேற்
சேந்தெரித் திடுது மென்று தென்மலை யரசர் சென்றார்
வாய்ந்துமற் றொழிந்த மன்னர் மேல்வர வலித்து நின்றார்.
reading: A report reaches the city that the southern-hill kings, having gathered with their allies at the cool foot of the mountain, mean to burn the city, while the other kings are resolved to march.
nuance: The enemy's decision is told in indirect speech as an envoy's report, as the next verse confirms.
event: Enemy kings gather and set out to burn the Vidyadhara city.

tamil: ஒற்றனாங் குரைப்பக் கேட்டே யொளியவன் பெயர னோடுஞ்
சுற்றமா யவருஞ் சூழ்நீர்ச் சுரமைநா டுடைய கோவும்
மற்றவன் புதல்வர் தாமும் வருகென வந்தார் மாற்றம்
உற்றவா றறியச் சொன்னா னொளிவரை யரசர் கோவே.
reading: After the spy's report the Vidyadhara king calls his kinsmen, the kings of the sea-ringed country and their sons, and lays the report before them as it was given.
event: The king summons his allies and repeats the spy's report.

tamil: விச்சையின் செருக்கி னாலும் வீங்குதோட் டருக்கி னாலு
கச்சையங் களிற்றோ டேனைக் கவனமா வலத்தி னாலுங்
அச்சுவக் கிரீவ னாதி அரசர்க ளழன்று வெம்போர்
நச்சிமேல் வருப வாயி னன்றது போல்வ துண்டோ.
reading: A voice among the council says that if Asvagriva and the other kings, proud of their arts, arms, elephants and cavalry, march in anger to war, nothing could be better than that.
nuance: Unnamed speaker; the 'it is good' of line 4 is bravado, answered by the fearful voices in the verses that follow.

tamil: எரியெனச் சுரிந்த கேசத் திருளெனத் திரண்ட மேனிப்
பெரியன வளைந்த வெள்ளை யெயிற்றினர் பிலங்கொள் வாயர்
அரியன செய்ப வன்றே யசுரரென் றுருவு கண்டே
இரிவன ரோடு வாரு ணம்மையு மெண்ணிற் றென்பார்.
reading: Some soldiers say that the enemy's fierce forms, with fire-like hair, dark bodies and white fangs, are the shape of demons and that onlookers will flee at the sight of them.
nuance: The sense of the last line (that even the Vidyadhara allies will recoil) is read loosely; the speakers are the council's soldiers speaking in turn, marked by என்பார்.

tamil: எரிபொங்க வெழுந்த வெள்ளை யெயிற்றிடை யிலங்க நக்குப்
புருவங்க ணெறிய வேற்றிப் புகுந்துநாம் வெருட்டும் போழ்தில்
உருவங்கள் பெரிய வாறு முள்ளங்கள் சிறிய வாறுஞ்
செருவங்கண் விளைந்த போழ்திற் காட்டுதுந் தெருட்டி யென்பார்.
reading: Others reply that they will glare, grin and charge in a rage, and that when the fight begins they will show that the foe's great frames hide small hearts.

tamil: இமையவ ரரசன் றானு மிகல்செயக் கருதி வந்தால்
அமையுமஃ தஞ்ச லாமோ யாண்கட னதுவ தானால்
நவையின ருளரென் றஞ்சி நடுங்கினர் தமக்கு நாளுஞ்
சுவைபெறு தோளும் வாளுஞ் சொல்லுமின் சுருங்க வென்பார்.
reading: Even if the king of the gods himself came to fight them, they say, the fear is needless since it is their duty, and they bid those who tremble at the thought of enemies to say how short the work of arm and sword would be.

tamil: மானமர் நெடுங்க ணார்தம் மனமென வெஃகி மைந்தர்
ஊனமி லகல மூழ்கி யுள்ளுறச் சிவந்த வொள்வாள்
ஈனமா மருங்கி னாரா திரைக்கிடந் தனல்ப வின்று
தானவர் குருதி மாந்தித் தம்பசி தணியு மென்பார்.
reading: The young warriors say their red swords, bathed in the foe's broad chests and thirsting like women's eyes, will drink the blood of the demons today and still their hunger.
nuance: The simile of the sword's longing against that of the women's eyes (line 1) joins love and war images, as the poet does elsewhere in the epic.

tamil: ஆள்வரை யனைய தானை யச்சுவக் கிரீவ னென்னு
நீள்வரை மருங்கிற் றாழ்ந்த திருவெனு மருவி நீத்தந்
தாள்வரை யிழிந்து வந்து தகைமணி நீல வண்ணன்
வாள்வரை யகல மென்னுங் கருங்கடன் மடுக்கு மன்றே.
reading: In a long figure the speaker says that the army of Asvagriva will pour down like the stream called Wealth from his mountain-like brow and fall as a flood into the dark sea of the gem-blue lord's broad chest.
nuance: The comparison is difficult: the 'stream' is the host streaming out of its chief and the 'sea' is the chest of the dark-hued lord Tivittan, but the grammar of lines 3 and 4 allows another reading.

tamil: ஆதலா லதனு ணாமு மயிற்படைப் புணைகள் பற்றி
யேதிலா மன்ன ரென்னு மிருமரக் கடப்பு வாரி
மீதுலாம் வெகுளி யென்னும் வெவ்வழன் முழங்க மாட்டிக்
காதலார் கண்கள் பூப்பக் காய்த்துதுங் கைகோ ளென்பார்.
reading: Therefore, the speakers say, they will take the peacock-banner as a raft, bind the two rafts of the enemy kings, and with the fierce fire of wrath roaring over the flood will reap the fruit with their loved ones' eyes blooming.
nuance: The mixed images of raft, flood and fire in a kind of ferry-crossing are hard to unpick; the sense of rage as the fuel of war is firm.

tamil: உயிரினு மதிக்கற் பால துள்ளப்பே ருறையி னுள்ள
தயிறரும் பனிக்குந் திண்மை யானநா ணதனை யேற்றி
வயிரவின் மனத்த தாகக் கையது வையங் காக்குஞ்
செயிரில்வில் லதனை நோக்கிச் செங்கதிர்ப் பெயரன் சொன்னான்.
reading: Looking at the spotless bow that guards the world, which he prizes above his life and strings with a bowstring named for shame, Arkakirti speaks.
nuance: நாண் is both the bowstring and the shame that guards honour, and the verse plays on the two.
event: Arkakirti addresses his bow before the war.

tamil: அடுந்திறல் வெகுளிக் காற்றோ டருக்கப்பே ருடைய மேகங்
கொடுஞ்சிலை குலவக் கோலிக் குருதிநீர் வெள்ள மோடக்
கடுங்கணை யென்னுந் தாரை கலந்துமேற் பொழிய வேந்தர்
நடுங்கினர் பனிக்கும் போழ்தி னம்மையு மறிவ தென்றான்.
reading: He says the clouds of wrath, with the bows bent as rainbows, will rain streams of arrows until flood-waters of blood run and the enemy kings tremble, and the kings will know.
nuance: His speech is a boast in the poet's war style; the poet does not say whether it comes true here.
event: Arkakirti boasts that his arrow-rain will drive the enemy to trembling.

tamil: அலைகடல் வண்ணன் றம்மு னலர்குழை புரளுங் காதிற்
சிலைபடு வயிரத் தோளான் செங்கதிர் முறுவ றோன்றி
இலைபடு வயிரப் பைம்பூ ணிமையவ ரல்ல ராயின்
மலைபடு கிருமி யோநம் மாறுநிற் பனக ளென்றான்.
reading: The elder brother of the sea-hued lord, with a smile that shines like the sun, says that if the enemies are not gods, they are only mountain-worms before them and will stand in their way.
nuance: The elder brother of the dark-hued one is Vijayan, by the epic's story (Tivittan's elder brother), and not named here.
event: Vijayan treats the enemies as worms and promises to meet them.

tamil: வானவர் மருள நாஞ்சின் மற்றிது மடுத்து மாற்றார்
தேனம ரகல மென்னுஞ் செறுவுசெஞ் சால்கள் போக்கி
ஊனமர் குழம்பு பொங்க வுழுதிட்டு வென்றி வித்தி
ஏனவர் செவிக ளார விரும்புகழ் விளைப்ப னென்றான்.
reading: Vijayan says that, with the gods looking on in amazement, he will take his plough, cut furrows through the enemy chests as fields, work the blood into mud, sow victory in it and reap far-heard fame.
nuance: The farming image gives war as a harvest of fame, the same trope that makes the plough Vijayan's weapon.
event: Vijayan describes battle as ploughing and sowing in the enemy's blood.

tamil: இன்னன பிறவு மேனை யிருநிலத் தரசர் பேச
மன்னவ குமரன் மாமன் மலரடி வணங்கி வாழ்த்தி
மின்னொடு விளங்கு வேலோ யுளங்கொடு விளம்பி யென்னை
என்னொடு படுவ தன்றே யினியிப்பால் வருவ தென்றான்.
reading: As the other kings speak, the king's son worships his maternal uncle's feet and says that the matter rests with him, since whatever comes next will be settled between him and the enemy.
nuance: The 'king's son' and 'uncle' are read from the wedding and the family of the preceding chapters; the verse names neither.
event: Tivittan bows to his father-in-law and takes the war as his own.

tamil: ஆங்கவன் மொழிந்த போழ்தி னமையுமிஃ தறிவ தன்றே
தேங்கம ழலங்கன் மார்ப வினிச்சிறி துண்டு நின்ற
தோங்கிய விஞ்சை நின்னா லுள்ளத்துக் கொள்ளற் பால
ஈங்கிவை யென்ன லோடு மிறைவனைத் தொழுது கொண்டான்.
reading: The Vidyadhara king answers that this is enough, but that the prince should still learn some high art held back for him, and the prince worships the king and takes it.
nuance: The tutor and pupil roles come from the context: the king gives and the man who worships and takes is the prince.
event: The Vidyadhara king gives the prince the remaining vidya, and he accepts it.

tamil: மந்திர வெழுத்து வள்ள லுள்ளத்துப் பொறித்த போழ்தே
அந்தர விசும்பிற் றெய்வ மணுகின பணியென் னென்னா
வெந்திறல் விஞ்சைக் கேற்ற வியன்சிறப் பியற்றி வேலோன்
நுந்தொழில் புகுந்த போழ்தி னோக்குமி னெம்மை யென்றான்.
reading: When the spell's letters are fixed in the prince's mind, gods of the air come to him asking what to do, and he honours them as the great art requires and bids them look to him when their work begins.
nuance: The mantra's power is reported as the story's marvel and is not argued as doctrine.
event: The vidya works and the gods appear before the prince.

tamil: ஓதிய விஞ்சை வாய்ப்ப வுலகடிப் படாது நின்ற
வாதிசா லமர கற்ப மாமென வமருங் காலைத்
தூதுவ ருருவக் காளை செவிசுடு சரம்பெய் தூணி
மாதிரத் தொசிந்த வேபோல் வந்தொருங் கிருவர் நின்றார்.
reading: As the art ripens and he stays like a part of the world that outlasts the ages, two envoys, with bags of arrows that burn the ear, come before him like the horizon bowed down.
nuance: 'Envoys' (தூதுவர்) are those of the discus-king who demands the girl in the next verse; the verse describes their manner more than their errand.
event: Two envoys arrive at the prince's presence.

tamil: பொன்னவிர் திகிரி யாளும் புரவல னுருவப் பைந்தார்
மன்னவன் றமரம் யாமே வாய்மொழி கேண்மின் மன்னீர்
கன்னியைத் தருதி ரோவக் கன்னியை மகிழ்ந்த காளை
இன்னுயிர் தருதி ரோவிவ் விரண்டிலொன் றுரைமி னென்றார்.
reading: The envoys, naming themselves as the men of the golden-discus king, offer a choice, to give up the maid or give up the life of the youth who loves her, and say one of the two must be named.
nuance: The ultimatum is the envoy's message as the sender's, and the poet does not endorse the claim.
event: The envoys put an ultimatum: the maid or the youth's life.

reading: At the words about the maid, the hearers' eyes grow red and smoke and sparks pour out, and a fire that takes the life is said to have caught in the prince's heart.
nuance: The verse has only four lines of three-footed length (it ends without the usual fourth full line) and the ending 'என்பவே' reports what is said of the prince's heart.
event: The prince flares into rage at the ultimatum.

title: அரசியற் சருக்கம் 1206-1230 (4/17)
theme: The envoys' insult burns Tivittan, who lets them go by custom and sets a worship-or-die choice; omens and divine word promise his win, and both hosts, the foe's Vidyadhara army, gather with drums and weapons.
source_issues: Verses 1213, 1214, 1219, 1221 and 1223 have broken syntax or corrupt lines and are held uncertain.
Verse 1221 line 1 has a stray 'திரிந்' fragment and line 4 a stray quote mark.
The speaker and the side of many verses (1210 to 1216) are inferred from the order of the embassy, not named.

cast.role: the warrior kings who rise with a roar to answer the archer
Tivittan, the hero
the gods of the sky who watch
the rival discus-lord whose envoys carried the demand
the Vidyadhara host of the discus-lord
the envoys of the discus-bearer

reading: The hero, his eyes spitting fire and his body beading with sweat like pearls, is scorched by the envoys' petty words, which stab like spears into wounds, and his anger heats the very heavens.
nuance: The verse names the hero only as வீரன், and who is scorched by the words is read from the sequence of the embassy; the tense of வெதுப்பினன் could also make the hero the one who scorches the heavens.
event: Tivittan blazes with anger at the insulting words the envoys have brought.

reading: As he laughs his anger-fire rises, fine drops of sweat fall, hot steam breathes from the pores, and the ears burn at the petty words, until he lifts his rage to the sky for all to see.
nuance: Anger is told wholly through the body (laughter, sweat, steam, burning ears), and it is not yet answered in speech, which the next verses hold back.
event: Tivittan's anger shows in his body as he hears the envoys' words.

reading: His look and his shining form change into an unlike, widespread brightness; he gives up speaking, and the divine youth shows what the goodness of a man is.
nuance: The phrase மனித்தன் நன்மையைத் தேற்றினன் is hard to fix: it can mean that his silence shows the restraint of a man, or that he declares a man's worth. Held loosely.
event: Tivittan's form changes and he falls silent.

reading: The foes' days are ended; the Earth-goddess has come to take her pleasure with him, and the gods gather in the sky saying they will see this youth's first battle.
nuance: The gods and the Earth treat his victory as already settled before the fighting starts, which prepares the divine word of 1216.
event: The gods gather to watch the youth's first war.

reading: A speaker bids the envoys be sent away: by old custom envoys come and go unharmed, though they have brought evil words that burned the ears; the fault of these fools is to be borne, and their going is the point.
nuance: The speaker is not named; the verse follows the hero's silence in 1208, so I read it as Tivittan, but a counsellor is possible.

reading: When the archer has spoken, the warrior kings rise with a roar and answer in a rage, each saying briefly that they have said these things with the great mountain in mind.
nuance: Line 4 is hard to construe (சொல்லிய தனெச்சிலர்), and who the kings are, the hero's allies or the foe's, is read from 1210.
event: The kings roar and answer after the archer's speech.

reading: The kings say that the broad-shouldered one, taking the discus and the wide fortune from the rival, will by his words know both the girl and themselves; they are likened in worth to diamond set on a plantain.
nuance: The simile of diamond on a plantain stem is unclear in force; the construction of lines 1 to 3 is also uncertain.
event: The kings declare the rival's discus and fortune will be taken.

reading: A verse on the terms of a message: what is to be said is said with a gleaming smile, and what comes after is to be weighed only once the foe has come within seeing range.
nuance: The syntax is badly broken and I cannot fix the sense; read only as a remark on speech and sight before a fight.

reading: The maid's sweet words, heard against the youth's garlanded chest, are set beside the feats of the bow-shouldered hero, who from a mountain-top speaks truly of what he can do.
nuance: The lines mix the maid's love and the hero's deeds without a clear join; held as uncertain.

reading: A voice puts the foes a choice: if he comes close and worships this hero's feet, his life is his own; if not, it is not his; will lives please them or is honour wanted, let them think what pleases my lord and come.
nuance: The speaker is read as the hero's side speaking to the departing envoys (1216 begins with them replying), not named in the verse; it ends in a question whether life or honour will weigh more.
event: The hero's side sets the envoys' king the terms: worship or lose his life.

reading: When they have spoken the envoys rise and go; at that point a divine word stands that this youth will win and reign, and the Earth-goddess puts away her sorrow.
nuance: தெய்வ வாய்மொழி may refer back to an earlier prophecy or to a new divine voice here; the verse does not say which.
event: The envoys leave; a divine word of victory is voiced and the Earth is relieved.

reading: Shell bangles of the women sound, divine war-drums circulate and beat, red eyes burn, the bows of warriors' brows bend and break, and without pause the hero's camp stands ringed for war.
event: Drums sound and the camp of the host is readied for war.

reading: The lion-like hero's gold body glows with long light, women's shoulders and the warriors' eyes throb with omens, the swords in warriors' hands seem to flower, and every heart opens.
nuance: Throbbing shoulders and eyes are read as omens of battle; the verse does not say whose omen is good.
event: The hero's body shines and omens throb as the host rises.

reading: Honey-like streams of ghee and honeycomb are poured over rows of pearl-hung umbrellas and the drums that strike down the foe-prince, so that the arms seem to be bathed in fat.
nuance: The syntax of 2 to 4 is broken; a ritual anointing of drums and umbrellas before battle is the likeliest sense.

reading: Crows scream facing the jewelled chariots' tops, the burning quarters pour a fresh rain of blood, and headless trunks rise and dance on the field.
nuance: The verse reads as battle seen in advance or the field of the first clash; it does not name the side whose chariots are meant.

reading: The delicate and the unwilling change their ways and fall out with their women; sapphire beauties of the soft women turn dark as those who cling to them fall in ruin.
nuance: Line 1 and line 4 are corrupt, and no firm reading is possible.

reading: Crowns and helmeted brows fall apart, the lustre of the victorious spears is dulled, and the war-hardened men's bows break and they fall.
nuance: The verse is one of a series of battle pictures and does not say which side falls.

reading: The women's flames-scorched bodies, garlands, burned eyes and their cruel, flower-petal eyes all throb at the left or right as their men go to war.
nuance: Left and right throbbing of the women's eyes reads as omen; the lines are partly corrupt and the left or right meaning is uncertain.

reading: The foe-kings, though they know that to fall in the thick of their host in the blood will bring ruin, will not let pride go, for they are kings of rage.
nuance: Which kings are named is read from the opening அரசர்-run; மானம் here is the pride that keeps them from submission, answering the choice of 1215.
event: The enemy kings hold to their pride though they sense defeat.

reading: The envoys who had gone return with the gold-shining discus and give the word to their lord, and when they speak he laughs like venom thrown by an angry cobra.
nuance: Laughter returns as the sign of anger, as in 1207; here it is the foe's laugh.
event: The envoys report the answer to their king, who laughs a venomous laugh.

reading: The foe speaks: having slain kings of the vast earth with her father and seized their lives and boasted of his fierce strength, he and the great elephant too are taken together; hurry.
nuance: The antecedent of 'he' in 2 to 3 is not clear and the verse is partly corrupt; held as uncertain.

reading: When the discus-lord has said this, those who live on the great mountain say 'long may you live' and ready elephants, horses and many chariots and rise.
event: The hill-dwellers arm their elephants, horses and chariots and rise.

reading: Cloud-dark drums are beaten, water-bright conches fill the line, fierce parai drums resound, the garland-hung host sounds, and the war-arrayed Vidyadharas bow over the earth.
event: The Vidyadhara host sounds drums and conches.

reading: Umbrellas, flags, cool chowries, weapons, crowns and many insignia press together, middle and sides and both flanks, so that the rank cannot be told from the weapon.
Gold-gleaming chariots, noisy horses and elephants stand with no gap, and the sword-army cry rings to the great directions.
nuance: A closing verse of massed description; the host is read as the foe's.

title: அரசியற் சருக்கம் 1231-1255 (5/17)
theme: The Vidyadhara war reaches its height: armies of elephants, chariots and archers clash, the hero's arrows blind and rout the foe, and the proud rival king, told his army has broken, answers with a laugh.
source_issues: Verse 1234 had a line repaired for a stray pulli.
Verses 1231 to 1255 have broken word division in many places and several readings are held loosely.
The speaker and referent of 1251 to 1255 are not named beyond their epithets; they are read from the story so far.

cast.role: the Vidyadharas of the rival host, who are routed
the young king of the southern mountain, who joins the battle
the staff-bearing man who reports the broken army to the king
the proud king whose army has broken; read as Acuvakanthan
the earth's kings who laugh and who are ashamed to retreat

reading: The host comes down on the wedding city like clouds rising and spreading into a great sea, swordsmen and bowmen darkening all eight quarters.
nuance: The verse does not say whose host it is; reading it as the Vidyadhara host of the rival king rests on the story so far.
event: A sword- and bow-bearing host descends on the city and darkens the sky.

reading: At the word 'army' the whole host rises without a gap, like two seas surging unchecked, and the work of war spreads on every side.
event: The two armies rise and spread for battle.

reading: Cloud meets cloud and dark sea meets sea as chariot with chariot and horse with horse crowd into the fight.
event: Chariots and cavalry of the two sides close with each other.

reading: Spear-bearing elephants and swarms of archers clash like mountains against mountains, the elephants bent on killing.
nuance: The Tamil of this verse has broken word division and one line was repaired in the core file; the sense of lines 1 and 2 is held loosely.
event: Elephants and bowmen meet in battle.

reading: Elephants' banners and horses leap over crowded elephants, kings' crowns and the clouds, the whole field heaving.
event: Horses leap over fallen elephants and crowns in the press.

reading: Chariot wheels crush heads, rolling them aside, and the fighters, dazed, cannot tell which way the chariot comes.
event: Chariot wheels crush heads and confuse the warriors.

reading: Maddened elephants roam among the crowded horses and chariots, tearing up and breaking the foe's arms and weapons.
event: Rutting elephants move through the enemy ranks.

reading: Warriors with fire in their eyes fall like fish when swords strike, as thunder-bright blades flash against thunder.
event: Fighters are struck down by sword blows.
