reading: Arrows set on the long bowstrings stand up like fish-baited hooks drawn taut, sharpened and flashing.
event: Bowmen draw arrows to the string.

reading: A bow named for the fire-eyed god pours a shower of blazing arrows, and the red flesh of the Vidyadharas swells into a flood.
nuance: The archer is not named; the bow's name is unclear in the printed text.
event: A fire-named bow rains arrows on the Vidyadharas and a river of blood forms.

reading: The young king of the southern hills, wanting a bow to match the Vidyadhara golden mountain, rises like a mountain of Kama and joins battle.
nuance: The identification of the young king rests on the story so far, and the compound in line 2 is obscure.
event: The southern young king attacks the Vidyadhara host.

reading: Vidyadharas with blazing swords and bows, arms like great mountains, appear before the youth as bright as Kama.
event: The Vidyadharas press on the hero.

reading: The Vidyadharas' arrows fly, the bows spit them out, and the quarters fill with darkness while the foes draw near.
event: The Vidyadharas shoot at the hero until the sky goes dark.

reading: The quiver sits at the hand, the bow stands, and the arrow runs in the time it takes to look: a picture of an archer too quick to see.
nuance: Pure description of speed in shooting; no event is told and the subject is not named.

reading: One arrow is loosed and becomes a thousand, uncountable, and they spread over the earth until they fill it.
event: The hero's shooting multiplies one arrow into a thousand.

reading: The arrows rise to the sky and strike the Vidyadharas in the eyes, the quarters go black, and they fall to the ground bewildered.
event: The hero's arrows blind the Vidyadharas, who fall to the ground.

reading: In the darkness the Vidyadharas puzzle, fear, hide and tumble, and break under arrows, some rolling on the ground.
event: The Vidyadharas are routed in the dark.

reading: The broken army scatters like a mountain collapsing, and the warriors who pound the foe like cobras struck go stumbling away.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 compare the pursuers to a cobra stirred by a touch; whether the comparison is for the pursuing heroes or the fleeing troops is not fixed.
event: The routed Vidyadhara army flees.

reading: Arrow-struck elephants scream, hold up their tails and stream water, and run with ears folded back.
event: Wounded elephants flee screaming.

reading: Drums are split and crowns submerged, royal power lies low, chariots clatter and horses stumble, and a river of blood runs down.
nuance: 'Crowns sunk' (முடிகள் மூழ்கின) and 'kings subdued' (அரசுகள் அவிந்தன) are the narrator's summary of a whole host breaking.
event: The rival army's drums, crowns and chariots are overthrown in a river of blood.

reading: The army has broken today like a sea beaten by the wind, says the staff-bearer, bowing to the proud king whose sea-like host has failed.
nuance: The identity of the proud king (taken as the rival king Acuvakanthan) and of the staff-bearer rests on the story so far.
event: The staff-bearer bows to the proud king and reports the breaking of the army.

reading: The speaker says that, as learning and subtle hearing bring many fruits, so war brings many fruits and fame; yet the foe has taken victory by the spear, and our men have taken fear in their feet.
nuance: The first two lines are a comparison and the grammar is hard to fix; the second half plainly reports the rout.

reading: The earth's kings, who came to fight alongside us and have now turned their backs, grin with long teeth like rolled fire, asking what is left that is hard.
nuance: Whether these kings are the rival's allies or the victor's side is not clear from the verse.
event: The allied kings laugh at the retreat of those who came to fight.

reading: Proud kings who did not break at the sea of arrows did break at the bow in the sun-like hand, and, ashamed of their own littleness, did not retreat to their own mountain.
event: The proud kings break before the hero's bow and are too ashamed to flee home.

reading: The mountain-shouldered king laughs: if one man with one bow and two arms has broken the army today, then war is good for our men.
nuance: The king's laugh takes the report of defeat as a boast, as the Kural's warrior laughs at his own wound.
event: The rival king laughs at the report of his broken army.

title: அரசியற் சருக்கம் 1256-1280 (6/17)
theme: The brothers of Accuvakkiriivan appear and scorn the human host, the two armies meet in a crowded battle of chariots, elephants and horses, and the warriors fight by a code of fearlessness and mercy.
source_issues: Verses 1274, 1275, 1277 and 1280 had a line repaired for a stray pulli.
Verse 1279 line 1 ends with a corrupt word (ஏற்க்) and its line 2 is metrically irregular.
Many words in 1257 to 1262 are run together, so speakers are held loosely.

cast.role: the kings who rose against Ratanupura and fled
an unnamed man who reports the temper of the discus-armed ones
the dark-bodied hero, likely the camper and the sapphire-hued one
the fierce lord of the Vidyadharas whose brothers fight
his younger brothers who lead the sky army
the eldest of the younger brothers
one of the brothers, who laughs at the human host
one of the brothers with curved teeth
one of the brothers who claps and laughs
the Vidyadhara host
the fighting men of the two armies
the kings in the battle

reading: Kings who rose against Ratanupura fought, were ruined and turned their backs in flight; the poet closes that none finishes what he has in mind unless it ripens with difficulty.
nuance: The verse names no cause for the failure, neither fate nor misjudged strength, and gives only the general rule that an aim is won hard.
event: The kings who marched on Ratanupura are broken and flee the field.

reading: When the enemy's stronghold battle is broken that day, one man reports the temper of the discus-armed ones, and it is like pouring ghee on the fire of the world's end.
nuance: The words at line 3 are run together, so who is reporting, and of whom, is held loosely.
event: One man tells of the temper of the discus-handed ones after the enemy's defeat.

reading: The news of those who went to the sky fainting and of the foes who went to the earth being cut down lodges in the mind like a spear thrust into a wound.
nuance: The subject whose mind is pierced is not named in the verse, so the sense is held loosely.

reading: A broad-minded dark-bodied one, saying that the other should rest and then rise against him, goes and pitches camp with his forces on the hill called Arungalam.
nuance: The verse never names the camper; his dark cloud-like body suggests Tivittan, but this rests on the story so far, not on the verse.
event: The dark-bodied commander encamps his army on the hill Arungalam.

reading: Younger brothers of Accuvakkiriivan, skilled in handling dark rutting elephants, spread a sea of troops across the sky and appear, smiling and breathing venom.
event: Accuvakkiriivan's younger brothers appear in the sky with a spread-out army.

reading: The eldest of the young brothers says that unless they destroy, with their kin, those who wronged their lord, they would sit with bangles and their hair tied.
nuance: Bangles and tied hair mark a woman's state, so the vow stakes manhood on revenge.
event: The eldest of Accuvakkiriivan's brothers vows to kill those who wronged their lord, with all their kin.

reading: Nilamanikantan, seeing the men with their umbrella-marks, laughs, with his bright tusk-white teeth showing, at these humans who dare to fight against them.
nuance: The first line is hard (மாலுமாங் குடையர்கொன்); the sense of the sneer is held loosely.
event: Nilamanikantan laughs with contempt at the human army.

reading: Vayirakandan, with curved teeth, says the foe will lie rolling on the battlefield, as the mud of garlands wet with honey and the breasts of women are kept for them.
event: Vayirakandan boasts that the enemies will lie rolling on the field.

reading: Sukandan claps hands together and laughs, as snakes would show hatred to Garuda.
nuance: The simile treats the Vidyadharas as serpents mocking the eagle Garuda, an image of overconfidence.
event: Sukandan laughs and claps his hands in scorn.

reading: The fierce one, his cruel heart cooled by his brothers' words, which fall like rain, looks at them and bids them set their names firm upon the earth where those who hated his name are loved.
nuance: The fierce one is probably Accuvakkiriivan speaking to his brothers, but the verse leaves him unnamed.
event: The fierce lord, cooled by his brothers' words, sends them to make their names stand.

reading: As the Vidyadharas press on, their rage swelling like poison burning poison, the sapphire-bright one's army rises without any fraud and stands against them.
event: The Vidyadharas attack and the sapphire-hued commander's army rises and meets them.

reading: The poet says it is not easy for us to count the spear-army that came as far as the sky and the sword-army that met it on the ground, two seas of troops.
nuance: The poet speaks in the first person plural of the effort of counting.

reading: If two seas existed and the land between them were a woman, the two forces would equal them, since the two unconquerable armies match each other.
To one who looks, the host seems to be nothing but crowded strong chariots, nothing but gathered war elephants and nothing but packed horses, all mingled together.
The warriors with right-handed weapons, anklets and sashes, red garlands and red eyes appear as if this world had no room for them and they ruled another.
nuance: The praise makes the warriors too great for this world, which sets the Vidyadharas' scorn in 1262 to 1264 against the foe's real stature.

reading: The armies joined battle; with no direction left for the fighting to spread, the troops stood in a war that was like the world's end.
event: The two armies join in a battle so dense it has no direction to spread.

reading: Some, with drums and flags and garlands struck back and forth, fight one another in their chariots, and their arrows fall thicker than rain from clouds.
event: Warriors in chariots strike drums and garlands and loose showers of arrows on each other.

reading: Feet are packed with feet, shoulders with shoulders, swords with swords; the poet asks in what days these could be counted.
nuance: The closing question asks whether the crush can be counted in any number of days.

reading: Umbrellas hide the ground, flags cover it, the earth is smeared dark, and weapons and the jewels of serpents flash across it.
Elephants strike with their trunks and throw fire between their eyes; as their tusks meet, the great ones seem mountains fighting mountains.
Horses circle like the wheels of time over the helmets of the fierce kings and the heads of rutting elephants.
nuance: The wheel of time (கால சக்கரம்) is a simile only; the verse makes no doctrinal claim.

reading: The bright-bossed shields, the shafts of the quivers and the bow-armed chariot throngs resemble clouds raining arrows.
The kings, with their minds failing to know who would do what and where, act in confusion with gleaming spears and crowded swords.
event: The kings fight in confusion, unsure what to do.

reading: The warriors, with sashes and dark anklets, glare and move about, not fearing even Death, calling that the fearful may leave and those who can bear it stay, and the leaders of unblemished lines go.
event: The warriors call on the fearful to leave the field while the brave stay and fight.

reading: The victors do not strike scornfully at an enemy who blinks, nor stare shamefully at one who fled, as though showing the foe the heroic path.
nuance: Kural 775 counts a blink at a flung spear as flight; this verse shows the winners declining to press the blinker.
event: Warriors spare the one who blinks and the one who fled, in the manner of heroes.

title: அரசியற் சருக்கம் 1281-1306 (7/17)
theme: A field battle of champions in the political sarukkam: Arisenan challenges and is cut down, Gunasenan and Indiran fight and Gunasenan falls, then the archers Varasenan and Kamukan meet.
source_issues: Verse 1303 is absent from the verse numbering (1302 is followed by 1304); the core file has 25 verses for 1281 to 1306.
Verses 1298 to 1302 were printed two short lines to a line and were split into four lines.
Verses 1295, 1304, 1305 and 1306 were printed in eight half-lines and were joined into four.
Verses 1281 to 1306 have many broken words and stray pulli repairs, so most readings are held loosely and the names of speakers and combatants are uncertain.

cast.role: the king's friend who proclaims his name and challenges the foe, and is cut down in a duel
the grandson of the tiger-chariot, who takes up Arisenan's challenge
the fighters of both sides
the younger youth who hews Arisenan
the kinsman of Azhalan who strikes Arisenan
the warrior who praises the discus-king and falls in the duel
the unnamed warrior who rushes in after Arisenan's fall
the king whose champions fight
a sword-bearing friend of the king, a golden-mountain figure
a fighter by name Indiran
those standing near who flee
the archer of the opposing army who takes his bow after Gunasenan falls
the learned archer who comes in answer to Varasenan

reading: Arrows lodged deep in their chests, the men pull them out by the root and read the lines written on the shafts, and some wander about asking who the named youth is, meaning to meet him.
nuance: The sense of the first half rests on a stanza that needed repair, and who is searched for is never named here.
event: Wounded men read the inscribed arrows and some go about searching for the archer.

reading: A youth bearing a shield on the left and a bright sword on the right, with ornaments, garland and war-wreath, thrusts through the enemy ranks and comes on hard.
nuance: He is not named in the verse; 1283 gives the name Arisenan, and the identification is the next verse's.
event: A shield-and-sword fighter forces his way through the enemy ranks.

reading: The king's friend names himself Arisenan and calls on the enemy to meet him, saying that any who want to live should turn back rather than face his sword.
nuance: Line 3 is damaged (வல்லிருளிராயின்); the offer of retreat is read from the last line.
event: Arisenan proclaims his name and challenges the foe to fight him or retreat.

reading: Hearing his words, a rival lets the arrow he had chosen go back and, saying this one is no match for a mighty man, comes forward himself to fight, the grandson of the tiger-chariot.
nuance: The man called அருக்கன் in line 1 is hard to place; he may be the grandson himself or his charioteer, and the verse does not decide.
event: The tiger-chariot's grandson answers Arisenan's challenge and comes to fight him.

reading: Taking up a gold-adorned shield and flashing his sword, he tells the newcomer that he has come where those who knew him not have fled, and warns him to turn back if he knows who he faces.
event: The challenged fighter takes up shield and sword and warns Arisenan off.

reading: The answerer laughs that he knows him well, a man who stood gorging in a mansion while another youth won a maiden who was his by right, and asks whether any news is left that is still new.
nuance: The taunt turns the fight on a marriage, but which maiden is meant is not told here.
event: One fighter mocks the other with the loss of a bride.

reading: He goes on that maidens follow the way of whoever wins them, as the poets' treatise has it, and that a man ignorant of this is a fool, so ignorance of him is still his rival's fault.
nuance: The claim is a taunting speaker's, not a doctrine of the work. The word ஏடர் is hard and the sense of the last two lines is held loosely.
event: The taunt is carried on: a maiden goes the way of the winner.

reading: Rather than trade words, the warriors resolve to settle it by the light of their swords, glare with burning eyes, exult, and leap up and fight in the wide sky.
event: The two sides give up words, glare and spring into the air to fight.

reading: Holding their gleaming jewelled shields and the others' red hair-crested ones, the fighters in the sky look like moon and sun in conjunction and like the moving spears.
nuance: The likeness to moon and sun is the poet's, and the last line leaves it unclear whether spears or men are compared.
event: The fighters hold shields aloft and fight in the sky.

reading: With pearl strings and gems flashing, swords and shields throwing shadow, they wheel in circling steps like a wheel turning on water.
event: The fighters circle one another with swords and shields.

reading: One thrusts with a spear while the other parries and turns back on his guard; since the onlookers see only the result and not the mind behind it, the poet asks what use is saying more.
nuance: The poet breaks off the description and says it cannot be told fully.
event: One fighter thrusts a spear and the other parries and recovers.

reading: The clash of iron makes a smithy of the field, sparks scatter like rain of vengai flowers on the ground, and fiery flecks of blades flung at each other fill every quarter.
event: Sparks fly from the clashing blades in every direction.

reading: Arisenan, whose strength is crushing, sees the sword thrown at him from his foe's shoulder and covers his body with his jewelled shield like the cool moon seized by a planet.
event: Arisenan guards himself with his shield against the thrown sword.

reading: As Arisenan strikes first and draws back, a younger youth hews his garlanded chest in two, and the watchers in the sky carry him off and hide him.
nuance: The man who hits Arisenan is called only the younger one of the Mal (மாற்கு இளைய காளை); the verse gives no name.
event: A younger youth cuts Arisenan down after Arisenan has struck and drawn back.

reading: A kinsman of one called Azhalan strikes Arisenan, the army cries out, some are burnt, some flee and many are crushed, and the others rush up with raised spears and are cut down.
nuance: The stanza was printed in eight half-lines and joined; the identity of the striker is not clear from the Tamil.
event: A kinsman of Azhalan strikes Arisenan and the armies clash, with many killed.

reading: Seeing Arisenan fall, a warrior with swinging shield and flashing sword comes whirling, cuts through horses and elephants and chariots alike, and the poet asks whether any can match such circling skill.
nuance: He is not named; line 4 is a rhetorical question on his skill, and the sense is held loosely.
event: A warrior rushes in after Arisenan's fall and slays the cavalry and elephants.

reading: Gunasenan, praising the discus-king's strength and wishing it to flourish, wears a mountain-tall crown and bright earrings and roams like a thundering cloud and a rutting elephant and a tiger.
nuance: The discus-king is Arukkakirthi in the verses that follow; here he is named only by the discus.
event: Gunasenan goes about the field praising his king and fighting.

reading: The spear-bearer who praises Arukkakirthi's greatness has a strength that burns the foe.
nuance: The warrior is not named in these four short lines; he is read as Gunasenan from the verse before.

reading: One like a golden mountain, bright sword in hand, the king's friend, comes thinking of the fight.
event: A sword-bearing friend of a king comes to fight.

reading: The newcomer's name is Indiran, a rutting elephant in his drive and like Kaman in beauty.
event: The newcomer is named Indiran.

reading: As the two meet to fight, those standing near fear and run away.
event: The two fighters face each other and the bystanders flee.

reading: One strikes off one of the other's shoulders with a sword, and the other with his remaining shoulder hurls his sword back.
nuance: The four short lines do not say which of the two loses the shoulder.
event: One fighter loses a shoulder to the sword and the other throws his sword in return.

tamil: குணசேனன் வீழக் கண்டு கூற்றினுங் கொடிய நீரான்
இணைசேனை தன்னு ளுள்ளோ னியம்பிய களிப்பின் மிக்கான்
கணைசேர்ந்த தூணித் தோளான் கைச்சிலை பிடித்துக் கொண்டு
திணைசேர வருக வென்று வரசேனன் றிகழ்ந்து நின்றான்.
reading: On seeing Gunasenan fall, Varasenan, fiercer than Death and delighted at the word of his comrade, takes up his bow and arrows and stands taunting, bidding the foe to come and match him.
nuance: Who is addressed by வருக is not named in this verse; the next verse gives the answering archer.
event: Varasenan, seeing Gunasenan fall, takes his bow and challenges the enemy.

tamil: மற்றவ னிற்ப தோர்ந்து மதகளி றனைய காளை
கொற்றவ னருக்க கீர்த்தி குணம்புகழ்ந் தாடிப் பாடிக்
கற்றவன் கலைக ளெல்லாங் காமுக னென்னும் பேரான்
பற்றிய வில்லு மம்பும் பாங்குடன் பரித்து வந்தான்.
reading: Hearing of him, Kamukan, a youth like a rutting elephant who has learned all the arts, praises the king Arukkakirthi's qualities and comes up bearing bow and arrow.
event: Kamukan arrives with bow and arrow to meet Varasenan.

tamil: வில்லொரு கையி னேந்தி வெங்கணை குழைய வாங்கிச்
சொல்லரு மாரி போலத் தொடுத்தவன் விடுத்த லோடும்
மல்லுறு காளை தன்மேல் வராமலே விலக்கி யிட்டுக்
கல்லெனக் கலங்கி வீழக் கைச்சிலை கணையே றிட்டான்.
reading: One draws his bow and showers arrows like rain, the strong youth wards them off before they reach him, and with an arrow of his own makes the archer reel and fall.
nuance: Which side falls is not named; it is read from 'the youth turned his arrows' that Kamukan wards off Varasenan's shafts.
event: An archer's volley is turned aside and the archer is shot down.

title: அரசியற் சருக்கம் 1307-1331 (8/17)
theme: The battle of the champions: the danava Arikethanan is cut down by Sarthulakan, Dhumaketu boasts and falls to the Vidyadhara king's younger brother, and Azhalvegan and Devasenan trade taunts.
source_issues: Verses 1307, 1317 to 1331 were printed as eight half-lines and joined into four.
Verse 1313 had a stray pulli removed.
The speakers of 1319 to 1322 and 1328 to 1330 are inferred from the epithets in the text, and the fallen man in 1325 is read from the kings' reaction.

cast.role: Tivittan, the dark-hued youth, the groom
the danava of the discus-lord's kin who is killed
the warrior who kills Arikethanan
the discus-lord's kin who comes after Arikethanan
the kin of the discus-lord
the Vidyadhara side and its kings
the Vidyadhara king's younger brother, the blazing chariot lord
the spear-skilled youth who comes in after Dhumaketu's fall
the lord of kings who goes out against Azhalvegan

tamil: கார்செயன் முழங்கி யார்ப்பக் காளையுங் கனன்று மிக்க
வார்சிலை வணங்க வாங்கி வாய்புக விடுத்த லோடும்
போர்செயுங் களத்து வீழ்ந்தான் புகழ்வர சேன னென்னத்
தார்செய்தா னவர்க டம்முட் டானவ னொருவன் வந்தான்.
reading: The youth draws his great bow and looses an arrow that lands in a warrior's mouth, so that a man named Pukazh Varasenan falls on the field, and then a danava of the foe steps out among them.
nuance: The youth is not named; he is taken to be Tivittan from the later epithet in 1319, and the clause naming the fallen man and the danava is hard to parse.
event: A warrior of the youth's side shoots down one enemy, and a danava comes out in his place.

reading: A danava wears garlands of entrails and skulls, hangs infants' heads in his ears, and strides among cut-off elephant trunks with a flaming trident.
nuance: The verse never names him; 1312 gives the name Arikethanan to the man who comes at this point, so the identification rests on that.
event: The danava prowls the field, hung with gore.

reading: Blood is his wine and his hands the cup, enemy bodies his meat; those behind him snap their fingers and whistle, saying that no one in this world will fail to think of such food.
event: The danava advances in blood-lust with followers behind him.

reading: Elephant tusks he tears out, enemy soldiers he drinks dry with his bright sword, and none who meets him unaware escapes.
event: The danava slaughters soldiers and elephants as he comes.

reading: Black as night, flame-like, with a lion's roar, he kicks the chariots and horses of the field so that they burst like popped grain; the poet calls this the splendour of his coming.
event: The danava smashes chariots and horses as he advances.

reading: The man named Arikethanan, the discus-lord's Death, tells himself that he has fought many armies and asks what use this poor army is as a match, and so comes on.
nuance: The text calls him the discus-lord's தமன், kin, and compares him to Yama; the boast in the second half is his own thought or speech.
event: Arikethanan, kin of the discus-lord, comes to the fight scorning the opposing army.

reading: Sarthulakan, joyful in battle though not drunk, draws his sword and meets the danava with the cry that he will drink his life.
event: Sarthulakan of the youth's side takes up the danava's challenge.

reading: As dark as hill, cloud and night, the foe swells like a sea and then shrinks into a single point on earth; the poet calls it the splendour of battle.
nuance: The verse is pure description of the two as they close.

reading: The danava, with fangs like the waxing moon and shoulders like wooded hills, drives his trident into the chest of his opponent.
nuance: The subject is not named; the sense depends on 1316, where the pierced man cuts back.
event: Arikethanan pierces Sarthulakan's chest with his trident.

reading: Pierced as he was, Sarthulakan hurls the sword and cuts the thrower in two with the very trident, the huge man falls like a mountain, and his own kin are broken.
nuance: Who falls is read from the next verse, which says the man's day of life was spent.
event: Sarthulakan kills Arikethanan and the discus-lord's kin lose heart.

tamil: வாழுநா ளுலந்து மற்றவன் மண்மேல் மலையென மறிதலு மலைமேல்
ஆழியான் றமர்க ளஞ்சினா ரஞ்சு மாயிடை யடுதிற லுடையான்
ஊழிநா ளெரியுங் கூற்றமு முருமு மொப்பவன் கைப்படை நவின்றான்
சூழிமா லியானைத் துளைமதஞ் செறிப்பத் தோன்றினான் றூமகே தனனே.
reading: His days of life spent, the fallen man lies like a hill while the discus-lord's kin on the mountain fear; then Dhumaketu, like the fire of the age's end and Death and thunder, arrives on a rutting elephant.
nuance: The phrase that his days were used up lets the poet put the death in fate beside Sarthulakan's skill; the text gives both without ranking.
event: Arikethanan is dead and Dhumaketu rides in to take the field.

tamil: மலையெ டுத்திடுகோ மாநிலம் பிளக்கோ மறிகட லறவிறைத் திடுகோ
உலைமடுத் துலகம் பதலையா வூழித் தீமடுத் துயிர்களட் டுண்கோ
சிலையிடத் துடையார் கணைவலத் துடையார் சிலர்நின்று செய்வதீங் கென்னோ
நிலையிடத் தவரு ணிகரெனக் குளரே னேடுமின் சென்றென நின்றான்.
reading: Dhumaketu boasts aloud: shall he lift the mountain, split the earth, drain the sea, burn the world and eat its lives; what can bow-men and archers do, and who among the foe equals him?
event: Dhumaketu boasts that no enemy equals him.

tamil: வண்டினம் பாடு மாலையன் வரித்த கச்சினன் வயிரப்பூ ணிரைத்த
தண்டினன் கழலன் றமனியத் தாரான் சார்ந்தனன் சார்தலு மவனைக்
கண்டன னன்றே கடலொளி மேனிக் காளைதன் மாமனுக் கிளையான்
உண்டினி நமக்கோர் போரென வெதிரே யுவந்துசென் றவற்கிவை யுரைத்தான்.
reading: The young brother of the dark-hued youth's father-in-law, wearing garlands, a diamond-studded mace and a golden gem-wreath, sees him coming and goes joyfully to answer that a battle has come.
nuance: Read as the king's younger brother (மாமனுக் கிளையான்), whom 1321 names as the owner of the blazing chariot; the speech opens in this verse and runs on in 1320.
event: The Vidyadhara king's younger brother goes to meet Dhumaketu.

tamil: மலையெடுத் திடுவாய் மாநிலம் பிளப்பாய் மறிகட லறவிறைத் திடுவாய்
உலைமடுத் துலகம் பதலையா வூழித் தீமடுத் துயிர்களட் டுண்பாய்
நிலையிடத் துளரோ நிகரெனக் கென்பாய் நின்றனை நிகருனக் காகித்
தொலைவிடத் தல்லாற் சொல்லிவை நுங்கட் கொழியுமோ தூமகே தனனே.
reading: He answers Dhumaketu's boast clause by clause: you would lift the mountain, split the earth, drink the sea and eat lives; will you claim no one is your equal? Stand, and your match will come until you are destroyed.
event: The Vidyadhara king's younger brother mocks Dhumaketu's boast.

tamil: என்றலு மதுகேட் டெரியுடைத் தேரோ னென்பவ னாமிவ னென்றே
நன்றுநன் றென்று நக்கன னக்கே நாணிலர் நம்மலை வாழ்வார்
இன்றெனக் கெதிராய் நீகொலோ பொருவா யென்றன னினையன மொழியாக்
குன்றினும் பெரியான் கூற்றினும் வெய்யோன் கொண்டனன் றண்டுகை வலித்தே.
reading: Dhumaketu hears him, laughs, and says that this is the one called the lord of the blazing chariot, and asks whether he will really fight him and not shrink, and raises his mace.
nuance: The title of the man he laughs at is எரியுடைத் தேரோன், which is what ties this scene to the chariot of the blazing fire in the Vidyadhara king's younger brother.
event: Dhumaketu mocks him and takes up his mace.

tamil: இன்றெனக் கெதிராய் நீகொலோ பொருவா யென்றிகழ்ந் துரைத்தனை யேடா
நின்றெனக் கெதிரா நீர்மையர் நின்போ னிரம்பவாய் திறந்துரைப் பவரோ
என்றன னெனலு மெதிர்தெழித் தவனு மெழுந்தன னெழுந்தன னிவனும்
அன்றுபோர் மலைந்தா ரதிர்ந்ததிவ் வுலக மமரொழித் தரசரு நின்றார்.
reading: The man answers that Dhumaketu was right to scorn him, and asks if any who stood against him ever stood speaking as loudly; they rise to the fight and the world shakes and the kings stand clear.
event: The two rise and join battle; the other kings stand aside.

tamil: ஆர்த்தன திசைக ளதிர்ந்ததிவ் வுலக மலைகடல் கலங்கின விருளாற்
போர்த்தது விசும்பு புலம்பின விலங்கல் புரண்டன பொருவரைத் துறுகற்
சார்த்தினர் புடைக்குந் தண்டின ரெதிரத் தாங்கியும் வாங்கியுந் தடுத்தும்
வேர்த்தனர் மெய்யால் வெதும்பினர் மனத்தால் விசும்பினை மயங்கவே திரிந்தார்.
reading: The directions roar, the earth shakes, the seas churn, darkness covers the sky and hills roll; the two strike with mace and shield and sweat though their hearts burn, circling in the sky.
event: The duel of the two shakes the world.

tamil: கண்டவர்க் கெல்லாங் கண்ணுளார் போல்வார் காண்டலுக் கரிதவ ருருவம்
தண்டின தொளியர் தங்களார்ப் பிசையுந் தயங்குதா ராரமும் விரவி
எண்டிசை மருங்கு மிடைநிலத் திடையு மிருள்கெழு விசும்பின தகமுங்
கொண்டன சிலம்பு குலுங்கின விலங்கல் கூற்றமுந் தலைபனித் ததுவே.
reading: To all who look, their forms are hard to see; mace, ring and garland, jewels and noise fill the eight quarters, the ground and the dark sky, the mountains tremble and even Death shivers.
nuance: The verse describes the fighting rather than telling an act.

tamil: தட்டுப்போ ரதனுட் டமனியக் கடிப்புந் தாரினோ டாரமுஞ் சரியப்
பட்டுப்போ யுருண்டா னவருளங் கொருத்தன் பருவரை கரியதொன் றனையான்
துட்டப்போ ரியானைத் தூமகே தனனுந் தோற்குமோ வொருவனுக் கென்று
மட்டுப்போ ரணிந்த மணிமுடி மன்னர் மயங்கினார் மானமு மிழந்தார்.
reading: One of the fighters, black as a great mountain, falls rolling from the fray with his gold ear-stud and garland shattered, and the crowned kings say, will even Dhumaketu lose to one man, and lose their pride.
nuance: Read as Dhumaketu's fall, from the kings' reaction naming him.
event: Dhumaketu is struck down; the kings who stood with him are dismayed.

tamil: பொருதாங் கழிந்து புகைகேது வீழ வரிகேது முன்ன முடிய
எரிதாங்கு வேலொ டினியீங்கு நின்று பெறுகின்ற தென்னை யெழுகென்
றரிதாங்க ணாவ தெளிதாகு மாறொ ரமர்செய்கை கொண்டு பிறர்முன்
கரிதாங்க ளான கழன்மன்ன ரேறு வருமங்கொர் காளை கடிதே.
reading: The mighty fall, banners drop and flames of the spear remain; the kings ask what they gain by standing and bid him rise, and a young man comes quickly.
nuance: The wording is difficult; the speakers are the discus-lord's kings and the arriving youth is identified as Azhalvegan from 1328.
event: After Dhumaketu's fall another young warrior is sent in.

tamil: கணிகொண் டலர்ந்த நறவேங்கை யோடு கமழ்கின்ற காந்த ளிதழால்
அணிகொண் டலர்ந்த வனமாலை சூடி யகிலாவி குஞ்சி கமழ
மணிகுண்ட லங்க ளிருபாலும் வந்து வரையாக மீது திவளத்
துணிகொண் டிலங்கு சுடர்வேலி னோடு வருவா னிததென்கொ றுணிவே.
reading: He comes with a spear, wearing flowered garlands, with scent in his locks and gems swinging at his ears, and the poet asks what is the resolve of this man.
event: Azhalvegan comes to the field.

tamil: அருமாலை வேல்வல் லழல்வேக னாகு மவனாயி லாக வமைக
எரிமலை வேல்வ லிளையார்க ணிற்க விவனென்னொ டேற்க வெனவே
பொருமாலை வாள்கை பொலிகே டகத்த னணிபோ திலங்கு முடியன்
செருமாலை மன்ன ரிறைதேவ சேன னெதிரே சிவந்து செலவே.
reading: Speaking of the spear-skilled Azhalvegan, he says: if it is he, let it be; let the young ones stand aside and let him face me; Devasenan, lord of kings, goes red before him.
nuance: The speaker of the opening is not named; Devasenan's words fit because he then goes out.
event: Devasenan goes out against Azhalvegan.

tamil: மலைமேலு மென்னை மதியாது வாழ்தி மனிசர்க் குவந்து படையாய்
நிலமேலு நின்று பொருவா னினைந்து வருவாய் நினக்கி துறுமே
சலமேலு மின்ன வுடையாயை வென்று தலைகொண்ட பின்னை நுமரைக்
குலம்வேர் களைந்து குடிபொன்று விப்ப னிதுயான் மகிழ்ந்த குணனே.
reading: Azhalvegan says to him: you live scorning me even on the hill and give nothing to men; you will fight on earth; when I win and take your head I will uproot your whole clan.
event: Azhalvegan threatens Devasenan with the destruction of his line.

tamil: மலைமேலு நின்னை மதியாது வாழ்வன் மனிதர்க் குவந்து படையாய்
நிலமேலு நின்று பொருவான் புகுந்த நிலைகண்டு நின்று மிஙனே
சலமே யுரைத்தி யிதுவோவு னாண்மை தழல்வேக வென்ன வெதிரே
உலமேசு தோளி னொளிவேலி னோடு மொருவா னெதிர்ந்து பொருவான்.
reading: Devasenan answers with the same words turned back, calls Azhalvegan's boast false, asks if this is his manhood, and meets him spear to spear.
nuance: The reply repeats the opening of 1329 almost word for word, so the exchange is a mirror.
event: Devasenan returns the taunt and the two fight.

tamil: வாள்வீசு மாறும் வடிவேலின் வந்த வடிவேல் விலங்கும் வகையுந்
தோள்வீசு மாறு மவைமீளு மாறு மிடைசொல்லும் வீர மொழியுந்
தாள்வீசு போழ்து கழலோங்கு மாறு மெதிர்தாங்க ளார்க்கு மொலியுந்
நாள்வீய லன்றி யுரைவீய யாவர் நவில்வார் நமக்கு மரிதே.
reading: The poet says no one could tell, except at the day's end, the ways of the sword and spear, the turns of the shoulders, the war-talk and the sounds of the fighters.
nuance: The narrator breaks off to say the fight cannot be fully described.

title: அரசியற் சருக்கம் 1332-1356 (9/17)
theme: The duel of Devasenan and Thazhalvegan ends in Suvarnaketu's arrival, a challenge to single combat, a shower of arrows and illusions, the fall of the golden-banner king, and Srisena's speech urging the kings not to flee.
source_issues: Verses 1332 to 1350 are printed in eight half-lines and were joined into four lines; verse 1341 had a stray pulli removed from line 4.
Verses 1351 to 1356 are short four-line verses in a different metre from those before them.
Speakers and the identity of the combatants are uncertain in 1336 to 1347 and 1349 to 1356, since the verses give epithets, not names.

cast.role: the king with the single sceptre who kills Thazhalvegan in 1332-1335
the foe who falls to Devasenan's sword in 1335
an ally of Suvarnaketu who has died by a sword before 1336
the golden-banner king who arrives in 1335 and falls in 1350-1351
the warrior who laughs and advances in 1352 and is taken to speak 1354-1356
the one who bears the Garuda banner and puts the challenge of 1339
the shining-crowned one who answers the challenge in 1340
the armies that clash in 1337-1338
the two war elephants that fight in 1348
the spearman taken prisoner in 1353
the Vidyadhara kings mocked and addressed in 1354-1356

tamil: மாலா லெதிர்ந்து மலைவாயை நீடு பொரவைப்ப தென்னை யினியென்
வேலா லழிப்ப னெனவே லெறிந்து விறல்வேக னார்ப்ப மறவோன்
மேலா லிலங்கு மணிகேட கத்தி னொருபால் விலங்கி யொருபாற்
றோலாத வாளி னெறியத் துணிந்து சுடர்கான்று வீழ்ந்த ததுவே.
reading: Seeing the foe stand against him and fix his long spear on the hill-like mass, the champion hurls his own spear to destroy it; the fierce Vegan roars, and the warrior's sword cuts him down, so that he falls blazing.
nuance: Who throws the first spear and who is struck cannot be fixed from the verse; the next verses name Devasenan as the warrior and Thazhalvegan as the one who falls.
event: A spear is hurled and answered; the warrior's sword fells Vegan in the duel.

tamil: எய்வே லறுத்து வறியானை நோக்கி யெறியாது நிற்ப வவனோர்
நெய்வேல் பெயர்த்து நிருமித்த தேந்தி யுருமொத்து நேர்ந்து பொருதான்
வெவ்வே றெருட்டி யொருதோ ணிமிர்த்தி விரலொன்று சுட்டி வரவே
வைவேலி னோடு நிமிர்கின்ற தோளை யறவீசி னானம் மறவோன்.
reading: The warrior cuts away the shaft that is thrown at him, waits without throwing, and when the other raises a ghee-tempered spear and charges like thunder, he lops off the raised shoulder together with its spear.
event: The warrior cuts down the spear and the arm that raised it.

tamil: நெய்யுற்ற வேலு மொருதோளும் வீழ வொருதோளி னீடு செருவைச்
செய்யுற்ற போழ்தி னெதிரே விலங்கி யிதுதேவ சேனன் மொழியும்
கையுற்ற தொன்று கவலே னுனக்கி துறுமாறு போக வெனவும்
மையுற்ற காளை வருவானை வாளி னுயிர்வவ்வி னானம் மறவோன்.
reading: With the spear and one arm already fallen, the foe fights on with the other; the warrior, calling out that he does not mind what is in the enemy's hand, cuts him down and takes his life.
nuance: The speech is given as Devasenan's own words; the one who falls is named only in 1335.
event: Devasenan answers the one-armed foe's attack with his sword and kills him.

tamil: தாம மார்ந்த மணியைம்பாற் றைய றாதை மைத்துனனாஞ்
சேம மார்ந்த தனிச்செங்கோற் றேவ சேனன் கைவாளாற்
சாம வண்ணன் றழல்வேகன் சாய்ந்தான் சாய்ந்த பொழுதத்தே
தூம மாரங் கமழ்குஞ்சிச் சுவண கேது தோன்றினனால்.
reading: By the sword of Devasenan, the king of the single sceptre and kinsman of the Aimpal land, the dark Thazhalvegan falls; at that moment Suvarnaketu, his hair fragrant with incense, appears.
nuance: The verse names the sceptre of Devasenan as the cause of the kill, so the royal sceptre stands behind the sword.
event: Devasenan kills Thazhalvegan, and Suvarnaketu comes onto the field.

tamil: அஃதே யஃதே யங்கார வேக னாங்கோ ரயில்வாளால்
வெய்தாங் குற்று வீடினனா னன்றே நன்றே மறுமாற்றம்
மைதோய் மலையும் மண்ணகமு நமதாச் செய்வென் செய்யேனேற்
செய்தா ரமர ருலகாள்வ னிரண்டி லொன்று திண்ணமிதே.
reading: A speaker cries that Angaravegan has died by a bright sword and vows to make the hill and earth his own, or else, if he fails, to rule the world of the gods: one of the two is sure.
nuance: The speaker is not named; Suvarnaketu is inferred from his arrival in 1335. The vow of earth or heaven is a warrior's vow, not a school's doctrine.
event: A vow of victory or heaven is made over a fallen ally.

tamil: என்னா விரண்டு மருங்கினுமற் றிளநல் யானைக் குழாஞ்சூழப்
பொன்னார் தேரும் புரவிகளு மிடைந்து பூமி பொறைகூர
முன்னாற் செல்ல வருவானை முந்நீர் வண்ணன் றன்மாமன்
மின்னார் விளங்கு விறல்வேலான் கண்டே வெகுண்டு மேற்சென்றான்.
reading: On both sides elephants, golden chariots and horses crowd in until the earth groans, and the sea-coloured one's uncle, seeing the champion come before the host, flies into rage and goes forward.
nuance: Whether the sea-coloured one is Thivittan and the uncle Devasenan, or the reverse, is not fixed by the verse.
event: The armies close and the uncle of the sea-coloured one charges.

tamil: கானற் புரவி கலிமாவோ டெதிர்ந்த கருங்கை மதவேழ
மான யானை தம்மோடே மலைந்த தேரு மாறேற்ற
ஈன மில்லா விளையாரோ டிளையார் திளைத்தா ரிவ்வகையே
தானை தம்முட் டாக்கலுறத் தாமுந் தம்முட் டலைப்பெய்தார்.
reading: Horses meet horses, elephants meet elephants, chariots meet chariots, and the armies strike each other with young fighters against young fighters.
nuance: Pure battle description built on pairing like with like.

tamil: அருவி யிலங்கு மதயானை யனல வூன்றி யணைபோழ்திற்
குருவ ரோடு படைபொருதல் கூடிற் றன்று குலவேந்தே
பொருவ ரென்னப் படுவாரங் கொருவர் போந்து பொரவொருவர்
ஒருவி நிற்ற லுரங்கொல்லோ வென்றா னுவண மேந்தினான்.
reading: A speaker tells the lord of a noble line that no army fights with elders; if one comes forward and another stands aside, can that be courage, he asks.
event: A challenge to settle the battle by one man against one is put.

tamil: குரவ ரென்னு முபசார மிருக்கக் கோதை மிளிர்வேலாய்
பொருவ ராயின் யாரோடும் பொருவர் பூமி வேண்டுபவர்
ஒருவி நிற்ப துரங்கொல்லோ வென்னு முரையு முணர்தியிவண்
இருவே முள்ளும் யார்பாலஃ துறுவ தென்றா னொளிமுடியான்.
reading: The shining-crowned one answers: even with the title of elder, those who fight will fight anyone who wants the earth; he asks which of the two of them such an act of standing aside suits.
event: A reply to the challenge, asking which of the two should fight.

tamil: ஆக வமைக வதுவேயவ் வரச நீதி யாகிவிடிற்
போக பொருவ னெனப்புகைந்து பொருவெஞ் சிலையொன் றிடனேந்தி
வேக யானை செலவுந்திச் சிறுநா ணெறிந்து வெஞ்சரங்கண்
மாக மெல்லா முடனடுங்கத் தொடங்கி னானம் மழைபோல்வான்.
reading: Agreeing that this should be the king's custom, he storms that he will fight, takes a bow in his left hand, drives his elephant forward, twangs the string and begins to shower arrows that make the whole sky tremble, like a cloud.
nuance: The rule of the duel is called அரச நீதி; the verse treats it as a king's custom, not as a doctrine.
event: The duel is accepted and the arrow-storm begins.

tamil: தொடங்கு கின்ற சுடுசரங்கள் சுருங்கி யொருகை செவிகாறும்
முடங்கு மொருகை சிலைவளையா நிமிருங் கண்ட தித்துணையே
இடங்க ளின்றி விசும்பெல்லா மிருள வீர்க்கோ டீர்க்குதையத்
தடங்க லின்றி யடுசரமே மிடைந்த தவனி வட்டமே.
reading: Arrows loosed from the string draw close, one hand to the ear, the other bent; no more is seen than this, for the sky is dark with arrows and the round earth is thick with them with no gap.
event: A dense shower of arrows fills the sky and earth.

tamil: சொல்லான் மலிந்த புகழினான் சுவண கேது சொரிகின்ற
கல்லார் கொண்டற் பெயல்போலுங் கணையின் மாரி கழல்வேந்தன்
வில்லாற் செய்த விசாலவட்ட மேலு நாலு மருங்கினுமாய்க்
கொல்லாற் செய்த வேலாற்குக் குடையாய் நின்று கவித்ததே.
reading: The golden-banner king, famed in word, pours arrows like a shower of stones, and his bows form a great round shield on all sides, covering the spearman as a canopy.
nuance: The verse says the arrow-shower becomes a shield for the spear-bearer; who the spearman is must be taken from the next verse.
event: Suvarnaketu's arrows form a canopy over the spearman.

tamil: வில்லாற் செய்த விசாலவட்டந் தன்னா லந்தில் விலக்கப்பட்
டெல்லாத் திசையுஞ் சரஞ்சிந்தி யிருள வீழு மெல்லைதன்னுட்
சொல்லாற் புகழ்தற் கரியான்பாற் றூணி வறிய வாதலுந்திண்
மல்லாற் செய்த தோளான்மேன் மாய வெம்போர் செய்குற்றான்.
reading: The wide round of bows turns the shower of arrows aside, they scatter to all quarters and fall; when the quiver is empty, the poet says, he turns to magic and makes ready to fight the strong-armed one with an illusion.
event: The arrows are turned aside and the quiver runs dry; magic begins.

tamil: செய்ய லுற்ற மாயமதுஞ் சிலையு நிலையுஞ் சுருங்கியவைத்.
தெய்ய லுற்ற பகழியையு மெண்ணி வேந்த னென்செய்தான்
மைய லுற்ற மதயானை மலைப்ப வுந்தி மாற்றானை
நைய லுற்றா யெனவுரையா நாம வாளி சிந்தித்தான்.
reading: The magic, bow and stand shrunk, and counting his remaining arrows, what did the king do? He calls out that the foe is wearied by the mad elephant and shoots the arrow named Naama.
event: The king counts his arrows and shoots the arrow named Naama.

tamil: தொடுத்த வாளி யதுபொழுதே சுவண கேது கையகத்து
மடுத்த சிலையும் பகழியும்வெம் மனத்துக் கொண்ட மாயமதும்
அடுத்துத் துணிசெய் தப்புறம்போ யரசர் குழாங்க ளிரியப்பாய்ந்
துடுத்த தூவி தோன்றாமை நிலத்தி னுள்புக் கொளித்ததே.
reading: The arrow cuts down the bow, arrows and the illusion in the foe's hand, flies past as kings scatter, plunges in and hides in the earth with no feather showing.
event: The shot arrow cuts the bow and the illusion, then buries itself in the earth.

tamil: அம்புஞ் சிலையுங் கைம்மறிய வகத்த விஞ்சை துணிப்புண்டு
வம்பு கொண்ட வளையங்கள் கணையம் விட்டு விட்டேறு
செம்பொன் னாழி யிவையெல்லாஞ் சென்று பாயச் சிந்தித்தான்.
reading: With his arrows, bow and illusion cut, the scorching foe, his mind in a rage, thinks to hurl rings, javelins, and golden discs at the champion all at once.
event: The foe, his magic cut, resolves to use rings, javelins and discs.

tamil: இப்பா லிவர்கள் பொரும்பொழுதி னியானை யிரண்டு மெதிர்தாக்கிக்
கைப்பா லெடுத்துக் கறைமருப்பு மிடைந்து கண்க ளெரிசிந்தி
மெய்ப்பா லெடுத்துக் குத்தியுமெய் விலங்கிப் பாய்ந்து மொன்றொன்றைப்
பொய்ப்பா லின்றி யெடுத்திட்டுப் புடைத்தும் பெயர்த்தும் பொருதனவே.
reading: While these two fight, the two elephants charge each other, lift with their trunks, lock tusks, rain sparks from their eyes, gore and pull aside, and in earnest lift and strike one another.
event: Two elephants fight, goring and flinging each other.

tamil: துண்ட வேகப் புள்ளுயர்த்தான் துளைக்கை யானைச் சுடர்முடியான்
கொண்ட வாளன் கேடகத்தன் குதிகொள் வான்போ லெழுந்தெதிரே
மண்டு வானை வயவேந்தன் கண்டு வாளி சிந்தினான்.
reading: The one with the swift Garuda banner, an elephant and a gleaming crown, rides in through a white-lotus pack of elephants, and as he passes, a man with sword and shield leaps at him; the brave king sees him and shoots arrows.
nuance: The one with the Garuda banner and the sword-bearer are not named; the elements follow the verse's own epithets.
event: A sword-and-shield man leaps at the Garuda-banner king, who shoots him.

tamil: மடுத்த வாளுங் கேடகமுங் கவசக் கண்ணு மார்பகமு
மடுத்துக் குத்தி னாற்போலக் கழிந்த தம்பு கழிதலுமே
எடுத்து மறிக்கப் பட்டான்போ லிலங்கு பூணு மாரமுந்தேந்
தொடுத்த தாம மாலையுமுன் சொரிய வீழ்ந்தான் சுடர்வேலான்.
reading: The arrow passes through the sword, shield, armour, eye and chest as if driven in; the shining-speared one falls, his jewels, chain and wreath of flowers spilling.
event: The arrow pierces the warrior, who falls with his ornaments scattering.

reading: As the golden-banner king falls, the great sea of the army, left without him, breaks off the fight and is crushed.
nuance: The verse is in a short four-line form with half-lines, unlike the long lines before it.
event: With Suvarnaketu fallen, his army breaks and is routed.

reading: On hearing the word that the victors stand and the others are down, Srisena, saying well, well and laughing, goes forward.
event: Srisena laughs at the report and advances.

reading: Like a churned dark sea mixing, the sword army broke, and the spear-bearing champion became a prisoner in the flood.
nuance: The verse is obscure; the water image and the captivity may belong to one figure or to two.
event: The sword army is broken and a spearman is taken prisoner.

reading: Saying that the Vidyadhara kings are the ones who fear, he laughs at the poisonous ones and speaks some small words.
event: A speaker mocks the Vidyadhara kings.

reading: If sword-bearing warriors, with anklets tied on their feet, break and run, tomorrow the shamefaced women will not be ashamed to embrace their shoulders.
nuance: The speaker is taken to be Srisena from 1352 and 1354; the verse is a warrior's rebuke, which this chapter does not set against any school.

reading: The speaker tells the kings who fight beneath the umbrella on the hill that this body perishes for the sake of fame that stands for ever; do not turn away today.
nuance: Spoken as a rebuke to the fleeing kings and not as a renunciant's teaching on the body; the body is spent for fame, not freed from.

title: அரசியற் சருக்கம் 1357-1381 (10/17)
theme: The great battle with the Vidyadharas: they are shamed back into the fight, Sri Sena and Sripala join it, a fall of the Vidyadhara king's crown breaks his army, and Kanaka Chitran taunts the kings who flee from fated men.
source_issues: Verses 1362, 1370-1377 have broken word division and several readings are held loosely.
Verse 1376 has a stray full stop at the end of line 3.
Who fights whom in 1369-1377 cannot be fixed from the Tamil alone.

cast.role: the Vidyadhara warriors and kings of the mountain, one side of the battle
the bright-spear Vidyadhara leader who rallies the men
the Vidyadhara king whose crown falls
a warrior of good conduct who enters the fight like Death
the hero who joins the fight and mounts the horse
son of the discus-holder, who steps in when the kings break

reading: A voice taunts the men who run, saying that flight to save a body costs the jewel of honour, and that a forest awaits those who fear.
nuance: The second half (lines 3-4) is obscure and the speaker is not named; the reading holds only line 1-2 firmly, and 1358 suggests the words are a rally to men who had begun to flee.
event: A speaker shames the fleeing Vidyadharas for abandoning honour to save their lives.

reading: At these words the Vidyadharas turn back and take up the fight, and the bright-spear leader urges them on.
event: The Vidyadharas rally and return to the battle at their leader's urging.

reading: The sword-bearing Vidyadharas crowd in against the enemy and the warriors are cut to pieces at the neck and the body.
event: Vidyadharas and the enemy's swordsmen close and cut each other down.

reading: Pieces of horses, saddle-gear and cut flanks lie mixed over the whole battlefield.
Sparks fly from the clashing swords like fire, and tusked elephants fall like mountains.
event: Elephants fall as swords clash.

reading: Men sink into mud made of gore, the tracks of the field fill with blood, and the fronts of golden chariots are broken.
nuance: Word division is broken in lines 1-3; the picture of the chariot-front shattered in blood is firm, the rest is held loosely.

reading: Sri Sena, a man of good conduct, comes into the sword fight like Death himself.
event: Sri Sena enters the battle.

reading: A boast that the speaker can fight those who live on earth and those who live in the sky alike.
nuance: No line names the speaker; I take it as Sri Sena because 1363 has just introduced him, and the sky-dwellers are the flying Vidyadharas.
event: A fighter boasts of fighting both earthly and sky-dwelling foes.

reading: Hearing the angry challenge to take up weapons if they can fight this kind of war, Sripala comes in.
event: Sripala, hearing the challenge, joins the fight.

reading: The chief mounts a horse decked with whisks that rises like a wave of the sea, and frightens everyone.
event: The hero mounts his horse and terrifies the enemy.

reading: Horses wheel and rise in their circling and the bow-and-arrow kings are bewildered in the fight.
event: The horses wheel and the opposing kings lose their order.

reading: Bow, sword and spear are laid aside as if by a word, and the combatants begin a fight without limit.
event: The fighters give up weapons and begin close combat.

reading: The victorious Vidyadhara, broad-chested, breaks the other's bow and hurled spear with ease.
event: The Vidyadhara breaks his opponent's bow and spear.

reading: With his spear broken the enemy cuts it down and strikes with a victorious sword at the king.
nuance: The word division is very broken and who strikes whom cannot be fixed.
event: A sword stroke is aimed at the king.

reading: The sword strikes a shining shoulder and the wounded man stretches himself out.
event: A sword wounds a shoulder.

reading: A wound made by the sword is said to be washed bright and clear in a garlanded man's honey-smelling flowers.
nuance: The verse is built on rhyming forms in -ளித and is very hard to parse; the reading is a guess at its main sense.

reading: After the laid-on sword has cut, the garlanded man urges his unruly horse not to go on.
event: A rider drives his horse away from the fight.

reading: He who let his horse run over the swift mount thinks of harming the other's shining crown.
event: A rider plans to strike at the enemy's crown.

reading: He thinks of cutting the crown, and the leap that follows is greater than any on earth or in the sky.
event: The rider leaps up to strike the crown.

reading: At the sign of his own sword he flies up on his course, through the sky, and reaches the world's edge.
event: The rider flies up through the sky.

reading: The great gem-crown of the flying Vidyadhara falls like a star at the other king's weapon.
event: The Vidyadhara king's crown is struck down by his rival.

reading: As the lord's bright crown falls, the mountain-folk's army gives up the fight and turns its back.
nuance: The verse shows that an army stands or falls with its king's crown; it is the narrator's picture, not a stated rule.
event: The Vidyadhara army breaks and flees when the crown falls.

reading: As the mountain kings break, Kanaka Chitran, the discus-holder's son, angry at heart, steps in and speaks.
event: Kanaka Chitran enters the fight and speaks.

reading: A speaker says that a man with drawn sword and girded belt who runs in fear of one man shows a manliness that is to be despised.
nuance: 1379 says Kanaka Chitran spoke; I take this as his speech, but the verse itself names nobody.
event: Kanaka Chitran taunts the fleeing kings for their cowardice.

reading: The Vidyadharas of the high mountain turn back in fear of men whom fate has marked, and the fanged youth laughs in wonder.
nuance: விதிபடு is read as 'fate-marked'; the identity of the laughing youth is not named and may be Kanaka Chitran or Sripala.
event: The Vidyadhara kings retreat; a fanged young man laughs at the marvel.

title: அரசியற் சருக்கம் 1382-1406 (11/17)
theme: The battle with the Vidyadharas continues: Kanaka Chitran taunts the foe and enters the fight, his kin's host rises, and the field fills with the wreck of men, horses and elephants described in a long run of similes.
source_issues: Many lines are corrupt or use rare words (1382-1384, 1397, 1400, 1402, 1404): the readings of these are hedged.
Verse 1395 has a stray comma in the first line.

cast.role: son of the discus-holder, who steps in when the kings break and fights in these verses
the enemy host the hero fights; side not named in the verse
Kanaka Chitran's kinsmen who say he has entered the fight
Grivan's younger brothers whose host rises
the charioteers who drive the chariots

reading: A taunt that once glances of women have pierced the broken-hearted, men who have joined the heroes' company have no cause to dread the killing weapons.
nuance: Lines 1-2 are cryptic (the women's quick glances as a piercing of hearts); the verse reads as the start of the speech announced in 1379, but the speaker is not named here.

reading: The speaker calls shameless men to witness that a warrior's strength stands praised with the sky even when the body is born, and asks whether the flesh body must be broken for the sake of taking human lives.
nuance: The last two lines can be read either as a challenge to the cowards or as doubt about the body's use; the sense turns on a rare construction.

reading: The speaker mocks the enemy lords, saying they have come as if to take balls of food in the same hands that dropped their bright oiled swords in fear in the fierce fight.
nuance: The speaker is read from 1379; no word here names him.
event: Kanaka Chitran mocks the enemy lords for dropping their swords in fear.

reading: Having spoken, the hero stands against the enemy's sea-like host and appears in the press with the sword, strong-armed, while the foe's broken pieces follow him.
event: The hero faces the enemy host and cuts into it with his sword.

reading: Thinking that to press on against foes dismayed, pushing aside the slanting spears, is honour, he walks the field with anklets sounding and bears the whole weight of the fight.
event: The hero advances through the spears and sustains the battle.

reading: The youth appears in battle dress, with ear ornaments, a garland of gold, a gem-linked girdle, a wreath of the war-band and a cluster of locks, and every side sees him.
event: The hero shows himself in the battle in full ornament.

reading: Horses cut in two and fallen gold chariots litter the field and elephants are left without their posts, yet the youth's sword is not wearied of the hot smell of flesh.
event: Horses, chariots and elephants fall before the hero's sword.

reading: Seeing the long-haired kings who stood against him bathe in streaming blood, the youth appears like a cloud-borne thunder and asks who now will face him.
event: The hero, after the kings are slain, appears like thunder and challenges the rest.

reading: On his kin saying that their bull-like Kanaka Chitran has pressed into the sword-fight, the brothers of Grivan rise in anger with the sea-like host.
nuance: Which side Grivan's brothers belong to is not said; they are taken as Kanaka Chitran's side because they rise at the news of him.
event: News that Kanaka Chitran is in the fight brings his kin's host out in anger.

reading: The foe that broke and withdrew earlier comes back to the field, and when the army's flood joins them it is like waves tossing on a roaring sea.
nuance: The simile (the army like the ocean's waves) is clear; who 'fled' and who 'returns' in line 1 is not.
event: The enemy that had broken returns to the fight and the armies surge together.

reading: The king's younger brothers, strong as diamond mountains, and the kings with their spear forces join, set on giving the foe grief, and burn into a hard battle.
event: The king's younger brothers and the kings join the battle in anger.

reading: With eyes red the warriors point and rage and drive their elephants on, so that no space is left in the press and the armies stand mingled everywhere.
event: The two armies close and mingle with no space left between them.

reading: Arrows go astray as feathers, bows as shafts, and the roaring chariot bands go astray like mountains while the elephants' great heads rock.
Jewelled shoulders snap, tusks are crushed, faces and many heads fall, the fearless run, and a flood of blood runs down.
nuance: The carnage is set out as a spectacle; no one grieves it here, unlike Purananuru 62, where both armies die and nothing is left to win.

reading: Yak-hair whisks float, white umbrellas roll like waves and rise like foam, and the elephants' trunks lie like banks along the flood.
Raw flesh rising in the blood and the mire sinks and the riders' rays of crowns show above it, so that the battlefield looks like an anthill.
nuance: Lines 2-3 are crowded with rare words and the exact picture is not certain.

reading: When warriors come and strike the backs of the riders with diamond clubs, the elephants' tusks break and fall like heaps of thorny screwpine petals.
event: Warriors strike down the riders with diamond clubs and the elephants' tusks fall.

reading: Kings' jewelled arms hurl at the elephants, and the weapons vanish into their wide-eared faces like the moon going into a rain-cloud.
event: Kings strike the elephants with thrown weapons.

reading: Among the kings' armies the shoulder-mountains, like peacocks entering a mountain pass, enter the elephants' great faces, the bundle of the dart.
nuance: The simile in lines 2-4 is hard and the last word is uncertain.

reading: The kings twist their arms and the arrows flying at the elephants are like stars of the sky falling on the heads of tall mountains.
The heads of the elephant-drivers fall cut off with their hair and cords, like bees' honey comb and flowers tumbling on mountain flanks.
nuance: The reading of the second half rests on rare words.

reading: The chariot-borne princes, with the charioteers driving by reins and goads and the shafts as bar, run the bright chariots through the sea of blood.
event: Charioteers drive the chariots through the sea of blood.

reading: Shields heaped up like crocodile backs in the blood water, with banners and poles, look like lotus stalks and the fish that gather round them.
Elephants fallen with arrows through their trunks lie in rows over the ground, like wounded mountains struck at the foot.
Gold-braceleted arms with shields fall scattered in every direction, like the shaken moon dropping from a serpent's grasp.

title: அரசியற் சருக்கம் 1407-1431 (12/17)
theme: The war of the plough-bearer against the Vidyadhara brothers: the young hero is attacked by four, the plough and lion bring his side back, Ratna Greevan's mountain breaks the army until an arrow fells him, and the grieving Asvagriva looses a spell that calls Death and the spirits against the world.
source_issues: Verses 1425-1431 were printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 lines by the repair tool.
Verse 1431 line 4 has a broken word division ('கிள ருலகை') and 1407 has an odd form 'பாய்ந்தழெக்'.
Who fights whom in 1409-1411 and who falls in 1423 cannot be fixed from the Tamil alone.

cast.role: the white plough-bearing hero, called வெள்ளியான் and அலாயுதன்; read as Vijayan
the younger brothers of Asvagriva (Kireevan) who attack the young hero
one of the attackers, with Vayira Kandan
the warrior who lifts the mountain
called also கனக நாமன், who fights the plough-bearer
the archer who looses the sun-bright arrow
those who report the deaths to Asvagriva
the lord of the gold discus, the Vidyadha king, who sends the spell
the spell that Asvagriva sends out
Death, called by the spell
the spirits and ghoul-hosts that gather

reading: Headless trunks dance with ringing anklets on the field, and the clotted flesh lit with fire looks like lamps set on stumps.
The white hero ploughs the field of battle with his plough, using the Vidyadharas' blood as water, and sows his fame in it.
nuance: The plough-warrior is not named by a proper name here; the plough (நாஞ்சில்) and the epithet 'the white one' point to Vijayan, and 1418 names the same fighter அலாயுதன், the plough-bearer.
event: The white hero ploughs the battlefield with his plough and sows fame in the Vidyadhara blood.

reading: The younger brothers of Kireevan, hearing of a merciless youth who has taken the field, ask who he is.
nuance: Lines 1-2 give the youth's red eyes and the field he now holds in broken word division; only the question in the closing lines is firm.
event: Greevan's younger brothers ask who the youth is that has taken over the battle.

reading: Resenting that this one is the eldest of the Suramai lord's sons, four young warriors drive their elephants at him alone.
nuance: Who the four are and who the one is cannot be fixed from the verse; I read the four as the younger Vidyadhara champions of 1409 and the one as the young hero the Suramai lord's son.
event: Four young warriors, burning with anger, drive elephants against one man.

reading: Ratna Kandan and the other warriors block the lanes of the oncoming force, burn them, and close on the young hero in fury.
event: Ratna Kandan and three others cut off and attack the young hero.

reading: A cry goes up that the young prince has fallen, and the Suramai king's army heaves like a dark sea over a whirlpool.
nuance: The cry may be a rumour; 1413 and 1414 show the young prince's side recovering at once, so the fall is not shown as final.
event: The army of the Suramai king is thrown into confusion by the cry that the young prince has fallen.

reading: A lion-like hero, new in the fight, mounts a fierce lion and takes up a new plough.
nuance: Line 1-2 are obscure and the rider is not named; the plough makes Vijayan the likely reader.
event: The hero mounts a lion and takes a fresh plough.

reading: The plough, the red-eyed lion and the elder brother arrive and the young king's army roars, while the enemy's elephants break in confusion.
nuance: 'The young king' here is the younger of the two brothers, which is why 1412's cry is answered now.
event: The elder brother arrives with plough and lion; the young king's army roars and the enemy's elephants scatter.

reading: In the thick of the fight he ploughs open the broad rich chests of the proud warriors, the youth who can bewilder even the best of them.
event: The young hero ploughs open the enemy warriors' chests with his plough.

reading: Kanaka Naman, hearing that one man with a plough has beaten two men and four elephants, comes to the fight, shoulders like a dark mountain.
event: Kanaka Naman, hearing of the plough-bearer's feats, joins the battle.

reading: Kanaka Chitran, angry, wipes his sword's edge and strikes, and the lion-like plough-bearer drives the plough's tip into his shoulder.
nuance: Chapter 60 casts Kanaka Chitran as a son of the discus-holder who steps in for the kings; here he fights the plough-bearer, so the two scenes are not shown to be on one side.
event: Kanaka Chitran strikes with his sword and the plough-bearer pins his shoulder with the plough's blade.

reading: Hearing that Vayira Kandan and all the others were beaten by Alaayudhan and what became of Kanaka Chitran, one man is left with a heart on fire.
nuance: The man who burns is not named; 1419 names Ratna Greevan as the next to act, so I read him.
event: A warrior, learning of the defeat of Vayira Kandan and the rest, is left burning with anger.

reading: Ratna Greevan rises in rage, resolved to finish the fight and manhood of those of the earth, and lifts a great mountain in his diamond-hard hands.
event: Ratna Greevan lifts a mountain with his hands.

reading: Belted, bearded and with brows knit, he blazes like fire and lifts the mountain and advances, and the army of the Suramai king scatters.
event: The army of the Suramai king scatters as Ratna Greevan advances with the mountain.

reading: As he comes close, an arrow gleams in the quiver of the king and into Arukka Kirti's drawn bow, and he sets it and drives it on.
nuance: Line 1-2 turn on a rare construction 'அருக்க கீர்த்தி கை'; the archer is read as Arukka Kirti.
event: Arukka Kirti fits a bright arrow to his bow and shoots.

reading: The arrow he strung, shot, set to the shoulder, tore through and drove into the earth, and it laid low even the onlookers: they call it the sun's arrow.
event: The arrow pierces its target, enters the earth and strikes down bystanders.

reading: The garlanded hero falls like one mountain on another and the sea churns while the hills grieve.
nuance: The faller is not named; it follows the arrow of 1421-1422 and the mountain-lifter of 1419-1420, so I read Ratna Greevan.
event: A great hero falls like a mountain and the sea and hills tremble.

tamil: தம்பியர் பாடு மக்க ளிறந்ததுந் தனக்குப் பாங்காய்
வெம்பிய வீரர் போருள் விளிந்ததும் விரைவி னோடிச்
reading: The staff-bearing messengers run to the lord of the gold discus and tell him that his younger brothers' sons and heroes died, the words falling on his ear like molten copper.
nuance: The words in line 4 'அரக்குண் கோலோர்' are rare; I read them as the staff-bearers of 055's report, not fixed.
event: Messengers report the deaths of his kinsmen and heroes to the discus-holding king.

tamil: ஆங்கவர் மொழிந்த போழ்தி னருவரை கரிய தொப்பான்
ஈங்கிவர் மாற்ற மாயி னிருந்தினி யென்னை யென்னா
வாங்குநீ ருலகில் வாழு முயிர்களை வாரிக் கொண்டு
வீங்குநீர்க் கடலுட் பெய்யும் விஞ்சையை விடுக்க நேர்ந்தான்.
reading: Dark as a mountain, he asks what is left to him if these are the news and chooses to loose the spell that sweeps up all living things of the world and pours them into the sea.
nuance: Grief and rage give the decision, and the verse states no claim on its justice; the Jain epic lets the reader see the sweep of the spell as the work of anger.
event: Asvagriva decides to send out a spell that gathers all life into the sea.

tamil: ஓர்ந்தவன் மனத்து விஞ்சை யொருபுடை யெய்த லோடுஞ்
சார்ந்தது சண்ட வேகை பணிபணி யென்று சார
வார்ந்தநீ ருலகின் வாழு மனிதரை வல்லை யாகில்
தேர்ந்துகொண் டொருவ ரின்றித் தெய்வமே செகுத்தி டென்றான்.
reading: At the thought the spell stands close, Chandavegai, and he bids it take every human of the sea-bound world, if it can, choosing them out and sparing none.
nuance: 'Choosing out and leaving none' (line 3-4) is odd: it can bid the spell to seek each person out, or to take them all without distinction; either way no sparing is allowed.
event: Asvagriva commands the spell Chandavegai to destroy mankind.

tamil: கொடியவன் விடுத்த போழ்திற் கூற்றுவன் றன்னைக் கூவி
வடியெயி றிலங்க நக்கு வாழிய தோள்க ளின்று
விடுகதி ராழி வெய்யோன் வேண்டவென் வாயுட் பட்டு
முடியுமிவ் வுலக நீயு முறைத்தொழின் முடித்தி யென்ன.
reading: When he sends the spell, it calls Death, laughs showing sharp teeth, tells him the world will end in its mouth at the sun-bright king's wish, and bids Death finish his own task too.
event: The spell Chandavegai summons Death and tells him to do his task as the world is ended.

tamil: அணங்குகள் குழுமி யாமும் பெருவயி றார்து மென்று
துணங்கைகோத் தாடி நக்குச் சுடரிலைச் சூல மேந்தி
வணங்குபு சூழ மற்ற மாபெருந் தெய்வம் வந்து
மணங்கமழ் சுரமை நாடன் றானைமேன் மடுத்த தம்மா.
reading: The spirits gather and say they will fill their great bellies too, dance with bright tridents and bow round, and the great goddess comes and drives the spell on the Suramai king's army.
event: The spirits and the great goddess come and the spell is loosed upon the Suramai king's army.

tamil: பட்டடி நெடிய வீங்கு பரட்டின நொடிக்குங் கால
ஒட்டிய வயிற்ற வற்ற லுகிரிடை மயிர முன்கை
கட்டிய கண்ணி பீலித் தலையின கழற்காய் போல
வட்டமா யுருளுங் கண்ண கணங்கள்வந் திரைத்த வன்றே.
reading: The ghoul-hosts come crying, long-footed, hollow-bellied, with hair-covered fingers and rolling round eyes like gall-nuts.

tamil: வரைகளை யுருள வுந்தி வந்ததோர் சண்ட வாயு
நிரைகிளர் சுடர தாகி நிமிர்ந்ததோ ருருவச் செந்தீ
திரைகளை மறிய வீசிச் சிறந்ததோ ரழுவ முந்நீர்
விரைகிள ருருவத் தெய்வ மிதுபடை விடுத்த வாறே.
reading: The spell shows as wind that rolls mountains, a fire that rises in rows, and a deep sea thrown up, as the god of rich colour sends it forth.
nuance: The scope of the destruction is as great as that of the end of an age, yet the target is one army; the epic holds both.
event: The spell appears as storm-wind, fire and sea.

tamil: வரைகளு மரனு மண்ணு மறித்திடும் வாயுச் செந்தீப்
புரைகிளர் பொடிக ளாரப் புணர்த்திடும் புணர்ந்த போழ்திற்
றிரைகிளர் பரவை முந்நீர் திரைத்துக்கொண் டொழுகு மிஃதால்
கிள ருலகைத் தெய்வ முண்ணிய வுடன்ற வாறே.
reading: The wind and fire shaking down mountains, trees and earth join, and the sea rolls over the world as if the god were devouring it.
nuance: Line 4 begins with a broken word 'கிள ருலகை' and the last sentence is held loosely.
event: Wind, fire and sea together destroy mountains, trees and earth.

title: அரசியற் சருக்கம் 1432-1456 (13/17)
theme: Tivittan's duel with Asvagriva: the hostile missile's deity shrinks before him, Garuda becomes his mount, the discus king boasts and is answered, and the two answer each other's divine weapons, naga with Garuda, fire with water, sleep with waking.
source_issues: Stanzas 1432-1443 and 1450-1456 were printed in half-lines and joined by the build; 1444 had a pulli removed.
1432-1433 and 1442 are obscure on whose host is in trouble.
The name 'அருக்கன்' (1434) is not identified in the verses and so is cast by the word alone.

cast.role: Tivittan, the sea-dark hero whose bow and Garuda come to him
the opposing discus-king, read as Asvagriva
a companion named only by this word, who warns of the missile
the host that breaks in 1432-1433
the kings and their host in 1442
the deity of the hostile missile
Garuda, who becomes Tivittan's mount
the divine weapon shaped like Garuda in 1452

tamil: மருங்கவை புணர்த்த பின்னை வானக வளாக மெல்லாங்
கருங்கலொன் றகன்ற மேலாற் கவித்தது கவித்த லோடும்
இருங்கலி யுலக மெல்லா மிருள்கொள வெருவி நோக்கிப்
பொருங்கலி யரசர் தானை போக்கிட மற்ற தன்றே.
reading: The sky is covered as if a great black stone had spread over it, the world goes dark, and the quarrelsome kings' host sees no way out.
nuance: Lines 1-2 are hard (what 'joins the flanks' and what the black stone is are not stated); the reading holds the darkening and the host trapped.
event: Darkness closes over the sky and the rival army finds no way to retreat.

tamil: வாளொடு வாள்கள் வீழா மைந்தரை மைந்த ருந்தித்
தாளொடு தாள்க டாக்கித் தலையொடு தலைகண் முட்டித்
தோளொடு தோள்க டேய்ப்பச் சுடரணி சுடர்ந்து சிந்த
ஆளுடை யரசன் றானை யரவமோ டுடைந்த தன்றே.
reading: Sword on sword, shoulder on shoulder, head on head, the lord's host breaks with a roar and scatters its bright ornaments.
nuance: 'ஆளுடை அரசன்' is not named; it is read as the king whose army was shown trapped in 1432, but the verse does not fix which side.
event: A host breaks in close fighting, with weapons and ornaments flying.

tamil: அன்னண முடைந்த போழ்தி னருக்கனை முகத்து நோக்கி
என்னிது விளைந்த வாறென் றிருங்கடல் வண்ணன் கேட்பக்
கன்னவில் வயிரத் தோளாய் காய்ந்தவன் விடுக்கப் பட்டு
மன்னுயி ருண்ணுஞ் சண்ட வேகையாம் வருவ தென்றான்.
reading: Asked by the sea-dark one what has happened, a companion answers that the angry foe has loosed a missile named Chanda Vegai which will come and drink the lives of the living.
nuance: The questioner is the sea-dark one (Tivittan, 'இருங்கடல் வண்ணன்'); the one addressed by the odd name 'அருக்கன்' is not otherwise identified, so the speaker is a guess from the word order.
event: Tivittan asks what is happening and is warned that the enemy's Chanda Vegai missile is coming.

tamil: செற்றலன் விடுத்த பின்றைச் செகுத்துயிர் பருகி னல்லான்
மற்றிது மறித லில்லை மறிப்பவர் பிறரு மில்லை
இற்றிதன் நிலைமை யென்ன விருங்கடல் வண்ண னக்காங்
கற்றமி லலங்கல் வேலோ யஞ்சினை போறி யென்றான்.
reading: The warning goes on: once sent in hate the missile does not turn back until it has killed, and no one can turn it; the sea-dark one asks its nature and teases the spearman for seeming afraid.
nuance: The claim is answered when the missile's own deity shrinks in 1439-1440. The last words ('you seem afraid') may be Tivittan's teasing; the verse does not mark the change of speaker.
event: The companion says the missile cannot be turned back, and Tivittan twits him for fear.

tamil: பேயெரி யுமிழ்ந்து நம்மேல் வருமெனப் பேசு கின்றாய்
நீபெரி தினியை யென்னா நெடியவன் றன்னை நோக்கிக்
மாயிரு விசும்பு மஞ்சும் வடிவினன் வள்ள லானான்.
reading: Answering that the missile will 'come spitting fire' he calls the speaker very gentle, and grows in anger and flame, taking a form that frightens even the sky.
nuance: 'நெடியவன்' (the tall one) is the sea-dark one, as in the earlier verses; 'வள்ளல்' (the generous one) as he grows reads as an epithet, not a change of subject.
event: Tivittan mocks the warning and swells in size and fire.

tamil: நலம்புரி செய்கை மேனாட் பெற்றநற் றோழ னேபோல்
உலம்புரி யுருவத் தோளாற் குற்றபோழ் துதவ லுற்று
வலம்புரி வலத்த தாக விடத்ததோர் வயிர வல்விற்
கலம்புரி கனபொற் பூணான் கைவந்து புகுந்த வன்றே.
reading: Like a good friend won in a former life, a vajra bow comes into his hand at the moment of need.
nuance: The simile ('நலம்புரி செய்கை மேனாட் பெற்ற நற்றோழன்') pictures help as the return of earlier good deeds, but the narrator uses it as a comparison, not as a statement of doctrine.
event: A diamond bow and its gem-set ornaments come into Tivittan's hands.

tamil: நெதிசொரி சங்க மேந்தி நெடுஞ்சிலை யிடங்கைக் கொண்டு
விதிதரு நீல மேனி விரிந்தொளி துளும்ப நின்றான்
மதியொரு பால தாக வானவின் மருங்கு கோலிப்
புதியதோர் பருவ மேகம் போந்தெழு கின்ற தொத்தான்.
reading: He stands with a conch in one hand and the long bow in the other, his dark body shining like a new rain cloud with a rainbow beside the moon.

tamil: வலம்புரி சிலம்ப வாய்வைத் திருஞ்சிலை வளைய வேற்றிக்
கலம்புரி கனபொன் னாழிக் கைவிரல் கதிர்ப்பச் சூட்டி
உலம்புரி வயிரத் தோளா னுரப்பினா னுரப்ப லோடுஞ்
சலம்புரி தெய்வ மஞ்சித் தன்னுரு வடைந்த தன்றே.
reading: He sets the conch to his mouth and sounds it, bends the bow and fits a ring on his finger and urges on his weapon; the deity of the hostile missile is frightened and returns to its own shape.
nuance: 'சலம்' can be anger, deceit or water; the deity is read as that of the missile from 1434-1435, which is why it is said to turn back.
event: Tivittan sounds the conch and shoots; the missile's deity shrinks back in fear.

tamil: நிலத்திடை நின்று வான முடியுற நிமிர்ந்து கண்ணின்
புலத்தின தளவு நீங்கிப் பொம்மென வுயிர்த்து விம்மிப்
பிலத்தின தளவிற் பேழ்வாய் பிறழ்ந்திலங் கெயிற்ற தாகிச்
சலத்தினைப் புரிந்த தெய்வந் தலைபனித் துடைந்த தன்றே.
reading: The deity, tall as the sky, breathes hard with gaping fangs, then trembles and shrinks.
event: The deity trembles and shrinks away.

tamil: தெய்வமாங் குடைந்து தன்பாற் படையினைத் திரைத்துக் கொண்டு
மையிரு விசும்பி னேறக் கண்டபின் மாற்று வேந்தன்
கையினைப் புடைத்துக் கண்கள் சிவந்துவா யெயிறு கவ்வி
வையக நடுங்க நோக்கி மழகளி றணைக வென்றான்.
reading: The rival king sees the deity retreat into the sky with its weapon, strikes his hands, glares and bites his lip, and orders the young elephant brought.
nuance: 'மாற்று வேந்தன்' (the opposing king) is read as Asvagriva, the discus-holder.
event: Seeing his missile fail, Asvagriva rages and calls for his elephant.

tamil: மாலுமால் களிறு நுந்தி மற்றவன் வருத லோடு
மாலுமால் புரவித் திண்டே ரரசர தரவத் தானை
வேலினா னுடங்கு நில்லா துடைந்திட வெகுண்டு நோக்கி
நீலமா மணிக்குன் றொப்பா னெடுஞ்சிலை யிடங்கைக் கொண்டான்.
reading: His elephant is driven in, the kings' host breaks before the spear, and the dark-gem-hill one looks on angrily and takes up the long bow.
nuance: Whose host breaks is not said; the reading takes it as the host in the path of the charge.
event: The enemy charges on an elephant; a host breaks; Tivittan takes the bow again.

tamil: வாய்ந்தநல் வயிரத் துண்டம் வளைந்தொளி துளும்ப வள்ளாற்
சேந்தன சிறுக ணோடு திசைமுகஞ் சிறகு தம்மால்
வேய்ந்தனெ விரித்து வீசி விசும்பிடை யிழிந்து வந்து
காய்ந்தெரி கணையி னாற்குக் கருடனு முழைய னானான்.
reading: Garuda, bright-eyed with winged diamond beak, comes down from the sky and stands at the side of the one with the fire-arrow.
event: Garuda descends and attends Tivittan.

tamil: கருடனை வலங்கொண் டேறிக் கார்முகங் கையி னேந்தி
மருடரு விசும்பி னேறி மணிவண்ண னெதிர்ந்த போழ்தின்
இருடனக் கெய்திற் றோரா னெரிகதி ராழி வேந்தன்
பொருடனக் கினியி லாத புகழ்ச்சிகள் புகல லுற்றான்.
reading: Tivittan mounts Garuda and rises with the bow to meet the sea-coloured foe; the discus king, black with rage, begins to speak boasts of no worth.
event: Tivittan rides Garuda into the sky; Asvagriva starts to boast.

tamil: தானவர் நின்னைப் போலத் தந்திற லறிவி லாதார்
ஈனவ ரிரங்கி வீழ்ந்தா ரேனையர் தொழுது வாழ்ந்தார்
வானவ ரென்னை யஞ்சி வானிடை மறைந்து செல்வார்
ஊனவர் தம்மு ணீயே யுயிரெனக் கிழக்க லுற்றாய்.
reading: Asvagriva boasts that the Danavas who were not like Tivittan fell weeping or bowed and lived, that gods hide in the sky from him, and that Tivittan alone has chosen to lose his life.
nuance: The boast is the foe's; the story soon shows its weakness in 1448 and in the failing weapons of 1451-1456.
event: Asvagriva claims the gods and Danavas fear him and that Tivittan is a fool to face him.

tamil: மண்ணுள்வாழ் சிதலைச் சாதி மற்றவை வாழு நாள்கள்
எண்ணியாங் கிகந்த பின்னை யிறகுபெய் தெழுங்கள் போலாம்
கண்ணினா லதனை நீயுங் கருடப்புள் ளதனை யேறி
விண்ணினா றெதிர்ந்து வந்தாய் வேற்கிரை யாகி யென்றான்.
reading: Like winged termites rising when their days are counted, you have come against my spear on Garuda as its prey.
event: Asvagriva calls Tivittan a termite flying to its death.

tamil: மாறலா மனிதர் தம்மேல் வண்சுட ராழி யானுஞ்
சீறினா னென்ற போழ்திற் சிறுசொலாய் நிற்கு மென்று
தேறினார் மொழிகள் கொண்டு செவிசுடு சொற்கள் கேட்டு
மாறினே னென்ப தோரா யளியற்றா யனல்விக் கின்றாய்.
reading: Asvagriva says he left off anger at men on hearing that even the discus-lord rose against them, but that Tivittan's ear-burning words prove he is pitiless, and so he is moved to wrath.
nuance: Lines 1-3 are tangled; the reading keeps only what is clear, that he answers insult with threat.
event: Asvagriva justifies his anger by Tivittan's words.

tamil: என்றலு மதனைக் கேட்டே யிருங்கடல் வண்ண னக்கு
நன்றுநன் றுரைத்தி மீட்டு நல்லையே பெரிது மேடா
குன்றின்மே லிருந்து நீநின் குழுவினுண் மொழிவ தல்லால்
இன்றுவந் தென்மு னின்று மிதுகொலோ கருதிற் றென்றான்.
reading: The sea-dark one says: good, good, you speak well, but this is what you say among your own band from a hilltop; can it be what you really mean to say to my face?
event: Tivittan answers that boasting among one's own band is not the same as facing the foe.

tamil: சிறியவ னுரைகள் வந்தென் செவிசுடும் பொறுக்க லாற்றேன்
எறிகடல் வளாகந் தன்னு ளிவன்பெய ரொழிப்ப னென்று
செறிமணிக் கடகக் கையாற் றிண்சிலை குழைய வாங்கிப்
பொறிநுதல் யானை மேலான் சரமழை பொழிவிக் கின்றான்.
reading: Asvagriva, hearing the small man's words burn his ears, vows to wipe out his name from the earth, draws the strong bow on his elephant and pours arrows.
event: Enraged, Asvagriva shoots a rain of arrows at Tivittan.

tamil: கடுத்தவ னெய்த போழ்திற் கருடன்றன் சிறகு தன்னாற்
புடைத்திட நெரிந்துப் பொங்கிச் சரங்கள்போய்ப் புரள நோக்கி
விடைத்திறல் விடலை தன்மேல் வெம்பிய மனத்த னாகிப்
படைத்திற லாளன் றெய்வப் படைத்தொழில் பறைக்க லுற்றான்.
reading: The arrows fall from Garuda's wing-beats; seeing them scattered, the bow-skilled one turns his mind to hostile divine weapons.
event: Garuda's wings beat the arrows aside; Asvagriva turns to divine weapons.
