tamil: காயிரும் பனைய வெய்யோன் கருமணி வண்ணன் றன்மேல்
ஆயிரம் பணத்த தாய வருமணி யாடு நாக
மாயிரும் புகழி னான்றன் வன்சிலை வாங்கி யெய்யச்
சேயிருஞ் சுடர்கள் சிந்தித் தீயுமிழ்ந் தோடிற் றன்றே.
reading: The foe shoots a weapon in the form of a thousand-hooded jewelled cobra at the dark-gem one, and fire sparks run from it.
event: Asvagriva looses a naga weapon at Tivittan.

tamil: கண்டன னதனை மற்றக் கருங்கடல் வண்ணன் கண்டே
ஒண்டிற லுவணப் புள்ளி னுருவினோர் தெய்வ வம்பு
கொண்டனன் றொடுத்த லோடுங் கொடுஞ்சிறை நுடங்க வீசித்
துண்டமா நாகந் தன்னைத் துண்டத்தாற் றுணித்த தன்றே.
reading: Tivittan sees it, takes a divine arrow in Garuda's form, and when it is shot the bird cuts the cobra to pieces with its beak.
event: Tivittan's Garuda weapon tears apart the naga weapon.

tamil: ஆயிடை யனன்று மீட்டு மழலுமி ழாழி வேந்தன்
தீயொடு புணர்த்த போழ்தத் தெய்வவம் பெய்த லோடும்
வேயுடை விலங்கல் சுட்டு விசும்பிடை வெம்ப வெம்பிச்
சேயிடை யெரிந்து சிந்திச் செல்வன்மேற் சென்ற தன்றே.
reading: The enraged discus-holder joins fire to the string and shoots a fire weapon that scorches the mountains and the sky and goes against Tivittan.
event: Asvagriva looses a fire weapon.

tamil: காரணி வண்ணன் கண்டே கதிர்மணிக் கடகக் கையால்
வாருண மென்னு மம்பு வாங்கினன் றொடுத்த லோடுஞ்
சீரணி விசும்பு மண்ணுந் திசைகளு மிருள வீழ்ந்து
நீரணி புயலின் றாரை நிரந்துவீழ்ந் தவித்த தன்றே.
reading: Tivittan draws the Varuna arrow; at its flight the sky, earth and quarters darken and rain falls in streams, putting out the fire.
event: Tivittan's Varuna arrow drowns the fire weapon in rain.

tamil: விண்களை வெதுப்பு நீர்மை வெய்யவன் வெகுண்டு மீட்டுங்
மண்களை மயக்கி மாக்க டுயில்கொள மரங்கள் சாயப்
புண்களை யணையும் வேலான் படைமுகம் புக்க தன்றே.
reading: The sun-hot one shoots a sleep arrow; creatures fall asleep, trees bend, and it enters the army's front.
event: Asvagriva looses a weapon that puts living things to sleep.

tamil: அயிலுடை யனல்செய் வேலோ னதனையு மறிந்து மற்றுத்
துயில்விடை செய்யு மம்பு தொடுத்தனன் றொடுத்த லோடும்
வெயிலிடை விரிந்து விண்பால் விளங்கிவீ ழிருளை நீக்கப்
பயிலுடை யுலகந் தேறிப் பட்டது முணர்ந்த தன்றே.
reading: Knowing it, the one with the fire-spear shoots an awakening arrow whose light drives off the dark and wakes the world, which understands what has happened.
event: Tivittan wakes the sleepers with his counter-weapon.

title: அரசியற் சருக்கம் 1457-1481 (14/17)
theme: The discus of Ayakantan wheels back to Tivittan, who hurls it and kills the king; onlookers draw lessons of impermanence, and the king's wives fall and lament over his body.
source_issues: Verses 1459-1460 and 1473-1481 are printed in eight half-lines and were joined into four lines; verse 1460 had a stray pulli removed from line 4.
Verses 1464-1465 are short four-line verses in a different metre from those before them.
Who speaks 1466-1468 and who is named by the cloud-hued epithet in 1468 cannot be fixed from the Tamil alone.

cast.role: the garlanded king whose discus turns on him, Tivittan's enemy
the young lord of Suramai who takes the returned discus and hurls it
those who see the king fall and speak their pity
Ayakantan's chief queen who faints and loses her life at the sight
the king's wives who come, fall and lament over him

tamil: சீற்றமொ டிரியுஞ் செல்வத் தெய்வவம் பெய்த வெல்லா
மாற்றின னறுப்ப நோக்கி மற்றவன் மாற்ற லான்பே
ராற்றலை யறிந்து வெய்ய வாழிகை யேந்தி யின்னும்
ஏற்றனை பொருதி யோவென் றிலங்கெயி றிலங்க நக்கான்.
reading: Seeing his weapons cut down and the other's strength, the king bares his teeth in a laugh and asks whether he will still stand and fight when the discus is raised.
nuance: Which weapons were cut and by whom is not named; lines 1-2 are read loosely.
event: Ayakantan, taking up his discus, laughs and taunts his opponent to fight on.

tamil: தாழியா தெய்யுந் தெய்வப் படைமுத லறுத்துச் சாலப்
பாழியான் மெலிந்தும் பண்டைப் பாவனை பயிற்றி யென்னை
ஆழியால் வெருட்ட லுற்றா யலந்தனை பெரிது மென்றான்
சூழிமால் யானை வல்ல சுரமைநாட் டிளைய கோவே.
reading: The young lord of Suramai answers that, though weakened by the long fight, he sees the old trick of frightening him with the discus, and says the king has only tired himself.
nuance: The speaker is fixed only by the vocative in line 4, which names the speaker of the reply.
event: Tivittan answers Ayakantan's taunt, saying the discus will not frighten him.

tamil: புனைகதி ரார மார்பன் புகைந்துகை முறுக்கி விட்ட
கனைகதிர்த் திகிரி கான்ற கனசுடர் வளைக்கப் பட்டு
வனைகதிர்க் குன்றம் போல மணிவண்ணன் மறைந்து போனான்.
reading: The king twists his hand in rage and hurls the blazing discus, and the dark-hued hero vanishes inside its fire as a mountain is lost in a burning forest.
event: Ayakantan hurls his discus and Tivittan is hidden by its flame.

tamil: உலங்கொண்ட வயிரத் தோளாற் குற்றதை யுணர மாட்டார்
நிலங்கொண்டு மனித ராழ நிரந்தழ லுமிழ்ந்து நேமி
புலங்கொண்ட வயிரக் குன்றின் புடைவரும் பரிதி போல
வலங்கொண்டு வந்து மைந்தன் வலப்புடை நின்ற தன்றே.
reading: The discus, spewing fire, does not strike the youth but wheels round and stands at his right side, like the sun beside a diamond mountain, while the onlookers cannot grasp what has happened.
nuance: The verse does not say why the discus spares him; a reader should not add a cause the Tamil leaves out.
event: The discus turns aside and halts at Tivittan's right.

tamil: கன்னவில் கடகத் தோளான் கண்டுகை தொழுது கொண்டு
மின்னவிர் விளங்கு நேமி விட்டனன் விடுத்த லோடும்
மன்னனை மார்பு கீண்டு மணிமுடி யெறிந்து மற்றைப்
பொன்னவி ரோடை யானைப் புகர்நுதற் புக்க தன்றே.
reading: The hero sees the discus, salutes it with joined hands, and sends it back; it splits the king's chest, strikes off his crown and enters the forehead of his elephant.
event: Tivittan hurls the returned discus and it kills Ayakantan on his elephant.

tamil: கழலவன் கனன்று விட்ட கதிர்நகை நேமி போழ
மழகளி யானை தன்மேன் மறிந்துவீழ் கின்ற மன்னன்
நிழலவிர் விலங்க னெற்றி நிமிர்ந்ததோர் காள மேகம்
அழலவன் றிகிரி பாய வற்றுவீழ் கின்ற தொத்தான்.
reading: The king, struck down, tumbles onto his elephant like a dark cloud on a mountain brow riven by a bolt of fire.
event: Ayakantan falls dead over his elephant.

tamil: நெறிதலை திரிவி லான்மே னினைவிலான் மொழியப் பட்ட
மறுதலை முடிக்கு மேது வாய்வழி யழிப்ப தேபோற்
பொறிதலை மணந்த காளை மேல்வரப் புணர்த்த நேமி
செறிதலை யிலாத மன்னன் றன்னையே செகுத்த தன்றே.
reading: The discus sent at a man of unwavering path rebounds and kills the king who lacked restraint, as a curse spoken against a blameless man ends in the speaker's own mouth.
nuance: The simile asks the reader to take the king's death as a rebounding of his own deed; it does not name a former birth, so it is not the karma of earlier lives.
event: The discus kills the king who sent it.

reading: Onlookers say that the man who came with elephants under a white umbrella and kings praising him is now cut down and brought low, and that impermanence has become plain.
Yesterday he came under the long umbrella with the discus before him and kings chanting his praise; today the same man lies felled by that discus, with his golden crown still bright.
nuance: The verse repeats the sense of 1464 with a day-to-day contrast of 'yesterday' and 'now'.

reading: A speaker says that the discus the king threw became his own enemy and that he died at the hands of mere youths, so that even a life the heavens know seems an illusion.
nuance: Line 2 calls his opponents 'boys', a mark of contempt for the king's fall rather than a statement of their age.

reading: Strength, killing power, wealth, beauty and splendour do not last to the end, he seems to say to those who live on earth, so do not be proud, and his fall shows it.
The discus he sent at the enemy came back and split his own broad chest, and he died; who can know what will come to pass?
nuance: The subject of line 1 is uncertain: it may name the king, whose body is dark, or the hero; the sense of the discus returning on its thrower is clear.
event: The king's discus returns and kills him.

reading: At such sights people pity him, and then the wives of Ayakantan, wearing gold earrings and with swelling breasts and slim waists, come near.
event: The king's wives come to the body.

reading: The chief queen sees her husband lying with his chest cut and her hand drops; her eyes drown in tears and life leaves her so that she is an empty body.
nuance: The Tamil says her life 'left' and her body was empty, which could be a faint or a death; she is not named again in these verses.
event: The chief queen faints and her life leaves her at the sight of the dead king.

reading: Their garlands slip, their waists give way, and the young women fall to the ground like peacocks, beating their eyes when they see their lord's chest.
event: The wives collapse on the field and beat their faces.

reading: They roll about like tangled creepers flung to the earth; after a time they get up, unable to leave their beloved's side, and melt like water.
event: The wives roll on the ground and rise to weep.

tamil: அரைச ரேறே யடலாழி வலவ வார்க்குந் தோலாதாய்
புரிசை நகரநூற் றொருபதுடையாய் பூமி முழு தாண்டாய்
செய் துலகம் பாராட்டு மொளியா யோடை யானையாய்
வரைசெய் தனைய திரடோளாய் மறிதல் பொருளோ வயவேந்தே.
reading: A lament addresses the king as lord of armies and of a hundred forts and asks if one who ruled the whole earth should be turned over in death.
nuance: The lament reads as grief rather than doctrine: the women ask whether the fall is fitting, and the work does not answer them here.

tamil: வானு மண்ணு முடனஞ்சும் வகையாய் மன்னர் மணிமுடிமேல்
தேனும் வண்டும் பலசென்று திளைக்குஞ் செம்பொற் செறிகழலாய்
நான மண்ணி யகிறேக்கி நாவி கமழு மெழிலாகம்
ஈன மண்ணி லிவர்காணக் கிடத்த லினிதோ விகல்வேந்தே.
reading: The lament asks whether it is fitting that the king whose feet were worshipped by kings and whose perfumed body smelled of musk should lie before all in the mean earth.

tamil: குழவி நாயிற் றெழிலேய்க்குங் குழம்பார் கோலக் குங்குமமே
மெழுகி மீதோர் மணியாரம் வீசிக் கிடந்த விரையாகம்
ஒழுகு குருதிச் சேறாடி யோடை யானை நுதன்மீது
வழுவி வீழ்ந்த வகைநாடின் மாயம் போலு மறவேந்தே.
reading: His chest, once smeared with saffron paste and a jewelled necklace, now lies bathed in a mud of blood on the elephant's forehead, which seems a thing of illusion.

tamil: பொன்னி னாய வமளிமேற் பூவி னாய வணைபொருந்தி
அன்ன மனையா ரடிவருட வமரும் பள்ளி யமராதே
மன்னு மிங்கோர் மதயானை நுதன்மேல் மறிந்து மணிமுடிசாய்த்
தென்னு முரையாய் துயில்கோட லிசையோ வங்கள் பெருமானே.
reading: Instead of the golden couch where wives rubbed his feet, he lies tipped over on a rutting elephant's forehead with the crown fallen aside; the speakers ask if that is fit sleep.
nuance: The contrast of couch and battle-elephant is the lament's argument; no claim is stated.

tamil: மகரப் பைம்பூண் மடவார்கள் வயிரக் குழையும் பொற்றோடுந்
தகரக் குழலு மளகமுந் திருத்திப் பயின்ற தாழ்தடக்கை
சிகர மனைய மதயானைச் செவிமேற் சரிந்து செங்குருதி
பகரக் கழுகு பாராட்டக் கிடத்த றகுமோ படைவேந்தே.
reading: The hands that the women adorned with jewels and perfumes now hang from the ear of a mountain-like elephant while vultures feed on the blood; the lament asks if that is fitting.

tamil: வெய்ய சுடரோன் றண்கதிரோ னெனவீங் கிவர்கண் மதிலியங்கார்
பைய வந்து தாமரையின் பரவைத் தடத்து மாளிகைமேல்
ஐய தலத்து மெலவிரிந்த தலராச் செல்லு மாணையாய்
செய்ய குருதிச் சேறாடிச் சிறுமா னிடர்க்கே தோற்றாயே.
reading: A lament says the king who gave orders like the sun and moon across the city and its halls was brought down by common men and sits bathed in blood.
nuance: Several words of lines 1-3 are run together in the edition and line 1 is read loosely.

tamil: பணங்கொ ணாகம் பலசூழ்ந்து பகல்செய் மணியின் சுடரேந்தி
அணங்கி யகலா துழைநிற்கு மாணை யுடைய வடல்வேந்தே
வணங்கி வந்து பலதெய்வம் வழிபா டாற்று மறநேமிக்
குணங்கொள் படையாய் கூடாரு முளரோ நினக்குக் கோமானே.
reading: The women remind him that gods came to worship his discus and snakes with jewelled hoods stood by him, and ask how foes could ever have joined against him.
nuance: The speakers presume the discus made him safe; the story has shown it was his own weapon that killed him.

tamil: பெருமா மழைக்கண் மாதேவி பிணையின் மாழ்கி யிவணழிய
வருமா முரசம் பிறர்பேர்கொண் டறைய வாழி யயனீங்கத்
திருமா நகருஞ் செல்வமுற்றுஞ் சிதையக் கண்டுஞ் சீறாயால்
உருமா லென்னுந் திறலினா யுலகம் வேண்டா தொழிந்தாயோ.
reading: The speakers ask why, with the great queen dying like a doe and other men's names being beaten on the war-drum in his own city, he does not rise in anger.
nuance: The reading of 'வாழி யயனீங்க' in line 2 is uncertain.
event: The wives say the conquerors are already claiming the king's city and drum.

tamil: மூரி முந்நீ ருலகங்கண் முழுதுங் காவன் முனிந்தாயோ
யாரு மில்லா வடியோங்கள் வழிபா டாற்ற மாட்டாயோ
சீரின் மன்னும் வளநாடுந் தெய்வப் படையுஞ் செல்வமுநீ
பாரின் மன்னர் பிறர்கொள்ளப் பணித்த தென்னோ படைவேந்தே.
reading: The lament closes asking if he was angry with the world, and why he has left to other kings his land, his divine weapon and his wealth, when none is left to serve him.

title: அரசியற் சருக்கம் 1482-1505 (15/17)
theme: After the discus kills the king of the Vidyadharas, the enemy dead are burned and their wives withdraw, the defeated bow and are shown mercy, the hero meets his father and is bathed and crowned Vasudeva, and the seven royal jewels come to him.
source_issues: Verses 1482-1485 were printed as eight half-lines and joined into four lines by the build.
Verse 1484 line 4 is broken in word division.
Verse 1500 line 1 had a stray pulli removed by the build.

cast.role: the red-eyed tall one, hero who takes the discus and is crowned Vasudeva
the elder prince, brother of Tivittan
the father of the two princes, named here as lord of the land of Surama
the Vidyadharas, who give up their pride and bow
the Vidyadhara and allied kings who crown and bathe the hero
the brahmins who lay the dead king on his pyre
the weeping women whose tears fall in 1482
the queens of the dead Vidyadhara king, called here Vayakkiriva

tamil: தொழுதுஞ் சூழ்ந்து மடிபற்றித் தொடர்ந்துஞ் சுரும்புண் கோதையும்
வழுவ மயங்கி மாழாந்து மருண்டுந் தெருண்டு மடவார்கள்
அழுத கண்ணீ ரகன்ஞாலத் தரச ருருக வருவியாய்
ஒழுக நெடுமான் முனிவென்னு மூழித் தீயு மவிந்ததே.
reading: The weeping of the women flows like streams, and with it the great king's wrath, likened to the fire at the world's end, is put out.
nuance: The first two lines are about the women and kings who weep, the last two about the anger that goes out; who exactly the kings melting are, and whose anger is meant, is not fixed by the words, so the reading keeps to the image of tears as water on fire.
event: The tears of the grieving women quench the victor's long-burning anger.

tamil: மஞ்சு தோயும் வரையார்தம் மன்னன் றன்னை மதயானை
மஞ்சு தோன்ற நுதலினிழித் தந்த ணாளார் மெய்தீண்டிப்
வஞ்ச மில்லாப் புகழானை வயங்கு செந்தீ வாய்ப்பெய்தார்.
reading: The brahmins lay the king of the mountain folk on a bed of cotton, silk and fine cloth, after he has been brought down from his elephant, and put him into the bright fire.
nuance: The dead king is called one of untainted fame (line 4), so the funeral is given with honour to the enemy slain; the verse does not name him, and he is taken from the context to be the lord of the mountain Vidyadharas.
event: Brahmins lay the dead Vidyadhara king on a rich bed and give him to the funeral fire.

tamil: மன்னன் றம்பி மார்களையு மக்க டமையு மற்றொழிந்த
பொன்னம் புனைதார் வேந்தரையும் பொருது பட்ட போர்க்களமீ
தென்னுஞ் சாடு மெரிவாய்ப்பெய் திரங்கி யழுதாங் கேகினரால்
உன்னி வந்த முடிக்ககிலா துடைந்த வேந்த னுழையாரே
reading: The kinsmen, sons and kings who fell in the battle are given to the fire on the field, and the king's defeated men leave weeping.
nuance: Line 4 is broken in the word division and the relation of 'those who could not complete what they thought' to the king is a guess.
event: The attendants of the beaten king burn the fallen on the battlefield and depart in tears.

tamil: ஆவி யாய வயக்கிரீவற் கமிழ்தம் பூத்த வஞ்சாயற்
றேவி மார்கள் கலனழித்துச் சேணி யுலகஞ் சென்றெய்தி
வீவில் காமன் வருவீதி கற்பு வேலி யால்விலக்கித்
தாவி னிறையின் றாழதனாற் பொறியின் வாயி றாழ்ப்பெய்தார்.
reading: The queens of the dead Vidyadhara king strip off their ornaments, go to the Vidyadhara world, and bar desire's way with the fence of chastity and the lock of restraint, shutting the doors of the senses.
nuance: Chastity is shown as a fence the widows themselves build around the senses, not as a guard set on them by others; whether this is a turn to renunciation or only widowhood is not said.
event: The widowed queens put off their jewels and shut out desire.

reading: A rain of flowers falls on the head of the red-eyed hero who has won the shining discus, and mingles with the sound of drums and conches.
event: Flowers are showered on the discus-winner as drums and conches sound.

reading: The divine arrows he shot are cut down and he takes the shining discus, and the sky is filled with a cry that it is a great marvel.
nuance: The subject is not named in the verse; 'the hero who took the discus' is taken from 1486 and 1499.
event: The hero cuts down the divine arrows and takes the discus, and the sky resounds with wonder.

reading: The Vidyadharas lay down their fierce anger and pride, and bow to the hero, the colour of a dark jewel-mountain, saying they were greatly afraid.
event: The Vidyadharas give up their pride and bow to the victor in fear.

reading: The hero shows mercy to the frightened kings and has a drum sounded for the kin of the king who died there, bidding them live again in the Vidyadhara world.
nuance: The speech is reported, not quoted, so the speaker is given as the hero from the action of line 4.
event: Tivittan has a drum proclaim that the dead king's people may return and live.

reading: The dark-cloud-coloured hero alights from Garuda, mounts a rumbling elephant, and enters the camp amid the kings' praise.
event: Tivittan comes down from Garuda and rides to the camp as kings praise him.

reading: Radiant like the moon, he goes with the great elder brother to the father's holy feet and bows, wearing a shoulder garland of gold.
nuance: 'The great one' is taken to be the elder brother Vijayan; the verse does not give the name.
event: Tivittan and his elder brother go to their father and bow at his feet.

reading: The king of the land of Surama, his eyes wide with delight at his sons' might, speaks to the kings who stand beside and bow.
event: The father, pleased with his sons' prowess, addresses the kings who bow around him.

reading: He says that he reached the name of father of these flawless young princes through his penance, and asks to see in their royal state the beloved jewel-adorned eyes of his sons.
nuance: The father credits his own tapas, not his sons' worth, for the blessing; this is the same turn of phrase as Kural 70's question of what penance the father did.
event: The father says his fatherhood is the fruit of penance and asks to see his sons crowned.

reading: At his word the Vidyadhara king and the kings joined with him gladly crown the princes, and the royal drum sounds that day.
event: The Vidyadhara king and the kings crown the princes to the beat of the royal drum.

reading: The kings bathe him in the waters of the Ganga and Sindhu, poured from golden lotus-mouthed pots in the auspicious way.
event: The kings pour Ganga and Sindhu water on him from golden pots.

reading: They pour on the king's curled head waters of the milk sea, taken up by the divine host and carried in pots of shining gems, so it is said.
nuance: Who the bearers are is carried by the verb alone; 'the divine army' (line 1) is taken as the source of the water.
event: Divine hosts pour milk-sea water from gem pots on the king's head.

reading: The brave Vidyadhara kings bathe the one like Indra with the flowers and waterfalls of the Mandara jewel-mountain and bow to him, as the tale says.
event: The Vidyadhara kings bathe him in waters of Mandara and bow.

reading: Lakshmi comes with love, and by the form, the light and the old rule of the book the king is anointed protector of the world.
nuance: The third and fourth lines turn on a rare phrase for the book's rule; the sense that the anointing follows a scripture's rule is held loosely.
event: The dark-cloud one is anointed protector of the world, with Lakshmi drawn to him.

reading: Because he took the discus after killing the discus-king, they set on him a bright crown and name him Vasudeva.
nuance: The title is given by the fact of winning the discus (line 2, 'because it was the discus'), not by birth or an earlier anointing.
event: The kings crown the discus-winner as Vasudeva.

reading: They crown the great hero in the old manner with a long crown of the gods, and bless him as the protector whose feet ring with anklets.
event: The kings and gods crown the great hero in the ancient way and bless him.

reading: At the great festival of the royal coronation they honour the gods, and the other precious things unsent also reach him.
nuance: Line 2 and 4 are not fully clear about whether the treasures come from the gods or from the festival.
event: The coronation festival is held and the remaining treasures come to the king.

reading: He wins the discus, staff, sword, conch, bow, parasol and fire-jewel, and shines as the god the kings of men bow to.
event: The king receives the seven royal jewels and shines as a god before kings.

reading: The two great treasures named Valampuri and the golden lotus pour out gems, bright gold and shining gold ore.
Crowned with a blazing crown, with all kings worshipping at his feet, the lord reaches the great hall of the discus's wealth.
event: The crowned lord enters the great hall of the discus's riches as kings worship.

reading: The great divine jewels each go to the city made ready, and the palace is held in honour because of the unwearying Garuda and the shining lord.
nuance: Lines 3-4 name Garuda and the lord together but the syntax is ambiguous about who is honoured by whom.
event: The divine treasures go to their prepared city and the royal palace is honoured.

title: அரசியற் சருக்கம் 1506-1530 (16/17)
theme: After the poets' chronicle of the discus-lords, the hero lifts the great gem mountain Kotisilai with his arms while kings and gods acclaim him, then returns in procession to Pothanam, where the city's women come out to him.
source_issues: Verses 1527, 1529 and 1530 print as eight half-lines; the tool joined them into four lines.
There is no verse numbered 1528 in the text; the chapter runs 1527 to 1529.
Verses 1521 to 1525 are yamaka and several readings are held loosely.

cast.role: Tivittan, the dark-hued hero who lifts the mountain and is hailed as lord
the poets who recite the chronicles of kingship
the kings who praise and bow to the hero
the women of the city who sing, rejoice and open their doors
the two women who enter the city with the hero
the people of Pothanam who welcome the lord

reading: The king of the war-drum and great host sits enthroned, and the poets then recite to this guardian of the sea-bounded land the old chronicles that teach kingship.
event: Poets recite the chronicles of kingship to the newly enthroned king.

reading: The poets set out the ancient code of royal conduct, and a few faultless deeds of the discus-lords are told on it.
nuance: திகிரியஞ் செல்வர், lords of the discus, are universal emperors; the verse sets the hero's coming feat inside that line of kings.
event: Poets recount the old code of kings and some deeds of the discus-lords.

reading: The poets list what a discus-lord has: seven rare jewels, two great treasures, sixteen thousand lands, festive cities and assemblies of kings.
nuance: Line 4 is hard (எழுவின முரைப்பின் ... எண்ண என்பவே); the sense that these are the things to be counted is held loosely.

reading: The old-story poets tell that such a lord went with many mighty gods, killed his foes, and then lifted a mountain.
nuance: The mountain-lift is first told as the deed of earlier lords; the hero repeats it in the following verses.
event: Poets recall an earlier lord who slew foes with the gods and lifted a mountain.

reading: Hearing this, the hero, without swelling pride, thinks that those who came before were as many as the sands of flowing water.
nuance: He answers the list of earlier feats with a thought of their number, not of his own power; line 2 is hard, so the sense is held loosely.
event: The hero hears the old feats and is not puffed up.

reading: On the word of those who know, the hero, his mind full of fitting wealth, rises with his sea of an army and reaches the hill Kotisilai.
event: The hero marches with his army to the Kotisilai mountain.

reading: The lord of the shining crown thrusts both bracelet-bright arms down beneath the great gem mountain, making the earth a pit, and lifts it.
event: The hero thrusts his arms under Kotisilai and lifts it.

reading: As he thrusts in his hand and lifts, the dark mountain rolls with a crash, and the red hollow it leaves rings as if the ground opened its mouth and called.
event: The mountain tilts as he lifts it and the hollow echoes.

reading: The tails of great snakes that lived in the hollows hang down as the garlanded one lifts, like bright roots of the torn-up hill.
Water from the blue-lily pools and streams falls from the lifted mountain, as if the dark hill wept at leaving the land.
Clouds slip from the broad slopes and fall, like the red cloth the mountain wore sliding off as it moves.
He sets one thigh firm and holds the bright mountain high in one hand, a blue-gem hill carrying another hill.
event: The hero stands holding the mountain aloft in one hand.

reading: While spear-kings praise him and flowers rain and the world of the gods cheers, the lord of gem-dark hue stands proud, the black mountain in one hand.
nuance: He is named by his hue and the Tirumal-like epithet திருமா மணிவண்ணன்; the verse gives no proper name.
event: Kings praise and the gods cheer while the hero holds the mountain.

reading: The verse pictures the hero's anklets and crest-jewel light and the gem-streamed mountain that rests on the hand of the garland-wearer.
nuance: Line 3 turns on கைத்தலத்தது அன்று, and the sense of the negative is not fixed; the reading is a cautious one.

reading: He lifts the mountain with his ruby-bright arm and stands, not even looking up as if he merely lifted it, and the garlanded kings, afraid, bow their gold crowns.
event: Frightened kings bow their crowns to the hero as he stands holding the mountain.

reading: The verse says the hero returns the great hill and that the king like the hill mounts the fierce elephant and calms it.
nuance: The verse turns on a yamaka of கோடிக் குன்றம் and the sense of the last line is uncertain.
event: The hero puts the mountain back and mounts and calms a killer elephant.

reading: After crossing the lotus-pooled moat and reaching the good watered land, fair women sing the cool fame of the hero and are honoured.
nuance: The verse is a யமகம் on தாமரை தங்கும் தண்புனல்; who crosses and who is honoured is not fixed.
event: Women of the land sing the hero's fame as he reaches it.

reading: Under his pearl parasol, bright as a moon, the people of the watered land rejoice, and the sea-ringed world comes under it.
nuance: The verse is a yamaka on மாலைத் தண்கேழ்; the last clause is read loosely.

reading: When the lord of the pond-rich land reaches the palace yard, the women of dark eyes are glad at his coming.
nuance: The yamaka on மையார் makes the exact words of their joy unclear.
event: The women of the mansions rejoice as the lord arrives.

reading: Red-lipped women shower flowers and, in their joy, lay aside their modesty as the famed king enters the city.
event: He enters the city while women throw flowers and drop their shyness.

tamil: தாமரை நாறுந் தண்பணை யெல்லா மகிழ் நாறச்
reading: With whisks waving and gold ear-rings flashing, the hero and the two women with him enter the flower-fenced city of Pothanam.
nuance: The hero is named by the epithet திருமால், and the two women are known only by epithets, the lotus-lady and the bright-jewelled one.
event: The hero and his two consorts enter the city of Pothanam.

tamil: சூழிணர்மென் மல்லிகையும் வளையமுமின் சூட்டுமெழி றுதையச் சூட்டி
யாழகவி மணிவண்டு மணிஞிமிறு மதுகரமு மிசைப்பச் செய்ய
காழகிலு நறுஞ்சாந்துங் கடிவாசப் பூம்பொடியுங் கமழ்ந்து கைபோய்
ஏழுலகு மணங்கொடுப்ப வெழினகரா ரெதிர்கொள்ள விறைவன் புக்கான்.
reading: Bees hum, incense and sandal scent the street, and the townsfolk welcome the lord as he enters decked in jasmine and ring-crest.
event: The townsfolk receive the lord as he enters the city.

tamil: கோபுரமுங் கழிந்துகுளிர் நகரைவலங் கொடுவீதி குடையோன் செல்ல
நூபுரமு மேகலையுங் கலந்தொலிப்ப நுண்மருங்கு னுடங்க வோடி
மாபுரத்து மாளிகைதம் மணிக்கதவந் தாழ்திறந்து மனத்தின் றாழும்
வேய்புரையு மென்பணைத்தோண் மெல்லியலார் மெல்லவே திறந்தா ரன்றே.
reading: Passing the gate and circling the cool city, the umbrella-lord goes down the street, and the slender women run out, clashing their anklets, and open their jewelled doors and the bolts of their minds as well.
nuance: தாழ் is bolt: the women open the door-bolt and, the verse says, the bolt of the mind; the epic makes desire the thing that opens their reserve.
event: The women of the mansions open their doors as he passes in procession.

tamil: போர் மேக மன்னதிறற் பொருகளிற்று மேலரசர் போற்றிக் கூவச்
சீர்மேக மெனச்செறிக ணிடி முரசங் கடிததிர்ந்து திசைமே லார்ப்ப
நீர்மேக முத்தினெடுந் தண்குடைக்கீழ் நிழற்றுளும்பு நேமி தாங்குங்
கார்மேக வண்ணனிவன் வருவானைக் காண்மினோ கண்க ளார.
reading: Kings on war-elephants hail him, drums sound like storm-cloud, and a voice bids the onlookers see with full eyes the cloud-hued bearer of the discus who comes under the pearl parasol.
nuance: The last line is a speech bidding the onlookers to look; who speaks it is not named, so narrator is a placeholder.
event: Kings hail him and drums sound as he approaches in procession.

title: அரசியற் சருக்கம் 1531-1554 (17/17)
theme: The end of the Arasiyal sarukkam: the king's young daughter is shown to the crowd and adorned, the city's festival darkens the sun, the prince enters the bride's chamber, is crowned beside her, gives her father the Vidyadhara realm and sinks into joy and wealth.
source_issues: Every verse but 1552 to 1554 prints in 8 half-lines in the source and was joined into 4 lines by the build.
1537 line 3 had a stray pulli removed by the build.
1534 line 3 reads ளிமானத்தின் for விமானத்தின், and 1535 line 2 reads திக்ழ்ந்து for திகழ்ந்து.
1532 line 4 (வருநனலர் தாரா ன்மற்) is garbled in word division.
1545 and 1546 name the actors only by epithets (மணிவரை அரசன், வளைவண்ணன், மகரப் பூணான்); the identifications are by sequence.

cast.role: an unnamed speaker who calls the onlookers to see the bride and groom
the crowd the speaker addresses
women who adorn the bride
young women at the windows
dancers, singers and praisers
the kings gathered for the wedding
the king of Podanam
Tivittan, the dark-hued young prince, the groom
heralds who proclaim by drum

tamil: செந்தாஅ மரைபுரையுஞ் செழுங்கண்ணுந் தடக்கையும் பவள வாயும்
அந்தாஅ மரைநாறு மடியிணையு மவையவையே காண்மின் காண்மின்
நந்தாஅ மரைநாட னகையிலங்கு மணியார நவின்ற மார்பம்
பைந்தாஅ மரை மடந்தை பாராட்டப் பொலிந்திலங்கும் படியுங் காண்மின்.
reading: A voice calls the onlookers to look at the bride: her lotus-red eyes, long hands, coral mouth, lotus-scented feet and the jewelled chest, shining as the lotus lady praises her.
nuance: The speaker is not named; the reading of the lotus (தாமரை) as Lakshmi in line 4 is read from பாராட்ட and the lotus-maiden, and may be only the poet's image.

tamil: உரற்கால முறச்செவிய வோங்கெருத்தி னோடைமால் யானைமே லொளிசூழ் மாலை
நிரற்கால மணிநிரைத்த நெடுங்குடைக்கீழ் முடிநிழற்ற நெடுமால் பின்னே
சரற்கால சந்திரனோர் தடவரைமேல் வெண்முகிற்கீழ்த் தயங்கி யாங்கே
யரக்காம்பல் வாயினிரிவ் வருநனலர் தாரா ன்மற் றவன்சீர் காண்மின்.
reading: The same voice shows the groom's glory: on a rutting elephant under a long jewelled umbrella, he shines like an autumn moon on a mountain beneath white cloud, with a red-lotus mouth and a garland.
nuance: Line 4 is garbled in the edition (வருநனலர் தாரா ன்மற்), so the last clause is held loosely.
event: A speaker presents the groom, riding an elephant under the royal umbrella, to the onlookers.

tamil: சேதாம்பல் வீழ்ந்தனைய செவ்வாயுஞ் செங்குவளை திளைத்த கண்ணு
மீதார்ந்த வெண்ணிலாச் சுடரொளியும் வெள்ளிக்குன் றனைய தோளும்
போதார்ந்த கருங்குஞ்சி மணிதொடர்ந்தாற் போற்புறந்தாழ்ந் திருண்ட வாறுங்
காதார்ந்த குழைதாழக் கதிருமிழ்ந்த திருமுகத்தின் கதிர்ப்புங் காண்மின்.
reading: The voice goes on to praise the groom's body: red lips, lily-dark eyes, a moon-bright light, shoulders like a silver hill, dark hair falling to his back and the glow of his face under swinging earrings.
nuance: That this is the groom and not the bride rests on the masculine shoulders and the sequence with 1532; no name is given.

tamil: வேய்காயு மென்பணைத் தோள் வெண்செந் தனமெழுகி முத்தந் தாங்கி
ஏகாய மிட்ட வெண்டுகிலின் மகளி ருழைநின் றேத்த
ஆகாய மியல்கின்ற வருமணிநல் ளிமானத்தி னகத்தாள் போலு
மாகாய வரையாளு மன்னர்கோன் மடமகளை வம்மின் காண்பாம்.
reading: The speaker says: let us go and see the king's young daughter, who sits among white-clad women praising her, like one inside a sky-travelling jewelled palace.
nuance: ளிமானம் in line 3 is an edition slip for விமானம்.
event: The speaker invites the crowd to go and see the king's daughter on her sky-palace.

tamil: அருமணி நீள்விமானத்தி னாகாயப் பளிங்கியன்ற விளிம்பி னாலுந்
திருமணியி னொளிமேனி நிழலெறிப்பத் திக்ழ்ந்திலங்கு தெய்வப் பாவை
கருமணியின் கதிர்குழற்றிக் கடைசுருட்டிக் கைசெய்து வளர்த்த போலும்
புரிமணிபொண் குழறிகழப் பொன்னணைமே லினிதிருந்த பொலிவு காண்மின்.
reading: In the jewelled palace with a crystal rim, the bride's own light shines back, and the poet says she is like a divine doll with hair dressed by hand and gem-set tresses, sitting on a golden couch.
nuance: திக்ழ்ந்து in line 2 is a misprint for திகழ்ந்து; the doll-image is the poet's own and it makes her seem made, not born, which the verse does not say outright.

tamil: மாநீல மிடைபதித்து வெண்பளிங்கிற் செவ்வரத்த விரேகை வாங்கிப்
பானீர வேல்வடிவு படத்திருத்தித் தாமரையுட் பாரித் தன்ன
தூநீல வாணெடுங்கண் குழைமுகத்தி னுள்ளி லங்கத் தோன்றுகின்ற
வாய்நீல மணியைம்பா லிவ்வணங்கு வரையணங்கோ வன்றோ காண்மின்.
reading: The speaker asks whether this is a mountain goddess, seeing the blue-gem eyes in her face like sapphires set in crystal and red lines drawn in a lotus.

tamil: எழுதாது மையொளிரு மிருமருங்கு மெறித்திடையே செங்கே ழோடித்
தொழுதார்க்கு வரங்கொடுக்குந் தடங்கண்ணி துணைமுலையின் வளாகஞ் சூழ
விழுதாய குங்குமத்தா லிலதையையுங் கொழுந்தினையு மிழைத்தார் பின்னு
முழுதார முத்தணிந்தார் நுண்மருங்கு லுளதாக முயன்றா ரல்லர்.
reading: Her eye-paint is not applied, kumkum lines and creeper-patterns are drawn on her breasts, and pearl strings are put on her; those who adorned her did not seem to try to make her waist exist at all.
nuance: The last line plays on her waist being so slender that the adorners made no effort over it; the sense is held loosely.
event: Her attendants adorn the bride with kumkum designs and pearls.

tamil: போதாவி யேகமழ்ந்து புரைவட்டம் பொன்னிழையாற் பொலிந்து தோன்றி
ஊதாவி யானுடங்கு மொள்ளரத்த நுண்கலிங்க மொன்று சேர்த்தி
மீதாடி வில்லுமிழு மிடைமணியொண் கலாபங்கண் மிளிர வீக்கி
யாதானு மிவரடக்க மிவளல்கு லகலாமை யறிந்து செய்தார்.
reading: They tie around her a fragrant, gold-edged red cloth fine enough to move with a breath, and gem girdles over it, knowing her hips never leave her.
nuance: The sense of line 4 (they know her hips never part from the cloth) is taken from the verb செய்தார் with அறிந்து and is not certain.
event: Attendants dress the bride in a red cloth and gem girdles.

tamil: கந்தாரங் கொளவீக்கிக் கடிவிரிந்து பூம்பாளை கமழுங் காலை
நந்தாஅ வனத்திளையா ரெழுவியாழ் நரம்பினுக்கு நலஞ்சா லின்சொன்
மந்தார மலர்கமழு மணியைம்பான் மைமதர்த்த மழைக்கண் மாதர்
செந்தாஅ மரையடியின் செவ்வியுமற் றிதுவாயிற் றெய்வ மேயாம்.
reading: When the flower-spathe season spreads, the lute-voiced young women's sweet words and the mandara-scented bride's lotus-red feet make the speaker say this is surely a goddess.
nuance: Line 1 (கந்தாரம் கொள வீக்கி) is obscure; it may mean a lute tuned in the gandhara mode, which would give the scene its music.

tamil: இன்னன பலவுங் காட்டி யிளையவர் காணும் போழ்தின்
மன்னவ ரரசர் தன்மேல் மாலையு மலருஞ் சிந்தி
மின்னவிர் சிவிறி தம்மால் விரைபொழி தாரை வீக்கித்
தொன்னக ரார்வ மென்னுங் களித்தொழி றொடங்கிற் றன்றே.
reading: After showing many such sights, the young people watching them join the kings in throwing garlands and flowers on the king and spraying him with scented water, and the old city's joy begins.
nuance: Whether the one showered (அரசர் தன்மேல்) is the groom or the old king is not fixed by the words.
event: The kings and young people shower the king with garlands, flowers and scented water as the city festival opens.

tamil: செம்பொன்செய் பொடியி னாலுஞ் சிவிறியின் றாரை யாலும்
அம்பொன்செய் மலரி னாலு மகிற்புகை யாவி யாலும்
பைம்பொன்செய் பதாகை யாலும் பரந்திருள் பட்ட வீதி
கம்பஞ்செய் யானை யானைக் கண்விளக் குறுத்த வன்றே.
reading: Gold dust, scented sprays, golden flowers, incense smoke and golden banners darken the streets, so that the elephant-bearing king's elephant lights the way by its eyes.
nuance: கம்பஞ்செய் யானையானை (line 4) is read as a shaking war-elephant and its rider; the lamp-eyed image is the poet's.
event: The festival's smoke and decoration darken the streets until only the elephant's eyes seem to give light.

tamil: மன்னிய புகழி னான்மேல் வாங்குவிற் புருவ மாக
மின்னவிர் பகழி கண்ணாப் புரிசைவெண் மாட மாகத்
துன்னிய சால வாயிற் றுளைகளே துளைக ளாகக்
கன்னிய ரெய்து தத்தங் கடிநகர் காவல் கொண்டார்.
reading: Maidens guard their own bright houses, with their brows as bows, glances as arrows, the white upper halls as ramparts and window-slits as the openings.
nuance: The poem turns houses into forts and glances into arrows to say that the king cannot pass unwounded; the verse does not say who passes, which is taken from the sequence.
event: Maidens at the windows shoot glances at the passing king.

tamil: ஆடுவா ரணங்கு கொள்வா ரார்வஞ்செய் கருவி வீக்கிப்
பாடுவார் கண்டு கூறிப் பரவுவார் பணிந்து முன்னாற்
கூடுவார் கொற்றங் கொள்ளக் கூறுவா ராகி யெங்கும்
ஊடுபோக் கரிய தாக வொளிநக ருழையர் சூழ்ந்தார்.
reading: Dancers, women armed with instruments, singers, praisers, and bowing men gather; the palace attendants surround the court in great numbers, so crowded that none can pass.
nuance: கொற்றம் கொள்ளக் கூறுவார் (line 3) means those who pronounce blessings for victory.
event: Entertainers and attendants crowd round the king in the palace city.

tamil: அங்குலாங் கொடியி னாலு மகிற்புகை யாலு மெங்கு
மங்குலாய் விசும்பு மூட மழுங்கிய சுடர னாகி
இங்குலா விளங்க மாட்டே னினியென வெண்ணி வெய்யோன்
கொங்குலாங் குளிர்கொள் சோலைக் குடவரைக் குவடு சேர்ந்தான்.
reading: Flags and incense smoke fill the sky like cloud and dim the sun, which thinks it cannot shine here any more and sets on the western hill.
nuance: The sun's withdrawal is an image of the festival outshining it; it is not claimed as an omen.
event: The sun goes down, dimmed by the smoke of the festival.

tamil: மணிவரை யரசன் மற்றை வாழ்நகர்க் கோயில் புக்கான்
பணிவரை யுழைய ராகிப் பயாபதி பக்க நின்றார்
தணிவரை யிலாத செய்கைத் தத்தமக் கியன்ற கோயில்
அணிவரை யனைய திண்டோ ளருக்கனோ டரசர் சேர்ந்தார்.
reading: The mountain-gem king enters his palace in the city, Payapati stands with his attendants, and the other kings go to their own palaces with the strong-armed Arukkan.
nuance: The 'mountain-gem king' of line 1 and the Arukkan of line 4 are not named by standard titles; identifying them with Tivittan and Arukkakirthi is the sequence's best guess.
event: The kings withdraw to their palaces at nightfall.

tamil: மஞ்சுடை மாடக் கோயில் வளைவண்ன் புக்க பின்னைச்
செஞ்சுடர் மகரப் பூணான் றிருவெதிர் கொள்ளச் சென்று
விஞ்சையம் பாவை மேய விடைமணி விமானஞ் சேர்ந்தான்
எஞ்சலில் செல்வந் தன்னா லிந்திர னிரட்டி யுள்ளான்.
reading: After the conch-white one enters his own tall palace, the red-bright, shark-ornamented prince goes with Fortune to meet him and enters the jewelled room of the Vidyadhara maiden, richer than Indra.
nuance: வளைவண்ணன் (conch-coloured) is an epithet read as Vijayan, the white elder brother; செஞ்சுடர் மகரப் பூணான் is taken as Tivittan. Both are guesses from epithets.
event: The prince enters the Vidyadhara bride's room.

tamil: மாலையாங் கடைந்த போழ்தின் மங்கலத் தேவிப் பட்டங்
காலையா மணிவ தென்று கண்ணதிர் முரசிற் சாற்றிப்
பாலையாழ் மழலை யாளைக் காப்பணி பயின்ற செல்வம்
வேலைசூ ழுலக மெல்லாம் விம்முற விளைந்த தன்றே.
reading: At evening a drum proclaims that the auspicious queen's coronation will be at dawn, and the world's joy grows over the sea-bound earth as the lute-voiced one is made ready.
nuance: The 'lute-voiced' woman (பாலையாழ் மழலையாள்) is the bride only by sequence.
event: Heralds beat a drum announcing the bride's coronation as queen for the next morning.

tamil: அங்கொளி விளக்கி னாலு மணிகலச் சுடரி னாலுந்
திங்களை யனைய செல்வி திருநுத லொளியி னாலு
மங்கல மரபிற் றல்லா மயங்கிருண் மறைந்து போகக்
கங்குலு மெல்ல மெல்லக் கையகன் றிட்ட தன்றே.
reading: Lamps, jewelled vessels and the bride's moon-like forehead chase the dark of the wedding night away, and the night slowly lets go.
event: The night passes in the glow of lamps and the bride's face.

tamil: காரிரு ளகன்ற போழ்திற் கமலினி யென்னுஞ் செல்விக்
கோருரு ளாழி வெய்யோ னருளிய வுதயஞ் சேர்ந்தான்
ஆரிரு ளனைய கூந்தற் கருளிய மனத்த னாகிப்
பேரரு ளாழி யானும் பெயர்ந்துபொன் மாடஞ் சேர்ந்தான்.
reading: As the dark clears, the sun, grantor of the rising to the lotus Kamalini, arrives, and the discus-bearing prince goes with a kind heart to the golden palace of his dark-haired love.
nuance: கமலினி is read as the lotus-bed that the sun favours and as a pun on the bride, not as a name; the prince as 'discus-bearer' is by epithet.
event: The sun rises and the prince goes to the bride's golden palace.

tamil: விஞ்சைய ருலகு மண்ணும் விண்ணுமொன் றாயதே போற்
செஞ்சுடர் மணியும் பொன்னு மாலையும் விரையுஞ் சேர்த்தி
அஞ்சுடர் வயிரப் பைம்பூ ணலைகடல் வண்ணன் றன்னாற்
பஞ்சுடை யல்குல் பாக வரசொடு பட்டங் கொண்டாள்.
reading: Gem, gold, garlands and perfume are gathered as the Vidyadhara world and the earth and the sky seem one, and the sea-hued prince has her crowned queen with him.
event: The sea-coloured prince crowns his bride queen beside him in a rich ceremony.

tamil: தேவிதன் றாதைக் கேற்ற பெருஞ்சிறப் பியற்றிச் செல்வன்
வேய்விரி வெள்ளிக் குன்றின் விஞ்சைய ருலக மெல்லாம்
ஓவில புகழி னானுக் குடன்கொடுத் துரிமை யோடும்
பூவிரி யுருவத் தாரான் பின்சென்று விடுத்துப் போந்தான்.
reading: He honours the queen's father with a great gift, hands him the whole Vidyadhara realm on the silver mountain with its rights, and walks behind to send him off.
nuance: The gift is a restoration of rule over Vidyadharas: the verse treats it as honour, not as a conquest being consolidated.
event: The prince gives his father-in-law the Vidyadhara kingdom and sees him off.

tamil: தெவ்வரங் கின்மை யாலுந் திசையினில் வணக்கற் பால
வவ்வழி யின்மை யாலு மருமணி வண்ண னாங்கு
reading: With no enemy left, no direction left to subdue, a wife, the earth and Fortune, the gem-hued prince becomes intoxicated with joy.
nuance: செருக்கிய களியன் (an elated, intoxicated one) uses a word that elsewhere can blame pride; here the poet does not.
event: The prince, with no rival left, is filled with the pleasure of his fortune.

reading: Two great treasures, guardians of the quarters, fall together at his feet, and the king, seeing the shining jewels, sinks into a sea of wealth.
nuance: The 'two treasures' (நிதி இரண்டு) are read as the nidhis of Jain and Hindu tradition; the verse names no number beyond two.
event: The two great treasures arrive at the king's feet and he is overwhelmed by wealth.

reading: In the golden city of Vamana of the lotus feet, a festival and sacrifice fills the fertile city with delight.
nuance: வேள்வி (sacrifice) is a Vedic word in a Jain work; whether it means a ritual or only a feast is not shown, and வாமன் is read as the king by epithet.
event: The festival and sacrifice celebrate the king's fortune in the city.

title: சுயம்வரச் சருக்கம் 1555-1578 (1/12)
theme: Opens the Swayamvara sarukkam: Tivittan after his victory, with the world at his feet, gives himself to pleasure; his chief queen asks to see the parijata tree wed to the Kamavalli creeper; and the brahmin jester Madhavan feigns a belly full of sweets, boasts of winning gifts in debate, and runs after fallen fruit in the grove.
source_issues: Verses 1555-1558, 1562-1565 and 1569 were printed in eight half-lines and repaired into four lines by the build; read as four.
1560 lines 3-4 and 1577 line 1 are hard to construe; the readings are marked uncertain.
1563 has the plural என்றார் where 1564 implies the maid (என்றவள்) spoke.

cast.role: Tivittan, called the dark gem-hued lord, the king
the gods who guard the quarters
the sixteen thousand kings who bow
the Vidyadhara kings who bow
the sixteen thousand kings' daughters, his wives
the king's chief queen, named only by her rank
the queen's maid who carries the message
the brahmin jester, named Madhavan, the king's companion

tamil: தேவரு மனிதர் தாமுஞ் செறிகழல் விஞ்சை யாரு
மேவருந் தகைய செல்வம் விருந்துபட் டனக டோற்ற
மாவர சழித்த செங்கண் மணிவண்ணன் மகிழ்ந்த காலைத்
தாவருஞ் செல்வ மொன்று தலைவந்த துரைக்க லுற்றேன்.
reading: The poet opens the new sarukkam, saying that after the dark-hued lord had destroyed the great ruler and was glad, he will tell of a further wealth that came to him.
nuance: Tivittan is named only by his epithets here (மணிவண்ணன், the gem-hued one); the identification rests on the previous chapters. The first-person உரைக்கலுற்றேன் is the poet's own voice.
event: The poet announces that another great fortune came to Tivittan after his victory.

tamil: பானிலா நிறைவெண் டிங்கள் பனிக்கதிர் பரப்பி யாங்கு
மேனிலா விரியும் வெள்ளி வெண்குடை விசும்பு காப்பக்
கோனுலா வுலக மோம்ப நிறீஇயபின் குவளை வண்ணன்
மானுலா மடக்க ணோக்கின் மகளிர்தம் வலையிற் பட்டான்.
reading: After setting the world under a white umbrella like the full moon, the dark-lily-hued lord is caught in the net of deer-eyed women.
nuance: The verse runs from rule to snare in one sentence: the umbrella that guards the world is followed at once by a net that holds the ruler.
event: Having established his rule, Tivittan falls into the net of women's glances.

tamil: திருமணி நிழற்றுஞ் செம்பொ னெடுமுடி முகட்டோர் தெய்வக்
குருமணி யுமிழுஞ் சோதி குலவிய வொளிகொள் வட்டம்
புரிமணி யோத வேலிப் புதையிரு ளிரியல் செய்யக்
கருமணி வண்ணன் றானே கதிரவன் றொழிலும் பூண்டான்.
reading: The dark-gem-hued lord takes on the sun's work, for the light of the gems in his crown drives off the thick darkness.
event: Tivittan's crown-jewels light up the dark as the sun would.

tamil: தேங்கமழ் தெய்வச் செம்பொற் றாமரை சுரிவெண் சங்கம்
ஈங்கிவை நெதிக ளாக வேழர தனங்க ளெய்தி
ஆங்கமர் செல்வந் தன்னா லற்றைக்கன் றமர்ந்த மாதோ
ஓங்கின னுருவத் தாலும் வில்லெண்ப துயர்ந்த தோளான்.
reading: Having gained the lotus, the conch and the other treasures and the seven jewels, the lord stands tall in body, eighty bows in height, and in his wealth.
nuance: Only the lotus and the conch are named; the verse does not list the rest of the treasures, and the numbers (nine treasures, seven jewels) are the tradition's, not counted here.
event: Tivittan gains the treasures and jewels of his wealth and stands eighty bows tall.

tamil: தெய்வங்கள் செப்பி னீரெண் ணாயிரந் திசைநின் றோம்ப
னொய்தியல் விஞ்சை வேந்தர் நூற்றொரு பதின்மர் தாழக்
கையமை திகிரி யானைக் காமனே கலவிக் கின்றான்.
reading: Sixteen thousand gods guard him from the quarters, sixteen thousand kings and a hundred and ten Vidyadhara kings bow, and the discus-bearer takes his pleasure like Kama.
nuance: நூற்றொரு பதின்மர் is read as one hundred and ten. The verse sets the homage of all three realms beside a lover's ease and passes no judgement on either.
event: Gods guard and kings and Vidyadhara kings bow to Tivittan while he takes his pleasure.

tamil: அன்னவ ரமிழ்தச் செப்பே ரணிமுலைக் குவடு பாயப்
பின்னிய தாது மல்கப் பில்கிய தேம்பெய் மாரி
துன்னிய சுரும்பொ டேங்கத் துணருடை கின்ற வன்றே.
reading: The sixteen thousand kings' daughters, like peahens, stand with the pollen of the flowers and a honey-rain pouring over their breasts as bees hum around them.
nuance: Lines 3-4 are hard to construe (பில்கிய தேம்பெய் மாரி, துணருடை கின்ற); the reading holds the picture of women, pollen, honey and bees and no more.

tamil: அன்னண மியலு நாளு ளக்கிரத் தேவி தங்கோன்
பொன்னணி யுலகின் வந்த பூவிரி பாரி சாத
மன்னிய லரும்பு வைப்ப மற்றத னோடு சேர்த்திக்
கன்னிய காம வல்லிக் கடிவினை காண லுற்றாள்.
reading: One day the chief queen, seeing the parijata flower of the golden world put out buds, resolves to see the wedding of the tree and the young creeper called Kama.
nuance: The verse treats a rite of marrying two plants as a courtly occasion; the tree is said to have come from a heavenly world (பொன்னணி உலகின்).
event: The chief queen decides to see the parijata tree wed to the Kamavalli creeper.

tamil: சுரும்பிவர் சோலை வேலித் துணர்விரி பாரி சாதம்
அரும்பிய பருவச் செல்வ மடிகளுக் கறிவி யென்று
பெரும்பிணா வொருத்தி தன்னைப் பெய்வளை விடுத்த லோடும்
விரும்பினள் சென்று வேந்தற் கிறைஞ்சிவிண் ணப்பஞ் செய்தாள்.
reading: The queen sends a bangled maid to tell the lord of the parijata's budding, and the maid bows to the king and makes the petition.
event: The chief queen sends a maid to inform the king, and the maid petitions him.

tamil: அடிகண்முன் னடித்தி யாரா லங்கைநீர் குளிர வூட்டி
வடிவுகொ டளிர்கண் முற்றி மகனென வளர்க்கப் பட்ட
கடிகமழ் பாரி சாத மதனோடொர் காம வல்லிக்
கொடிமணம் புணர்க்க லுற்ற குறிப்பறி நீசென் றென்றார்.
reading: The message says that the parijata, raised like a son by the women with water from their palms, is to be wed to the Kamavalli creeper, and the king is asked to understand the wish.
nuance: The tree is spoken of as a son reared by the attendants, so the wedding is a family occasion; the next verse has the king repeat the word 'son'. The plural என்றார் may mean the queen's words are quoted by the maid.
event: The maid delivers the queen's request that the reared parijata be wed to the creeper.

tamil: என்றவண் மொழிந்த போழ்தி னிலங்கொளி முறுவ றோற்றி
நன்றது பெரிதி யாமு நங்கைதன் மகனைக் காண்டும்
என்றவ னருளக் கேட்டே யிளையவள் பெயர்ந்து போக
மின்றவழ் வேலி னாற்கு விதூடக னுழைய னானான்.
reading: The king smiles and says that he will see the lady's son, at which the maid goes and the jester becomes the king's companion.
nuance: 'The lady's son' is the parijata tree, so the king takes up the queen's way of speaking.
event: The king agrees to see the plant 'son', and the jester takes his place at the king's side.

tamil: காதுபெய் குழையுஞ் செம்பொற் சுருளையுங் கலந்து மின்னப்
போதலர் குஞ்சி யாங்கோர் பூந்துணர் வடத்தின் வீக்கி
ஓதிய மருங்கு றன்மே லொருகைவைத் தொருகை தன்னால்
மீதியல் வடகம் பற்றி வெண்ணகை நக்கு நின்றான்.
reading: A man stands laughing with ear-rings, a golden curl and a garland knotted into his hair, one hand on his waist and the other holding his garment.
nuance: He is not named until 1566 (அந்தணன்) and 1569 (மாதவன்); the identification follows 1564, which ends on the jester's arrival.
event: The jester takes his place in comic dress and laughs.

tamil: மூடிய புகழி னாற்கு முகிழ்நகை பயந்து காட்டுங்
கோடிய நிலையின் முன்னாற் குஞ்சித்த வடிவ னாகிப்
பாடிய சாதிப் பாடல் பாணியோ டிலயங் கொள்ள
reading: Bent low before the king of spotless fame, the brahmin dances to the rhythm of a song.
nuance: He is a brahmin, but a comic one; the poem gives him no Vedic learning in the verses that follow.
event: The brahmin jester dances in front of the king to entertain him.

reading: As the jester dances again and again with many beats, the long-crowned king laughs and calls it good.
event: The king laughs and praises the jester's dance.

reading: With his ear-rings slipping and his garment bunched about him, the jester puffs his belly out, rolls in the dust and groans.
event: The jester puffs out his belly, rolls in the dust and groans.

reading: Holding his belly, the man named Madhavan answers the king's question about his trouble by saying that it is full of many modakas, puffed up and swallowed.
nuance: மாதவன் elsewhere means a great ascetic; for the jester it is either his name or an irony, and the reading cannot settle which.
event: Asked what ails him, the jester says his belly is full of modakas.

reading: Asked when he ate so many modakas, he says he has eaten none; they are to be eaten at the festival in the queen's fragrant grove.
nuance: The joke turns on the time: his groaning is for a feast he has not yet eaten.
event: The jester says the sweets are still to come, so that his belly is swollen with greed only.

reading: The king laughs and asks what the trouble is, then says that no gift is given except to brahmins with Vedic tongues, and asks what he will do.
nuance: The king states the rule as a tease to a glutton who has shown no learning; the work does not take it as its own teaching, and the jester answers with a joke, not an argument, so it is `reported`.
event: The king tells the jester that gifts go only to Veda-learned brahmins.

reading: The jester says that he is skilled in debate, which can defeat the Veda-learned, and that he will get the gift that way; women have long known his merit.
nuance: A boast of skill, not a doctrine: the jester sets debate-skill against Vedic learning as a title to the king's gift.
event: The jester boasts that he can win the gift by beating the Vedic brahmins in debate.

reading: He explains his way of winning debate: he will beat those who aim to win by recitation, with his stick, until his word prevails.
nuance: The cudgel turns the idea of debate into a farce, so nothing of the debate's own arguments appears. The line 3 reading (தடியாலே) is not certain.
event: The jester says his method of debate is to beat the reciters with a stick.

reading: The king says 'good, let us see this debate', goes to the grove's wall gate with the guards, and enters the garden.
event: The king goes with the guards to the grove gate and enters.

reading: In the garden the jester in his mock dress runs about before the king and sees rich fruits fallen in heaps.
event: The jester sees ripe fruit lying fallen in the grove.

reading: At the sight of the fruit his mouth waters and his teeth run, and he runs to the king and says 'look, let us eat, let us eat'.
event: The jester runs to the king and urges him to eat the fallen fruit.

reading: A speaker, probably the king, says that if they are to pass this limit of the grove the other should come quickly, and then one of the two goes ahead singing loudly.
nuance: Neither the speaker of lines 1-3 nor the one who walks ahead is named; the line 1 wording is obscure and the roles are inferred from 1574-1576.
event: One of the pair urges the other to hurry on past the fruit and walks ahead singing.

reading: The grove is full of sandal, mango and other trees whose bunched flowers bow down and shower honey and pollen like rain.

title: சுயம்வரச் சருக்கம் 1579-1602 (2/12)
theme: In the grove, Tivittan and the jester walk past fruit, shade and flowers; the jester is afraid of dark, of thieves and of petals, the king teaches him the grove's blooms and cures, the jester jokes about the queen's foot and is struck by a flower, then flees from a spirit that proves to be his own shadow, before the queen arrives.
source_issues: 1583 is hard to construe; the guards (கருமுகத்தர்) are read as the grove's monkeys by 1584.
1587 சாலிகை is a rare word; the verse is read from the reply in 1588.
1594 ஏதிலாள் ஒருத்திக்கா is unclear; speaker and sense are uncertain.
1586 சால காண் is hard to construe.

cast.role: Tivittan, the king, called the sea-hued one
the brahmin jester Madhavan, the king's companion
the king's chief queen, named only by her rank
the maidens who attend the queen

reading: Seeing the ripe fruit on the grove's mango trees, with the madhavi creeper growing over them, the speaker says they will run and pick them.
nuance: The speaker is not named; the greed for fruit fits the jester of the previous chapter, but only the story so far says so.
event: The jester sees the ripe fruit and proposes to run and take it.

reading: Where bees swarm in the cool grove, fruit lies spilled on one side, and the dull-minded man who ran up to it grows angry.
nuance: மூடு கொண்ட மதியன் is taken as a gibe at the jester; the Tamil does not name him.
event: The jester, running to the fallen fruit, finds it spoiled by bees and is angered.

reading: Speaking to the lord, the jester says that this grove, which even the sun does not think to enter, has not the least guard.
event: The jester tells the king the grove is unguarded.

reading: The spear-bearing king answers that many warriors guard the golden wall, so he asks how the grove can be said to lack guards.
event: The king denies that the grove is unguarded and says warriors keep the wall.

reading: The speaker says that the guards of the rare fruit are the fierce-eyed, black-faced ones who shake the fruit down and come, so the grove is guarded after its own kind.
nuance: The black-faced, fierce-eyed guards look like the monkeys that 1584 names; the verse itself does not say so, and the lines are hard to construe.
event: The king explains who guards the fruit.

reading: As a langur of the grove shows its tricks, the jester says that all of them are thieves, so they should go on to the queen's grove.
nuance: The joke turns on the king's own claim of guards (1582-1583): the guards are the thieves.
event: The jester calls the grove's monkeys thieves and proposes that they move to the queen's grove.

reading: The sea-hued king hears the jester's remark that thieves are many, with a laugh hidden in his own words, and the jester, shrinking, looks to both sides and walks close to him.
nuance: Who is ashamed (வெள்கி) is not fixed by the verse; it is read here as the jester.
event: The king laughs inwardly at the jester's remark, and the frightened jester walks close beside him.

reading: In the tamala avenue, where hanging shoots shade the path, the jester takes the shade for darkness and is afraid, and the garlanded king removes his fear.
nuance: The quoted words சால காண் are hard to construe; the reading follows the sentence's frame.
event: The jester takes shade for darkness and trembles; the king calms him.

reading: The jester, seeing fallen petals at the foot of a bakula tree, asks the sea-hued king in fear whether the grove too will begin a war.
nuance: The word சாலிகை is rare; the sense of the question is taken from the reply in 1588, which says there is no war here.
event: Frightened, the jester asks if fallen petals mean a fight is starting.

reading: The king tells him not to fear, since there is no battle here, and says the bakula's longing is cured when women's coral mouths spill the five-taste liquor on it.
nuance: The verse gives the bakula a longing (வயவு நோய்), cured by the women's mouth-wine; it treats the tree as a lover, with no claim beyond the poem's own image.
event: The king explains that the bakula blooms when women pour liquor on it.

reading: Calling the jester a man of great learning, the king explains that bees do not rise from the flowers' scent but have swarmed at the foot of the tree.
nuance: ஓங்கிய கேள்வியாய் is likely ironic, since the king is teaching the jester.
event: The king explains why the bees gather at the tree's foot.

reading: The king also tells him plainly that the jasmine rising among thorny stems has petals shaped like blood and will open on its own day.
event: The king explains the jasmine to the jester.

reading: The jester asks the banner-armed king what the asoka is, which bears fresh shoots at its foot, when other branches carry them at the tip.
event: The jester asks about the asoka's shoots at its foot.

reading: The king shows him that these are no leaves but the lac stains of dancing women's feet, laid there to cure the tree's longing.
event: The king explains that the red at the foot is women's lac-footprints.

reading: The jester teases that when the dark-eyed queen puts her small foot to the king's head, he blooms at once, so the asoka's way is his.
nuance: The joke reverses the 'longing' of 1588-1592: the lord of sixteen thousand wives is the one cured by his wife's foot.
event: The jester jokes that the king, like the asoka, blooms at the queen's foot.

reading: After the jester has spoken, the king strikes him with a flower, and the jester says he will tell the queen of the wrong done him for the sake of a stranger.
nuance: The grammar of ஏதிலாள் ஒருத்திக்கா is unclear; the sense is read as the jester's complaint that he is struck for the king's own failing.
event: The king strikes the jester with a flower, and the jester threatens to tell the queen.

reading: The king takes his hand, says he will do nothing like it again, and climbs a gem-set rock platform.
event: The king seizes the jester's hand, promises not to repeat the blow, and goes up on the rock seat.

reading: The jester, who sits beside him on the bright stone, looks around, is afraid, and with trembling body and hair on end steps back.
event: The jester, seated on the stone, is seized by fear and draws back.

reading: Asked what he has seen, the brahmin cries out that a spirit lives in this place which strikes and eats, so they must leave quickly.
nuance: The brahmin's words are a report of his fear, not a doctrinal claim; the story soon shows the spirit to be his own shadow.
event: The jester answers the king's question by claiming that a spirit lives in the stone and eats those who stay.

reading: Asked for its form, the jester describes it: a golden ear-leaf, bright gem earrings, ears and eyes rolling, a hand gesture, and a swollen belly.
nuance: Every feature he lists is a feature of a man with ear-ornaments, which sets up the king's answer in 1599.
event: The jester describes the spirit he thinks he has seen.

reading: With a quiet laugh the bright-jewelled king says that it is not his own shadow but the jester's, so let it stand, since his shadow goes with him and cannot be seen inside rock.
nuance: The king's words are cryptic in the first lines; the reading follows the next verse, where the jester is told to see his own deeds in the shadow.
event: The king laughs and begins to show the jester that the spirit is his own shadow.

reading: The jester is told to look at the shadow and see his own acts in it; he bows, sees it doing what he does, understands, and sits quietly in the cool shade.
nuance: The jester is called இலங்கு நூலினான், the one with the shining thread or learning: the learned brahmin is cured by looking.
event: The king makes the jester watch his shadow copy him, and the jester's fear ends.

reading: The king says that while the queen is on her way they will sit on this gem stone and look at the beauty of the grove, and the two sit contentedly.
event: The king proposes that they wait on the stone, and the two sit down.

reading: With her girdle ringing and her anklets sounding, the queen comes into the grove like a swan, ringed by maidens and guards.
event: The chief queen arrives at the grove with her maidens and guards.

title: சுயம்வரச் சருக்கம் 1603-1626 (3/12)
theme: The queen overhears the king praise a stranger's footprint, storms out and is won back by the king's bow and embrace; the jester is hunted down, bound in garlands and let loose to sing yamaka songs about fruit; the couple then begin the wedding of the parijata and the Kama creeper and the king is caught again in women's glances.
source_issues: Verse 1624 was printed in eight half-lines and repaired into four lines by the build; read as four.
1618-1620 are yamaka songs in a short metre whose last foot repeats the first; the sense is thin and marked uncertain.
The woman of 1603 and the footprint of 1606-1607 follow chapter 69 (1578-1602), which is not yet marked; her identity is read from 1607.

cast.role: Tivittan, called the gem-hued lord, the king
the king's chief queen, named only by her rank
the brahmin jester Madhavan, the king's companion
the Vidyadhara's daughter whose footprint is read
the queen's attendants who fetch Madhavan
the king's other queens
the women of the queen's following

reading: A woman, hidden by her magic craft in a fragrant grove and longing for play, stands in worship like a peahen.
nuance: The woman is not named in the verse; she is read as the Vidyadhara maiden of the next verses (விஞ்சையன் மடந்தை, 1607) and the verse itself does not say whom she worships.
event: A woman hidden in the grove by magic stands in worship.

reading: The rain-hued king sits at ease on a soft couch inside the glow of his gem-circle while Madhavan keeps him amused.
nuance: மருட்ட is read as 'amuse, bewilder'; the verse does not say with what Madhavan holds the king.
event: Tivittan sits on a soft couch with Madhavan beguiling him.

reading: As a soft-fingered woman with muffled anklets draws near, the king, thrown off, puts one nectar-sweet question to the brahmin.
nuance: The grammar leaves open who asks and who is asked; the next verse gives the question in the king's voice, so he is read as the asker.
event: The woman approaches and the bewildered king questions the brahmin.

reading: The king asks whether the one whose red-dyed footprint is under the asoka is of the earth or of the great mountain.
nuance: The king asks about her from her footprint alone, before he has seen her; this is what the queen overhears in 1608.

reading: The truthful brahmin reads the red, round-fingered, fleshy footprint and says she is a Vidyadhara's daughter, fit for the world's lord.
nuance: The speaker is the one questioned in 1605, called அறிவன் here; his reading from the foot is what sets off the queen's anger.
event: Madhavan names her a Vidyadhara maiden from her footprint.

reading: At his word the queen's lily-dark eyes redden, she breaks into sweat, and burning with anger she steps out in front of the king.
nuance: The scene turns on the verse before: praise given to a stranger's foot is what she takes as the wrong.
event: The queen, who had overheard, steps forward in anger.

reading: Madhavan, shaking, slips away into the garden, and the king, forgetting the speech meant to answer her, stands asking what harm will now follow.
nuance: The jester who read the footprint is the first to flee; the king is left to face the queen alone.
event: Madhavan hides in the grove and the king stands at a loss.

reading: The king pleads that he is no wrongdoer, calling her king's daughter and sweeter than nectar, but with her brows knitted she grows angrier.
event: The king tries to soothe her and she grows more angry.

reading: The queen says she will go to her own palace and he may play with that woman; the king rises and lays his crown on her small feet.
nuance: The great crown that all kings bow to is here laid at his own wife's feet; the bow ends the quarrel's first round and the next verse is his speech while bowing.
event: The queen turns to leave and the king lays his crown at her feet.

reading: As the crowned head bows, the king tells her she has learned much craft, and asks her to hear out any fault of his and give judgement.
nuance: கைதவம் is read as the queen's feigned anger, said in jest; the sense is a little uncertain.
event: The king, bowing, asks her to judge whether he is at fault.

reading: She tells her people that the king has done no wrong and orders them to seek Madhavan and bring him; they find him in the grove and drag him back by his cloth.
nuance: The speaker of the order is not named; the queen is read as the speaker because the next verse shows her still giving commands.
event: Attendants hunt Madhavan down in the grove and bring him by his garment.

reading: With a smile on her gem-like mouth she looks at the cowering Madhavan and orders him tied with garlands and brought, then goes to the flowering garden.
nuance: Her anger turns into a game here: the penalty falls on the jester, in flowers, and not on her husband.
event: The queen smiles and has Madhavan bound with garlands.

reading: The king, delighted, folds the soft-voiced queen to his breast, the smile at her mouth shining, and says he has now received her grace.
event: The king embraces the queen in reconciliation.

reading: Pressing her in a close embrace as their garlands crush together, the king persuades her to give up her fault-finding, since Madhavan is faultless.
nuance: The king settles the matter by the embrace and by clearing his companion; he does not answer why he asked about the footprint.
event: The king embraces the queen and calms her anger.

reading: Freed of the garland bonds from his shoulders, Madhavan puts on a loving manner and sings many songs and dances many dances.
event: Madhavan, released, sings and dances for the couple.

reading: The jester's first song says that at the sight of fruits in the grove his heart runs, runs, and asks the garland-wearer whether it will gather together.
nuance: Each verse is a yamaka song in which the last foot repeats the first; the sound play is the point and the sense is slight. The addressee is feminine (கோதையாய்), so the queen.

reading: The second song says that at the sight of fruits in the mud his teeth water, and calls to the woman of the spreading garland.
nuance: A yamaka song again, in which the last foot repeats the first; the fruit lies in mud (சேறு), where the first song had it in the wood (காடு).

reading: The third song says that at the sight of long mango fruit his heart wants, wants, and addresses the golden-chested one.
nuance: The address here is masculine (மார்பினாய்), so the song turns from the queen to the king.

tamil: இன்னன பாடி யாட வீர்ங்கனி பலவுங் கூவி
முன்னவ னார வூட்டி முறுவலோ டமர்ந்த பின்னை
மன்னிய பாரி சாத மணமக னாக நாட்டிக்
கன்னியங் காம வல்லி கடிவினை தொடங்க லுற்றார்.
reading: After singing and dancing they call for many sweet fruits, feed the elder one until he is full, then set the parijata as bridegroom and begin the wedding rites of the maiden creeper.
nuance: The wedding of the tree and the creeper that the queen resolved on in 1561 is now carried out; the jester's hunger is fed first.
event: They feed the jester, set the parijata as bridegroom and start the wedding of the Kama creeper.

tamil: திருமணி நிழற்றுஞ் செம்பொற் றிலதமா முடியி னானுங்
அருமணி யரும்பித் தாழ்ந்த வந்தளிர்ப் பொதும்பர் சார்ந்தார்.
reading: The king in his gold crown and the queen with the long eyes enter a bower of gem-flowering shoots, with the parijata on its jewelled altar.
event: The king and queen enter the garden bower.

tamil: வரிவளை வயிரொ டேங்க வாரணி முரச மார்ப்பக்
திருவள ரலங்கன் மார்பிற் செங்கணான் றேவி மார்கள்
உருவளர் கொம்ப ரன்னா ளருளறிந் துழைய ரானார்.
reading: With conches sounding and drums beating through the golden grove, the king's queens, knowing the will of the branch-like one, become her attendants.
nuance: Whose will the queens learn (உருவளர் கொம்பரன்னாள்) is read as the chief queen's.
event: The other queens come to wait on the chief queen as the drums sound.

tamil: செங்கய லுருவ வாட்கட் டேவிதன் குறிப்பிற் சேர்ந்த
மங்கையர் வனப்பு நோக்கி மணிவண்ணன் மகிழ்ந்து மற்றப்
பொங்கிய விளமென் கொங்கை மகளிர்தம் புருவ வில்லால்
அங்கய னெடுங்க ணென்னும் பகழியா லழுத்தப் பட்டான்.
reading: Seeing the beauty of the women who have joined the queen, the dark-hued king is pleased, and the arrows of their long eyes pierce him, bent with the bows of their brows.
nuance: The poet says the king 'was pressed' by the arrows, as in the net of 1556; the pleasure in women's eyes that the queen's anger was about is fully back.
event: The women's glances pierce the pleased king.

tamil: குடங்கையி னகன்று நீண்டு குவளையின் பிணையல் செற்று
மடங்களி மதர்வைச் செங்கண் மான்பிணை மருட்டி மையாற்
புடங்கலந் திருள்பட் டுள்ளாற் செவ்வரி பரந்த வாட்கண்
இடங்கழி மகளிர் சூழ விந்திர னிருந்த தொத்தான்.
reading: Ringed by women whose red-streaked eyes outdo the deer's and press into the dark of the kohl, the king sits like Indra.
nuance: The simile gives the king the place of Indra among heavenly women; it is praise of his pleasure, not a judgement of it.

tamil: ஆங்கவ ரோடு மற்ற வணிபொழிற் கரச னாய
பாங்கமை பாரி சாதம் பருவஞ்செய் பொலிவு நோக்கி
ஈங்கிவற் கிசைந்த கோல மினிதினி னியற்று கென்றான்
ஓங்கிய வுருவத் தார்மே லொளிநிலா வுமிழும் பூணான்.
reading: Looking at the parijata's season-wrought splendour in the grove, the king in his shining ornaments tells his people to dress the pair in fitting finery.
nuance: The command begins the wedding adornments of the tree and creeper whose rites were opened in 1621.
event: The king orders the plant bridal pair to be decked.

title: சுயம்வரச் சருக்கம் 1627-1650 (4/12)
theme: Opens the garden sport after the plants' wedding: the groves are dressed, the queens marry the parijata to the Kama creeper, the king hides by art among his women with Madhavan, and the women, sent out by the chief queen, play in leaves and flowers, paint his portrait, sing his fame and complain of their delicacy, until they reach the artificial hill, where guards post watch and the echo mocks them.
source_issues: Verses 1627-1634, 1636-1642 and 1631 were printed in eight half-lines and repaired into four lines by the build; read as four. 1631 line 1 had a pulli removed after a vowel sign, and so did 1640 line 7.
1633 lines 3-4 print மரவம்பூம் and குரவம்பூங் with an extra nasal, and 1645 line 4 (குலகறிவோ) is hard to construe; those readings are marked uncertain or hedged.
1644 ends in தாழ்ந்த without a finite verb; read here as a participle completing the sentence.

cast.role: Tivittan, the dark gem-hued lord, the king
the king's wives, the sixteen thousand kings' daughters
the king's chief queen
the brahmin jester Madhavan, the king's companion
the grove, given speech and acts in 1644 and 1645
the chamberlains and old guards who search and guard the grove
the artificial hill, whose echo answers in 1649-1650

tamil: எந்திர மிழிந்த தாரை யருவிநீ ரினிதி னாட்டிக்
கந்தனெத் திரண்ட திண்டோட் கனகசா லங்கள் காட்டிப்
பைந்தழைப் பொழிலுக் கெல்லா மரசெனப் பட்டஞ் சேர்த்தி
அந்தளிர்க் கொம்பர் தோறு மணிபல வணிந்தா ரன்றே.
reading: The grove is made ready: fountains pour from engines like waterfalls, golden frames stand about, every green grove is given a king's crown, and jewels are hung on each tender-leaved branch.
nuance: The verse crowns the groves as kings (line 3), so the garden is made a court before the women of the king's court take it in 1643. The second line is hard to construe: கந்தனெத் may stand for a post-like shape, and the sense of கனகசாலங்கள் (golden frames or halls) is not fixed.
event: Unnamed workers dress the garden with fountains, golden frames and jewels for the festival.

tamil: கன்னியங் காம வல்லிக் கனங்குழை மடந்தை தன்னை
மன்னவன் றேவி மார்கண் மணவினைக் கோலஞ் செய்து
பின்னத னோடு சேர்த்திப் பெருகிய களிய ரானார்
இன்னகைப் புதல்வர் செல்வம் யாவரே யினிதென் னாதார்.
reading: The king's queens dress the young creeper Kama in bridal finery, join her to the tree, and grow glad, for who would not call the wealth of sweet-smiling sons sweet?
nuance: The tree was called a son raised by the women's hands (1563), so the closing question turns the wedding of two plants into a parent's joy in a child; the verse does not say the joy rests on the child's merit.
event: The queens finish the wedding of the parijata and the Kamavalli creeper and rejoice.

tamil: மாதரார் மனத்தி னுள்ளும் மணிவண்ண னினைப்பி னுள்ளுங்
காதலுஞ் செறிந்த தாகக் காமனு முழைய னாகப்
போதலர் பருவச் சோலைப் பொழினல நுகரும் போழ்தில்
ஓதநீர் வண்ண னங்கோ ருபாயத்தா லொளிக்க லுற்றான்.
reading: While the women enjoy the grove in its flowering season, with love thick in their minds and in the dark-hued lord's, and Kama at his side, the lord hides himself by a stratagem.
event: Tivittan hides by a ruse while the queens enjoy the grove.

tamil: பொன்னவிர் குழையி னாரைப் பொழில்விளை யாட லேவி
மன்னவன் மதலை மாட வளநக ரணுகு வான்போற்
றன்னைமெய் மறைத்தோர் விஞ்சை தாழிரு ளெழினி யாகப்
பின்னைமா தவனுந் தானும் பிணையவ ருழைய னானான்.
reading: Having kept the women playing in the grove, the king's son hides himself by an art that makes the dark a curtain, and he and Madhavan are then close beside the women.
nuance: The verse does not say who sent the women to play; 1631 shows the chief queen sending others, so the hiding and the queen's answer are two halves of one game.
event: Using a magic art that makes darkness a screen, Tivittan and Madhavan hide near the women.

tamil: மன்னவன் மறைந்த தெண்ணி மாபெருந் தேவி மற்றப்
பொன்னவிர் கொடியன் னாரைப் பொழில்விளை யாட லேவக்
கன்னியங் கோலஞ் செய்து கதிர்மணிக் கலங்க டாங்கி
இன்னகை மழலை தோற்றி யிளையவ ரினைய ரானார்.
reading: Guessing that the king has hidden, the great queen sends the other golden-vine women to play in the grove, and they dress as girls with bright jewels, sweet smiles and lisping speech.
event: The chief queen, guessing Tivittan is hidden, sends more women to play and they act like children.

tamil: அம்பொன்செய் கலாப வல்கு லந்தழை புனைந்த வஞ்சிக்
கொம்பஞ்சு மருங்கு னோவக் குவிமுலை முறிகொண் டப்பிச்
செம்பொன்செய் சுருளை மின்னச் செவிமிசைத் தளிர்கள் சேர்த்திக்
கம்பஞ்செய் களிற்றி னான்றன் கண்களைக் களிப்பித் திட்டார்.
reading: Wearing gold girdles and skirts of leaves, with sprouts bound on the breasts and tender shoots at the ears, the women delight the eyes of the lord of the trembling elephant.
nuance: The dress is made of the grove itself, so the women become part of what they play in; the king who is looking is the one who hid in 1629-1630.
event: The women dress in leaves and gold to please the king's eyes.

tamil: விரவம்பூந் தளிரும் போது மிடைந்தன மிலைச்சு வாரும்
அரவம்பூஞ் சிலம்பு செய்ய வந்தளிர் முறிகொய் வாரும்
மரவம்பூம் கவரி யேந்தி மணிவண்டு மருங்கு சேர்த்திக்
குரவம்பூங் பாவை கொண்டு குழவியோ லுறுத்து வாரும்.
reading: Some set tender leaves and flowers in their hair, some pluck sprouts while their anklets ring, some hold chowries of flowers with bees beside them, and some hush a flower doll like a child.
event: Women play at dressing and at nursing flower dolls in the grove.

tamil: பாவையும் விலங்கு சாதிப் படிமமும் பறப்பை தாமுங்
கோவையு முகத்து மாக்கிக் குலவிய விதழ தாக
ஓவியர் புனைந்த போலு மொளிமலர்ப் பிணையன் மாலை
தேவியர் மருளச் செய்து சிகழிகை சேர்த்து வாரும்.
reading: Some make dolls, beasts, birds and faces out of flowers, with petals laid as if painters had drawn them, so that the queens marvel, and then bind these into their hair.
event: Women weave flower figures and garlands so fine that the queens marvel.

tamil: சிகரமா யிலங்கு சென்னித் தென்மலைச் சாந்து மூழ்கிப்
பகருமா மணிவண் டோவாப் பணைமுலைப் பாரந் தாங்கித்
தகரவார் குழல்பின் றாழத் தாழ்குழை திருவில் வீச
மகரயா ழெழுவி மன்னன் வண்புகழ் பாடு வாரும்.
reading: Bathed in sandal of the southern hill, bees hovering, hair trailing behind and ear-pendants flashing like rainbows, some play makara lutes and sing the king's rich fame.
nuance: They sing his fame while he is hidden among them, so the praise is addressed to a man who may be listening.
event: Some women play lutes and sing the king's fame.

tamil: அருமலர்த் தழையும் போது மடியுறை யாக வேந்தித்
திருமலர்ப் பாவை யன்ன தேவியைச் செவ்வி காண்பார்
உருமல ரிழைத்த பாவை யொளிமண நயந்து மாதோ
குருமலர்க் கொம்பி னொல்கிக் குரவையின் மயங்கு வாரும்.
reading: Some, carrying leaves and flowers in their laps, wait for the lotus-goddess-like queen to be in the mood to be seen; others, longing for the wedding of the flower doll, bend like shoots and sway in the kuravai dance.
event: Women bring flower gifts to the chief queen and join in the kuravai dance.

tamil: வட்டிகைப் பலகை தன்மேன் மணிவண்ணன் வடிவு தீட்டி
ஒட்டிய வடிவிற் றம்மை யூடலோ டிருப்பக் கீறித்
திட்டமிட் டுருவ நுண்ணூற் றுகிலிகை தெளிர்ப்ப வாங்கிப்
பட்டமுங் குழையுந் தோடும் பையவே கனிவிப் பாரும்.
reading: Some paint the gem-hued lord on a board and draw themselves beside him in a lovers' sulk, drawing sure lines with a fine brush and softening his crown and ear-rings.
nuance: The sulk is painted, not spoken: the women set the quarrel of love in a picture for a man who is hiding nearby.
event: Women paint Tivittan's portrait and themselves sulking at him.

tamil: மாம்பொழின் மருங்கு சூழ்ந்த மணிச்சிலா தலத்து மேலாற்
காம்பழி பணைமென் றோண்மேற் கருங்குழ றுவண்டு வீழப்
பூம்பொழில் விளங்கத் தோன்றும் பொன்னிதழ் மறிந்து நோக்கித்
தேம்பொழி செய்யு ளின்பஞ் செவிமுதற் சேர்த்து வாரும்.
