reading: Some sit on a jewelled stone slab by the mango grove, hair spilling over their bamboo-like shoulders, and look back at the sweet-dripping verse they gather to the ear.
nuance: This is the one verse of the run that makes poetry the play; the sense of the last two lines turns on reading செய்யுள் as the verse they hear or recite.
event: Women sit on a stone slab and enjoy verse.

tamil: கோதையுங் குழைவின் பட்டின் கொய்சகத் தலையுந் தாழ
மாதர்வண் டொருங்கு பேர மழையிடை நுடங்கு மின்போற்
போதலர் பொதும்பிற் றாழ்ந்த பொன்னெழி லூச றன்மேல்
ஓதநீர் வண்ணற் பாடி நூழிலூ ழியங்கு வாரும்.
reading: Some, garlands and hair-ends hanging and veils swaying, sing of the sea-hued lord as they swing to and fro on a golden swing in the bower, like lightning in a cloud.
event: Women sing of Tivittan while swinging.

tamil: கள்ளுமிழ்ந் துயிர்க்குஞ் சோலைக் கனமடற் குமரி வாழை
உள்ளெழு சுருளை வாங்கி யொளியுகிர் நுதியி னூன்றிப்
புள்ளெழு தடமும் போர்மான் றொழுதியு மிதுன மாய
ஒள்ளெழி லுருவுங் கிள்ளி யுழையவர்க் கருளு வாரும்.
reading: Some pull the inner curled leaf from a young plantain and scratch with bright nail-tips a lake with birds, herds of fighting deer and loving pairs, then give them to the women beside them.
nuance: The pairs (மிதுனம்) scratched into the leaf echo the portrait of the lovers' sulk in 1637: the women picture couples while waiting for the king.
event: Women scratch pictures into plantain leaves and pass them to each other.

tamil: மயிலுடை யாடல் கண்டு மகிழ்ந்துமெய்ம் மயங்கி நிற்பார்
குயிலொடு மாறு கொள்வார் குழைமுகஞ் சுடரக் கோட்டிக்
கயிலொடு குழல்பின் றாழக் கண்டுநீர் கொண்மி னென்றாங்
கயிலுடைப் பகழி வாட்க ணங்கையின் மறைத்து நிற்பார்.
reading: Some, delighted by the peacock's dance, sway with it; some rival the koel; some, with their hair behind, hide their arrow-keen eyes behind a hand as they say something to be taken up.
nuance: The third line is hard to place: whether கண்டு நீர் கொண்மின் is a call to look or to take is not settled by the Tamil.
event: Women imitate the peacock and the koel, and some cover their eyes with a hand.

tamil: செழுமலர்த் தாது கொய்து மெல்விரல் சிவந்த வென்பார்
விழுமலர்த் துகள்வந் தூன்ற மெல்லடி மெலிந்த வென்பார்
கொழுமலர்ப் பிணைய றாங்கிக் கொடியிடை யொசிந்த வென்பார்
எழுமலர்த் தனைய தோளான் றேவிய ரினைய ரானார்.
reading: Some say their fingers reddened gathering pollen, others that dust of petals hurt their soft feet, others that a flower garland bent their slender waists, and so the queens of the flower-shouldered king became.
nuance: The women claim delicacy as a boast, the way a lover praises it; the king who is meant to hear is hidden in the grove.
event: The queens make playful complaints of their delicacy.

reading: The women's waists sway like creepers without touching them, their long glances run like jewel-bees, their feet and hands show like tender shoots, and so they conquer the scented flower-grove.
nuance: 1627 crowned the groves as kings; here the women take the crown by being more garden than the garden.
event: The women's beauty outdoes the grove.

reading: The flowers of the grove, bowing as they catch the women's body-fragrance, say they have no way to repay them and gather in clusters, bending with offerings.
nuance: A speech given to the grove, not to a person; the plants admit a debt and not a claim.
event: The grove's flowers bow to the women and offer themselves.

reading: The ashoka gives the women an ashoka, the red tilaka tree gives them tilaka, as if saying that they would serve those who came; the meaning of the last line, about the grove's knowing, is unclear.
nuance: The verse plays on the tree names as gifts: the ashoka is given as an ashoka and the tilaka as a forehead mark.
event: The ashoka and tilaka trees give the women their own sprigs.

reading: Silver-white boulders wrapped in fresh gold spathes, swaying golden coconuts and bird-filled gold plantains frame the artificial hill with clear gem waterfalls, which the women reach.
event: The women reach the artificial hill.

reading: The chamberlains and old guards search the jewelled caves, long thickets and cloud-sleeping groves, and the sweet-spoken ones then take the watch on every side.
nuance: The verse says nothing of finding anyone; the king has hidden himself by art (1630), so the search and the guard are around the only man the women expect.
event: Chamberlains and guards search the grove and then guard its approaches.

reading: Like peahens spreading through the grove, the dark-cloud-hued lord's beloved women enter the hill-slope grove, jewels rolling and girdles sounding.
event: The women enter the grove on the hill-slope, ornaments sounding.

reading: As the girdles at their waists ring, the hill's own girdle rings back, and as their golden anklets sound, a row of golden anklets answers exactly.
nuance: The answering 'girdle' belongs to the hill (வரை மேகலை); only an echo fits the verse, and 1650 confirms it.
event: The women's girdles and anklets are answered by an echo.

reading: The hill takes the women's jewelled lisping, as it was uttered, and answers it back, mimicking what they do and mocking them, in the fragrant grove of the red-eyed tall one.
nuance: The hill acts as a speaker of its own; the red-eyed tall one is the king of the opening (verse 2). The word அசதியாடின்று (made fun of) is read here as mockery in play.
event: The artificial hill echoes and mocks the women's talk.

title: சுயம்வரச் சருக்கம் 1651-1674 (5/12)
theme: The women play on the gem hill, dressing the stones as grass and flowers and singing the king's deeds; the king has a god take the form of a rutting elephant to frighten them, then comforts them, goes down at noon to the pool, and enters it with them, where the swirling water begins a water-fight.
source_issues: Verses 1663-1674 were printed in eight half-lines and repaired into four lines by the build; read as four. 1669 line 1 had a pulli removed after a vowel sign.
1657 line 3 ends புனக்கிளிக with a lost letter; 1670 line 4 has a doubled காட்டி and a doubtful போலக்காட்டி; those readings are marked uncertain.

cast.role: Tivittan, the dark gem-hued lord, the king
the king's wives and women
the king's chief queen
the god the king commands to become an elephant
the king's attendants at the pool

reading: The women of the court clear the gems that the stream has washed down the misty slope and, laying out streets, build a fine toy city.
nuance: The sense of சீலம் புனைவார் in line 3 is not fixed; read here as the women giving the play-city its fitting adornment.
event: The women build a toy city from the gems the stream brought down.

reading: Women call the emerald's cool rays tender grass, step on them gingerly, and, their small feet aching, sink softly onto a bed of flowers.
event: The women walk on gem-light as on grass, and rest on a flower bed.

reading: Seeing the fresh-leaved grove and saying it is like their lord, the women bathe in the gem waterfall with a fresh glow of love in their looks.
nuance: Line 3 makes the grove's beauty a likeness of the king; the women's love shapes how they see the place.
event: The women praise the grove as like their lord and bathe in the waterfall.

reading: Taking the cool moonstone, bright inside, for the moon, the women see the drops it throws as rain from a cloud and hide in the grove.
nuance: The verse is built on mistaking: stone for moon, drops for rain.
event: The women mistake moonstone drops for cloud rain and hide in the grove.

reading: The women stroke the ruby's red rays with their ring-bright fingers, calling them ashoka sprouts, and bend over them with a small smile.
event: The women take ruby rays for ashoka shoots and stroke them.

reading: Seeing a great shining ruby, the women think of it as kaya flowers fit for the hair; bees follow, and they cover their eyes and walk on.
nuance: Line 2 reads the gem as blossom and line 3 the women as ready to wear it; the last line's covered eyes is read as a play against the following bees.
event: The women take a ruby for kaya blossoms and hide their eyes from the bees.

reading: The king's women, in the guise of watchers of a ripe hill-field, call to the parrots there in sweet lisping speech and coax them to come.
nuance: Line 3 ends புனக்கிளிக and line 4 has மாயோன் மடந்தைமார்; the lost letter in line 3 is supplied as கிளிகளை, and 'the dark lord's women' is read as the king's women.
event: The women call the parrots of the hill-field and delight them.

reading: On the gem-set rocks of a gold hill covered with fresh leaves, some tender-bodied women gather in pleasant company.
event: Some women gather on the rocks of the hill.

reading: On the gold slab they set a coral for the pestle, pour in gems, lift the tusk, and, as the golden hill sounds, sing of the dark one in the rhythm of a pounding song.
nuance: The pounding song (அம்மனை வள்ளை) turns grain-work into play with gems; the dark one of line 4 is the king, as the next verses' refrain shows.
event: The women pound gems in play and sing of the dark lord.

reading: The song names the dark cloud-hued one's deeds: he lifted a bow, tore open the lion's mouth, struck down the rutting elephant Ayakkiriva, and held the white hill.
nuance: Verses 1660-1662 carry a refrain of the dark-hued one; the deeds named are of the song, and the verse does not tell them as events.
event: The women sing the king's heroic deeds.

reading: The song says he put the conch to his mouth and took the bow, saw the foe's head tremble in the war, and embraced the lotus-lady's gold body.
nuance: The song joins war (conch, bow, enemy's trembling) and love (the lotus-lady's body) as the one fame of the king.
event: The women sing the king's war and his embrace of the lotus-lady.

reading: The song says he is the wearer of the golden discus and long crown, who took the wealth and ornaments of enemies and enjoyed the pleasures of the trusted lady.
nuance: The same verse sets conquest and enjoyment side by side as his praise.
event: The women sing of his wealth, his crown and his love.

tamil: மடந்தையர் பாட வாங்கு மாபெருந் தேவி நிற்ப
அடைந்தவ ரோடு மாடு மார்வநீர் வெள்ளம் வாங்க
உடைந்தழி மனத்தன் வேந்த னுழையதோர் தெய்வங் கூவிப்
படந்தவா முகத்தோர் வேழ மாகெனப் பணித்து விட்டான்.
reading: While the women sing and the chief queen looks on, the king, his heart breaking at their joy in the others, calls a divine being near him and bids it become an elephant with a spread face-cloth.
nuance: The whole verse joins a grieving heart and a ruse; the stated reason in line 2 and 3 is that love's flood and his breaking mind move him, and the poem calls the king's heart both hurt and playful. The text of the verse is printed in eight half-lines and repaired.
event: The king, wishing to frighten the women, orders a god to take elephant form.

tamil: மைவரை யொன்று கோல மணிதயங் கருவி தாழ
ஐவனங் கலந்த சார லருகுவந் தணைவ தேபோற்
றெய்வமோர் வேழ மாகிச் செய்கடாந் திரண்டு வீழ
மைவரு நெடுங்க ணல்லார் நடுங்கவந் தணைந்த தன்றே.
reading: A god becomes an elephant like a dark mountain, with its rut flowing, and comes like a mountain nearing a millet field, so that the dark-eyed women tremble.
event: The god in elephant form approaches the women, who tremble.

tamil: கயில்கலந் திருண்டு தாழ்ந்த கருங்குழன் மருங்கு சோர
வெயில்கலந் திலங்குஞ் செம்பொன் மிடைமணிக் குழைவில் வீச
அயில்கலந் திலங்கு வேற்க ணையரி பிறழ வேட்டி
மயில்கலந் திரிந்த போல மடந்தையர் நடுங்கி னாரே.
reading: The women's dark hair slips about their sides, the rings in their ears swing, their spear-like eyes flicker, and they shake like peahens scattered by fear.
event: The women tremble before the elephant.

tamil: நாண்டனா னிறைந்த நங்கை நடுங்குபு நுடங்கி நோக்கி
யாண்டையா ரடிக ளென்னு மாயிடை யஞ்சல் பொன்னே
ஈண்டையே னென்னை பட்ட தென்றுசென் றணுகி னானால்
வேண்டிய விளைத்துக் கொள்ளும் விழுத்தவம் விளைத்து வந்தான்.
reading: A trembling woman looks about and cries for her lord's feet; he comes up, tells her not to fear, and says that he is here; he has done the great penance that brings whatever one wants.
nuance: The last line gives the king's power as the fruit of a past penance; it states a claim about tapas in a verse of love-play, and speaks of the king as the hero of the ruse, not as one who has renounced.
event: The king comes to the frightened woman and reassures her.

tamil: மலைமுக மதநல் யானை மற்றது மறித்து நங்கை
முலைமுக நெருங்கப் புல்லி முருகுவேய் கோதை சூட்டிக்
கலைமுகந் திருத்திக் காதிற் கனபொன்செய் சுருளை நீவி
இலைமுகங் கலந்த செம்பொற் கலங்களை யிலங்க வைத்தான்.
reading: Turning the rutting elephant back, the king embraces the woman, sets a fragrant garland on her, tidies her clothes, smooths the ear-roll and sets her gold ornaments in place.
event: The king drives off the elephant and comforts the woman.

tamil: மங்கையர் தம்மை யெல்லா மணிவண்ணன் மருட்டி மற்றிக்
கொங்கவிழ் குளிர்கொள் சோலைக் குன்றினின் றிழிந்த போது
வெங்கதிர் விரிந்த வெய்யோன் விசும்பிடை வெதும்ப வெம்பிச்
செங்கதிர்க் கூடங் குத்திச் செந்நடு வாக நின்றான்.
reading: After the dark-hued king has deceived all his women and comes down from the grove-hill, the sun stands at noon, burning the sky.
event: The king comes down the hill at noon, having deceived the women.

tamil: அணங்கனார் நுதலின் மேலி லரும்பிய வாரத் தெண்ணீர்
மணங்கம ழலங்கன் மார்பன் மனத்தினை வாங்க மற்றக்
கணங்குழை மடந்தை மாரைக் கடிபுன லாடல் காண்பான்
மணங்கொள்பூந் துணர்கொள் சோலை மண்டுநீர் வாவி சார்ந்தான்.
reading: Beads of sweat on the women's brows pull the king's heart, so he goes to the pool in the flowering grove to see them bathe.
event: The king goes to the pool to watch the women bathe.

tamil: சாந்துநீர் நிறைந்த வாவி தயங்குசெங் குவளை வாவி
பூந்துக ளவிழ்ந்த பொற்றா மரைமலர் புதைந்த வாவி
தேந்துண ரகன்ற தெண்ணீர்த் திருமணி யுருவ வாவி
வாய்ந்தவை போலக்காட்டி காட்டி யுழையவர் வணங்கி நின்றார்.
reading: The attendants show the king pools of sandal-water, red lilies, golden lotuses and clear gem-blue water, and then bow and stand aside.
nuance: Line 4 ends with a doubled காட்டி and the clause வாய்ந்தவை போல is hard to place; read as the attendants showing the pools.
event: The attendants point out the pools to the king.

tamil: அன்னவா றமைந்த தெண்ணீ ரலைபுன லாடும் போழ்தில்
இன்னவா றியற்று கென்றாங் குழையரை மறைய வேவிப்
பொன்னவாஞ் சுணங்கு போர்த்த புணர்முலை மகளி ரோடு
மன்னவாம் வயிரத் தோளான் வலஞ்சுழி வாவி புக்கான்.
reading: At the king's order that they hide, the attendants withdraw, and he enters the whirling pool with the women, whose gold-freckled breasts are pressed together.
event: The king sends the attendants away and enters the pool with the women.

tamil: மலங்குபாய் தயங்கு பொய்கை மணக்கல்வா யடுத்த செம்பொற்
கலங்கினா றிழிந்து கீழே கலந்துவந் தெழுந்த தெண்ணீர்
அலங்கலான் மடந்தை மார்த னரும்புணை யாக வீங்கி
வலங்குலாய்ச் சுழித்து வாய்த்த வாவி வாய் மடுத்த தன்றே.
reading: Water that comes down the gold channels from the gem stones fills the pool and swirls, and the women's floats lift on it.
nuance: The verse describes the pool's source and its swirling; the connection of the waters with the women's floats in line 3 is read loosely.
event: The pool fills and swirls as the women bathe.

tamil: அலைபுனல் பெருக லோடு மலைகடல் வண்ணன் றன்னை
மலைபுனை கொடியிற் புல்லி மடந்தையர் மயங்கு வாரும்
மிலைபுனை கோதை சோர விடுபுணை தழுவு வாரும்
கலைபுனை துகிலுந் தோடு மொழியப்போய்க் கரைகொள் வாரும்.
reading: As the water rises, some women cling to the sea-hued king like creepers to a hill, others seize a float and lose their garlands, and others lose their clothes and ear-ornaments and make for the shore.
event: The rising water scatters the women, who cling to the king or flee.

tamil: ஆர்புனல் சுழித்து வாங்க வனையரா யணிபொன் வாவி
நீர்புனை தடத்தி னுள்ளா னிலைகொண்டு நெடுங்கண் சேப்பத்
தார்புனை மார்பன் றன்மேற் றரங்கநீர் தயங்கத் தூவி
வார்புனை முலையி னல்லார் மயங்கமர் தொடங்கி னாரே.
reading: With the swirling water drawing round him, the king stands firm in the pool, his eyes reddened, and the women begin a water-fight, flinging water on his chest.
event: The king stands in the pool and the women start a water-fight against him.

title: சுயம்வரச் சருக்கம் 1675-1698 (6/12)
theme: Water-sport and the envoy: Tivittan's wives play against him in a garden pool, the play ends with drying, scenting and garlanding, and a Vidyadhara envoy flies down from the sky with a letter that begins to tell of a bride and her suitor.
source_issues: Verses 1675-1680, 1695-1698 were printed in eight half-lines and repaired into four lines by the build; read as four.
1677 line 2 is corrupt or hard (தரையாய்க் குறளுஞ் சிந்து மிதந்தன சில்ல சிந்தி) and line 4 ஓரையாய் is obscure.
1695 lines 1-3 are hard to construe and the speaker of the question is a reading.
1696 and 1697 leave unclear who reads the letter and who speaks.

cast.role: Tivittan, the dark-hued king, called by his colour
the kings' daughters who are his wives, who play in the water
attendants who open the pool's sluice
young attendants who tell the king the hour
the Vidyadhara who flies down with a letter
the woman of the queen's household who reads the letter

tamil: திரளிருஞ் சிவிறி வீக்கிச் செழுமழைத் தாரை பெய்வார்
மருளிரும் பிணையன் மாலைப் படைபல வழங்கிச் சூழ்வார்
சுருளிருந் தோடு வாங்கித் தோண்மிசை துளங்கி வீழ்ப்பார்
இருளிருங் குழலி னார்க ளிறைவன்மே லினைய ரானார்.
reading: The king's wives, dark-haired, fill their syringes and pour streams like rain, fling garlands in play and shake the ear-ornaments from their shoulders, so turning themselves against their lord in sport.
nuance: இறைவன்மேல் இனையர் ஆனார் says they became his foes in play; the poet uses the vocabulary of war for a bath, and the verses that follow keep it.
event: The wives begin a water battle against the king, spraying him and throwing garlands.

tamil: சாந்தெழு சிவிறித் தாரை சதுர்முக மாக வீக்கிப்
பாய்ந்தன பவழச் செங்கே ழங்கையான் முகந்த தெண்ணீர்
வேய்ந்தன திவலை யாகி விழுந்தன வேரி மாலை
நாந்தகக் கிழவன் பொய்யே நங்கைமார்க் குடைந்து நின்றான்.
reading: The jets of scented water, aimed four ways from the syringes, fall on the wives like drops of fine rain, and the lord of the Nandaka sword, though the sport is only feigned, gives way before the women.
nuance: Nandaka is the sword of Vishnu; calling Tivittan its lord keeps his godlike standing while he plays at losing. பொய்யே, 'only in pretence', is the poet's own word.
event: Tivittan feigns defeat before the wives' water-jets.

tamil: காரையார் வண்ணன் மாலைக் காற்படை யுடைந்த போழ்தில்
தரையாய்க் குறளுஞ் சிந்து மிதந்தன சில்ல சிந்தி
வேரியார் குவளை வேய்ந்த மெல்லிய லவர்க்குத் தோற்ற
ஒரையாய் முதலை யாகிக் கூன்மடை யொளித்த வன்றே.
reading: As the lord's line of foot-guards breaks in the play, the water-toys and floating things are scattered, and, losing to the lily-wreathed women, he is said to have hidden like a crocodile in the pond's bent sluice.
nuance: Line 2 (தரையாய்க் குறளுஞ் சிந்து மிதந்தன சில்ல சிந்தி) and the word ஓரையாய் in line 4 are obscure; the picture of a game lost and a hiding place is firm and the objects named are not.
event: Tivittan, beaten at the water-play, hides in the pond's sluice like a crocodile.

tamil: வென்றனம் வீரன் றன்னை வீக்குமின் சிவிறித் தாரை
சென்றெனச் சிறந்த காதற் றேவியர் திளைக்கும் போழ்தில்
ஒன்றிய வுழையர் கீழ்நீ ரோப்பறித் திடுத லோடு
நின்றகஞ் சுழிந்த தெண்ணீர் நெரேலென விழிந்த தன்றே.
reading: The queens cry that they have beaten the hero and tell one another to pour the spray on him; while they play, their attendants open the lower sluice and the still water of the pool runs out with a rush.
nuance: The words வென்றனம் வீரன் றன்னை வீக்குமின் are the queens' own cry; the draining of the pool is the poet's addition and shows the day's play ending.
event: The queens declare victory over Tivittan, and attendants let the pool's water drain.

tamil: மாலையுந் துகிலும் வார் வார்புன லொழுகும் போழ்தின்
ஆலையின் கரும்பி னின்சொ லணங்கனா ரவிழத் தத்தம்
கோலமென் றுகில்க டாங்கிக் குழைமுகஞ் சுடரக் கோட்டி
வேலைநீர் வண்ணன் முன்னர் நாணினான் மெலிவு சென்றார்.
reading: With garlands and cloth streaming water, the cane-sweet-voiced women loosen their dress, then draw their wet garments close and turn their shining faces aside, shy before the sea-hued lord.
nuance: Shyness comes only after the play is over and the cloth clings; the poet puts modesty at the end of the sport and not at its start.
event: The soaked queens gather their clinging garments and turn away shyly from Tivittan.

tamil: அருமணிக் கலாப வல்கு லவிழ்துகி லசைத்து மீட்டும்
திருமணி வண்ண னோடுந் தேவியர் திளைத்துத் தெண்ணீர்ப்
புரிமணிப் பொன்செய் வாவிப் புணைபுறந் தழுவிப் புக்கார்
கருமணி வண்டுந் தேனுங் கையுறக் கலந்த தன்றே.
reading: The queens tie up their jewelled girdles and loosened cloth, and with the gem-hued lord go down again into the golden pond, clinging to the floats at its side.
nuance: Line 4 has dark bees and honey joining the hand-clasped play; the bees stand for black eyes or hair mingling with the flowers.
event: Tivittan and the queens re-enter the pond with floats.

reading: Women play in the water, now diving with swelling breasts, now clinging to a float with soft young-leaf hands, now ducking until their red carp-like eyes redden, and the poet says the water-play bewildered them.
nuance: The verse is a series of three actions closed by மயங்கிற் றென்பவே, a hearsay close that keeps the poet at a distance from the scene.

reading: Red saffron from their feet, evening-red powder and the dark collyrium dissolved from their long eyes mix together in the pool, so that the water seems to have been made red and dark at once.
nuance: The water is described as the colour of what the women wash into it; nothing in the verse says it is stirred by the king.

reading: The saffron paste of the women's breasts, the scented powder shaken from their hair and the sandal on the red-eyed lord's chest all mingle, and the great pool turns to mud.
nuance: The turning of clear water into mud is meant as sign of the sport's abundance and not of spoiling; the poet makes no complaint.

reading: The women strike the water with their broad hips and with their breasts under fine down, and bend their slim waists, so that the waves of the pool seem to be joining them.

As the women press into the water with garlands trembling on their young breasts, the lotuses that rose sank, and when the girls came up from their dive the new brightness of their faces showed to the lotuses.
nuance: The conceit is that the lotuses show the girls' faces by contrast; the poet does not say they were outshone, only that the faces brought out something the flowers had not.

reading: The clear waves tossed by the women with bangled hands rise, and as the tired women step towards the jewelled bank the water follows a little way up on their small feet and falls back again.

When the hours of the day had passed, the young attendants bow at his flower-anklets and tell him the time, and the king, with the vine-like painted-lipped women around him, goes to the day-time palace in the grove.
event: Attendants tell Tivittan the time and he goes with his queens to the pleasure-house in the grove.

reading: The wives dry the water from their jewel-coloured bodies, put fine cloth on their hips, and with smoke of aloe in a crow-beak vessel they perfume and dry one another's damp hair.
nuance: It is not said whose body is dried; the grammar leaves open that the wives dry themselves or the lord. காகதுண்டம் (crow-beak) is a kind of aloe-wood.
event: The queens dry and dress after the water-play and scent their hair with incense.

reading: A garland is made of cool blue lilies, the dark-edged petals of the neythal, and the fragrant damanaka shoot, and it is received with joy.
nuance: No one is named as maker or wearer; whose garland it is, and who rejoiced, is not said.
event: A garland of lilies and damanaka is made and welcomed.

reading: The wives rub the golden mountain-hued sandal of the southern hills into their skin and sprinkle lotus pollen over it, and their soft breasts become a feast for the king's eyes.
nuance: விருந்து பட்டவே, 'became a feast', gives the breasts as what is offered to the lord; the poet's word fits a guest's treat and carries no blame.
event: The queens paint their breasts with sandal and lotus pollen.

reading: The young ones of beauty beyond counting come, bringing the cool bunches of kallaara lilies, the lily garlands they threw, and the shining lotuses, and embracing them.
nuance: Whether இளையர் are young attendants or the young queens themselves is not clear; the verse names no giver and no receiver of the flowers.

reading: The queens, with bunches of kallaara flower in their hands waved as fans, and lotus leaves held over them as umbrellas, appear like the lotus-seated goddess and her kind.
While the guardians of the quarters watch and the lord enjoys his sweet food, the girls stand around the destroyer of the great king, drinking him in with their dark eyes.
nuance: மாவரசு அழித்தவன் recalls the earlier victory over the great king (the sarukkam's opening); the poet holds the war and the harem side by side in a single phrase.

tamil: வஞ்சியங் கொம்ப னாரு மன்னனு மிருந்த போழ்தின்
விஞ்சைய னொருவன் றோன்றி விசும்பினா றிழிந்து வந்து
மஞ்சிவர் சோலை வாயில் வாயிலோன் வாயி லாக
அஞ்சன வண்ணன் செந்தா மரையடி வணங்கி னானே.
reading: As the king sits with the women, a Vidyadhara descends from the sky, enters the grove gate through the gatekeeper, and bows to the feet of the dark-hued lord.
event: A Vidyadhara arrives from the sky, is let in by the gatekeeper, and bows to Tivittan.

tamil: வந்தவன் வணங்க லோடு மாமனை நுவலி யென்னை
கந்தணை யானை வேந்தன் கழலடி செவ்வி யோவென்
றந்தமி லாழி யாள்வான் வினவலி னருளு மாறென்
றிந்திர னனைய நீராற் கிறைஞ்சலு மிருக்க வென்றான்.
reading: When the visitor bows, the ruler of the wheel-ruled earth asks after the visitor's uncle and the welfare of the king whose feet he serves, and bids him rise, and, because the visitor bows as to Indra, bids him sit.
nuance: Lines 1-3 are hard to construe: மாமனை நுவலி என்னை ... செவ்வியோ என்று can be read as Tivittan's question about the uncle, or the envoy's report of him; the reading follows the first.
event: Tivittan asks after the sender and tells the bowing Vidyadhara to sit.

tamil: உரிமையோ டிருந்த போழ்தி னுணர்த்துதற் குரித்தென் றெண்ணித்
திருமுகந் தொழுது காட்டத் தேவிதன் மருங்கு நின்ற
உரிமைகொ ளுழைய ருள்ளா ளொருத்திவா சித்து ணர்த்த
அருமுடி யொழிய வெல்லா வணிகளு மவனுக் கீந்தான்.
reading: When they have settled, the envoy shows the letter, bowing to it; an attendant of the queen's household reads it aloud, and the king gives the envoy every ornament he wears except his crown.
nuance: The gift comes before the sense of the message is told: the king rewards on seeing the letter, and the verse leaves the contents for the next verse. வாசித்து can mean 'reads' or 'discerns'; the reading takes it as read aloud.
event: The envoy presents a letter, an attendant reads it out, and Tivittan gives the envoy all his ornaments but the crown.

tamil: கனிவளர் கிளவி யாருங் கதிர்மணிக் கலங்கள் வாங்கிப்
பனிமதி விசும்பின் வந்தான் பால்வரப் பணித்த பின்னை
இனியிது பெயர்த்து நீயே யுரையென வெடுத்துக் கொண்டு
துனிவள ரிலங்கு வேலான் கழலடி தொழுது சொன்னான்.
reading: The queens take the jewelled vessels from the visitor who has come through the cool moonlit sky, and, bidden to go on, he takes the letter again, and, told to say it again himself, bows to the feet of the king of the bright spear and speaks.
nuance: The king's order இனியிது பெயர்த்து நீயே யுரை, 'now say this yourself, turned', makes the envoy answer in his own mouth what the paper holds; the verse does not say the paper's text was unfit.
event: Tivittan has the envoy restate the message, and the envoy bows and begins.

tamil: சுடர்மலைத் திருண்ட சோலைச் சுரேந்திர காந்த மென்னும்
வடமலை நகர மாளு மன்னவன் றேவி பெற்ற
தடமலர்ப் பெரிய வாட்கட் டையன்மற் றவளை யெங்கோன்
விடமலைத் திலங்கு செவ்வேல் வெய்யவன் பெயரன் வேட்டான்.
reading: The envoy begins: the king who rules the northern-ridge city of Surendrakanta has a daughter, broad-eyed and born of his queen, and the grandson of the fierce spear-bearing Veyyavan has asked for her in marriage.
nuance: He names the bride by her father's city and her mother, and the suitor by his grandfather; who the suitor is, and what he wants of Tivittan, is for the verses after this chapter. The speaker is known from 1697.
event: The envoy announces that a suitor has sought the daughter of the king of Surendrakanta.

title: சுயம்வரச் சருக்கம் 1699-1722 (7/12)
theme: Opens the night of Tivittan's household joy: after dismissing the Vidyadhara envoy he spends the night in love-play, ending with the queen, who sees the moon enter her mouth; he reads it as the coming of a son, and the sun and moon give the child form; the son is born, the city feasts, the rites, kin, gifts and praise follow, and the child is named Vijayan.
source_issues: Verses 1699 to 1709 are printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 lines by the tool.
1716 சிறைநகர் சீத்தன is a hard phrase; the reading of cleaned or emptied prisons is not fixed.
The queen is named only by her rank (தேவிகை); the earlier chapters' name for her is not in these verses.

cast.role: the Vidyadhara envoy who is sent away
Tivittan, the dark gem-hued lord, now a father
the sun, who sets and later takes the child's form
the moon, who rises, enters the queen's mouth and sets
the women of the palace who entangle the king
the queen who conceives, named only by her rank
the newborn son of Tivittan, called Vijayan at 1722, not to be mixed with the elder prince Vijayan
the plough-bearing elder brother of Tivittan, uncle of the child
the people of the city who feast and perform the rites
the kin, father, queens and relatives who gather and name the child
the brahmins, kings and elders who praise the child's parents

tamil: என்றவன் பெயர்த்துஞ் சொல்ல வின்பநீர் வெள்ள மூழ்கி
மின்றவ ழிலங்கும் வேலான் விஞ்சைய னவனைப் போக்கிச்
சென்றுதன் கோயில் சேர்ந்தான் செங்கதிர்த் திகிரி யானு
மன்றழல் சுருங்க முந்நீ ரலைகட லழுவம் பாய்ந்தான்.
reading: After the Vidyadhara has spoken again and been sent away, the lord returns to his palace as the sun plunges into the sea at evening.
nuance: The sun is named only by the epithet of the one holding the discus; the identification rests on the sinking into the sea in line 4.
event: Tivittan dismisses the Vidyadhara envoy and goes to his palace while the sun sets.

tamil: அழலவன் குளித்த பின்னை யணங்கிவ ரந்தி யென்னும்
மழலையங் கிளவிச் செவ்வாய் மடந்தையு மடைந்த போழ்தில்
குழலமர் கிளவி யார்தங் கூந்தலுட் குளித்து விம்மி
எழிலகி லாவி போர்ப்ப விருவிசும் பிருண்ட தன்றே.
reading: Dusk and the sweet-voiced young woman arrive together, and darkness spreads like the smoke of women's hair over the wide sky.
nuance: Evening is made a woman (அந்தி) entering with the night; the dark is likened to the hair of women, and the scene moves from the public court to the bedchamber.

tamil: விரவின பரவைப் பன்மிமீன் மிடைமணிக் கலாப மாக
மருவின பரவை யல்குன் மயங்கிருட் டுகிலை வாங்கிப்
புரிவணன் மதிய மென்பான் பொழிகதிர்த் தடக்கை நீட்டி
இரவெனு மடந்தை செல்வ நுகரிய வெழுந்து போந்தான்.
reading: The moon takes the night's dark cloth from her, as a lover takes the garment of a woman jewelled with stars, and rises to enjoy her wealth.
nuance: Moonrise is told as a man's undressing of a woman, preparing the poem's turn to Tivittan's own night.
event: The moon rises and draws off the garment of night.

tamil: ஏரணி விசும்பி னங்கே ழெழுநிலா விரிந்த போழ்தில்
சீரணி மணிவண் டார்க்குஞ் சிகழிகைப் பவழ வாயார்
காரணி வண்ண னென்னுங் கருங்களி வேழந் தன்னை
வாரணி யிளமென் கொங்கை வாரியுள் வளைத்துக் கொண்டார்.
reading: As the moon spreads its light, women with coral lips trap the dark-hued lord, likened to a rutting elephant, in the hollow between their breasts.
nuance: Tivittan is the 'dark-clouded' lord and also a mad elephant; the verse begins an elephant figure that runs to 1705.
event: The women of the palace draw Tivittan into love-play.

tamil: பங்கய முகத்து நல்லார் பவழவாய்க் கவளங் கொண்டு
பொங்கிய களிய தாகி மயங்கிய பொருவில் வேழம்
குங்குமப் பொடிநின் றாடிக் குவட்டிளங் கொங்கை யென்னும்
தங்கொளி மணிமுத் தேந்துந் தடத்திடை யிறைஞ்சிற் றன்றே.
reading: The elephant-lord, drunk on the mouthfuls of coral-lipped women, bows in the pool of their pearled breasts.
nuance: The elephant figure continues; the 'mouthful' is the kiss, in an image of an elephant being fed.
event: Tivittan sinks into the women's embrace and is intoxicated.

tamil: வேய்மரு ளுருவத் தோளார் வெம்முலைத் தடங்க ளென்னும்
பூமரு தடத்துட் டாழ்ந்து பொற்பொடி புதைய வாடிக்
காமரு காம மென்னுங் கருங்கயம் படிந்து சென்று
தேமரு குழலஞ் சாயற் றேவிகைப் பட்ட தன்றே.
reading: The elephant wallows in the pools of other women's breasts and bathes in the dark pool called desire, then comes to the chief queen.
nuance: The elephant moves from pool to pool and finally to one woman, the queen (தேவிகை, a term for a queen, not a given name). The closing 'came into her keeping' is the hinge of the sequence.
event: After the other women's embraces Tivittan comes to the queen.

tamil: காதலா லுரிமை பாங்கிற் கடிகமழ் காம வல்லித்
தாதலொந் ததர்ந்து சிந்தத் திளைத்தவத் தடக்கை வேழம்
மாதரா ளமிழ்தின் சாயற் றோட்டியால் வணக்கப் பட்டுப்
போதுலாம் புணர்மென் கொங்கைக் குவட்டிடைப் பூண்ட தன்றே.
reading: The great elephant is bent by the queen's goad of nectar-like grace, and settles on the hill of her breasts, bound there.
nuance: The goad (தோட்டி) is the woman's grace; love is a binding the elephant accepts, and the image makes the queen the one who governs the king.
event: The queen holds Tivittan fast in love.

tamil: செங்கயற் கண்ணி னாளுஞ் செல்வனுந் திளைத்துத் தீந்தேன்
பொங்கிய வமளி மேலாற் புணர்முலை நெருங்கப் புல்லித்
தங்கிய பொழுதிற் றாழ்ந்து தண்கதிர் மதியந் தானே
மங்கைதன் பவழச் செவ்வாய் மடுத்தக மடைந்த தன்றே.
reading: The red-lipped queen and her lord embrace on the honeyed bed, and the cool moon itself, sinking, enters the red mouth of the woman.
nuance: The moon entering the mouth is the poem's omen of conception, a motif that the narrator tells as a wonder of the bed, and the next verses show it read as a dream.
event: In union the queen sees the moon enter her mouth.

tamil: அடைந்தது மதிய மாக வாயிடை யரசன் றிண்டோள்
மிடைந்ததோ ணெகிழ விம்மி மெல்லியல் வெருவ லோடு
மடங்கலை யலைக்கு நீரான் மருட்டினன் வினவ மாதோ
வடந்தவ ழிளமென் கொங்கை மெல்லவே மிழற்றி னாளே.
reading: The moon having entered, the king's arms slacken; the frightened woman is asked in a voice that conquers lions, and whispers her tale.
nuance: The asker's voice is likened to a lion's roar softened to coax: the king's power is turned into gentleness at the bedside. The queen's own words are not given.
event: Tivittan questions the trembling queen, who tells him quietly what she saw.

tamil: வணங்கியிவ் வுலக மெல்லா மகிழ்ந்துகண் பருகு நீர்மை
அணங்கிவர் சிறுவன் வந்துன் அணிவயிற் றகத்துப் பட்டான்
கணங்குழை யஞ்ச லென்று கருமணி வண்ணன் றேற்றப்
பணங்குலாம் பரவை யல்குற் பாவையும் பரிவு தீர்ந்தாள்.
reading: The dark-gem lord comforts her: a child before whom the whole world will bow and rejoice has come into your womb, so do not fear.
nuance: The king himself reads the dream, not an astrologer as in the earlier dream of 106 to 111. The child is already spoken of as a son the world will worship.
event: Tivittan interprets the queen's vision as the coming of a son and calms her.

tamil: கங்குல்வாய் மடந்தை கண்ட கனவுமெய் யாகல் வேண்டி
மங்குல்வா னகட்டுச் சென்று மதியவன் மறைந்த பின்னை
அங்குலா யிருளை நீக்கு மாயிரங் கதிரி னானும்
கொங்குலாங் குழலி காணுங் குழவிய துருவங் கொண்டான்.
reading: So that the dream the woman saw in the night would prove true, the thousand-rayed sun leaves the sky after the moon sets and takes the child's form.
nuance: The poem gives a reason from the dream: the sun takes a shape so the vision is made true. Moon, then sun, are the two lights that make the child, and the audience is told that the dream was real.
event: The sun takes the form of the child the queen has seen in her dream.

reading: Bearing the noble child, she is lit by a shine as of a conch that holds a precious pearl, and becomes a woman of fortune.
nuance: The conch with its pearl (வலம்புரி மணிக் கரு) is the womb with the child; the bearing is shown through her radiance.

reading: As the dark gem grows within her, her slow-moving body loses its former beauty and glows with the gold-bright look of a land that gives gems.
nuance: The change in the body from old beauty to a golden glow is presented as a sign of the child's growth.

reading: The young lord is born, with a light that grows through the cool sky, a body gleaming like saffron and a modest brilliance.
nuance: The birth is told in one sentence of radiance: he appears with a saffron-bright body and a shy radiance. The newborn's name is not given until 1722.
event: The queen's son is born.

reading: The call of 'Be glad!', the sound of gem-set instruments and the drum of the offering rise together like the sea of the end of the age.
nuance: The cosmic simile for a festival of joy is the sea of the end of an age, the ocean at dissolution. Joy at a birth borrows the sound of the world's ending.
event: The city's drums and voices break out at the birth.

reading: Flutes and tabors, conches and horns sound together, and the garlanded city shakes with the din.
nuance: The garlands drop their pollen as the city quakes with the sound; the verse is pure festival, with no new event.

reading: At the doors of houses, girls with garlands dance with young men to the drum, the song of love and the clapping of hands.
nuance: The festival of the king's birth is a general holiday for the city, in which the sound of love-song is the town's own.

reading: The prisons are cleaned, sandal marks are set on brows, the king's city is decked for festival, and townsfolk forget their work in the feast.
nuance: The cleaning or emptying of prisons (சிறைநகர் சீத்தன) at a royal birth is a common sign of mercy, but the phrase is hard and the reading is uncertain.
event: The city is made ready for festival; the people give up their ordinary work.

reading: After days of bathing and fragrant oils, the people honour the child with a rite of merit and place on him the flower-remnant from the feet of the lord.
nuance: Placing flowers from the feet of the 'excellent one' (புங்கவன்) on the infant is the Jain way of marking the child with the blessing of the Arhat, shown here as the first rite of his life.
event: The people perform the birth rites and lay the flowers from the god's feet on the child.

reading: His father with the golden discus, the plough-bearing elder brother, and the queens and all seven great kinsfolk gather happily.
nuance: The plough-bearer and the golden-discus lord are the two brothers of the story, now uncle and father of the newborn.
event: The father, the plough-bearer and the queens and kin gather around the child.

reading: When the child appears like the young sun with his hands joined, they all embrace him and bathe in a sea of unending joy.
nuance: The young sun is the simile for the child, as the earlier verse made the sun take the child's form.
event: The kin embrace the child.

reading: Groups of virtuous brahmins, brave kings and the town's wise elders all gather and speak the praise of those who bore this lord.
nuance: The praise falls on those who bore him, as much as on the child himself: the three orders of society speak for the parents.
event: Brahmins, kings and elders gather and praise the child's parents.

reading: The lord shows the heaps of jewelled strings, the golden hills, the precious ornaments and red cloth and invites them to take them into the city.
nuance: The royal gift is given with the words 'enter the city and take', an open handing-out of wealth at the birth.
event: Tivittan lays out riches and offers them to all.

reading: Because he shines with fortune and is joined to victory, they name the one with the fortune on his chest 'Vijayan', the victor.
nuance: The child is named Vijayan, the same name as the elder brother Vijayan, the plough-bearer of 1718, so the name recurs in the next generation; the reason is the child's own fortune and victory, not the uncle's name.
event: The kin give the child the name Vijayan.

title: சுயம்வரச் சருக்கம் 1723-1746 (8/12)
theme: A Vidyadhara sky-car lands to bring joy over the birth in Tivittan's house, a Vidyadhara messenger tells how the sun-named lord's wife dreamt of a gem and bore the boy Amitatejas, Tivittan rewards him, and his own son grows, goes to teachers at five, and a younger daughter is born and named amid kin and joy.
source_issues: 1736 line 1 had a pulli after a vowel sign removed by the build.
1738 line 3 had a pulli after a vowel sign removed by the build.
1743-1746 are in a different metre and their last lines are hard to construe; the sense of 1743 line 2, 1744 lines 1-2 and 1745 line 2 is not fixed.
The identity of the girl born in 1744-1746 is not stated; chapters 76-78 may call her Sayambavai.

cast.role: Tivittan, the dark-hued lord with the discus, host of the Vidyadhara guests
the men whom Tivittan orders to bring the welcome
the Vidyadhara women who alight with chamberlains and pour the ghee
the Vidyadhara man who bows to Tivittan and reports the birth
the mountain-king's daughter, wife of the sun-named Vidyadhara lord, who conceives and bears Amitatejas
the Vidyadhara prince born in the messenger's story; id as in chapter 77
Tivittan's own son, who grows, crawls and is sent to school; id as in chapter 74
Tivittan's queen, who bears a daughter; id as in chapter 74
the many kin who gather and name the girl

reading: After word of the joy has been sent to the Vidyadhara world as well and the dark-hued lord has given his leave, a red-gold sky-car comes down out of the cloudy heavens.
nuance: The sense of lines 1-2 (what is sent, and what the dark-hued lord grants) is not fixed; ஓகை is taken as 'joy', the news of the birth in chapter 74.
event: A red-gold flying car descends from the sky to the lord's city.

reading: Seeing a gem-bright flying car come down and reach the city, the spear-bearing lord tells his people it is the lords' own visit and bids them bring what is due to the guests.
nuance: Line 3 (பணிவரை கொணர்மினீர்) is hard; 'bring what is fit for service' is the reading taken.
event: Tivittan sees the sky-car land and orders his men to bring the welcome.

reading: The Vidyadhara women, bright of body, come down with their chamberlains from the car that enters the rain-cloud, and reach the king's lodging in the walled city.
event: The Vidyadhara women and their attendants alight and reach the palace.

reading: At the cry 'Let it flourish!' the women pour fragrant ghee over the long golden crown, and a great laugh of love rises loud as the roaring sea.
nuance: Whose crown or head is anointed is not said; given the birth in chapter 74 it may be the child's, but the verse names only the king (புரவலன்) and the women.
event: The women pour ghee at the lord's word and the hall breaks into joyful laughter.

reading: After the ghee-anointed women are sent to the women's palace and the seated company settles, one man bows to the queen's lord and begins to tell him a tale.
nuance: 'பாவை கோயில்' is taken as the women's quarters, and 'யாங்கிருந்த' as the company's sitting; who 'we' are is not stated.
event: A Vidyadhara messenger bows to Tivittan and begins his report.

reading: The messenger says that our lord, whose name is the shining sun, dwells in delight with the garlanded daughter of the mountain-king whose hair is like a dark cloud.
nuance: 'எறிகதிர்ப் பெயரன்' is taken as Arkakirti (the sun-named), the Vidyadhara prince of the earlier chapters; the wife is called சோதிமாலை, which may be a name or an epithet.
event: The messenger names the Vidyadhara lord of the sun's name and his wife, daughter of the mountain king.

reading: One night while the king's wife sleeps the moon rises in the sky with its rays and opens the blossoms of the wide heavens.
nuance: The rising of the moon over her sleep is the frame for her dream of the next verse, as the moon's entry is the frame of the dream in chapter 74.
event: The moon rises over the sleeping queen.

reading: After a cool gem has come to her in a dream, her breasts swell and she takes the form of a bright goddess like a gold figure.
event: After her dream of the gem the queen shows the signs of pregnancy.

reading: Climbing the gem-bright sky-car and seeing the wish-tree groves, the doe-eyed woman lets her pregnancy craving be satisfied.
nuance: 'வயா' is the craving of pregnancy; in the verse the satisfaction of the craving is told as a flight over the wish-tree groves.
event: The queen rides the sky-car through the heavenly groves and her craving is satisfied.

reading: After she has become like a gold figure, a youth appears with a body so bright that even the moon in the bent sky would be shamed by it.
event: The queen's son is born, radiant as a young moon.

reading: The child, with a red lily's petals, a coral mouth, eyes like fragrant flowers and a face like the inside of a lotus, is like a babe of gold in the flower.
As the boy appears, gem lamps burn in the sky, flower rain falls with bees, conches sound like the sea's waves, and light spreads in every direction.
event: Heavenly signs accompany the child's birth: lamps, a rain of flowers, conches and light.

reading: Sovereign kings of boundless strength had their old white umbrellas wilt as he rose with boundless strength, and they gave him a name that says that very might: Amitatejas.
nuance: The name 'அளப்பருந் திறலினன் அமித தேசன்' is repeated word for word in each line to make the meaning, 'of unmeasurable might', plain; who gives it is left to 'they'.
event: The boy is named Amitatejas ('boundless might').

reading: The speaker ends his report: the dark-cloud-hued uncle, to let the lord's beauty be drunk by the eyes, said 'tell the world's master and come', and so he has come with ghee; such is the matter.
nuance: Who is meant by மாமனார் (the child's uncle) and by 'the master of the world' is not clear; the text says only that a message of 'come' was sent. Line 1 carries a repaired pulli.
event: The messenger finishes his report and states that he came bringing ghee.

reading: On hearing him the lord of the discus gives him treasure shining in the vault, joins him to royal wealth, and the messenger goes happily to his own world.
event: Tivittan rewards the messenger with treasure and he returns to the Vidyadhara world.

reading: Tivittan's son, the child of the foe-less lord of the golden discus, grows with a beauty that makes onlookers glad, guarded by women with hair full of bees.
nuance: After the news of Amitatejas the verse returns to Tivittan's own son (called the lord's child, not by name here); the earlier chapter names him Vijayan.
event: Tivittan's son grows up in the care of his nurses.

reading: Guarded by many shining gods and blessed by the lotus lady, he grows like the cool-rayed sun in the sky, a lord of cool light over the earth.
nuance: The 'many gods' who guard him are the poem's own picture of a fortunate birth; the verse does not link them to any school.
event: The child grows under the care of gods and the goddess of the lotus.

reading: With golden-corded anklets ringing, gem strings shining at his waist and golden bells on his feet, he crawls about the courtyards of the women who wear gold-corded jewels.
event: The boy crawls about the women's courtyards in his jewels.

reading: Shown the golden lotuses of the pond and called by women of gentle form, he is glad, and his ear-rings flash like lightning as he creeps through the pollen-laden gardens.
event: The boy plays among the garden pools while women call him.

reading: The ones who see him see the wealth of eyes, the earth's wealth grows with his joy each day, and like the red sun of the heavens he plays and tires, pulling the little golden wheel.
nuance: Three kinds of wealth (of the eyes, of the earth, of the sky) are used for the child, as one fortune seen from three sides.
event: The boy plays with a golden wheel-toy until he is tired.

reading: At the age of five the boy is brought to teachers rich in unfailing learning, so that the lord of the bright discus unites him with them.
nuance: 'காதலி நாவின் மகளாக' (line 2) is hard; it may mean the boy is joined to learning as to a loved one's own daughter. The reading here takes only the sure part: teachers and the boy at five.
event: Tivittan hands his five-year-old son to learned teachers.

reading: The queen of the guardian lord bears a girl, younger than the boy, whom all the world calls the god of love's wealth and who rises praised in every direction like the fire-offering's wealth.
nuance: Lines 1-2 are hard: 'காமச் செல்வன்' may name the boy, or praise the girl, who is the one 'ஒளியாள்' who is praised.
event: Tivittan's queen gives birth to a daughter younger than her son.

reading: The assembled kin, the Vidyadhara kinsfolk among them, name her in keeping with victory, are sent back to the Vidyadhara ranks, and the dark-hued lord sinks happily in a sea of love and joy.
nuance: The name given, 'பெயரிட்டு' with 'கொன்றிய வாறு', is not given in the verse and is hard to construe; 'in keeping with victory' is a guess.
event: The kin gather and give a name; the Vidyadhara guests leave; Tivittan is full of joy.

tamil: ஐயன் றானு மவ்வகை யாலே வளர் வெய்த
reading: So the boy grows, the great queen is full of joy, and the girl, whom they obtained by worshipping the gods like fortune itself that the people worship, has a name of lightning for her body's light.
nuance: 'மின்னின் பெயராளும்' ends the verse with her name as the name of lightning; the name is not spelled out and a later chapter's heroine may be this girl or another.
event: The boy and the girl grow up; the queen rejoices.

title: சுயம்வரச் சருக்கம் 1747-1770 (9/12)
theme: In the Swayamvara sarukkam, Tivittan's daughter grows up and plays ball with her friends, the parents call the tired girl to them, the father weighs her ripeness, takes counsel and has the swayamvara drum proclaimed, and the kings and the Vidyadhara lords gather round the city.
source_issues: Verses 1748-1757 and 1759? were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four lines by the build; read as four.
1755 line 4 prints பூங்குழ்லுங் for பூங்குழலுங்.
1757 line 6 had a pulli after a vowel sign removed by the build.
1770 line 4 prints அரைசெதிர் for அரைசு எதிர்; the receiver of Arkkan's son is not named.

cast.role: Tivittan's daughter, the maiden of the swayamvara
the mothers and nurses who surround her
her companions and attendants at ball-play
mothers and friends who protest at her play
Tivittan, the dark-hued lord and the girl's father
the king's chief queen, named by rank
the king and queen speaking together
counsellors learned in the science of wealth
the herald who proclaims the swayamvara by drum
the people of the city to whom the herald speaks
the kings who gather
the Vidyadhara kings from the silver mountain
the son of Arkkan, who arrives with his lady
the ruler of this mountain who receives him, not named

reading: Bees hum to the flowers and the girl, slender as a flowering creeper, grows up like a great peahen among her mothers and playmates.
nuance: The girl is not named in the verse; she is Tivittan's daughter only from the next verses (1754 calls her the dark-hued one's daughter). Bees and flowers surround her as they do a creeper.
event: The princess grows up amid her mothers and companions.

tamil: மழலைக் கனிவாய் மணிவண்டு வருடி மருங்கு பாராட்ட
அழனக் கலர்ந்த வரவிந்த வமளி சேர்ந்த விளவன்னம்
கழனிச் செந்நெற் கதிரென்னுங் கவரி வீசக் கண்படுக்கும்
பழனக் குவளை நீர்நாடன் பாவை வார்த்தை பகருற்றேன்.
reading: After a picture of the watery land, with bees, lotus beds, a resting swan and paddy ears like fans, the poet says he now begins the tale of the daughter of that land's lord.
nuance: The land and the girl are paired through the first-person பகருற்றேன் (I begin to tell); the picture of the countryside serves as a frame for her. Printed in 8 half-lines and joined by the build.

tamil: செம்பொற் சிலம்புங் கிண்கிணியுஞ் செல்வச் செஞ்சீ றடிபோற்ற
வம்பத் துகிலின் வடஞ்சூழ்ந்த வல்குன் மணிமே கலை மருட்ட
அம்பொற் சுருளை யிருபாலு மளக வல்லி யருகிலங்கப்
பைம்பொற் சுடிகை நிழறுளங்கப் படர்ந்தா டாயம் படிந்தாளே.
reading: The girl, adorned with gold anklets, tiny bells, a fresh silk wrap, a gem girdle and hair curls and head ornaments, joins the crowd of her playmates.
event: The girl, dressed and ornamented, goes to join her playmates.

tamil: நங்கை நல்லார் பாராட்ட நகையாட் டாயம் புகலோடு
மங்கை மடவார் பந்தாடன் மயங்கி யாடன் மணிநிலத்துக்
கொங்கை சேர்ந்த குங்குமத்தின் குழம்புங் கோதை கொய்தாதும்
அங்க ராகத் துகளும்பாய்ந் தந்தி வான மடைந்ததுவே.
reading: The young women's ball-play scatters saffron paste, garland pollen and body powder, so that the air turns red like the evening sky.
nuance: The evening-red sky is made by the cosmetics of the players themselves; the game is shown as beauty at its most active.
event: The women play ball and the dust of their ornaments reddens the sky.

tamil: காவி நாணுங் கண்ணார்தங் கையி னேந்துங் கந்துகங்கள்
ஆவி தாமு முடையனபோ லடிக்குந் தோறு மடங்காது
பூவி னார்ந்த மணிநிலத்துப் பொங்கி யெழுந்து பொன்னேந்தி
நாவி நாறு மிளங்கொங்கைத் தடங்கள் சென்று நணுகியவே.
reading: The balls in the girls' hands rebound as if alive and, however they are struck, fly up from the jewelled floor and settle on the scented breasts.
nuance: The verse gives the balls a will of their own (ஆவி உடையன போல்), which the next verse turns into a simile of lovers.
event: The balls struck by the women spring back and land on their breasts.

tamil: கரிய குழலும் பொற்றோடுஞ் செய்ய வாயுங் கதிர்முறுவல்
மரிய திசையு மதிமயங்கு மம்பொன் முகத்து மடவார்கள்
திரியத் தம்மைப் புடைத்தாலுஞ் சென்று சேர்ந்து திளைக்குமால்
அரிய செய்யுங் காமுகர்போ லளிய வந்தோ வடங்காவே.
reading: Even when the women strike them away, the balls return to cling to them, like lovers who do harsh things and still will not be restrained.
nuance: Ball-play is read as courtship: the ball plays the lover who is driven off and returns. The comparison is the poet's and does not judge the lover.
event: The women strike the balls and the balls keep returning to them.

tamil: செம்பொற் சுருளை மெல்விரலாற் றிருத்திச் செறிந்த தேரல்குல்
வம்பத் துகிலின் வடஞ்சூழ்ந்து மணிமே கலையுந் தானேற்றி
அம்பொற் குரும்பை மென்முலைமே லணிந்த பொன்ஞா ணருகொடுக்கிப்
பைம்பொற் றிலத நுதலொதுக்கிப் பாவை பந்து கைக்கொண்டாள்.
reading: The girl tidies her curls, ties her silk wrap and gem girdle, tucks in her gold waist-string, sets her forehead mark straight and takes up the ball.
nuance: She makes herself ready with her own hands before she plays; the same silk and gem girdle dress a bride in 1538, which gives the game a look of rehearsal.
event: The princess dresses herself for play and takes up the ball.

tamil: கந்தாடு மாலியானைக் கார்வண்ணன் பாவை கருமேகக் குழன்மடவார் கைசோர்ந்து நிற்பக்
கொந்தாடும் பூங்குழலுங் கோதைகளு மாடக் கொய்பொலந் துகிலசைத்த கொய்சகந் தாழ்ந்தாட
வந்தாடுந் தேனுமுரல் வரிவண்டு மாடமணி வடமும் பொன்ஞாணும் வார்முலைமே லாடப்
பந்தாடு மாடேதன் படைநெடுங்க ணாடப் பணைமென்றோ ணின்றாடப் பந்தாடு கின்றாள்.
reading: Dark-hued Tivittan's daughter plays ball while her attendants stand with weary hands, her flower-hair, garlands, silk folds, girdle, eyes and arms all swaying with the game.
nuance: The verse names her father by the epithet கார்வண்ணன் (the dark-hued one, Tivittan by the earlier chapters), the first time here that she is placed as his daughter.
event: The princess plays ball while her attendants stand tired beside her.

tamil: கந்துகங்கள் கைத்தலத்தா லேறுண்டு பொங்கிக் கருங்கண்ணுந் தாமுமுறக் கலந்தெழுந்த போழ்தின்
வந்தனவுஞ் சென்றனவும் வானத்தின் மேலு மணிநிலத்து மீதுநெறி மறிகுவன வாகி
அந்துகிலி னிடைத்தோயு மகலல்கு றீண்டு மணிமருங்கு சூழுமணியார் வடமுந் தாக்கும்
கொந்தவிழும் பூங்குழ்லுங் கோதைகளு மூழ்குங் குவளை வாட் கண்ணிவருங் குறிப்பறிய மாட்டாள்.
reading: The balls rise and fall about the sky, the jewelled floor, her silk, girdle and breasts, and the lily-eyed girl, absorbed in the game, cannot make out their coming.
nuance: The last clause, குறிப்பறிய மாட்டாள், can be read as the girl failing to follow where the balls go or failing to read their drift; the second reading would hint at what the game means. Line 4 prints பூங்குழ்லும் for பூங்குழலும்.
event: The princess plays on among the rising and falling balls.

tamil: நறுமாலை வந்தலைப்ப நன்மேனி நோமா னங்காயிப் பந்தாட னன்றன்றா மென்பார்
இறுமாலிம் மின்மருங்கு லென்பாவ மென்பார் இளமுலைமே லேர்வடம்வந் தூன்றுமா லென்பார்
செறுமாலிங் கிவைகாணிற் றேவிதா னென்பார் செங்கண்மால் காணுமேற் சீறானோ வென்பார்
பெறுமாறு தாயருந் தோழியரு நின்று பிணையனா டன்மேற் பன்மொழி மிழற்றுகின்றார்.
reading: Her mothers and friends stand about her and say that ball-play is no good for her tender body, that her waist will break and her breasts be pressed by her pearl strings, and that the queen or the red-eyed lord would be angry to see it.
nuance: Their worry is for her body and for the anger of her parents (தேவி, செங்கண்மால்), not a rule of conduct; nothing in the verse says the girl stops.
event: Her mothers and friends protest that ball-play is not fit for her.

tamil: நீராலிக் கட்டி நிரந்தெழுந்து பொங்கி நிழறயங்கும் பொன்னறைமே னின்றாடுகின்ற
காராலி மஞ்ஞை களிசிறந்தாற் போலக் கருங்குழலி பந்தாடல் காதலித்த போழ்தில்
சீராலி மால்வண்ணன் றேவியுந் தானும் செவ்வரத்த நுண்ணெழினி சேர்ந்தொருங்கு நோக்கி
வாராலி மென்கொங்கை மையரிக்கண் மாதர் வருந்தினா ணங்கையினி வருகவீங் கென்றார்.
reading: The dark-hued lord and the queen watch from behind a fine red curtain as she plays like a peahen on a gold floor, and, seeing her tired, call her to come to them.
nuance: The speech is given jointly to the two parents, who watch unseen behind the curtain. Line 6 had a pulli repaired and the stanza was printed in 8 half-lines.
event: The king and queen watch their daughter play and call her to them because she is tired.

reading: At the crowned king's gracious word she lets go of her jewelled ball and, her hair streaming behind, comes and reaches the feet of the dark-lustred one.
nuance: The words அருளிது என்றலும் can be taken as the king's call or as a general phrase of grace; 1757 gives the call. அருமணி முடியவன் and கருமணி ஒளியவன் are read as the same man, Tivittan.
event: At her father's call the princess leaves the game and goes to his feet.

reading: He seats her on his right thigh, wipes the sweat from her brow with his palm and sits in quiet gladness, then looks over her blooming body.
nuance: The father's tenderness and his appraising look sit in one verse: the sweat he wipes comes from the ball-play, and the look prepares the decision of 1762.
event: Tivittan seats his daughter on his lap, wipes her brow and looks at her.

reading: Seeing her young breasts, her richness of form and the beauty of her figure, he feels a joy that makes his heart sigh.
nuance: உளமயா உயிர்ப்பதோர் உவகை can be read as joy that makes the heart sigh, a mixture of pride and anxiety at her ripeness, or as a plain sigh of gladness; the verse does not say a marriage is in his mind, but 1762 follows.
event: The lily-garlanded father sees that his daughter has come of age.

reading: He arranges her fine hair, sets her happily on the queen's lap and goes off to the council-hall of the palace.
nuance: The mantra-sala (மந்திர சாலை மண்டபம்) is a room for counsel, not for ritual; the next verse shows what he does there.
event: Tivittan sets his daughter in the queen's lap and goes to the council hall.

reading: After counsel with men of the science of wealth, whose view agrees with his own, the king commands that the swayamvara drum be struck from an elephant's neck.
nuance: The decision is taken in council, with the ministers named by their learning (அருத்தநூல், the policy texts), and not by the father alone.
event: Tivittan takes counsel with his ministers and orders the swayamvara drum proclaimed.

reading: The drum, smeared with white sandal paste and hung with peacock-feather garlands, is struck with a roar like hail.
nuance: This is the drum that receives offerings (பலிபெறு முரசம்); its sound announces the wedding to everyone.
event: The swayamvara drum is struck.

reading: A herald calls for the king's long life, the earth's welfare, enemies sunk, virtue spreading, cool rain, ripe crops and grief brought low, and bids the people hear the proclamation.
nuance: The blessing runs from the king through the country's rain and harvest and its virtue; the ruler stands at the head of every wish, as in the Kural's picture of just rule.
event: The herald opens the proclamation with blessings on the king and land.

reading: The herald bids the people decorate the city of the forest-ringed gold town, raise festival arches, welcome white festival dress and honour guests, and put flowers and vessels in order.
event: The herald orders the city decorated and guests honoured.

reading: The thunderous drum is said to have declared that the swayamvara is fixed for ten days from today and that the world should gather with the kings who live in concord.
nuance: ஈரைஞ் ஞாள் is read as ten days counting today; the verse closes with என்பவே (they say), so the narrator reports the proclamation at a remove.
event: The drum announces the swayamvara for ten days later and summons the kings.

reading: The drum thunders through the royal city's streets like a cloud-burst, and the peacocks in the mansions, taking it for rain, are bewildered.
nuance: Peacocks that mistake the drum for rain-clouds belong to the poet's stock of images; the whole city is shown shaken by the news.

reading: With drums, conches and heavy armies, kings and those who are not kings pour like the sea round the city and fill the outer ring of its wall.
nuance: The line names both kings and non-kings (அரசரல்லாரும்), so the crowd is more than suitors: those who come to watch are counted too.
event: Kings and others arrive in force and surround the city walls.

reading: The Vidyadhara kings from the silver mountain, with sea-like armies and a blinding radiance, come and camp among the eight mountains.
nuance: எண்மலைச் சிலம்பு (the slopes of the eight mountains) is hard to place; the verse likely means the camp-ground outside the city.
event: The Vidyadhara kings arrive with their armies and encamp.

reading: The son of Arkkan, who is lord of that mountain's kings, comes with a lady with dark long eyes while the ruler of this mountain goes out to greet him.
nuance: The verse does not give his name. Who receives him (இவ்வரை அரைசு) is not stated: it may be Tivittan or a kinsman of the city. Line 4 prints அரைசெதிர் for அரைசு எதிர்.
event: Arkkan's son arrives with his lady and is received by the local ruler.

title: சுயம்வரச் சருக்கம் 1771-1793 (10/12)
theme: The swayamvara hall is built and adorned; the kings of Ayodhya, Hastinapura, Kundalapura, Varanasi, Suriyapura and Madurai arrive in state, and the prince Amitatejas outshines them all before the maiden is called in.
source_issues: Verses 1784-1789 and 1791-1793 are printed in 8 half-lines in the source and joined into 4 lines; 1771, 1784 and 1785 and 1786 have pulli repairs flagged by the checker. Verse 1783 line 3 prints a bracketed (சு) in மாமுர(சு).

cast.role: the lord of kings who sits in the hall
the lord of the city who receives the guests
the dark-hued, discus-handed lord, taken to be Tivittan from the earlier chapters
the white-gleaming lord who arrives with him
the Vidyadhara lord of golden hue
the builders of the choosing hall
the band of musicians
the one who proclaims the hour
the assembled kings
king of Ayodhya, Ikshvaku line
king of Hastinapura, Kuru line
king of Kundalapura
king of Varanasi, Ugra line
king of Suriyapura, Hari line
king of Madurai
the prince Amitatejas, who outshines the kings
the young women watching the assembly
the gentle maiden the king calls in to choose

reading: In the golden city a walled grove-garden holds a shining hall; the lord of kings sits there and the city's own lord comes to receive him.
nuance: The two lords are named only by their rank (the lord of kings; the lord of this city), so who is who rests on the earlier chapters.
event: The city's lord goes out to receive the overlord of kings who has come to sit in the hall.

reading: The dark-hued lord with the bright spear, the white-gleaming one, and the Vidyadhara of cool golden hue together make the earth blaze with their light.
nuance: The three are given only by colour and kind (dark, white, a Vidyadhara of gold), so naming them rests on the story so far.
event: Three lords arrive, each known by the hue of his body, and their brightness lights the ground.

reading: As streets, courts and the rest fill on both sides, the sea-girt earth looks as if the world of the gods had come down.
nuance: The simile makes the city a heaven set on earth, which prepares the pomp of the kings who arrive.

reading: A pillared mansion with golden-crowned jewelled gate-towers and four doors shows fine jewel-work on every side.
Crystal slabs, coral pillars, golden vessels, silver bamboo-work and pearls of young light make the hall bright.
The white court of the hall, with its altars chilling the moonlight, seems to laugh at the four-faced Brahma's quarters.
nuance: The poet sets the hall beside the Creator's own realm and says it laughs at it, a boast of the hall's worth.

reading: The raised stages, five bow-lengths in measure, rise on gold pillars set with coral, with cloud-like hangings, as if the sky's stages had descended.
On balconies edged with emerald, thrones carried by young lions stand raised high.
nuance: The thrones are held up by lion figures, the usual sign of royal seats.

reading: Seats shaped like crocodile-thrones and swan-down cushions are set with gems.
Strings of pearls, crystal-bright garlands, gold wreaths and honeyed flower-ropes are hung through the hall.
Cotton seats are spread, flowers laid, and clouds of incense rise as though the hall were feasting the fierce sun.
nuance: Honouring the sun-god with an incense feast turns the hall's preparation into a form of worship.
event: Attendants spread seats and flowers and burn incense in the hall.

reading: When the builders finish the hall of the choosing and spread couches in sandal shade, the musicians stand and play to say the work is done.
event: Builders complete the choosing hall, and the musicians rise and begin to play.

reading: At the auspicious hour a herald calls the kings to come and take their seats, conches sound, and the great drums roar as the kings appear.
event: A herald calls the assembled kings to come in; conches and drums answer and the kings appear.

tamil: எரிமணி வயிரப் பூணா னிக்குவா குலத்துட் டோன்றி
அருமணிப் புரிசை வேலி யயோத்தியாள் கின்ற வேந்தன்
திருமணி நிழற்றுஞ் செம்பொன் னெடுமுடி திருவில் வீசப்
புரிமணி யாரந் தாழப் பொன்னகர் பொலியப் புக்கான்.
reading: The lord of Ayodhya, born in the Ikshvaku line, enters the golden city with a splendid crown and strings of gems.
event: The king of Ayodhya enters the city.

tamil: குழவியம் பருகி போல்வான் குருகுலங் குளிரத் தோன்றி
அழுவநீர்ப் புரிசை வேலி யத்தின புரம தாள்வான்
முழவங்க ளிரண்டு செம்பொன் முளைக்கதிர்க் கனக வல்லி
தழுவிய தனைய தோளான் றன்னொளி தயங்கச் சார்ந்தான்.
reading: The king of Hastinapura, of the Kuru line, with arms like twin drums and shining with his own light, arrives.
event: The king of Hastinapura arrives.

tamil: நண்டுபொன் கிளைக்கு நாட னாதவன் குலத்துட் டோன்றிக்
குண்டல புரம தாளுங் குங்குமக் குவவுத் தோளான்
கண்டிகை தவழப் பூண்டு கதிர்மணி முடியின் மேலால்
வண்டுகள் பரவச் சென்று வளநகர் மருளப் புக்கான்.
reading: The lord of Kundalapura, of the Nathavan line, with saffron-smeared shoulders and wreathed crown, enters with bees swarming over him.
event: The king of Kundalapura enters the city.

tamil: ஊழிகாண் பரிய தோன்ற லுக்கிர குலத்து வேந்தன்
வாழைதாழ் சோலை வேலி வாரண வாசி மன்னன்
சூழிமா லியானை யுந்திச் சுடர்குழை திருவில் வீச
ஏழையர் கவரி வீச வெழினக ரிசைப்பச் சென்றான்.
reading: The lord of Varanasi, of the Ugra line, rides in with a crested elephant, flashing earrings and women waving fly-whisks.
event: The king of Varanasi rides into the city.

tamil: சொரிமது கலந்த சோலைச் சூரிய புரம தாளும்
அரிகுலத் தரசர் கோமா னவிர்மணி யாரந் தாங்கிப்
பொருமலைப் பகடு நுந்திப் புயலலைத் திருண்டு வீழ்ந்த
புரிமலர்க் குஞ்சி தாழப் பொன்னகர் புகழப் புக்கான்.
reading: The lord of Suriyapura, born of the Hari line, comes forward on a mountain-like war-elephant, hair loose with its flowers, as the city praises him.
event: The king of Suriyapura enters the city on an elephant.

tamil: சொன்மலர்ந் துலக மேத்துஞ் சுடரவன் மருகன் றோலா
மன்மலர்ந் திலங்கு செய்கை வளங்கெழு மதுரை யாள்வான்
தென்மலை வளர்ந்த தெய்வச் சந்தனந் திளைத்த மார்பன்
மின்மல ராரந் தாங்கி வியனகர் விரும்பப் புக்கான்.
reading: The lord of Madurai, kin of the shining one the world praises, wearing the gem-necklace and sandal on his chest, enters as the city wishes him well.
event: The king of Madurai enters the city.

tamil: ஐம்பெருங் குலத்த ராய வரசரும் பிறரு மாங்கண்
கம்பெறி களிநல் யானைக் கடற்படை புறத்த தாக
வம்பெறி வளாகஞ் செம்பொன் மஞ்சங்கண் மலிர வேறி
வெம்பரி விளங்குந் தானை வேலவர் விளங்கு கின்றார்.
reading: The kings of the five great lines and others stand outside with their elephants and hosts, and the spear-bearers shine on golden seats.
event: The kings take their seats, their armies waiting outside.

tamil: திருந்திய திலதக் கண்ணித் தேவிளங் குமரன் போலும்
அருந்தகை யரச நம்பி யடுதிற லமித தேசன்
பரந்தபின் பசலை கூரப் பனிக்கதிர் வருவ தேபோல்
விரிந்தொளி சுடர வேந்தர் விளங்கொளி மழுங்கச் சென்றான்.
reading: The prince Amitatejas, strong in battle and wearing the garland, goes in so brightly that the other kings' light is dimmed, as the moon is when it rises.
nuance: The poet likens him to a young god and to the moon, so the verse sets up the contest by the one who dims the rest.
event: Prince Amitatejas enters, outshining the assembled kings.

tamil: மழைபுரை மதத்த தாய மழகளி யானை தன்மேல்
வழைவளர் சோலை சேர்ந்த மணிவண்டு மறிவ வேபோல்
எழுதெழி லழகன் றன்மே லிளையவர் கருங்கண் வீழ்ந்து
விழவயர் நகரின் வந்த வேந்தரை விட்ட வன்றே.
reading: The young women's dark eyes fall on the handsome prince as bees fall on a maned elephant, and they leave the other kings they had come to the festival for.
nuance: The eyes act before the bride does: the choice is anticipated in the gaze of the onlookers.
event: The young women's eyes turn from the kings to the handsome prince.

tamil: வரைசெறிந் தனைய செம்பொன் மஞ்சங்கண் மலிரத் தோன்றி
அரைசர்க ளிருந்த போழ்தி னாழியந் தடக்கை வேந்தன்
விரைசெறி குழலங் கூந்தன் மெல்லியல் வருக வென்றான்
முரைசொலி கலந்த சங்கு வயிரொடு முரன்ற வன்றே.
reading: When the kings are seated on their golden thrones, the discus-handed king calls the gentle maiden to come in, and drums and conches sound together.
nuance: The calling voice is the king's, with the discus-hand; that he is Tivittan rests on the epithet and the earlier chapters.
event: The king calls the maiden to come in and the drums and conches sound.

title: சுயம்வரச் சருக்கம் 1794-1816 (11/12)
theme: Sayambavai is dressed, guarded and walks in procession to the swayamvara hall, her women praise her, and a herald names the assembled kings to her one by one, praising each by line, deeds, appearance and country, and twice by the merit or austerity that wins his embrace.
source_issues: 1799-1816 were printed in eight half-lines and repaired into four lines by the build; read as four.
1794 line 2 carries the editor's mark (கு) and lines 2-3 are hard to construe.
1798 line 1 (சராவி), 1800 line 3 (திரைமகளிர்) and 1809 line 1 (சயம்பூறான்) are rare or damaged words.
1806 line 5 had a pulli after a vowel sign removed by the build.

cast.role: the Vidyadhara king's daughter, whose swayamvara this is
the armed maidens who guard Sayambavai
the attendant women who praise her as she goes in
the man with the gold-bound cane who names the kings to Sayambavai; his office is not named in the verses

reading: The king's daughter, in her jewelled upper room, is told something about the lord ladies' grace and steps down from her flowered seat above the golden couch.
nuance: The verse names no one; 'the king's daughter' is taken as Sayambavai because this is the swayamvara sarukkam. Line 3 is hard to construe and carries the editor's mark (கு) on line 2.
event: Sayambavai rises from her couch in the palace and steps down from her seat, to go out to the wedding hall.

reading: Women like creepers bind the jewelled girdle on her, tie up her hair, tighten her bodices and close around the peacock-like girl with spears in their hands.
nuance: The spears carried by her attendants make the bride's procession a guarded one, as the armed maidens of 862-975 are.
event: The maidens of her guard dress Sayambavai and surround her with spears.

reading: With her companions and nurses she goes through the courts, the girl who rules the hearts of kings, like the moon moving among stars and reflected in the clear jewelled waters.
nuance: The moon-and-stars simile gives her the kings' longing before any king is shown.
event: Sayambavai walks with her retinue towards the hall.

reading: As she walks, bees follow her, the minds of the kings follow, the eyes of onlookers delight, and the praise and music of the eight quarters follow, and she steps gently over fallen petals.
event: Sayambavai walks on among following bees, kings' thoughts and the sounds of praise.

reading: Her soft feet ache, the kings' thoughts throb, their desire swells and she enters the gem-set mansion, dark and bright as a flower.
nuance: Line 1 is hard: 'சராவி' is a rare or damaged word, so the cause of the pain in the soft feet is not fixed.
event: Sayambavai reaches the jewelled mansion where the kings are seated.

tamil: பொன்னேநன் மணிக்கொம்பே பூமிமே லாரணங்கே போற்றி போற்றி
அன்னேயெம் மரசர்குலத் தவிர்விளக்கே யாரமிர்தே போற்றி யுன்றன்
மின்னேர்நுண் ணிடைநோமான் மென்மலர்மேன் மென்மெலவே யொதுங்கா யென்று
மன்னேர்சே யயினெடுங்கண் மங்கைமார் போற்றிசைப்ப மாடம் புக்காள்.
reading: Her women cry 'honour, honour' to her as gold, as a gem-branch, as the lamp of the kings' line, and beg her to step slowly on the soft flowers lest her fine waist hurt, as she enters the hall.
event: Her attendants praise her and warn her to tread softly as she goes into the hall.

tamil: அணிதயங்கு சோபான வீதிவா யணங்கனையா ரடியீ டேத்த
மணிதயங்கு மாளிகைமேல் வாணிலா வளர்முன்றின் மருங்கு சூழ்ந்து
கணிதயங்கு வினைநவின்ற கண்டத் திரைமகளிர் கையி னீக்கித்
துணிதயங்கு வேலரசர் மனந்துளங்கச் சுடர்ந்திலங்கித் தோன்றி னாளே.
reading: At the shining steps her attendants salute her, and in the moonlit court of the mansion, when the screen-women draw back, she appears blazing before the kings, whose minds waver.
nuance: Line 3 (கணிதயங்கு வினைநவின்ற ... திரைமகளிர்) is hard to construe; I read it as women who hold a screen and remove it.
event: Sayambavai appears before the assembled kings and they are shaken.

tamil: வடியரத்த மிடைவழித்துக் கருங்கண்ணுஞ் செம்பொன்னால் வளைத்த சூரல்
கொடியரத்த மெல்விரலாற் கொண்டரசர் குலவரவு கொழிக்கு நீராள்
முடியரக்குப் பூங்கண்ணி மூரித்தேர் வேந்தர்தமை முறையாக் காட்டிப்
படியரக்கும் பாவைக்குப் பைபையவே யினையமொழி பகரா நின்றான்.
reading: A man with a gold-bound cane, who shows the kings in order and speaks softly to the girl, begins to name them.
nuance: The verse does not give the speaker's office; 'herald' is my label for the man who names the kings, as the speakers of 1802-1816 do.
event: The herald points out the kings to Sayambavai one by one and begins to speak to her.

tamil: அங்கார வலர்கதிர மணிசுடரு மரியணைமே லமர்ந்து தோன்றித்
தங்கார மணிநிழற்றுந் தடவரையா ரகலத்தான் றகர நாறுங்
கொங்கார வார்குழலார் குவிமுலைகண் முகம்பொருத குவவுத் தோளான்
இங்காரு நிகரில்லா விக்குவா குலத்திறைவ னிருந்த கோவே.
reading: He points to the first king, broad-chested and scented with the sandal that the women's breasts touch, who sits on a lion seat, the lord of the Ikshvaku line with no peer here.
event: The herald points Sayambavai to the king of the Ikshvaku line.

tamil: ஆதியா னருளாழி தாங்கினா னாயிரச்செங் கதிரோ னாணுஞ்
சோதியான் சுரர்வணங்கு திருவடியான் சுடுநீறா நினையப் பட்ட
காதியா னருளியபொற் கதிர்கொள்முடி கவித்தாண்டார் மருகன் கண்டாய்
ஓதியா மொழியினிவ னுறு வலிக்கு நிகராவா ருளரோ வேந்தர்.
reading: The herald says this king is descended from one who bore the wheel of grace of the First Lord and was crowned by the one who burned the harmful karmas, and asks who among kings could match his strength.
nuance: The praise runs through the king's descent from the First Lord and his line, not through any deed of his own; the Jain colouring of 'அருளாழி' and 'காதி' is the poet's, but the verse makes no doctrinal claim.

tamil: ஆழித்தே ரொன்றேறி யலைகடலி னடுவோட்டி யமரர் தந்த
மாழைத்தேர் மருங்கறா மணிமுடியு மணிகலமுந் திறையா வவ்வி
ஊழித்தே ரரசிறைஞ்ச வுலகெலா மொருகுடைக்கீ ழுறங்கக் காத்த
பாழித்தோட் பரதன்பி னிவனிவனா னிலமடந்தை பரிவு தீர்ந்தாள்.
reading: He mounted a single wheel-chariot, drove it across the middle of the sea, seized the gods' gold chariots and crowns and jewels as tribute, and kept the whole world under one umbrella, so that after Bharata the earth lost her sorrow.
nuance: Bharata is the measure: the earth's relief 'after Bharata' is set on this king, as 397 sets Bharata's rule on the First Lord's grace.

tamil: இன்னவன துயர்குலமு மிளமையுமிங் கிவன்வடிவுஞ் சொல்ல வேண்டா
மன்னவன்றன் மடமகளே மற்றிவனுக் கிடமருங்கின் மஞ்சஞ் சேர்ந்து
பொன்னவிரு மணியணைமேற் பொழிகதிரீண் டெழுந்ததுபோற் பொலிந்து தோன்றுங்
கொன்னவின்ற வேற்குமரன் குருகுலத்தார் கோனிவனே கூறக் கேளாய்.
reading: Skipping his lineage, youth and looks, the herald tells the king's daughter to hear of the king beside him, seated on a gem couch at his left, the lord of the Kuru line.
event: The herald moves on to the king of the Kuru line seated beside the first.

tamil: அருளாழி யறவரச னருளினா லகன்ஞாலம் பரிவு தீர்த்தான்
உருளாழி யுடையரிவ னடைவின்மிக்க கடைப்பணிகொண் டுழையோர் போல
இருளாழி நிழற்று ளும்பு மெரிபொன்மணி நெடுமுடிசாய்த் திறைஞ்சப் பட்டான்
மருளாழுங் கழிவனப்பின் மற்றிவனே குலமுதற்கண் வயவோன் கண்டாய்.
reading: By the grace of the lord of dharma, the herald says, the wheel-holder removed the world's sorrow; kings bow their crowns to him like servants, and he is the foremost in his line.
nuance: 'அறவரசன்' may name the Jain teacher or a king; the verse does not say. Whether 1806-1807 praise the Kuru king of 1805 or begin another is not fixed by the text.

tamil: சூழிருங் கடற்றானை யுடன்றுளங்கச் சுரர்கொணர்ந்து சொரிந்த மாரித்
தாழிரும்பல் புயறாங்கிச் சரகூடஞ் சந்தித்த தகையோ னன்னோன்
யாழிரங்கு மணிவண்டு மிலங்கிழையார் கருங்கண்ணு மருங்கு நீங்கா
வீழிரும்பொற் சுடரார வரைமார்ப னிவன்சீர்யான் விளம்ப வேண்டா.
reading: He bore the rain of weapons poured by the gods' sea-host, and met the arrow-tower, and bees and women's dark eyes never leave his chest; his greatness, says the herald, needs no telling.

tamil: இங்கிவன திடமருங்கி னெழில்றயங்கு மணிமஞ்ச மிலங்க வேறிச்
சங்கிவர்வெண் சாமரையுந் தாழ்குழையின் நீள்சுடருந் தயங்கி வீசக்
குங்குமஞ்சேர் கொழும்பொடியிற் புரண்டுதன்னி னிறஞ்சிவந்த குளிர்முத் தாரம்
செங்கதிரோ னொளிபருகுஞ் செவ்வரைநே ரகலத்தான் றிறமுங் கேளாய்.
reading: At his left side another king sits on a gem couch, fanned by white fly-whisks, his chest red with kunkuma and as broad as a red mountain, and the herald asks her to hear of him too.
event: The herald points Sayambavai to the next king seated beside him.

tamil: தகரநா றிருஞ்சோலைச் சயம்பூறான் றுறவரசாய் நின்ற காலை
மகரயாழ் நரம்பியக்கி வரங்கொண்டு வடமலைமே லுலக மாண்ட
சிகரமா லியானையான் வழிமருகன் செந்தாமந் தவழ்ந்து தீந்தேன்
reading: When the First Lord stood in the sandal grove as a king of renunciation, one played the harp, won a boon and ruled the world on the northern mountain, and this king is the descendant praised by the gods.
nuance: The harp-playing boon-winner on the northern mountain matches the story of Nami told at 538-547; 'சயம்பூறான்' (line 1) is not a word I can read, so the identification is not fixed.

tamil: சக்கரர்தாம் பிறந்துவரித் தரங்கநீர் வளாகமெல்லாந் தங்கீழ்க் கொண்ட
உக்கிரமெய்க் குலத்தரச னொளிவேலிவ் விளையவன துருவே கண்டாய்
அக்கிரநற் பெருந்தேவி மடமகளே யரசணங்கு மணங்கே யின்னும்
விக்கிரமக் கடற்றானை விறல்வேந்த ரிவர்சிலரை விளம்பக் கேளாய்.
reading: This young king, spear shining, comes of the Ugra line which the wheel-kings founded and which held the sea-bound earth, and the herald tells the king's chief daughter that he will name a few more.
event: The herald points to the young Ugra-line king and promises to name a few more.
