tamil: ஏலஞ்செய் பைங்கொடியி னிணர்ததைந்து பொன்னறைமேற் கொழுந்தீன் றேறிக்
கோலஞ்சேர் வரைவேலிக் குண்டலத்தார் கோமானிக் கொலைவேற் காளை
ஞாலங்க ளுடன் பரவு நாதவன்றன் குலவிளக்கு நகையே னம்பி
போலிங்க ணரசில்லை பொன்னார வரைமார்பன் பொலிவுங் காணாய்.
reading: The herald points to the lord of Kundalam, whose line lights the lord of the world's house, a spear-armed youth, and says there is no king like him here.
nuance: 'நாதவன்' and 'குண்டலத்தார்' may be names of line and place or epithets; the verse does not fix them.
event: The herald points to the lord of Kundalam.

tamil: சொரிமலர்த்தண் மலரணிந்த சோலைசூழ் சூரியத்தார் கோமான் றோலா
அரிகுலத்தார் போரேறிவ் வரியேறு போலிருந்த வரச காளை
வரிமலர்த்து மணிவண்டு புடைவருடு மாலையார் மகளிர் வட்கண்
புரிமலர்த்தண் வரையகலம் புராதார் புண்ணியங்கள் புணரா தாரே.
reading: The herald names the lord of the Surya garland, a lion of the Hari line, and says that the women who have not embraced his broad chest have not met merit.
nuance: Line 4 can be read with the women as those who have not embraced him, or those who have not 'united' with merit (புண்ணியங்கள்); I give both as one claim. The herald is selling a suitor, so the claim is his own.
event: The herald points to the king of the Surya garland of the Hari line.

tamil: வேலைவாய்க் கருங்கடலுள் வெண்சங்கு மணிமுத்தும் விரவி யெங்கும்
மாலைவாய்க் கரும்பறா வகன்பண்ணை தழீஇயருகே யருவி தூங்கும்
சோலைவாய் மலரணிந்த சூழ்குழலா ரியாழிசையாற் றுளைக்கை வேழம்
மாலைவாய் நின்றுறங்கும் மதுரைசூழ் வளநாடன் வடிவுங் காணாய்.
reading: The herald points to the lord of the rich land around Madurai, where white conches and pearls mingle in the sea, sugarcane grows thick, waterfalls hang and elephants sleep to the women's lutes in the groves.
event: The herald points to the lord of the Madurai country.

tamil: விண்சுடரு நெடுங்குடைக்கீழ் விறல்வேந்தன் றிறமிதனை விளம்பக் கேளாய்
தண்சுடரோன் வழிமருகன் றென்மலைமேற் சந்தனமுஞ் செம்பொன் னாரத்
தொண்சுடரும் விரவியநல் வரைமார்ப னுலகிற்கோர் திலதங் கண்டாய்.
reading: The herald says that this king under a tall umbrella, with elephants like thundering clouds, is a descendant of the moon-line, with the sandal of the southern hills on his chest, a tilaka on the brow of the world.
nuance: The moon-line, the southern hill and the Madurai verse before suggest the Pandya, but the verse does not name him.
event: The herald points to the king under the tall umbrella of the moon-line.

tamil: மழைக்கரும்புங் கொடிமுல்லை மருங்கேற வரம்பணைந்து தடாவி நீண்ட
கழைக்கரும்பு கண்ணீனுங் கரபுரத்தார் கோமானிக் கதிர்வேற் காளை
தழைக்கரும்பின் முருகுயிர்க்குந் தாரகலஞ் சார்ந்தவர்க டவஞ்செய் தாரே.
reading: The herald names the lord of Karapuram of the sun-line, a bright-spear youth in a land of sugarcane and creeper, and says the women who have won his garlanded chest had done austerity.
nuance: 'தவஞ்செய்தாரே' makes past austerity the cause of present good fortune, as 1812 does with merit; the herald uses a doctrine of former deeds as part of the king's praise.
event: The herald points to the lord of Karapuram of the sun-line.

tamil: வண்டறையு மரவிந்த வனத்துழாய் மதர்த்தெழுந்த மழலை யன்னம்
உண்டுறைமுன் விளையாடி யிளையவர்க ணடைபயிலு முறந்தைக் கோமான்
கொண்டறையு மிடிமுரசுங் கொடிமதிலுங் குளிர்புனலும் பொறியும் பூவும்
ஒண்டுறையு மும்மூன்று முடையகோ வேயிவன தெழிலுங் காணாய்.
reading: The herald points to the lord of Urandai, in whose city swans play and young women walk, and says he keeps a war-drum, a banner wall, cool water, machines and flowers, and three ghats in each of three kinds.
nuance: Lines 3-4 list the king's possessions in threes; I cannot fix what each three is.
event: The herald points to the king of Urandai.

title: சுயம்வரச் சருக்கம் 1817-1839 (12/12)
theme: The herald names the last of the kings to the bride, who gives her heart to a young prince before he is named and garlands him; the rejected kings accept it as karma, the wedding is held and the swayamvara closes; a second swayamvara gives the girl Sutara to Srivijayan, and the poet ends the sarukkam by telling all to remember the fruit of deeds.
source_issues: 1817-1837 were printed in eight half-lines and repaired into four lines by the build; read as four.
Chapter 78 casts the herald as a man (நின்றான்); 1820 line 4 uses the feminine சொன்னாள், so the guide may be a woman; one id is kept.

The bride of the first choosing is never named in these verses (chapter 78 names her Sayambavai); the second bride is named சுதாரை at 1835, and 1837 line 3 names a lady 'of light'. Who is which is not settled by the Tamil here.
1822 line 2 (வெங்கதிரோன் பெயரவனுக்கு ... எனொ) and 1828 line 1 (நெய்த்தலைப் பாலுக்காங்கு) are hard to construe.

cast.role: the guide who names the kings to the bride (a man in chapter 78; here the verb சொன்னாள் is feminine)
the king's daughter shown the kings and who garlands the prince; not named in this chapter's verses
the rejected kings of the swayamvara
the flaming-discus king who sees a wedding completed and whose son the second bride chooses; probably Tivittan, not named
the groom's father of the first wedding, named at 1832; at 1829 the unnamed spear-bearer is taken to be him
the prince the first bride garlands; probably Amitatejas of chapter 77, not named here
the mountain-king who describes the kings to the girl at the second swayamvara
the bride of the second swayamvara, named at 1835
the groom of the second wedding, the sea-hued one's son, named at 1838
the hearers the poet addresses at the close

tamil: தழலவாந் தாமரையி னீரிதழுஞ் செங்குவளைத் தாதும் வாரி
அழலவாஞ் செந்தோகை யலங்குபொலங் கதிர்ச்செந்நெ லலைத்த வாடை
பழனவாய்ப் பைங்கரும்பின் வெண்போது பவழக்காற் செம்பொன் மாடத்
தெழினிவாய்க் கொணர்ந் தசைக்கு மியலேமாங் கதநாட னிவனேகண்டாய்.
reading: The guide points out the lord of the Hemangada land, whose northern wind carries lotus petals, lily pollen and the white flowers of sugarcane to the coral-legged gold mansions.
nuance: The verse is praise of the king's land more than of the king; the man himself is named only by his country.
event: The herald shows the bride the lord of the Hemangada country.

tamil: காந்தளங்கட் கமழ்குலையாற் களிவண்டு களிறகற்றுங் கலிங்க நாடன்
பூந்தளவங் கமழ்சாரற் பொன்னறைசூழ் தண்சிலம்ப னன்றே பொன்னே
ஏந்திளஞ்சிங் காதனத்தி னினிதிருந்த விளவரச னிப்பா லானோன்
மாந்தளிர்கண் மருங்கணிந்த மணியருவிக் குன்றுடைய மகதைக் கோவே.
reading: The guide shows the lord of Kalinga and the young king of Magadha, who sits on a lion throne and owns hills of gem-bright streams.
event: The herald shows the bride the lord of Kalinga and the king of Magadha.

tamil: அங்கநா டுடையவர்கோ னவ்விருந்தா னிவ்விருந்தா னவந்திக் கோமான்
கொங்குவார் பொழிலணிந்த கோசலத்தார் கோமானிக் குவளை வண்ணன்
கங்கைதா னிருகரையுங் கதிர்மணியும் பசும்பொன்னுங் கலந்து சிந்தி
வங்கவாய்த் திரையலைக்கும் வளநாட னிவன்போலும் வைவேற் காளை.
reading: The guide names the kings of Anga, Avanti, Kosala (the lily-hued one) and Vanga, praising the Ganga-washed land of the last as she points to the spear-armed youth.
event: The herald shows the bride the lords of Anga, Avanti, Kosala and Vanga.

tamil: வஞ்சியின்மெல் லிடையவளை வானிலா வளர்முன்றில் வலமாய்ச் சூழ்ந்து
பஞ்சியின்மெல் லடிநோவ நடைபயிற்றிப் படைவேந்தர் பலரைக் காட்டி
மஞ்சிவரு மாளிகையின் வடமருங்கின் மணிமஞ்ச மலிரத் தோன்றும்
விஞ்சையர்த முலகாளும் விறல்வேந்தர் குழாங்காட்டி விரித்துச் சொன்னாள்.
reading: The bride is led round the moonlit courtyard, her soft feet aching, past many armed kings, and the guide then shows her in detail the Vidyadhara kings who sit on gem couches on the north side of the mansion.
nuance: The verb சொன்னாள் is feminine, whereas chapter 78 casts the herald as a man; the guide is kept as one figure here and the discrepancy is noted in source_issues.
event: The herald walks the bride round the hall and names the earthly kings, then the Vidyadhara kings on the north side.

tamil: மாடிலங்கு மழைதவழ்ந்து மணியருவி பொன்னறைமேல் வரன்றி வம் பூந்
தோடிலங்கு கற்பகமுஞ் சுரபுன்னை வனங்களுமே துதைந்து வெள்ளிக்
கோடிலங்கு நெடுவரைமேற் குடைவேந்த ரிவர்குணங்கள் கூறக் கேட்பின்
ஏடிலங்கு பூங்கோதா யிமையவரின் வேறாய திமைப்பே கண்டாய்.
reading: The guide tells the bride that the Vidyadhara kings, whose qualities she can hear, are no different from the gods save that they blink.
nuance: The praise rests on the old mark of the gods that they do not blink; the herald uses it to say these kings differ from gods only in that one thing.
event: The herald praises the Vidyadhara kings of the silver mountain as godlike.

tamil: வெங்கதிரோன் பெயரவனுக் கிளவரசிவ் வேந்தனெனொ முன்னந் தானே
கொங்கிவருங் கருங்குழலி பெருந் தடங்கண் இருங்குவளை பிணையல் போலச்
செங்கதிரோ னெனவிருந்த திருந்துவே லிளையவன்மேற் றிளைத்த வன்றே.
reading: While the guide still tells of the kings' cities and lines, the bride's large eyes had already settled on the young spear-bearing prince, heir of the king named for the sun.
nuance: The heir is named only by the sun-king's epithet; line 2 is hard to construe, and that the heir is the groom later called the cousin prince (1828) is inferred.
event: The bride's gaze settles on the prince whom the herald has not yet reached.

tamil: கடாமிகு களிநல் யானைக் கவுளிழி கான வீதி
விடாமிகை சுழன்று வீழும் விரைகவர் மணிவண் டேபோல்
படாமுகக் களிற்றி னான்றன் பவழக்குன் றனைய மார்பில்
தடாமுகை யலங்க றன்மேற் றையல்கண் சரிந்த வன்றே.
reading: Her eyes fall on the garland of his chest like a bee drawn by the rut-scent of a great elephant.
event: The bride's eyes fall on the prince of the elephant with the face-cloth.

tamil: ஏட்டினார் குழலி னாளுக் குழையவ ளின்ன னென்று
காட்டினா ளாவ தல்லாற் காரிகை தன்னின் முன்னம்
ஓட்டினா ணிறையுங் கண்ணு முள்ளமுங் களித்த தங்கே
பாட்டினா லென்னை போக பான்மையே பலித்த தன்றே.
reading: The guide had only pointed him out, but her restraint and her heart had already gone to him, and the fruit of her enjoyment-lot had ripened, so the herald's words were no use.
nuance: போக பான்மை is read as the portion of enjoyment owed her; the verse does not say it is the fruit of a past deed, so no link rests on that.
event: The bride gives up her restraint at the sight of the prince before the herald has done naming him.

tamil: விண்டழி நிறைய ளாகி மெல்லவே நடுங்கி நாணி
வண்டிவர் மாலை நோக்கி மாதராள் மறைத லோடும்
கொண்டதோர் குமரன் போலக் குங்குமக் குவவுத் தோண்மேல்
ஒண்டொடி மாலை வீழ்த்தா ளுலகொலி படைத்த தன்றே.
reading: Her restraint broken, trembling and ashamed, she lets the bee-covered garland fall on the saffron-heaped shoulders of the prince, and the hall roars.
event: The bride puts the garland on the prince's shoulders, choosing him.

tamil: ஆர்த்ததங் கரவத் தானை யாலித்த முரசுஞ் சங்கும்
தேர்த்தன மலருஞ் செம்பொற் சுண்ணமுந் திசைக ளெல்லாம்
போர்த்தன பதாகை பொங்கிப் பூமியங் கிழவ ருள்ளம்
வேர்த்தன வேர்த்துத் தாமே வெய்துயிர்த் தொழிந்த வன்றே.
reading: Drums, conches and war-drums sound, flowers and golden powder fill the quarters, and the rejected kings sweat and sigh.
nuance: The rejected kings are the same men the herald praised in 1817-1821, now left without comment.
event: The hall erupts in noise and flowers as the rejected kings sweat and sigh.

tamil: புனைவுதா னிகந்த கோதைப் பொன்னனாள் பூமி பாலர்
நினைவுதா னிகந்து காளை வடிவெனு நிகளஞ் சேர
வினைகடாம் விளையு மாறியாம் வேண்டிய வாறு வாரா
வினையதால் வினையின் றன்மை யெனநினைந் தாறி னாரே.
reading: Their hope gone and their eyes held by the prince's form as by a fetter, the kings calm themselves with the thought that deeds ripen as they will, not as one wishes, and that this is how deeds go.
nuance: The kings' consolation is the same doctrine the poet urges on all in the last verse of the chapter (1839); here it is reported as their thought and not argued.
event: The rejected kings give up their claim by thinking that the outcome is the work of karma.

tamil: நெய்த்தலைப் பாலுக் காங்கு நெடுவரை யுலகின் வந்த
மைத்துன குமரன் றன்னை மடமொழி மாலை சூட்ட
இத்தலை யென்ன செய்தா னெரிகதி ராழி வேந்தன்
கைத்தலை வேலி னாற்குக் கடிவினை முடிவித் தானே.
reading: The question is put of what the flaming-discus king did when the soft-speaking girl garlanded the cousin prince from the mountain world, and the answer is that he saw the wedding completed for the spear-bearer.
nuance: Line 1 (நெய்த்தலைப் பாலுக்காங்கு) is obscure, and who the flaming-discus king is, host or kinsman, is not stated.
event: The discus-king completes the wedding rites for the spear-bearing prince.

tamil: விண்ணகம் புகழு நீர்மை விழுக்கலம் பரப்பி யார
மண்ணக வளாகத் துள்ள மன்னரான் மண்ணு நீர்தந்
தெண்ணகன் புகழி னாரை யெழிலொளி துளும்ப வாட்டிப்
புண்ணகங் கமழும் வேலான் பொன்மழை பொழிவித் தானே.
reading: The spear-bearer spreads out fine ornaments before the kings of the earth, bathes the renowned in splendour and has a rain of gold fall.
nuance: The sense of lines 2-3 (the kings bringing water, being bathed) is uncertain; read as honouring the guests with gifts.
event: Gifts of jewels and gold are poured out to honour the kings who came.

tamil: தருமணன் மணிமுத் தாகத் தண்டுல மியற்றிக் கான்யாற்
றருமணற் றருப்பை சூழ்ந்தாங் கதன்மிசை பரிதி பாய்த்திப்
பெருமண மன்னற் கேற்ற சமிதையாற் பெருக்கப் பட்ட
திருமணி யுருவிற் செந்தீச் செல்வத்திற் சிறந்த தன்றே.
reading: The wedding fire is laid with jewel-bright rice, river sand and darbha, with fuel fit for a great king, and shines richer than any wealth.
nuance: Pure description of the rite's setting; no one acts in the verse.

tamil: தங்கழல் வேள்வி முற்றித் தையலக் காளை யோடும்
பொங்கழல் வலஞ்செய் போழ்திற் குழைமுகம் பொறித்த தெண்ணீர்
பைங்கழ லமரர் பண்டு படைத்தநீ ரமிழ்தப் புள்ளி
அங்கெழு மதியந் தன்மே லரும்பியாங் கணிந்த வன்றே.
reading: When the fire sacrifice is done and the bride circles the flame with the youth, the drops of sweat on her ear-ringed face are like nectar dots on the moon.
event: The bride and groom circle the sacred fire.

tamil: மன்னவ குமர னாங்கு மடந்தையைப் புணர்ந்து மாடத்
தின்னகி லமளி மேலா லிளமுலைத் தடத்து மூழ்க
அன்னவன் றாதை செங்கோ லாணைவே லருக்க கீர்த்தி
தன்னமர் மடந்தைக் கேற்ற சயமர மறைவித் தானே.
reading: The prince lies with the girl in the mansion on the aloe-scented couch, while his father Arkkakirti, whose sceptre and spear rule, has the swayamvara brought to its close.
event: The groom consummates the marriage and his father ends the swayamvara.

tamil: சயமர மறைந்த நன்னாட் டமனிய மஞ்சம் பாவி
இயமரந் துவைப்ப வேறி யிகன்மன்ன ரிருந்த போழ்தில்
பயமலை மன்னன் பாவைக் கவரவர் பண்பு கூறிக்
கயமலர் நெடுங்க ணாளோர் காரிகை காட்டி னாளே.
reading: On the day after the first choosing, kings take seats on gold couches to the sound of drums, a mountain-king tells the girl each one's character and a lotus-eyed woman is shown.
nuance: The verse is hard to parse: whether the lotus-eyed woman is the guide or the bride, and who the mountain-king is, are not said.
event: A second swayamvara is held; the mountain-king describes each king to the girl.

tamil: வரிகழன் மன்ன ரென்னு மணிநெடுங் குன்ற மெல்லாம்
சுரிகுழன் மடந்தை யென்னுந் தோகையம் மஞ்ஞை நோக்கி
எரிகதி ராழி வேந்தன் றிருமக னென்னுஞ் செம்பொன்
விரிகதிர் விலங்கற் றிண்டோட் குவட்டினை விரும்பிற் றன்றே.
reading: The girl, like a peahen, looks over the kings as a range of hills and longs for the golden peak that is the flaming-discus king's son.
event: The girl's eyes choose the discus-king's son from the assembled kings.

tamil: மாதராள் சுதாரை வாட்கண் மலரொடு மணிவண் டார்க்கும்
போதுலாம் பிணையல் வீரன் பொன்வரை யகலஞ் சூழ
ஏதிலா மன்னர் வாட விருபுடைக் கிளைஞ ரெல்லாம்
காதலாற் களித்துச் செல்வக் கடிவினை முடிவித் தாரே.
reading: Sutara's garland of flowers and bees falls on the hero's golden chest while the other kings wither, and kin on both sides gladly complete the wedding.
event: Sutara garlands the hero and her kin complete the wedding.

tamil: கழல்வலம் புரிந்த நோன்றாட் கடல்வண்ணன் புதல்வன் காமர்
குழல்வலம் புரிந்த கோதை குழைமுகம் வியர்ப்ப வேட்டான்
அழல்வலம் புரிந்து சூழ்ந்தாங் கத்தொழின் முடித்த பின்னைத்
தழல்வலம் புரிந்த வேலான் றடமுலை வாரி சார்ந்தான்.
reading: The sea-hued one's son, whose feet wear the warrior's anklet, circles the fire with the bride and after the rite joins her.
event: The groom circles the fire with the bride and is united with her.

tamil: மாதரஞ் சாய லாளு மணிவண்ணன் சிறுவன் றானும்
ஓதநீ ரின்ப மென்னு மொலிகடற் றரங்க மூழ்கச்
சோதியம் பெயரி னாளுஞ் சுடரவன் புதல்வன் றானுங்
காதலிற் களித்துத் தங்கள் கனவரை யுலகஞ் சார்ந்தார்.
reading: Both couples, the lady of gentle grace with the dark-gem lord's son and the lady named for light with the sun's son, delight in love and go to their homes on the great mountain.
nuance: Which bride is which of the two named in lines 1 and 3 is not said; they are read as the two weddings of the chapter.
event: The two newly wedded pairs depart for the mountain land.

reading: Srivijayan, whose command stands against enemy kings' victory, enters the joyous palace of victory with his wife as lovely as Tiru.
nuance: The wording of lines 1-2 plays on the word விசயம் (victory) and is a pun on his name; read as praise.
event: Srivijayan enters his palace with his bride.

reading: The poet closes by saying that such wealth here and the pleasure of the flower-decked gods are the fruit of one's deeds, and bids people of good nature to remember it daily and keep to the way.
nuance: The closing moral sets the kings' resigned thought at 1827 as the poet's own teaching, and prepares the opening of the next sarukkam (1840-1844), where Payapati reasons from his kingship to merit.

title: துறவுச் சருக்கம் 1840-1862 (1/10)
theme: Opens the Renunciation sarukkam: King Payapati, delighting in his grandchildren, thinks that his kingship is the fruit of past good deeds and the body is foul and brief, then asks his ministers whether any statecraft can defeat Death; they cannot, and a minister proposes seeking the sages.
source_issues: Verses 1840-1855 were printed in eight half-lines and repaired into four lines by the build; read as four.
1842 line 5 and 1849 line 6 carried a pulli after a vowel sign, repaired by the build.
1848 and 1850 are hard to construe; 1860 to 1862 turn on rare words and the speaker of 1859 and 1861 is not named; the readings are marked uncertain.

cast.role: King Payapati of Podanam, called Prajapati in 1841, who turns to renunciation
Tivittan, the red-eyed lord, the king's son
the king's grandchildren, the young sons of the discus-ruler
the king's counsellors

tamil: மன்னிய புகழி னான்றன் மகன்வழிச் சிறுவர் வாயுள்
இன்னகை மழலை கேட்டாங் கினிதினி னிருந்த காலைப்
மன்னுமெய்த் துறவிற் புக்கான் பயாபதி மன்னர் மன்னன்
அன்னதன் பகுதி தன்னை யறியுமா பகர லுற்றேன்.
reading: The poet opens the Renunciation sarukkam: while Payapati, king of kings, sat happily listening to the sweet babble of his son's children, he entered true renunciation, and the poet will tell how.
nuance: The turn is set in a moment of family joy, not of loss: the call to renounce comes with the grandchildren's laughter in the room, so the sarukkam begins from fullness, not grief.
event: The poet announces that King Payapati took to renunciation while delighting in his grandchildren.

tamil: திருமகி ழலங்கன் மார்பிற் செங்கணான் வணங்கச் செல்வப்
பெருமகிழ் வெய்தி வேந்தன் பிரசாபதி பெரிய வாட்கண்
உரிமையோ டிருந்த போழ்தி னொலிகல னொலிப்ப வோடி
அருமைகொ டிகிரி யாள்வான் சிறுவர்சென்ற ணுகி னாரே.
reading: As the red-eyed lord bows, King Prajapati sits glad among his own, and the grandchildren, their ornaments ringing, run up to the ruler of the discus.
nuance: Payapati and Prajapati name the same king of Podanam in these verses; the red-eyed bowing lord and the 'ruler of the discus' are taken as Tivittan on the strength of the earlier chapters, and the children as his sons.
event: Tivittan bows to Prajapati, and Tivittan's young sons run to their grandfather.

tamil: ஆங்கவ ரணைந்த போழ்தி னமிழ்துகொப் புளித்த போலும்
தேங்கமழ் பவழச் செவ்வாய் முறுவனீர் பருகித் தேங்கி
ஈங்கிவை யனைய தோற்றி யின்பமே பருக நின்ற
வீங்கிய தவத்திற் கின்னும் வித்திடற் பால தென்றான்.
reading: Seeing the children's nectar-sweet smiles, the king says that the swollen merit which has brought such pleasure still has more seed to be sown.
nuance: The pleasure is read as a harvest already drawn from a field, so the same sight that delights him prompts the thought of sowing; the verse does not say the pleasure is bad, only that the stock behind it is finite.
event: Payapati, watching his grandchildren, speaks of sowing more seed for the austerity that bore these pleasures.

tamil: அலகுடன் விளங்கு மம்பொற் குடைநிழ லரசர் சூழ
உலகுடன் வணங்க வோடை யுயர்களிற் றெருத்த மேலால்
பலகுடை பணியச் செல்லும் பண்பிது நமக்குத் தந்த
நலனுடைத் தளிய நங்க ணல்வினைத் தெய்வ மன்றே.
reading: The umbrellas, the kings who surround him, the world's bowing and the ride on a tall elephant are all a gift to us from our good-deed deity.
nuance: நல்வினைத் தெய்வம் makes karma itself the divinity who grants the kingship; no god of the Veda is named. The king receives what he has earned.

tamil: தன்னையோ ரரச னாக்கித் தரங்கநீர் வளாக மாள்வித்
தின்னுயி ராகிச் செல்லு நல்வினை யென்னு மின்ன
முன்னுப காரி தன்னை முதல்கெட முயலுங் கீழ்மை
நன்னரின் மாந்த ரன்றே நரகங்கட் கரச ராவார்.
reading: Those who try to destroy the root of the good deed that made them king and gave them the sea-girt earth, the only helper that goes with the life, are base men and will be kings in the hells.
nuance: நரகங்கட்கு அரசர் turns kingship upside down: the same word that names his rank names the hell-lord's dominion for the heedless.

tamil: சென்றநாள் பெயரு மேனுஞ் செல்வமுஞ் செருக்கு மாக்கி
நின்றநா ணிலவு மேனு நெறிநின்று வருந்த வேண்டா
இன்றுபோல் வாழ்து மன்றே யிப்படித் தன்றி யாங்கள்
பொன்றுநாள் வருவ தாயின் வாழ்க்கையோர் பொருள தன்றே.
reading: Whether the days gone by pass and wealth and pride stand, one need not suffer on the path; we live as today, but if the day of our perishing comes our life is worth nothing.
nuance: The verse is hard to construe in lines 1-2; the reading takes it as the king's inward objection that he is content as things are, answered at once by line 4.

tamil: எரிபுரை யெழில தாய விளந்தளி ரிரண்டு நாளின்
மரகத வுருவ மெய்தி மற்றது பசலை கொண்டு
சருகிலை யாகி வீழ்ந்த கரிந்துமண் ணாதல் கண்டும்
வெருவிலர் வாழ்து மென்பார் வெளிற்றினை விலக்க லாமோ.
reading: Two days make a bright young leaf green, then pale, then a dried leaf that falls and burns to dust; the ignorant who see it and still say 'we will live' cannot be held back.
nuance: The leaf stands for the body in three stages, flame-red, emerald and withered, so the argument from nature rests on colour change, not only on loss.

tamil: பிறந்தனர் பிறந்து சாலப் பெருகினர் பெருகிப் பின்னை
இறந்தன ரென்ப தல்லா லியாவரு மின்று காறு
மறைந்துயிர் வாழா நின்றா ரில்லையால் வாழி நெஞ்சே
சிறந்தது தவத்தின் மிக்க தின்மையே சிந்தி கண்டாய்.
reading: People are born, grow great, then die, and no one has lived on hidden; so, heart, think that nothing is better than austerity.
nuance: The king addresses his own heart (நெஞ்சே); the same address runs through 1848 and 1849.

tamil: பிறந்துநாம் புறஞ்செய் கின்ற பேதையிவ் வுடலந் தானும்
இறந்தநாள் போல்வ தின்றா யிற்றையின் னாளை வேறாய்ப்
பறைந்துநாம் பற்றப் பற்றப் பற்றுவிட் டகலு மாகிற்
சிறந்தனர் பிறர்க கள்யாரே சிந்தைநீ சிந்தி யென்றான்.
reading: The foolish body we tend is as good as dead; if we leave attachment and stop clinging, who is better than we; think this over, he told his heart.
nuance: Lines 1-2 are hard to construe and the reading is tentative; line 3 and 4 are clearer.

tamil: தொகைமல ரலங்கல் சூடித் தூநறுஞ் கண்ண மப்பிப்
புகைநனி கமழ வூட்டிப் புறஞ்செயப் பட்ட மேனி
சிகையினோர் சிறுமுட் டீண்டச் சிதைந்தழுக் கொழுகு மாயி
நகைபெரி துடைத்து நாணா மிதனைநா மகிழ்த னெஞ்சே.
reading: The body wreathed, perfumed and smoked for display falls apart and runs with filth when a tiny thorn from the hair pricks it, yet we are glad of it without shame, heart.
nuance: The adornment is listed step by step (garland, paste, incense) before the thorn undoes it, which makes the care itself the evidence of folly.

tamil: ஒழுகிய முடையு நீரு முதலகை யிகப்ப வூறும்
அழுகலிவ் வள்ளல் யாக்கை யகம்புற மாயிற் றாயில்
கழுகொடு கவருங் காக்கை கைத்தடி கொண்டு காத்தும்
அழகுள சுழலு மன்னோ வாயிரச் சாதி மாதோ.
reading: The foul flowing fluid of this body, which the demon spirits would mock if it were turned inside out, would be fought over by kites and crows, who are kept off with a stick, and so do a thousand kinds of 'beauty' circle it.
nuance: The crow guarded off with a hand stick (line 3) is the very picture Naladiyar 41 uses; the shared image makes the point that the body must be defended from what will eat it. Line 4 is hard to construe.

tamil: வல்வினை விளைத்த மாந்தர் மற்றதன் வித்து மாட்டிப்
புல்வினை கான மண்டிப் புலியின்வாய்ப் பட்ட தேபோல்
நல்வினை யினிதி னூட்டு நல்வினை முதல்கண் மாறி
இல்வினை யின்பம் வெஃகி யிறுபவே யறிவி லாதார்.
reading: Those who did evil deeds take its seed and sow it; like a man in a tiger's mouth, they leave the root of good deeds that feeds them sweetly and die wanting the pleasure of what has no root, which fools do.
nuance: The verse repeats 1844's root image in the plain voice of a warning and ends the king's inward reflection before 1852 opens the council.

tamil: இன்னன பலவுஞ் சிந்தித் திருந்தது மிகையென் றெண்ணி
மன்னவ னுழையர் தம்மான் மந்திரத் தவரைக் கூவிப்
பொன்னவிர் பவழத் திண்காற் புரிமணிக் கூட மெய்திக்
தன்னம ரமைச்ச ரோடு தானமர்ந் திருந்து சொன்னான்.
reading: Having reflected on all this and judged that waiting is excess, the king summons his counsellors through his attendants and, seated with his ministers in the coral-pillared gem hall, speaks.
event: Payapati calls his ministers to a council in the gem hall.

tamil: மலைபயில் களிநல் யானை மன்னரால் வவ்வ லின்றாய்க்
கலைபயில் மகளிர் கண்போற் கள்வர்கைப் படாது நாளும்
நிலையின செல்வக் கூனம் வருவன வுரைமி னென்றான்
இலைபயின் மகரப் பைம்பூ ணெரிமணிக் கடகக் கையான்.
reading: The king asks the ministers to tell what losses may come to his enduring wealth, which kings cannot seize like a mountain elephant nor thieves steal like women's glances.
nuance: The wealth is described by what cannot take it (kings, thieves), which prepares the answer that only Death remains.
event: Payapati asks the council to name any danger to his wealth.

tamil: ஆள்வினை மாட்சி யென்னு மிரண்டினு மரசு காத்துத்
தோள்வினைக் களவு காவ லுள்வழித் துன்னல் செல்லா
வாள்வினைத் தடக்கை வேந்தே வருவது மற்று முண்டோ
கோள்வினை பயின்ற கூற்றங் குறுகல தாயி னென்றார்.
reading: The ministers answer that, with effort and good order guarding the realm, no theft or force can reach it; is anything more to come, they ask, unless the ranging Death should come near?
nuance: The ministers name the one danger they cannot guard against, so the council turns by their own words from the state to Death.
event: The ministers reply that nothing threatens the realm but Death.

tamil: கோள்வினை பயின்ற கூற்ற வரசனாற் கொள்ளற் பால
கேள்வினை பயின்ற நூலிற் கிளர்ந்துநீ ருரைமி னென்ன
வாள்வினை புரிந்த தோளான் மனத்ததை யுணர்ந்து மாதோ
நாள்வினை புரிந்து நங்க ளுயிர்நிறை கொள்ளு மென்றார்.
reading: At the king's bidding to speak from learning about what Death can take, the ministers, reading his mind, say that Death will do his day's work and take their lives whole.
event: At the king's bidding, the ministers say Death will take their lives.

tamil: சந்தினாற் றவிர்க்க லாமோ சார்பினா லொழிக்க லாமோ
பந்தியா முன்னந் தாமே பகைத்திருந் துய்ய லாமோ
வெந்திறற் காலன் றன்னை மேற்சென்று வெல்ல லாமோ
உய்ந்துயிர் யாங்கள் வாழு முபாயநீ ருரைமி னென்றான்.
reading: The king asks whether Death can be turned back by conciliation, by alliance, by making enemies first, or by attacking and conquering him, and bids them name a way to live.
nuance: The questions are the four ordinary expedients of a ruler against an enemy; the king tests whether statecraft reaches Death.
event: Payapati asks the ministers if statecraft can defeat Death.

tamil: பீழைமை பலவுஞ் செய்து பிணிப்படை பரப்பி வந்து
வாழுயிர் வாரி வவ்வி வலிந்துயிர் வாங்கி யுண்ணுங்
கூழைமை பயின்ற கூற்ற வரசனைக் குதிக்குஞ் சூழ்ச்சி
reading: The ministers answer that they have not learned a stratagem to leap at the king of Death, who spreads sickness, takes lives by force and eats them.
event: The ministers confess that statecraft has no means against Death.

tamil: ஆயினக் காலன் பாணி யாம்பிற வரச செல்வம்
பாயிய வெழுந்த வேங்கை பாரிக்கு மளவிற் பைம்புன்
மாயிருஞ் சுருளை மேயு மான்மறி போலு மென்றான்.
reading: Then, says the king, the pleasures of royal wealth we enjoy and the life we wish to live are like a fawn grazing the green weed while the tiger prepares to spring.
nuance: The simile is the king's answer to the council's silence; it turns their confession into his own resolve.

tamil: இருங்களி யாணர் வாழ்விற் கிமைப்பிடை பெரிது கண்டாய்.
reading: The speaker answers that there is not even that much time: like a morsel falling into a rutting elephant's mouth, Death, glad with his crescent tooth, takes life in the space of a blink.
nuance: The speaker is not named; he addresses the king as வேந்தே, so a minister is meant.

tamil: முன்னிய முகமன் மாட்டா முற்றிய வறிவி னாரை
மன்னவன் மகிழ்ந்து நோக்கி வாழுயிர் வவ்வுங் காலன்
தன்னைநா மிகந்து சேருஞ் சரண்பிறி துரைமி னென்றான்.
reading: The king, who loses his life, says that flatterers who cannot serve the lord's interest with sweet words cannot help; look to the learned who advise him, and tell of some refuge we can reach beyond Death.
nuance: Lines 1-3 are hard to construe; the verse is read as the king rejecting courtly flattery and asking for refuge.
event: Payapati asks what refuge lies beyond Death.

tamil: இனியன போன்று தோன்றி நுகர்ந்தவற் கிறுதி செய்யும்
கனிபுரை கிளவி நீக்கிக் கண்ணனார் கருத்துட் கொண்டு
துனிவன நினையுங் காலன் றுணிவன துணியுஞ் சூட்சி
முனிவரை வணங்கிக் கேட்டு முயறுமோ வடிக ளென்றார்.
reading: Dismissing the pleasant flattery that ends only in ruin, the speaker, taking the king's thought to heart, asks, lord, whether they should try after bowing to the sages and hearing them.
nuance: கண்ணனார் is taken as the speaker's own epithet in line 2; the verse is uncertain in lines 2-3.
event: A minister proposes to seek the sages' counsel.

tamil: குருகயா வுயிர்க்குஞ் சோலைக் குளிரணிப் பழன நாட
முருகயா வுயிர்க்கும் பூவார் முறிமிடை படலை மாலைத்
திருவயா வுயிர்க்கு மார்பற் செறிதவர் சரண மூலத்
தருகயா வுயிர்ப்பி னல்லா லரண்பிறி தாவ துண்டோ.
reading: Lord of fertile lands, there is no refuge but to stay at the foot of the austere sage's feet, close under the tree of his refuge; what other refuge can there be?
nuance: The refuge is a person, the sage under his tree, not a god or a rite; the verse sets the sage's feet against the king's palace as a shelter.

title: துறவுச் சருக்கம் 1863-1885 (2/10)
theme: The king orders a drum proclaimed for a festival of the Lord at his golden temple under the Ashoka tree; the poet promises merit and a heavenly body to those who watch, the city and its folk dress and throng the streets, and the king rides out in full royal state while the poet says the onlookers' deeds died.
source_issues: Verses 1864 to 1867 were printed in eight half-lines and 1868 and 1869 likewise, and repaired into four lines by the build; read as four.
1871 lines 2 and 3 are corrupt as printed (சிந்தினார் யினா லென்னையவ் ...).
1863 line 2 names விசோதி, which is unclear as written.
1874, 1879 and 1882 carried a pulli after a vowel sign, repaired by the build.

cast.role: the king of Podanam who orders the festival, unnamed in these verses
the heroes whose words ease the king's mind in 1863
the people of the city who come out for the festival
the brahmins who carry flower offerings in the procession
the garlanded and gold-adorned folk of the procession
the women who wave the fly-whisks for the king

tamil: எரிகின்ற சுடரி னெய்பெய் திடுதிரி தூண்டி யாங்கு
விரிகின்ற புலமை வீரர் மொழிதலும் விசோதி யன்னாற்
பரிகின்ற வுரிமை வல்ல படரொழி மனத்த னானான்
சொரிகின்ற மதுவின் மாரித் துவலையி னனைந்த தாரான்.
reading: As the heroes speak, like a wick trimmed in a burning lamp of ghee, the king grows light of mind, free of the grief that weighed on him, and sits wet with the rain of honey from his garland.
nuance: The name in line 2, விசோதி, is not clear as written; it may be a name or a corrupt word, so who is likened to whom is not fixed. The lamp-wick simile makes the heroes' words the stirring that raises the king's flame; the verse does not say what they said.
event: The learned heroes speak and the king's mind is eased of its sorrow.

tamil: கரும்பணி மொழியி னார்தங் கருந்தடங் கண்ணும் வண்டும்
சுரும்பணை முலையி னாருந் தொடையலுந் துதைந்த மார்பன்
அரும்பணி யசோக நீழ லடிகள தணிபொற் கோயில்
விரும்பணி விழவு சாற்றி வியன்முர சறைக வென்றான்.
reading: The king, whose chest is thick with garlands and the dark eyes of women, orders a drum to be proclaimed for a festival in the lord's adorned golden temple under the Ashoka tree.
nuance: The speaker is taken to be the king of the previous verses because no other is named; the verse itself gives only 'he said'. The Ashoka shade names the Jina's tree, so the temple is the Arhat's, and the festival is a Jain royal act, though the verse does not say Jain.
event: The king commands that a drum proclaim a festival at the Lord's golden temple under the Ashoka tree.

tamil: ஒளியவ னுலகம் தன்னுட் கரந்தவ னுயிர்க ளுய்யும்
அளியவ னருள்செய் யாழி யுடையவ னடிமை செய்வார்க்
கெளியவ னெந்தை பெம்மாற் கியற்றிய விழவின் மிக்க
களியவ ரென்ப செம்பொற் கதிர்முடி சூடு வாரே.
reading: The poet praises the Lord as the radiant one hidden in the world, gracious to living beings, holder of the wheel, easy for his servants to reach, and says those most gladdened at the festival made for him will wear the golden crown.
nuance: The Lord is praised in the vocabulary of a world-ruler (the wheel, the hidden light) and the reward promised is kingship, so devotion is paid for in the coin the king already holds.

tamil: அருள்புரி யழலஞ் சோதி யாழியா னாதி யில்லான்
மருள்புரி வினைகட் கென்று மறுதலை யாய வாமன்
இருள்புரி யுலகஞ் சேரா வியனெறி பயந்த பெம்மான்
பொருள்புரி விழவு காண்பார் புண்ணிய வுலகங் காண்பார்.
reading: The Lord, the fire of grace and the beginning-less one, is the enemy of the deeds that bring delusion and showed the wide way that does not enter the dark world; whoever sees the festival made for him sees the world of merit.
nuance: The way out of the dark world is placed with the Lord, who is called beginning-less, but the verse does not say a maker: he shows the path, he does not grant release. The promise of merit's world for the onlooker sits beside the claim that he is the foe of deeds, so the festival is presented as a good deed done to one who stands against deeds.

tamil: கண்ணிய வறிவன் செல்வ விழவினுட் களித்த மாந்தர்
புண்ணியத் துகள்க ளென்னும் பொற்சுண்ணம் புதைய வாடிப்
பண்ணியன் மொழியி னார்தங் கருங்கண்ணாற் பருகு நீர்மை
விண்ணிய லுருவ மெய்தி விளங்கிவீற் றிருப்ப ரன்றே.
reading: Those who have rejoiced at the Lord's rich festival, bathed in the golden powder called the dust of merit and drinking the beauty of the sweet-voiced women with their dark eyes, will gain a celestial form and shine.
nuance: The powder is called merit's dust (புண்ணியத் துகள்) and is literally the festival's gold; the gaze on women is part of the pleasure that earns heaven, which the epic voices without reproof here, though the same sarukkam turns to renunciation.

tamil: எல்லைசான் முரசிற் சாற்றி யின்னன வறைத லோடும்
மல்லன்மா நகரங் கேட்டே வானுல கிழிந்த தேபோன்
முல்லைவான் கண்ணி சூடி முகிழ்நகைக் கலங்க டாங்கிச்
செல்லும்வாய் தோறுஞ் செல்வ விழவணி தேர்த்த தன்றே.
reading: At the proclamation by the great drum the city rejoices as though the sky-world had fallen to earth: people with jasmine garlands and smiling jewels fill every street, and the festival chariots go through every lane.
event: The drum is sounded and the whole city comes out adorned for the Lord's festival.

tamil: இன்னிசை முரசங் கேட்டே மெய்பெரி தினிய கேட்டா
மன்னிய நங்கள் வாணாள் வாழ்கநம் மிறைவ னென்னாப்
பொன்னியன் மலருஞ் சாந்துஞ் சுண்ணமும் புகையும் பொங்கத்
துன்னிய நகர மாந்தர் துறக்கம்பெற் றவர்க ளொத்தார்.
reading: Hearing the sweet drum, the people of the city say that their long lives are secure and bless their lord, and with flowers, sandal, powder and incense rising they seem to have gained heaven.
nuance: Whether நம் இறைவன் (our lord) is the king or the Jina is not fixed by the verse; both are possible, and the blessing's wish for long life reads with a sharp irony, since the king is moving toward renunciation.
event: The townspeople bless their lord on hearing the drum.

reading: Golden festoons hung with full jars were raised, white banners pressed together, and the sound of drums and conches silenced the roar of the cloud-dark sea.
The streets, plastered with fragrance, are strewn with pearls and gems, and the bright city is like the golden world fallen to earth.
nuance: The second and third lines are corrupt as printed (சிந்தினார் யினா லென்னையவ் ...), so who strews, and with what, is a reading from the first and last lines only.
event: The people strew pearls and gems on the festival streets.

reading: The smoke of thick aloe rising over the jewelled mansions looks like young clouds resting on a bright hill.
The people dress in white cloth, smear their bodies with white sandal, wear garlands of jasmine, and carry pearls, diamonds and other ornaments as their festival finery.
event: The townsfolk put on white clothes and ornaments for the festival.

reading: Elephants with two white tusks carry lotus-flower offerings that dazzle the eye and rival the sky, and brahmins bearing them stand in order in a way that perplexes the earth.
nuance: Lines 2 to 4 are hard to construe; brahmins here take part in a Jain-framed festival as bearers of offerings, a detail the verse states without comment.
event: Brahmins carry flower offerings on elephants in the procession.

reading: Garlanded folk with red-flowered chaplets and gold necklaces, with sandal ground with saffron and bracelets flashing on their hands, wearing body-flowers and finery, become kings.
event: The adorned throng stand dressed like kings.

reading: People with blue-lily crowns and red robes of the same colour, their bodies red, appear on elephants mingled with flowers in their hands.
event: Crowned riders appear on elephants.

reading: Folk in golden garlands scatter gold powder that gleams on their lightning-bright bodies, and the lords of the two treasures come in with soft flowers and ornaments.
nuance: The 'lords of the two treasures' (இருநிதிக் கிழவர்) is taken as a title of the wealthy; the verse does not say whom it names.
event: The throng and the lords of the two treasures gather.

reading: Wearers of yellow robes with bright golden jewels, carrying flower offerings, file on war-elephants with the women of full breasts, as they say.
event: Yellow-robed men on war-elephants process with women.

reading: As the city rises in uproar, with the conch and the drum sounding louder than the dark sea, the lord of the great army appears on a mountain-like elephant.
nuance: The rider is called செல்வன் without a name; he is taken as the king who ordered the festival in 1864.
event: The king rides out on a great elephant at the head of his army.

reading: Women with spear-bright eyes wave white chauris, and the king, in the shade of an umbrella with coral shaft and lord of the sea-girt earth, appears like a sea of horses surrounding him.
nuance: The umbrella, chauris and army are the insignia of kingship, set out at full height here.
event: The king appears under the white umbrella with fly-whisks waving.

reading: The horses spread in all directions, and many rutting elephants with diamond tusks, spouting a rain of rut and blowing out the fire of anger, press together in many kinds.
The instruments sounded, the elephants trumpeted, the chariots rolled, the many living things were covered by banners and the shower of flowers, and, they say, their deeds sweated and died.
nuance: The close reading of 'deeds sweated and perished' (வினைகள் வேர்த்தன விளிந்தன) is a figure of exhaustion and death; the verse puts it in the hearsay form என்ப, so the poet reports the claim without vouching for it in his own voice, and it turns on a rare word.

reading: On every side umbrellas of silver spread, and the fly-whisks waving in all directions look like the foam of the wide Milk Ocean rising in waves.
Fans of peacock feather and rounded screens hide the radiant one as they are set up, and the crowd finds no room to walk.
nuance: The radiant one (ஒளியவன்) is taken as the sun, as the umbrellas and fans cover the sky; 1865 uses the same word for the Lord, so the pun may be intended or the reading may be wrong.

reading: Fragrant sandal fills the censers and cool scent the incense boxes, and the flower-heaped baskets press close, one upon another.

title: துறவுச் சருக்கம் 1886-1908 (3/10)
theme: Payapati reaches the Jina shrine with flower and water offerings; the Lord appears under an asoka tree with throne, halo, umbrella, whisks, flower rain and heavenly music, and the king bows and sings a hymn praising his feet, his freedom from deeds and his rule above Indra and the dark-blue god.
source_issues: Verses 1903 to 1908 are printed in eight half-lines in the source and were joined into four lines each by the build; the joins follow the metre.
Lines 3 and 4 of 1908 and line 4 of 1904 are hard to parse; the readings given are marked uncertain.

cast.role: King Payapati, who comes to the Jina shrine and sings his hymn
the Lord or Jina, the knower, who appears under the asoka tree
the singers, dancers and praisers who crowd the shrine
the yakshas who hold the whisks beside the Lord
the gods who worship from the sky
the Vidyadharas who gather in the air with the kinnara pairs
the gem-hued red-eyed lord, with the golden-discus lord, who come beside the Lord
the queens who accompany the two lords

reading: Flower offerings fall in rows like a rain, bee-loud clusters of blossom pour down, auspicious banners spread, and the hosts of binding deeds are said to have hidden away.
nuance: The last line is reported speech (என்பவே), so the vanishing of karma is the poet's report of the scene, not an event he claims to see; the verse does not say whose presence drives the karma away.
event: Flowers rain and banners spread as the hosts of karma are said to hide.

reading: Singers, those who wish long life, dancers and those who praise the knower gather in crowds until no open space is left anywhere.
The poet asks us to hear how the oil-bright spearman fares as the seven-fold festival goes to the feet of the one who cast out the foes that are his deeds and taught the scripture's way aright.
nuance: The verse turns the story from the hall to the shrine and names the Lord only by what he did; the festival's seven parts are not listed.

reading: Arranging offerings of water, perfume and bee-loud flowers, the king, among the roar of his army, reaches the fair Jina shrine of the meritorious one.
nuance: The king is not named in the verse; he is known from the sarukkam's earlier verses.
event: Payapati arrives at the Jina shrine with water, perfume and flower offerings.

reading: At the gate of the high-towered shrine the king halts his young elephant, climbs down, takes bright flowers and circles the rich city with its gardens before arriving.
event: Payapati dismounts at the shrine gate and circles it with flowers in his hand.

reading: As the king arrives, the Lord appears seated on a lion throne beneath an asoka tree in the gold-adorned city, shining together with its light.
nuance: The asoka and the throne begin a series of the Jina's signs, the shade tree, flowers, music, whisks, throne, halo and umbrella, that the next verses spread across the scene.
event: The Lord appears to Payapati on a lion throne under an asoka tree.

reading: The throne is said to be gold set with rows of red gems, carved with elephant-trunk lions and sea-monster mouths, and its look spills five kinds of light.
nuance: Only the throne is described; the Lord seated on it is not.

reading: When the world sees the thousand-ray light, the darkness of the seven worlds leaves and deeds are said to wither; a ring of light appears around the Lord.
nuance: The second line is hard (ஆழியல் வினை கேளாடவிய), so whether the deeds wither or the dark withdraws from them is a reading; the halo (பாமண்டலம்) is not named.

reading: Yakshas with shoulders like tall trees raise whisks that look like milk-white moonbeams settled on masses of gem, their hands joined in worship.
nuance: The whisks stand among the eight signs of the Jina, borne by divine servants, not by the king's own men.

reading: The umbrella of the fragrant-tree Lord is a cluster of three, drinkable-bright with moonlike pearls, hemmed with gold and rich with light.
nuance: The three umbrellas answer the single white umbrella of the earthly king, who elsewhere rules the world under one; here a triple one rises over the Jina.

reading: Flaming flowers on the asoka that seem to feed a fire, ponds of lotus, and swarms of bees on the leafy asoka cool the place.
nuance: The asoka's red blooms look like fire but cool, so the image of heat is turned to calm.

reading: Banners like the sides of cloud-eyed women spread in rows, shapes like rain of song appear, and a rain of flowers buries the golden ground.
nuance: The flower rain here is the divine counterpart of the offered flowers in 1886.

reading: Gods clap their hands in worship, and sweet music sounds sadly on every side beneath rain-heavy flowers that mingle in the dark sky.
nuance: இரங்கி suggests the music sounds yearning, as if grieved; the verse does not say for what.

reading: Vidyadhara men and women with dark-eyed, wide-hipped companions mingle with pairs of kinnaras rising all over the upper air.
nuance: Each class of heavenly being is named by line, without any word on what the Lord does for them.

reading: The red-eyed gem-coloured one of the flame-bright crown, the one of the golden discus, and their queens appear beside the Lord of the rare gem hue.
nuance: The two gem-coloured figures are not named; the red eyes point to Tivittan of the earlier sarukkam and the golden discus to a discus-holder, but the verse does not fix who they are.
event: Two gem-hued lords and their queens come to stand beside the Lord.

reading: Seeing the gem-and-gold city that heaven's builders made, a sight to take away the eye, the king, whose deeds were shaking loose, stood as sovereign.
nuance: விண்டுதிர் வினையினன் vaguely says the king's deeds are dropping away; the verse leaves open whether that is cause or result of what he sees. The last words (வேந்தனாயினான்) are unusual, since he was already king.
event: Payapati sees the divine city and stands before the Lord.

reading: Having anointed the ground with perfume and set many flowers as ornaments, the king bows until his gem-crown touches the earth and, his deeds already cut, begins his hymn to the Lord.
nuance: துணிபடு வினையினன் is said of the worshipper before the hymn begins, so the cutting of deeds comes with the act of devotion, not after the praise.
event: Payapati prepares the ground, bows with his crown to the earth and begins to praise the Lord.

tamil: மூவடிவி னாலிரண்டு சூழ் சுடரு நாண முழுதுலக மூடியெழின் முளைவயிர நாற்றித்
தூவடிவி னாலிலங்கு வெண்குடையி னீழற் சுடரோ யுன்னடிபோற்றிச் சொல்லுவதொன் றுண்டால்
சேவடிக டாமரையின் சேயிதழ்க டீண்டச் சிவந்தனவோ சேவடியின் செங்கதிர்கள் பாயப்
பூவடிவு கொண்டனவோ பொங்கொளிகள் சூழ்ந்து புலங்கொளா வாலெமக்கெம் புண்ணியர்தங் கோவே.
reading: The king asks of the Lord, whose white umbrella's shade and gem-bright light put the sun and moon to shame, whether his red feet were reddened by the lotus-petals touching them or whether their red rays took the shape of flowers.
nuance: The poet turns the Lord's feet into a question about cause (do the lotuses redden them, or the feet the lotuses?), a conceit of praise, not a doctrine; the stanza is printed in eight half-lines and was joined into four.
event: Payapati's hymn begins with a question about the Lord's red feet.

tamil: கருமாலை வெவ்வினைகள் காறளர நூறிக் கடையிலா வொண்ஞானக் கதிர்விரித்தா யென்றும்
அருமாலை நன்னெறியை முன்பயந்தா யென்றும் அடியேமுன் னடிபரவு மாறறிவ தல்லால்
திருமாலே தேனாரு மரவிந்த மேந்துந் திருவணங்கு சேவடியாய் தேவாதி தேவ
பெருமானே நின்பெருமை நன்குணர மாட்டார் பிணங்குவார் தம்மைவினைப் பிணக்கொழிக்க லாமே.
reading: The king says the Lord cut the dark garlands of fierce deeds, spread the bright light of unending knowledge and gave a fair path; his servants know only to praise his feet, but those who do not know his greatness and quarrel can have the quarrel of deeds removed.
nuance: The last line (பிணங்குவார் தம்மை வினைப் பிணக்கொழிக்கலாமே) is hard: it may say the disputants' own deeds are ended by worship, or the Lord's power could end the quarrel of deeds in them. Also read the half-line division: the stanza is printed in eight half-lines and was joined into four.

tamil: ஒளியாகி யுலகாகி நீவிரிந்தா யென்கோ உலகெலா நின்னொளியி னுள்ளடங்கிற் றென்கோ
அளியார யுலகநீ யாள்கின்றா யென்கோ அமருலகு தானின்ன தடியடைந்த தென்கோ
விளியாத மெய்ப்பொருளை நீவிரித்தா யென்கோ நீவிரித்த வாறேமெய்ப் பொருள்விரிந்த தென்கோ
தெளியாம லில்லைநின் றிருவடிகண் மெய்ம்மை தெளிந்தாலுஞ் செவ்வனே தெரிந்துரைக்க லாமே.
reading: Shall I say you spread as light and as the world, or that the world lies within your light, that you rule the world with grace, that heaven has taken your feet; shall I say you spread true being, or that true being spread as you spread it? Only by understanding your feet will it be known.
nuance: The repeated என்கோ (shall I say) lets the hymn put two ways of speaking side by side, the Lord as source and the Lord as container, without choosing; the king says the choice is settled only by understanding.

tamil: களியானை நாற்கோட்ட தொன்றுடைய செல்வன் கண்ணொரா யிரமுடையான் கண்விளக்க மெய்தும்
ஒளியானை யூழி முத லானானை யோங்கி உலகளவு மாகியுயிர் தமக்குறுகண் செய்யா
அளியானை யாரழலஞ் சோதிவாய் சூழ்ந்த அருளாழி யானையிணை யடிபரவு வார்கட்
கெளியானை யெந்தை பெரு மானையே யல்லால் இறையாக வீங்கொருவ ரெண்ணுமா றென்னே.
reading: The Lord is the one who gives light to the thousand-eyed Indra, who is the beginning of ages, spreads to the world's measure, harms no living thing, is easy for those who worship his feet; how then can anyone count any other as god?
nuance: Indra, the four-tusked elephant's owner of thousand eyes (line 1), is placed beneath the Jina as a receiver of his light, which turns the heaven's lord into a worshipper. The rival god is not named; the claim is aimed at any other claimant.

tamil: தெருளாமை யால் வினவற் பாலதொன் றுண்டு திருவடிகள் செம்பொனா ரரவிந்த மேந்த
இருளாழி யேழுலகுஞ் சூழொளியின் மூழ்க இமையாத செங் கண்ணி னிமையோர்வந் தேத்த
உருளாழி யானு மொளி மணிமுடிமேற் கைவைத் தொருபாலில் வரவுலக நின்னுழைய தாக
அருளாழி முன்செல்லப் பின்செல்வ தென்னோ அடிப்படா தாய்நின்ற வான்ஞால முண்டோ.
reading: The king asks why, when the golden feet are held by celestials with unblinking eyes, the dark gods' world is flooded by his light, and the discus-lord with his hand on his crown stands to one side, the wheel of grace goes in front and others follow; is there a heaven that does not lie at his feet?
nuance: The question pattern (தெருளாமையால் வினவற்பாலது) is a deferential form: the poet claims not to know why, though the question itself carries the claim. The discus-lord is not named and may be Vishnu or a world-emperor.

tamil: வானோர்த முலகுடைய மானீல வண்ணன் மகிழ்ந்திறைஞ்சு மாலையணி மணிமுடிமேல் வைகா
ஊனாரு மறவாழி யோடைமால் யானை உடையான்ற னொளிமுடியின் மேலுரையோ நிற்கத்
தேனாரு மரவிந்தஞ் சென்றேந்தும் போழ்து திருவடிகள் செந்தோடு தீண்டாவே யாகில்
ஆனாவிம் மூவுலகு மாளுடைய பெம்மான் அடியுறுவா ரின்மைதா மறிவுண்ட தன்றே.
reading: The king says that the Lord's feet are above even the talk about the garlanded crown of the dark-blue lord whom the heavens praise, and that if the feet do not touch the lotus offered by those who go to carry it, it means that the lack of those who would stand at his feet has been known.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are very hard and turn on the sense of அடியுறுவார் இன்மை; the reading here is cautious. If the dark-blue lord is Vishnu, the verse shows a Jain poet placing Vishnu at the Jina's feet, a claim the poet voices, not a view of Vaishnavas.

title: துறவுச் சருக்கம் 1909-1931 (4/10)
theme: After worshipping the Jina, the king bows to a sage, and the sage, at the ministers' plea to turn away births, lists his topics, names the four states and the seven hells, and describes the first hell's pits and the sufferers who entered by their own deeds.
source_issues: 1909-1912 print as eight half-lines in the source; the tool joined them into four lines.
1917 and 1918 are obscure and their speakers are not fixed by the text.

cast.role: King Payapati of Podanam, who turns to renunciation
the Lord the king worships, taken as the Jina
the sage of great austerity whom the king meets
the king's counsellors who ask the sage to turn away births
those born in the hell pits
the tormentors who crowd round the sufferers

tamil: தேனருளி மந்தாரச் செந்தாமந் தாழ்ந்து திரளரைய செம்பவளம் வம்பாக வூறி
வானருளி மாணிக்கச் செங்கதிர்கள் வீசி மதிமருட்டும் வெண்குடையோர் மூன்றுடைய வாமன்
யானருள வேண்டியடி யிணைபணியும் போழ்து இமையவர்கோ னாயிரச் செங்கணான் வந்து
தானருளு மாறென்று தாள்பணியும் போழ்துந் தகையொன்ற தேலிறைமை தக்கதே யன்றே.
reading: The speaker says that when even Indra of the thousand red eyes comes and bows at the feet of the lord under the three white umbrellas, seeking his grace, then that lord's godhead is surely fitting.
nuance: The verse does not name its speaker or the Lord; both are taken from the praise that closes at 1913, where the king bows to the Lord, so the speaker is the king by inference.

tamil: விண்டாங்கு வெவ்வினை வெரூஉவுதிர நூறி விரிகின்ற மெய்ஞ்ஞானச் சுடர் விளக்கு மாட்டிக்
கண்டார்க ணின்னிலைமை கண்டொழுக யானின் கதிர்மயங்கு சோதியாற் கண்விளக்கப் பட்டுத்
தண்டாஅ மரைமலரின்மே னடந்தா யென்றுந் தமனீயப் பொன்னணையின் மேலமர்ந்தா யென்றும்
வண்டார சோகி னிழல் வாயமர்ந்தா யென்றும் வாழ்த்தினால் வாராயோ வானவர்தங்கோவே.
reading: The speaker praises the Lord as one who has struck down fierce deeds, lit the lamp of true knowledge, walked on the lotus and sat on the golden seat and under the ashoka's shade, and asks whether the king of the gods will not come when so praised.
nuance: The lotus, golden seat and ashoka tree are the stock marks of an arhat's court; the verse uses them as praise epithets, not as events.

tamil: கருவார்ந்த பொருணிகழ்வுங் காலங்கண் மூன்றுங் கடையிலா நன்ஞானக் கதிரகத்த வாகி
ஒருவாதிங் கவ்வொளியி னின்னுள்ள வாகில் உலகெல்லா நின்னுளத் தேயொளிக்க வேண்டா
திருவார்ந்த தண்மார்ப தேவாதி தேவ திரளரைய செந்தளி ரசோகமர்ந்த செல்வ
வருவாரும் வையகமு நீயும்வே றாகி மணிமேனி மாலே மயக்குவதிங் கென்னோ.
reading: The speaker tells the Lord that things that come to be and the three times lie inside his endless light of knowledge, and asks why he should be dazed by a world that is no different from himself.
nuance: The last two lines are hard: the verse seems to ask what use there is in an all-knowing lord being dazzled by the world, but the sense of the vocative lines is not firm.

tamil: செங்க ணெடுமாலே செறிந்திலங்கு சோதித் திருமுயங்கு மூர்த்தியாய் செய்யதா மரையின்
அங்கணடி வைத்தருளு மாதியா யாழி அறவரசே யென்றுநின் னடிபணிவ தல்லால்
எங்க ணிட ரகலுமா றிந்நிலைமை யெய்தி இருளுலக நீக்குமரு டருகநீ யென்று
வெங்கணிரு வினையையற வென்றாய்முன்னின்று விண்ணப்பஞ் செய்யும் விழுத்தகைமை யுண்டோ.
reading: The speaker addresses the Lord as the holy king of dharma and says that bowing at his feet and begging him to remove their distress and light the dark world is a merit greater than any, since he has wholly conquered the two deeds.
nuance: The two deeds (இருவினை) are read as good and bad deed; the verse does not say so.

reading: Having praised and bowed to the Lord, the king lays his head at the conqueror's feet, circles his shrine, and enters another golden pillared hall.
nuance: The king is not named here; he is the subject carried over from the praise.
event: The king worships the Jina, circles his shrine and enters the pillared platform hall.

reading: In that hall sits a sage, firm like a great mountain with his many austere virtues, and the king wipes the dust from his lotus feet with the garland on his golden crown.
nuance: The king's crown-garland becomes a cloth for the sage's feet: the ruler lowers the sign of his rank before an ascetic.
event: The king touches the sage's feet with the tip of the garland on his crown.

reading: The sage, whose great austerity has closed the springs that feed deeds and whose word is a mantra none can turn back, sits, and the king takes the seat that was fitting.
nuance: ஊற்றுச் செறித்த is a Jain image of closing the channels of inflow (asrava); the verse has the word for springs only.
event: The king takes the seat offered him before the sage.

reading: As the king sits bowed, the garlanded ministers say to the sage that he should feed them the nectar that ends torment and turn aside the tangled births so that they may be saved.
nuance: The ministers ask for the teaching as a drink of nectar, so the plea is for relief from rebirth, not for advice on statecraft, which they could not give at 1857.
event: The ministers ask the sage to feed them teaching that will turn away their births.

reading: A speaker, with the king seated on his throne, remarks that the king who has had so much of the sweet wealth is asking about the holy greatness of dharma, and asks what it is that he is asking.
nuance: Who asks and who answers is not fixed by the words: this is read as the king's turn to speak, but it could be the sage testing him.
event: The king puts a question about dharma, or is questioned about it, before the sage.

reading: The verse says of one who eats the food laid before him that he does not know how to bring his course to an end and does not mind its long-hated nature, and says the same of the handsome lord.
nuance: The verse is obscure: it seems to describe a lord who enjoys his meals and has not learned how to end his round of births. The identification of the handsome lord with the king is a guess.

reading: After the ministers have spoken, the king of austerity, whom the gods of the sky honour and whom the rule of his teaching has made great, begins to set out the matter for the king as if for Indra.
nuance: The king is likened to Indra, as the sage is likened to a king of austerity: each is named in the other's terms.
event: The sage begins his exposition for the king.

reading: The great ascetic tells the lord to listen, and lists what he will tell: the states of rebirth, the deceit within them, the deed that fixes fate, the ways of conquering deeds, and the glory of the release the wise desire.
nuance: This is a table of contents for what follows: hells, then (outside this chapter) the other states, then deeds and release.
event: The sage sets out his five topics: rebirths, deeds and their conquest, and release.

reading: The sage says that souls whirl like the turning cart wheel, the ring thrown by one without release and the drifting dust, and that there are four states they seek.
nuance: Wheel, ring and dust are three pictures of the same turning: the soul has no fixed place and is moved by what it has done.
event: The sage names four destinies that turn the souls.

reading: The sage names the four states as the hell-dwellers, the beasts, men and the good gods, and says an account of their kinds would grow long, so the king, whose heart melts, hears one way of telling it.
nuance: The sage promises brevity here and then spends the rest of the chapter on the hells.
event: The sage names the four states and says he will tell them briefly.

reading: The sage says the lower hells are cut into forty-nine layers, and that the dwellings of those who go to them number eighty-four lakhs.
nuance: The numbers rest on a reading of ஏழாயிருபத்திரட்டியோடொன்பது as seven hells made of forty-nine layers; the verse gives only the numbers.
event: The sage counts the layers and dwellings of the lower hells.

reading: The sage says the hells are named by what they are: darkness of darkness, darkness, smoke, merciless mire, sand, gravel and the bright stone, and the king should take each as its name says.
nuance: The last of the seven, மணி, is read as the gem-stone of the first hell; the verse says only மருளின் மணி.
event: The sage names the seven hells.

reading: The sage says that the pain of those who have gone into the hells would make even the tellers shudder, and that he will give the words for the first of them.
nuance: The sage says the telling itself would chill the speakers: the verse turns the description into a warning to a listener already uneasy.
event: The sage begins to describe the first hell.

reading: The sage says the first hell has thirteen levels with thirty lakh of dwellings, pits blazing with fire, and that there is no end to their number.
event: The sage counts the pits of the first hell.

reading: The pits are like chests split open, like cave mouths, like jars and pots, deep and wide with slippery mire, and are the place where wicked men are born.
nuance: Birth, not arrival, is the word: the hell-dweller is born in the pit rather than sent to it.

reading: When the pits have taken shape and wailing bodies fill them, the beings slip onto burning rock and lie rolling, scorched and crumbled like worms.
event: The pit-born beings fall on burning rock and writhe like worms.

reading: Crumbled like worms they swell and rise, and after the smoke has risen they fall again and tumble in the same way, in a torment that never ceases for as long as their life lasts.
nuance: The pain is endless only for the life-span there: the verse limits the torment to it, not to eternity.

reading: Those who cry 'alas, dharma' find no one who says 'we have come' and takes them out; burned and still not dying, they entered the pit through their own earlier striving in deeds.
nuance: The cry is to dharma, not to a god, and no rescuer answers; the verse makes the cause the sufferers' own earlier striving, not a judge's decree.
event: The sufferers cry out and no one answers, because their own earlier deeds sent them in.

reading: Some of cruel and licentious craft crowd around the sufferers and torment them, telling them to take in turn the many fruits of the deed they did before.
nuance: The identity of the tormentors is not given beyond their trade; they are read as hell's attendants because they act on the sufferers.
event: Hell's attendants torment the sufferers and tell them to take the fruit of their own earlier deeds.

title: துறவுச் சருக்கம் 1932-1954 (5/10)
theme: The sage, answering King Payapati's turn to renunciation, describes the hells in detail: the matched tortures of adulterers, meat-eaters, slanderers and oppressors, then the doubling of pain, size and life span down the layers, and then who falls there.
source_issues: 1941 line 1 has an unclear bracketed ending in பெரிது.
1946 line 1 (எழுவின்) and line 4 (முக்காவதமே) are hard to read, so the size figures are uncertain.
1949 lines 1-2 contain words that look corrupt (உடையந்தலி).
1954 lines 3-4 are hard to construe.
The speaker is not named in these verses: the sage's identity and the start of his speech come from the earlier verses, which are not in this chapter.

cast.role: the sage who tells King Payapati of the hells, named only by his speech; the text of these verses gives no name
the wardens of hell who inflict the torments, not named in the verses
the beings suffering in hell
King Payapati, the sage's hearer, addressed by vocatives such as 'one with the jasmine garland'

reading: In the dark of night the guilty went to a neighbour's house and took pleasure there; in hell the wardens say 'see, this is she' and make them embrace figures of blazing fire set in copper heated to the red of coals.
nuance: The punishment answers the offence in kind: the secret night-visit becomes a forced embrace, and the wardens' mocking 'see, this is she' repeats the lover's own pleasure back to him.
event: Hell's wardens make adulterers embrace fiery copper figures of women.

reading: Dogs the wardens have raised in cages for this purpose, with sharp claws and huge gaping mouths, tear at the victims, who scream and try to climb a tree built of thorns.
nuance: The dogs are reared for the task, so the torment is an orderly institution, not the chance cruelty of passing demons.
event: Hell's dogs seize the victims, who flee up a thorn tree.

reading: The wardens show the victims great lumps of flesh as the food they craved and, saying 'look at these', pour into their open mouths masses of copper that has drunk fire.
nuance: The offered 'flesh' is the bait the offender once craved, which makes the metal a grim parody of the meal.
event: Wardens force molten copper into the mouths of those who ate flesh.

reading: Those who killed many deer and fawns and ate the meat are cut limb by limb and fed their own limbs by the wardens, in one quarter of hell.
nuance: The penalty reverses the act exactly: the eater becomes the carved animal and the food together.
event: Wardens carve meat-eaters limb by limb and feed them the pieces.

reading: Those who used many words against the weak and, wanting their goods, punished them are beaten on their foul bodies with thorn clubs and tremble and roll, as the fruit of that wrong.
event: Wardens beat with thorn clubs those who wronged the weak for their property.

reading: Those who did hateful things and spoke slander against their betters have the tongue torn out with pincers, and diamond-hard thorns are driven under the nails of some.
nuance: The word the verse uses for the slander (குறிப்பு) is a hint or insinuation, so even veiled speech is punished with the tongue.
event: Wardens pull out slanderers' tongues and drive thorns under their nails.

reading: Wardens roast the imprisoned in blazing fire, boil them in heated caustic, make many turn inside an oil-press mortar and flay the body, in one quarter of hell.
event: Wardens roast, boil, press and flay the hell-beings.

reading: Wardens seize and tear, split chests with axes and impale on stakes quickly, and the sage tells the king, wearing great ornaments, that this is the fruit of their deeds.
nuance: The last line turns a catalogue of cruelties into a verdict: no judge is named, only vinai ripening.
event: Wardens tear, split and impale the hell-beings while the sage names it the ripening of deeds.

reading: Wardens seize the hands, cut off the fingers, scrape the body, crush the bones so that they fall apart, and hurl others down from a mountain.
event: Wardens maim the hell-beings and throw them from a mountain.

reading: Hell-beings tortured by a terrible thirst cry for water; the wardens show them pools of rare poison, and they rush, drink, and cry out with rotting tongues.
nuance: The relief offered is itself the harm: the pools are the form their thirst takes.
event: Wardens show poison pools to the thirsty, who drink and cry out.

reading: Unable to bear the heat they run, and entering a long grove thinking it shade, fire-wind pours on their heads and they fall down burning.
nuance: Shade is another false relief, like the pools of the previous verse.
event: The hell-beings flee into a grove that burns them.

reading: The sage tells the king, wearing a garland of jasmine buds, that in the first layer there are thousands of crores of sorrows, and that each lower layer holds twice that unbounded pain.
nuance: The first-person 'I told' in the next verse shows that the whole description of the hells since 1932 is the sage's speech to the king.
event: The sage tells Payapati that the pain of hell doubles with each lower layer.

reading: He says that he has told the span of the sufferers' fall, their order and other matters, doubling in each lower layer, leaving aside the one thing he calls shining knowledge.
nuance: The last line seems to set aside a knowledge that only a knower can tell, but the grammar is doubtful.

reading: The poison that is not rained, the great pits of fire, the pits no one dug and the ponds of foul water make such a stench that no other living thing survives within a yojana of the hell.
nuance: The stench is described as a force that kills outsiders, which marks hell as a sealed region.

reading: The first layer's beings are given a measure in bows, cubits and fingers, and the beings of the lower layers grow larger without limit, to a size stated in yojanas and kavatams.
nuance: The measures are stated in units whose reading is hard to fix.

reading: The lowest life span is ten thousand years, the longest life is the measure of the sea, and the life spans increase going down; the least in each lower layer is the greatest of the one above.
The life spans are listed in sea-measures: three, seven, ten, seventeen, twenty-two and thirty-three, rising down the layers.
nuance: The list gives six figures, with the first layer's one sea measure implied.

reading: The foul-eared, bright-toothed wicked ones eat poison, and the others of the hell, kindling a fight for them to watch, crowd in, fall and suffer great pain.
nuance: Some words (உடையந்தலி) are corrupt, so the exact sense of the first two lines is uncertain.
event: Hell's inhabitants are set to fight while others watch, and suffer.

reading: They are cooked in fire but do not die, they lie in the mire and do not perish, they wander in smoke without rest, and their pitiable pain would make even a hunter with arrow and bow feel pity.
nuance: The hunter who would pity is the very kind of killer that earlier verses of the list put in hell.

reading: Asking who falls into the deep sorrow of that place, the sage answers the king, wearing a fresh garland, that it is those who give up their own wives and lie with other men's women with flowered hair.
nuance: From here the sage turns from the torments to the sins that earn them.

reading: Cruel-hearted people who love killing, and those with a cruel nature who take others' goods, will reach hell, the sage says to the king who struck down his foes.
nuance: The address to the king as one who felled enemies leaves open that the sage may point at the king's own acts.

reading: Those who scorn good dharma, gather wealth with toil, and die hard-fisted without doing householder's dharma, and those who revile poets who do not take up petty dharma and do wrong from ignorance, are also in the list.
nuance: Householder's dharma is here a duty whose neglect is punished, not a lesser way next to renunciation.

reading: The sage says the king has joined to the list the sea-dwelling fishers with boats and rafts who take life for bait, and those the king himself had punished.
nuance: The last line may say that the king has already put such people in the same company as those he punished; it is unclear.

title: துறவுச் சருக்கம் 1955-1977 (6/10)
theme: The sage ends his account of hell and tells Payapati of the beasts: their one- to five-sensed births and the nigoda below, the tortures men inflict on them, the deceit and hatred that cause a beast's birth, and the deniers sent to the nigoda, then the island peoples counted among animals.
source_issues: 1964 line 3 carried a pulli after a vowel sign, repaired by the build.
The words சேகர், மிலைச்சர் and கடிப்பியர் (1971 to 1977) are rare technical terms of the Jain scheme of human kinds, so 1971, 1972 and 1977 are marked uncertain.
1959, 1961, 1963, 1964, 1966 and 1969 turn on hard words or lines and are marked uncertain.

cast.role: King Payapati, addressed by the sage as king, who has turned toward renunciation
the sage who instructs the king; these verses do not name him
those who say there is no soul and no rebirth, as the sage describes them

reading: The sage closes his account of hell: those sunk in its unquenchable fire do not grasp the good teaching, and some who do rise to a better state do not stay there, so nothing more need be said of them.
nuance: It closes the long hell passage (1932 to 1954) and turns, in the next verse, to animal births, so the sarukkam's tour of the bad states runs hell first, then animals, then the island peoples.

reading: The sage tells the king to consider the animal births as they multiply, running from the one-sensed up to those that end with the five senses, spread through the good earth.
In the long-suffering nigoda births many souls labour having reached only one sense, and a few of them do move out of that state.
nuance: The nigoda is the lowest stratum of Jain life-forms; the verse says only that some leave it, not how or why.

reading: One-sensed lives suffer, and few are wise enough to know how they are destroyed, so those of dull understanding kill them.
nuance: Harm is traced to a failure of perception, not to malice: the killers are those lacking sharp knowledge (கூரறிவில்லவர்).

reading: Apart from one of the six classes of life, the other named classes of birth are destroyed by people who act as if enraged while the world trembles, without cherishing them.
nuance: Which one of the six classes is excepted cannot be told from the four lines; the verse does not name them.

reading: The remaining moving kinds, from elephants down, are the harmless beasts, and men seize and torment them by force, so that on one side the fat of their flesh runs.
nuance: The suffering is described at its worst in the seizing and cooking of the animal: the line about melting fat (ஊனெய் உருகும்) is the grimmest of the run.

reading: Beasts ridden and loaded with great weights, with legs broken and sinking, are cut and refused and chosen for killing by those who enjoy meat, while some waste away.
nuance: The lines move from the animal as burden-bearer to the animal as meat; the same owner's use and his appetite are laid side by side. Several rare words make the sense of the third line less sure.

reading: Beasts are cut down by the sellers of flesh, crushed by those who cannot stop, and killed by cruel-bowed hunters, so that the animals' pain, the sage tells the king, never lets up.
nuance: Three trades of killing are named in turn: the flesh-seller, the one who breaks the animal, and the hunter. The sage lists occupations that live on animal death, without saying here that each earns its own rebirth.

reading: The sage says that the pitiable beasts look to everyone with their pain, and that even those who stand before them as good people try to be free of them and be done.
nuance: The last two lines are hard to construe: they may say that even people of worth, shown the animals' pain, turn from it rather than help. The reading is a best guess.

reading: The longing of maidens, the sickness that grips even the gods and the burning pain of the suffering animal, the sage says, are known only to ones like himself, so the king should not suppose them small.
nuance: The line pairing the maidens' longing and the gods' sickness with the animals' pain seems to place all three as kinds of suffering, but the third verse line is not clear; the pulli after a vowel sign in line 3 was repaired by the build.

reading: Some animals waste away shrinking from the loud or the foul, and some perish at the hands of cruel people who offer them to deities that take offerings, as the king is told.
nuance: The verse does not argue against sacrifice; it lists it among the ways an animal dies. The Jain objection to offerings is in the choice of that list.

reading: While mothers rear their young, the young look at them and think of them in love and lie apart or cling, and even so, on one side, they meet countless troubles.
nuance: The verse seems to say that even the tenderness between animal mothers and young does not spare them harm. The construal of line 3 is not secure.

reading: Asking who becomes these suffering beasts, the sage says: those who take up great austerity and afterwards work deceits are born as these.
nuance: The sage names the cause of animal birth as hypocrisy after vows, not as ordinary wrongdoing, so the fault is falling from a state the person had taken up.

reading: Those who join deceit to wealth, who bewilder others into folly with dark hearts that count none of their own faults, and who lack grace, also become these beasts.
Those who cling and hate, speak many angers and go out in wrath, and who draw near to what destroys kin, enter the births that these beasts have.
nuance: The third line is hard to construe (the word துவர்ப்பகை is not clear); the verse is read here as stating the causes of animal birth from clinging, hatred and rage.

reading: Sinners who say that there is no soul, no rebirth and no good or evil if one examines it, and who feast on harm, go without pause to the nigoda state.
nuance: The denial is given in the Jain sage's summary and is answered by the penalty it is said to bring, not by argument here; the school is not named, so the view is the sage's account of such deniers, not a statement a materialist would sign.

reading: Cloud-like generous kings' sons and sky-travelling folk, and many kinds of humans such as the Segar and Milechchar, are counted in the sage's scheme as enjoyers' humans.
nuance: The rare words (சேகர், மிலைச்சர், கடிப்பியர்) name classes of humans in the Jain scheme; I read the verse as a list of human kinds, not as a claim about any one of them.

reading: The ten kinds of the Segar, in the declining age of Bharata and Airavata, lack clear mind, conduct and knowledge, as if their understanding were dead.
nuance: The declining age is named only by the word இழிவு (fall); the verse is a cosmological tag for the kind of human the sage is describing.

reading: Among humans who live in the island lands, those called Milechchar are counted, the sage says, among animals, and beings of that sort die as such.
nuance: The verse ranks a whole people by birth-state; it states the Jain classification and does not argue it. The rest of the passage (1974 to 1977) gives the marks of the class.

reading: They have long tails and curved teeth, one leg each, no learning, ears four in number and harmful tusks, lack conduct and live in the island.
nuance: The portrait is of an imagined people at the edge of the world, drawn with marks of beasts; the verse says nothing of real peoples.

reading: Except for the bare fact of human birth they are pale animals, naked, shameless in conduct, gathered on the soil and living by digging and eating earth.
nuance: The verse faults nakedness together with shameless conduct (நாணா ஒழுக்கினர்); it does not say nakedness alone is the fault.

reading: Eating flowers and fruit, many Milechchar live in garden trees, and the sage tells the king to consider that their lives last without end for one palyopama.
nuance: The palyopama is the Jain unit for a vast span of years; the verse gives the lifespan, not the reason for it.

reading: Those joined to the Milechcha lands, though of faultless human form, are of shrinking mind and cruel livelihood, and the sage says that these base ones too he lowers like water.
nuance: The last line (நீச அவரையும் நீரின் இழிப்பாம்) is hard to construe; it is read as a statement that even the human-looking among them are put down.

title: துறவுச் சருக்கம் 1978-2000 (7/10)
theme: In the Renunciation sarukkam a sage tells the king which kinds of people are low and how rare is a human birth, shows pleasure as honey over a pit, names the four paths of effort and spends the rest on giving: its three grades, the giver's seven qualities, its fruit in kingship and the harm of giving to the cruel.
source_issues: The teacher is not named in 1978-2000; he is taken as the sage Payapati's ministers proposed seeking in chapter 80, from the sarukkam, and the addressee as the king (1997 கோவே, 2000 மன்ன).
1979 line 2, 1981 line 4, 1993 lines 1-2, 1994, 1995 lines 1-2 and 2000 turn on rare or damaged words; their readings are marked uncertain or hedged in nuance.

cast.role: the teaching sage who instructs the king on the rarity of human birth and on giving; unnamed in these verses and taken to be the sage the ministers sought in chapter 80
King Payapati, addressed as the garlanded one and the king (கோவே, மன்ன)

reading: Asked who the Koodar, Milechchar and Kumanudar are, the teacher answers: those who, spinning endless quibbles, weigh good qualities and yet will not accept them, and have nothing good in them.
nuance: The verse opens a list of lesser kinds of men and names them only by their quibbling; the three labels are the teacher's, and the outsider word மிலைச்சர் is used here as a term of low standing, not as a tribe the verse describes.
