reading: The same low company includes those of unrestrained lineage who cannot be restrained, those who eat flesh together with other forbidden things, and those who begin deeds that the high-minded never begin.
nuance: The verse measures the low by what they eat and do, not by birth alone, though line 1 speaks of lineage. Line 2 is hard: the word விடங்கார் may be 'poison-black' or a damaged form, so exactly what is eaten is not fixed.

reading: Among such births some become these kinds, some sink into low states and dwindle away soon after joining, and others, the teacher says, are past the reach of knowledge.
nuance: The verse lists fates after the types of 1978-1979 without naming them, and its last half-line is hard to construe, so it is read loosely.

reading: Even among those born in the lands where humans live, within the two and a half continents, many are no better than hangers-on, for their efforts never join the three classes.
nuance: The 'two and a half continents' is the Jain measure of the human world; the three classes are not named here, and the comparison to kinsfolk (ஒக்கல்) may rather mean 'like the household's hangers-on'. Both are uncertain.

reading: Those mingled with the three classes who are fools in a crowd and cannot judge what is fit and unfit are not to be called people, and the king is told to treat them as chaff thrown aside.
nuance: Humanity is made a matter of discernment (தக்க தகா), not of birth; this is the teacher's judgment, spoken to a king who must himself discern.

reading: Good lands and good forms are not found just where one chooses to be born, so to pass beyond the countless wombs and reach them is very hard.
nuance: The verse says good births are hard to win; it does not say here by what means, which 1985 gives.

reading: No one counts the eunuch, the blind and the like as human, and even when everything else is in order, birth as a woman is not an honoured one.
nuance: This is the teacher's view in a Jain work, set among marks of a lesser birth, and the epic gives it without reply here; it is the epic's view of women's standing as a birth, not a general truth about women. The first word அண்ணை is obscure.

reading: Of the eighty-four hundred thousand kinds of birth, only those who hold firmly to a gladdening good deed come to this human body.
nuance: The figure 84 lakh of yonis is the classical Jain count of kinds of birth; the verse makes karma the sole means of reaching the human body.

reading: Even a child who, from the first days in the womb, forms and grows without fault will meet many sufferings that cannot be fully told.
nuance: The verse puts the pain of life before birth, so even a fair birth is not a good fortune.

reading: The infant crosses the harsh wilderness of childhood and the faults of youth; if one gets through the forest with difficulty, one reaches old age and, failing, goes to another state.
nuance: Life is drawn as a wilderness with three stages; the 'other state' (கதி) is the next birth, not extinction.

reading: As a man chased by an elephant hangs over a deep pit with a snake in it and licks a falling drop of honey, so the king should weigh the pleasure of human life.
nuance: This is the well-known parable of the man hanging in a pit between an elephant and a snake; the verse gives its parts compactly and does not say what gnaws the rope, so the image is read in its common form. It makes pleasure real but small, not unreal.

reading: For two people living together in love, wanting pleasure, many sufferings arise with the ties between them; the verse is read as saying that without these ties effort would be wholly work.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are hard: the sense of முற்றும் தொழிலே is not fixed, and the verse may say that without those ties effort would be pure labour.

reading: For those born into this state there is one lasting thing, won by vows: the firm effort that leads to the golden lands of the heavens and of enjoyment.
nuance: The reward is the heavens and enjoyment lands, not release; the epic does not here say vows lead to liberation.

reading: Though the ways of firm effort are many in telling, count them as four: one's own conduct, giving, austerity and worship.
nuance: The first of the four, தன்னியல், is read as one's own conduct; the verse gives no more than the list, and 1992 onwards deal with the second, giving.

reading: Giving is said to be of best, middle and lowest grade, depending on a faultless receiver, the giver and the gift, and the gift itself must be beyond reproach.
nuance: The three grades are named, but which factor ranks a gift first is not said here. Compare the seven qualities of the giver in 1995.

reading: The verse tells of givers who have mastered the senses and think of future births rather than this life, and whose faultless merit comes back to them multiplied threefold.
nuance: The first lines use rare words (ஐமை, இமைபதம்) and cannot be fixed; the threefold multiple is clear from line 3 but what the three are is not.

reading: Wise people list renunciation, restraint, doing good to others, guarding kin and holding to truth as duties, and the teacher has given giving as the quality of one who lacks nothing and fits the receiver.
nuance: Both halves are hard to join and the last line may speak of the receiver rather than the giver.

reading: The giver's seven qualities are listed: patience, capacity, eagerness to give, love for the receiver, non-attachment, discernment and the absence of regret.
nuance: Only the count of seven is plain; several words of lines 1-2 (போதிசை, பொன்றுதறு, கட்பம்) are rare, so the names are read from the context and not fixed.

reading: One who is himself restrained, gives to the restrained and feels the hurt of all living things, grows in knowledge and conduct and reaches the blameless lands of joy.
nuance: The syntax of the second line is hard, so the verse is read with some doubt.

reading: Those who, seeing the distress of the people at the door, give food as far as they can will become kings with armies, elephants and umbrellas.
nuance: The fruit is kingship in a later birth; this ties the giving to the king's own rank, which Payapati ties to past deeds in 1843.

reading: One who gives to evil-doers wealth that causes many injuries and harms to lives will earn a fruit the teacher would only laugh to tell.
nuance: The mock tone of 'I would laugh to say it' is the teacher's. This makes harmlessness (கொல்லாமை) a limit on giving.

reading: He is like a man who loses his own wealth and builds for himself the door to a wretched state, or hands great wealth to cruel wretches and asks them to serve him.
nuance: The simile finishes 1998: the one who gives to cruel men gets his own harm back.

reading: The gifts made to those fit to receive by one who has grasped the true principles do not fall among the three grades, but lead him up among the best of the gods.
nuance: The 'three grades' may be those of 1992 or the fruits of the gift in three realms; the verse is hard and its reading uncertain.

title: துறவுச் சருக்கம் 2001-2023 (8/10)
theme: The sage's lesson on austerity continues: the vows and their fruit, the seven doors of merit, compassion and equanimity, knowledge as a lamp, the four kinds of meditation, and the great ones who conquered their deeds, down to the lands of enjoyment won by givers.
source_issues: 2001, 2002, 2004, 2006, 2011 and 2016 turn on compressed or damaged lines and are marked uncertain.
The speaker of these verses is the sage by the story, not named in any of the lines; 2004 may be in the king's voice.

cast.role: the austere sage who teaches King Payapati
King Payapati, who is taught and who is told his own line conquers karma

reading: The sage says that the vows, though many and widely spread, are gathered into five, and that to tell their fruit across the heads that follow would leave the fitting vow short of its due.
nuance: The count and the closing comparison (line 4) turn on the compressed phrase in lines 2 to 3 and cannot be fixed with confidence.

reading: All vows are alike in kind, the sage says, yet for those who are like the vowless the vow of not killing is the one that, if kings keep it, leaves nothing they cannot conquer.
nuance: Winning (வெல்லா வகையில்லை) is put in the language of a king's conquest, so non-killing is offered to a ruler as a form of victory, not as a surrender of power. Lines 1 to 2 are hard to construe.

reading: The austerity borne by those who possess themselves is hard even for the sages to tell if asked, the sage says; it belongs to those who have left this life with the zeal that shines in the next world.
nuance: The sage answers the king's search for a refuge at his feet (1862) by saying first that what he asks is hard to put into words.

reading: Those who came having done austerity stand firm in it, but for those who came having done wrong it is greatly hard, and the sage asks what can be done for people who suffer from the deeds they have done.
nuance: Lines 3 to 4 may be the king's question to the sage; the sage is taken as the speaker because 2005 answers directly in his voice.

reading: The wealth of austerity that the clear-sighted take up grows in two kinds and many, so do not be bewildered when it comes, but understand it fully.
nuance: The king's own talk of sowing more seed (1842) is answered here: austerity is called wealth, and wealth that increases.

reading: The sage says that if one strives to give worship without measure to the great lord of the three worlds, the gods themselves come to hail one as their chief.
nuance: கலகையில் in line 2 may be a damaged spelling of 'countless' (அளவற்ற); the sense follows that guess.

reading: The sage says that the doors of merit that he has praised gather into four, yet those who have looked closely along the subtle texts count still more doors.
nuance: Four is named here and seven in the next verse; the sage offers his four as a summary and defers to the finer count of the texts, so the two numbers are not a contradiction.

reading: The seven doors are named: compassion, clarity, love for virtues, praise that reaches the object, faultless austerity, pure knowledge, and meditation that clears the dark.
nuance: Compassion heads the list and meditation closes it, so the order runs from feeling to inner discipline.

reading: When a dear life suffers, one should melt as for one's own life and save it; where that cannot be done, a moist heart is still the nature of compassion.
nuance: Line 3 allows that rescue may not succeed and still counts inward tenderness as compassion, which makes the heart's state, not the result, the measure.

reading: Whether abused, praised or left alone, those of clear mind feel no hot anger, no cool delight and no dislike, and are free of the three kinds of delusion.
nuance: The three delusions (மும்மூடம்) are not named in the verse; the reading stays with what the Tamil says.

reading: The sage names love of the feet of the knowing, honouring the conduct of the great and looking to their many virtues as attachments that bring wealth when they do not bind.
nuance: The line 'செறிதலி லார்வங்கள்' (attachments without binding) is the key phrase and is not fully secure.

reading: Taking up austerity by one's strength, practising it, mastering it, standing first in conduct and praising it: this, the sage says, is the course that carries to the two heavens.
nuance: The verse names the two heavens (இருவிசும்பு) without saying which they are.

reading: Those who have cut off their astringent stain and reached the rare state, standing first in this conduct, are what the sage calls good austerity, and it brings rule of the heavenly world.
nuance: துவர்ப்பு, the astringent taste or dye, is read here as the stain of passion that the renouncer has shed; this reading is not certain.

reading: Knowledge is what the learned grasp on hearing the meaning of the texts: it clears the confusing darkness and is the lamp that shows the truth.
nuance: Knowledge is a lamp, and the same lamp is lit in 2018 for vision, so the sage joins hearing and seeing.

reading: The sage says that the meditation which grows on and on, fully told, is of four kinds, of which two bring the opposite of good and the rest give victory, heaven and release.
nuance: The four are not named in the verse; the reading rests on the count and the two fruits.

reading: Those who strive in praise of merit find these things within, the sage says, and if one takes up the reverse of them it is a ripening that wears one down and torments.
nuance: The first line is obscure; it probably speaks of the two bad meditations of 2015.

reading: Those worthy who have lit the lamp named vision, though without vows, rule not a dark realm but the world of the gods, or plunge into the flood of great bliss from which there is no return.
nuance: The verse sets vision above vows without dismissing vows, and it leaves open which of the two destinations is meant.

reading: The sage says that seeing the true thing is the lamp of vision, and if it is lit the fire-darkness called deeds cannot stay, so he urges the king to make it his own wealth.
nuance: Karma is called both fire and darkness, the lamp ending it by showing the true thing and by no act of a god.

reading: If one traces the gods and men in order, the sage says, Vijayan and the discus-lord are the first of eighteen who will come to bewilder this world.
nuance: The eighteen and the identity of the discus-lord (Tivittan) turn on a compressed line and a rare form, so this reading is uncertain.

reading: The sage says he has told of Ayakanthan who lost the discus and of the nine foes of the strong lord who fell, and that such falls are without end through the ages of the wide world.
nuance: The names are as printed; line 2 is hard to parse and the count of foes is read from மும்மூவர்.

reading: Among the gods and men who conquer their deeds, the sage says, the king himself is one, and with him Bharata, the first of his line, and the discus-rulers are those very ones.
nuance: The king is told that his own line belongs to those who conquer karma, so renunciation is shown as a family inheritance and not an alien road.

reading: Those with the sacred mark on the breast, who hold the glory of never being born again, are the best in this world, the sage says, and they come through austerity.
nuance: The sacred mark on the breast (திருமறு மார்பர்) is taken as the Jain sign of a teacher of the path; other readings are possible.

reading: The people who stand first in giving and like virtues, the sage says, are of this kind, having entered the grace of the gods and reached lands of enjoyment, though their nature cannot be fully told.
nuance: The verse marks the lower rung of merit as enjoyment of lands, after 2022 has named release as the higher.

title: துறவுச் சருக்கம் 2024-2046 (9/10)
theme: In the Renunciation sarukkam the teacher tells the king of the land of enjoyment where twin children grow, meet, unite and rise to heaven after their span, and then lists the four orders of gods: Bhavana, Vyantara, Jyotishka and the kalpa heavens.
source_issues: Verses 2024 to 2046 carry no build flags; 2033, 2036, 2041 and 2042 turn on rare technical words (palla) or a likely corrupt word (கெளாண் in 2042 line 3) and are marked uncertain.
The speaker, a teacher addressing the king (வேலோய், 2024 and 2036), is not named in these verses; the 'sage_teacher' is inferred from the closing of the previous chapter's call to seek the sages.

cast.role: the unnamed teacher who speaks of the lands of enjoyment and the orders of gods to the king
King Payapati, the addressee of the teaching (வேலோய்)
the girl born in the enjoyment land
the boy born with her in the enjoyment land

reading: The teacher tells the spear-bearing king that the best, the middle and the lowest ranks of beings are three, and that each one's way of life follows the fruit of the good deeds it did.
nuance: Line 3 names some tenfold deed or tree (பத்துவகை பாதவம்) whose fruit sets the rank; the sense of 'ten kinds of tree' is not fixed, so the reading keeps only that rank follows earlier merit.

reading: The teacher says that to tell the ways of the pair of couples there, the king should think of the two pairs here, who with their parents are raised by two gods.
nuance: The grouping of the 'two pairs', the 'parents' and the 'two gods' (lines 3-4) cannot be fixed from this verse alone; it opens the account of birth in the land of enjoyment.

reading: When the forty-nine days of the laughing infant stage are complete, the pair become bright-bodied and reach the proper youth.
event: The twin children of the enjoyment land pass their forty-nine days of infancy and reach youth.

reading: The girl grows into full maidenhood: slender waist swaying, breasts swelling, coral-red lips and bright teeth.
event: The girl of the enjoyment land reaches full maidenhood.

reading: The boy likewise comes into his fullness: dark hair, a lotus face, and a body like a jewelled mountain smeared with saffron.
event: The boy of the enjoyment land reaches full youth.

reading: Adorned with flowers and wishing-tree shoots, her gold ear-coils flashing, the girl enters the flowering garden.
event: The girl, adorned, enters the flowering garden.

reading: The lord, shoulders like coral hills and ornaments gleaming, comes into the same garden like a rutting elephant.
event: The young man comes into the garden where the girl is.

reading: The young man's eyes and the girl's eyes, like lotus-petal and dark water-lily, come together and press against each other.
event: The eyes of the youth and the maiden meet.

reading: The girl's four womanly qualities and the youth's four manly qualities fall away at once; the two draw near and melt together, which the teacher calls the way of fate.
nuance: The 'four qualities' of each are not listed here, but their loss is the reason for the union; fate (விதி) is given as the cause, not choice or marriage.
event: The pair lose their reserve and unite.

reading: From that day on, for three palla spans of life, they enjoy desire without a break like the gods, and this the teacher says is the whole of the life the shadow of which is their merit.
nuance: Lines 3-4 are hard to construe; the verse says only that the long pleasure is a standing life 'like a shadow' of their earlier deed.
event: The pair enjoy unbroken pleasure for their life span.

reading: There is no night, no quarrel, no suffering for them; the pleasure they eat through their days is the fruit of what they gave to austere kings.
nuance: Gift to ascetic kings (தவத்தரசர்க்கு ஈந்த) is named as the cause of the enjoyment-land birth, so the pleasure is itself a reward for renunciation's patrons.

reading: After enjoying the pleasures and completing the three palla spans, they look upon their descendants and rise to the heavenly world.
event: The pair complete their span, look at their children, and go up to the world of the gods.

reading: The teacher lists how those of one, two and three palla portions, in order, go to the lands, times and heights they have earned, and says the whole account is too long to give.
nuance: The terms palla and the numbered portions (lines 1-2) are rare technical words; the sense is that the length of life and the later rise are graded by merit.

reading: Their bodies are like red coral, white crystal and green sprout, and their scent is like the scent of champak, jasmine and kongu blossoms.
Beasts and birds born in the enjoyment land, when they leave their bodies, also rise to the kalpa world of the gods.
nuance: Even animals are drawn into the ladder of merit, which differs from the Naladiyar's picture where a beast's birth is a mark of fall.
event: Animals of the enjoyment land die and rise to the kalpa heaven.

reading: The teacher says that the gods' ways are hard to tell even for gods, but he will speak them briefly, since they spread out in four kinds.
nuance: The speaker marks his own account as a short one of something hard to say, and opens the list of the gods.

reading: He names the four orders of gods: the ten Bhavanas, the eight Vyantaras, the five Jyotishkas and the sixteen kalpa gods, who are without end in this world.
Above those he names are nine and nine upper gods, and above them eight kinds, and the teacher says they have no sickness, anger or enmity.
nuance: The tally of the upper ranks (lines 1-3) is hard to fix; the verse stands as a rough ladder of higher heavens.

reading: The ten Bhavana lords wear crowns of a thousand hoods set with jewels, some with flaming hair, and live in dwellings of gem-bright halls.
nuance: A word in line 3 (கெளாண்) looks corrupt and the sentence is left loosely read.

reading: Of the Vyantaras, beginning with the Kinnaras, some live in the world of men, hear the sound of soft strings, watch the god-possession rites, and bow to kings.
The Vyantaras show themselves or hide, dwell in mountains, groves, tanks, islands, seas and cities, and are many.
The Jyotishkas are the moons and suns, the stars and constellations and the fierce planets, who circle Mount Meru in the sky, some moving and some fixed.
The three kinds of gods with their wives lit the lamp of right faith; those who do not reach it do not, but those who kept good vows shine in the company.
nuance: The first lines name the gods only as 'three' and the second half is hard to attach, so the reading is tentative.

title: துறவுச் சருக்கம் 2047-2068 (10/10)
theme: The teacher finishes his account of the gods: the splendour of the heavens and their pleasures, the powers and spans of the four orders and the kalpa heavens up to thirty-three seas, and the highest gods under no lord; he notes that heaven's wealth, won by austerity, ends, and says that right vision with austerity keeps one from hell and brings endless bliss, as the king bows.
source_issues: 2064 line 4 has a broken glyph (சேயிடையொள் ெளாளிநிழற்ற, vowel sign U+0BC6 after a space); the intended word is lost.
2062, 2063 and 2066 turn on technical lifespan words and cryptic numbers; they are marked uncertain.
The teacher is not named in these verses; as in chapter 88 he is inferred from the sarukkam's frame.

cast.role: the unnamed teacher who tells the king of the heavens and the orders of gods
King Payapati, who listens to the teaching

reading: Those who stay true to their beloved, give up wine and flesh, give gifts and keep the home, together with the young women of their houses, are said to rise as gods among the highest, with light, the eight qualities and their pleasures.
nuance: Line 3 ஓதினமுத்தேவராய் is read as 'the gods we have named'; the sense of முத்தேவர் here is not fixed, so the reading keeps only that these householders become gods.

reading: The teacher says the gods in the sky above Mount Mandara show themselves like a rainbow, shining like images of fine gems while the heavenly ones hail them.
At that moment of birth as gods they are showered with flowers, bathed in nectar water, dressed in many ornaments, hailed and sung to, fanned with flower-gem whisks, and joined by women.
event: A newly born god is showered with flowers, bathed in nectar and adorned while others hail him.

reading: The gods' bodies shine without being dyed, their wreaths do not fade and their robes do not dull, and they bathe long in a great flood of delight.
The teacher says the gods who reach heaven have golden mansions, soft couches, gem hills and flying cars, and that there is nothing more to say of them than this.
nuance: The 'nothing else to say' of line 4 turns the picture into an inventory: heaven is a list of comforts, and 2060 then says that even it has an end.

reading: In the gods' assembly of musicians they watch a play, sit pleasantly with Indra while young women praise them, and live on jewelled upper terraces; this is all the sky holds for those who reach the gods' world.

With honey-voiced women to ravish the eye, a Mandara grove and drums sounding on a gem stage, the gods have such pleasures and their feats of power, and that is the report of them, the teacher says to the garlanded king.
nuance: Line 4's செய்திறற்றொழில் is taken as the deeds the gods' power allows; the word is rare and the reading is not fixed.

reading: When festivals are held for the Tirthankaras and light spreads over all directions, the peacock-like women and fruit-laden assemblies of the gods' own world are still not left behind by the gods.
nuance: Line 1 தீர்த்தங்கள் திறந்தவர்க்கு and line 4 தம்முருவி னகலாரே are hard; the verse is read as the gods' worship of the Tirthankaras while they keep their own form, and the sense is not secure.

reading: The gods have red eyes that never close, know neither night nor day, neither fire nor cold, and bear tall crowns heavy with strung gems.
nuance: 'அமையாத பிறப்பறியார்' in line 2 is read as 'know no unfitting birth'; the phrase may mean something else.

reading: The gods' powers are to shrink to an atom or swell very large, to arrive at a thought, to take whatever form they wish and many forms at will, and the like.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are read as the remainder of the list of qualities; the construction is loose.

reading: The teacher tells the king that heaven has levels and that the higher joy belongs to the higher beings; right vision, once perfected, is easy for the great, while others seldom get it.
nuance: Line 4 can be read as saying the great find it easy or that it is mostly beyond the lesser; the reading keeps both halves.

reading: The god's body shines as if rays of light had poured down on a gem image, and his gem crown and ruby bracelet burn with light of their own.
nuance: Line 4's இனமுதலாச் சிடர்ந்தினிதி னியல்பாய் is corrupt-looking; only the shining is certain.

reading: The wives of the divine kings have bodies of bright figurines and shining jewels, speak little, stay forever young and never wither.

Heaven's great wealth is all joy, with no pain even for a blink, and it comes through great austerity; but it ends some day, and those who understood the Lord's teaching saw that something higher lies above it.
nuance: மிசை in line 4 may mean 'above' or 'further on'; the verse hints at release beyond heaven without naming it, and the following verses go on counting heaven's spans.

reading: The Bhavana gods live a sea of years and a bit more, the equal gods here a palya, and the sun and moon gods similarly; after their span each one's destiny follows his own lot.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are technical (கடல், பல்லம்) and the lines are read as the lifespans of the Bhavana, Vyantara and Jyotishka orders; the hit on exact figures is uncertain.

reading: The lowest of the kalpa heavens are counted in pairs and groups, and their spans rise with each step up to twice eleven seas.
nuance: The numbers of lines 1 to 3 are cryptic; the last line's twice eleven seas (twenty-two) fits the span of the highest of the kalpa heavens.

reading: Above these come the three triples and the nine, each a step higher, and the span rises to thirty-three seas for the highest, the teacher says to the crowned king.
nuance: The count of three, nine and fifteen doubled and three more reads as thirty-three; the arithmetic is the reading's own.

reading: As for the divine kings of those realms, they are great beings who feel no longing for women and sit proudly in a lasting pleasure under their own radiance.
nuance: Line 4 has a damaged word (சேயிடையொள் ெளாளிநிழற்ற); the sense of radiance is guessed.

reading: The highest gods have bodies without flesh and limbs of light that spread over all the worlds, shining like crystal, with no one above them and none greater.
nuance: Line 3's வெண்சங்கே ரிலைச்சையாம் is obscure; கோனிலா in line 4 is taken as 'having no king'.

reading: Beyond that is a realm where equals live in a joy that never changes and no fall comes after long ages, the teacher says, a wide world where their kings sit enthroned.
nuance: Line 1's அத்திதியா மதனிலமைந் தாலூணின் is hard; the reading keeps only an unchanging realm of equals.

reading: The teacher closes by saying that the four destinies and the doors to them are as told, and that a person who stands in firm right vision and bears austerity avoids hell and the animal births and keeps a great, unfailing wealth.
event: The teacher ends his account of the destinies and states the way to the unfailing wealth.

reading: When the king bows and asks for grace, the sage, the highest of those of great austerity, sets out how one reaches unending bliss, since a talk of welfare is not a place for flattery.
nuance: Line 1 is read as the narrator's remark; it could also be the teacher's, and உறுதிகணன் is a doubtful word.
event: King Payapati bows to the sage, who then lays out the way to endless bliss.

title: முத்திச் சருக்கம் 2069-2089 (1/3)
theme: In the Renunciation sarukkam the teacher closes his account of release, the king resolves to strive for it, his ministers urge him to lay down the crown, and he warns his young sons that both the goddess of wealth and the goddess of the earth are faithless.
source_issues: Verse 2072 line 1 carries a repair of a pulli after a vowel sign; no sense is affected.
Verses 2069, 2070, 2073, 2076, 2077, 2085 and 2089 have compressed or doubtful lines; they are marked uncertain.
The teacher is named by no word in 2069 to 2074 and is taken from 2075 line 1 as the speaker.

cast.role: the unnamed ascetic teacher whose teaching on release the king hears
King Payapati, who resolves on renunciation and warns his sons
the king's ministers, who urge him to give up the crown
the king's young sons, addressed in 2081 to 2089

reading: The teacher says that with the two kinds of deeds gone nothing new can come on this road, and that for the faultless great ascetics there is one broad way, the one leading to the summit, and nothing else to tell.
nuance: The two kinds of deeds (இருவகை வினை) are not named here; they are most likely good and bad deed, but the verse does not say so. சூளிகை in line 3 is read as a summit or pinnacle, a rare word, and line 4 is compressed.

reading: The teacher says that the one born is bound to the objects of his senses, that once those objects have matured he feels desire and hatred, and that by heaping up hidden deeds through them even the dead man meets the same nature again.
nuance: Line 3 says the deeds are gathered where there is no door (வாயிலா); I take this as deeds heaped unseen, which is a reading of a compressed phrase.

reading: The teacher says that one who greatly fears this wheel of births resolves on renunciation, becomes pure, guards a conduct full of compassion toward kin and living things, and reaches a greatness free of forgetfulness.
nuance: உறவிக்கண் in line 3 may mean toward kin or toward all that live; the reading keeps both open.

reading: The teacher says that when right vision and knowledge shine and the mind has conquered the pride of the senses and is pure, the hero who has long practised the road of meditation reaches the world of release from which there is no return.
nuance: The way is the Jain road of vision, knowledge and conduct, reached by the hero's own effort; nothing in the verse gives a god or a grace any part in it.

reading: The teacher says that the final state belongs to the heroes who have cut desire and craving at the root, and asks whether others can know it.
nuance: கடையிலெண் குணத்தது in line 1 is read as the state of the eight qualities (எண்குணம்) with no end; the sense turns on compressed words and on line 2, which is hard to parse.

reading: The teacher says the bliss of release is like the light that pours from a jewel, the coolness of a sandal chip and the scent of a flower close at hand.
nuance: சிவகதி here means the state of release; it does not name Siva. The three pleasant comparisons are all sensory, though the verse is about a state said to lie beyond the senses.

reading: When the faultless ascetic has spoken, the victorious king, who has drunk the nectar of the teacher's word, says he will strive to reach the world where there is no return.
nuance: மாதவ னுரைப்ப is read as the great ascetic speaking; the sage is the one the epic's earlier chapters name as the teacher, but the name does not appear here.
event: Payapati, having drunk the teacher's words, declares that he will strive for release.

reading: The king speaks fittingly that his resolve cannot be hindered and that the world has agreed to it, but the ministers, who have not agreed, answer him.
nuance: The first two lines are hard: போதிகை, விலக்க றக்கதன்று and ஒக்க நன்றுடன்படல் can be read as the king's resolve that none may bar, or as a general maxim of agreement, and who exactly speaks in lines 1 and 2 is not fixed. The verse's last line leads straight into the ministers' words in the next verses.
event: The ministers reply to the king who has announced his resolve.

reading: The ministers ask whether one who lived in a dark pit of unbearable pain, with no comfort from anyone, and who has got out through a door by good fortune, would gladly seek the man who would roll him back in.
nuance: The verse is a simile with the application left unsaid; it is given its sense by 2079, where the ministers urge the king to throw off the crown. உருட்டுவான் ஒருவனை is read as one who rolls him back.

reading: The ministers add a second image, asking whether one who has fled a heavy prison and escaped would go back into the cruel jail of rough guards.
nuance: Prison and pit are the same figure for worldly life; the ministers' point is made by questions, and the second image repeats the first with a harsher keeper.

reading: The ministers say that one who resolves on the great austerity that ends the disease of birth will not look for ties, and ask the jewel-crowned king to give up the crown.
nuance: Here the king's own counsellors urge the renunciation they might have been expected to oppose; the objection sketched in 2076 resolves into their agreement. The verse's last words ('so the ministers are said to have spoken', என்பவே) pass the speech on as report.
event: The ministers urge Payapati to lay down his crown and renounce.

reading: After the ministers speak, the king rises, calls his young sons with their bright spears, and says this to them without anger.
nuance: இனலிலான் in line 4 is taken as without hurt or anger, the king speaking calmly to those he is about to leave in charge.
event: Payapati calls his sons together to speak to them.

reading: The king tells his sons that the goddess of wealth does not favour the unclear-minded, as the pleasure of the senses is not for the poor, the fruit of dharma for the merciless or the understanding of a text for a restless mind.
nuance: The three comparisons set a lack against what it would need (money for pleasure, compassion for dharma's fruit, steadiness for learning); Lakshmi's favour is put on the same list, so the verse does not say wealth is bad, only that it does not stay with the unwise.

reading: The king bids the wealthy hear the goddess's nature: she leaves the men she has joined and never gives herself to any, wanting always someone new.
nuance: Wealth is a woman who stays with no one; the verse does not say any man can hold her by merit.

reading: The king says that when a man's merit is spent the goddess leaves the poor like courtesans who turn their backs on the penniless, and slights everyone, with no friendship for anyone she has reached.
nuance: Line 1 makes wealth depend on merit (புண்ணியம்); the loss is a spent deed, not a changed fortune. The courtesan simile belongs to the epic's own habit of using the courtesan for fickleness, and it looks at her as the narrator's side does.

reading: The king says that if she stays by one man she hides his good qualities and breeds in him hatred, anger and pride, and makes even the learned look at others with scorn.
nuance: Even her staying does harm; the verse says wealth, not her leaving, is what spoils the learned.

reading: The king says that the wealth of young men who trust courtesans with long arrow-like eyes is spent away, and that such is the nature of those who enjoy the lotus-creeper of the goddess.
nuance: The last two lines are compressed and the link between the lotus-creeper and the courtesans is not spelled out; I take it as Lakshmi again, so the courtesan and the goddess are set side by side.

reading: The king tells his garlanded sons not to trust her, and says that the ones who love those she scorns as strangers are the learned.
nuance: The verse turns the warning into a rule of choice: attach to the learned, who do not leave. காதலாராபவர் is read as 'those who love', though the text is compressed.

reading: The king turns to the goddess of the earth and tells the sons that she has no family and no virtue as her rule, and that she goes along with men who are clever in strategy.
nuance: The earth is spoken of as a woman who follows the strong and cunning king; the verse does not say whether the sons should fight for her. உலமிகு வயிரத்தோள் in line 4 is a praising address to the sons.

reading: The king says that the earth has enjoyed more men than there are grains of sand and left them, and has not stayed even with those who came after, which is her nature even now.
nuance: மூரித் தானையீர் addresses the sons as men with great armies; the verse tells them they are one more in a long line.

reading: The king says that she has no bond with the victorious crowned kings, clings to no one, and keeps only those who cling to her, like an old woman between her watery clothes.
nuance: The close of the line, முற்றுநீர்த் துகிலிடை முதுபெண் நீர்மையே, is hard: it may be an old woman wrapped in a wet cloth or a figure taken from the sea-girt earth. The reading is held loosely.

title: முத்திச் சருக்கம் 2090-2110 (2/3)
theme: The Renunciation sarukkam continues with King Payapati announcing to the young princes that he has resolved to leave, his queens and ministers taking up austerity with him, his crown cast into the milk sea by the gods, the thousand kings laying down theirs, the sons' grief and its consolation, and the king's arming himself with the five vows, virtues and disciplines against karma.
source_issues: Verses 2090 to 2092 are only partly clear: the 'her' of 2090 and 2091 and the sense of 2092 line 3 cannot be fixed, so they are marked uncertain.
2109 and 2110 print as eight half-lines in the build and are repaired to four lines; 2110 line 3 is obscure.
The speaker of the consolation in 2105 is inferred as the sages; the sons' names are inferred from epithets in 2101.

cast.role: King Payapati of Suramai land, who renounces and gives the realm to his sons
the young princes, the king's sons and kin, as a group
the conch-coloured prince, taken to be Vijayan
the discus-bearing prince with Fortune on his chest, taken to be Tivittan
the queens
the ministers who practise austerity
the gods who carry off the crown
the thousand kings who take off their crowns with the king
the sages who console the princes

reading: The poet recalls the king who once ruled while kings bowed at his feet, the sounds of royal drums, and a younger brother, and then turns to the manner of the chastity of a woman who enters the wedding.
nuance: The verse is broken: the line about the 'chastity of her who enters the bridal home' (line 4) has no stated link to the king in lines 1 to 3, and the younger brother is not named, so the verse is read only as a closing view of the old royal state before the renunciation begins.

reading: The king tells his hearers that such is her nature and that they should not cherish her as wealth, for once the people uphold the protector of living beings, they should look to their own duty.
nuance: 'She' (இவள், அவள்) is not named here; she may be royal fortune or the land, but the verse does not say, so the reading keeps the warning against loving her as property and nothing more.

reading: The king tells the garlanded ones that the guarding of the sea-fenced land, with its spear-bearing warriors, now rests with them, and that he has begun to set his own rule, so they should look to the time.
nuance: The sense of line 3 (யானினி எனக்கு அரசாக்கல் உற்றனன்) is not fixed: it may mean he has turned to rule himself, or has taken up some other sovereignty, and the verse leaves it open.
event: The king hands over the guardianship of the land to the young princes and announces his own turn to another rule.

reading: The king says that the days left to him with them are few and their own days many, so the learned should put away grief, for he has resolved today.
event: Payapati tells his people he has resolved to leave.

reading: The young princes bow and ask what fault they have committed against their lord, and he, already like a stranger to them, answers that they have done nothing wrong.
event: The young princes ask what fault they have done; the king answers that it is nothing they did.

reading: He calls the queens, dear as nectar, and asks why their long eyes weep; they take up austerity before the king.
event: The king asks the queens why they weep; they take up the vow before him.

reading: The ministers who had practised austerity, trembling at the disease of birth, now by the grace of the king-of-kings throw off the great burden they bore.
event: The ministers, who have been practising austerity, put down the burden of the body by the king's grace.

reading: The lord of the land of Suramai, with resolution, bathes in water from the milk sea and takes off his many jewelled ornaments for the great ascetics.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are tangled (the gods' part in bringing the milk-sea water and the crown's place); only the bath and the taking off of ornaments are firm.
event: Payapati bathes and puts off his ornaments in the presence of the ascetics.

reading: The king gives up his hard-won crown, and the gods take the gem-clustered crown away and cast it into the milk sea as if it were a great crown of their own sea.
nuance: The throwing of the king's crown into the sea of the gods turns a loss of rank into an offering; the verse itself does not say who sees this.
event: Payapati renounces the crown; the gods carry it off and cast it into the milk sea.

reading: The king gives the drum-loud army and the sea-ringed earth to his sons and goes, and a thousand kings with their king-of-kings take their fragrant crowns off and put them aside.
event: Payapati gives the kingdom to his sons and a thousand kings follow him in taking off their crowns.

reading: The crowns, bracelets, pearl necklaces, earrings and ornaments thrown off shine like blazing fires where they lie.
event: The kings throw away their crowns and jewels.

reading: As the blazing gem crown comes down from the lord's head, the two sons, conch-coloured Vijayan and discus-chested Tivittan, cry out like the sea of coiled conches.
nuance: The two are identified only by epithets (the conch-coloured one and the discus-bearer with Fortune on his chest); the names are the reader's inference from the story.
event: Vijayan and Tivittan wail as their father's crown falls.

reading: Though they are dear to him, his love has gone beyond reach and the lord has become one with no tie to them, so they melt like wax in a bellows-fire and their flower eyes fill with water.
event: The princes melt in grief at the lord's detachment.

reading: The princes lament that the lord who once drew them to his fragrant chest while kings bowed has become like a stranger, and that this is cruel and great.
nuance: The speaker is the two princes together as a pair (the cast has no id for a pair), so the speaker is given as the one named elsewhere, Tivittan, which is only a convenience.
event: The princes complain that their lord has turned away from them.

reading: They ask who now will take the garland from his chest and mount to him, and who will honour them as their own in the way he did, and so they depart in grief with flowered crowns.
event: The princes leave in sorrow.

reading: The sage tells the young princes that the might which, by unmoving valour, bends the world was given up today by the lord, so there is nothing for them to grieve.
nuance: The line 1 phrase (நின்றிலா நிலைமையில் நீங்கி) is hard; the reading keeps only that the consolation turns on the king's act being a higher victory.
event: The sage consoles the young princes.

reading: The proud princes bow to the sages and say that if this is the grace of the lord, then their quarrelsome prattle was foolish, neither his quality nor his intent.
event: The princes accept the king's act and bow.

reading: The princes resolve not to grieve the lord's mind further by their talk, bow low with blazing crowns and go back to the rich city.
event: The princes return to the capital.

reading: The warrior returns to the king and says it is not fitting to serve here, since the lord had held the broad wealth and the sea-ringed earth as dust underfoot, and bows to the spear-bearer.
nuance: The returning figure and the 'spear-bearer' (வேற்படை வீரன்) are not named in the verse.
event: A warrior worships the spear-bearing lord and goes back.

tamil: வேற்படை விடுத்து வீரத் தவவர சதனை மேவி
நூற்படை முனிவர் கண்ணா னோக்கிய நயத்த னாகிப்
பாற்படு விரத நோன்மைப் படைப்பெருந் தலைவ ரைவர்
மேற்படை செய்யச் செல்லும் வினைவரை விலக்க வைத்தான்.
reading: The lord lays down the spear and enters the ascetic's kingdom of heroic austerity, looks with the eye of the sages of the scripture, and stations five great captains of the vow-army to hold back the karma that advances.
event: Payapati lays down his spear and sets five vows as guards against incoming karma.

tamil: குணப்படை யிலக்க மெண்பான் குலவுநான் காகுஞ் சீலக்
கணப்படை பதினெட் டாகு மாயிரங் கருவி யாகத்
துணைப்படை பிறர்க்குச் செய்யுந் துருநயத் தளவு நீக்கி
மணப்புடை சிந்தை யென்னு மடந்தையைச் செறிய வைத்தான்.
reading: The lord arrays the army of virtues, the army of disciplines in eighteen thousand and the aids as instruments, and sets the maiden called mind firmly in their keeping.
nuance: Line 3 (துணைப்படை பிறர்க்குச் செய்யும் துருநயத் தளவு நீக்கி) is obscure; the counts of the virtue-army are read as the poet's figures, not checked.
event: Payapati arms himself with virtues and disciplines and guards the mind.

title: முத்திச் சருக்கம் 2111-2130 (3/3)
theme: In the closing verses of the Release sarukkam, the lord guards the fortress of the self, mounts the elephant of knowledge, draws the sword of meditation, kills the karmic enemies one by one, throws the sword away, enters the city of no return and becomes the crest-jewel of the world, while the gods worship and the princes of the story rule on.
source_issues: Verses 2123 to 2126 carry no build flags but 2123 line 1 (கருமால் வினையரசு காறளர நூறிப்து) and 2125 line 3 (a stray ங் in முடிவென்னும் ங்கொடியுந்) are corrupt, so those verses are marked uncertain.
Verses 2111 to 2122 and 2127 were printed as eight half-lines and joined into four by the build; 2130 had a stray pulli after a vowel sign removed.
The lord who wins release is not named in 2111 to 2130; the cast id hero_lord is inferred from கோன் in 2122 and 2127, and the verses do not say who he is.

cast.role: the unnamed lord who fights karma as a war and wins release; the verses do not name him
the karmic enemy kings and their host
the gods who shower and praise
Prajapati, who rules the Brahma world in 2128
Tirumal of the discus, who rules the earth in 2128 and 2129
the one white as a conch who worships in 2130
the one with a jewel-blue body who worships in 2130
Death and Desire, who flee in 2127

tamil: செறிவெனப் படுவ மூன்று செழுமதில் செறியச் செய்து
பொறியெனும் வாயி லைந்து பொற்கத வடைத்து மாற்றி
அறிவமை சிந்தை யின்மாட் டகம்படி யுழைய ராக்கிக்
கறையிலீ ரறுவர் நிற்ப விறைவராக் காக்க வைத்தான்.
reading: The lord is shown raising a fortress of the self: three rich walls, five sense-gates shut with golden doors, a knowing mind set inside, and twelve faultless ones stationed as guards.
nuance: The verse never says what the three walls or the twelve guards stand for; the allegory is read from the five gates (பொறி, the senses) alone, so the sense of the numbers is left open.
event: The hero builds a walled fortress with its five gates shut and posts twelve faultless guards.

tamil: படைகெழு புரிசை வெல்வார் புறநின்று பதின்மர் காக்க
விடையவர் தம்மு ளாரே யுழையரீ ரறுவ ராக
உடையதன் னுலக மூன்று மொருவழிப் படுக்க லுற்று
மிடைகெழு வினைவர் தானை மெலியமேற் சென்று விட்டான்.
reading: Ten guards stand outside the walls and twelve serve inside, and the lord, wishing to bring his three worlds under one road, sends his force out against the thinning host of the karmic enemy kings.
nuance: The numbers ten and twelve are given without their referents.
event: The hero stations his guards and marches out against the army of the karmic enemies.

tamil: பின்னணி யோகு நான்மை யபரகாத் திரம்பெற் றேனைத்
தன்னவ யவங்கண் முற்றித் தயங்குநூன் மனங்க ளோவா
துன்னிய திசையி னுய்க்கு முணர்வெனும் வயிரத் தோட்டி
இன்னியன் ஞான வேழத் தெழிலெருத் தேறி னானே.
reading: Having gained four kinds of discipline, the lord mounts the splendid elephant of knowledge, driven by a diamond goad that is awareness itself and kept on the path of the sacred texts and the mind.
nuance: The four named in line 1 (பின்னணி, யோகு, நான்மை, அபரகாத்திரம்) are partly unclear words, and the clause about the texts and the mind in line 2 may be read two ways, so only the picture of knowledge as an elephant under a goad is kept.
event: The hero climbs the elephant of knowledge, steering it with the goad of awareness.

tamil: தருக்கெயில் காப்பு வாங்கத் தடக்கைமால் பகடு நுந்தித்
திருக்கிளர் குணமேற் சேடிச் செழுமலைக் குவட்டி னோட்டி
முருக்கிய வுருவு வேட்கை முனைப்புல மகற்றி முற்றிச்
செருக்கிய வினைவர் வாழுந் திண்குறும் பழிக்க லுற்றான்.
reading: Driving the great elephant to break the guard of the proud fort, he rides it up a ridge of good qualities, crushes the shape of desire, drives off the outposts of the senses and attacks the stronghold where the karmic enemies live.
event: The hero storms the fort of the karmic enemies on his elephant, crushing desire and the outposts of the senses.

tamil: நிறையிலார் பொறுத்த லாற்றா நிலையிது நிறைந்த நோன்மைக்
கறையி லீராறுக் கொத்த கண்ணியர் கவரி வீச
முறையினாற் பெருகு முள்ளச் சமாதிநீர் முறுக வுண்ட
குறைவிலாத் தியான மென்னுங் கொற்றவா ளுருவிக் கொண்டான்.
reading: Unable to bear the enemy's unrestraint, he draws the sword of unending meditation, steeped in the water of samadhi, while women suited to the twelve faultless ones fan him with whisks.
nuance: The fanning women are the twelve faultless ones in female form as far as the grammar of line 2 shows, but the verse does not say it outright.
event: The hero draws the sword of meditation while attendants fan him.

tamil: விண்கடாஞ் செய்யும் வெய்ய வினைவர்கட் கரண மாகிக்
கண்கடா மிறைக்கு மோரேழ் கடிவினை பொடிசெய் திட்டே
கொண்கடா நவின்ற வீரெண் கொடிமதிற் கோட்டை குட்டி
எண்கடா முடைய வெண்மர் குறும்பரை யெறிந்து வீழ்த்தார்.
reading: Serving as the means against the fierce enemies, the lord crushes a group of fierce karmas, razes the sixteen walled forts he has already named, and eight strike down the chieftains.
nuance: Lines 2 and 3 count karmas and forts (seven, sixteen) and line 4 an eight; the verse itself gives no key, and the words கொண்கடா and எண்கடா are hard.
event: The hero and eight of his men break the enemy's forts and cut down its chieftains.

tamil: ஈடிலர் வெகுளி யுள்ளிட் டெண்மரை யெறியத் தீயுட்
பேடுவந் தொன்று பாய்ந்து முடிந்தது முடிந்த பின்னை
ஓடிவந் தொருத்தி வீழ்ந்தா ளுழையவ ரறுவர் பட்டார்
ஆடவன் றானும் போழ்து கழித்துவந் தொருவ னாழ்ந்தான்.
reading: With anger and its fellows (eight in all) struck down, a neuter figure leaps into the fire and dies, then a woman falls, six attendants die, and last the man himself sinks after a while.
nuance: The neuter, woman and man with six attendants may be the nine minor passions of the Jain list, but the verse names them only as figures; I follow the picture and not that list.
event: A run of enemy figures led by anger dies in sequence: the neuter, the woman, six attendants and the man.

tamil: பின்னுமோர் நால்வர் தெவ்வர் முறைமுறை பிணங்கி வீழ்ந்தார்
அன்னவர் தம்மு ளானே குறைப்பிண மொருவ னாகித்
தன்னைமெய் பதைப்ப நோக்கி யவனையுந் தபுப்ப நோனார்
துன்னிய துயிலு மேனைத் துளக்கஞ்செய் திருவர் பட்டார்.
reading: Four more enemies fall in turn, one of them rising as a half-corpse that is cut down again, and two others who shake the sleeping die as well.
nuance: The grouping of the four and the two, and the sense of the half-corpse, cannot be fixed from the verse.
event: Four enemies fall one by one, and two more die with them.

tamil: தாங்கியீ ரிருவர் தாக்கித் தலைதுணிப் புண்ட பின்னை
வீங்கிய வனந்த ஞான்மை விழுநிதி முழுதுங் கைக்கொண்
டோங்கிய வுலகிற் கெல்லா மொருபெருங் கிழவ னானான்.
reading: After those fall, two kings and four more are struck and beheaded, and the lord takes the whole treasure of infinite knowledge and becomes the single master of all the raised-up worlds.
event: The hero kills the last enemy kings, takes the treasure of infinite knowledge and rules all the worlds.

tamil: நெடிதுட னாய தெவ்வர் நால்வரை நீறு செய்திட்
டடிகள்பின் முடிவென் பாளை யகப்படுத் தனைய ராக
இடிமுர சதிருந் தானை யரசரோ டிங்க ணீண்டிக்
கடிகம ழமரர் வீரன் கடிவினை முடிவித் தாரே.
reading: Having reduced four old enemies to ash, he ends the fierce karma; the verse then speaks of the woman called முடிவு, whom he reaches, while gods and kings gather in a host.
nuance: முடிவு (end, completion) is spoken of as a woman in lines 2 and in the verses that follow, so the end of karma is both a deed and a person to be won; the grammar of lines 2 and 3 is hard and the clause is read loosely.
event: The hero reduces four long-standing enemies to ash and ends the karma that bound him.

tamil: கொடிகளுங் குடையுங் கோலக் கவரியு மமரர் தங்கள்
முடிகளு மடந்தை மாரு முகிழ் நகைக் கலங்க ளுஞ்செற்
றடியிடு மிடமின் றாகி மூடியா காய மெல்லாம்
கடிகமழ் மலருஞ் சாந்துஞ் சுண்ணமுங் கலந்த வன்றே.
reading: Flags, umbrellas, whisks, the crowns of the gods, their women and their jewels press so close that there is no place left for a foot, and the whole sky is mixed with flowers, sandal and powder.
event: The gods crowd the sky with their regalia and rain flowers, sandal and powder.

tamil: பொன்னரி மாலை பூவின் பொழிமதுப் பிணையன் முத்தின்
மின்னிவர் விளங்குந் தாம மெனவிவை விரவி வீசித்
துன்னிய வினைவர் கூட்டந் துணித்துவீற் றிருந்த கோனைப்
பன்னிய துதிய ராகி யமரர்கள் பரவு கின்றார்.
reading: The gods scatter gold-threaded garlands, flower-rain honey, pearl strings and jewelled wreaths and praise the lord who cut the crowd of enemies and sits in glory.
event: The gods shower garlands and praise the lord who cut the enemy host.

reading: Having wiped out the king of dark karma and wanting the princess called the Lord's end without parting, he enters a rich city from which none returns even after the ages turn.
nuance: Line 1 is corrupt (கருமால் வினையரசு காறளர நூறிப்து) and the third line's வேட்டு எய்தி may mean wedding the woman called முடிவு or merely winning her; the sense of the destroyed king is kept, the details are not.
event: The hero destroys the king of karma and enters the city of no return.

reading: After the mind-maid's sword of meditation has burned the karmic kings, he throws it away, embraces the girl called முடிவு and enters the rich city to which one comes back no more.
nuance: The sword is the same weapon as in 2115; here it is discarded, which means that even meditation is a means and not the goal. Liberation is pictured as marriage to a maiden named முடிவு, so release is described in the language of the bridegroom.
event: The hero casts away the sword of meditation, embraces the girl called end and enters the city of no return.

reading: Casting off the coverings, the boundless one swallows the world and the non-world together and stands unmoving, with the maiden called end, in the shining state of release.
nuance: சிவகதி here names the liberated state in a Jain poem and is not a claim about the god Siva; line 3 has a stray ங் (முடிவென்னும் ங்கொடியுந்) that is corrupt.
event: The hero removes the coverings of karma, takes in all knowable things and stays in the state of release.

reading: After many praises and bows, the gods make a fire-offering, bathe in the nectar of the wheel of virtue, shine with joy and, praising, each go to his own place.
nuance: The gods' fire-offering (வேள்வி, line 2) sits inside a Jain scene of worship; the verse does not say it is the Vedic sacrifice.
event: The gods worship with a fire-offering, bathe in the nectar of the dharma wheel and return to their places.

reading: After the field is lost and Death and Desire leave his side, he sees the truth by the pure light of full knowledge and, undimmed in heaven's worlds, becomes the crest-jewel of the world.
nuance: சூளாமணி, the work's own title, is used here of the liberated one, so the poem names itself from this verse.
event: Death and Desire flee, and the hero attains full knowledge and becomes the crest-jewel of the world.

tamil: திருமால் பெரு நேமி திகழ்ந்த செந்தா மரைத்தடக்கைக்
reading: With karma gone, the gods praise his feet each day; Prajapati rules the Brahma world sweetly, and Tirumal of the discus guards the sea-bound earth.
nuance: Prajapati and Tirumal are the princes of the epic's story; here they are shown ruling after the story's close, and the verse does not say whether Prajapati is the one who is liberated.
event: The gods worship the liberated lord's feet while Prajapati rules Brahma's world and Tirumal rules the earth.

reading: While the lord who is theirs sweetly rules the gods' world, Tirumal clears the earth of common rule, lifts a straight sceptre under the gods' guard, and lives while kings praise his feet.
event: Tirumal rules the earth with a straight sceptre, protected by the gods and praised by kings.

reading: The one white as a conch and the one blue as a jewel of the sea, with arms like pillars, bow with the whole world to the lord who won the deceiving karma and keep a daily festival under his lotus feet.
nuance: Reading the white one and the dark one as the two brothers of the story is from the colours alone; the verse does not give their names.
event: The two brothers and the whole world worship the lord who won karma, keeping a festival at his feet each day.

title: பாயிரம் 1-4
theme: The poet's opening: he worships the tirthankara under the pindi tree and Vani, bows to the lord on the lion throne and announces the tale of Udayanan, apologises for his poor words with the image of a gem wrapped in cloth, and ends on the ripening and shedding of karma.
source_issues: Verse 4 lines 3-4 are hard to parse; the reading is provisional.
Verse 2 வாமன் is not clearly the same lord as verse 1.

cast.role: the tirthankara Nemi, seated under the pindi tree, whose feet the poet worships

tamil: மணியுடன் கனக முத்த மலிந்தமுக் குடையி லங்க
அணிமலர்ப் பிண்டி யின்கீ ழமர்ந்தநே மீசர் பாதம்
பணிபுபின் வாணி பாதம் பண்ணவர் தாள்க ளுக்கெம்
இணைகரஞ் சிரத்திற் கூப்பி யியல்புறத் தொழுது மன்றே.
reading: The poet joins his hands over his head and worships the feet of Lord Nemi, seated under the pindi tree beneath the three jewelled umbrellas, and the feet of Vani and the gods.
nuance: The Jain invocation names a tirthankara, Nemi, and not a creator; the worship asks for no boon here.
event: The poet raises his joined hands and worships the lord's feet.

tamil: பொன்னெயில் நடுவ ணேங்கும் பூநிறை யசோக நீழல்
மன்னிய வாமன் பாதம் வந்தனை செய்து வாழ்த்தி
reading: The poet worships the feet of the lord enthroned on the lion seat in the shrine beneath the asoka tree within a golden rampart, and says he will spread out the tale of the great Udayanan.
nuance: The lord here, named only வாமன், is probably the same tirthankara as in verse 1, but the verse does not say so.
event: The poet bows to the lord and declares he will tell Udayanan's story.

tamil: மணிபொதி கிழியு மிக்க மணியுட னிருந்த போழ்தில்
மணிபொதி கிழிய தன்னை மணியுட னன்கு வைப்பார்
துணிவினிற் புன்சொ லேனுந் தூயநற் பொருள்பொ திந்தால்
அணியெனக் கொள்வார் நாமு மகத்தினி லிரங்கல் செல்லாம்.
reading: The poet says that as people keep a gem-filled cloth bundle safe with the gem, and take even a humble word as an ornament when it holds pure meaning, so he asks that his own flawed words be received with pity.
nuance: The apology rests on the worth of meaning over the poverty of words; the cloth that carries the gem is the poem's plain language.

tamil: ஊறுந்தீ வினைவாய் தன்னை யுற்றுடன் செறியப் பண்ணும்
கூறுநல் விதிபு ணர்ந்து குறையின்றிச் செல்வ மாமுன்
மாறுறு கருமந் தன்னை வரிசையி னுதிர்ப்பை யாக்கும்
வீறுறு முதிர்ப்பின் றன்மை விளம்புதற் பால தாமோ.
reading: The poet speaks of the deed that comes on like a rising fire and binds the self, and of the fine law by which, before wealth is reached, the opposing deed is shed in order, and asks whether the nature of its ripening can be told.
nuance: The sense is held loosely: the ripening and the orderly shedding of deeds is the Jain account of karma, but the last two lines are hard to parse.

title: உஞ்சைக் காண்டம் 5-28 (1/5)
theme: The poem moves from the lord's age and the land to Kausambi, King Sathanikan and Queen Mirukavathi, then tells how a bird carries the queen to her father the sage, how her son Udayanan is born and grows up in the hermitage with Yugi, wins a lute and a divine elephant, and how his uncle Vikraman and then his father Sathanikan hand him a throne and turn ascetic, ending with his crowning and four ministers.
source_issues: Verse 12, line 2: a pulli after a vowel sign was removed by the repair step.
Verse 16, line 1: the word 'கண்ணினாடான்' is damaged; the sense is taken from the rest of the verse.
Verse 22, line 1: 'ராமி' is damaged and gives no clear sense.
Verse 28, line 2: the minister's name 'சாருரு மண்ணு வாவும்' is broken across words; read as Urumannuvan.
The poem's named lord at verse 5 is Veeranathan, a form of Mahavira.

cast.role: the lord, a tirthankara, at whose time the story is set
king of the Vatsa land at Kausambi, Udayanan's father
his queen, Udayanan's mother
the huge bird that carries off the queen
the queen's father, a sage in the hill forest
the queen's son, born in the hermitage
Udayanan's friend and later minister, son of the yogi Brahmasundaran
the divine elephant tamed by Udayanan's lute
King Vikraman, the queen's brother, who gives his kingdom to Udayanan

tamil: இஞ்சிமூன் றுடைய கோமா னெழில்வீர நாத னிந்தப்
புஞ்சிய நிலத்தோர்க் கெல்லாம் பொற்புநல் லறநன் மாரி
விஞ்சவே சொரியுங் காலம் வெண்மதிக் குடைக்கீழ் வாழும்
எஞ்சலில் காட்சி மன்ன னிருக்கைநா டுரைத்து மன்றே.
reading: The poet turns to the age when the lord of the three ramparts, fair Veeranathan, pours a rain of virtue on this crowded earth, and says he will tell of the land of a king who rules in that time.
nuance: Virtue falls as rain from the tirthankara here, where the Kural makes the rain follow the king's justice; the poem sets its king inside the lord's age.

tamil: பூவுநற் றளிருஞ் செற்றிப் பொழின்மிகச் சூழ்ந்தி லங்கும்
நாவலா மரத்தி னாலே நாமமாய்த் துலங்கி நின்று
தீவுநற் கடல்க டாம மொன்றிற்கொன் றிரட்டி சூழ்ந்த
நாவலந் தீவு நந்தி னன்மணி போன்ற தன்றே.
reading: The poet says the jambu-named continent, ringed by seas each twice as wide as the one inside it, is like a fine gem among the islands.

tamil: வேதிகை சிலைவ ளைத்து வேதண்ட நாணே றிட்டுப்
போதவும் வீக்கி னாற்போற் பொற்புடைப் பரதந் தன்னில்
ஓதிய தரும கண்டத் தோங்கிய காவு நின்று
வாதத்தாற் சுகந்தம் வீசும் வத்தவ னாட தாமே.
reading: Within the Bharata part of that continent, in its land of dharma, the poet places the Vatsa country, where the wind carries the scent of its groves.
nuance: The first two lines compare the land to a bow drawn with a string; the figure is hard to follow, and only the placing of Vatsa in Bharata's dharma-land is firm.

tamil: இஞ்சிமிக் கெழுந்தே யோங்கி யிலங்கிய வமர லோகம்
எஞ்சலி லெல்லை காணா வெழில்பெற நிற்ற னோக்கி
அஞ்சலில் வருக வென்றே யணிபெற விலங்கி நீண்ட
குஞ்சிநன் கொடிக்க ரத்தாற் கூவியிட் டழைக்கு மன்றே.
reading: The poet says the heavenly world, seeing the limitless beauty of the city, calls it with a hand of tall flags to come without fear.
nuance: Who calls whom is not clear in the Tamil: the heaven may call the city up, or the city's flags may call the gods down. Either way the city is praised as the match of heaven.

tamil: முகிறவழ் மாட மீதின் முத்தணி மாலை நான்றே
இகலுறு மமளி யின்மே லெழின்மங்கை மைந்தர் தாமும்
பகலிர வின்றிப் போகம் பண்பினாற் றுய்த்தி ருப்பார்
நகரிகௌ சாம்பி யென்னு நாமமார்ந் திலங்கு மன்றே.
reading: The poet names the city Kausambi, where men and women in cloud-high mansions live in pleasure by day and night.
nuance: The city is praised by its pleasure, not its virtue, and the poem will later make renunciation the end of such a life.

tamil: ஊனுமிழ்ந் திலங்கும் வேலா னுன்னத முகிலெ ழுந்து
வானுமிழ் வாரி யன்ன வண்கையன் வண்ட ரற்றும்
தேனுமி ழலங்கற் றோளான் செல்வத்திற் குபேர னன்னான்
reading: The poet introduces King Sathanikan, spear-bearing, as generous as a rain-cloud and as rich as Kubera.

tamil: மன்னவ னுள்ளத் துள்ளாண் மாமணி மயிலஞ் சாயல்
அன்னமென் னடைவேற் கண்ணா ளருந்ததி யனைய ஙங்கை
பொன்னணி சுணங்கு பூத்த புணர்முலை யமிர்த மன்னாள்
மின்னு நுண் ணிடையா ணாம மிகாவதி யென்று மிக்காள்.
reading: The poet names the king's beloved queen, delicate as a peahen and as faithful as Arundhati, Mirukavathi.
nuance: Her fidelity is praised by the comparison to Arundhati, the star-wife, before any event shows it.

tamil: கற்புடைத் திருவி னங்கை காரிகை தன்வ யிற்றிற்
சற்புரு டொருவன் வந்து சார்ந்தவ தரித்து மிக்க
நற்புடைத் திங்க ளொன்பா னன்கமைந் திருக்கு மோர்நாட்
பொற்புடை மஞ்ச மீதிற் பொலிவுட னிருந்த போழ்தில்.
reading: The chaste queen, in the ninth month after a good soul had entered her womb, sits one day on a fine couch.
nuance: A virtuous being 'taking birth' in her womb is told as a plain fact of rebirth; no earlier life is named for him here.
event: Mirukavathi, in the ninth month of pregnancy, sits on her couch.

tamil: செந்துகின் மூடிக் கொண்டு திருநிலா முற்றந் தன்னில்
அந்தமாய்த் துயில்கொள் கின்ற வாயிழை தன்னைக் கண்டே
அந்தரத் தோடு கின்ற வண்டபே ரண்டப் புள்ளொன்
றந்தசை யென்று பற்றி யன்றுவான் போயிற் றன்றே.
reading: As the queen sleeps in a red cloth on the moonlit terrace, a huge bird seizes her, taking her for flesh, and flies up.
nuance: The bird's mistake is the whole cause; no fault of hers or the king's is named.
event: A huge bird seizes the sleeping Mirukavathi and carries her into the sky.

tamil: மற்றவ டந்தை தானு மாமுனி யாகி நிற்கும்
சற்கிரி விபுல மன்னுஞ் சாரலவ் வனத்திற் சென்று
நற்றவ னருகில் வைப்ப நற்றுயில் விட்டெ ழுந்தாள்
பற்றுயி ருண்ணாப் புள்ளும் பறந்துவான் போயிற் றன்றே.
reading: The bird sets her down in the forest where her father, now a great sage, lives; she wakes, and the bird, which does not eat the life it seized, flies off.
nuance: The same bird that was a menace in the last verse is shown to be harmless; the verse says it did not eat the life it had seized.
event: The bird sets Mirukavathi down by her father the sage and flies away without harming her.

tamil: நிறைமதி முகநன் மங்கை நிரம்பிய கெர்ப்ப மாதல்
பொறைவயி னோய்மீக் கூரப் பொருவில்வான் கோள்க ளெல்லாம்
முறையினல் வழியை நோக்க மொய்ம்பனத் தினத்திற் றோன்ற
அறையலை கடலிற் சங்க மாணிமுத் தீன்ற தொத்தாள்.
reading: With the child ripening, the queen suffers pains, and on a day the planets look kindly the son is born, like a pearl from a conch.
event: Mirukavathi bears a son on an auspicious day.

tamil: பொருகயற் கண்ணி னாடான் போந்ததை யறிந்த ழுங்கித்
திருமணி கிடந்த தென்னச் செழுமகன் கிடப்பக் கண்டு
பெருகிய காத லாலே பெருந்துயர் தீர்ந்தி ருப்ப
மருவுநற் றாதை யான மாமுனி கண்டு வந்தான்.
reading: Learning where she has come, the queen grieves, then sees her son lying like a gem and her sorrow ebbs with love; her father the sage comes and sees them.
nuance: Line 1 has a damaged word in the queen's description, and its first half is hard to join to the rest; the grief and the sage's arrival are clear.
event: The sage comes and finds his daughter and her newborn son.

tamil: தவமுனி கொண்டு சென்று தாபதப் பள்ளி சேர்த்தி
அவணினி தோம்ப வப்பா லருக்கன துதய காலத்
துவமையின் றுதித்தா னாம முதயண னாக வென்றார்
இவணமத் தாயுஞ் சேயு மிருடிபா லிருந்தா ரன்றே.
reading: The sage takes mother and child to his hermitage and tends them; the boy, born like the sun rising, is named Udayanan, and they stay with the sages.
nuance: The name 'rising' fits the verse's comparison of his birth to a sunrise.
event: The sage brings Mirukavathi and her son to the hermitage, where the boy is named Udayanan.

tamil: பிரமசுந் தரயோ கிக்குப் பிறந்தவன் யூகி யோடும்
இருவரும் வளர்ந்தே யின்பக் கலைக்கட னீந்திக் கானக்
கரிணமும் புள்ளு மற்றுங் கண்டடி வீழுங் கீதப்
புரந்தரன் கொடுத்த யாழும் பொறைமுனி யருளிற் பெற்றான்.
reading: Udayanan, born to the royal line, and Yugi, son of the yogi Brahmasundaran, grow up together, master the arts, and by the sage's grace Udayanan gains Indra's lute.
nuance: The lute comes as a gift of grace from the sage, not of his own skill, and it sets up the elephant scene.
event: Udayanan and Yugi grow up together and he receives Indra's lute from the sage.

tamil: மைவரை மருங்கி னின்ற மலையென விலங்கு கின்ற
தெய்வநல் லியானை கண்டு சென்றுதன் வீணை பாடப்
பையெனக் களிறுங் கேட்டுப் பணிந்தடி யிறைஞ்சி நின்று
கையது கொடுப்ப வேறிக் காளையும் பள்ளி சேர்ந்தான்.
reading: Seeing a mountain-like divine elephant, the youth plays his lute; the elephant listens, bows at his feet and offers its trunk, and he mounts it and rides to the hermitage.
nuance: Music, not force, tames the elephant, the first sign of the lute's power.
event: Udayanan plays the lute, tames the divine elephant and rides it to the hermitage.

tamil: நன்றிருட் கனவி னாக நயமறிந் தினிது ரைக்கு
பன்னிடும் பாகன் வந்து பற்றியே யேறி னாலும்
இன்றைநாண் முதலா நீநா னின்றியே முன்னுண் டாலும்
அன்றுன்பா னில்லே னென்றே யக்கரி யுரைப்பக் கேட்டான்.
reading: The elephant pledges to him in a dream that, though a keeper mount it, it will not stay with him on the day he eats before it; he hears this.
nuance: The condition of the pledge turns on a hard sentence in lines 2 and 3; the sense given is the likeliest, not certain.
event: The elephant pledges itself to Udayanan in a dream.

tamil: செல்லுமக் காலந் தன்னிற் செறிதவன் புதல்வ னான
வெல்களிற் றியானை வேந்தன் விக்கிரன் றனக்கு மக்கள்
இல்லையென் றெவ்வங் கூர்ந்தே யினிமையின் வந்து நல்ல
சொல்லருண் முனிவன் பாதந் தொழுதுநன் கிருந்தா னன்றே.
reading: At that time King Vikraman, son of a sage, grieving that he has no children, comes and sits worshipping the sage's feet.
event: Vikraman, childless, comes to worship the sage's feet.

tamil: புரவல னினிய ராமிப் புதல்வர்க ளார்கொ லென்ன
வரமுனி யருளக் கேட்டு மகிழ்ந்துதன் னாய மெல்லாம்
சிரசணி முடியுஞ் சூட்டிச் செல்வற்குக் கொடுத்துப் போக்கி
விரவிய தவத்த னாக வேண்டுவ தெண்ண மென்றான்.
reading: Asking whose sons these are, he hears the sage's answer, gladly crowns the boy and gives him his retinue, and says he will take up the ascetic life.
nuance: Line 1 has a damaged word ('ராமி'), so who is said to be whose son has to be taken from the next lines, where he gives up kingship to the boy.
event: Vikraman learns who the boys are, crowns Udayanan and resolves to become an ascetic.

tamil: முனியொடு தங்கை தன்னை முயன் றிரந் தெய்தி நாகம்
தனையன வெங்க யத்திற் றனையனை யேற்றிப் போய்த்தன்
மனனிறை நாட்டை யந்த மருகனுக் கீந்து போந்து
முனிவனம் புகுந்து மாமன் முனிவனாய் நின்றா னன்றே.
reading: Vikraman gets his sister and the sage's leave, seats the boy on a fierce elephant, hands his own kingdom to his sister's son, and goes into the forest as an ascetic.
nuance: He ends his childlessness by making his sister's son the heir, and the same act is his turn to renunciation; the kingdom passes to a sister's son, not a son of his own.
event: Vikraman gives his kingdom to his nephew Udayanan and becomes a forest ascetic.

tamil: இளமையை இகந்து மிக்க வினியநற் குமர னாகி
வளமையிற் செங்கோ றன்னை வண்மையி னடத்தி னானாங்
கிளமயி லனைய தேவிக் கிரங்கிய சதானி கன்றான்
உளமலி கொள்கை யான்ற வொருதவற் கண்டு ரைத்தான்.
reading: Udayanan, grown into a handsome youth, rules justly with a straight sceptre; Sathanikan, pining for the queen, speaks of one fault he has seen.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are obscure: what the fault is, and whose, is not stated in the verse.
event: Udayanan rules justly; Sathanikan, longing for his queen, names a fault.

tamil: தேவியின் வரவு நல்ல திருமகன் செலவுங் கேட்டு
மாவலன் மனம கிழ்ந்து வந்தூர்புக் கிருக்கு நாளில்
தேவியும் வந்து கூடிச் சிறந்தநற் புதல்வர் தம்மைத்
தேவிளங் குமரர் போலச் செவ்வியிற் பயந்தா ளன்றே.
reading: Hearing of the queen's return and the prince's going, the king is glad and enters the city; the queen joins him and bears two sons like young gods.
event: Sathanikan welcomes Mirukavathi back and she bears two sons.

tamil: பிங்கல கடக ரென்று பேரினி திட்டு மன்னன்
தங்கிய காத லாலே தரணியாண் டினிது செல்லக்
குங்கும மணிந்த மார்பக் குமரனும் யூகி யும்போய்
அங்குள தேச மெல்லா மடிப்படுத் தினிதி ருந்தார்.
reading: The king names the two sons Pingalan and Katakan and rules the land lovingly, while Udayanan and Yugi go out and bring all the lands there under their sway.
event: Sathanikan names his sons; Udayanan and Yugi conquer the surrounding lands.

tamil: உதயண குமரன் றன்னை யுற்றுட னழைத்துப் பூமிப்
பதமுனக் காக வென்று பார்த்திபன் கொடுத்துப் போகிக்
கதமுறு கவலை நீங்கும் காட்சிநற் றவத்த னாகி
இதமுறு யோகந் தன்னி லெழில் பெறநின்றா னன்றே.
reading: Sathanikan calls Udayanan, gives him the throne of the earth, and himself takes up ascetic life, freed from anger and cares, and stands in yoga.
nuance: The king chooses the throne's heir, Udayanan, over the two sons he has just named, and leaves while still living, not at death.
event: Sathanikan hands the throne to Udayanan and becomes a yoga-practising ascetic.

tamil: மணிமுடி கவித்த போழ்தின் வத்தவர்க் கிறைவ னானான்
அணியுநாற் படையுஞ் சூழ்ந்த அமைச்சரு நால்வர் நாமம்
தணிவில்சீர் யூகி யோடு சாருரு மண்ணு வாவும்
துணைவயந் தகனுந் தொல்சீர் விடபக னென்ப வாமே.
reading: At his coronation Udayanan becomes lord of the Vatsa people, with four ministers around him: Yugi, Urumannuvan, Vayantakan and Vidapakan.
nuance: Line 2 has the second minister's name broken in word division, and the reading 'Urumannuvan' is taken from that.
event: Udayanan is crowned king of the Vatsa people and four ministers are named.

title: உஞ்சைக் காண்டம் 29-51 (2/5)
theme: The search for Udayana's vanished divine elephant is set beside Pradyota's court in Ujjain, where, enraged by a tribute-roll and by his ministers' praise of Udayana, the king lets them build a mechanical elephant packed with ninety-six armed men; Udayana ignores omens and Vayantakan's warning, plays his veena before it, and is surrounded.
source_issues: The order of verses 29 and 30, which belong to Udayana's own court, before verse 31 introduces Ujjain, is not marked by any change of scene in the text.
Verse 48 line 1 has an unclear phrase (நக்க கணத்தை) that is read here as a group he did not look at, which is doubtful.
The word division of the edition splits many words across lines of the verse, as in வனச்சரர் and சாலங்காய.

cast.role: Udayana, the Vatsa king who is hunting for his lost divine elephant (called வத்தவன், உதையன்)
the Vatsa king's minister who rules while he is absorbed in plays (verse 29, uncertain)
Udayana's companion who warns him and brings five hundred heroes
King of Ujjain who rules with the discus and plots against Udayana
Pradyota's ministers, who praise Udayana and then build the decoy
Pradyota's minister who rides the artificial elephant and is sent with it
the ninety-six armed men hidden inside the machine elephant
the hunters and forest-dwellers who see the decoy and report it
Udayana's army that searches for the lost elephant

tamil: அரசனுக் கினிய ராகி யமைச்சிய னடத்திச் செற்றே
வருபகை பலவுந் தேய வரச்செங்கோ லுய்க்குங் காலை
அரியநா டகங்கள் கண்டே யரசனு முளமா ழாந்து
reading: The king's minister, dear to him, drives out the swarming enemies and runs the realm in the king's name, while the king, watching rare plays and sunk in feeling, forgets Karinam and dines with his beloved.
nuance: The verse sets the minister's labour beside the king's ease in one sentence, so the loss in the next verse follows a stretch of heedless pleasure. The word அமைச்சியன் is not a name; that it is Yugi, as verse 38 suggests, is an inference.
event: While his minister crushes the enemies and rules for him, the king, absorbed in plays, forgets Karinam and eats a meal with his beloved.

tamil: மன்னிய தெய்வ யானை மாயமாய் மறைந்து போக
மன்னனு மனந்த ளர்ந்து மணியிழந் தரவு போலத்
reading: The lasting divine elephant vanishes by magic; the king, spent like a serpent that has lost its jewel, falls into grief, bids the elephant be sought, and the great army goes searching all over the earth.
event: The divine elephant disappears and Udayana orders his army to search the whole land for it.

reading: Where the waters of the Sindhu and the Ganga join and feed the land, in the fair country of Avanti, stands the rich fortified city Ujjain, whose crowding mansions touch the moon.
nuance: The scene moves to Ujjain; the story of Udayana's side stops while the rival's court is set out.

reading: Pradyota, whose armies cannot be counted, rules the earth with the discus he bears, while kings in rows bring tribute in wealth, and he stays on with his roaring great elephant and chariot.
When the matchless king calls for the gold tribute, he has not seen that a mark has been put against one name on the roll of the kings' tribute; when it is told him he flares up.
nuance: The words ஒருமகன் புள்ளி are hard: it may be a single man or a son who made the mark, or a dot against a name. The sense of a mark on the roll is the likely one, but it is not fixed by the line.
event: Pradyota calls for tribute, is told of a mark on the tribute-roll that he had missed, and grows angry.

reading: His eyes blazing like a lotus on fire, the lord asks his ministers what excuse they have for hiding so well, until he forgot it, the wrong done by the king of the sea-girt land.
nuance: The accused is left unnamed in the verse; that the sea-girt king is Udayana comes from the next verses, which praise his gifts. A king who accuses his counsellors of concealing a fact is the case Kural 638 and 639 reverse.
event: Pradyota questions his ministers for concealing the offender's act from him.

reading: The ministers begin to list what the man has: courage proved in the field, learning that brings gain, his way of checking the fierce-eyed elephant, and his flawless mastery of the veena.
nuance: The two skills at the centre of the list, handling elephants and playing the veena, are the ones the ambush later uses against him.
event: The ministers name Udayana's skills of arms, learning, elephant-taming and the veena to the angry king.

reading: They go on to his inherited wealth, his youth and beauty, his jewels and good family, and say, in measured words, that since he is all this what he did is his due.
nuance: The ministers answer the king's accusation by praising the man, not by denying the fault. The sense of உற்ற கடனென, that what he did is fitting to his rank, is doubtful.
event: The ministers finish listing Udayana's merits and speak of what is due to him.

reading: The king hears and rages, orders them to seize the man who has come and bring him, and the ministers gathered there ask what must be done, then settle among themselves on something else.
nuance: The king's anger overrides the ministers' praise at once, and the ministers do not oppose it openly but turn to a scheme.
event: Pradyota orders Udayana seized; his ministers instead decide on another plan.

reading: The proud ministers take counsel on several matters, Yugi's going to war against the weak foes, the king's pity at the elephant's going, and catching a forest elephant by showing one, and join in one counsel.
nuance: The verse names three things on the table; which one they choose has to be read from what they build in the next verses.
