event: Pradyota's ministers deliberate and agree on a plan of taking an elephant by displaying another.

reading: With lac, thread hardened with wax, wood, painted lime and hair, with stretched hide and whatever else they needed, they made an elephant with their own hands.
nuance: The materials are the ones used for dolls and models: the elephant is made to be taken for a real one, not for use as a siege engine.
event: The ministers build an artificial elephant out of lac, thread, wood, hair and hide.

reading: A mechanical elephant with levers and a swollen belly holds ninety-six men, weapons hidden, and they drive it along the road like a blue mountain.
nuance: The men inside are the weapon and the elephant a shell: its likeness to a real elephant is its only force.
event: Ninety-six armed men hide inside the mechanical elephant and drive it on.

reading: As the elephant trumpets like thunder, the minister Salankayan, one of the ministers, rides the battle-elephant before the king and shows it.
event: Salankayan rides the artificial elephant before Pradyota to show it to him.

reading: At the ruler's word, Salankayan, go and bring it, he sets off swiftly with spear, with the white umbrella, the sceptre and the feather fan of kings.
nuance: That Salankayan carries the king's insignia may mark him as the king's envoy or may be a part of the disguise; the verse does not say.
event: Pradyota sends Salankayan out; he sets off carrying royal insignia.

reading: Sixteen thousand elephants of the eight hills, sixteen thousand fine horses, sixteen thousand decorated chariots and sixteen thousand archers go with them.
nuance: The word எண்வரை before elephants is rare and its sense (of eight kinds, or of the eight hills) is not fixed here.
event: A force of sixteen thousand each of elephants, horses, chariots and archers is named to go with the machine.

reading: With all this in good order, the one who sends them says come softly, and the elephant of well-made levers arrives in the forest of the Vatsa king.
nuance: The verse does not name who gives the order to come softly; it may be the king or Salankayan.
event: The artificial elephant and its host are sent to the forest of the Vatsa king.

reading: In that forest the hunters look with love at the cow-elephants and at the great bull whose rut sets bees rising, holding a leafy bough in its trunk like a storm cloud.
nuance: The decoy is made to behave like a bull in rut, so the shell is dressed in the signs of a living elephant.
event: The forest-dwellers see the decoy among the real cow-elephants and take it for a rutting bull.

reading: Thinking it is our lord's elephant, they run to tell Udayana; with a splendid horse in jewelled trappings, the proud king mounts and sets out.
nuance: Whether எம் இறை means Udayana, as the story of the lost divine elephant would suggest, or only the hunters' lord in general is not fixed in the line.
event: The hunters report the elephant to Udayana, thinking it his own, and he rides out.

tamil: புள்ளிடை தடுப்பத் தீய பொய்க்குறி செய்யக் கண்டும்
வள்ளலு நடப்பா னாக வயந்தகன் விலக்கப் போந்து
கள்ளவிழ் மலர்க்கா னத்துக் கள்ளநல் லியானை கண்டே
உள்ளமெய் மொழிக டம்மா லுணர்ந்தவ னினிய னானான்.
reading: Though birds cross his path and ill signs show, the generous king walks on, Vayantakan holds him back in vain, and in the honey-dripping grove he sees the false elephant and grows glad by words he trusts.
nuance: Omens and a warning both reach him before he sees the decoy; the verse offers no excuse for him. The sense of line 4 is not clear.
event: Udayana ignores the omens and Vayantakan's warning and walks to the grove where he sees the false elephant.

reading: Without a glance of desire at the company named in line 1, he is glad at heart and plays his great veena, strings true, in the right raga.
nuance: He answers a decoy of his own sort with his own art: the skill that the ministers praised is his lure.
event: Udayana takes up his veena and plays it in the proper raga.

reading: As the music reaches the wide ears of the mechanical elephant and he rides on eagerly, the hidden men burst the hand-made beast, the fittings fall away, and it becomes a fighting host.
nuance: The words of line 3 can also be read as the hidden men destroying the elephant's shell for the sake of the attack; the sense is the same.
event: The hidden men break out of the machine as Udayana rides in, and it turns into an army.

reading: Seeing in the enemy's deed a clever picture, he smiles, and Vayantakan and five hundred faultless heroes come and join him.
event: Udayana smiles at the trick and is joined by Vayantakan and five hundred warriors.

reading: The army hidden in the elephant spreads out and closes round them; the angry Vatsa king cuts down hundreds, then his own force breaks and dies at the front.
nuance: Whose army is meant by சேனை in line 4 is not marked; it may be his own five hundred.
event: The hidden host encircles Udayana's party; he kills hundreds before the force at the front is broken.

title: உஞ்சைக் காண்டம் 52-74 (3/5)
theme: The capture and its answer: Udayanan's sword wins in the fighting until an elephant's tusk breaks it and he is seized; the dream of Vasavadatta foretells a taker, and Yugi, hearing of the capture, plans a rescue by guile, spreading news of his own death and entering the enemy's city disguised as a madman.
source_issues: Verse 54 line 4 reads மன்றன் where மன்னன் is expected; the subject of the sword is inferred from verse 55.
Verses 56, 61 and 74 are unfinished clauses with no main verb and run on into the next; verse 68 line 3 பெருமகன்கணிகைமைந்தர் is hard to parse; verse 63 lines 1-2 are speech not marked as speech.

cast.role: the hero, king of Vatsa, called வத்தவன் in verse 53, who is captured
the minister whose four-fold army surrounds Udayanan
king of Ujjain, Vasavadatta's father
Pradyotanan's daughter, who has the dream
Udayanan's companion who writes the letter and carries it to Yugi
Udayanan's chief minister, who plots his rescue
the harsh-spoken men who seize the king, Pradyotanan's side by the context
the readers of the book of dreams who interpret Vasavadatta's dream

reading: Salankayan, enraged, closes in with the four-fold army, which rises up and ringed the king from all four quarters while his eyes redden like Death's.
event: Salankayan's four-fold army surrounds the king from the four quarters.

reading: Like a tiger in a herd of deer, the sword-wielding king of Vatsa makes the bowmen fall and feeds Death a feast, giving the blade its food.
event: Udayanan cuts down the bowmen who ring him.

reading: As blood runs like a river and the men standing about flee, the furious Salankayan comes on, and the king sets his sword on his head.
nuance: The word மன்றன் in line 4 is not a clear word for king, so the verse does not name who lays the sword; the next verse, which has the king spare the man, is what fixes the reading.
event: Udayanan overpowers Salankayan and lays his sword on his head.

reading: Kings do not put ministers to death, so the king, heeding the words of the wise, does not press down his sword and lets that minister go in affection.
nuance: The sparing is given as a rule of kings and as the advice of the learned, not as the king's own softness. In this chapter the same king is soon taken captive by men who show him no such restraint.
event: Udayanan spares the minister Salankayan and sets him free.

reading: Elephants in a mass close in, and the war-elephants fall like hills, the rows of jewelled chariots roll on the ground and horses surge and fall on the earth.
nuance: The verse is one long clause with four falling things and no finite verb; verse 57 supplies the sentence, so read the two together.
event: A battle of elephants, chariots and horses brings down the combatants; the verse has no main verb and runs on into the next.

reading: As the king's rage cuts through another rank and his sword snaps on an elephant's tusk, harsh-speaking men seize the garlanded king, left without refuge.
nuance: The captors are called only harsh-spoken men; that they are the Ujjain king's people follows from the letter and the dream of the verses that come after.
event: Udayanan's sword breaks on an elephant's tusk and Pradyotanan's men seize him.

reading: A catalogue of what the captive's hand used to do for women: set fresh flowers in their hair, draw the moon-like mark on their brow, smear saffron on their breasts and fit anklets on their lotus feet.
nuance: The verse never names a hand's owner. It sets four tender acts of the hand beside the fact, told in the next verse, that the same hand is now tied.

reading: The hand that plays the lute, daubs scented paste and gives to those who ask, the hand of my faultless crowned king, is bound with white cloth for all outside to see.
nuance: The speaker says என்முடி மன்னன் ('my crowned king') and is not named, so he may be a lamenting follower or the poet in a follower's voice; the reading keeps the speaker open. The giving hand is the one that is bound: the verse links his generosity to his helplessness.
event: Udayanan's hands are bound with white cloth while the onlookers outside cry out.

reading: Vayanthakan writes a palm-leaf letter to the loving Yugi, as one binds a fine lion in a spider's thread, and hands it over with his own fair hand.
nuance: The simile means the lion is held by a thread that would be nothing if he were free; it puts the captivity as a binding by guile more than by strength.
event: Vayanthakan writes a letter to Yugi telling of the king's capture and gives it to him.

reading: As the king is carried under guard on a bright chariot, Vasavadatta, the beloved daughter of the great Pradyotanan, in a dream of her own sees something that is worked out in the next verses.
nuance: The verse is one unfinished clause: the guarded chariot and the dream are put side by side with no main verb. That the passenger is the captive king is read from the context of verses 57-60.
event: The captive king is taken to Ujjain while Vasavadatta has a dream.

reading: In bed as the young sun rose she dreamed that someone clasped her breasts and carried her off with him; she told it to her good father, who asked those who knew the book of dreams.
nuance: The dream is told in the narrator's voice without naming the man who takes her; the reading of verse 63 is what turns it into a prophecy.
event: Vasavadatta tells her father her dream and he asks the dream-readers about it.

tamil: இவண்மு லைக்கி யைந்தநல் லெழின்ம ணம்ம கன்வந்தே
துவளி டையி ளமுலை தோய்ந்து கொண்டு போமென
அவள்க னவு ரைப்பக்கேட் டண்ண லும்ம கிழ்ந்தபின்
திவளு மாலைத் தேர்மிசைச் செம்மல் வந்த டைந்தனன்.
reading: The readers tell that a bridegroom will come and take her away, touching her young breasts, and when her father hears the dream he is glad, and a lord arrives on a garlanded chariot.
nuance: The speech of lines 1-2 is assigned to the readers of verse 62 and is not marked off as speech; the odd wording இவண்முலைக்கியைந்த makes its parse uncertain. The father's gladness follows from the foretelling and the captive is the one said to be arriving, so the verse sets prophecy and arrival side by side.
event: The dream-readers tell Pradyotanan that a bridegroom will come and take Vasavadatta, and the captive king arrives.

tamil: மன்ன னைமி கவும்நொந்து மாந கரி ரங்கவும்
துன்னி வெஞ்சி றைமனையிற் றொல்வி னைது ரப்பவும்
இன்ன நற் படியிருப்ப வியல்வ யந்த கனுந்தான்
சென்று யூகி தன்னிடைத் திருமு கத்தைக் காட்டினான்.
reading: With the king pitied and the great city weeping, an old deed driving him into the fierce prison-house, Vayanthakan goes to Yugi and shows him the letter.
nuance: Line 2 puts the captivity in an old deed (தொல்வினை); nothing in the verse says the king's own folly or the enemy's guile as its cause, though the poet's account of the battle shows both.
event: Vayanthakan brings the letter to Yugi and shows it.

tamil: அண்ணல் கோயி லெங்கணு மரற்றி னும்பு லம்பினும்
கண்ணி னீர ருவிகள் கால லைத்தொ ழுகவும்
அண்ண லோலை வந்தசெய்தி மான யூகி கேட்டுடன்
புண்ணில் வேலெ றிந்தெனப் பொற்ப ழிந்து வீழ்ந்தனன்.
reading: Cries ring out in every palace and eyes stream, and Yugi, hearing the message of his lord's letter, falls broken like one struck on a wound by a spear.
event: Yugi hears the letter's news and collapses.

tamil: தேறி னனெ ழுந்திருந்து தீயர் கள்ள யானையை
மாறு தரக் காட்டியெம் மன்ன னைப்பி டித்தனர்
வீறு தர வந்நகரை வெங்க யத்த ழித்துப்பின்
கூறு மன்ம களுடன் கொற்ற வனை மீட்குவம்.
reading: Rising steadied, Yugi says: the wicked showed a false elephant and took our king; we shall destroy their city with fierce elephants and recover the king along with the famed king's daughter.
nuance: The words that name the trap, கள்ள யானை, tell the reader that the capture was by a decoy elephant; verse 57 shows only the seizure. The vow also takes in the king's daughter, which makes the rescue a winning of a bride as well.
event: Yugi recovers and resolves to take the king back and destroy Ujjain.

tamil: மீள்கு வம்யா ருமென் றெணி வெகுண்டு போர்க்க ளத்தினில்
வாண்மு னைக டந்தவர்க்கு வஞ்ச னைசெய் வோமென
நீள்வி ழிநன் மாதரோடு நின்ற சுற்றத் தோர்களைக்
கோள் களைந்து புட்பகத்திற் கொண்டு வந்து வைத்தனன்.
reading: Resolving that they would all return, and that those who had passed through the sword's edge would be met with guile, he took the king's kin and wives out of danger and set them in Pushpakam.
nuance: The resolve is Yugi's thought in the narrator's frame, and the work does not say here whether guile is right in itself, only that it is his answer.
event: Yugi moves the king's kin and women from the battlefield to Pushpakam.

tamil: உருமண் ணுவா வினுட னிடப கன்ச யந்தியும்
திருநி றைந்த புட்பகமுஞ் சேர்ந்தி னிதி ருக்கவென்
பெரும கன்க ணிகை மைந்தர் பிங்க லக டகரை
அரசு நாட்டி யாள்கவென்றே யன்பு டன்கொ டுத்தனன்.
reading: With Urumannuvan, Idabakan and Jayanti kept safe in prosperous Pushpakam, he gives the rule lovingly to Pingala and Kadaka, bidding them reign.
nuance: பெருமகன்கணிகைமைந்தர் can be read as the sons of a courtesan or as parts of names; the reading takes the two named rulers and leaves their parentage open.
event: Yugi appoints Pingala and Kadaka to rule Pushpakam and keeps Urumannuvan and others there.

tamil: மன்ன வற்கி ரங்கியூகி மரித்த னனென் வார்த்தையைப்
பன்னி யெங்க ணும்முறை பரப்பி வைய கந்தன்னில்
அன்ன தன தொப்புமை யமைந் ததோர்ச வந்தனை
reading: Pitying the king, Yugi has the news of his own death spread everywhere and, thinking of a corpse that matches his own, burns it in a bright fire of forest wood.
nuance: The false death serves the plan of getting to the captive king unwatched; it costs him the loyalty of the realm that verse 70 states.
event: Yugi has it said that he is dead and burns a body made to pass as his.

tamil: தன்ன கர்பு லம்பவெங்குந் தன்னை யுங்க ரத்தலின்
உன்னி வந்து மாற்றரச ரோங்கு நாடு பற்றினர்
என்ற றிந்து யூகியு மினிச்சி றையின் மன்னனைச்
சென்ற வட்காண் டுமென்று தேய முன்னிச் சென்றனன்.
reading: Hearing that his own city is crying out and enemy kings, thinking him hidden, have seized the high lands, Yugi decides to go and see the king in prison and sets out to that country.
event: Yugi hears that his lands are taken and sets out for the prison to see the king.

tamil: துன்ன ருநற் கானமோடு தொன்ம லையிற் சாரலும்
செந்நெல் கள்வி ளைவயற் செழும்பு னன திகளும்
மன்னு நாடுந் தான்கடந்து மாகொ டிநி றைந்திலங்கு
நன்ன கருஞ் சேனையி னன்க மைச்சன் சென்றனன்.
reading: Through wild forest, old hills, their slopes, fields of ripening red rice, lush streams and settled lands, the good minister goes on with his army toward the splendid city of banners.
nuance: Most of the verse is a catalogue of the land he passes; the one event is his march, and it adds the army to the picture of the lone disguised man in the verses that follow.
event: Yugi crosses forest, hills and farmland with his army toward the city.

reading: He leaves his strong army hidden behind the wall of a crowded settlement at the shining Tiger-face gate, a place loud as the roaring sea.
nuance: புலிமுகவாயில் is read as the name of a gate or place; the verse does not say whose city it is, so only the army's hiding is stated.
event: Yugi lodges his army in hiding at the Tiger-face gate settlement.

reading: Drilling in the words that would draw out each question and its answer, speech of feigned madness that the king would know, he takes a fixed disguise and walks into the middle of the city street.
nuance: மருளுரை is read as speech that bewilders others but carries a sense the king would recognise; the verse makes the king, not the onlookers, the speech's real hearer.
event: Yugi prepares coded mad talk, puts on a disguise and enters the city's main street.

reading: He scatters his dark hair so that it falls loose, winds on a garland that bewilders, rubs coloured powder over his body and fixes a mark in the right place.
nuance: The verse is one unfinished list of acts of dress, with no main verb; line 4 is obscure and the reading takes it as a forehead mark.
event: Yugi dresses himself as a madman with loose hair, garland and powder.

title: உஞ்சைக் காண்டம் 75-97 (4/5)
theme: Yugi, disguised as a mad performer, signals Udayanan in prison through music, rouses the king's elephant, which wrecks Ujjain; the ministers advise freeing the captive, and the vina of Udayanan brings the elephant to bow.
source_issues: Verses 75-76 do not name the figure described; identification with Yugi rests on verse 81.
Verse 82 line 2-3 (நாகத்தின் கோடு பாய்ந்த... வடுவ்வை) is corrupt.
Verse 89 line 2 (கண்டமாந்தரை தரைதத்ன்) looks corrupt.
Verse 90 numerals in lines 1-2 are garbled.
Verse 95: சீவகன் appears with no explanation; may be a scribal intrusion.

cast.role: Udayanan's minister, who comes disguised to free him
the Vatsa king, held captive in Ujjain
Yugi's friend and helper
the king of Ujjain, who holds Udayanan
the Ujjain king's counsellors
the king's guards and soldiers
the people of Ujjain
the king's war elephant, set loose against the city
the mahouts who try to hold the elephant
the speaker of verse 95; name unexplained in the verse

reading: A figure is described in costume: a golden band on the brow, sandal paste on the chest, a golden girdle at the waist and a garment slit with arrows.
nuance: The verse never names the wearer; that this is the disguised Yugi is known only from verse 81, where the king knows him by his music.

reading: The same figure is dressed in a garland and upper cloth, earrings, anklet bells, a dried waist-cloth, a playing flute and a water pot carried on the head.
nuance: A strange mixed costume that suits a mad entertainer; the verse leaves the guise unnamed.

reading: The figure appears in the middle of the flag-hung old city's fine street, dancing, passes through the steps of the dance and comes along sweetly, roaring like thunder.
nuance: Yugi is not named; the entry as a public performer is the first stage of the rescue plan.
event: A dancing, thundering stranger comes down the main street of the city.

reading: The figure cries out that Indra has left Indra's world and come, that he sits in the sky and has come in love, and that he is lord of the sons who are Indra's lord, in words whose last two lines are broken.
nuance: The claim to be Indra is part of a mad-man's act, not a belief of the poem; lines 3-4 are too broken to parse with confidence.
event: The disguised man proclaims himself Indra come down.

reading: The speaker says a five-headed snake with spotted stripes was caught from its anthill and put, held, inside this city's prison, and that they showed it so that it should be known everywhere.
nuance: The snake is most likely a veiled name for the imprisoned Udayanan, so a madman's babble tells the crowd what the guards cannot take as news; the verse itself does not say so.
event: The disguised man speaks in riddling words of a captured snake kept in the city's prison.

reading: After teaching bewilderment and clarity without measure, with crowds gathering around him, he leaves the great streets behind and comes to the hard prison hall.
event: The disguised man draws a crowd, then reaches the prison.

tamil: கிளைத்தலை யிருவர் கற்ற கிளர்நரப் பிசையுங் கீதம்
உளத்தியல் பாட்டைக் கேட்டு யூகியா மென மகிழ்ந்து
களைந்தனன் கவலை யெல்லாங் காவலற் குணர்த்திப் போந்தான்.
reading: Two kinsmen's song learned on the strings is played on the flute he enjoys for the chained king to hear; the king hears the song of his own mind, knows that it is Yugi and rejoices, casts off every care, and Yugi, having told the king, leaves.
nuance: The tune is the secret message: the guards hear a mad piper, the king hears his minister. Line 1, 'two of the kin', is unclear.
event: Yugi plays music at the prison so that the captive Udayanan knows him and takes heart.

tamil: பலகொடி வாயிற் செல்லப் பார்மன்னன் சேனை வந்து
நலமுறு வடிவு நோக்க நாகத்தின் கோடு பாய்ந்த
கலனணி மார்வ டுவ்வைக் கஞ்சுகத் துகிலின் மூடத்
தலைமுத லடியீ றாகத் தரத்தினாற் கண்டு போந்தார்.
reading: The king's soldiers come through many gates to see the fine form of the man and, from his head to his feet, look him over as he goes; the line about the ornament on his chest and the cloth over it is broken.
nuance: Line 2 and the word வடுவ்வை in line 3 read as corrupt; only the sense that he was looked over and passed is secure.
event: The king's men examine the strange performer and let him go.

tamil: பித்தனற் பேய னென்று பெருமகற் குரைப்பக் கேட்டு
வெற்றிநற் சேனை மற்றும் வெஞ்சிறை காக்க வென்றான்
மற்றினி யூகி போந்து மலிகுடி பாக்கஞ் சேர்ந்தே
அற்றைநா ளிரவில் யானை யனல்கதம் படுக்க லுற்றான்.
reading: They tell the great king that the man is a ghost-possessed madman; hearing it, the king bids his victorious army to keep the cruel prison still, while Yugi goes to the village and that night sets about rousing the elephant's rage.
nuance: The guise works: the king's caution falls on the prison guard, not on the stranger.
event: The guards dismiss the stranger as mad; Yugi that night sets out to enrage the elephant.

tamil: வாளொடு கைவில் லேந்தி வயந்தகன் றன்னோ டெண்ணித்
தோளன தோழன் கூடத் தூபத்துக் கேற்ற வத்தும்
வேளையீ தென்று கொண்டு விரகினாற் கயிறு பற்றித்
தாளொத்த கொம்மை மீதிற் றரத்தினா லிழிந்தா னன்றே.
reading: With sword and bow in hand he reckons with Vayanthakan, his arm-like friend, that the hour is right for the fumigating materials, and by cunning he takes hold of a rope and goes down, by skill, onto the elephant's mass.
nuance: The words after the rope in lines 3-4 are hard; whether he drops onto the elephant's back or its legs is not clear.
event: Yugi and Vayanthakan choose the hour and go down a rope to the elephant.

tamil: ஆனைதன் னிலைகண் டெய்தி யகிலிடும் புகையு மூட்டிச்
சேனைமன் னகர ழித்துச் சிறைவீடுன் கடனே யொன்று
மானநல் யூகி யானை செவியின்மந் திரத்தைச் செப்ப
யானைதன் மதக்கம் பத்தி லருந்தளை யுதறிற் றன்றே.
reading: He sees the elephant's place, makes aguru smoke rise, and, telling the beast that it should destroy the army and the city and that freeing the captive is its task, the wise Yugi whispers a mantra into its ear, and in its maddened rut the elephant shakes off its heavy chain.
nuance: The elephant, the king's weapon, becomes the means of the captive's rescue; this is the stratagem the whole sequence turns on.
event: Yugi smokes the elephant, whispers a mantra into its ear and the elephant breaks its chain.

tamil: நீங்கிட மிதுவென் றெண்ணி நிலைமதி லேறிப் போகத்
தூங்கிரு டன்னி லானை சுழன் றலைந் தோடப் பாகர்
பாங்கினால் வளைப்பப் பொங்கிப் படுமுகின் முழக்க மென்ன
reading: Thinking this the way to leave, Yugi climbs the standing wall and goes; in the thick darkness the elephant whirls and runs, and when the mahouts try to enclose it, it roars like a bursting cloud, tears loose and kills them with its trunk.
nuance: The keepers die at the hand of the beast they were set to guard, the cost of the stratagem falling first on men who did nothing.
event: The freed elephant kills the mahouts who try to enclose it.

tamil: வேழமும் மதங்கொண் டோட வேந்தன்கேட் டினிதெ ழுந்து
வேழநன் வேட்டங் காண வெம்முலை மாத ரோடும்
ஆழிநல் லிறைவன் றானு மணிமிகு மாட மேறிச்
சூழநன் மாதர் நிற்பத் துளக்கின்றி நோக்கி னானே.
reading: The elephant runs in rut, the king hears, rises and, with his full-breasted women, climbs a jewelled mansion to watch the hunt, looking on without a tremor.
nuance: The king watches it as a spectacle; the next verses show how soon his own city pays for it.
event: The Ujjain king climbs a mansion to watch the elephant he thinks he controls.

tamil: கூடமா ளிகைக ளெல்லாங் கோட்டினாற் குத்திச் செம்பொன்
மாடமு மதிலு மற்று மறித்தஃதி டித்துச் செல்ல
ஆடவர் கூடி யோடி யயில்குந்தந் தண்ட மேந்தி
நாடி நற்கையாற் றட்டி நாற்றிசை சூழ்ந்து நின்றார்.
reading: The elephant gores the storeyed halls and golden mansions and walls and pulls them down as it passes, while men gather, run, hold spears and staffs and strike it, standing around it on all four sides.
event: The elephant batters the city's mansions while men try to surround it.

tamil: கூற்றுரு வெய்தி யோடிக் கோட்டிடைக் குடர்க ளாடக்
காற்றென முழக்கி வேழங் கண்டமாந் தரைதத்ன் கையால்
நாற்பத்தெண் பேரைக் கொன்று நடுவுறப் பிளந்திட் டோடி
மாற்றருங் கோட்டை வாயின் மதிற்புறம் போந்த தன்றே.
reading: In the shape of death, its tusks hung with entrails, it roars like the wind and kills forty-eight men with its trunk, splits the crowd through its middle and runs outside the wall to the unconquerable fort gate.
nuance: The words கண்டமாந்தரை... தரைதத்ன் in line 2 look corrupt and the sense is partly guessed.
event: The elephant kills forty-eight and breaks out toward the fort gate.

tamil: அறுநூற்றின் மீதி லைம்ப தானநற் சேரி தானும்
உறுநூற்றி லேழை மாற வுள்ளநாற் பாடி யோடும்
நறுமலர்க் கந்தம் வீசு நன்குள காவு மற்றும்
பெறுமத யானை கோட்டாற் பெருநக ரழித்த தம்மா.
reading: By its tusks the great elephant ruins the great city: so many streets of the six hundred and fifty, the seven hundred, the four wards and the fragrant gardens are wrecked.
nuance: The numerals of lines 1-2 are garbled in the edition and cannot be added up.
event: The elephant's tusks wreck streets, wards and gardens.

tamil: பாடுநன் மகளி ரெல்லாம் பாட்டொழிந் தரற்றி யோட
ஆடுநன் மாதர் தாமு மாடல்விட் டலந்து செல்லக்
reading: The singing women stop their song and run crying, the dancers leave the dance and wander off, the couples scatter, and many take shelter on the upper floors of the golden mansions.
event: Singers, dancers and couples flee to the upper storeys.

tamil: மத்துறு கடலின் மிக்கு மறுகிய நகரத் தாரும்
வற்றிநல் வேந்த னோடு வினவினா ரமைச்ச ரெண்ணி
இத்தின நகரம் பட்ட விடரது விலக்க னல்ல
வத்தவன் கைய தென்ன வகுத்துரை கேட்ட மன்னன்.
reading: The townspeople, churned like the sea by a churning stick, ask the king; the ministers consider and say the disaster of this city can not be turned aside, that it lies in Vatsa's hand, and the king hears the explanation.
nuance: The ministers' point turns the captive into the only remedy of the harm; whether they know of Yugi's scheme is not said.
event: The citizens question the king and his ministers say only Udayanan can stop the elephant.

tamil: போரினி னிற்க லாற்றாம் பொய்யினிற் றந்த மைந்தன்
சீரொடு சிறப்பும் வௌவிச் சிறையினில் வைத்த தன்றிப்
பேரிடிக் கரிமுன் விட்டாற் பெரும்பழி யாகு மென்று
தாருடை வேந்தன் சொல்லத் தரத்தினா லமைச்சர் சொல்வார்.
reading: The king says he could not stand against him in battle, brought the son by a lie, took his glory and held him in prison, and that sending him before the thundering elephant would bring a great stain; the ministers then answer.
nuance: The king admits that the capture was by a lie and that war had been beyond him; his fear is of blame, not of the wrong.
event: The king hesitates to send his captive before the elephant, and the ministers reply.

tamil: இந்திர னானை தானு மிவன்கையா ழிசைக்கு மீறா
திந்திரன் வேழ முங்கேட் டேழடி செல்லு மற்றிக்
கந்திறு கைம்மா விக்கோன் கைவீணை கடவா தென்ன
மந்திரத் தவர்சொற் கேட்டு மன்னனப் படிச்செய் கின்றான்.
reading: The ministers say that Indra's own elephant does not go beyond the sound of this man's lute, and that if it hears it goes but seven steps, so this tusked elephant cannot pass the king's vina; hearing the mantra-knowers' words, the king does as they say.
nuance: The ministers' claim of the vina's mastery over elephants is a promise whose test comes in verse 97.
event: On the ministers' advice the king sends for Udayanan to play against the elephant.

tamil: சீவகன் வத்த வற்குச் செவ்விதிற் செப்பு கின்றான்
தேவ விந் நகரிடுக் கண் டீர்க்கைநின் கடன தாகும்
போவதுன் றேசத் தென்றல் புரவலன் கடன தாகும்
பூவல னுரைத்தா னென்னப் புகழ்ந்தவன் சிறை விடுத்தான்.
reading: Civakan tells Vatsa straightly that this city's distress is seen and that to end it is his duty, that to go to his own land is the guardian's duty, and praising him as one that the flower-hand has spoken, he frees him from the prison.
nuance: Civakan, the name Jivaka of the Cintamani, appears here with no explanation; the form may be an editor's slip or a second name of the Ujjain king, so the speaker is held with doubt.
event: The speaker frees Udayanan after asking him to end the city's distress.

tamil: உருவுள சிவிகை யேறி யுயர்மன்னன் மனைபு குந்து
திருமயி ரெண்ணெ யிட்டுத் திறத்தினன் னீரு மாடி
மருவிநன் பட்டு டுத்து மணிக்கல னினிது தாங்கித்
தெருவிடைத் திகழப் புக்கான் றிருநகர் மகிழ் வன்றே.
reading: The king takes a bodied palanquin to the palace, oils his hair, bathes with care, puts on silk and a fine jewel, and enters the street gleaming while the great city rejoices.
event: Udayanan is freed, bathed and dressed, and rides into the street.

tamil: பருந்துபின் றொடர யானை பறவைகண் மற்றுஞ் சூழப்
பெருந்தெரு நடுவுட் டோன்றப் பீடுடைக் குமரன் றானும்
திருவலித் தடக்கை வீணை சீருடன் பாட லோடும்
மருவலிக் களிறுங் கேட்டு வந்தடி பணிந்த தம்மா.
reading: With hawks following, elephants and birds around, the honoured prince appears in the middle of the great street, singing with his great hand on the vina, and the rutting elephant, hearing, comes and bows at his feet.
nuance: The vina does what the mantra started and the guards could not undo; the claim of verse 94 holds.
event: Udayanan plays the vina and the raging elephant comes and bows at his feet.

title: உஞ்சைக் காண்டம் 98-120 (5/5)
theme: Udayanan wins the king of Ujjain's trust by mastering the elephant, teaches Vasavadatta, is granted leave and an army, and flees with her by Yugi's fire-trick on the she-elephant, which dies and is reborn a god, then fends off the hunters and reaches Jayanti.
source_issues: Verse 102: the speaker and identity of திருமகள் is not clear.
Verse 105 lines 3 to 4: the grammar is hard and who forgives whom is uncertain.
Verse 107 line 4 and verse 108 line 3 are hard to read.
Verse 113 lines 1 to 3: the measure and the speaker are not clear.
Verse 109 line 3 is hard to parse.

cast.role: the king of Vatsa, held at Ujjain, who tames the elephant and teaches Vasavadatta
the king of Ujjain, Vasavadatta's father (named by titles in these verses)
the king of Ujjain's daughter, Udayanan's pupil
Udayanan's minister who plans the escape
Udayanan's friend
Vasavadatta's friend
a lady who tells a dream in verse 102; identity not clear
the princes of Ujjain, the king's sons
the brahmins who fix the hour
the elephant Udayanan makes kneel
the she-elephant on which they flee
Udayanan, Vasavadatta and their companions riding the she-elephant
the forest hunters who attack the fugitives

tamil: பிரிந்தநற் புதல்வர் வந்து பெற்றதந் தந்தை பாதம்
பரிந்தநற் காத லாலே பணிந்திடு மாறு போலே
இருந்துதற் பணிந்த யானை யெழின்மருப் படிவைத் தேறிப்
பெருந்தகை யேவிக் கோட்டு பெருங்கையாற் றோட்டி கொண்டான்.
reading: The elephant kneels to Udayanan like sons long parted who come back and bow to their father's feet, and the great man, secure in his seat, takes up the goad in his big hand and drives it.
nuance: The simile of sons returning to a father makes the animal's submission an act of love, not of force; the verse does not say which elephant this is, nor how it was brought to kneel.
event: The elephant bows down to Udayanan, who mounts, steadies himself and takes the goad.

tamil: வைத்தநன் மணியும் யாழும் வரிக்கயி றதுவு நீட்ட
வெற்றிநல் வேந்தன் வாங்கி வீக்கிமிக் கார்த்துக் கொண்டே
உற்றநல் வீதி தோறு மூர்ந்துநற் சாரி வட்டம்
பற்றிநன் கோட்டக் கண்டு பார்த்திபன் மகிழ்ச்சி கொண்டான்.
reading: Udayanan takes the gem, the lute and the striped rope that are held out, ties them on, rides the elephant along every street in circles, and the king who watches him is glad.
event: Udayanan, riding the elephant through the streets in circles, delights the king of Ujjain.

tamil: முடிப்புவி யரச னீய மொய்ம்பனு மணிந்து கொண்டு
கொடிப்புலி முகத்து வாயிற் கோட்டையுட் கொண்டு வந்தான்
இடிக்குரற் சீய மொப்ப விலங்கிய குமரன் றானே.
reading: The king of Ujjain gives a priceless pearl necklace, which the strong youth puts on, and he rides into the fort gate under the tiger banner like a roaring lion.
event: The king gives Udayanan a pearl necklace; Udayanan wears it and enters the fort on the elephant.

tamil: சால்கவென் றிறைவன் செப்பத் தன்னுடைக் கையி னோச்சிக்
கால்களின் விரலி னெற்றி கனக்கநன் கூன்றி நின்று
மால்கரி கால் கொடுப்ப மன்னனு மகிழ்ந்து போந்து
வேல்கவின் வேந்தன் காண வியந்துடன் தழுவிக் கொண்டான்.
reading: At the king's word that it is enough, Udayanan raises his hand, braces his toes on the elephant's brow, and makes it give its legs; the king, pleased, embraces him.
nuance: The only words spoken are the king's brief 'enough', which ends the display.
event: At the king's command Udayanan makes the elephant kneel, and the king embraces him.

tamil: மருமக னீயே யென்று மன்னவ னினிமை கூறி
வருமுறை நயந்து கொண்டு மகிழ்ந்துட னிருந்த போழ்தில்
திருமகள் கனவு கூறிச் செல்வநீ கற்பி யென்னப்
பெருவலி யுரைப்பக் கேட்டுப் பெருமக னுணர்த்த லானான்.
reading: The king calls Udayanan his son-in-law, speaks kindly, and as they sit in pleasure a lady tells of a dream and asks him to teach, whereupon the great man agrees to instruct.
nuance: மருமகன் may be a courtesy of the king's here and not a settled marriage; later verses still speak of Vasavadatta as a pupil.
event: The king calls Udayanan his son-in-law; a lady reports a dream and Udayanan agrees to teach.

tamil: வேந்தன்றன் மக்கட் கெல்லாம் வேன்முதல் பயிற்று வித்தும்
பூந்துகில் செறிம ருங்குற் பொருகயற் கண்ணி வேய்த்தோள்
வாய்ந்தவா சவதத் தைக்கு வருவித்தும் வீணை தன்னைச்
சேர்ந்தவ ணிகரி லின்பிற் செல்வனு மகிழ்வுற் றானே.
reading: The king has weapons taught to all his sons, and has the slender-waisted Vasavadatta brought to learn the lute, and the lord is glad.
nuance: The verse does not say who teaches whom the lute; the sense follows the preceding verse where Udayanan agrees to instruct.
event: The king has his sons trained in arms and brings Vasavadatta to learn the lute from Udayanan.

tamil: உரையினி லரிய னாய வுதயண குமர னோர்நாள்
அரசிளங் குமரர் வித்தை யண்ணனீ காண்க வென்ன
வரைநிகர் யானை யூர்ந்து மாவுடன் றேரி லேறி
வரிசையிற் காட்டி வாள்வில் வகையுடன் விளக்கக் கண்டான்.
reading: The young princes ask 'elder brother' Udayanan to watch their skill, and ride elephants, horses and chariots and show him their ways with sword and bow in order, which he watches.
event: The princes of Ujjain display their riding and weapon skills before Udayanan.

tamil: வாசவ தத்தை வந்து மன்னனை யிறைஞ்ச நல்யாழ்
பேசவை தளரக் கேட்டுப் பெருமக னினிய னாகி
ஆசிலா வித்தை யெல்லா மாயிழை கொண்டா ளென்றே
ஏசவன் சிறைசெய் குற்ற மெண்ணுறேல் பெருக்க வென்றாள்.
reading: Vasavadatta comes and bows to the king with her lute; hearing it falter, the great man is kind, saying the lady has all faultless arts, and she asks that the fault of imprisoning him not be counted.
nuance: Line 4 is the first mention in the chapter of Udayanan's imprisonment as a wrong to be forgiven, and who asks whom is not clear.
event: Vasavadatta bows to the king, and she speaks of the fault of Udayanan's imprisonment.

tamil: விசும்பியல் குமரர் தாமும் வியந்துட னிருப்பப் புல்லும்
பசும்பொனி னிலத்தில் வீழப் பாவையர் மயக்க முற்றார்
வசம்படக் குறுக்கி நீட்டி வரிசையிற் பாட லோடும்
அசும்பறாக் கடாத்து வேழத் தரசனு மகிழ்ந்தா னன்றே.
reading: The princes watch amazed while Udayanan, singing by the rules and drawing the strings short and long, makes the girls fall in a swoon on the golden floor, and the elephant-riding king rejoices.
nuance: Who plays the lute here is not named; the sense follows the lines 3 to 4 and the preceding performance.
event: Udayanan sings and plays; the women faint, and the king is pleased.

tamil: வத்தவன் கையைப் பற்றி மன்னவ னினிது கூறி
வத்தவ னோலை தன்னுள் வளமையிற் புள்ளி யிட்டும்
வத்தவ நாட்டுக் கேற வள்ளலைப் போக வென்ன
reading: The king takes the Vatsa lord's hand and speaks kindly, writes on a palm-leaf the royal marks of the Vatsa land, and tells him to go there; the brahmins name the next day as the hour.
nuance: The king here lets him go openly, yet verse 109 turns to Yugi's trick; the poem does not reconcile the two, and the last line is hard.
event: The king dismisses Udayanan to Vatsa with a written grant, and the brahmins fix the next day for departure.

tamil: ஓரிரண் டாயி ரங்க ளோடைதாழ் மத்த யானை
ஈரிரண் டாயி ரங்க ளெழின்மணிப் பொன்னின் றேரும்
போரியல் புரவி மானம் பொருவிலை யாயி ரம்மும்
வீரர்க ளிலக்கம் பேரும் வீறுநற் குமரற் கீந்தான்.
reading: The king gives the young lord two thousand rutting elephants, four thousand jewelled golden chariots, a thousand war horses and a very large number of soldiers.
nuance: The numbers are as the lines print them; line 3 is dense and the horse count is read only roughly.
event: The king gives Udayanan a great army.

tamil: யூகியும் வஞ்சந் தன்னை யுற்றுச்சூள் வழாமை நோக்கி
வாகுடன் குறத்தி வேடம் வகுத்தனன் குறிகள் கூற்றாம்
நாகத்தி னகர ழிந்த நடுக்கங்க டீர வெண்ணிப்
போகநன் னீரி லாடப் புரத்தினி லினிது ரைத்தான்.
reading: Yugi, holding to his sworn vow, takes a trick and the guise of a fortune-telling woman, and tells the city in pleasant words to go and bathe in the water in order to ease the fear of the trembling beast.
nuance: Yugi's deceit is done to keep a vow, not for his own gain, and the poem does not blame it; the sense of line 3 is uncertain.
event: Yugi, disguised as a kuratti, sets a stratagem and tells the city to go bathing.

tamil: மன்னவன் றன்னோ டெண்ணி மாநகர் திரண்டு சென்று
துன்னிய நீர்க்க யத்திற் றொல்புரப் புறத்தி லாட
நன்னெறி வத்த வன்றான் னன்பிடி யேறி நிற்ப
உன்னிய யூகி மிக்க வூரிற்றீ யிடுவித் தானே.
reading: The king, after consulting, goes with the city to the pool outside the old town to bathe; Udayanan stands on a good she-elephant, and Yugi has the town set alight.
event: The city goes to bathe; Yugi sets fire to Ujjain while Udayanan waits on the she-elephant.

tamil: பயந்துதீக் கண்டு சேனை பார்த்திபன் றன்னோ டேக
வயந்தகன் வந்து ரைப்ப வத்தவ குமரன் றானும்
நயந்துகோன் மகளை மிக்க நன்பிடி யேற்றத் தோழி
கயந்தனை விட்டு வந்த காஞ்சனை யேறி னாளே.
reading: Frightened at the fire, the army goes off with the king; Vayantakan comes and tells Udayanan, who gladly lifts the king's daughter onto the she-elephant, and her friend Kanchanai mounts too.
nuance: Whether Vasavadatta goes willingly is not said; the verse says only that Udayanan 'gladly' lifts her.
event: The fire scatters the court; Udayanan seats Vasavadatta on the she-elephant and Kanchanai joins her.

tamil: வயந்தகன் வீணை கொண்டு வன்பிடி யேறிப் பின்னைச்
செயந்தரக் கரிணி காதிற் செல்வன்மந் திரத்தைச் செப்ப
வியந்துபஞ் சவனந் தாண்ட வேயொடு பற்ற வீணை
வயந்தகன் கூற மன்னன் மாப்பிடி நிற்க வென்றான்.
reading: Vayantakan takes his lute and mounts the strong she-elephant, the lord speaks a mantra in her ear, and as they cross the Panchavanam forest the lord tells her to halt.
nuance: The mantra of line 2 is not named and its use here is as a charm for steadiness, not the dying mantra of verse 114.
event: Udayanan whispers a mantra to the she-elephant; Vayantakan rides; the elephant is made to stop.

tamil: நலமிகு புகழார் மன்ன நாலிரு நூற்று வில்லு
நலமிகத் தருமின் றென்ன பண்ணுகை நம்மா லென்னக்
குலமிகு குமரன் செல்லக் குஞ்சர மசைந்த தன்றே.
reading: The lines hail a noble king and say that the elephant has crossed a great stretch of eight hundred bows' length of land, which the god gave, and as the prince goes on the elephant begins to waver.
nuance: The measure in lines 1 to 2 and the speech in lines 2 to 3 are hard, and the speaker is not named.
event: The prince rides on and the elephant begins to give way.

tamil: அசைந்தநற் பிடியைக் கண்டே யசலித மனத்த ராகி
தசைந்தகை யுதிரம் பாயச் சாலமந் திரமங் காதில்
இசைந்தவர் சொல்லக் கேட்டே யின்புறத் தேவா யிற்றே.
reading: Seeing the she-elephant sink, the riders get down troubled; she falls to the earth bleeding, and as the great mantra is spoken into her ear she joyfully becomes a god.
nuance: The verse says only 'mantra' and does not name the five-fold salutation by which Jain accounts of such a death are known.
event: The exhausted she-elephant falls and dies; the riders speak the mantra in her ear and she is reborn a god.

tamil: உவளகத் திறங்கிச் சென்றே யூர்நிலத் தருகு செல்லப்
பவளக்கொப் புளங்கள் பாவை பஞ்சிமெல் லடியிற் றோன்றத்
தவளைக்கிண் கிணிகண் மிக்க தரத்தினாற் பேச லின்றித்
துவளிடை யருகின் மேவுந் தோழிதோள் பற்றிச் செல்வாள்.
reading: The lady gets down and walks toward the nearby ground, her feet, soft as cotton, blistered red like coral, her anklets silent in her weariness, and she goes holding her friend's shoulder.
event: Vasavadatta, footsore, walks on leaning on her friend's shoulder.

tamil: பாவைதன் வருத்தங் கண்டு பார்த்திபன் பாங்கி னோங்கும்
பூவைவண் டரற்றுங் காவுட் பூம்பொய்கை கண்டி ருப்ப
வாவுநாற் படையுங் கொண்டு வயந்தகன் வருவே னென்றான்
போவதே பொருளூர்க் கென்று புரவல னுரைப்பப் போந்தான்.
reading: Udayanan sees the lady's distress and the lotus pool in the grove; Vayantakan says he will come back with the four-fold army, the king tells him to go to the city, and he goes.
event: Vayantakan goes to bring the army while Udayanan stays with the weary Vasavadatta by the pool.

tamil: சூரியன் குடபாற் சென்று குடவரை சொருகக் கண்டு
நாரியைத் தோழி கூட நன்மையிற் றுயில்க வென்று
வீரிய னிரவு தன்னில் விழித்துட னிருந்த போழ்து
சூரிய னுதயஞ் செய்யத் தொக்குடன் புளிஞர் சூழ்ந்தார்.
reading: At sunset Udayanan bids the lady sleep with her friend and stays awake through the night; at sunrise the hunters gather round them.
event: Udayanan keeps watch through the night; at dawn the hunters surround him.

tamil: வந்தவ ரம்பு மாரி வள்ளன்மேற் றூவத் தானும்
தந்தனு மேவிச் சாராத் தரத்தினால் விலக்கிப் பின்னும்
வெந்திறல் வேடர் வின்னாண் வெந் நுனைப் பகழி வீழ
நந்திய சிலைவ ளைத்து நன்பிறை யம்பி னெய்தான்.
reading: The hunters rain arrows on the generous lord, who wards them off with his bow and, as their cruel arrows keep falling, bends his great bow and answers with crescent arrows.
event: The hunters shoot at Udayanan; he defends himself and shoots back with crescent-headed arrows.

tamil: செய்வகை யின்றி வேடர் தீவனங் கொளுத்த மன்னன்
உய்வகை யுங்க ளுக்கின் றுறுபொரு ளீவ னென்ன
ஐவகை யடிசில் கொண்டே யானநாற் படையுஞ் சூழ
மெய்வகை வயந்த கன்றான் வீறமைந் தினிதின் வந்தான்.
reading: Helpless, the hunters set fire to the wood; the king says he will give them wealth to live on, and Vayantakan arrives well turned out with five kinds of food and the four-fold army.
nuance: The offer to the hunters follows their defeat, so the gift is a settlement and not a ransom; whether they accept is not said here.
event: The hunters fire the forest; Udayanan promises them wealth; Vayantakan arrives with food and the army.

tamil: நன்புறச் சிவிகை யேற நங்கைநாற் படையுஞ் சூழப்
பண்புறு சயந்தி புக்குப் பார்த்திப னினிதி ருந்தான்.
reading: They eat the food gladly and stay that day; next morning the king mounts the fine elephant, the lady rides a palanquin with the army about them, and they enter Jayanti where the king sits at ease.
event: The party eats, rests and travels on to the city of Jayanti.

title: இலாவாண காண்டம் 121-135 (1/2)
theme: Settled at Jayanti, Udayanan sinks in pleasure with Vasavadatta and forgets his lost kingdom; Yugi, reading this, plans to part the king from the queen by stratagem, sends a Sankhya woman ascetic with a portrait, and the king, after a sage's prophecy, garlands Virisikai.
source_issues: Verses 125, 127 and 128: the order of events and the speaker are not clear.
Verse 131 lines 1 to 2: the painted eye and its sense are hard to read.
Verse 135 line 4: the grammar is loose, so Yugi's role in the parting is uncertain.

cast.role: king of Vatsa, living at Jayanti with Vasavadatta
Udayanan's minister who plans to part him from the queen
Udayanan's wife, daughter of the king of Ujjain
Udayanan's friend
a minister to whom Yugi tells his plan
the king of Ujjain (named by title)
the Sankhya woman ascetic, called the old woman, who carries the portrait
the sage Udayanan consults
the sage's daughter, whom Udayanan garlands
the hunters recalled in verse 128
the she-elephant of the flight

reading: The poet turns to what Udayanan did after reaching Jayanti, having left Ujjain, and says he gave himself to his love for the parrot-voiced lady.
event: Udayanan, settled at Jayanti, turns to enjoying Vasavadatta.

reading: He joins the bright-jewelled lady in the sweet manner of a sacrifice and enjoys the great pleasures of the senses with her, his love growing.
nuance: The comparison of union to a sacrifice (வேள்வி) and to the union of the serpent-folk is the poet's own image for the richness of the pleasure; the verse does not blame it.
event: Udayanan enjoys the pleasures of union with Vasavadatta.

reading: Unable to see the shore of his desire, the elephant-lord sinks in it, and the god of love's arrows plunge him deeper, until he swims the sea of desire with the lady's breast for a raft.
nuance: Desire is drawn as a sea he cannot cross; the raft that keeps him afloat is the very thing that holds him in it.

reading: He no longer thinks of the land he lost or of his lowly state, forgets virtue and his own self, lets neither night nor day go, and the king sinks, fallen in the lady's charms and bewildered.
nuance: The poet blames the king's forgetting directly (மறந்து, விழுந்து), and this is what the minister's later plan answers; it is the poet's judgement, not the lover's own.
event: Udayanan, absorbed in Vasavadatta, forgets his lost kingdom and his duty.

reading: While the king goes on like this, Yugi, dearer than life, looks on at the departure of Vatsa, freed from prison by Yugi's own scheme, with the fair lady on the young she-elephant.
nuance: Lines 1 and 4 can be read as Yugi watching the flight or as the poet recalling it; the grammar of the verse is loose.
event: Yugi, having freed the king from prison by his scheme, watches him ride off with the lady.

reading: Yugi, thinking lovingly of returning, hears that the king of Ujjain is grieving inwardly, learns by stratagem that the great army has not risen, leaves Ujjain's bounds and goes to Pushpakam.
nuance: The king of Ujjain is named only by title (உஞ்சைநகர்க் கரசன்); his grief at the escape is told, not shown.
event: Yugi, learning that Ujjain's army has not moved, leaves its border and goes to Pushpakam.

reading: Yugi tells Idabakan his own purpose and asks what effort is now fitting for their golden-crowned king; and as he comes on a she-elephant and has crossed a wide land, the elephant cannot bear to step and falls to the ground.
nuance: Lines 3 to 4 seem to recall the she-elephant's fall already told in verse 114, mixed into Yugi's talk; the verse's order of events is not clear.
event: Yugi confides his plan to Idabakan; the she-elephant on which the king rides collapses.

reading: A list of what befell: the hunters closed round them, the king beat them, he went with the matchless Vayantakan, entered Jayanti with its white flags, and joined the lady in love.
nuance: Only a string of nouns in -ததும்; who recites the list, the poet or Yugi, is not stated.
event: The verse recalls the hunters' siege, the king's victory and arrival at Jayanti.

reading: Hearing that the king, absorbed in pleasure, thinks nothing of the land he lost, Yugi smiles, his teeth shining, and decides that if the king is parted from his queen by a trick, the lost kingdom will come back to his hand.
nuance: Yugi's reasoning is given as his own thought (எண்ணினான்); the poem has not yet shown whether the plan is wise.
event: Yugi plans to part the king from the queen by stratagem in order to win back the kingdom.

reading: Yugi meets a woman ascetic of the Sankhya school, tells her what to say, and, as if his own life had left him, paints on a cloth the three ministers and the king's form.
nuance: The word சாங்கிய is used only to name the woman's order; the verse states no Sankhya doctrine.
event: Yugi instructs a Sankhya woman ascetic and has a portrait made of the king and his ministers.

reading: One figure in the portrait is set with the upper eye wide and the left one removed; with this and a message to be made known to the crowned king, the old woman goes and sees the lion-voiced lord.
nuance: Lines 1 to 2 on the painted eye are hard to parse; what the missing eye signals is not clear from the verse.
event: The old woman takes the portrait to Udayanan.

reading: The king sees her and, wishing to honour her, bids her sit; the kinswoman speaks kindly and then asks why Yugi, who freed him from prison, has not come back with him, and bids him tell.
event: The old woman asks Udayanan why Yugi did not return with him.

reading: The king has no word of Yugi, so the seated woman shows him the portrait; the king sees it, laments and grieves much, and then bows to a sage rich in penance and asks him.
event: The old woman shows the portrait; Udayanan laments, then bows to a sage and asks him.

reading: The sage assures him firmly that he will regain his crowned rule and his companion in bodily form; the king, trusting this, garlands the slender-waisted Virisikai, the sage's daughter he sees in the scented hill-slope.
nuance: The verse does not make clear whether the garlanding is part of the sage's counsel or a separate act; the prophecy is told by the poet, in the sage's words only in sense.
event: A sage foretells Udayanan's return of rule and friend; Udayanan then garlands the sage's daughter Virisikai.

reading: He unites with her, and when she is called away to the forest by her friends and the king goes, Yugi, in his mind, appears to the king to part the queen from him for some days.
nuance: The last line is not clear; it can be read as Yugi's thought of parting the queen or as his appearance for that purpose.
event: After the union, Udayanan leaves, and Yugi sets about parting the king from the queen for some days.

title: இலாவாண காண்டம் 136-150 (2/2)
theme: Yugi's false fire is played out: the king believes the queen has burned, mourns and wishes to die, is turned by his ministers, and sets out for the Magadha sage on Vayantakan's advice.
source_issues: Verse 147 line 2 had a pulli after a vowel sign, repaired by the build; the verse is hard to read.
Verses 137 to 139: who is the minister, who brings the news and who the savarar are is not stated; read from the story.
Verse 144 lines 3 and 4 and verse 149 line 2 are hard to read.

cast.role: the king of Vatsa, mourning the queen he believes dead
Udayanan's minister who arranged the false fire
Udayanan's friend and counsellor
the queen, hidden in the minister's house
the Sankhya woman who brings the queen through the tunnel
the men hidden in the king's house who set it on fire
the hunters said to have fired the house
the king's ministers who restrain and advise him
the guards who search for the body

reading: Those hidden in the king's house are told to stay together, and having made an underground tunnel from the king's house to the queen's, they set the whole house on fire.
nuance: Who gives the order and who the hidden men are is not said; the verse gives only the tunnel and the fire, which prepare the false death in the next verses.
event: The men hidden in the king's house, who have a tunnel dug below, set it alight.

reading: Through the underground passage the Sankhya woman brings the just king's queen, finely adorned, to the minister's house, and the minister bows at her feet and speaks gently.
nuance: The minister is not named; the story so far makes him Yugi, but the verse does not say so.
event: The Sankhya woman brings the queen through the tunnel to the minister's house; the minister bows to her and speaks kindly.

reading: The minister calls her his own good mother and asks a boon: her king will be away from her only some days, and without it the land will not be theirs; she agrees and he hides her as the case requires.
nuance: Both speaker and addressee are known only from the story; line 2 may also be read as the minister speaking for the queen to the Sankhya woman.
event: The minister asks the queen to bear a short parting and she agrees, and he hides her.

reading: On the hunters' fire seeming to be their own deed, the king sees evil omens, learns that the queen is hurt, and falls down, grieving and shaken, when the minister tells what has happened.
nuance: Line 1 puts the burning on the hunters; the verse does not say who tells the king that it was they, only that he is told.
event: The king, told that the queen is lost in the fire, collapses in grief.

reading: The king rolls on the ground and rises saying he will die with the dead queen, and the tall ministers hold him and beg him; he asks to be shown her burnt body.
nuance: The line 2 words are the king's, but the verse gives only the report and not the speech itself.
event: Udayanan resolves to die with the queen; ministers restrain him, and he asks to see the burnt body.

reading: When the guards say the charred body cannot be found, the ornaments of burnt gold are set before him, and he, thinking she fell in the fire and that it is no trick, cries out for her.
nuance: The ornaments are the proof the plan lets the king have, and the verse tells us he reads the lack of a body as the fire's work, not a ruse.
event: Guards bring burnt ornaments in place of a body; the king, believing she died in the fire, laments.

reading: The king, grieving over her, calls her the lamp of the earth who came as a boon and a lamp among women hard to win, the light of his eyes.
event: The king laments, calling the queen the lamp of the world and of his eyes.

reading: He calls her a deer, a peacock, a lotus-borne Lakshmi, a honey, a creeper, and one born of great penance, and asks whether it is right that she died and he suffers.
nuance: Pure lament; the praise names the queen by images only (deer, peacock, creeper) and gives no new fact.
event: The king addresses the dead queen with a list of comparisons and asks if his grief is justified.

reading: The king laments her breasts, her hair, her face as a golden ear-ring, her ornament, and her cool moon-like face as he cries out.
nuance: Several words in line 3 and 4 (சிங்கார முனதுரையும், பொங்காரம்) are hard to take and the sense is only approximate.
event: The king mourns the queen, naming her features.

reading: He calls her the lute-mistress, the wise one, the doll of modesty and the shining gem, and cries that she should come to his sight and show her face.
event: The king cries to the dead queen to appear and show her face.

reading: As the sorrow swells beyond words, the good ministers say that to put aside love for the queen is wiser, and the king listens, leaves his weeping and turns from her as a loving husband would.
nuance: The advice is sound in the ministers' eyes and the king takes it, but the queen is alive, so the counsel rests on a false fact only Yugi's side knows.
event: The ministers advise the king to give up his lament; he agrees and withdraws from it.

reading: Yugi, knowing the king's state, says the work is firm and the course good, tells Vayantakan to do again at the king's side what they had in mind.
nuance: Lines 2 to 4 are damaged and the sense of the verse is a probable one; the text was repaired at line 2 by the build.
event: Yugi tells Vayantakan to carry on the plan beside the king.

reading: Vayantakan, wise in true knowledge and skilled in hard counsel, bows at the king's golden feet and speaks again of what is best for him, while the king listens.
nuance: The verse only opens the speech that fills the next one.
event: Vayantakan bows to the king and begins to advise him.

reading: Vayantakan says that in the land of the Magadha king there is a learned sage who shows the dead their fate and sees the truth by sight and knowledge, and urges they go to him.
nuance: Line 2 (இற்றவர்க் காட்டும் இயல்பினன்) is hard; it may be that the sage shows the dead, or shows the way to those who are gone, and the reading is not fixed.
event: Vayantakan tells the king of a sage in Magadha and proposes going there.

tamil: வத்தவ குமரன் கேட்டு வயந்தகன் றன்னை நோக்கி
அத்திசை போவோ மென்றே யகமகிழ்ந் தினிய கூறி
வெற்றிநாற் படையுஞ் சூழ வெண்குடை கவரி மேவ
reading: The king hears Vayantakan, agrees gladly to go that way, and sets out with the four-fold army, white umbrella and fans.
event: Udayanan agrees to Vayantakan's plan and sets out with his army.

title: மகத காண்டம் 151-168 (1/2)
theme: Udayanan reaches Magadha still grieving, is deceived by a promise of his lost queen, is joined to Padmavati, and then Urumannuvan, Yugi's model in mind, turns the threat of seven kings into a stratagem of disguise and rumour.
source_issues: Verses 167 and 168 are in a different, shorter metre and lines are broken; the readings are tentative.
Verse 163 lines 3 to 4 are hard to parse; the speaker of line 1 is not named.
Verse 161: the speaker is inferred from the last line of verse 160.

cast.role: the king of Vatsa, in exile in Magadha
Udayanan's friend
Udayanan's minister who planned the escape from Ujjain
the learned brahmin of the Soma ascetics' hall who is deceived and then promises the king his queen
commander of the Magadha army
king of Magadha
the Magadha king's sister
Padmavati's friend
Udayanan's ministers
Udayanan's minister
the three hundred kinsmen Urumannuvan sends
the seven allied kings who march on Magadha

tamil: சயந்தியி னெல்லை விட்டுச் சாலவு மகத நாட்டுக்
கியைந்துநன் கெழுந்து சென்றே யிரவியி னுதய முற்றான்
நயந்தனன் றேவி காத னன்மனத் தழுங்கிப் பின்னும்
வியந்துநல் லமைச்சர் தேற்ற வெங்கடுங் கானம் புக்கான்.
reading: The king leaves the Jayanti border, travels on into the Magadha country, and arrives at dawn; grieving in heart for his queen even as his ministers console him, he enters a harsh forest.
nuance: The subject is never named in the verse; the king is known from the story so far, and the sense of line 3 (his love for the queen weighing on him despite comfort) is not fully fixed.
event: Udayanan crosses into the Magadha country and enters the forest, still grieving for the queen.

tamil: செத்தநற் றேவி தன்னைத் திருப்பவு மீட்க லாமென்
றத்திசை முன்னி நல்ல வருவழிப் பட்டுச் செல்ல
அத்தியும் பிணையு மேக வாண்மயி லாடக் கண்டு
வத்தவன் கலுழ்ந்து ரைக்கு மனனமை மனையை யோர்ந்தே.
reading: Hoping the dead queen may yet be brought back, the king heads that way; seeing a stag with its doe and a peacock dancing, he weeps and speaks of his lost wife.
nuance: The verse calls the queen dead (செத்த) yet lets him hope to bring her back; the hope comes from the earlier plan and is not explained here.
event: Udayanan, going toward Magadha, weeps at the sight of paired animals and a dancing peacock.

tamil: கோட்டுப்பூ நிறைந்தி லங்குங் கொடிவகைப் பூவுங் கோலங்
காட்டுநந் தேவி யென்று கால்விசை நடவா மன்னன்
காட்டினன் குன்ற மேறிக் கானகங் கழிந்து போந்து
சேட்டிளஞ் சிங்க மன்னான் திருநிறை மகதஞ் சேர்ந்தான்.
reading: The king, who cannot walk on, points to flowers on branches and creepers as showing his queen's adornment; he climbs a hill, passes the forest and reaches rich Magadha.
nuance: Grief makes every sight a likeness of the lost wife; the same habit of seeing her in other things returns in verse 157.
event: Udayanan sees flowers as the queen's ornament, climbs a hill, crosses the forest and reaches Magadha.

tamil: மருவிய திருவி னானம் மகதவர்க் கிறைவ னாமம்
தருசக னென்னு மன்னன் றானைவேற் றலைவன் மாரன்
இருந்தினி துறையு மிக்க விராசநற் கிரியந் தன்னிற்
பொருந்திச்சென் னகர்ப்பு றத்திற் பொலிவுட னிருந்தா னன்றே.
reading: Maran, commander of the army of Tarusakan, lord of the Magadhas, lives in splendour in the town of Rajagiri, just outside the capital.
nuance: The verse only places Maran and Tarusakan; it gives no action of the king himself.
event: Maran, the Magadha king's army commander, is settled at Rajagiri outside the city.

tamil: காமநற் கோட்டஞ் சூழக் கனமதி லிலங்கும் வாயிற்
சோமநற் றாப தர்கள் சூழ்ந்தமர் பள்ளி தன்னில்
நாமநல் வயந்த கன்னும் நன்கறி காக துண்ட
மாமறை யாளற் கண்டு வஞ்சகஞ் செப்பி னானே.
reading: At the Kamakottam gate, among ascetics of the Soma sort, Vayantakan finds the learned brahmin Kakatundan and tells him a deceitful tale.
nuance: The deceit is named but its content is not given; the verse is the start of a plan, not a statement of belief.
event: Vayantakan meets Kakatundan in the ascetics' hall and feeds him a false story.

tamil: திருநிறை மன்னன் றன்னைச் சீர்மறை யாளன் கண்டே
இருமதி யெல்லை நீங்கி யிப்பதி யிருப்ப வென்றும்
மருவியங் கிருக்கு மோர்நாண் மகதவன் றங்கை தானும்.
reading: The brahmin meets the king and says that if he stays in this town for two months he will restore the lost queen and the earth with her; meanwhile the Magadha king's sister appears one day.
nuance: The promise is part of the deceit begun in verse 155 and answers the king's hope in verse 152; the verse breaks off before the sister's coming is told.
event: Kakatundan promises the king the lost queen and the earth if he waits two months.

tamil: பருவமிக் கிலங்குங் கோதைப் பதுமைதே ரேறி வந்து
பொருவில்கா மனையே காணப் புரவலன் கண்டு கந்து
மருவும்வா சவதத் தைதான் வந்தன ளென்று ரைப்பத்
திருநகர் மாதுங் கண்டு திகைத்துளங் கவன்று நின்றாள்.
reading: Padmavati, in full bloom, drives up in a chariot to see the god of love himself; the king, seeing her, is glad and says that Vasavadatta has come, and the lady stands troubled at the sight of him.
nuance: The king's eyes mistake Padmavati for the dead wife because his mind is full of her; compare the flowers he took for her ornament in verse 153.
event: Padmavati comes in a chariot, and Udayanan takes her for Vasavadatta.

tamil: யாப்பியா யினியா ளென்னு மவளுடைத் தோழி சென்று
நாப்புகழ் மன்னற் கண்டு நலம்பிற வுரைத்துக் கூட்டக்
காப்புடைப் பதுமை யோடுங் காவலன் கலந்து பொன்னின்
சீப்பிடக் கண்சி வக்குஞ் சீர்மங்கை நலமுண் டானே.
reading: Padmavati's friend Yappiya Iniyal goes to the king, praises her charms and brings them together; protected by his guards, the king unites with her.
event: Yappiya Iniyal brings Padmavati to the king and they unite.

tamil: எழில்பெறு காமக் கோட்டத் தியற்கையிற் புணர்ந்து வந்து
வழிபெறு மமைச்ச ரோடு வத்தவ னினிய கூறும்
மொழியமிர் தந்ந லாளை மோகத்திற் பிரியே னென்னத்
தொழுதவர் பெறுக போகந் தோன்றனீ யென்று சொன்னார்.
reading: After joining her at Kamakottam as nature has it, the Vatsa king tells his ministers sweetly that he will not leave the nectar-voiced girl for desire; they bow and say 'may you gain enjoyment, appear'.
nuance: The ministers' reply (line 4) is brief and its last word is not clear; they appear to approve the king's pleasure.
event: Udayanan tells his ministers he will not leave Padmavati, and they bless the match.

tamil: மாட்சிநற் சிவிகை யேறி மடந்தைதன் னோடும் புக்குத்
தாழ்ச்சியின் மாளி கைக்குட் டக்கவண் மனங்கு ளிர்ப்பக்
காட்டினன் வீணை தன்னைக் காவலன் கரந்தி ருப்ப
ஓட்டிய சினத்த னாய வுருமண்ணு விதனைச் செப்பும்.
reading: Riding a splendid palanquin with the girl into a mansion, the king shows her the lute, which he has kept hidden; the angry Urumannuvan is moved to speak of this.
nuance: The cause of Urumannuvan's anger is not given in the verse; the verse prepares his speech in verse 161.
event: Udayanan takes Padmavati to a mansion and shows her the lute; Urumannuvan, angered, speaks.

tamil: ஆகிய தறிந்து செய்யு மருளுடை மனத்த னான
யூகியங் குஞ்சை தன்னை யுற்றருஞ் சிறைவி டுக்கப்
போகநற் றேவி யோடும் போந்தது போல நாமும்
போகுவ மன்னன் மாதைப் புதுமணம் புணரு வித்தே.
reading: Yugi, whose mind is kind and who knows events, freed Kunjai from prison and left with the queen; so Urumannuvan proposes that they too go, after the king has been married afresh to this girl.
nuance: The speaker is Urumannuvan only because verse 160 ends by saying he will speak; verse 161 does not name him. The model he cites is Yugi's earlier escape from Ujjain, told in the preceding kandam.
event: Urumannuvan proposes that the king be married to Padmavati before they all leave.

tamil: உருமண்ணு வாவ னுப்ப வுற்றமுந் நூறு பேர்கள்
மருவிய விச்சை தன்னான் மன்னவன் கோயி றன்னுள்
மருவினர் மறைந்து சென்றார் மன்னவன் றாதை வைத்த
பெருநிதி காண்கி லாமற் பேர்க்குநர்த் தேடு கின்றான்.
reading: Urumannuvan sends three hundred kinsmen, who by their art slip unseen into the king's palace while the king, unable to find the great treasure his father laid up, searches for those who moved it.
nuance: Line 4 can be read as the king looking for the thieves of the treasure; the verse does not say that Urumannuvan's men took it.
event: Urumannuvan's three hundred men hide in the Magadha palace while the king hunts for his father's lost treasure.

tamil: யானறிந் துரைப்ப னென்றே யரசனைக் கண்டு மிக்க
மாநிதி காட்டி நன்மை மகதவ னோடுங் கூடி
ஊனமில் விச்சை தன்னா லுருமண்ணு பிரித லின்றிப்
பானலங் கிளவி தன்னாற் பரிவுட னிருக்கு நாளில்.
reading: A speaker says he will tell what he knows, meets the king and shows him a great treasure; thereafter the Magadha king, with goodwill, lives happily beside Urumannuvan, who is never parted from him, by means of his art.
nuance: The verse does not name who says 'I will tell what I know'; the story points to Urumannuvan, but the speaker is a guess, and line 4 (பானலங் கிளவி) is also hard to place.
event: Urumannuvan shows Tarusakan a great treasure and the two live as close allies.

tamil: அடவியா மரசன் மிக்க வயோத்தியர்க் கிறைவன் றானைப்
படையுறு சாலி யென்பான் பலமுறு சத்தி யென்பான்
முடிவிரி சிகையன் மல்லன் முகட்டெலிச் செவிய னென்பான்
உடன்வரு மெழுவர் கூடி யொளிர்மக தத்து வந்தார்.
reading: Seven kings, among them the lord of Ayodhya's army chief Shali, Palamuru Sakti, Mudiviri Sikaiyan and Mukatteli Seviyan, come together to Magadha.
nuance: The names are listed by title; some of them are hard to separate (the verse mixes names and nicknames).
event: Seven allied kings of the forest and Ayodhya arrive in Magadha with their forces.

tamil: தருசகற் கினிதி னாங்க டருதிறை யிடுவ தில்லென்
றெரியென வெகுண்டு வந்தே யினியநா டழிக்க லுற்றார்
தருசக ராசன் கேட்டுத் தளரவப் புறத்த கற்ற
உருமண்ணு வாம னத்தி லுபாயத்தி லுடைப்ப னென்றான்.
reading: The seven, angry, say they will not pay tribute to Tarusakan and come to destroy his pleasant land; he is shaken at the news, and Urumannuvan says that he will break them by a stratagem.
nuance: The verse prefers plan (உபாயம்) to open battle for the defence; line 4's first words are hard to parse.
event: The seven kings refuse tribute and march to ravage Magadha; Urumannuvan promises to defeat them by stratagem.

tamil: கள்ளநல் லுருவி னோடுங் கடியகத் துள்ளே யுற்ற
வள்ளலை மதியிற் கூட்டி வாணிக வுருவி னோடு
பள்ளிப்பா சறைபு குந்து பலமணி விற்றி ருந்தார்.
reading: In disguise, Urumannuvan and the king, joined by his wit to the Magadha king, go as merchants who sort jewels, swap a few, and set up a shop in the enemy camp selling many gems.
nuance: Line 1's 'false form' and 'merchant form' suggest a change of guise for both; the jewels are a pretext for getting inside the camp.
event: Urumannuvan and Udayanan, disguised as jewel merchants, set up a stall in the enemy camp.

reading: In an unclear verse, words the king and the Magadhas would not wish to hear spread among the troops as they come into the four-fold camp by night, hidden talk of many kinds.
nuance: The verse is in a different, shorter metre and its words are broken; the reading is a guess.
event: Hidden rumours spread through the camp at night.

reading: Those who heard the talk lose heart, the troops give way and run, and the enemy leaders gather in confusion, until the doubt in their minds is gone.
nuance: Line 4 (ஐயம் மனத்திடை நீங்கினார்) is hard: it can be read as the leaders' doubt ending, or as their giving up their purpose.
event: The rumours break the enemy's nerve and its army runs.

title: மகத காண்டம் 169-185 (2/2)
theme: Udayanan wins the war for Tharusakan of Magadha, is given Padumai and a dowry of troops, then wins the Panchala war, enters his city in honour and heals the fallen.
source_issues: Verse 173: the e-text prints this verse without its number; it stands between 172 and 174.
Verse 177, line 1: the phrase 'வெல்லுமண்ணலை ம்மிக' is damaged; the sense is taken from the rest of the verse.
Verse 170, line 2: the minister's name is run together with the next word.
Verse 175: the count of women is garbled in the edition.

cast.role: the Vatsa king, called also the lord of the lute
king of Magadha, who gives his sister to Udayanan
Tharusakan's sister, Udayanan's new bride
a minister of Udayanan
the spies who report to the king
Udayanan's minister sent to the Panchala king
the Panchala king, Udayanan's enemy
two princes who join Udayanan with an army
the kings who bow to Udayanan
the women of the city who bless the king
the bards who sing at the king's return

reading: Spies report to the king what the men who camped by night did, how they went off and then gathered and came back and let go, and the king, hearing it, calls it the work of 'kar'.
nuance: The verse leaves out who the campers are and what was let go; the king's remark is a single word of judgment, and the reader must take the rest from the next verses.
event: Spies tell the king of the night-campers' doing, and the king names it a 'kar' deed.

reading: The minister Urumannuvan tells the fair-armoured kings the doings of the Vatsa lord, and the earth-king is glad in himself.
nuance: The name is run together with a following word in the edition and the telling may be the spies' or the minister's; what is sure is that a report of Udayanan's deed makes the king glad.
event: Urumannuvan reports Udayanan's deed to the king, who rejoices.

reading: Full of unending joy, the king goes out to meet the lord of the sweet lute, embraces him in honour and vows to drive out the foes who will not come to terms.
event: The king meets Udayanan, embraces him and promises to remove their enemies.

reading: Udayanan with his four-fold army marches and destroys the enemy force in battle, and the king returns with tribute.
event: Udayanan wins the battle and the king comes home with tribute.

reading: The king of Magadha, Tharusakan, welcomes the victorious Vatsa lord to his house and gives his sister, the lady Padumai, to him in the rite of the sacrifice.
nuance: The wedding is made by a sacrifice (வேள்வி), a rite the Jain poet narrates without comment; the marriage is also the reward for the victory of the last verse.
event: Tharusakan welcomes Udayanan and gives him his sister Padumai in marriage by the sacred fire.

reading: After the wedding adornments are made, the king gives a dowry of a thousand rutting elephants, two thousand horses and twelve hundred chariots.
nuance: The gift is counted in fighting strength; nothing in it is domestic wealth.
event: Tharusakan gives the bridal gift of elephants, horses and chariots.

reading: The dowry goes on with sixty-eight thousand soldiers and a body of fragrant-garlanded women, and the king names Varudakari, Sakthi and Dharmadattan to go with it.
nuance: The number of the women is given in a tangled phrase and I take it only as a few hundred.
event: Tharusakan adds soldiers, women and three named men to the dowry.

reading: With Satyakayan and the ministers added, the king tells the four-fold force to follow Udayanan, and gives the bride's gift with a glad face and sends them off in good order.
event: Tharusakan sends ministers and army with Udayanan and sets the bridal party on its way.

reading: The king speaks some gentle words in friendship, sends the lord off, and as the Vatsa king reaches his own land his younger brothers come to him.
nuance: Line 1 is damaged, so who speaks the gentle words, and to whom, is read from the sense.
event: Tharusakan takes leave of Udayanan with kind words, and Udayanan reaches his border.

reading: Pingalan and Kadakan, two princes with twelve thousand brave troops, come to the lord, bow at his feet and join him, and the army is set in the field outside Kausambi.
event: Pingalan and Kadakan arrive with their army and join Udayanan before Kausambi.

reading: Udayanan calls Varudakaran and tells him to go to the Panchala king, who holds a proud army, and drive the crowned kings away by skill; when he goes with wealth they begin the war.
nuance: Whether the 'strategy' is a bribe, or a stratagem, turns on the word பொருளின் in line 4; 'wealth' is the likelier use.
event: Udayanan sends Varudakaran with wealth to the Panchala king to break the other kings, and the fighting starts.

reading: The minister goes and drives the kings off in battle, but the Panchala king comes against him with a four-fold force, and arrows from both bows shut out the sun.
event: Varudakaran drives off the kings; the Panchala king counterattacks and the arrows fly thick.

tamil: விரிந்த வெண்குடை வீழவும் வேந்தர் விண்ணுற வேறவும்
பரிந்து பேய்க்கண மாடவும் பலவா நரிபறைந் துண்ணவும்
முரிந்த முண்டங்க ளாடவும் முரிந்த மாக்களி றுருளவும்
வரிந்த வெண்சிலை மன்னவன் வந்த வன்கண் சிவந்தவே.
reading: The field is shown as a scene of ruin: white umbrellas fall, kings rise to heaven, ghouls dance, jackals feed, headless trunks dance, and the king's eyes grow red.
nuance: The verse sets the dancing ghouls and feeding jackals beside the kings' ascent to heaven, so the carnage is told as a feast and a glory together; the poet gives no word of pity.
event: The battle reaches its height, with corpses and scavengers filling the field.

tamil: மாற்ற வன்படை முறிந்தென மன்ன வன்படை யார்த்திடத்
தோற்ற மன்னன்வந் தெதிர்த்தனன் றூய காளைதன் வாளினால்
மாற்ற லன்றனைக் கூற்றுண வண்மை யிவ்விருந் தார்கென
ஏற்ர வகையினி லிட்டன னிலங்கு வத்தவ ராசனே.
reading: When the enemy army breaks and the Vatsa army roars, the beaten king comes forward again, and Udayanan, with his sword, feeds him to Death.
nuance: Line 2's 'தோற்ற மன்னன்' is read as the beaten king; the verse does not say outright that he is the Panchala king.
event: Udayanan kills the Panchala king in single combat after his army is broken.

tamil: பகைய றவேயெ றிந்துடன் பாங்கிற் போர்வினை தவிர்கென
வகைய றவேப டுகளங் கண்டு நண்ணிய மற்றது
தொகையு றுந்தன தொல்படை சூழ வூர்முக நோக்கினன்
நகையு றுந்நல மார்பனு நகர வீதியில் வந்தனன்.
reading: Having cut down the foes and ordered the fighting to stop, the king looks over the field, sets out for the town with his old army about him, and comes smiling into the streets.
event: Udayanan halts the war, inspects the field and rides back toward the city.

reading: Women climb up on the mansions on both sides to bless the king, bards sing, and he enters the golden palace among the banners.
event: The townswomen and bards honour Udayanan and he enters his palace.

reading: The king has the fallen on the field smeared with oil and medicine and given wealth, the kings come and bow at his feet, and he wears the crown and rules in joy.
nuance: The care for the wounded comes after the victory has been told as a feast of scavengers; both appear in the same chapter.
event: Udayanan tends the wounded and rewards them, kings submit, and he takes the crown.

title: வத்தவ காண்டம் 186-204 (1/3)
theme: Udayanan, back among his people, rules with gifts, is told by sages that Vasavadatta lives and will bear a world-ruling son, welcomes Urumannuvan and then Vasavadatta and Yugi, hears Yugi's confession of his plot, and, after a sulk, reconciles with Vasavadatta.
source_issues: Verse 192, line 2: a pulli after a vowel sign was removed by the repair pass.
Verses 194, 199, 200: several words and the identities of the people they name are unclear.

cast.role: the Vatsa king
envoys of hostile kings who bring tribute
a brahmin who finds the king's lute and brings it back
Padumai, the Magadha king's sister, the king's wife
the goddess who gives the lotus in the king's dream
the great sages and ascetics who read the dream
the king's minister, freed by the Magadha men
the king's wife, Ujjain's princess
the king's minister who planned the escape
the king's friend
the women attending the king's bath
the bodiless god of love

tamil: மின்சொரி கதிர்வேற் றானை வீறடி பணிய வெம்மைப்
பொன்சொரி கவரி வீசப் பொங்கரி யாச னத்தில்
தண்சொரி கிரண முத்தத் தவளநற் குடையி னீழல்
மின்சொரி தரள வேந்தன் வீற்றி ருந்த போழ்தின்.
reading: The king sits enthroned in glory, his feet bowed to by armies and fanned with golden whisks, under a white pearl umbrella.

tamil: மாற்றலர் தூதர் வந்து வருதிறை யளந்து நிற்ப
ஆற்றலர் வரவ வர்க்கே யானபொன் றுகில ளித்தே
ஏற்றநற் சனங்கட் கெல்லா மினிப்பொரு ளுவந்து வீசிக்
கோற்றொழி னடத்தி மன்னன் குறைவின்றிச் செல்லு கின்றான்.
reading: Envoys of hostile kings come and stand with the tribute they owe; the king gives them gold and cloth, spreads wealth among his people, and rules by the sceptre without lack.
nuance: The king answers tribute with gifts; the verse sets his giving beside his ruling by the sceptre as one habit.
event: Envoys of enemy kings bring tribute, and Udayanan rewards them and gives wealth to all his people.

tamil: மதுரவண் டறாத மாலை மகதவன் றங்கை யாய
பதுமைதன் பணைமு லைமேற் பார்த்திபன் புணர்ந்து செல்ல
துதிக்கைமா வீழ்ந்த கானந் தோன்றலு மாடம் பண்ணிப்
பதியினு மமைத்துப் பாங்கிற் படிமமு மமைத்தா னன்றே.
reading: As the king lies with Padumai, the Magadha king's sister, he builds a pavilion and a town where the elephant fell in the forest, and puts up an image beside it.
nuance: The verse joins the king's love for Padumai with the marking of the place where the elephant died; whether the image is of the elephant is not said.
event: Udayanan builds a pavilion, a town and an image where the elephant fell, while he is with Padumai.

tamil: அருமறை யோதி நாம மருஞ்சன னந்த ணன்றான்
திருவுறை யுஞ்சை நின்று திகழ்கொடிக் கௌசாம் பிக்கு
வருநெறி வேயின் மீது வத்தவன் வீணை கண்டு
பொருந்தவே கொண்டு வந்து புரவலற் கீந்தா னன்றே.
reading: A brahmin learned in the rare Veda, going from Unjai to Kausambi, finds the Vatsa king's lute on the bamboo along the road and brings it to the king.
event: A brahmin finds Udayanan's lute on a bamboo by the road and brings it to the king.

tamil: மதுமலர்க் குழலி விண்மின் மாலைவேல் விழிமென் றோளி
பதுமைவந் தரசற் கண்டு பன்னுரை யினிது கூறும்
மதியின்வா சவதத் தைதன் வண்கையி னதனைப் போல
விதியினான் வீணை கற்க வேந்தநீ யருள்க வென்றாள்.
reading: Padumai comes to the king and begs that he teach her the lute as he taught Vasavadatta with his own generous hand.
nuance: She names Vasavadatta, her rival, as the measure of what she asks for.
event: Padumai asks Udayanan to teach her the lute as he taught Vasavadatta.

tamil: பொள்ளென வெகுண்டு நோக்கிப் பொருமனத் துருகி மன்னன்
ஒள்ளிதழ்த் தத்தை தன்னை யுள்ளியே துயிலல் செய்ய
வெள்ளையே றிருந்த வெண்டா மரையினைக் கொண்டு வந்து
கள்ளவிழ் மாலைத் தெய்வங் கனவிடைக் கொடுப்பக் கண்டான்,
reading: The king, angered and melting in grief, falls asleep thinking of Thattai and sees in a dream a goddess bring the white lotus of the white bull.
nuance: The verse does not say whom he is angry at; it may be Padumai's request, which names Vasavadatta, or his own grief.
event: Udayanan sleeps thinking of Vasavadatta and dreams a goddess brings him a white lotus.

tamil: கங்குலை நீங்கி மிக்கோர் கடவுளை வினவச் சொல்வார்
அங்கயற் கண்ணி தானு மாரழல் வீந்தா ளல்லள்
கொங்கைநற் பாவை தன்னைக் கொணரநீ பெறுவை யின்பம்
இங்குல கெங்கு மாளு மெகழிற்சுதற் பெறுவ ளென்றார்.
reading: At dawn he asks the sages what the god gave him, and they say the fish-eyed lady did not die in the fire, that he will find joy by bringing her back, and that she will bear a fair son who rules the whole world.
nuance: The verse's first reading line carries a corrupt mark, repaired by the editor; the sages speak of the lady only in images.
event: Sages read Udayanan's dream and tell him Vasavadatta is alive and will bear a son who rules the world.

tamil: வெள்ளிய மலையின் மீதே விஞ்சைய ருலக மெல்லாம்
தெள்ளிய வாழி கொண்டு திக்கடிப் படுத்து மென்ன
ஒள்ளிய தவத்தின் மிக்கோ ருறுதவ ருரைத்த சொல்லை
