reading: Addressing his mother, the king says her family never did cruel killing, and that if the sin of killing a life brings many sorrows today, all she has urged is no kindness to him.
nuance: He turns his mother's care against her counsel: what she calls help would be harm to him.
event: The king appeals to his family's past and to the sorrow that killing breeds.

tamil: என்றலு மெனது சொல்லை யிறந்தனை கொடியை யென்றே
சென்றனள் முனிவுச் சிந்தைத் தீருவிலி பிறிது கூறும்
கொன்றுயிர் களைத லஞ்சிற் கோழியை மாவிற் செய்து
சென்றனை பலிகொ டுத்துத் தேவியை மகிழ்வி யென்றாள்.
reading: Angered that he has defied her, the mother calls him cruel, then offers another way: if he fears taking a life, let him make a cock of flour, offer it as a sacrifice and please the goddess.
nuance: The proposal is a loophole in the king's refusal, offered in the same breath as her anger.
event: The mother proposes a flour cock as a substitute for a living offering.

tamil: மனம்விரி யல்குன் மாய மனத்தவை வகுத்த மாயக்
கனவுரை பிறிது தேவி கட்டுரை பிறிதொன் றாயிற்று
எனைவினை யுதயஞ் செய்ய இடர்பல விளைந்த என்பால்
வினைகளின் விளைவை யாவர் விலக்குந ரென்று நின்றான்.
reading: The king, in a verse whose first half is hard, sets the queen's false dream-tale against his mother's counsel and says that, with his deeds now rising and many sorrows come upon him, no one can keep the ripening of deeds away.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are hard (the sense of the queen's 'dream-tale' set against 'the goddess's counsel'). The reading of the first half is provisional; the king's words in lines 3 and 4 are clear.
event: The king, standing before his mother, says that no one can turn back what his deeds are ripening.

tamil: உயிர்ப்பொருள் வடிவு கோற லுயிர்க்கொலை போலு மென்னும்
பயிர்ப்புள முடைய னேனும் பற்றறத் துணிவில் மன்னன்
செயிர்த்தவ ளுரைத்த செய்கை செய்வதற் கிசைந்த தென்றான்
அயிர்ப்பதென் அறத்தின் திண்மை யறிவதற் கமைவி லாதான்.
reading: Although the king shrinks even from making the shape of a living creature, as it is like killing, he is not firm enough to cut his ties, and so consents to do what his mother angrily told him.
nuance: The last line is hard (அயிர்ப்பதென் அறத்தின் திண்மை). The reading takes it as the narrator's remark that his hold on dharma was not firm enough to be sure.
event: The king agrees, against his own misgiving, to the flour-cock offering.

tamil: மாவினின் வனைந்த கோழி வடிவுகொண் டவ்வை யாய
தேவிதன் னிடைச்சென் றெய்திச் சிறப்பொடு வணக்கஞ் செய்தே
ஆவயின் தன்கை வாளா லரிந்துகொண் டருளி தென்றான்.
reading: The king takes the flour-made cock with his mother to the goddess's place of slaughter, bows with honour and cuts it with his own sword, saying that it was offered to her.
nuance: The place is called the place of killing (படுகொலைக்கிடம்); the king goes not as the sacrificer's helper but as the one who strikes.
event: The king beheads the flour cock before the goddess with his own sword.

tamil: மேலியல் தெய்வங் கண்டே விரும்பின தடையப் பட்ட
சாலியி னிடியின் கோழி தலையரிந் திட்ட தோடி
கோலிய லரசன் முன்னர்க் கூவுபு குலுங்கி வீழ
மாலிய லரசன் தன்கை வாள்விடுத் துருகி னானே.
reading: The goddess is pleased, and the flour cock, its head cut, runs before the king crying, shakes and falls, so that the king drops his sword and is moved with pity.
nuance: The narrator treats the flour bird as a creature that cries out; the work thereby answers the mother's claim that a likeness is a harmless substitute.
event: The flour cock cries and falls when the king's sword strikes it, and the king drops the sword.

tamil: என்னைகொல் மாவின் செய்கை யிவ்வுயிர் பெற்ற பெற்றி
சென்னிவா ளெறிய வோடிச் சிலம்பிய குரலி தென்கொல்
பின்னிய பிறவி மாலைப் பெருநவை தருதற் கொத்த
கொன்னியல் பாவ மென்னைக் கூவுகின் றதுபோன் மென்றான்.
reading: The king asks what has happened to the flour cock that received life, why it ran and cried under his sword, and whether the sin that brings the chain of births its great fault is calling him.
nuance: The fear is put as a question; the deaths at 153 are the poem's later answer.
event: The king questions the living cry of the flour cock and fears the sin has come to him.

tamil: ஆதகா தன்னை சொல்லா லறிவிலே னருளில் செய்கை
ஆதகா தழிந்த புள்வா யரிகுர லரியு நெஞ்சை
ஆதகா தமிர்த முன்னா மதியவள் களவு கொல்லும்
ஆதகா வினைக ளென்னை யடர்த்துநின் றடுங்கொ லென்றான்.
reading: In regret, the king cries out that he did a graceless thing by his mother's words, that the cry of the bird tears his heart, and that his deeds may now stand over him and crush him.
nuance: Lines 2 and 3 are obscure (the repeated ஆதகா and a clause about the 'nectar' lady); the reading rests on lines 1 and 4.
event: The king laments the graceless act and fears his deeds.

tamil: இனையன நினைவு தம்மால் யசோதர னகர மெய்தித்
தனையனி லரசு வைத்துத் தவவனம் படர லுற்றான்
அனையதை யறிந்துந் தேவி யவமதித் தெனைவி டுத்தான்
எனநினைந் தேது செய்தா ளெரிநர கத்து வீழ்வாள்.
reading: Thinking so, Yasodharan goes back to the city, sets his son on the throne and sets out for the forest of austerity; the queen, knowing it and thinking that he spurned her, does something that will send her to the burning hell.
nuance: The narrator names the queen's end before her act, so the poison that follows is told as already judged.
event: The king hands the kingdom to his son and leaves for the ascetic forest, and the queen resents it.

tamil: அரசுநீ துறத்தி யாயின் அமைகமற் றெனக்கு மஃதே
விரைசெய்தா ரிறைவ வின்றென் வியன்மனை மைந்த னோடும்
இரசநீ ரமிர்து கைக்கொண் டருளுதற் கிசைதல் செய்வாய்
அரசுதா னவன தாக அவிது நா மடிக ளென்றாள்.
reading: The queen tells the king that if he gives up the kingdom, so will she; she begs him to come to her house that day with his son and take the sweet drink, and let the kingdom be the son's while they become ascetics.
nuance: The speech is a pretence, as 152 says (வஞ்சனை வலித்து): her renunciation is the bait.
event: The queen feigns agreement with the king's renunciation and invites him to her house.

tamil: ஆங்கவ ளகத்து மாட்சி யறிந்தன னரச னேனும்
வீங்கிய முலையி னாய்நீ வேண்டிய தமைக என்றே
தாங்கல னவ்வை தன்னோ டவள்மனை தான மர்ந்தான்
தீங்கது குறுகின் தீய நயமுநன் னயம தாமே.
reading: Though the king knows what lies in her heart, he tells her to do as she wishes and, bearing his mother with him, goes to sit in her house; the verse adds that when ruin is near even a wrong course seems the right one.
nuance: Line 1 can be read as the king's knowledge of her intent or of her worth; the reading takes the first.
event: The king, knowing her mind, goes with his mother to the queen's house.

tamil: நஞ்சொடு கலந்த தேனி னறுஞ்சுவை பெரிய வாக
எஞ்சலி லட்டு கங்கள் இருவிரு மருந்து கென்றே
வஞ்சனை வலித்து மாமி தன்னுடன் வரனுக் கீந்தாள்
நஞ்சொடு படாத தானு மகனொடு நயந்து கொண்டாள்.
reading: The queen mixes poison with honey and sweet food, gives it to her husband and his mother as a dish for both, and takes the unpoisoned part herself with her son.
nuance: The honey's sweetness hides the poison: the same sweetness the Kural praises in speech here covers murder.
event: The queen serves poisoned food to the king and his mother.

tamil: நஞ்சது பரந்த போழ்தின் நடுங்கினர் மயங்கி வீழ்ந்தார்
அஞ்சினர் மரணஞ் சிந்தை யடைந்தது முதல தங்கண்
புஞ்சிய வினைகள் தீய புகுந்தன பொறிகள் பொன்றித்
துஞ்சினர் துயரத் துஞ்சா விலங்கிடைத் துன்னி னாரே.
reading: As the poison spreads they tremble and fall in a swoon, fear death, and the deeds they had heaped come in; the senses fail and they die, to fall into the animal state that knows no end of pain.
nuance: Both are given as causes: the queen's poison is the means, and the ripening of the family's own deeds is the narrator's reason. The poem does not say that the woman's act is excused by karma.
event: The king and his mother die of the poison and are reborn among animals.

tamil: எண்களுக் கிசைவி லாத இறைவியா மிவள்தன் செய்கை
கண்களுக் கிசைவி லாத கடையனைக் கருதி நெஞ்சின்
மண்களுக் கிறைவ னாய வரனுக்கு மரணஞ் செய்தாள்
பெண்களிற் கோத னாளே பெரியபா வத்த ளென்றார்.
reading: The mourners say that this queen, unfit even for counting, thought of a low man unfit for eyes to see, killed her husband the lord of lands, and is the most wrathful and sinful of women.
nuance: This is the people's judgment in their own grief, not the narrator's; the narrator has already judged her at 149.
event: The mourners condemn the queen who killed her husband for a base lover.

tamil: தீதகல் கடவு ளாகச் செய்ததோர் படிமை யின்கண்
காதர முலகி தன்கண் கருதிய முடித்தல் கண்டுஞ்
சேதன வடிவு தேவிக் கெறிந்தனன் தெரிவொன் றில்லான்
ஆதலால் வந்த தின்றென் றழுங்கினர் சிலர்க ளெல்லாம்.
reading: Some of the mourners say that the king made an image of a god free of evil, yet, though he saw the world's wishes fulfilled before such an image, threw a living-shaped offering to the goddess without discernment, and so this has come today.
nuance: The mourners join the offering at 145 to the poison; the poem gives the same link in the narrator's voice at 153 only as ripened deeds, not as this one offering.
event: Some mourners trace the king's death to his flour-cock offering.

tamil: அறப்பொருள் நுகர்தல் செல்லா னருந்தவர்க் கெளிய னல்லன்
மறப்பொருள் மயங்கி வையத் தரசியல் மகிழ்ந்து சென்றான்
இறப்பவு மிளையர் போகத் திவறின விறுதி யின்கண்
சிறப்புடை மரண மில்லைச் செல்கதி யென்கொ லென்றார்.
reading: Others say that the king did not enjoy the wealth of dharma, was not easy for the great ascetics to reach, and was deluded by wrong things and joyful in rule; he died young while others were stingy with pleasure, and no good death waits at the end, so what is his destination?
nuance: The mourners judge the king by his rule alone; the narrator's account of his refusal to kill at 138 to 140 shows what they cannot see.
event: The mourners doubt the king's destination.

tamil: இனையன வுழையர் தாமும் எழில்நக ரத்து ளாரும்
நினைவன நினைந்து நெஞ்சின் நெகிழ்ந்தனர் புலம்பி வாடக்
கனைகழ லரசன் தேவி கருதிய வதுமு டித்தாள்
மனநனி வலிதின் மாழ்கி மைந்தனை வருக வென்றாள்.
reading: The attendants and the townspeople weep at these thoughts, while the queen, who has done what she wished, her mind weakened by the strain, calls her son.
event: The people mourn while the queen calls her son.

tamil: இனையனீ தனியை யாகி யிறைவனிற் பிரிந்த தென்கண்
வினையினால் விளைவு கண்டாய் விடுத்திடு மனத்து வெந்நோய்
புனைமுடி கவித்துப் பூமி பொதுக்கடிந் தாள்க வென்றே
மனநனி மகிழ்ந் திருந்தாள் மறைபதிக் கமுத மாவாள்.
reading: The queen tells her son that he is alone now, that the loss of the king came from the fruit of her own deeds, bids him leave off the heart's sorrow, wear the crown and rule the earth, and sits glad, the nectar of her secret lord.
nuance: The queen speaks the poem's own doctrine of karma to hide a deed that is hers; the poem uses the same words to expose her.
event: The queen consoles her son and bids him rule.

tamil: வாரணி முரச மார்ப்ப மணிபுனை மகுடஞ் சூடி
ஏரணி யார மார்ப னிசோமதி யிறைமை யெய்தி
சீரணி யடிகள் செல்வத் திருவற மருளல் செல்லான்
ஓரணி யாக மாத ருவகையங் கடலு ளாழ்ந்தான்.
reading: With the drums beating, Yasomati puts on the jewelled crown and takes up lordship; he does not turn to the teacher's gift of dharma but sinks into a sea of the delight of women.
event: Yasomati is crowned and gives himself to pleasure.

tamil: இனையன வினையி னாகு மியல்பிது தெரிதி யாயின்
இனையன துணைவ ராகு மினையரின் விளையு மின்பம்
இனையது தெளிவி லாதார் இருநில வரசு செய்கை
வனைமலர் மகுட மாரி தத்தனே மதியி தென்றான்.
reading: The teller says to Maridattan that if he understands that such things arise from deeds, these will be his companions and from them joy will grow, while those without that clarity only rule the earth and wear the flowered crown.
nuance: The speaker is taken to be the teller of the tale to the king Maridattan, from the frame laid in the second chapter; the verse itself names only the addressee.
event: Sudattan draws the lesson of the king's death for Maridattan.

title: மூன்றாஞ் சருக்கம் 161-182 (1/3)
theme: The king and his mother, dying in attachment, are reborn as peacock and dog, then boar and snake, then fish and crocodile, each birth ending in a violent death at the other's hands, with the poet naming deed as the cause.
source_issues: Verse 161 line 1 has the clipped form 'மதிமதி' for Chandramathi.
Verse 166 line 1 has 'மாமயின்' for 'மாமயில்'.
Verses 177, 178 and 181 are partly obscure; who kills whom in 177-178 and the sense of கொல்கராத்தந்து in 181 are inferred.

cast.role: the former king, now reborn as peacock, boar and fish
the king's mother, reborn as dog, snake and crocodile
the son, now king, who receives the peacock and dog
the former queen, read from 172 as the woman with Ashtavakran
the hunchbacked elephant-keeper
the Vindhya hunter who shoots the peahen
the hunter woman who rears the egg
the hunters who give the animals to the king
a dancing hunchback seized by the crocodile
the net-people who catch the crocodile

reading: The poet says that the king and Chandramathi died still bound by attachment, and that what follows is the account of their many births.
nuance: 'Mathi' in line 1 is the edition's clipped form of Chandramathi, the king's mother, whom the next verses make the dog; the verse sets out the plan of the whole section on births, as 147 foresaw it.

reading: A chief of the Vindhya hills, coming with a dog, shoots a great peahen that carries an egg in her belly.
nuance: The verse names only 'the king of the hill called Vindhya' and a cruel hunter; that the egg holds the former king is learned from verse 172 on.
event: A Vindhya hunter shoots a pregnant peahen.

reading: The man takes the egg that the arrow's mouth has spilled, sets it among a wild fowl's eggs and gives it to a loving hunter woman to rear.
nuance: The same hand that kills the mother-bird saves the egg; the verse gives no reason, and the later births show the lives it leads to.
event: The hunter hands the rescued egg to a hunter woman to be reared.

reading: Chandramathi, the king's mother, comes to the lane outside the great city by her earlier deed and is born a dog with sprouting fangs.
nuance: 'The deed done before' (முந்து செய்வினை) is left unnamed here; the reader supplies the urging of a blood-offering and the poisoning from the earlier chapters.
event: Chandramathi is reborn as a dog in the outcaste lane outside the city.

reading: When the peacock and the dog have grown, the hunters give them to the king as a fitting gift, and they come to the palace of Yasomathi, the king.
nuance: வயிரியாகும் in line 3 may mean one who will be their enemy; the sense is not fixed. The two gift animals are the father and the grandmother of the king who receives them.
event: The hunters present the grown peacock and dog to King Yasomathi, and they enter his palace.

reading: The peacock that was a king does not rise before those who rise before him, is startled even at his own body, and grows up in the palace in fear.
nuance: Where in his man's life all rose before him, the bird shrinks from those who rise. The poet does not say the fear is remembered; that the bird is the king comes from line 1.
event: The bird that was once king lives timid in the palace.

reading: Women stroke the feet of the sleeping king on his soft bed, and the peacock with its tail moves timidly on the ground.
nuance: The couch the women tend is the very bed from which the same soul once rose; the verse sets the sleeper at ease and the bird in fear.

reading: The king eats sweet food from a gold dish in the company of women, while the bird that was a king waits outside the hall for scraps.
nuance: அரையன் in line 3 is the king at table, Yasomathi; the same word is used of the peacock in line 3, so 'the lord' belongs to the bird only as what he once was.
event: The former king, now a peacock, waits outside the bed hall for food as the new king dines.

reading: The dog, once Chandramathi, eats the sweepings of the dung-heap, grabs the leavings and grows weak in the yard.
nuance: A queen mother who once dined in her palace is now at the refuse; verse 168 had the peacock waiting outside the hall in the same way.
event: The dog scavenges scraps and grows weak.

reading: The poet says that those who did not hold to the good vow and the way of virtue came into great suffering that could not be borne, by the cruelty they had done before, and that the fruit of deed is hard to overcome.
nuance: The only verse in this run to state the rule outright; it comes after both the peacock's and the dog's lowered state is shown. 'Vow' (வதம்) is the Jain term, so the school tag follows the word.

reading: One day the peacock sees, by the side of the jewelled hall, the woman with full breasts embracing the hunchback Ashtavakran after a great feast.
nuance: The verse does not name the woman; that she is the former queen is inferred from verse 172, which calls her the bird's beloved of the earlier birth.
event: The peacock sees the woman embracing Ashtavakran by the hall.

reading: Recalling, after it understood, the peerless deed of its beloved of the earlier birth, the bird pecks out the guiltless lover's bright eyes.
nuance: The bird that remembers an earlier birth is the one thing in the chapter so far that does remember; it answers with its beak what the king had stopped his sword from doing.
event: The peacock pecks out Ashtavakran's eyes.

reading: The woman, enraged, flings a handful of stones from her hand; they strike the bird's head and it falls to the ground.
nuance: 'She of the pearl-white smile' (முத்த வாள்நகையாள்) is the woman of 171, here seen in anger.
event: The woman hurls stones and knocks the peacock down.

reading: The dog, the mother born again, runs behind and bites; the peacock dies in her mouth, and the poet says this is how harmful deeds come to their fruit.
nuance: The mother who once urged the son to a blood-offering kills him, a bird, in her mouth; neither knows the other. The verse says deed bears fruit but not whose deed it is here.
event: The dog seizes the peacock and kills it.

reading: Thinking that the dear life of the peacock trembling in the dog's mouth had left, a woman says so; and Yasomathi, not understanding, beats the dog with a board.
nuance: The beater is the dead bird's son and the dog's grandson; he acts without knowing it, so the harm done is the work of ignorance not of choice.
event: Yasomathi strikes the dog with a board, not knowing who she is.

reading: The king that was a peacock is born in the Vindhya hills as a boar with bristles like thorns and brings pain to others; the poet calls this the fruit of a hard deed.
nuance: The poet moves the soul on at once: the one who was in 175 beaten for its sake is not heard of again.
event: The former king is reborn as a boar in the Vindhya woods.

reading: The dog too comes to the hillside, as a black snake, and coils; the boar's bowels burn and his hunger leaves him.
nuance: 'Hunger left the boar' may mean the snake swallowed him or that he died; the sense turns on a rare phrase. Verse 178 calls this boar the one that killed the mother, so the two kill each other.
event: The dog is reborn as a black snake and attacks the boar.

reading: As the boar that killed its mother wearies, a fierce bear charges it like a lion; it falls tormented and dies.
nuance: The verse calls the boar 'the mother-killing boar' (தாய்கொல் பன்றி), so by the poem's count the boar had killed the snake that was Chandramathi; a bear, with no part in the story, ends him.
event: A bear attacks the boar and kills it.

reading: The soul that was king and boar becomes a fish named Lohita in the river Shiprai, whose waters bring pain.
nuance: The fish's name (உலோகித) is given only here; the birth takes the soul from the land to the water.
event: The former king is reborn as the fish Lohita in the river Shiprai.

reading: The dog, as black snake, goes before and becomes a crocodile, and burning with heat it strains to swallow the fish.
nuance: The mother has been dog, snake and now crocodile, each time moving to meet the son in his next form; the poem does not say she knows him.
event: The former snake is reborn as a crocodile and tries to swallow the fish.

reading: A hunchback woman dances in the air; the crocodile seizes her in its mouth, and the king orders the crocodile given to killers to be killed.
nuance: கொல்கராத்தந்து is unclear in the edition; the reading takes கொல்க as the order to kill. The king who gives the order is the crocodile's own grandson.
event: Yasomathi orders the crocodile that took the hunchback killed.

reading: The fishers catch the crocodile in a net and drag it by ropes, heat skewers and surround it, and the killers cut and tear it; the poet says many tormented it and who can tell it all.
nuance: The poet turns away from the telling ('who can tell it'), as he does not at the beast's earlier deaths; the verse gives the cruelty its own weight.
event: Fishers and killers capture the crocodile and cut it to pieces.

title: மூன்றாஞ் சருக்கம் 183-204 (2/3)
theme: The queen mother and the king, reborn as a goat and a fish, are taken for the rite of the dead by the brahmins and by the king who is their son; the brahmins bless the dead with heaven as they eat him, and the kid, hearing it, recalls his birth, names his city and wealth as the fruit of his deed, and dies into another birth.
source_issues: Verse 183 line 1 splits the name as 'சந்தி ரம்மதி' in the edition.
Verse 188 line 2 'ஒரு வன்றகர்' may be a different word division (ஒருவன் தகர்).
Verses 193 and 194 are obscure in lines 1-2 and 3-4; the sense is a provisional reading.
Verse 201 lines 3-4 and verse 202 are partly obscure.
Verse 204's சினை could be an embryo or an egg; the edition's division is kept.

cast.role: Asokan's queen and Yasodharan's mother, now reborn as a goat
the dead king, reborn through peacock, boar, fish and ram-kid
his son, the king of Ujjayini, who hunts and orders the rite
the brahmins who claim the flesh for the rite of the dead and bless it
some who recite rules after the buffalo is given
the king's spies sent to fetch the kid
a strong ram that kills the mating kid

reading: The mother, once Chandramathi, passes through the births of a dog, a black snake and a crocodile caught in a long net, and after that death comes as a young female goat to the hamlet of the outcaste people.
nuance: The verse puts a queen's soul in a string of animal births and ends in the lowest settlement; it gives no reason for the order of births here, and the earlier chapters' account of her deed is not repeated.
event: Chandramathi, reborn as a dog, a snake and a crocodile, dies in a fisher's net and is born as a young goat in an outcaste hamlet.

reading: The other fish, the one that was once the king, is also caught in a long net, and the brahmins who came that day see it and tell the king it is a fit thing for the rite due to his kin.
nuance: The fish is Yasodharan, though the verse says only 'the other fish' (மற்றை மீன்); the reader has to carry the identity from the births in the earlier verses.
event: Brahmins see a netted fish and tell King Yasomathi it suits the rite for his lineage.

reading: The brahmins, whom the poet calls doers of evil, tell Yasomathi to eat one limb of the cut fish so that Yasodharan may prosper in heaven, which is hard to die into, and so that he may guard the earth.
nuance: The word தீவினையாளர் is the poet's own verdict on the speakers, set into the narration, not something the brahmins say of themselves; the work answers the claim through what the father is, not in this verse (see 196-197).
event: The brahmins bid Yasomathi eat a piece of the fish to raise his dead father in heaven.

reading: The life standing in the fish's throat departs; it understood the birth it had come from and, with the thought that eating after eating sets one up in heaven, it wasted away and died saying 'good, good'.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are hard: 'eating and eating to set one in heaven, good, good' can be the dying creature's bitter echo of the brahmins, or a mere report of what they said; I read it as the fish's own bitter echo, and the reading is provisional.
event: The fish remembers its former birth and dies as the rite proceeds.

reading: The king, after the births of peacock, boar and fish, ends in the womb of the goat of before, takes the form of a male, and when grown falls upon the very mother who bore him.
nuance: The verse says the birth ended in the womb of 'the goat of before' (முன்னை ஆடு); that this goat is Chandramathi of 183 is the reader's inference. The poet states the union flatly and does not comment on it; the work's own sin-and-fruit line is carried by the verses around it.
event: Yasodharan, reborn as a ram-kid from the goat who was once his mother, grows and mates with her.

reading: While he enjoys the goodness of his mother, a strong ram, angered, charges at him; he runs, writhes and loses life, and joins the womb of the same mother through the seed.
nuance: 'ஒரு வன்றகர்' is read as 'a certain strong ram'; if the edition's word division is 'ஒருவன் தகர்' (a man's ram) the sense is the same. How the dead creature 'joins' (சார்ந்தது) the womb is told in a word and not explained.
event: A rival ram attacks Yasodharan as he mates; he dies and enters his mother's womb again.

reading: The soul becomes a young kid in its mother's womb; when it has grown, the flower-crowned king, wishing to hunt, kills the mother goat with an arrow on his way back.
nuance: Read with 183 and 187, the doe is Chandramathi, the king's own grandmother, and the kid is his own father; the verse itself names neither, and the hunting king does not know.
event: King Yasomathi, back from the hunt, shoots the pregnant goat dead.

reading: The lion-strong king takes pity on the kid that falls from the arrow, and orders the outcaste man to raise it and spare its feet hardship.
nuance: The kindness comes at the moment he has killed its mother, and the closing என்பவே marks it as the poet's report.
event: The king has the orphaned kid saved and raised by an outcaste man.

reading: On another day, by his usual custom, the king goes on a great hunt, kills the many creatures that come to hand, and brings them back to offer, with a buffalo as the chief offering, to the goddess of war.
nuance: The poem calls the buffalo the king's victorious offering (கொற்றமிக்கு) in plain description; the reader sets it against what the king's father refused at 139.
event: King Yasomathi kills many animals in a hunt and offers a buffalo to the goddess.

reading: The brahmins say that the buffalo killed today would be good if it could be eaten in the rite for the dead, and the king gives it to them; then some others stand up and recite rules.
nuance: The rite is named சிராத்தம். The speaker of the rules (சிலர்) at line 4 is different from the brahmins who claimed the flesh.
event: The brahmins claim the fresh buffalo for the rite and the king gives it; others begin to cite rules.

reading: Some say that since the buffalo has dried in the sun and crows may have seized it, it is no good for the rite, and add that there is still another way.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are broken by the edition's word division; the sense 'dried in the sun, crows may have taken it' is a provisional reading.
event: Rule-reciters object that the sun-dried flesh may be spoiled and offer another way.

reading: They go on that even flesh named bad may be judged by choice, and that if good cooked rice is set before the ram's face the books of merit count it as proper; the rest of the line is obscure.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are very hard (பூதம், நாதனார், அத்துராதிகள்); what is firm is that the ram is chosen, and that is the turn to the kid of 190. The rest is a provisional reading.
event: The rule-reciters name the ram as the right victim, with rice laid before its face.

reading: On hearing this, the king says the kid they once sent off to be reared is the very thing, and sends spies to fetch it; the brahmins approve it as good.
nuance: The decisive moment is the king's own choice of the animal he had saved; the father is brought to the rite by the son's order, with no word of knowing.
event: The king sends spies to bring back the reared ram-kid for the rite, and the brahmins approve.

reading: They eat what was brought, and the brahmins, learned in the four Vedas, bless the dead King Yasodharan to live in the world above together with his mother.
nuance: The claim is stated as the brahmins' belief and is turned in the next verse, where the eaten kid recognises himself as the blessed man; the verse itself does not mark the irony.
event: The brahmins eat the kid's flesh and bless the dead Yasodharan and his mother with life in heaven.

reading: Having heard that, the goat of that place remembers its birth and, grieving, understands that the one who rules here, King Yasomathi with his rutting elephant, is its own son.
nuance: The eaten animal recovers its memory of the former birth only as the rite is spoken over it; the Jain epic presents memory of births as a gift of understanding, not a punishment.
event: Hearing the blessing, the kid recalls its birth and knows the king as its son.

reading: It sees that this is its own great city of Ujjayini, this its palace and treasure, these its servants, and that this is how it has come to be.
nuance: The repeated 'this is mine' (இது என்) in every line is the king's old claim of ownership, now said by a goat.
event: The kid surveys what was once its city, palace and servants.

reading: It says that these heaps of wealth it made, these rutting elephants it reared, these fine horses it bred, are what the deed it produced has now ripened into.
nuance: The line is open: 'what I made is the fruit of the deed I produced' may mean the wealth was the fruit, or that the fallen state is; the verse sets both against each other. The voice is a kid's, and the work lets it stand.
event: The kid names the wealth, elephants and horses it once made as the fruit of its own deed.

reading: It adds that these men are its gate guards, its army chiefs, its singers and dancers, its own attendants.
It wonders what the poison-giving queen Amirthamathi, who gave it this end, is doing, whether she lives on with the hidden lover, and what became of her, since she is not here.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are obscure; 'her lasting hidden one' (தன் மறையான்) is read as the secret lover of ch. 6 and the last clause is a provisional reading.
event: The kid wonders what became of the wife who poisoned it.

reading: It asks whether this blamed king, with flesh-eaters such as these, who has made me suffer without cause, can send me to the heaven he wishes.
nuance: The claim is put as a doubtful question by the eaten man himself, who is the dead one the rite claims to lift; it answers the brahmins' claim of 185 and 196 from inside the story. The grammar of lines 1 to 3 is hard.

reading: With what the foolish woman's poison left of him gone from this earth and city, he asks what he did and what he will do, and says he knows nothing.
nuance: The grief is without a way out; he does not yet link his state to the Jain account of deeds that the youths gave at 34 and 35.

reading: As such thoughts rise, the great pain made by countless deeds presses on him; before he can look at his son's palace, the kid's life leaves and goes to be born again as an embryo.
nuance: The poet carries the claim by naming the pain as 'made by deeds' (வினையினாகிய); the next birth is stated in 'சினை' (an embryo or egg) and the shape it takes is left to the next verse.
event: The kid dies and is born again.

title: மூன்றாஞ் சருக்கம் 205-226 (3/3)
theme: The buffalo killed by the king's men for the loss of a horse is eaten by Amirthamathi, who is then struck by leprosy, which onlookers call the fruit of her deeds; one who understands visits and reproaches her, and the soul is born as a cock that the king has reared, while the chapter closes on the spring.
source_issues: Verse 205 is hard in its second and third lines (வாடது) and who is the snake is unclear.
Verse 207 line 4 'மா' is read as 'horse' from 208, not stated.
Verse 210 சரணம் may be feet or the four refuges.
Verse 215 மேனியன் is masculine where the sense is the queen; compare 216.
Verse 219 வத்தகர் is obscure; who the visitor is is inferred.
Verses 220 to 222 leave speakers and the person who goes with the buffalo open.

cast.role: the buffalo of the merchants, the next rebirth of the one the story follows; identity from the sequel
the merchants whose buffalo kills the royal horse
the king's attendants who report the horse's death and carry out his order
the king of Ujjain, unnamed in these verses; Yasodharan's son by the story so far
Yasodharan's widow, who poisoned him and eats the buffalo's flesh
the others who say she is working an illusion
those who speak behind the queen's back; named only in 219
the one who goes to see the leprous queen; by 221 the man she poisoned, but the Tamil does not say
the cock into which the soul is born
the cock-keeper to whom the king gives the cock

reading: The verse lists the rebirths so far (Chandramathi a dog, a black snake after) and says that the one now followed came to the goods-rich land of Kalinga as a buffalo and grew up there.
nuance: The line 'வாடது' and who the snake is are hard; that the buffalo is the poisoned king reborn is taken from the sequel (the queen's eating of it, 212, and the accusation at 221), not stated in the verse.
event: The one passing through rebirths is born and grows as a buffalo in Kalinga.

reading: The buffalo travels with merchants, bearing their goods without rest, and one day the merchants halt their caravan outside Ujjain by the river.
event: Merchants and their burden-buffalo come and camp on the bank beside Ujjain.

reading: Wearied by the load it carried, the buffalo runs into the Sipra river, bathes its fill, and coming to the bank it strikes the horse that has come there.
nuance: The word மா in line 4 is read here as 'horse', since 208 names the royal mount as lost; the edition leaves it as 'the animal'.
event: The buffalo, freed of its load, bathes in the Sipra and gores a horse on the bank.

reading: The king's attendants announce that the royal mount named Arasavannam, killed by the merchants' buffalo, is gone.
nuance: The attendants lay the loss on the merchants through their buffalo, which sets up the king's seizure in 209.
event: The royal attendants report to the king that his horse is dead through the merchants' buffalo.

reading: The king, in a rage, orders the merchants' wealth and the buffalo seized and brought to him, and his men go and carry off goods past counting.
nuance: The verse itself does not condemn; the claim is the reader's reading of the report. The king is unnamed here; he is taken to be Yasomati by the story so far.
event: The king orders the merchants' goods and the buffalo taken, and his men plunder them.

reading: The merciless men, knowing the king's order, bind the beast's four feet and strip it of all its means, leaving it with only dharma as its fortress.
nuance: சரணம் நான்கு can be 'four feet' or the four refuges of Jain practice; the first is followed here, and the line 'only dharma is its fortress' may carry the second meaning.
event: The king's men bind and disable the buffalo as ordered.

reading: The buffalo is killed in stages: boiled in caustic water, cut apart, its belly emptied, a rod stirred through ghee, and at last it is finished with a thorn-sharp whip.
nuance: The step-by-step account of the butchery is a Jain teaching device: the pain of the animal is set out so that the later eating of its flesh (212) is felt as cruelty.
event: The king's men slaughter and prepare the buffalo with cruelty.

reading: The queen, a vine of a woman named Amirthamathi, puts the well-cooked buffalo flesh in her mouth and fattens her belly; the others say she is working some illusion.
nuance: The queen is Yasodharan's wife and, if the buffalo is the poisoned king reborn (205 and 221 suggest it), she is eating her victim; the verse does not say this, the sequel does.
event: Amirthamathi eats the cooked flesh of the buffalo while others comment.

reading: The queen says she still has hunger, that a ram lives close by, and that biting its thigh and eating it today would put her craving to an end.
nuance: Her words show appetite growing as it is fed; the epic's own voice holds the opposite, that craving is not ended by eating.
event: Amirthamathi asks for a ram to be killed so she may eat its thigh.

reading: The verse looks back: in anger she took the life of the great lord whose beauty matched Kama's, mixing his poison with her passion, and joined a man she had made a human dog.
nuance: 'Human dog' is the narrator's contempt for the man, not a name; the earlier chapters name him Ashtavakran (ch.6).
event: Recalled: Amirthamathi poisons her husband and takes the hunchback as her lover.

reading: After she had sported with the low-born hunchback of leprous body, a day comes when one of beautiful frame, now spoiled, is plunged in leprosy.
nuance: மேனியன் in line 3 is masculine, while 216 uses feminine forms for the sufferer; the sense is taken as the queen, but the form could point at the hunchback.
event: Amirthamathi falls ill with leprosy after her years with Ashtavakran.

reading: Her limbs rot and wither, she oozes sores, flies crowd in the stench, and many more diseases gather upon her.
event: Leprosy and other diseases ravage Amirthamathi's body.

reading: Those who see her say that she has no understanding by the strong karma of a former birth, that this is the fruit of what she did in this birth, and that this karma does not lie, and does not die even if she dies.
nuance: The speakers are named in 219 only as those who said this behind her back; 'எம்மையும்' (us too) is hard to place.

reading: They wonder whether it was craving for the disease, want of fine discernment, or the gathering of heavy evil karma that made her eat the dead buffalo, and say this delusion will seize her again.
So they spoke behind her back; then one who fully understood it all went to see her, pained in mind.
nuance: The word வத்தகர் is obscure and who the visitor is is not fixed by the Tamil; 220 and 221 let him be the man she poisoned.
event: Her attendants speak, and one who understood goes to see her.

reading: The visitor reproaches the queen: she was angry at him, she went and delighted in a sinner, and now her body is thus and she has seized him too.
nuance: 'Sinner' (பாவி) is used for her lover, for her, and for the speaker's own fate, so the verse is open to two readings of who has seized whom.

reading: The visitor says she tormented him with his mother by poison, that her wrath has not ended though she is dying, and asks whether, with the buffalo lying in her belly, she will plot against him too.
nuance: This is the verse that makes the visitor the poisoned king; the buffalo here is a third party, 'that buffalo' in her belly, so whether the buffalo is he or his mother is left open.
event: The visitor accuses the queen of the poison and of the eaten buffalo.

reading: Seeing her so, he asks what reproach can do; one thing still burns in his heart, and the life undone by the queen's torment went on its way with the buffalo.
nuance: Whether the life that goes with the buffalo is the queen's or the visitor's is not settled by the grammar.

reading: In that great city, in a Paraiya street of small houses and many people, the soul takes the form of a cock, and the victorious spear-king wishes to see it.
nuance: The street is named only as the place of the birth; the verse does not judge the birth by it.
event: The soul is born as a cock and the king wants to see it.

reading: The king is delighted at the sight and orders Chandakarmi to be given charge to raise it; he takes it to his cage and rears it, and it grows skilled in war.
nuance: This Chandakarmi is a cock-keeper, whom the Tamil does not equate with the Chandakarman who brought the youths in ch.2 and 3.
event: The king has the cock reared by Chandakarmi, who trains it for fighting.

tamil: தரள மாகிய நயனத்தொ டஞ்சிறை சாபம்போற் சிகியென்ன
மருளு மாகன சிகழிகைச் சுடர்க்கண மணிமுடி தனையொத்த
ஒளிரு பொன்னன சரணங்கள் வயிரமுள் ளொப்பில போரின்கண்
தளர்வில் வீரியந் தகைபெற வளர்ந்தன தமக்கிணை யவைதாமே.
reading: The cock grows, its eyes like pearls, its wings like a bow, its crest bright like a gem-crown, its golden feet with diamond spurs matchless in battle, and its strength unflagging.

tamil: செந்தளிர் புனைந்த சோலைத் திருமணி வண்டுந் தேனுங்
கொந்துகள் குடைந்து கூவுங் குயிலொடு குழுமி யார்ப்பச்
செந்துண ரளைந்து தென்றற் றிசைதிசை சென்று வீச
வந்துள மகிழ்ந்த தெங்கும் வளர் மதுப் பருவ மாதோ.
reading: The grove with its red shoots, bees, honey and koel calls fills with the south wind, and the heart rejoices everywhere in the season of honey.

title: நான்காஞ் சருக்கம் 227-244 (1/2)
theme: King Yasomathi sits in his garden among dancers, and his executioner Chandakarman meets the ascetic Akampanan, to whom he says he cut thieves and never found a soul; the sage answers with fire in wood and a conch's sound, names the final state of the soul, and gives the man of the world knowledge, faith and the vows as his way.
source_issues: Verse 227 spells the king's name விசோமதி; it is read as Yasomathi (இசோமதி) of chapter 5.
Verse 228 line 4 had a pulli after a vowel sign, repaired by the build.
Lines of 230 and 232 to 238 are obscure or compressed; speakers are taken from 231, 234 and 239.
Verse 242 and 244 give புலைசு தேன்கள் for the abstentions, read as flesh, honey and toddy.

cast.role: the king, here sitting in his garden
the king's queen
dancing women who play before the king
the king's executioner of thieves, who questions the sage
the ascetic who meditates in the grove and answers him

tamil: இணர்தகைப் பொழிலி னுள்ளா விசோமதி யென்னு மன்னன்
வணர்தகைக் குழலி புட்பா வலியெனுந் துணைவி யோடு
புணர்தகை வல்லி புல்லி வளரிளம் பிண்டி வண்டர்
இணர்ததை தவிசி னேறி யினிதினி னமர்ந்தி ருந்தான்.
reading: The king Yasomathi sits happily on a seat laid with young asoka blossoms in his garden, with his queen Pushpavali beside him, the creeper-like wife who clings to him.
nuance: The king's name is spelled விசோமதி with an initial வி in the edition; it is read as the Yasomathi of the earlier chapters (இசோமதி).
event: King Yasomathi sits in his flower garden with Queen Pushpavali.

tamil: பாடக மிலங்கு செங்கேழ்ச் சீறடிப் பரவை யல்குற்
சூடக மணிமென் தோளின் தொழுதனர் துளங்கத் தோன்றி
நாடக மகளி ராடு நாடக நயந்து நல்லார்
பாடலி லமிர்த வூறல் பருகினன் மகிழ்ந்தி ருந்தான்.
reading: Dancing women with ringed ankles and bangled arms bow and sway into view and dance, and the king, glad, drinks in their sweet song as though it were nectar.
nuance: The scene is the pleasure of a king at ease; the next verse breaks it with the arrival of the ascetic's finder.
event: Dancers perform before the king, who delights in their song.

tamil: வளையவர் சூழ லுள்ளான் மனமகிழ்ந் திருப்ப மன்னன்
தளையவிழ் தொடையன் மார்பன் சண்டமுற் கருமன் போகி
வளமலர் வனத்துள் தீய மனிதரோ டனைய சாதி
களைபவன் கடவுள் கண்ணிற் கண்டுகை தொழுது நின்றான்.
reading: While the king sits happy among his women, the king's punisher Chandakarman, who rids the land of thieves and such people, goes into the flowery grove and stands with folded hands before one he takes for a god.
nuance: Chandakarman's office, one who removes the evil sort of people, is implied by the words அனைய சாதி களைபவன், which the verse does not explain; he is the king's executioner of thieves in the verses that follow.
event: Chandakarman goes into a flowering grove, sees a holy man and stands before him with folded hands.

tamil: அருவினை முனைகொ லாற்ற லகம்பன னென்னும் நாமத்
தருமுதல் யோகு கொண்டு தன்னள விறந்தான் முன்னர்
மருவிய நினைப்பு மாற்றி வந்தது கண்டி ருந்தான்.
reading: There sits alone to one side under an asoka tree the ascetic Akampanan, who has gone beyond himself in deep concentration and is now returning from it, and Chandakarman watches.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are hard: 'went beyond his own measure' and 'turned away his former thought and came back' are taken as the coming out of trance, which the Tamil does not say outright.
event: Chandakarman sees the ascetic Akampanan rise out of deep meditation beneath an asoka tree.

tamil: வடிநுனைப் பகழி யானு மலரடி வணங்கி வாழ்த்தி
அடீகணி ரடங்கி மெய்யி லருள்புரி மனத்தீ ராகி
நெடிதுட னிருந்து நெஞ்சி னினைவதோர் நினைவு தன்னான்
முடிபொருள் தானு மென்கொல் மொழிந்தருள் செய்க என்றான்.
reading: Chandakarman bows at the sage's feet, praises him, sits long with a quiet mind and asks him what final object it is that he has been fixing in his heart.
nuance: Chandakarman is called the one with the sharp arrow (வடிநுனைப் பகழியான்), a hunter or killer by trade, who asks like a pupil.
event: Chandakarman bows to Akampanan and asks what the sage's meditation was aimed at.

tamil: ஆரருள் புரிந்த நிஞ்சி னம்முனி யவனை நோக்கிச்
சீரருள் பெருகும் பான்மைத் திறத்தனே போலு மென்றே
பேரறி வாகித் தம்மிற் பிறழ்விலா வுயிரை யன்றே
கூரறி வுடைய நீரார் குறிப்பது மனத்தி னாலே.
reading: The sage looks at him, judges him fit to grow in grace, and answers that the keen-witted point to the soul, whole in great knowledge, by the mind.
nuance: Whether the quoted words begin at line 2 or line 3 is not fixed by the edition; the sage's answer is taken from the closing lines.
event: Akampanan looks at Chandakarman and begins to teach him about the soul.

tamil: அனந்தமா மறிவு காட்சி யருவலி போக மாதி
நினைந்தவெண் குணங்க ளோடு திருமல நித்த மாகிச்
சினஞக்செறு வாதி யின்றித் திரிவித வுலகத் துச்சி
அனத்தகா லத்து நிற்ற லப்பொருட் டன்மை யென்றான்.
reading: The sage says that the freed soul has endless knowledge, vision, strength and bliss among its eight qualities, is eternal and without stain, and stands for ever at the top of the three worlds; that is the soul's own nature.
nuance: The verse names only the first four of the eight qualities. Nothing in it makes this state the gift of a god; the soul has it as its own nature once the stain is gone. The words திருமல நித்த மாகி are not sure.
event: Akampanan tells Chandakarman what the final state of the soul is.

tamil: கருமனு மிறைவ கேளாய் களவுசெய் தோர்கள் தம்மை
இருபிள வாகச் செய்வ னெம்மர சருளி னாலே
ஒருவழி யாலுஞ் சீவ னுண்டெனக் கண்ட தில்லை
பெரியதோர் சோர மென்றான் பின்னமாச் சேதித் திட்டும்.
reading: Chandakarman tells the sage that he has cut thieves in two by the king's order and nowhere found a life in them, which he takes for a great cheat.
nuance: No school is named here; the claim is the materialist one that what cannot be seen on cutting does not exist, put by a man whose trade is killing. The sage answers it in verses 236 to 238.
event: Chandakarman tells of cutting condemned thieves in two and finding no soul.

tamil: மற்றொரு கள்வன் தன்னை வதைசெய்யு முன்னும் பின்னும்
இற்றென நிறைசெய் திட்டு மிறைவனே பேதங் காணேன்
உற்றதோர் குழியின் மூடி யொருவனைச் சிலநாள் வைத்து
மற்றவ னுயிர்போ யிட்ட வழியொன்றுங் கண்டி லேனே.
reading: He adds that he weighed another thief before and after killing and saw no difference, and that when a man was shut in a pit for some days to die he saw no way by which a life went out.
nuance: The speaker is known from verse 234. The two tests are the man's own, the first by scale and the second by sealing; the sage's reply in 237 takes up the breath and the conch.
event: Chandakarman describes weighing a thief before and after killing him, and burying another in a pit.

tamil: பையவே காட்டத் தன்னைப் பலபின்னஞ் செய்திட் டன்று
வெய்யெரி கண்ட துண்டோ விறகொடு விறகை யூன்ற
ஐயனே யங்கி தோன்றி யதனையு மெரிக்க லுற்ற
திவ்வகைக் காண லாகு மென்றுநீ யுணர்தல் வேண்டும்.
reading: The sage asks whether anyone ever found fire in a log by cutting it up, and says that when wood is rubbed on wood the fire appears and burns the wood; so what is real can show itself without being found by cutting.
nuance: This is the first reply to 234. It argues from analogy and does not prove the soul, only that failure to find it by cutting proves nothing. Line 1 is hard.
event: Akampanan answers Chandakarman with the fire hidden in wood.

tamil: சிக்கென வாயு வேற்றித் தித்திவாய்ச் செம்மித் தூக்கிப்
புக்கவவ் வாயு நீங்கிப் போயபின் னிறைசெய் தானும்
ஒக்குமே யொருவன் சங்கோ டொருநில மாளி கைக்கே
திக்கெனத் தொனிசெய் திட்ட தெவ்வழி வந்த தாகும்.
reading: The sage says that when breath is blown into a conch and then gone, the one who blew it is as the blown breath was, and asks from where the sound that rang through the mansion came, when no cutting of the conch will show it.
nuance: The second reply to 234 and 235. Lines 1 to 3 are corrupt or very compressed and the exact comparison is not fixed.
event: Akampanan answers the weighing and the pit with the sound of a conch.

tamil: இவ்வகை யாகுஞ் சீவ னியல்புதா னியல்பு வேறாம்
வெய்ய தீ வினைக ளாலே வெருவுறு துயரின் மூழ்கி
மையலுற் றழுங்கி நான்கு கதிகளுட் கெழுமிச் செல்வ
தையமில் காட்சி ஞானத் தொழுக்கத்தோ ரறிவ தாகும்.
reading: The sage ends that the soul has a nature of its own, distinct from the body, which because of cruel deeds sinks in suffering through the four states of rebirth; this is what those of right faith, knowledge and conduct know.
nuance: The earlier chapter gave the same teaching to the young ascetics at the place of killing (verses 49 and 50); here a murderer of thieves is the pupil.
event: Akampanan concludes his answer on the soul.

tamil: ஆகமத் தடிக ளெங்கட் கதுபெரி தரிது கண்டீர்
ஏகசித் தத்த ராய விறைவர்கட் கெளிது போலும்
போகசித் தத்தோ டொன்றிப் பொழிவழிப் படரு நீரார்க்
காகுமற் றுறுதிக் கேது அருளுக தெருள என்றான்.
reading: Chandakarman says that the Agamas are great and hard for people like him, though easy for those lords of single mind, and asks what will serve for the final good of those who follow the stream of enjoyment.
nuance: Chandakarman is called a man of mixed mind; his question is why the work gives a further, lighter way for householders in 240 to 244.
event: Chandakarman asks for a way to the final good that a man of the world can follow.

tamil: அற்றமி லறிவு காட்சி யருந்தகை யொழுக்க மூன்றும்
பெற்றனர் புரிந்து பேணிப் பெருங்குணத் தொழுகு நீரார்க்
குற்றிடு மும்ப ரின்ப முலகிதற் கிறைமை தானும்
முற்றமுன் னுரைத்த பேறும் வந்துறும் முறைமை யென்றான்.
reading: The sage says that for those who hold faultless knowledge, rare vision and rare conduct, all three, the fruit is heavenly joy, lordship in this world and the release named before.
nuance: The three are not named in the verse by their later names; அறிவு, காட்சி and ஒழுக்கம் are 'knowledge', 'vision' and 'conduct'. Heaven and earthly power are given as by-fruits, with release the end.
event: Akampanan names the three that lead to the final good.

tamil: உறுபொருள் நிலைமை தன்னை யுற்றுணர் வறிவ தாகும்
அறிபொரு ளதனிற் றூய்மை யகத்தெழு தெளிவு காட்சி
நறுமலர்ப் பிண்டி நாதன் நல்லறப் பெருமை தன்பால்
இறுகிய மகிழ்ச்சி கண்டாய் இதனது பிரிவு மென்றான்.
reading: The sage defines knowledge as knowing real things as they are, vision as the clarity and purity that rises within, and the third as firm joy in the great dharma of the Lord of the asoka.
nuance: The verse says 'these are its parts' of the third, joy in the Jina's dharma; knowledge and vision are given first. Lines 3 and 4 may name the same thing as faith or as a part of it.
event: Akampanan defines the first two of the three.

tamil: பெருகிய கொலையும் பொய்யுங் களவொடு பிறன்ம னைக்கண்
தெரிவிலாச் செலவு சிந்தை பொருள்வயிற் றிருகு பற்றும்
மருவிய மனத்து மீட்சி வதமிவை யைந்தோ டொன்றி
ஒருவின புலைசு தேன்கள் ஒருவுத லொழுக்க மென்றான்.
reading: The sage says that conduct is turning the mind away from killing, lying, stealing, going unthinkingly to another's wife and tight clinging to wealth, together with giving up flesh, honey and toddy.
nuance: புலைசு தேன்கள் is read as flesh, honey and toddy; the first word is odd.
event: Akampanan lists the five vows and three abstentions that make up conduct.

tamil: கொலையின தின்மை கூறிற் குவலயத் திறைமை செய்யும்
மலைதலில் வாய்மை யார்க்கும் வாய்மொழி மதிப்பை யாக்கும்
விலையில்பே ரருளின் மாட்சி விளைப்பது களவின் மீட்சி
உலைதலில் பெருமை திட்ப முருவலி யொழிந்ந தீயும்.
reading: The sage says what each vow yields: not killing brings lordship, truth a respected word, giving up theft great and priceless grace and standing.
nuance: These are worldly rewards put to a man who has just said he cannot follow the ascetic's road; they are offered to him as householder fruit. Lines 3 and 4 are obscure.
event: Akampanan lists the rewards of the first three vows.

tamil: தெருளுடை மனத்திற் சென்ற தெளிந்துணர் வாய செல்வம்
பொருள்வயி னிறுக்க மின்மை புணர்த்திடும் புலைசு தேன்கள்
ஒருவிய பயனு மற்றே யொளியினோ டழகு வென்றி
பொருள்மிகு குலனோ டின்பம் புணர்தலு மாகு மாதோ.
reading: The sage ends with the rest: wealth of clear mind and freedom from clinging to wealth, and giving up flesh, honey and toddy, which together bring radiance, beauty, victory, good birth and pleasure.
nuance: The lines 1 and 2 do not say clearly which vow brings which fruit.
event: Akampanan lists the remaining rewards of the vows.

title: நான்காஞ் சருக்கம் 245-261 (2/2)
theme: In the second half of the sage's reply to Yasomathi, the king's claim that life cannot go on without killing is answered by compassion and by the story of his father and grandmother, who suffered in every birth for killing a flour cock and who now sit as cocks in a cage beside him; they take the vow, are killed by his arrow and pass into human birth, and the chapter ends with Pushpavali's three children and the youngest prince's schooling.
source_issues: Verses 254 and 257 end without a full stop in the edition, and 254's last line runs into 255.
246 line 1 reads 'சண்ட இசைத்தது' (probably 'சண்டன் இசைத்தது'), apparently a name for the king, which does not appear elsewhere in this chapter.
The speakers of 245 and 255 are not marked by the text; the readings are inferred from 246 and from the cocks' crowing in 256.

cast.role: the king of Ujjayini, son of Yasodharan; speaks to the sage in this chapter
the sage who answers Yasomathi and tells him who the cocks are; unnamed in this chapter
the two cocks in the cage beside the king, who are his father and grandmother reborn
Yasomathi's father, who with his mother killed a flour cock
Yasomathi's grandmother, the king's mother in the earlier chapters
Yasomathi's queen, who bears the twins and a third son
the youngest son of Yasomathi, named like his grandfather

tamil: சிலைபயில் வயிரத் தோளாய் செப்பிய பொருளி தெல்லாம்
உலைதலின் மகிழ்வோ டுள்ளத் துணர்ந்தனை கொள்க என்னக்
கொலையினி லொருவ லின்றிக் கொண்டனென் அருளிற் றெல்லாம்
அலைசெய்வ தொழியின் வாழ்க்கை யழியுமற் றடிக வென்றான்.
reading: Bowing, the king answers the sage's teaching by saying he has taken in all he was told but cannot give up killing, since life would fall apart if the harassing stopped; the second line may still be the sage's words that he quotes.
nuance: The speaking voices are tangled: line 1 and the start of line 2 address a 'diamond-shouldered' hearer and may be quoted from the sage, and the next verse's opening (என்றடி பணிந்து) shows that all of this is the king's answer. The sage's reply in 246 and 252 is what answers the claim here.
event: Yasomathi replies to the sage that he has accepted the teaching but not the giving up of killing.

tamil: என்றடி பணிந்து சண்ட விசைத்தது கடவுள் கேட்டு
நன்றினித் தெளிந்தா யல்லை நவிலிசை யமுத நல்யாழ்
ஒன்றிய செவிடு மூமும் ஒருவனாற் பெறுத லுண்டோ
இன்றுநீ யுரைத்த தற்றே யியம்புவ துளது கேண்மோ.
reading: The sage, hearing him, says he has not understood well: a man deaf and dumb cannot get the nectar of music or a good lute, and what the king has said is just that.
event: The sage tells Yasomathi he has not truly understood and says more remains to be heard.

tamil: ஆருயிர் வருத்தங் கண்டா லருள்பெரி தொழுகு கண்ணால்
ஒருயிர் போல நெஞ்சத் துருகிநைந் துய்ய நிற்றல்
வாரியின் வதங்கட் கெல்லா மரசநல் வதம தற்கே
சார்துணை யாகக் கொள்க தகவுமத் தயவு மென்றான்.
reading: When one sees a living being's distress, the sage says, to melt and waste away in the heart as though the life were one's own is the support the king-vow of non-killing needs, with restraint and compassion as its companions.
nuance: Line 3 reads 'among the sea-like vows, the kingly vow'; I take 'அரச நல் வதம்' as the chief of vows (non-killing) and 'அதற்கே' as pointing back to it, which the following verses support.
event: The sage names compassion for a creature's pain, felt as one's own, as the base of the chief vow.

tamil: இறந்தநா ளென்னு முள்ளத் திரங்குத லின்றி வெய்தாய்க்
கறந்துயி ருண்டு கன்றிக் கருவினை பெருகச் செய்தாய்
பிறந்துநீ பிறவி தோறும் பெருநவை யுறுவ தெல்லாஞ்
சிறந்தநல் லறத்தி னன்றித் தீருமா றுணரி னுண்டோ.
reading: The sage tells the king that, lacking pity, he cruelly drained and took life from a cock, swelling karma, and that the great suffering he gets in birth after birth could end by no means except good dharma.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are hard (the 'day that is gone' and the milking-and-eating image); the sage seems to be speaking of the earlier killing of the flour cock, and the reading rests on 250 and 251.
event: The sage tells Yasomathi that a killing without pity has made karma swell and that only dharma can end its fruit.

tamil: நிலையிலா வுடம்பின் வாழ்க்கை நெடிதுட னிறுவ லென்றிக்
கொலையினான் முயன்று வாழுங் கொற்றவ ரேனு முற்றச்
சிலபக லன்றி நின்றார் சிலரிவ ணில்லை கண்டாய்
அலைதரு பிறவி முந்நீ ரழுந்துவ ரனந்தங் காலம்.
reading: Even kings who live by killing, thinking to keep this impermanent body long, have stood only a few days, the sage says, and they sink in the sea of rebirth for endless time.
nuance: The argument is that killing to prolong life defeats itself because the body does not last and the killing makes the next birth worse; it answers the king's claim in 245 from the body's brief span.
event: The sage says that kings who kill to keep the body last only a few days and then sink in rebirth.

tamil: இன்னுமீ தைய கேட்க யசோமதி தந்தை யாய
மன்னவ னன்னை யோடு மாவினற் கோழி தன்னைக்
கொன்னவில் வாளிற் கொன்ற கொடுமையிற் கடிய துன்பம்
பின்னவர் பிறவி தோறும் பெற்றன பேச லாமோ.
reading: Listen further, the sage says: the king who was Yasomathi's father, together with his mother, killed a cock of flour with a sword and then suffered in every birth a pain worse than the cruelty of the killing, which cannot be told.
nuance: The cock was of flour (மாவினால்), not a living bird; the sage counts the intent of killing as the deed (see 252). The king named here is Yasodharan of the earlier chapters and the mother Chandramathi.
event: The sage tells Yasomathi that his father and grandmother, who killed the flour cock, have suffered in every birth since.

tamil: வீங்கிய வினைகள் தம்மால் வெருவரத் தக்க துன்பம்
தாங்கினர் பிறந்தி றந்து தளர்ந்தனர் விலங்கிற் செல்வார்
ஆங்கவர் தாங்கள் கண்டா யருவினை துரப்ப வந்தார்
ஈங்குநின் னயல கூட்டி லிருந்தகோ ழிகளா யென்றான்.
reading: Swollen by their karma, they bore fearful pain and wore down in birth and death, going into animal births; the sage says they are the cocks sitting in the cage near the king.
event: The sage tells Yasomathi that the two cocks in the cage beside him are his father and grandmother reborn.

tamil: உயிரவ ணில்லை யேனு முயிர்க்கொலை நினைப்பி னாலிம்
மயரிகள் பிறவி தோறும் வருந்திய வருத்தங் கண்டால்
உயிரினி லருளொன் றின்றி யுவந்தனர் கொன்று சென்றார்
செயிர்தரு நரகி னல்லாற் செல்லிட மில்லை யென்றான்.
reading: Although the flour cock held no life, the sage says, the thought of killing a life made these deluded ones suffer in every birth, and those who killed without pity for life have no refuge but the fierce hell.
nuance: Intent is made the measure of the deed: no life was taken, yet the fruit is as if one had been. This is the sage's final answer to the king's claim in 245.

tamil: மற்றவன் இனைய கூற மனநனி கலங்கி வாடிச்
செற்றமுஞ் சினமு நீக்கித் திருவறத் தெளிவு காதல்
பற்றினன் வதங்கள் முன்னம் பகர்ந்தன வனைத்துங் கொண்டு
பெற்றன னடிகள் நும்பாற் பெரும்பய னென்று போந்தான்.
reading: Hearing this, Yasomathi is shaken and grieves, puts away his hatred and anger, loves the clear holy dharma, takes the vows told before, and leaves saying he has won great fruit from the lords.
event: Yasomathi gives up anger, takes the vows and leaves, grateful to the sage.

tamil: கேட்டலு மடிகள் வாயிற் கெழுமிய மொழிகள் தம்மைக்
கூட்டினு ளிருந்த மற்றக் கோழிகள் பிறப்பு ணர்ந்திட்
டோட்டிய சினத்த வாகி யுறுவத முய்ந்து கொண்ட
பாட்டருந் தன்மைத் தன்றே பான்மையிற் பரிசு தானும்
reading: The cocks in the cage, hearing the words that came from the lord's mouth, learn of their births and take up the vows in anger left behind; the sentence is left open for the next verse.
nuance: The verse ends mid-sentence (the last line of 254 is its own clause that is closed in 255).
event: The two cocks hear the sage and, learning of their births, take the vows.

tamil: பிறவிக ளனைத்து நெஞ்சிற் பெயர்ந்தன நினைத்து முன்னர்
மறவியின் மயங்கி மாற்றின் மறுகின மருகு சென்றே
அறவிறை யடிகள் தம்மா லறவுமிர் தாரப் பெற்றேம்
reading: All their births pass through their hearts, once clouded by forgetfulness; going near, they say that by the lord of dharma they have been given the nectar of dharma and have escaped the hot disease of rebirth.
nuance: That the cocks speak is my reading of lines 3 and 4 (அறவுமிர்தாரப் பெற்றேம், 'we have received'), which could also be the poet's voice for them.
event: The two cocks recall their past births and give thanks for the teaching that frees them from rebirth.

tamil: அறிவரன் சரண மூழ்கி யறத்தெழு விருப்ப முள்ளாக்
குறைவிலா வமுதங் கொண்டு குளிர்ந்தக மகிழ்ந்து கூவச்
செறிபொழி லதனுட் சென்று செவியினு ளிசைப்ப மன்னன்
முறுவல்கொண் முகத்து நல்லார் முகத்தொரு சிலைவ ளைத்தான்.
reading: Having bathed in the sage's feet, the cocks drink the full nectar of dharma and crow gladly in the grove, and the king, hearing it, bends a bow with a face that smiles beside the faces of fair women.
nuance: The last line is obscure (the bow bent 'with the face of fair women') and leaves it unclear whom the king aims at.
event: The cocks crow in the garden and the king bends his bow.

tamil: சொல்லறி கணையை வாங்கித் தொடுத்தவன் விடுத்த லோடும்
நல்லிறைப் பறவை தம்மை நடுக்கிய தடுத்து வீழச்
சில்லறி வினைக ளேனுந் திருவறப் பெருமை யாலே
வல்லிதின் மறைந்து போகி மானுடம் பாய வன்றே
reading: The king takes the knowing arrow and looses it, and the good birds shake and fall; yet by the greatness of the holy dharma their small karmas hide away and they pass into human birth.
nuance: The poem does not explain how Yasomathi, who has just taken the vows in 253, looses the arrow; the verse stresses that the dharma the cocks took turns the killing into a rebirth as human beings. The verse ends without a full stop in the edition.
event: Yasomathi's arrow strikes the cocks, which die and are reborn as humans.

tamil: விரைசெறி பொழிலி னுள்ளால் வேனலின் விளைந்த எல்லாம்
அரசனு மமர்ந்து போகி யகநகர்க் கோயி லெய்தி
முரசொலி கழுமப் புக்கு மொய்ம்மலி குழலி னாரோ
டுரைசெய லரிய வண்ண முவகையின் மூழ்கி னானே.
reading: The king goes through the scented grove, then back into the palace to the sound of drums, and sinks into untellable delight among women with fragrant hair.
event: Yasomathi returns to his palace and gives himself to pleasure.

tamil: இன்னண மரச செல்வத் திசோமதி செல்லு நாளுள்
பொன்னிய லணிகொள் புட்பா வலியெனும் பொங்கு கொங்கை
இன்னிய லிரட்டை யாகு மிளையரை யீன்று சின்னாள்
பின்னுமோர் சிறுவன் தன்னைப் பெற்றனள் பேதை தானே.
reading: As Yasomathi lives on in royal wealth, Pushpavali bears twins and, after a few days, another son.
event: Pushpavali bears Yasomathi twins and then a third son.

tamil: அன்னவர் தம்முள் மன்னோ னபயமுன் னுருசி தங்கை
அன்னமென் னடையி னாளு மபயமுன் மதியென் பாளாம்
பின்னவர் வளரு நாளுட் பிறந்தவ னிறங்கொள் பைந்தார்
இன்னிளங் குமர னாம மிசோதர னென்ப தாகும்.
reading: Of the twins, the boy is Abhayaruchi and the girl is Abhayamati, and the son born after them is named Yasodharan.
nuance: The verse does not say that the twins are the cocks reborn; that follows from 257 and from the youth's own words (73), which this link rests on. The younger brother bears the name of his grandfather the king.

tamil: பரிமிசைப் படைப பியின்றும் பார்மிசைத் தேர்க டாயும்
வரிசையிற் கரிமேற் கொண்டு வாட்டோழில் பயின்று மன்னர்க்
குரியஅத் தொழில்க ளோடு கலைகளின் செலவை யோர்ந்தும்
அரசிளங் குமரன் சென்றா னடுத்தது கூற லுற்றேன்.
reading: The young prince grows up and learns the arts of horse, chariot and elephant and the work fit for kings, together with the sciences, and the poet says he will tell what came next.
event: The youngest prince is trained in arms and learning.

title: ஐந்தாஞ் சருக்கம் 262-284 (1/3)
theme: The king, out hunting, turns his killing on the ascetic Sudatta, looses hounds that will not come near him and draws his sword; the merchant Kalyanamitran stops him with the greatness of the ascetic, a former king of Kalinga, and with the rule that lives, even one's own, are not to be taken; the king bows and begs to hear of births, and Sudatta begins by his avadhi knowledge.
source_issues: Verse 263 line 2 reads விளைத்துகள் where வினைத்துகள் is meant.
Verse 266 lines 2 and 3 do not parse; 275 line 3 is damaged; 282 lines 1 to 3 and 283 line 4 are hard to construe.
Verse 272 line 3 spells இமையின் as விமையின்.

cast.role: the hunting king; unnamed in these verses
the ascetic Sudatta, a former king of Kalinga
the merchant who stops the king
the king's hounds
Asokan, whose heaven the ascetic names; perhaps the king of Ujjayini of chapter 5

reading: With nets, snares and a hundred other hunting devices, and packs of tusk-toothed hounds baying, the king takes up his spear and speeds to the hunt in the midst of his four-fold army, like Death himself in the middle of a sea.
nuance: The simile makes the king Death (நமன்) before he has met the ascetic of the next verses; the poet loads the hunt with the image of killing.
event: The king sets out at speed on a hunt with his army, hounds and nets.

reading: The ascetic Sudatta, whose nature is to give living beings good, and who wipes away the dust of the two clinging kinds of deed, stands in his vow-posture; the king, proud and raging like a rutting elephant, thrusts in on him.
nuance: Line 2 reads தொத்திருவிளைத்துகள்; the sense is தொத்து இருவினைத் துகள் (clinging dust of the two deeds), so விளை stands for வினை. The last line, with இழித்து and அடுசுடத்திடை, is hard: whether the king dismounts, reviles, or sets something on the ascetic cannot be fixed, so the reading keeps to 'confronts'.
event: The raging king confronts the standing ascetic Sudatta.

reading: Like Death combing the forest's edge, he has found nothing to kill that fits today, and so, saying he will end his whole business and take the sweet life of the one before him, he comes with unstoppable rage upon the great ascetic.
nuance: வினை முற்றும் பாற்றி may mean 'ending his whole day's labour' (the hunt) or, as a pun, 'wiping out [his] deeds'; the verse is ironical either way, since the ascetic is the one who wipes deeds away (263).
event: Finding no game, the king turns his killing intent on the ascetic.

reading: He looses at the lord, from whom a rain of grace pours, a pack of fire-breathing, barking hounds, as many as fifty doubled with five, as though they were going to seize red flesh.
nuance: The count (ஐந்தினொடு பொருத தொகை ஐம்பதின் இரட்டி) is read as about a hundred and five; the wording is loose. The contrast is the poem's: the one who rains grace is met with hounds sent for flesh.
event: The king sets his pack of hounds on the ascetic.

reading: By the power of the penance that does great dharma the hounds fear to touch him and stand off at a bow's distance; the king, black-hearted and swollen with rage, then thinks of loosing the cruel weapon himself and draws his sword.
nuance: The grammar of lines 2 and 3 is broken. The reading rests on 279, where the merchant says the hounds do not come near, and so on the hounds standing off; it is not certain that the verse says the hounds are what stand.
event: The hounds are held back by the ascetic's penance, and the king draws his sword.

reading: A strong merchant named Kalyanamitran, dear as the king's own life, comes between and cries that he is undone, for a sword is being drawn before the great ascetic.
nuance: எனை (line 4) can read as 'me': that the blade is drawn on him as he steps between, or that the king's sword, drawn at the ascetic, ruins the merchant too. Kalyanamitran is named only here in the chapter and the verse calls him a kinsman of the king, not his minister.
event: The merchant Kalyanamitran enters and protests the drawn sword.

reading: Cast off this rage, he says; instead of honouring the feet of one who bears the mountain-load of great dharma, why does a mind burning with anger take up a cruel weapon, O king of the garland and the fierce spear?

If they say 'let it be', it is; if they say 'let them be destroyed', they are; if they say 'let the cloud come here', it comes, and that too by fate: such is the greatness of the one-minded ascetics, O lord with the cloud-generous hand and the elephant-like heart.
nuance: விதியின் (line 2) makes the ascetic's power run through fate (விதி); it is not clear whether the ascetic's will is itself fate or whether fate is what lets the will take effect. The verse does not say the ascetic works by a god.

reading: Those who come to them with love become lords of the gods, those who pass beyond them in contempt fall to the lowest hell; the venerable ones are like shade that one takes refuge in, with neither favour nor anger, and the course of the world beyond is the doing of the divine ones.
nuance: The fruit of honour and scorn falls on the doer, yet the ascetics themselves are said to hold neither favour nor wrath (அருளும் முனிவும் இலர்); the verse does not say who dispenses the result.

reading: Even if Indras come to bow at their feet, or others inflict endless bitter pain, they do not think 'ours' or 'others', only 'each one's own deed', these ascetic kings who have risen far above the world, O wearer of the garland.

Every life in the world is like my own life, they hold; so, putting away cruelty and pouring grace, they raise up lives; bow at the holy feet of those who stand guard like the eyelid, and you will cross beyond your deeds, O victorious spear-bearer.
nuance: இமையின் in line 3 is read as 'like the eyelid' (which guards the eye); the text spells it விமையின், a possible misprint.

reading: The king, not rejecting the merchant's gentle words, lays down his anger and the weapon in his hand, then asks who this pitiable man is that he, the king, should bow to, a dark-skinned man thick with dust.
nuance: He yields to the plea, not to the ascetic: the weapon goes down while contempt remains, so his turn to reverence is not yet made (283).
event: The king puts aside his anger and weapon but still scorns the dust-grimed ascetic.

reading: If you ask whom the world worships, hear: he is the ornament of the Ganga line, lord of Kalinga, who ruled the whole land alone like a lion with no shared strength of arm; know this clearly, king.
nuance: The ascetic is not named in these lines; that he is Sudatta (263) is from the context. கங்கைகுல திலகன் is the Ganga dynasty of Kalinga, a claim about a person the verse does not date.
event: The merchant tells the king that the ascetic was once a king of Kalinga.

reading: Thinking that pleasure, wealth and youth pass quickly like cloud, lightning and the rainbow, he resolves on renunciation, the dharma in which grace grows, and sets his mind on entering the pleasure-rich golden world.
nuance: Line 3 is damaged (ஆகதுற வருள்பெருகு மறெனெடத னியலே). The aim named in line 4 is the heaven of pleasures, not release; compare 284, where the fruit is a divine world.
event: The king of Kalinga reasons that enjoyment is fleeting and resolves to renounce.

tamil: ஆடுகொடி யானை அதிர் தேர் புரவி காலாள்
reading: Lands and cities, the women of fair loveliness, banner-waving elephants, chariots, horses and foot soldiers, crown, garland, earrings, shoulder-bangles, necklace and clothes: 'let all go away from me', he said, and gave them up.
event: Sudatta gives up kingdom, women, army, ornaments and clothes.

reading: Gods, kings of the earth and the mountain dwellers come to worship him as he takes the ascetic form, and with no taint in his mind, thinking only of what is good for lives, he wanders through forest, hills and lands.
nuance: Gods and kings worship him now, as the merchant said at 270 of those who come near.
event: Sudatta takes the ascetic form and wanders the forests while gods and kings worship him.

reading: Holding that 'I' is nothing, 'mine' is nothing and even benefit is nothing, the dignified ascetic delights not in his body; the dirt of other deeds does not stay in his form, and each day he wears the virtues that smile with the light of knowledge.
nuance: இதம் (benefit) is added to the pair 'I' and 'mine': he gives up even the good he might claim for himself, which goes past the Kural's pair.

reading: This is the greatness of the matchless ascetic's yoga, lord: the killing deed of the forest and the fierce karma that were to join you have ceased to join you today; why seek killing, spear-bearer? See, the hounds do not come near.
nuance: The deed is said to have stopped through the ascetic's greatness, which reads the stopping of karma as brought about by the ascetic's yoga; the verse does not say how.

reading: When the merchant has said this, to move his mind, the king goes, sets the holy lotus feet on his head, and thinks: 'to dissolve my fault today I will cut off my head and stand in refuge at his feet.'
nuance: The king's own measure of the fault is a life; the merchant answers it in 281 and 282.
event: The king resolves to cut off his own head as atonement.

reading: Seeing him think this, the merchant raises his hand and says: let go what is in your mind, king; if one raises others' lives as one's own life, that is right; if you take your own life, what grace is that?
nuance: The same word for life, உயிர், covers both: the verse extends the rule that protects others' lives to the king's own.
event: The merchant stops the king from cutting off his own head.

reading: The matter he spoke before is not finished; more remains to be said, and the sense of what he thinks to say now comes to him: having decided this earlier, do not fill up the fault; what you now think of is a great harm, he said.
nuance: Lines 1 to 3 are very hard; பிழைதூராய் may mean 'do not heap fault' or 'do not leave the fault undone'. Only the last line, that the new plan is a great harm, is certain.

reading: Giving up the king's rage and growing in grace, he goes to the feet of Sudatta, whose speech is full of eloquence, bows so that the flowers of his crown touch them, and speaks of all of their births.
nuance: The last line is cut short: எமர் பவமுழுதும் is read as asking to hear the whole of their births, which the muni's knowledge in 284 can supply. He has gone from the weapon of 266 to the crown-flowers on the feet, and it is the merchant, not the ascetic, who brought this about.
event: The king bows at Sudatta's feet and asks him of their births.

reading: Then the ascetic, setting out by his avadhi knowledge what it had shown him so that the king could take it in, tells that Asokan, by the penance he did before, rejoiced in a divine world of high fame.
nuance: Whether this Asokan is Yasodharan's father of ch. 5 is not stated in the verse; same name is not shown to be same person. அவதி is the clairvoyant knowledge of the Jain ascetic, here used for knowledge of former births.
event: Sudatta begins to reveal by his avadhi knowledge that Asokan reached a heaven through earlier penance.

title: ஐந்தாஞ் சருக்கம் 285-307 (2/3)
theme: The muni Sudattan tells the king the fruits of deeds: Asokan in a god's world, the poisoner Amritamati tortured through the hells and eating her own flesh, and Yasodharan and his mother through beast births to birth as the king's own twin children; the twins remember their births, the king weeps for what his deeds have done and the muni bids him not fear.
source_issues: Verse 285 says only 'he'; the father Asokan is read from verse 284.
The muni and the king are not named in this chapter; Sudattan (verse 283) and Yasomati are inferred from the story and from 'your son' in verses 298 and 299.
Verse 287 gives six names of the seven hells; verses 289 and 295 are partly obscure.
Verse 300 lines 1 to 3 are partly obscure and spaced oddly in the edition; verses 303 to 306 are spaced as a different edition would be.
Verse 279 line 4 and verse 300 line 4 lack their closing marks as in the edition; the verse boundaries are the edition's.

cast.role: the muni who tells the king the fruit of the births; named in verse 283, unnamed here
the king the muni addresses; read as Yasomati, father of the twins, unnamed in this chapter
the king's grandfather, now a god, who renounced in chapter 5
the queen who plotted to poison the king, now in hell
the old mother, born as animals and now as the king's daughter
the former king, born as animals and now as the king's son
the beings of hell who torment the fallen
the twin brother, the former Yasodharan
the twin sister, the former Chandramathi
the twins speaking together
the man the king sends to fetch the twins

reading: The muni says that the king's father, Asokan, is now a god shining like a rare gem in Brahma's world, glad among divine women for more than ten oceans of years.
nuance: The verse says only 'he'; the father is read from verse 284, where Asokan reaches a world of the gods. The muni speaking, and the king he addresses as 'you', are not named in this chapter: Sudattan is the muni of verse 283 and the king is read as Yasomati, since verses 298 and 299 call the twins his son and daughter.
event: Asokan, who took renunciation, enjoys a god's life in Brahma's world.

reading: The muni says that the queen Amritamati, who with the old mother plotted by guile to kill the king with poison, became wholly a leper and fell into dire hell, her deeds like poison consuming her.
nuance: The verse shows the punishment answering the crime: she planned his death by poison and her deeds are called 'poison-like' that wear her down.
event: Amritamati, who plotted the king's poisoning with his mother, is struck with leprosy and falls into hell.

reading: The muni lists the seven pits of hell by their grounds: the darkness of darkness, darkness, smoke, mire, sand and gravel, each place bringing the pain its deeds earn.
nuance: Only six grounds can be read in the lines; the seventh name is not clear in the edition.

reading: The muni says five of the hells have ground that would melt even Mount Meru as hot and cold water, and that Amritamati fell into the smoke hell, where she has no helper and no dharma.
event: Amritamati falls and melts into the smoke hell.

reading: Hell's dwellers run up as she falls into the pit, set her in smoke and fire, burn and split her and grind her bleeding wounds; the verse asks whether any who face a deed's wrath would not themselves be wrathful.
nuance: Line 4 is hard to construe. 'If the sunk deed is angry, are there any who are not angry' may mean that no one can be gentle toward her when her own deed is angry with her.
event: The beings of hell burn, split and grind the fallen Amritamati.

reading: Hell's keepers cry that she had eaten cooked flesh before and now force molten copper into her mouth until her face melts and runs.
nuance: The reproach 'you ate' is voiced by the tormentors; it is the muni's account, which the work holds, that makes the punishment the answer to the deed. The word இந்திரர்கள் here names the tormentors, as written.
event: The keepers of hell pour molten copper into Amritamati's mouth, reproaching her for eating flesh.

reading: She is burnt to crisp, and a fair image is heated in the fire; they say 'this is very sweet', bid her embrace it, and she cries out as her whole body crumbles to powder.
nuance: The scorching image set against her love is not spelled out as the elephant-keeper, and the speaker of 'this is very sweet' is not named.
event: Amritamati is made to embrace a heated image and her body crumbles.

reading: They pour poison down her until her tongue rots, and she melts in her thirst but cannot die; in a land where blameless deeds bear no fruit, nothing sweet can grow.
